docs.title: IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver
docs.text: A Kubernetes CSI driver that pools multiple PVCs as subdirectories within shared IBM Cloud VPC file shares, instead of the traditional 1:1 PVC-to-share mapping.

docs.title: Why Pooling?
docs.text:
The standard IBM VPC file CSI driver creates one VPC file share per PVC — a 1:1 mapping. That hits three walls fast:

  • Quota — VPC accounts cap at 300 file shares. A busy cluster with lots of small PVCs burns through that quickly.
  • Speed — Creating a VPC file share takes 30-90 seconds. Pods sit waiting for storage.
  • Cost — Each share has a 10 GB minimum and its own billing line. Hundreds of tiny PVCs mean hundreds of minimums.

Pooling flips the model: pre-provision a few large shares, then hand out subdirectories within them. Creating a subdirectory is instant, shares nothing with the VPC API, and lets many PVCs share the capacity of a single share. Think of it like a VMware datastore — one NFS export holds many volumes.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Traditional CSI drivers create one VPC file share per PVC. This driver takes a different approach: a FileSharePool CR defines a pool of VPC file shares, and each PVC gets a subdirectory on an existing share.

VPC File Share (1 TB)
├── /pvcs/pvc-aaa...    ← PVC-1 (10 GB quota)
├── /pvcs/pvc-bbb...    ← PVC-2 (50 GB quota)
└── /pvcs/pvc-ccc...    ← PVC-3 (20 GB quota)

This reduces VPC API calls, speeds up PVC provisioning (mkdir vs. 30-90s share creation), and lowers cost by consolidating storage.

docs.text:

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Key components:

Component Location Role CSI Controller pkg/driver/controller.go gRPC handlers for volume lifecycle CSI Node Agent pkg/driver/node.go NFS mount + bind-mount into pods Pool Manager pkg/pool/manager.go Core brain: allocation, deallocation, expansion, snapshots, clones Share Selection pkg/pool/share.go Spread (most free) or binpack (least free) strategy Clone Worker pkg/pool/clone_worker.go Async clone operations Replication Controller pkg/pool/replication_controller.go Cross-region disaster recovery with incremental rsync Hook Orchestrator pkg/hooks/ Lifecycle hooks (exec + HTTP) for replication Admission Webhooks pkg/webhook/ Validating webhooks for all CRD types Migration CLI pkg/migrate/ Migrate PVCs from stock IBM CSI driver IBM VPC Client pkg/ibmcloud/client.go Thin wrapper around VPC file share API CRD Types api/v1alpha1/ FileSharePool, SubVolume, Snapshot, ReplicationPolicy, BackupPolicy, BackupRestore, VolumeGroupSnapshot (not active), Hook

docs.title: CRDs
docs.text:
• FileSharePool (cluster-scoped) — defines a pool of VPC file shares with allocation strategy, auto-expansion, and capacity limits
  • SubVolume (cluster-scoped) — tracks individual PVC allocations: which share, subdirectory path, requested size, and clone/snapshot state
  • Snapshot (cluster-scoped) — tracks a snapshot of a SubVolume on the same share
  • ReplicationPolicy (cluster-scoped) — defines replication from a pool to a destination, with pre/post-sync lifecycle hooks and incremental rsync
  • BackupPolicy (cluster-scoped) — backs up the PVCs and VMs it selects into a snapshot pool, on a schedule
  • BackupRestore (cluster-scoped) — one request to restore a backup into a new PVC
  • VolumeGroupSnapshot (cluster-scoped) — not active; nothing acts on it

The words used here (pool, share, moment, snapshot pool and others) are defined once in CONTEXT.md.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: The project's own words (pool, share, SubVolume, tier, drain, golden image, clone, hook and the rest) are defined once in CONTEXT.md.

docs.title: IBM Cloud VPC
docs.text: Term Definition dp2 The only VPC file share profile. IOPS range from 100 to 96,000; if spec.iops is not set, each share gets 100 IOPS whatever its size IOPS I/O Operations Per Second; the performance budget for a share, shared by all PVCs on that share VPC Access Mode The older file share access control mode. Shares are exported under a shared FQDN and differ by their NFS export path. Existing shares still work. The driver no longer creates them Security Group Mode The file share access control mode the driver uses for every new share. A security group on the mount target's virtual network interface decides who can mount. By default it is the cluster's own security group root_squash NFS server mapping of root (UID 0) to nobody (UID 65534); always enabled on VPC file shares, cannot be disabled initial_owner VPC API parameter setting the UID/GID ownership of the share's root directory at creation time Transit Gateway IBM Cloud service connecting VPCs across regions over the private backbone; required for cross-region replication

docs.title: NFS
docs.text: Term Definition NFSv4.1 Network File System protocol version 4.1; adds session trunking and directory delegation over v4.0. Required by VPC file shares. sec=sys NFS security flavor using standard Unix UID/GID credentials (AUTH_UNIX); required for chown to work on VPC shares sec=null NFS security flavor using anonymous authentication; VPC shares negotiate this by default, making all files UID 99 soft mount NFS mount option that returns I/O errors after a timeout; prevents pods from hanging when the NFS server is unreachable hard mount NFS mount option that retries I/O indefinitely until the server responds; can cause pods to hang permanently timeo NFS mount option: timeout per RPC attempt in deciseconds (default 600 = 60 seconds) retrans NFS mount option: number of RPC retransmissions before a soft mount returns an error (default 3) rsize / wsize NFS mount options controlling read/write buffer sizes in bytes (typically negotiated to 1 MB) close-to-open NFS consistency model: changes to a file become visible to other clients only after the writer calls close() and the reader calls open() bind-mount Linux mount operation that makes a directory accessible at a second mount point; used to expose individual subdirectories into pod paths

docs.title: CSI (Container Storage Interface)
docs.text: Term Definition Provisioner The CSI driver identifier in a StorageClass (e.g., vpc-file-pool.csi.ibm.io); determines which driver handles PVC requests Sidecars Standard Kubernetes CSI helper containers (csi-provisioner, csi-resizer, csi-snapshotter, liveness-probe, node-driver-registrar) that translate Kubernetes events into CSI gRPC calls NodeStageVolume CSI RPC that mounts the entire NFS share at the staging folder kubelet gives for the volume; called once per staged volume on a node NodePublishVolume CSI RPC that bind-mounts a SubVolume's subdirectory from the staging path into the pod's volume path VolumeContentSource Field in CreateVolume indicating the new volume should be populated from an existing snapshot or volume (clone) fsGroupPolicy CSI driver spec field controlling whether kubelet recursively chowns mounts to the pod's fsGroup; set to None to avoid failures with root_squash StorageClass Kubernetes resource that maps PVCs to a provisioner and its parameters (pool name, tier, UID/GID, mount options)

docs.title: KubeVirt / OpenShift Virtualization
docs.text: Term Definition CDI Containerized Data Importer — KubeVirt component that imports, clones, and uploads VM disk images into PVCs DataImportCron CDI resource that periodically imports OS images from a registry into golden image PVCs on a schedule DataSource CDI resource pointing to a bootable disk PVC; appears in the OpenShift Virtualization InstanceTypes catalog tab DataVolume CDI resource that combines PVC creation with data import/clone in a single object. The pool's golden image syncer makes one per golden image VolumePopulator Kubernetes mechanism CDI uses to populate PVCs StorageProfile CDI resource auto-created per StorageClass; defines access modes, volume mode, and clone strategy for CDI operations Template OpenShift resource defining a complete VM blueprint (CPU, memory, disks, network); appears in the Templates catalog tab InstanceType KubeVirt resource defining a CPU/RAM preset; paired with a DataSource (image) to create a VM from the InstanceTypes tab virt-handler KubeVirt DaemonSet component on each node that manages VM lifecycle; calls chown(107, 107) on filesystem-mode PVC mount directories virt-launcher KubeVirt pod that runs the QEMU process for a single VM QEMU Open-source machine emulator used by KubeVirt to run VMs; requires raw format disk images for filesystem-mode PVCs qcow2 QEMU Copy-On-Write disk image format; cloud images are distributed as qcow2 but must be converted to raw for KubeVirt filesystem PVCs

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: Term Definition Finalizer Kubernetes metadata that prevents a resource from being deleted until a controller removes it; used on pools to block deletion while SubVolumes exist Leader Election Pattern ensuring only one controller replica actively reconciles at a time; prevents concurrent pool state corruption OwnerReference Kubernetes metadata linking a child resource to its parent; enables automatic garbage collection (e.g., auto-created StorageClasses deleted with their pool) Admission Webhook Kubernetes extension that validates or mutates resources on create/update; the driver uses validating webhooks on all CRD types SCC (SecurityContextConstraints) OpenShift resource controlling pod security permissions; the node agent requires the privileged SCC (standard for CSI drivers)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Kubernetes 1.28+
  • IBM Cloud VPC infrastructure
  • kubectl and helm (v3)

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# Apply CRDs
make deploy

# Or install via Helm
make helm-install

See INSTALL.md for full setup instructions including IBM Cloud API key configuration.

docs.title: Create a Pool
docs.text:
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: my-pool
spec:
  zone: us-south-1
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 1000
  maxShares: 5
  autoExpand: true
  allocationStrategy: spread

docs.title: Use a PVC
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: my-app-data
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  storageClassName: ibm-vpc-file-pool
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The CSI driver authenticates to IBM Cloud using secret-common-lib, the same library used by the stock IBM block and file CSI drivers. This means:

  • On managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters: Credentials already exist. No setup required — the driver reuses the cluster's existing storage-secret-store or ibm-cloud-credentials secret.
  • On self-managed clusters: You create an ibm-cloud-credentials secret manually (one-time setup).

The library supports two authentication methods: API keys (traditional) and pod identity via Trusted Profiles (no long-lived secrets).

docs.title: Managed Clusters (ROKS / ROVS / IKS) — Zero Setup
docs.text:
On managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters, the storage-secret-store secret in kube-system is pre-populated by the IBM Cloud add-on system. It contains the API key and VPC endpoint configuration that the stock IBM CSI drivers already use.

Our driver reads the same secret via secret-common-lib. There is nothing to create.

docs.title: Verify the credentials exist
docs.text:
# Check for the legacy secret (present on all managed clusters)
kubectl get secret storage-secret-store -n kube-system

# Check for the newer secret (may or may not exist yet)
kubectl get secret ibm-cloud-credentials -n kube-system

# Check the cluster configmaps
kubectl get configmap ibm-cloud-provider-data -n kube-system
kubectl get configmap ibm-cloud-cluster-info -n kube-system

If storage-secret-store exists and holds an API key, the driver will work. That's it.

docs.title: Clusters That Use a Trusted Profile (ROKS or ROVS)
docs.text:
Some managed clusters do not store an API key. They log in to IBM Cloud with a cluster trusted profile instead. A trusted profile trusts only the Kubernetes service accounts linked to it, which by default are the stock IBM file CSI driver's accounts. The driver then fails to start, and the storage-secret-sidecar container logs:

Error fetching iam token using trusted profile ... Selected trusted profile not eligible.

To fix it, link the driver's controller service account to the cluster's trusted profile:

# Find the profile: it has links for ibm-vpc-file-controller-sa
ibmcloud iam trusted-profiles
ibmcloud iam trusted-profile-links <profile-id>

# Link the driver's controller service account
ibmcloud iam trusted-profile-link-create <profile-id> \
  --name link-ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller \
  --cr-type ROKS_SA \
  --link-crn crn:v1:bluemix:public:containers-kubernetes:<region>:a/<account-id>:<cluster-id>:: \
  --link-namespace kube-system \
  --link-name ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller

# Restart the controller
kubectl rollout restart deployment/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller -n kube-system

Copy the --link-crn value from the existing ibm-vpc-file-controller-sa link. The driver then has the same access as the stock file driver. Check that the profile has at least the permissions in Minimum IAM Permissions.

docs.title: How It Works on Managed Clusters
docs.text:
1. The IBM Cloud add-on system creates storage-secret-store with a TOML config containing the API key, IAM endpoint, and VPC endpoint.
  2. Our driver initializes secret-common-lib with IKS_ENABLED=true (managed mode).
  3. The library runs a sidecar that watches the secret, exchanges the API key for IAM tokens, caches them, and auto-refreshes before expiry.
  4. The driver calls GetDefaultIAMToken() before each VPC API operation to get a valid bearer token.

The managed provider also supports automatic token refresh without pod restarts when the API key changes.

docs.title: Self-Managed Clusters (OCP / Kubernetes) — Manual Setup
docs.text: On self-managed clusters, you need to create the credentials secret yourself.

docs.title: Option A: API Key Authentication (Simpler)
docs.text:
# 1. Create a Service ID with VPC Infrastructure Editor permissions
ibmcloud iam service-id-create vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --description "Service ID for IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver"

ibmcloud iam service-policy-create vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --roles Editor \
  --service-name is

# 2. Create an API key
ibmcloud iam service-api-key-create vpc-file-pool-csi-key vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --description "API key for VPC File Pool CSI Driver" \
  --output json

# 3. Create the Kubernetes secret (use the newer ibm-cloud-credentials format)
cat > /tmp/ibm-credentials.env << 'EOF'
IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=iam
IBMCLOUD_APIKEY=<paste-api-key-here>
EOF

kubectl create secret generic ibm-cloud-credentials \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --from-file=ibm-credentials.env=/tmp/ibm-credentials.env

rm /tmp/ibm-credentials.env

# 4. Create the provider-data configmap
kubectl create configmap ibm-cloud-provider-data \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --from-literal=vpcID=<your-vpc-id> \
  --from-literal=subnetID=<your-subnet-id>

docs.title: Option B: Pod Identity with Trusted Profiles (No Long-Lived Keys)
docs.text:
Trusted Profiles eliminate the need for a static API key. The driver authenticates using a Kubernetes service account token that IBM Cloud IAM validates.

# 1. Create a Trusted Profile in IBM Cloud
ibmcloud iam tp-create vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --description "Trusted Profile for VPC File Pool CSI Driver"

# 2. Create a claim rule linking it to the Kubernetes service account
ibmcloud iam tp-rule-create vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --type Profile-SAML \
  --conditions <conditions-json>
# (see IBM docs for the exact claim rule format for your cluster)

# 3. Assign VPC Infrastructure Editor policy to the Trusted Profile
ibmcloud iam tp-policy-create vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --roles Editor \
  --service-name is

# 4. Create the Kubernetes secret with pod identity auth type
cat > /tmp/ibm-credentials.env << 'EOF'
IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=pod-identity
IBMCLOUD_PROFILEID=<trusted-profile-id>
EOF

kubectl create secret generic ibm-cloud-credentials \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --from-file=ibm-credentials.env=/tmp/ibm-credentials.env

rm /tmp/ibm-credentials.env

The controller Deployment also needs a projected service account token:

volumes:
  - name: vault-token
    projected:
      sources:
        - serviceAccountToken:
            path: vault-token
            expirationSeconds: 600
containers:
  - name: csi-controller
    volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
        name: vault-token

Pod identity is the preferred approach for production because there are no static credentials to rotate or leak.

docs.title: Minimum IAM Permissions
docs.text:
Regardless of auth method (API key or Trusted Profile), the identity needs:

IAM Service Role Why VPC Infrastructure Services (is) Editor Create, read, update, delete file shares and mount targets

The driver does NOT need:

  • Administrator — it doesn't manage security groups, subnets, or access policies
  • Kubernetes Service roles — it doesn't interact with the IKS/ROKS control plane
  • Cloud Object Storage roles — no object storage involved
  • Key Protect / HPCS roles — unless using customer-managed encryption keys (then add Reader on the KMS instance)

docs.title: Managed Clusters
docs.text:
On managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters, the storage-secret-store is managed by the IBM Cloud add-on system. If the cluster's API key is rotated (e.g., via ibmcloud ks api-key reset), the add-on system updates the secret automatically.

With the managed secret provider (IKS_ENABLED=true), the sidecar detects the secret change and refreshes tokens without a pod restart.

docs.title: Self-Managed Clusters
docs.text:
# 1. Create a new API key
ibmcloud iam service-api-key-create vpc-file-pool-csi-key-new vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --description "Rotated key $(date +%Y-%m-%d)" \
  --output json

# 2. Update the credentials env file
cat > /tmp/ibm-credentials.env << 'EOF'
IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=iam
IBMCLOUD_APIKEY=<new-api-key>
EOF

# 3. Update the Kubernetes secret
kubectl create secret generic ibm-cloud-credentials \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --from-file=ibm-credentials.env=/tmp/ibm-credentials.env \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

rm /tmp/ibm-credentials.env

# 4. Restart the controller (unmanaged provider doesn't auto-detect changes)
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n kube-system ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller

# 5. Verify and delete the old key
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=controller -c csi-controller --tail=20
ibmcloud iam service-api-key-delete vpc-file-pool-csi-key vpc-file-pool-csi

Pod identity doesn't need rotation — the Kubernetes service account token is short-lived (600 seconds) and automatically refreshed by the kubelet.

docs.title: What Happens When Credentials Are Invalid
docs.text:
Scenario Existing Mounts New PVCs Pool Reconciliation API key expired/deleted Unaffected Fail (Pending) Fails (no new shares) Wrong IAM permissions Unaffected Fail (403 on share create) Fails Secret deleted from K8s Unaffected Fail Fails Pod identity profile revoked Unaffected Fail Fails IAM service outage Unaffected Fail (retry with backoff) Fails (retry)

Key point: Credential issues never affect running pods. NFS mounts are kernel-level and have no ongoing dependency on the IBM Cloud API. Credentials are only needed when the pool manager creates, expands, or deletes VPC file shares.

docs.title: Diagnosing Credential Issues
docs.text:
# Check controller logs for auth errors
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=controller -c csi-controller --tail=50 | grep -i "auth\|token\|401\|403\|iam"

# Verify the secret exists
kubectl get secret -n kube-system ibm-cloud-credentials storage-secret-store 2>/dev/null

# Test the API key manually
ibmcloud login --apikey <key>
ibmcloud is shares

docs.title: Private Network Access
docs.text:
secret-common-lib automatically uses private endpoints when configured in the credentials:

Via storage-secret-store (TOML format — managed clusters): 

[VPC]
g2_riaas_endpoint_url = "https://us-south.private.iaas.cloud.ibm.com/v1"
g2_token_exchange_endpoint_url = "https://private.iam.cloud.ibm.com"

Via cloud-conf configmap: 

{
  "riaas_private_endpoint": "https://us-south.private.iaas.cloud.ibm.com",
  "token_exchange_url": "https://private.iam.cloud.ibm.com"
}

The driver calls secretProvider.GetPrivateRIAASEndpoint() and uses it if available, falling back to the public endpoint.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use pod identity (Trusted Profiles) in production — eliminates static API keys entirely. No rotation, no leakage risk.

  2. On managed clusters, don't create a separate key — reuse storage-secret-store. Fewer secrets = smaller attack surface.

  3. On self-managed clusters, use a Service ID — never a personal API key. Service IDs can be scoped and revoked independently.

  4. Scope IAM policies tightly — Editor on VPC Infrastructure is the minimum. If resource-type scoping to share is available, use it.

  5. Never log credentials — the controller MUST never log API keys or tokens. Log the secret name/namespace for debugging, never the contents.

  6. Restrict secret RBAC — only the controller's ServiceAccount should have get access to credential secrets.

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: vpc-file-pool-csi-secret-reader
  namespace: kube-system
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["secrets"]
    resourceNames: ["ibm-cloud-credentials", "storage-secret-store"]
    verbs: ["get", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: vpc-file-pool-csi-secret-reader
  namespace: kube-system
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller
    namespace: kube-system
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: vpc-file-pool-csi-secret-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

  1. Use private endpoints — route IAM and VPC API traffic over the IBM private network.

  2. Enable Activity Tracker — audit all VPC API calls made by the driver's identity.

docs.title: Architecture Reference
docs.text: For the meaning of project words such as pool, share, SubVolume and moment, see CONTEXT.md.

docs.title: 1. CSI Controller (Deployment)
docs.text:
The gRPC server that implements CSI Controller RPCs. Runs as a Deployment with 1–2 replicas using leader election.

Responsibilities: - Receive CreateVolume / DeleteVolume / ControllerExpandVolume calls from the Kubernetes CSI sidecar containers. - Delegate to the Pool Manager for allocation decisions. - Return volume info (NFS server IP, share path, subdir path) to the kubelet via the CSI protocol.

Sidecar containers (standard CSI sidecars, deployed alongside the controller): - csi-provisioner — watches PVCs, calls CreateVolume/DeleteVolume - csi-resizer — watches PVC size changes, calls ControllerExpandVolume - liveness-probe — health checks

Does NOT: - Mount anything. - Call IBM VPC API directly (goes through Pool Manager → IBM VPC Client). - Create VPC file shares on purpose in the CreateVolume path. The one exception is auto-expand: when no share fits and autoExpand is on, Allocate calls CreateFileShare once (see Pool Manager). The call waits for the new share to become stable. If the share is ready and has a mount target when the call returns, CreateVolume uses it. If not, CreateVolume returns a retriable error (Unavailable) and the provisioner retries.

docs.title: 2. CSI Node Agent (DaemonSet)
docs.text:
Runs on every worker node. Implements CSI Node RPCs.

Responsibilities: - NodeStageVolume: Mount the VPC file share (NFS) at the staging folder that kubelet gives for this volume. If that staging folder is already mounted (a second pod on the same volume), reuse the mount. A different volume on the same share has its own staging folder, so the share is mounted again. - NodePublishVolume: Create the subdirectory on the share if it does not already exist (with uid/gid/permissions from VolumeContext), then bind-mount it into the pod's volume path. - NodeUnpublishVolume: Unmount the bind-mount from the pod path. - NodeUnstageVolume: Unmount the NFS mount at the volume's staging folder. Kubelet calls this when no pod on the node uses the volume any more. - NodeGetVolumeStats: Return capacity/usage stats for the subdirectory (via du or statfs).

Mount tracking (one NFS mount per staged volume):

Node filesystem:
  <kubelet dir>/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/<driver>/<hash for volume aaa>/globalmount/
    └── NFS mount of the whole share (one per staged volume)
        └── pvcs/pvc-aaa/             ← subdirectory for PVC aaa
  <kubelet dir>/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/<driver>/<hash for volume bbb>/globalmount/
    └── NFS mount of the same share, mounted again for volume bbb
        └── pvcs/pvc-bbb/             ← subdirectory for PVC bbb

  <kubelet dir>/pods/{pod-uid}/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/{pv-name}/mount/
    └── (bind mount of <staging folder>/pvcs/pvc-aaa/)

The volume ID is {pool}/{share-id}/{pv-name}, so it includes the PV name. Kubelet therefore stages each volume in its own folder, and the node agent keeps an in-memory list of staged folders (not a reference count). A second pod on the same volume reuses the mount. A different volume on the same share is mounted again. Kubelet calls NodeUnstageVolume when the last pod on the node stops using the volume.

NFS mount via nsenter wrapper:

The node agent container includes a /usr/local/bin/mount wrapper that routes NFS mounts through the host's mount namespace using nsenter --mount=/proc/1/ns/mnt --root=/proc/1/root. Bind mounts use the container's local /usr/bin/mount. This requires hostPID: true on the DaemonSet so /proc/1 refers to the host's PID 1.

Cross-zone server selection:

When volumeContext contains server.<zone> keys (from pools with accessor zones), the node agent selects the IP matching its own zone (topology.kubernetes.io/zone label). This ensures NFS traffic stays within the zone for lower latency. Falls back to the default server key if no zone match is found.

docs.title: 3. Pool Manager
docs.text:
The core logic component. Runs within the controller pod but is architecturally distinct.

Two modes of operation:

docs.title: A. Synchronous allocation (called from CSI Controller)
docs.text:
type PoolManager interface {
    // Allocate finds a share with room, records the SubVolume CR, and returns
    // the share's mount info. Subdirectory creation is deferred to NodePublishVolume.
    Allocate(ctx context.Context, req AllocationRequest) (*AllocationResult, error)

    // Deallocate deletes the SubVolume CR and updates pool tracking.
    // Does not remove the subdirectory on the NFS share (nfsOps is nil in controller mode).
    Deallocate(ctx context.Context, subVolumeName string) error

    // Expand updates the allocation size for an existing SubVolume.
    Expand(ctx context.Context, subVolumeName string, newSizeGB int64) error

    // CreateSnapshot creates a directory-level copy of a SubVolume.
    CreateSnapshot(ctx context.Context, snapshotName, sourceVolumeID string, params map[string]string) (*SnapshotResult, error)

    // DeleteSnapshot removes a snapshot directory and its CR.
    DeleteSnapshot(ctx context.Context, snapshotName string) error

    // ListSnapshots lists snapshots, optionally filtered by source volume.
    ListSnapshots(ctx context.Context, sourceVolumeID string) ([]SnapshotResult, error)

    // RestoreSnapshot creates a new SubVolume from a snapshot.
    RestoreSnapshot(ctx context.Context, snapshotName string, req AllocationRequest) (*AllocationResult, error)

    // CloneVolume creates a new SubVolume that is a copy of an existing one.
    // The copy always runs asynchronously: the SubVolume CR is created with
    // cloneStatus=Pending and the clone worker copies the data with a Job.
    CloneVolume(ctx context.Context, sourceVolumeID string, req AllocationRequest) (*AllocationResult, error)

    // CreateVolumeGroupSnapshot creates snapshots for multiple SubVolumes in sequence.
    // Does NOT execute hooks -- the CSI controller handles hook orchestration.
    CreateVolumeGroupSnapshot(ctx context.Context, req GroupSnapshotRequest) (*GroupSnapshotResult, error)

    // DeleteVolumeGroupSnapshot deletes all member snapshots and the group CR.
    DeleteVolumeGroupSnapshot(ctx context.Context, groupName string) error
}

type AllocationRequest struct {
    PVName        string
    PVCName       string
    PVCNamespace  string
    PoolName      string
    RequestedGB   int64
    Zone          string
}

type AllocationResult struct {
    ShareID         string            // VPC share ID
    MountTargetIP   string            // Primary mount target IP
    SubPath         string            // Subdirectory path, e.g., "/pvcs/pvc-abc123"
    SharePath       string            // NFS export root, e.g., "/"
    UID             *int64            // Unix user ID for the subdirectory
    GID             *int64            // Unix group ID
    Permissions     string            // Unix permissions string (e.g., "755")
    MountTargets    map[string]string // Zone -> IP mapping (nil for single-zone)
    AccessibleZones []string          // All zones this volume is accessible from
}

docs.title: B. Asynchronous reconciliation (controller-runtime reconciler)
docs.text: Watches FileSharePool CRs and reconciles pool state: - Ensure a matching StorageClass exists for the pool (auto-created, with OwnerReference for GC). - If total allocated capacity exceeds expandThreshold percentage, create a new VPC file share and add it to the pool. - If a share is unhealthy (VPC API reports degraded), mark it as draining — no new allocations, but existing PVCs remain. - Periodically scan SubVolume CRs and reconcile actual share state. - Update FileSharePool.Status with current share inventory and capacity.

docs.title: 4. IBM VPC Client
docs.text:
Thin wrapper around the vpc-go-sdk. Isolates all IBM Cloud API calls.

Operations: - CreateFileShare(ctx, spec) → share ID, mount target IP - DeleteFileShare(ctx, shareID) → error - ExpandFileShare(ctx, shareID, newSizeGB) → error - GetFileShare(ctx, shareID) → share details (state, size, IOPS, mount targets) - ListFileShares(ctx, filters) → list of shares (for discovery/reconciliation) - CreateShareMountTarget(ctx, shareID, input) → mount target for a share that has none - GetSubnetZone(ctx, subnetID) and FindSecurityGroupID(ctx, vpcID, name) → the subnet and security group for a mount target

Shares use security group access mode: each share has one mount target, with a network interface in the worker subnet of the pool's zone.

All operations are idempotent or check-before-act. All have context-based timeouts.

docs.title: 5. Clone Worker
docs.text:
Background component within the controller pod that handles every volume clone. All clones are asynchronous.

Responsibilities: - Process SubVolumes with cloneStatus=Pending or cloneStatus=InProgress. - Create a Kubernetes Job that performs the cp -a data copy (same-share or cross-share). The controller pod has no NFS access, so the Job does the copy. - Update SubVolume CR status as clone progresses: Pending → InProgress → Complete or Failed. - Handle crash recovery by restarting incomplete clones on controller restart.

Does NOT: - Block CreateVolume — the CSI controller returns immediately after recording the clone. - Allow pod access before clone completes — the node agent gates NodePublishVolume on cloneStatus=Complete.

docs.title: 6. Replication Controller
docs.text:
Standalone reconciler that handles cross-region disaster recovery by copying SubVolume data between pools.

Responsibilities: - Watch ReplicationPolicy CRs and execute replication cycles on a configurable schedule. - Mount source shares (read-only) and destination shares (read-write, cross-region via Transit Gateway). - Copy each matching SubVolume's subdirectory from source to destination in one of two modes. Direct NFS mode runs a Job that uses rsync (SyncDir incremental, or CopyDir full copy). Receiver mode (destinationEndpoint set) tars the whole folder and uploads it to the receiver each cycle; only direct NFS mode uses rsync. - Execute pre-sync and post-sync lifecycle hooks via the Hook Orchestrator for application-consistent replication. - Track replication progress, RPO, bytes transferred, and consecutive failures in ReplicationPolicy.Status. - Expose Prometheus metrics for replication lag, RPO, and error counts.

Does NOT: - Create or delete VPC file shares (destination pool must already exist). - Interfere with the CSI controller, node agent, or pool manager. - Provide crash consistency or cross-file transactional consistency (file-level consistency only, unless application quiesce hooks are configured).

docs.title: 7. Migration CLI
docs.text:
Utility package (pkg/migrate/) for migrating PVCs from the stock IBM VPC file CSI driver to the pool-based driver.

Components: - Planner (planner.go) — analyzes existing PVCs and generates a migration plan. - Executor (executor.go) — executes the migration plan: creates SubVolume CRs, spawns data-copy pods, and rebinds PVCs. - Pod (pod.go) — manages ephemeral pods used for data transfer during migration.

docs.title: 8. Hook Orchestrator
docs.text:
Sequential hook execution engine (pkg/hooks/) that runs pre/post lifecycle hooks for replication and group snapshot operations.

Responsibilities: - Dispatch hooks to the correct executor based on hook type (exec or http). - ExecHook: Find pods via Kubernetes label selector and execute commands via the pod exec API (SPDY remote command). - HTTPHook: Send HTTP requests (GET/POST/PUT) with custom headers to webhook endpoints and validate 2xx responses. - Enforce per-hook timeouts via context deadlines (default 30 seconds). - Respect OnError policy: Abort stops the operation on hook failure, Continue logs and proceeds. - Collect HookResult records with success/failure, timing, and truncated output for CRD status.

Wired into: - Replication Controller — pre/post-sync hooks for application-consistent DR replication. - VolumeGroupSnapshot — pre/post-snapshot hooks for coordinated multi-PVC snapshots.

docs.title: 9. Admission Webhooks
docs.text:
Validating admission webhooks (pkg/webhook/) registered with the controller-runtime manager. Enforce CRD field constraints at admission time, rejecting invalid create/update requests before they are persisted.

Validators: - FileSharePoolValidator — field ranges, required fields, immutable zone/profile on update. - SubVolumeValidator — required fields, subPath regex validation with path traversal protection. - ReplicationPolicyValidator — required fields, Go duration parsing for schedule, maxRetries range. - SnapshotValidator — required sourceSubVolume and poolName. - VolumeGroupSnapshotValidator — required fields, failurePolicy enum validation. - PoolBenchValidator — share size and IOPS against IBM's dp2 table, disks of the largest step fit the share, load and knee ranges, events at a step; settings fixed once the run has started.

docs.title: 10. CRD Controllers
docs.text:
Six CRD types, managed by controller-runtime:

  • FileSharePool — defines a pool of VPC file shares; reconciler ensures the pool has enough capacity.
  • SubVolume — tracks a single PVC's allocation: which share, subdirectory path, requested size, and clone/snapshot state.
  • Snapshot — tracks a point-in-time directory copy of a SubVolume, stored under /pvcs/.snapshots/.
  • VolumeGroupSnapshot — coordinates multiple Snapshot CRs for multi-PVC consistent snapshots, with pre/post-snapshot lifecycle hooks.
  • ReplicationPolicy — defines a cross-region replication relationship between a source pool and a destination pool, with pre/post-sync lifecycle hooks. Direct NFS mode can use incremental rsync; receiver mode uploads the whole folder each cycle.
  • Hook (embedded type) — defines a lifecycle hook with exec or HTTP execution, timeout, and on-error policy. Embedded in VolumeGroupSnapshot and ReplicationPolicy specs.

See CRD-SPEC.md for full type definitions.

docs.title: Data Flow: CreateVolume
docs.text:
1. The user creates a PVC with the pool's StorageClass (auto-created, named after the pool).
  2. The csi-provisioner sidecar calls the CreateVolume gRPC.
  3. The CSI Controller receives CreateVolume. It takes the pool name from the StorageClass parameters and the requested size from the PVC spec.
  4. It calls PoolManager.Allocate(ctx, request):
  5. 4a. Read the FileSharePool CR for the named pool.
  6. 4b. Read all SubVolume CRs for that pool (or use cached state).
  7. 4c. Calculate the allocated capacity of each share.
  8. 4d. Pick a share with enough remaining capacity (strategy: spread or bin-pack, per pool config).
    • If no share has room and pool.spec.autoExpand is on and shares < maxShares: create a new VPC file share through the IBM VPC Client (slow: 30-90 s), wait for it to become "stable", and add it to FileSharePool.Status.Shares. If the new share is ready (stable, with a mount target), use it. If not, return a retriable codes.Unavailable error ("pool is expanding") and the provisioner retries.
    • Otherwise (autoExpand is off, or the tier is at maxShares): return a retriable codes.ResourceExhausted error.
  9. 4e. Create the SubVolume CR that records the allocation.
  10. 4f. Return an AllocationResult (share IP, subpath, uid, gid, permissions).

The subdirectory is not created here. It is created in NodePublishVolume on the node agent. The controller does not create directories on the NFS share (nfsOps is nil). 5. The CSI Controller returns CreateVolumeResponse with: - volume_id: "{pool}/{share-id}/{subdir-name}" - volume_context: 

server: "10.240.1.5"                  # Primary (home zone) IP
server.us-south-1: "10.240.1.5"       # Zone-keyed IPs (when accessorZones configured)
server.us-south-2: "10.240.2.10"      # Accessor zone IP
share: "/"
subDir: "/pvcs/pvc-abc123"
pool: "general-purpose"
shareID: "r006-a1b2c3d4-..."
permissions: "0755"   # optional
uid: "1000"           # optional
gid: "1000"           # optional
- accessible_topology: [zone] 6. Kubernetes creates the PV and binds it to the PVC. 7. The pod is scheduled, and kubelet calls NodeStageVolume and NodePublishVolume. 8. The node agent mounts the share (if not cached), creates the subdirectory if it does not exist (with uid/gid/permissions from VolumeContext), then bind-mounts the subdirectory into the pod.

docs.title: Data Flow: DeleteVolume
docs.text:
1. The PVC is deleted (reclaimPolicy: Delete).
  2. The csi-provisioner calls the DeleteVolume gRPC.
  3. The CSI Controller receives DeleteVolume and parses the volume_id to get the pool, share ID and subdir name.
  4. It calls PoolManager.Deallocate(ctx, subVolumeName):
  5. 4a. Read the SubVolume CR to get the share details.
  6. 4b. Update FileSharePool.Status (decrement allocated capacity).
  7. 4c. Delete the SubVolume CR.

The controller does not remove subdirectories on the NFS share (nfsOps is nil in controller mode). Subdirectory cleanup is a future enhancement or handled by an external garbage collection process. 5. The CSI Controller returns success.

docs.title: Data Flow: Pool Reconciliation (Background)
docs.text:
Every 60 seconds, or on a FileSharePool CR change:

  1. The reconciler reads the FileSharePool CR.
  2. For each share in Status.Shares, it calls the IBM VPC API to verify share health. If a share is "degraded" or "failed", it marks the share as draining in Status.
  3. It calculates the total pool utilization: the sum of all SubVolume allocations, compared with the total pool capacity.
  4. If utilization is above expandThreshold:
  5. If shares.count < maxShares: create a new VPC file share (IBM VPC Client) and add it to Status.Shares when it becomes "stable".
  6. Otherwise: emit a Warning event ("pool at capacity").
  7. It updates FileSharePool.Status with the current metrics.
  8. It emits Prometheus metrics:
  9. pool_total_capacity_gb
  10. pool_allocated_capacity_gb
  11. pool_pvc_count
  12. pool_share_count
  13. share_allocated_capacity_gb (per share)
  14. share_pvc_count (per share)

docs.title: Data Flow: CreateSnapshot
docs.text:
1. The user creates a VolumeSnapshot that references a PVC.
  2. The csi-snapshotter sidecar calls the CreateSnapshot gRPC.
  3. The CSI Controller receives CreateSnapshot and parses the source volume ID to get the pool, share ID and subdir name.
  4. It calls PoolManager.CreateSnapshot(ctx, snapshotName, sourceVolumeID, params):
  5. 4a. Read the source SubVolume CR.
  6. 4b. Create the Snapshot CR. It is not ready yet. Its folder is /pvcs/.snapshots/snap-{name}/.
  7. 4c. Start a share data Job. The Job copies the source subdirectory to the snapshot folder with cp -a. The controller pod has no NFS access, so it never copies data itself. A disk that a running VM writes to is copied with QEMU instead (see VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md).
  8. 4d. When the Job succeeds, mark the Snapshot CR ready.
  9. The CSI Controller returns CreateSnapshotResponse. The snapshot is ready to use after the copy ends.

docs.title: Data Flow: CloneVolume
docs.text:
1. The user creates a PVC with a dataSource that references an existing PVC.
  2. The csi-provisioner detects the dataSource and sets VolumeContentSource.
  3. The CSI Controller receives CreateVolume with VolumeContentSource.Volume.
  4. It calls PoolManager.CloneVolume(ctx, sourceVolumeID, req). This creates a SubVolume CR with cloneStatus=Pending and returns at once (the pod waits).
  5. The background Clone Worker updates the CR to cloneStatus=InProgress, creates a Job that runs cp -a from the source to the target, then updates the CR to cloneStatus=Complete or Failed.
  6. NodePublishVolume gates pod access on cloneStatus=Complete. Kubelet retries with backoff until the clone finishes.

docs.title: Volume ID Format
docs.text:
The CSI volume ID encodes everything needed to locate the subvolume:

Format: {pool-name}/{share-vpc-id}/{subdir-name}

Example: general-purpose/r006-a1b2c3d4-5678-90ab-cdef-1234567890ab/pvc-abc123

Parsing:
  pool-name: general-purpose
  share-vpc-id: r006-a1b2c3d4-5678-90ab-cdef-1234567890ab
  subdir-name: pvc-abc123

This format is: - Deterministic (same inputs → same ID) - Parseable without external lookups - Human-readable in kubectl get pv output

docs.title: RBAC
docs.text: The controller ServiceAccount needs: - FileSharePool, SubVolume: full CRUD - PersistentVolumes: get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete (CSI provisioner creates PVs) - PersistentVolumeClaims: get, list, watch, update, patch - PersistentVolumeClaims/status: patch - Nodes: get, list, watch (for topology) - Secrets: get, list, watch - ConfigMaps: get, list, watch - StorageClasses: get, list, watch, create - Events: create, patch - Leases: get, create, update (for leader election) - CSINode: get, list, watch

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
• On managed clusters (ROKS/ROVS/IKS), authentication is provided by the storage-secret-sidecar which populates the storage-secret-store secret. No standalone API key secret is needed.
  • On self-managed clusters, an IBM Cloud API key is stored in a Kubernetes Secret (ibm-cloud-credentials).
  • Never logged, never included in CRD status or events.

docs.title: NFS Security
docs.text:
• Shares use VPC security group rules (TCP 2049).
  • Mount options: nfsvers=4.1,sec=sys (or sec=krb5p if encryption-in-transit is enabled).
  • Subdirectories created with specific UID/GID/permissions per StorageClass config.
  • Node agent validates all paths before mount/unmount to prevent traversal attacks.

docs.title: Pod Isolation
docs.text:
• Pods get a bind-mount of their specific subdirectory, NOT the whole share.
  • A pod cannot traverse above its subdirectory because the bind-mount is the filesystem root from the pod's perspective.

docs.title: Failure Modes
docs.text: Failure Impact Recovery Controller pod crash New PVCs queue; existing PVCs unaffected Pod restarts; leader election transfers Node agent crash New pod mounts fail on that node DaemonSet restarts; existing mounts survive (kernel-level) VPC file share unavailable All PVCs on that share lose access IBM HA (99.999%); pool manager marks share as draining IBM VPC API down No new shares can be created; existing PVCs unaffected Pool manager retries with backoff; allocations to existing shares still work SubVolume CR accidentally deleted Allocation tracking lost for that PVC Data still on share; operator can recreate CR from share contents FileSharePool CR deleted Pool manager stops reconciling Don't delete it; use finalizers to prevent accidental deletion Disk full on a share Writes fail for all PVCs on that share Monitoring alerts; auto-expand or manual expand

docs.title: Backup & Recovery Guide — IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver
docs.text: Data protection strategy using the driver's snapshot, clone, backup, and replication features. For the meaning of words such as moment, restore point and snapshot pool, see CONTEXT.md.

docs.title: Data Protection Options
docs.text: Method RPO RTO Scope Best For Volume Snapshots Point-in-time Minutes (copy speed) Single PVC Regular backups of individual volumes Volume Clones Point-in-time Minutes (the time to copy the data) Single PVC Dev/test copies, pre-migration backup Group Snapshots (not active) None: the driver does not act on them None Multiple PVCs Do not use. A snapshot of a running VM already covers all its disks Backups to a Snapshot Pool Schedule-based (minutes to hours) Minutes to hours (copy speed) Selected PVCs and VMs, all disks of a VM together Keeping many moments of a volume or VM in the same region, on shares of their own Cross-Region Replication Schedule-based (minutes to hours) Manual failover Full pool or label-selected Disaster recovery Application-Level Backup Varies Varies Application-specific Databases, VMs, crash-consistent workloads

docs.title: Volume Snapshots
docs.text: A snapshot is a copy of one volume that stays on the same share as the volume (see CONTEXT.md). It does not protect you from the loss of the share. See USER-GUIDE.md — Snapshots for basic usage.

docs.title: Scheduled Snapshots with CronJob
docs.text:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: snapshot-myapp-data
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "0 */6 * * *"  # Every 6 hours
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: snapshot-creator
          containers:
            - name: snapshot
              image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
              command:
                - /bin/sh
                - -c
                - |
                  TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
                  cat <<SNAP | kubectl apply -f -
                  apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
                  kind: VolumeSnapshot
                  metadata:
                    name: myapp-data-${TIMESTAMP}
                    namespace: default
                    labels:
                      app: myapp
                      snapshot-type: scheduled
                  spec:
                    volumeSnapshotClassName: ibm-vpc-file-pool
                    source:
                      persistentVolumeClaimName: myapp-data
                  SNAP
                  echo "Snapshot myapp-data-${TIMESTAMP} created"
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
---
# RBAC for the CronJob
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: snapshot-creator
  namespace: default
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: snapshot-creator
  namespace: default
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["snapshot.storage.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["volumesnapshots"]
    verbs: ["create", "get", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: snapshot-creator
  namespace: default
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: snapshot-creator
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: snapshot-creator

docs.title: Snapshot Retention Script
docs.text:
Delete snapshots older than a retention period:

#!/bin/bash
# delete-old-snapshots.sh
# Usage: ./delete-old-snapshots.sh <namespace> <label-selector> <max-age-days>

NAMESPACE=${1:-default}
SELECTOR=${2:-snapshot-type=scheduled}
MAX_AGE_DAYS=${3:-7}

CUTOFF=$(date -u -d "${MAX_AGE_DAYS} days ago" +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ 2>/dev/null || \
         date -u -v-${MAX_AGE_DAYS}d +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

echo "Deleting snapshots older than ${MAX_AGE_DAYS} days (before ${CUTOFF})"

kubectl get volumesnapshots -n "$NAMESPACE" -l "$SELECTOR" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.metadata.creationTimestamp}{"\n"}{end}' | \
while read name timestamp; do
  if [[ "$timestamp" < "$CUTOFF" ]]; then
    echo "Deleting snapshot: $name (created $timestamp)"
    kubectl delete volumesnapshot -n "$NAMESPACE" "$name"
  fi
done

Run as a CronJob for automated retention:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: snapshot-retention
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"  # Daily at 2 AM
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: snapshot-creator
          containers:
            - name: cleanup
              image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
              command:
                - /bin/sh
                - -c
                - |
                  # Keep snapshots for 7 days
                  CUTOFF=$(date -u -d "7 days ago" +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
                  kubectl get volumesnapshots -n default -l snapshot-type=scheduled \
                    -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {.metadata.creationTimestamp}{"\n"}{end}' | \
                  while read name ts; do
                    if [ "$ts" \< "$CUTOFF" ]; then
                      kubectl delete volumesnapshot -n default "$name"
                      echo "Deleted: $name"
                    fi
                  done
          restartPolicy: OnFailure

docs.title: Snapshot Performance
docs.text:
A snapshot of a plain volume is a full directory copy (cp -a). Performance depends on data size. A snapshot of a VM disk is faster: it is a QEMU copy, or an instant snapshot where the Sidecar gate is on (see VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md).

Data Size Approximate Snapshot Time 1 GB 5-15 seconds 10 GB 30-90 seconds 100 GB 5-15 minutes 1 TB 1-2 hours

Snapshot creation consumes share capacity equal to the source data size. Monitor pool capacity to ensure room for snapshots.

docs.title: Volume Clones
docs.text: Full copies of existing PVCs. See USER-GUIDE.md — Volume Cloning and VOLUME-CLONING.md for design details.

docs.title: Pre-Change Backup via Clone
docs.text:
Before a risky operation (upgrade, migration, schema change):

# 1. Create a clone of the data PVC
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: myapp-data-backup
  namespace: default
  labels:
    backup-reason: pre-upgrade
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  storageClassName: ibm-vpc-file-pool
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
  dataSource:
    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
    name: myapp-data
EOF

# 2. Wait for clone to complete
# The SubVolume is named after the new PV (pvc-<uuid>)
PV=$(kubectl get pvc myapp-data-backup -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}')
kubectl get subvolume ${PV} -w
# Wait for cloneStatus to show "Complete"

# 3. Proceed with the risky operation
# ...

# 4. If rollback needed, swap PVC references in your deployment
# 5. Clean up the backup clone when no longer needed
kubectl delete pvc myapp-data-backup

docs.title: Clone from Snapshot (Point-in-Time Restore)
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: myapp-data-restored
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  storageClassName: ibm-vpc-file-pool
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
  dataSource:
    name: myapp-data-20260221-060000   # Snapshot name
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io

docs.title: Restore in the console
docs.text:
The console can do the same without YAML. Open a snapshot in the IBM VPC File Pools page (Snapshots tab) and choose Restore to new PVC, on the details page or in the row menu.

  • The form has defaults: the name is <source claim>-restored, the size is the snapshot's size (you can make it bigger, not smaller), and the storage class, access mode and volume mode come from the source claim when it still exists.
  • The namespace is fixed to the namespace of the snapshot. This is a Kubernetes rule.
  • The action only creates a new claim. It never replaces an existing volume.
  • The claim stays Pending until the copy ends, and becomes Bound only then. A Job runs the copy. If the copy fails, the driver keeps the new volume's record and starts a new copy at the next retry. The claim is not deleted.
  • The action is off, with a reason, when the snapshot is not ready or when no VolumeSnapshot points to it. A snapshot made directly as a Snapshot object has no VolumeSnapshot: create one first.
  • The form warns when a VM uses the source claim. The warning text says a snapshot of a running VM is a plain file copy that may not boot. That text is older than the driver: a snapshot of a running VM's disk is now a QEMU copy or an instant snapshot (see the KubeVirt VMs section). Check status.consistency on the Snapshot before you restore.

docs.title: Group Snapshots
docs.text:
Not active (issue #100). The driver does not act on VolumeGroupSnapshot records: nothing watches them, the hooks below never run, and the CSI group snapshot service is not registered, so Kubernetes' own group snapshot API cannot reach the driver. There is no plan to turn it on. A running VM with several disks does not need it: its snapshots show one moment already (see KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md). This page describes the design, not a working feature.

Coordinated multi-PVC snapshots for applications with related volumes. See USER-GUIDE.md — Volume Group Snapshots and VOLUME-GROUP-SNAPSHOTS.md for design details.

docs.title: Application-Consistent Group Snapshot with Hooks
docs.text:
For applications that support quiesce/thaw operations:

apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: VolumeGroupSnapshot
metadata:
  name: mydb-consistent-snap
spec:
  poolName: general-purpose
  sourcePVCs:
    - pvcName: mydb-data
      pvcNamespace: default
    - pvcName: mydb-wal
      pvcNamespace: default
  failurePolicy: Abort
  preSnapshotHooks:
    - name: quiesce-db
      type: exec
      exec:
        podSelector:
          app: mydb
        namespace: default
        container: db
        command: ["pg_ctl", "stop", "-m", "fast"]
      timeoutSeconds: 30
      onError: Abort
  postSnapshotHooks:
    - name: resume-db
      type: exec
      exec:
        podSelector:
          app: mydb
        namespace: default
        container: db
        command: ["pg_ctl", "start"]
      timeoutSeconds: 30
      onError: Continue

docs.title: Best-Effort Group Snapshot (No Hooks)
docs.text:
For workloads where brief inconsistency is acceptable:

apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: VolumeGroupSnapshot
metadata:
  name: myapp-group-snap
spec:
  poolName: general-purpose
  sourcePVCs:
    - pvcName: myapp-data
      pvcNamespace: default
    - pvcName: myapp-config
      pvcNamespace: default
    - pvcName: myapp-logs
      pvcNamespace: default
  failurePolicy: Continue

The inconsistency window (time between first and last member copy) is tracked in status.inconsistencyWindow. For the smallest window, order PVCs from largest to smallest so the longest copy runs first.

docs.title: Backups to a Snapshot Pool
docs.text: A BackupPolicy backs up the PVCs and VMs you select into a pool that holds only backups. The pool has its own VPC file share, so losing or filling a data share does not take the backups with it. The pool must hold only backups: the policy stops backing up while it holds any volume. So the driver refuses to make a volume (a new claim, a clone or a restore) on a pool that a policy uses as its snapshot pool, and the console leaves that pool's storage class out of its lists. A running VM is backed up at one moment for all its disks, with the guest file systems frozen for a fraction of a second, and only changed blocks are copied after the first backup.

docs.title: What a backup looks like
docs.text:
A backup is a set of files on a share of the snapshot pool. You cannot browse backups from the cluster or the console yet (issue #92). kubectl backup list shows what exists. The folders are below /backup/<policy>/ on the share. Each volume has a folder named after its PersistentVolume (pvc-<uuid>), not after its claim.

  • A plain volume is a folder of files. /backup/<policy>/pvcs/pvc-<uuid>/ holds the files as they were at the latest backup. Each earlier moment is a folder of hard links, named by its UTC time (for example 20261021T093000Z), in /backup/<policy>/.moments/pvcs/pvc-<uuid>/. A file that did not change takes no extra space.
  • A VM disk is one file, disk.img. The folder /backup/<policy>/pvcs/pvc-<uuid>/ holds the latest backup as a whole raw disk. Earlier moments are not separate disks. They are undo files in the folder .repl-undo next to the disk. Each undo file holds the old contents of the blocks that the next backup changed. A restore of an earlier moment applies the undo files, newest first.
  • A VM with several disks has one folder for each disk. All its disks show the same moment, so a restore at that moment gives a VM that boots.

The words moment and restore point are defined in CONTEXT.md.

apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata: {name: backups}
spec:
  zone: eu-de-3
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 2000
  iops: 3000
  maxShares: 1          # more than one share is allowed; each volume stays on one of them
  initialShares: 1
  autoExpand: false
---
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: BackupPolicy
metadata: {name: nightly}
spec:
  snapshotPool: backups
  schedule: 6h
  keepFor: 14d
  namespaces: [vms, apps]
  selector:
    matchLabels: {backup: "yes"}     # a label on the PVCs

Check it, and list the moments you can restore:

kubectl get backuppolicy nightly
kubectl backup list --policy nightly

Restore a volume as it was at a moment, to a new PVC (the volume may be gone). A VM has one PVC for each disk: restore each disk at the same moment, then make a VM from the new PVCs.

kubectl backup restore --policy nightly --pvc vms/web-root --to vms/web-root-restored \
  --moment 2026-10-20T09:00:00Z --wait

Things to know: - Size the snapshot pool for one whole copy of the selected data plus the changes kept for keepFor. A VM that rewrites half its disk a day, kept for 14 days, needs up to 7 extra disks of undo files. When the share is more than 85% full, the policy stops new backups: its status.phase is Error and status.message says how full the share is. The controller starts a small Job on the share about every 10 minutes to read its usage (df), and pauses the policy's ReplicationPolicy objects with the same annotation that suspend uses. Backups are never deleted to make room. Backups resume by themselves when usage falls to 85% or less, for example after you lower keepFor or remove the backups of a volume. Alert on vpc_file_pool_backup_snapshot_pool_used_percent (see MONITORING.md) so you act before the limit. - A volume that is not a VM disk is synced with rsync and each sync is kept as a folder of hard links, so a backup of a running database is only as consistent as its files. Use the hooks of replication for such volumes. - Backups are in the same VPC as the data. They do not cover the loss of the VPC; use cross-region replication for that. - A volume that is deleted, or no longer matches the selector, keeps its backups until keepFor has passed since its last backup, and can be restored until then. Deleting a policy keeps its backups on the share; kubectl backup delete removes them (below). - A VM restored from an earlier moment may need its guest to run a file system check, as after a power loss, if the backup is CrashConsistent. A backup that says FileSystemConsistent does not.

Remove the backups of a volume you no longer want (for example a volume that is gone and will never be restored). This is the only way to remove them before keepFor has passed, and only this command does it: the controller never removes backups by itself.

kubectl backup delete --policy nightly --pvc vms/web-root

It measures the backup folder and the folder of earlier moments with a Job on the snapshot pool's share, shows both paths and the size, and asks you to type vms/web-root. Use --yes instead of the typed answer; in a shell that is not interactive (a script, CI) --yes is required, and without it the command stops before it starts a Job. The Jobs run in the driver namespace (--driver-namespace, default kube-system), so you need the right to make, read and delete Jobs and PersistentVolumeClaims there, to list the pods of those Jobs (it reads the size from their termination message), and to make, read and delete PersistentVolumes (cluster-wide). You also need to read backuppolicies, backuprestores and filesharepools (cluster-wide).

It refuses, and changes nothing, in these cases: - The policy still backs up the volume. Remove the label that selects the claim (or delete the policy), wait for one backup cycle so kubectl backup list shows the volume as retained, then run it again. - A restore of the volume has not ended (any BackupRestore for that policy and claim that is not Done or Failed).

If the policy is already deleted, its status can no longer say where the backup is. Name the snapshot pool and the volume yourself: --pool backups --volume pvc-.... The volume name is the folder under /backup/<policy>/pvcs/ on the share.

docs.title: Backups in the console
docs.text:
The Backups tab of the IBM VPC File Pools page shows the same facts as kubectl backup list, with no kubectl.

  • The list has one row for each policy: snapshot pool, schedule, keep time, phase, number of volumes, the age of the stalest backup, and whether the COS export is on.
  • A policy page shows its settings and one row for each volume: the claim, the VM, the newest and oldest backup, the restore points, what the newest backup wrote (VM disks only: a plain volume shows -, because its file copy does not count bytes), the consistency, the last error and the export state. A volume the policy no longer backs up is marked with the date its backups are kept until. A crash consistent copy has an orange label.
  • When new backups are stopped because the snapshot pool is more than 85% full, a banner says so on both pages and links to the pool. Nothing is deleted to make room; see Backups stopped.
  • Restore is in the console too (next section). The COS tab and restore from COS are described below.

docs.title: Make and change a policy in the console
docs.text:
On the Backups tab, Create BackupPolicy opens a form that makes the same BackupPolicy as the YAML above. Edit on the list or on a policy page opens it again.

  • Snapshot pool. Only a pool that holds no workload claims and has a ready share can be chosen; the other pools are listed, switched off, with the reason.
  • Schedule and keep for. The page checks the same limits as the admission webhook (a schedule of at least 1 minute, a keep time of at least 1 hour) and shows the webhook's own message if it refuses the policy.
  • Labels and namespaces. The page counts, live, the claims the labels match (and says when a VM's other disks join), so a wrong label shows at once. A policy with no labels is refused. Match expressions cannot be edited in the form; an edit keeps them, and keeps the export block.
  • VM copy speed limit. Explained as on the replication form, with the note that Red Hat does not support copying a running VM.
  • The form explains the 85% stop: when a share of the snapshot pool is more than 85% full, no new backups are made for the volumes on it, and nothing is deleted to make room.
  • Suspend and Resume are on the list menu and on the policy page. They set spec.suspend; existing backups stay.
  • Delete asks first. Deleting a policy stops new backups; the backups already made stay on the snapshot pool. Remove them with Delete backups on the volume (while the policy exists) or with kubectl backup delete.
  • Without the right to create, update or delete BackupPolicy objects, the action is off, the page names the missing right, and (for create and edit) shows the YAML for an administrator.

docs.title: Restore a backup in the console
docs.text:
Open a policy, and choose Restore in the menu of a volume. This does what kubectl backup restore does: it makes one BackupRestore object, and the driver makes the new claim and copies the backup into it.

  • Volume. Any volume the policy has backups of, including a volume that is gone (marked "no longer backed up").
  • Latest backup, or a moment. For a moment, choose a time in your time zone. The restore uses the newest backup at or before it, and the banner tells you which backup it used. The page shows the oldest and the newest backup, and refuses a time before the oldest. It cannot list the moments one by one, because the policy status holds only the count of restore points.
  • Namespace and new claim name. The name must not exist; the page checks the namespace live and refuses a name that is taken, as a restore never writes over a volume.
  • Storage class. The default is the class of the backed-up claim. Only classes of this driver are offered.
  • A confirmation says that a new claim is made, that nothing is overwritten, and that the copy takes time.
  • The page then follows the restore: Pending, Provisioning, Restoring, Done (with the restored moment) or Failed (with the message). The new claim cannot be used until it is Done.
  • A crash consistent VM disk shows a warning: the guest may need a file system check when it starts.
  • If your account may not create BackupRestore objects, the button is off, the page names the missing right, and it shows the YAML an administrator can apply for you.
  • Other pages can link to the page with ?claim=<namespace>/<name> and ?moment=<time>.

docs.title: Delete the backups of a volume in the console
docs.text:
Delete backups in the menu of a volume does what kubectl backup delete does, as a dialog. It is the only destructive action of the Backups tab.

  1. Refusals. The dialog refuses, and starts nothing, while the policy still backs up the volume (the label that selects it is still there; remove it, or delete the policy, and wait for one backup cycle so the volume shows as "no longer backed up"), and while a restore of the volume has not ended. It uses the words of the command line.
  2. Measure. The console starts the same measure Job as the command, on the snapshot pool's share, and shows how much would go, for example "12.0 GiB, 9 moments". The Job only reads. If the folders are empty or missing, the dialog says so and stops.
  3. Confirm. You type the claim as namespace/name. Only then does the console start the delete Job. The backups cannot be recovered; the volume itself is not touched.
  4. Result. The dialog follows the Job and says "Removed the backups of ... (size)", or the error. The console removes each Job, its claim and its PV when the Job ends.

The Jobs run in the driver namespace (kube-system) with your own rights: to make and remove Jobs and claims there, to make and remove PersistentVolumes, and to list pods. Without them the dialog is off, names the missing rights, and shows the YAML of the delete objects for an administrator to apply (applying it removes the backups without the measure step or the typed confirmation, so only apply it knowingly). A link can open the dialog with ?claim=<namespace>/<name> on the policy page. After a policy is deleted, its status can no longer say where its backups are; use kubectl backup delete --pool ... --volume ....

docs.title: The COS tab and restore from COS in the console
docs.text:
The COS tab of a policy page shows what kubectl backup cos-list shows, without kubectl.

  • Export settings. Bucket, endpoint, folder, keep time, lock, schedule, and the names of the Secrets and the Key Protect key. The console shows Secret names only and never reads a Secret.
  • Export state of each volume. When the newest copy in COS was sent and how big it was, or the export error. A failed export is tried again by itself and never stops the local backups.
  • List COS contents. Runs the same read-only Job as cos-list in the driver namespace and shows the volumes and their moments. It needs the right to make and remove a Job there and to list pods; without it the button is off, the missing right is named and the Job YAML is shown for an administrator. A long list is cut: enter one volume to see all its moments.

Set up the export is a guide at the top of the COS tab. The console does not run cos-setup: it needs your own IBM Cloud login, and the console has none and must not hold an IBM Cloud API key. So the guide shows the command with your names filled in and what each flag means (run it with --dry-run first). After it has run, you paste what it wrote:

  1. The contents of the two Secret files (the COS key and the wrapped backup key), and the Key Protect API key. The console makes the Secrets in the driver namespace from them. It sends each once, never reads a Secret back, and leaves a Secret that exists already as it is. It refuses Secrets in another namespace, Secrets with other keys, and the readable backup key (keep that outside IBM Cloud).
  2. The spec.export block that the command printed. The console checks it with the same rules as the admission webhook, shows the webhook's message if it still refuses, and writes it into the policy.
  3. A line then says whether the export works: how many volumes have been sent to COS, or that a volume has an export error. The first export runs after the next local backup.

Without the rights to make Secrets or to change the policy, the buttons are off and the missing right is named.

Restore from COS (link on the Backups list and on the COS tab) makes one BackupRestore with spec.fromCOS, as kubectl backup restore --from-cos does, and works in a cluster that has no policy and no snapshot pool. Fill the settings from a policy of this cluster, or type them for another cluster's bucket. COS keeps neither the claim name, the storage class nor the size, so you give them. The Secrets (COS key, wrapped backup key, Key Protect API key) must already exist in the driver namespace. Two things the console cannot do, because it has no IBM Cloud login: it does not remove delete markers in the bucket (use the command if a backup you can see is not found), and it does not fetch the wrapped backup key from the bucket into a missing Secret. The readable emergency key as a file (--backup-key-file) is a command-line option only. The page takes ?policy=, ?volume= and ?moment=.

docs.title: Export to COS (built; proved in stage 18 except the emergency-key and DR-cluster restores)
docs.text:
A policy can also send its backups to an IBM Cloud Object Storage bucket, encrypted before they leave the cluster, with a lock that nobody can shorten. The controller does this with the spec.export block:

spec:
  export:
    bucket: pool-backups
    endpoint: s3.eu-de.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud
    prefix: lab
    credentialsSecret: cos-credentials   # in the driver namespace
    backupKeySecret: cos-backup-key      # in the driver namespace: the backup key, wrapped by Key Protect
    keyProtect:                          # which root key unwraps it (all four are required)
      instanceID: <Key Protect instance GUID>
      region: eu-de
      rootKeyID: <root key ID>
      apiKeySecret: keyprotect-apikey    # Secret, key "apikey": an API key with the Reader role on the root key
    emergencyKeySecret: ""               # optional; see "Backup key handling" below
    keepFor: 30d                         # default; at least 25h with lock Compliance
    lock: Compliance                     # or None
    schedule: 6h                         # optional; default: after each local backup

After each local backup of a volume, an export Job reads the snapshot pool's share (read-only, so a running VM is never slowed) and sends the changes to the bucket. kubectl get backuppolicy NAME -o yaml shows exportedTime, exportedBytes and exportError for each volume. A failed export is tried again after 5 minutes and never stops the backups to the snapshot pool. While the export of a volume runs, the next local backup of that volume waits (the volume's status says held: export to COS running), so the export never reads a disk that changes under it; other volumes are not held, except that all disks of a running VM are held together, because one VM copy takes all its disks. A hold ends with the export, or after 6 hours, when the export is stopped and tried again. Restore points of a volume get older by the length of its export. A maintenance Job runs once a day (hourly for the shortest keep time of 25 hours) and deletes snapshots older than keepFor. Alert rules for a late export are in MONITORING.md.

kubectl backup cos-setup makes the IBM Cloud side with your own login (IBMCLOUD_API_KEY, IBMCLOUD_IAM_TOKEN or your ibmcloud login; it needs no cluster; it deletes only the instance-wide policy that IBM Cloud adds for the new HMAC key). Run it with --dry-run first: it prints every step and the exact objects.

kubectl backup cos-setup --dry-run \
  --region eu-de --resource-group my-rg --bucket my-backups-0123 \
  --root-key crn:v1:bluemix:public:kms:eu-de:a/ACCT:INSTANCE:key:KEYID \
  --vpc-crn <cluster VPC CRN> --admin-address <your public address>[,more] \
  --key-file ~/.config/pool-csi/cos-key.yaml --secret-file ~/.config/pool-csi/backup-key-secret.yaml

It makes (or reuses, by name) the COS instance, a versioned bucket with object lock and no default keep time, the PoolCsiBackupWriter role, a service ID limited to that one bucket, an HMAC key, a CBR zone and rule, and a backup key wrapped by your Key Protect root key. You must give an existing Key Protect root key; it does not make one. It refuses to run with --cbr-mode enabled (the default) when your own address is not in the zone, so you cannot lock yourself out; use --zone-id to reuse a zone. It refuses a bucket it did not make unless you pass --existing-bucket. It writes the COS key to --key-file (a Secret manifest, mode 0600, never printed), shows the readable backup key once and waits until you type that you saved a copy outside IBM Cloud, then stores only the wrapped copy in the bucket and in --secret-file. A keep time above 90 days needs a typed confirmation because a Compliance lock cannot be undone. Run it again at any time: what exists is left as it is. It prints the spec.export block to paste. It was run against real IBM Cloud in stage 18 of the release test.

Backup key handling. The readable backup key is never stored in the cluster or in the bucket. Only the copy wrapped by Key Protect is: in the Secret backupKeySecret (key wrappedKey) and next to the backups in the bucket. Each export and maintenance Job asks Key Protect to unwrap it. The driver has no identity of its own in Key Protect. It uses the API key of a service ID that has the Reader role on the root key, and that API key is held in the Secret keyProtect.apiKeySecret (key apikey; cos-setup does not make this Secret, it prints the command), keeps the readable key in memory (a memory-backed folder, mode 0400, removed as soon as Kopia has read it) and never logs it. The controller never reads these Secrets and never calls Key Protect. If you remove the API key's access in Key Protect, exports and maintenance stop. Key Protect runs in one region. If it is unreachable, a Job fails with a message that says so, and tries again later; to keep exporting through a Key Protect outage, set emergencyKeySecret to a Secret (key backupKey) with the readable key: the Job then uses it and logs that it did. That Secret is a readable copy in the cluster, so it weakens the protection against someone who takes over the cluster; the safer emergency copy is the one cos-setup shows you once, kept outside IBM Cloud, and used by the restore. A wrong root key or a bad API key is always an error, never a reason to use the emergency key. The unwrap was proved against a real Key Protect root key in stage 18 of the release test (see DEPLOYMENT-NOTES.md). Not yet proved: the emergency-key restore (--backup-key-file) and a restore from COS in the other (DR) cluster.

docs.title: Restore from COS
docs.text:
This is the way back when the pools are gone. It works in any cluster that runs the driver: it needs no BackupPolicy and no snapshot pool, only a pool to restore into, the bucket, and the keys.

  1. In the new cluster, make the two Secrets in the driver namespace that cos-setup wrote manifests for: the COS key (cos-credentials) and the Key Protect API key (keyprotect-apikey). The wrapped backup key Secret is made for you from the copy in the bucket if it does not exist.
  2. List what is in the bucket:
kubectl backup cos-list --policy nightly --bucket my-backups-0123 \
  --endpoint s3.eu-de.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud --prefix lab \
  --kp-instance <GUID> --kp-region eu-de --kp-root-key <ID>

It prints each volume (pvc-<uuid>) and the moment of each export. It runs a read-only Job in the driver namespace, so the cluster must be able to reach the bucket. The answer is cut at about 3.5 KB; add --volume pvc-... to see every moment of one volume. COS keeps no claim names, so the volume name is how you identify a backup; the size and the class are not kept either. 3. Restore one volume to a new PVC:

kubectl backup restore --from-cos --policy nightly --volume pvc-11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555 \
  --to apps/db-restored --storage-class ibmc-vpc-file-pool --size-gb 40 \
  --bucket my-backups-0123 --endpoint s3.eu-de.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud --prefix lab \
  --kp-instance <GUID> --kp-region eu-de --kp-root-key <ID> --moment 2026-10-21T09:30:00Z --wait

The same flags as cos-list, plus the new PVC, its class and size, and an optional --moment. With your own IBM Cloud login (IBMCLOUD_API_KEY, IBMCLOUD_IAM_TOKEN or the ibmcloud login) the command first removes delete markers in the policy's area of the bucket: a delete made with the driver's key only hides data, and a hidden chunk looks missing to Kopia. It removes markers only, by version, and never a real version. The endpoint must be a COS S3 host (s3.[direct.|private.]<region>.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud); your token is sent to no other host. Symlinks in a backup are removed from the scratch copy, and the restore Job refuses a symlinked backup folder, disk or moment folder. Use --skip-marker-cleanup if nothing was deleted and your login cannot reach the bucket.

The restore makes a BackupRestore with spec.fromCOS. It reuses the restore of a local backup: the export is copied from the bucket into a scratch folder on the share of the new volume, the restore Job copies it into the volume (a VM disk is rewound to the moment), and the scratch folder is removed. The new PVC is held back from pods until the copy ends, and the restore never writes over a PVC that exists. The share needs room for a second copy of the volume while the restore runs.

If Key Protect or the root key is gone, restore with the readable backup key that cos-setup showed you once: --backup-key-file ./backup-key.txt, and leave out the --kp-* flags.
