The command puts the key in a temporary Secret, never calls Key Protect, waits for the restore, and removes the Secret when the restore ends. If the wait times out, the Secret stays for the running Jobs and the command prints the kubectl delete secret line to run when the restore ends. This path needs the COS key Secret too. --backup-key-file is for restore only; cos-list uses Key Protect.

Proved against a real COS bucket and a real Key Protect root key in stage 18 of the release test (export, cos-list, restore into the same cluster and into the DR cluster, and the emergency-key restore with --backup-key-file in both; see DEPLOYMENT-NOTES.md). Last full pass: release run 1029-2259 on v0.16.2, 30 Oct 2026, with the Jobs running the driver image. For the bucket and its lock, see TUTORIAL-09-COS-BACKUP-BUCKET.md. The design is in docs/specs/2026-10-21-backup-cos-export.md.

A Compliance lock cannot be undone, not even by IBM. Locked data is billed until its lock ends, also after you delete the policy.

docs.title: Browse a backup and restore files (in development)
docs.text:
The goal (issue #92) is to look inside a backup and get back one file or folder without restoring the whole volume. The design is in docs/specs/2026-10-22-backup-file-restore.md. Only the first part exists:

  • The browse helper (cmd/browse, image browse). It reads one backup folder, read-only. It lists a folder in pages of 1000 names, describes a name, reads a byte range of a file, and streams a folder as a tar. It never follows a symbolic link: a link is listed with its text, a download of a link is refused, and a tar keeps it as a link. A path is a list of names, so a name with a newline or bytes that are not text works. Every call needs the session token. The helper ends by itself after 15 minutes without use, or after 2 hours.
  • Browse sessions (part 2). A BackupBrowse resource per open session; the controller starts the helper pod for it, with a random token and a per-session TLS certificate in a Secret, and removes everything when the session ends. The helper serves only over TLS. Defaults: 15 minutes idle, 2 hours hard limit, 5 open sessions in the cluster and 2 for each namespace; all are Helm values (backupBrowse.*).
  • The gateway and kubectl backup (part 3). kubectl backup ls, get and browse list and download files and folders of a plain volume's backup, at the latest copy or at a moment. See "Browse from the command line" below.
  • Restore of files (parts 4 and 5). A BackupFileRestore copies chosen files and folders out of a backup into a new claim or into a new folder of an existing claim. Users ask for it with kubectl backup restore-files, through the gateway, which checks their rights on both namespaces. See "Restore files into a claim" below.
  • The console file browser (phase 3, first half). A Browse files action on each volume of a policy opens a page that lists folders and files, with a moment picker and downloads. See "Browse and download files in the console" below.
  • Backups in COS (phase 4). The same commands read a plain volume's backup from the policy's COS bucket. See "Files from a backup in COS" below.
  • The console restore dialog (phase 3, second half). See "Restore files in the console" below.
  • VM disks (phase 5, in development). The files inside a VM disk, without starting the VM. See "Files inside a VM disk" below.
  • Not built yet: VM disks in COS (phase 6), and in the console a switch to read from COS by hand.

docs.title: Browse from the command line
docs.text:
kubectl backup ls  --policy nightly --pvc apps/db [--moment 2026-10-21T09:30:00Z] [/var/www]
kubectl backup ls  --policy nightly --pvc apps/db --moments            # the moments that can be browsed
kubectl backup get --policy nightly --pvc apps/db /var/www/index.php --out ./restored/
kubectl backup get --policy nightly --pvc apps/db /var/www --extract ./www-copy
kubectl backup browse --policy nightly --pvc apps/db                    # prints a session name
kubectl backup ls --session bb-abc12 /                                  # reuse it
kubectl backup browse --close bb-abc12

A file is saved under its own name in --out (a folder), under the name you give, or on standard output with --out -. A file that exists is never replaced. A folder is saved as NAME.tar, or unpacked with --extract, which writes only folders and regular files below the folder you name and skips links and special files (it says which). A symbolic link in a backup is shown as a link and is not downloaded. A name that is not text is shown as \xNN, and you can type it the same way.

Without --session, each command reuses an open session of the same user, volume and moment, or opens one, and waits for the helper pod (a few seconds). A session ends after 15 minutes without use.

Who may browse. kubectl backup sends your own token from your kubeconfig (a token or an exec plugin; a client certificate alone has no token to send). The gateway checks the token with the Kubernetes API, then checks, on every call, that you may get the rights-only resource backupfiles (group storage.ibmcloud.io) in the namespace of the backed-up claim. No object of that kind exists: it only lets RBAC say "may read the backups of this namespace".

Who May browse the backups of namespace N Admin of N (the built-in admin role) Yes, with no setup: backup-file-reader is aggregated into admin A user with only view or edit in N No Anyone with a RoleBinding to backup-file-reader (or backup-file-restorer) in N Yes Cluster administrator Yes Admin of another namespace No

To let someone read another namespace's backups: kubectl create rolebinding NAME -n N --clusterrole=backup-file-reader --user=alice. A deleted claim's backup still belongs to its old namespace. A person without the right gets the same "forbidden" whether the volume exists or not. Removing the binding stops access on the next call; a session of that person cannot be used by anyone else.

Audit. Each session start, file download, folder download and close writes a Kubernetes Event on the BackupBrowse (in the driver namespace, on the ConfigMap backup-gateway-info, with the session in related): the user, the namespace, the volume, the moment and the path, never contents or tokens. People without rights in the driver namespace cannot read them.

How the gateway is reached. Through the reencrypt Route on OpenShift (the router answers with the cluster's ingress certificate and encrypts again to the gateway); elsewhere through the …-gateway Service and an ingress of your own. kubectl backup finds the address in the ConfigMap backup-gateway-info (readable by every signed-in user) or from --gateway or KUBECTL_BACKUP_GATEWAY. It trusts the system certificate roots; if your ingress certificate is from a private CA, --gateway-ca-file names that CA.

Where it runs. Helper pods and their Secrets are in their own namespace, ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-browse (backupBrowse.namespace), which holds nothing else, so the gateway can read Secrets only there. The namespace allows root pods without capabilities (Pod Security level baseline); on OpenShift one SCC allows exactly that.

docs.title: Restore files into a claim
docs.text: A BackupFileRestore (cluster scoped, short name bfr) copies the files and folders you list out of one backup into a claim. It is the file version of a BackupRestore. Users do not make it: kubectl backup restore-files asks the gateway, which checks their rights and makes it (below). A cluster administrator may also make it by hand, as here.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
kubectl backup restore-files --policy nightly --pvc apps/db --path /var/www/index.php --path /etc/app --to apps/db-files --wait
kubectl backup restore-files --policy nightly --pvc apps/db --moment 2026-10-21T09:30:00Z --paths-file paths.txt --to apps/db --existing --wait
kubectl backup restore-files --status bfr-abc12

--path is given once for each file or folder, as kubectl backup ls prints it (a name that is not text is \xNN); --paths-file reads one path on each line. --to NAMESPACE/CLAIM is the target. The default is a new claim (--new-claim, with --size-gb and --storage-class if you want to choose); --existing writes a new folder into a claim that exists. --wait follows the restore to the end and says where the files are; without it the command prints the name of the restore and --status NAME shows it later. A restore is shown only to the user who asked for it. A user may have 10 restores that have not ended (backupGateway.maxOpenRestores); more are refused. The limit is enforced by numbered object names (bfr-<user hash>-<n>), so parallel requests cannot pass it; a slot whose restore has ended is freed for the next one.

What you ask for You need Any restore get backupfiles in the namespace of the backed-up claim (the built-in admin role has it; backup-file-reader and backup-file-restorer carry it) Into a new claim also create on persistentvolumeclaims in the target namespace Into an existing claim also update on persistentvolumeclaims and create on pods in the target namespace (writing files into a claim is the same power as mounting it)

So an admin of namespace B can restore a file from the backup of namespace A into a claim of B only if someone with rights in A gave them backup-file-reader there. Without it they get the same "forbidden" whether the volume exists or not. The gateway reads the existing claim only after both rights are known, and takes its UID, so a claim that is deleted and made again before the restore runs is refused. Each request writes an audit Event FileRestoreRequested on the restore (in the driver namespace, on the ConfigMap backup-gateway-info, with the session in related): the user, the volume, the moment, the target and the paths, never contents or tokens. The controller writes FileRestoreDone or FileRestoreFailed with counts only.

apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: BackupFileRestore
metadata:
  name: web-files-1
spec:
  policy: nightly
  sourceNamespace: web          # the claim that was backed up
  sourceName: data
  moment: "2026-10-21T09:30:00Z"   # optional: the newest backup at or before it; unset is the latest copy
  paths:                           # a folder is restored with everything in it; "/" is the whole volume
    - /var/www/html/index.php
    - /etc/app
  targetNamespace: web
  targetName: data-restored
  existing: false               # false: make a new claim. true: write a new folder into targetName

Two targets.

Target What happens A new claim (existing: false) The claim must not exist. The controller first runs a Job that only reads and adds up the size of the chosen files (skipped if you set sizeGB). The claim gets that size plus 20%, rounded up to a whole GiB, at least 1 GiB, and the class of the backed-up claim (or storageClassName). Pods are held back from the claim until the copy ends, as in a whole-volume restore. The tree under the volume's root is kept: /var/www/html/index.php becomes /var/www/html/index.php in the new claim An existing claim (existing: true) The files go into a new folder at the top of the claim, named restored-<policy>-<moment> (the latest copy is named by its newest moment, or -latest before the first moment; -2, -3 if the name exists). Nothing else of the claim changes. The claim keeps working for its pods

A restore never writes over a file that exists, and nothing is put back in place. Download a file with kubectl backup get instead, or copy from the restored folder.

What is copied. Regular files, folders and symbolic links. A link is copied as a link and never followed. Devices, pipes and sockets are left out and counted. A file or folder the reader cannot read inside a chosen folder is left out and counted (status.unreadable); a chosen path that is missing or unreadable ends the restore with an error. File times are kept. The setuid and setgid bits are removed. Extended attributes and ACLs are not copied.

Owners and modes. Everything restored gets the owner that the claim is configured with (defaultUID and defaultGID of the pool, for example 107 on KubeVirt pools); modes are kept. If the pool configures no owner, the files keep the owner they had in the backup. The folder itself gets the pool's defaultPermissions (or 0755). The Job sets times, then mode, then owner, for each file, and finishes a folder only after everything in it is written, so a folder with mode 0500 or a file with mode 0600 owned by another user is restored whole. If an owner cannot be set, the restore fails and removes what it wrote: files that nobody can read are worse than no restore. NFS maps root to an ordinary user on VPC file shares; reading was proven on the lab in phase 1 (below), and writing is checked by stage 20 of the release test.

Safety. The list of paths is a file in a ConfigMap that the restore owns, never an argument or part of a script. The Job is the driver program itself (--mode=restore-files), not a shell. It reads the backup read-only through the same handle-based reader as browsing, and writes the destination the same way: every name is made with mkdirat, symlinkat or openat with O_EXCL and O_NOFOLLOW, in a folder reached one name at a time without following a link. A person who puts a link into a claim while the restore runs makes it fail; it cannot make it write somewhere else. Into an existing claim the Job writes a hidden folder first (.restoring-<restore UID>) and renames it to its final name at the end, so nobody sees a half-written folder, and a failed or repeated try leaves nothing. The Job has no service account token, a read-only root file system and no capability except CHOWN and FOWNER.

Refused. A claim that holds a VM disk (disk.img): a VM disk is never a target. A claim with no data folder yet (start a pod that uses it first). A claim that is being restored, or that another restore is writing into (the second restore waits). A claim that was deleted and made again since the request (the claim's UID is pinned when the request is first seen, or when the gateway checked the user's rights). Files that do not fit: the Job checks before it copies, against the least of 200 GiB (backupBrowse.restoreMaxBytes), the free space of the share, and, for an existing claim, its size less what it holds.

Status. phase (Pending, Measuring, Provisioning, Restoring, Done, Failed), message, folder, restoredMoment, latest, sizeGB, the counts files, dirs, links, skipped, unreadable and bytes, and endedTime. A failed copy into a new claim leaves the claim held back; delete it and ask again. An ended restore is removed after 24 hours. The controller writes an Event on the restore when it ends. The Job gets 4 hours. At most 5 restores run at once in the cluster (backupBrowse.restoreMaxRunning); the others show Pending and "waiting" and go on, oldest first, when one ends.

docs.title: Browse and download files in the console
docs.text:
On a policy page, the Browse files action of a volume opens the file browser. The action shows only when the driver was installed with the backup gateway on (backupGateway.enabled and backupBrowse.enabled, the defaults) and only if you may get backupfiles in the claim's namespace; otherwise it names the missing right. The rules for who may browse are the ones in the table above.

  • Starting. The page opens a session and shows "Starting the reader" until the reader is ready (a few seconds). It asks the gateway again every 2 seconds; no request waits for the reader. If the session ends (15 minutes without use, 2 hours, or another tab closed it), the page says so and offers Open again. The session is closed when you leave the page.
  • Folders. The page lists a folder 1000 names at a time (Load more for the next page), with breadcrumbs back up the path. It shows size and time of change. A symbolic link is shown with the text it points to, marked "Link, not followed", and is never opened or downloaded. A file that the reader cannot open is marked "Not readable". A device, pipe or socket is marked as a special file.
  • Names. A name is always shown as text, never as HTML. Characters that are not printable, and bytes that are not valid text, are shown as \xNN (and a backslash as \\), the same as kubectl backup ls, so you can find the same file with both.
  • Moment. The picker offers Latest copy and every moment folder, newest first. Choosing one closes the session and opens a new one at that moment. The latest copy can change while you look, because the next backup replaces files in it one at a time; an older moment does not change until the keep time removes it.
  • Download. Download saves one file; Download as tar (on a folder, or Download this folder as tar above the table, which at the root is the whole backup) saves a folder as a tar. They are plain links to the gateway through the console's plugin proxy: the console session supplies your token, so no token is in the link, and the browser writes the file to disk as it arrives (no copy in memory). The gateway answers with Content-Disposition: attachment, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Content-Security-Policy: sandbox; default-src 'none', Cache-Control: no-store and a type of application/octet-stream (application/x-tar for a folder), so a backup file can never be shown as a page of the console. The audit Event is the same as for kubectl backup get. A download is one file or one folder at a time, up to the gateway limit (backupGateway.maxDownloadBytes, 50 GiB); a tar does not tell the browser what it left out (the command line shows that).
  • Restore. Tick files, folders and links, and press Restore selected (see "Restore files in the console" below).
  • Not in the console yet. A switch to read from COS by hand, and the moments that only COS holds (the picker lists the moments of the snapshot pool; the gateway does choose COS by itself when a session or restore asks for a moment older than every local restore point). VM disks.

Security notes. The browser holds only your own token, which the console proxy adds; the gateway checks it and your right on every call. The link of a download holds the names of the path (base64), so the console's and the browser's logs can show them; file contents and tokens are never in a link. A failed download shows as a failed download in the browser (the error text is not shown there): the usual causes are a file over the limit or a session that ended. kubectl backup get gives the exact message.

docs.title: Files from a backup in COS
docs.text:
A policy with an export block sends its backups to a COS bucket (see "Export to COS" below). You can browse and restore files from there, with the same commands and the same rights as for the snapshot pool. The moments that the local keep time has removed are still in COS until the COS keep time ends.

kubectl backup ls  --from-cos --policy nightly --pvc apps/db --moment 2026-09-01T09:00:00Z /var/www
kubectl backup get --from-cos --policy nightly --pvc apps/db /etc/app.conf --out ./restored/
kubectl backup restore-files --from-cos --policy nightly --pvc apps/db --path /etc/app --to apps/db-files --wait

Which source. --from-cos asks for COS. Without it the gateway chooses: COS when the moment is older than the oldest local restore point, or when no local copy is left and the volume has been exported; the snapshot pool otherwise. The gateway's volume list (GET /v1/volumes) shows exported and exportedTime for a volume that has a copy in COS; kubectl get backuppolicy NAME -o yaml shows exportedTime too. A session on COS and a session on the snapshot pool are never mixed up: a request for one never reuses a session of the other. The reply names the source of the session.

Which backup in the bucket. The policy's export block names the bucket, the prefix, the Secrets and the Key Protect key, so a user names none of them. The volume is the one the policy keeps for the claim. For a moment, the reader takes the oldest export made at or after it (it holds the earlier moments too), then the newest moment folder at or before it, the same rule as ChooseRoot for a folder on a share. The latest copy is the newest export. ls --moments lists the moments in every export, so it shows what only COS holds.

A bucket that no policy describes. After a loss, in a new cluster, a cluster administrator can name the bucket: --from-cos --policy AREA --bucket B --endpoint HOST --volume pvc-<uuid> [--prefix P] with the key flags of restore --from-cos (--kp-instance, --kp-region, --kp-root-key, --credentials-secret, --backup-key-secret, --kp-api-key-secret). --policy is the policy's area in the bucket, and there is no --pvc. A readable key is given as a Secret in the driver namespace (--emergency-key-secret NAME --emergency-key-only), not as a file: a session lasts too long to keep a Secret that the command made. The gateway allows this only to someone who may get every Secret the request names, in the driver namespace (checked for each Secret by name, and again on every later call), because the helper would mount them. A new claim needs --storage-class, because COS does not keep it. The endpoint must be a COS S3 host (the key is sent to it); the request is checked by the command, the gateway and the controller.

How it works. The helper pod runs the pinned Kopia program as a child process, read-only (kopia repository connect --readonly, no credentials stored). It does not mount a share. It reads the COS key, the wrapped backup key and the Key Protect API key as read-only files, unwraps the backup key with Key Protect in its own memory (the controller never holds it), and gives Kopia the COS key and the backup key in an explicit environment and nowhere else: the Key Protect API key and the wrapped key never reach Kopia, and no key is on a command line. Kopia is run for the list of snapshots (snapshot list --json) and for one object at a time (show <object ID>); a folder is a JSON list that the reader parses. The file restore Job uses the same reader and writes the claim with the same safe writer as for a local backup.

What keeps one volume out of another. The helper's keys can read the whole policy area, which holds other namespaces' volumes. So: only snapshots whose tag names the volume and whose source path is exactly /share0/backup/<policy>/pvcs/<volume> (or its .moments twin) are used, a test tries a tag of this volume on another volume's path, a path of this volume on another volume's tag, another policy's area, and paths that look like these with .. or an extra name. A user's path is never an argument to Kopia: the reader starts at the root object of the chosen snapshot and walks down by the object IDs that it reads from the repository, comparing each name with the names in that one folder. Each object ID is checked to be letters and digits before it is given to Kopia, so it cannot be an option. A name that cannot occur in a path (empty, ., .., with / or a NUL byte) is left out of the list and cannot be reached, and the same name twice in a folder is reported as damage. There is no file system under the reader, so a symbolic link is only text: it is listed with its target, a path through one is refused, and a download of one is refused.

Where it runs. The helper pod and the file restore Job for COS run in the driver namespace, next to the COS and Key Protect Secrets (a pod can mount only Secrets of its own namespace). The keys are not copied to the browse namespace, where the gateway may read Secrets. The controller keeps a second copy of each session's token and certificate in the driver namespace for the pod to mount, owned by the session and removed with it; the gateway reads only the first copy. The pods have no service account token, a read-only root file system, no capabilities, run as an ordinary user, and are reachable only by the gateway (a NetworkPolicy). The controller may make and delete Secrets in the driver namespace, nothing more (a Role); it checks from their metadata that the Secrets the export block names exist, and does not read them.

When it fails. The helper stops before it listens and puts the reason in the session status, in words and with no key in them:

Cause What you read A Secret named by the export block is missing the Secret "x" that the export block names does not exist in namespace kube-system A Secret lacks a key, or the image cannot be pulled After five minutes: the helper pod was not ready after 5m0s. Check that the Secrets ... hold the keys access_key_id, secret_access_key, wrappedKey and apikey Key Protect refuses the root key or the API key the backup key could not be unwrapped: ... (the emergency key does not hide a refusal) Key Protect cannot be reached and there is no emergency key cannot reach Key Protect and no emergency key is set The COS key is wrong or may not read the bucket COS refused the key: check the COS key Secret, that it may read this bucket, and the context-based restriction (CBR) rules The bucket or the endpoint is wrong the bucket does not exist at this COS endpoint or COS cannot be reached from the cluster Wrong prefix or policy there is no backup repository at this bucket and prefix The backup key does not open the repository the backup key does not open the repository in COS No export of the volume no backup of volume pvc-... was found in the COS bucket area of policy ... No moment at or before the time no backup at or before ...

Limits. Each folder step and each file is one run of the Kopia program, which opens the repository first. On a local repository that takes about 0.2 seconds; against a real bucket it will be more (not measured yet). A folder listing is cached, and at most 16 runs happen at once, so browsing is quick but a restore of many thousands of small files is slow. For a whole volume use kubectl backup restore --from-cos. A folder can hold up to a million names, and the helper pod gets 1 CPU and 1 GiB by default (backupBrowse.cos.*). A file name that is not valid text may come back under a different name: Kopia writes names into a JSON list, and JSON cannot hold arbitrary bytes (to be checked on the lab; the snapshot pool keeps such names exactly). A file's content is read from the start each time, so reading backward costs a restart of that file. VM disks in COS are phase 6 of the design.

docs.title: Restore files in the console
docs.text:
In the file browser, each file, folder and link has a checkbox (an entry the reader cannot open, and a device, pipe or socket, has none). The line above the table says how many you chose and how big the files are: for example "3 chosen: 2 files (3.0 KiB), 1 folder with everything in it". A folder is restored with everything in it, and a link is restored as a link (it is not followed). Your choice stays when you open another folder, and is dropped when you change the moment. Clear drops it at once. If you choose a folder and a file inside it, the file is not written twice.

Restore selected opens a dialog. It shows what will be written, from which backup and moment, and where it goes:

Where What happens A new claim (the default) The claim is made in the namespace you type (the namespace of the backed-up claim by default), named <claim>-restored by default. Leave the size empty and the driver measures the chosen files first and makes the claim that size plus 20%, at least 1 GiB; or type a size in GiB. The storage class is the one of the backed-up claim unless you choose another A new folder in an existing claim The files go into a new folder at the top of the claim, named restored-<policy>-<moment>. Nothing else in the claim changes. The choice is turned off, with the missing rights named, if you may not do it (see below)

A restore never writes over a file or a claim that exists, and never puts a file back in its old place. The dialog says so before you confirm. If you chose the Latest copy, it also warns that the next backup can change files while they are copied; choose a moment for a copy that stays as it is.

Rights. You need get backupfiles in the namespace of the backed-up claim (you have it, or you could not browse). For a new claim you also need create on persistentvolumeclaims in the target namespace; for an existing claim also update on persistentvolumeclaims and create on pods there. The dialog asks the cluster about the namespace you type, and turns off what you may not do; the gateway checks again.

Progress. After you confirm, the dialog shows the phase: Waiting to start (Pending), Measuring the size of the chosen files (Measuring), Making the claim (Provisioning), Copying the files (Restoring), then Done or Failed. It asks the gateway every 2 seconds with a short request, and stops when the restore ends or the dialog closes; the restore goes on without the dialog, and a restore you closed is still shown by kubectl backup restore-files --status NAME (the dialog shows the name when it cannot follow the restore any more). When it is done, the dialog links to the claim and names the folder, and shows the counts (files, folders, links), the size, anything left out, and the moment that was restored. When it fails, it shows the reason; a claim made for the failed restore stays held back from pods, so delete it before you ask again.

Refusals, in plain words.

Answer The dialog says 403 Which right is missing: get backupfiles in the source namespace, create (and update) on persistentvolumeclaims in the target namespace, or create on pods for an existing claim 404 There is no backup of this volume any more, or the chosen existing claim does not exist 409 A claim with that name already exists; a button fills in another name (name-2, name-3) 429 You have too many open restores (10 by default, backupGateway.maxOpenRestores); wait for one to end

A restore takes at most 1000 chosen entries; choose a folder that holds them instead. Names are shown as text only, in the same escaped form as kubectl backup ls, and the console sends them to the gateway in that form. The browser holds only your own token; no file content is ever in a request.

docs.title: Files inside a VM disk (in development)
docs.text:
The backup of a VM disk is one raw disk, disk.img, plus an undo file for each older moment. To look inside it without starting the VM, a helper pod runs a small read-only appliance VM (libguestfs) that reads the guest file systems, and a read-only disk server shows it the disk as it was at the moment you chose. Built so far:

  • The disk view (replication.OpenDiskView). It shows the disk as it was at any restore point, read-only, with no copy and no scratch space: a read takes the bytes from the latest disk and applies the undo files, newest first, to just the range that was asked for. A test checks, for random histories (writes, zeros, growing and shrinking disks, partial and full copies), that every moment reads byte for byte what RestoreDisk writes. The view never writes: it does not roll back a copy that stopped half way and does not remove a half-written undo file. If the disk or the undo folder changes while a view is open, for example because a new copy started, every read fails and the session must be opened again.
  • The disk server (pkg/nbd). It gives a view to the appliance as a network block device on a private local socket. Only reads are answered; a write, trim or zero request is refused, and the export is marked read-only. The appliance parses file systems that someone else wrote, so the server treats it as hostile: it bounds every request, answers every option it does not know with "unsupported" and never allocates more than a read may ask for.
  • The hold. A session on a VM disk (BackupBrowse.spec.guest) holds the disk's next backup copy while it is open, because a half-applied copy has the disk and the undo files out of step. The controller takes the hold before the helper starts, then waits until a copy that is already running has ended; the session shows Pending with the reason. A held volume gets no new copy (held: waiting for a browse session in the policy status, and all disks of a running VM are held together, because one VM copy takes all its disks). The hold ends when the helper is gone, at the latest at the session's hard limit (2 hours); a hold older than 3 hours is ignored, so a stopped controller cannot stop backups for good. Other volumes are not held. A backup of that one volume can be late by up to 2 hours.
  • The guest helper (Dockerfile.browse-guest, browse --guest). A pod with the same read-only mount as the plain helper, an ordinary root user with every capability dropped, a read-only root file system, two scratch folders (/tmp and /var/tmp, 1 GiB each) and 1 CPU and 1 GiB of memory. It shows the disk to the appliance through the disk server and lists what is inside. The image is CentOS Stream 9 (pinned by digest) with libguestfs, libguestfs-xfs, libguestfs-winsupport and guestfs-tools, and the browse binary; the appliance is built into the image, so a pod does not build it at every start. With backupBrowse.guest.kvmDevice the pod asks for the KVM device (about 1.5 seconds per appliance start instead of about 12). The guest part is off until backupBrowse.guest.enabled is set, because it needs that image.
  • The top level is the list of file systems. In a VM disk session, the first listing shows the guest's file systems as folders (sda1, rhel-root), each with its type and label. A volume that cannot be read is listed too, with the reason in plain words and no way to open it: LUKS and BitLocker (nobody can read them without the guest's key), ReFS, ZFS, a RAID member, swap, or a type the reader does not know. For those the whole-disk restore is the way. Below a file system the paths are the guest's own paths. LVM physical volumes are not listed (their logical volumes are).
  • Crash copies. A backup of a running VM is a crash copy unless the freeze worked. The appliance's drive is read-only, so a journal can never be replayed. A file system that does not mount is tried once more without replaying its journal (norecovery for XFS, noload for ext3 and ext4), and then the session says so on the file system and in its notices. When the policy status says the newest copy is crash-consistent, XFS and ext4 start without the journal at once. The session shows "this copy was taken while the VM was running; the newest changes may be missing". Only the newest copy's consistency is recorded, so for an older moment the notice follows that record.
  • Cost and limits. Each folder opened and each file read runs one of the libguestfs tools (virt-ls, virt-cat; NTFS is readable only through them), and each starts an appliance. Listings are kept for the session. One tool runs at a time, because each holds about 550 MiB. A big download therefore holds the reader, and a listing waits for it. Without KVM a folder takes about 12 seconds. virt-ls prints a long listing in CSV only with -R, so each listing reads the whole tree below the folder and keeps the first level: a folder with a very deep tree (the root of a big system disk) is slow to open. The appliance may take 10 minutes at most to start; after that the session fails with the reason.
  • Restore of files from a VM disk (BackupFileRestore.spec.guest). The restore Job runs in the guest image with the same restore code as for a plain volume (browse --mode=restore-files), reads the guest's files through the appliance, and writes them to a new claim or a new folder of an existing claim. Paths begin with the file system (/sda1/etc/hosts), and that first name is kept in the restored tree. The pod has a reader, which parses the disk and has no write access to the target and no capability, and a writer, which holds only the target and the CHOWN and FOWNER capabilities and never sees the disk. The disk is held for as long as the restore runs: the restore may hold it for 2 hours 45 minutes at most from the first hold, each Job gets what is left of that time (and never more than 2 hours; a plain restore has 4), and the restore fails when the time is used up. Speed: every folder opened and every file read starts an appliance (about 1.5 seconds with KVM, about 12 without), so a restore of a few files or folders is quick and a restore of thousands of small files is not: at 1.5 seconds a file, 5,000 files take over two hours and would hit the limit. Restore the files you need, or restore the whole disk.
  • Using it. The gateway makes a guest session or a guest restore for every volume that the policy status shows as a disk of a VM (vmName), so the same commands and the same console page work for it, with the same access rule (get backupfiles in the namespace of the claim). A VM disk in COS is refused with a sentence (phase 6). See "VM disks in the commands and the console" below.
  • Two ways a VM disk is stored. A running VM is copied by QEMU and keeps one undo file for each earlier moment. A VM that was stopped when it was backed up is copied as plain files, and each earlier moment is a folder with its own disk.img. The controller tells them apart by the consistency in the policy status (FileCopy is the plain copy), and the reader uses the moments folder for the second kind.

docs.title: VM disks in the commands and the console
docs.text:
kubectl backup ls  --policy P --pvc NS/NAME [--moment TIME]              # lists the file systems of the disk
kubectl backup ls  --policy P --pvc NS/NAME --fs rhel-root /etc          # lists a folder inside one
kubectl backup get --policy P --pvc NS/NAME --fs sda1 /Users/me/a.docx --out .
kubectl backup restore-files --policy P --pvc NS/NAME --fs rhel-root --path /etc/hosts --path /home --to NS/CLAIM --wait

--fs takes the name ls prints at the top (sda1, rhel-root) or the device (/dev/rhel/root), and puts it in front of the path. Without it you give the full path (/rhel-root/etc/hosts). A session on a VM disk is given 20 minutes to start instead of 5 (it waits for a backup copy that is being written, and the appliance can take minutes without KVM). Notices that the session reports (a copy taken while the VM was running; a file system read without its journal) are printed to standard error as note: .... ls shows the reason beside a volume that cannot be read.

In the console, Browse files on a VM disk shows "Starting the reader of the VM disk", then a page that asks you to choose a file system. A volume that cannot be read is shown with a "Cannot be read here" label and its reason, and cannot be opened or chosen. Warnings (crash copy, journal) appear above the table. The page says that the next backup of the disk waits while it is open. The restore dialog explains that the file system name stays at the top of what is written.

Speed and limits: a download of a folder as a tar, and a restore of many files, start one appliance for every folder opened and every file read. With the KVM device that is about 1.5 seconds each; without it about 12. Restores of a few files and folders are quick; thousands of small files are not (a restore of a VM disk has a 2 hour limit). One reader tool runs at a time, so a big download makes folder listings wait.

docs.title: Can the helper read other users' files?
docs.text: Yes. VPC file shares map root to an ordinary user, so this was a real question. It was tested on the lab (22 Oct 2026) with a volume filled by users 1000, 2000 and root: files with mode 0600, folders with mode 0700, a link to /etc, a name with a newline. The helper (user 0, no capabilities, read-only NFS mount with sec=sys) listed and read all of them. A cp -a as root, which is how the whole-volume restore Job copies, read all of them too. The file restore Job reads the same way as the helper. The only failures in that copy were changes of owner into a scratch folder that was not on the share, which the restore Job does on the share. A pipe could not be created on the share by a normal user (mkfifo is refused), so the share holds none.

docs.title: Cross-Region Replication
docs.text: Schedule-based replication for disaster recovery. See CROSS-REGION-DR.md for architecture and consistency analysis.

docs.title: Setting Up DR
docs.text:
Prerequisites: 1. Transit Gateway connecting source and destination VPC regions 2. A FileSharePool in the destination region with shares mounted and accessible 3. The destination NFS server IP reachable from the source cluster

apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: ReplicationPolicy
metadata:
  name: prod-to-dr
spec:
  sourcePoolName: production
  schedule: "15m"                    # Sync every 15 minutes
  incrementalSync: true              # Use rsync for delta-only transfer
  maxRetries: 3                      # Pause after 3 consecutive failures
  destinationNFSServer: "10.245.0.100"   # DR region mount target IP
  destinationExportPath: "/"
  destinationBasePath: "/pvcs"       # Base path on destination share
  subVolumeSelector:                 # Optional: replicate only labeled SubVolumes
    matchLabels:
      backup: required
  preSyncHooks:                      # Optional: quiesce before sync
    - name: quiesce-apps
      type: http
      http:
        url: "http://myapp:8080/quiesce"
        method: POST
      timeoutSeconds: 60
      onError: Abort
  postSyncHooks:
    - name: resume-apps
      type: http
      http:
        url: "http://myapp:8080/resume"
        method: POST
      timeoutSeconds: 60
      onError: Continue

docs.title: Monitoring Replication Health
docs.text:
# Check replication status
kubectl get replicationpolicies -o wide

# Detailed status
kubectl get replicationpolicy prod-to-dr -o yaml

# PromQL: Current lag
# pool_csi_replication_lag_seconds{policy="prod-to-dr"}

# PromQL: Sync success rate
# rate(pool_csi_replication_sync_total{policy="prod-to-dr",result="success"}[1h])

docs.title: DR Failover Drill
docs.text:
Validate your DR readiness periodically:

# 1. Verify replication is current
kubectl get replicationpolicy prod-to-dr -o jsonpath='{.status.lastSyncTime}'

# 2. On the DR cluster, verify data exists
kubectl debug node/<dr-node> -it --image=busybox -- sh -c \
  "ls /host/var/data/kubelet/plugins/vpc-file-pool.csi.ibm.io/staging/<dr-share-id>/pvcs/"

# 3. Create test PVCs on the DR cluster pointing to replicated data
# 4. Deploy a test workload and verify data integrity
# 5. Clean up the test deployment

docs.title: Failover Procedure
docs.text:
Failover is manual by design (see CROSS-REGION-DR.md for why). Use the kubectl failover CLI plugin for structured DR promotion:

# 1. Stop replication on the source cluster to prevent partial syncs

# 2. Review what will be failed over and check RPO
kubectl failover plan --nfs-mount-path /repl/dst/10.245.3.8

# 3. Dry-run to preview resources that will be created
kubectl failover execute --nfs-mount-path /repl/dst/10.245.3.8 \
  --dr-pool dr-production --dr-share-ip 10.245.3.8 --dry-run

# 4. Execute failover — creates SubVolume CRs, PVs, and PVCs on the DR cluster
kubectl failover execute --nfs-mount-path /repl/dst/10.245.3.8 \
  --dr-pool dr-production --dr-share-ip 10.245.3.8

# 5. Verify PVC binding
kubectl failover status

# 6. Deploy workloads on the DR cluster
# 7. Update DNS/load balancer to point to the DR cluster

See CROSS-REGION-DR.md — Failover CLI for full flag reference and details.

docs.title: Application-Level Backup
docs.text: For workloads that require crash consistency beyond what NFS directory copies provide.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
Database Recommended Backup Method PostgreSQL pg_dump or pg_basebackup + WAL archiving MySQL mysqldump or xtrabackup MongoDB mongodump or filesystem snapshots with db.fsyncLock()

Pool CSI snapshots can supplement application-level backups for non-critical data (configs, logs).

docs.title: KubeVirt VMs
docs.text:
A snapshot of a running VM's disk is safe. The driver sees that a running VM uses the claim and copies the disk with QEMU at one moment, with the guest file systems frozen for a fraction of a second. The Snapshot says FileSystemConsistent when that worked. The copy adapts its speed so the VM keeps its speed: it starts at 15 MB/s, speeds up while the share the VM reads is quiet, and slows down when the share is busy. Set vmCopySpeedLimitMBps on the VolumeSnapshotClass to set the highest speed, or vmCopyAdaptive: "false" to copy at that fixed speed instead (default 20 MB/s). Without the node agents' metrics the copy runs at the fixed speed. A VM with several pool disks gets one moment for all of them: when the first disk's snapshot starts, the driver copies every pool disk of the VM at once, and the snapshots of the other disks (KubeVirt asks for them together) join that copy. Their status.copyMoment and status.copyID are the same. A KubeVirt VirtualMachineSnapshot is done after a few seconds, but each disk's VolumeSnapshot is ready only when its copy ends; wait for all of them before you restore.

kubectl get snapshots.storage.ibmcloud.io <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.consistency}{" "}{.status.copyMoment}{"\n"}'

To match the disks of a VM today, or if you cannot use the QEMU copy: 1. Stop the VM with virtctl stop <vm-name> 2. Create a volume snapshot of each disk PVC 3. Restart the VM with virtctl start <vm-name>

For ongoing VM protection, use a BackupPolicy or replication. Both copy a running VM at one moment for all its disks. You can also use application-level backup tools such as Velero with the KubeVirt plugin, or Trilio.

docs.title: Strategy Recommendations by Workload Type
docs.text: Workload Primary Protection Secondary Protection Notes Stateless apps None needed — Redeploy from source Config data Scheduled snapshots (daily) Cross-region replication Low RPO tolerance Application data Scheduled snapshots (6h) + clone before changes Cross-region replication Label-select critical PVCs Databases Application-level backup (pg_dump, etc.) Pool snapshots as secondary Never rely solely on NFS snapshots KubeVirt VMs Snapshot of the running VM (all pool disks are copied at one moment), or a BackupPolicy Application-level backup See KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md ML training data Scheduled snapshots (model + checkpoints) Cross-region for final models Intermediate checkpoints are expendable CI/CD artifacts None or short-lived snapshots — Easily reproducible

docs.title: Single PVC Recovery
docs.text:
# 1. Find available snapshots
kubectl get volumesnapshots -n <namespace> -l app=<app-name>

# 2. Restore from snapshot
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: <pvc-name>-restored
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  storageClassName: ibm-vpc-file-pool
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: <original-size>
  dataSource:
    name: <snapshot-name>
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
EOF

# 3. Update application to use the restored PVC
# 4. Verify data integrity
# 5. Delete the old PVC if the restored one is confirmed good

docs.title: Full Pool Recovery
docs.text:
If an entire pool is lost (all shares destroyed):

# 1. Recreate the FileSharePool CR
kubectl apply -f pool-backup.yaml

# 2. Wait for shares to be provisioned
kubectl get filesharepools -w

# 3. Restore SubVolumes from the CRD backup
#    (This restores tracking metadata only — data must come from DR or backups)

# 4. If cross-region replication was configured:
#    - Switch to DR cluster (see "Failover Procedure" above)
#    OR
#    - Reverse-replicate from DR back to the recovered pool

docs.title: Cross-Region Failover Recovery
docs.text: See the DR Failover Procedure section above.

docs.title: Capacity Planning Guide — IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver
docs.text: Decision framework for sizing pools, selecting profiles, and planning growth. This guide wraps the raw performance data in PERFORMANCE-TUNING.md into actionable sizing guidance.

docs.title: Decision Flowchart
docs.text: Use this to determine your pool configuration:

docs.title: How Many Pools?
docs.text:
Create separate pools for each distinct combination of:

Dimension When to Separate Example Trust boundary Different teams that should not share NFS storage team-a-pool, team-b-pool Performance tier Workloads needing different IOPS levels standard-pool (dp2), high-iops-pool (dp2 with a higher spec.iops) Zone Zone-local data residency requirements us-south-1-pool, us-south-2-pool Lifecycle Different retention or backup policies persistent-pool, ephemeral-pool Workload class VMs need different UID/GID than app workloads app-pool (UID 1000), vm-pool (UID 107)

Rule of thumb: Start with fewer pools and split only when you have a concrete reason. Each pool consumes VPC share quota.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
Minimum share size = (target PVCs per share) × (average PVC size) / (target utilization)

Example:
  Target: 100 PVCs per share
  Average PVC size: 10 GB
  Target utilization: 80%
  Minimum share size = 100 × 10 / 0.8 = 1250 GB → round up to 2000 GB

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
Share Size Pros Cons 500 GB - 1 TB Lower blast radius, faster creation, finer control Uses more VPC quota, more management overhead 2 TB (recommended start) Good balance of quota efficiency and blast radius — 4+ TB Fewer shares, more room for growth Higher blast radius, longer creation time

See PERFORMANCE-TUNING.md — Share Sizing Strategy for workload-specific sizing tables.

docs.title: dp2 (the only profile)
docs.text:
dp2 is the only profile VPC file shares offer. It accepts 100 to 96,000 IOPS and 10 to 32,000 GB per share. If you do not set spec.iops, the VPC gives each share 100 IOPS, whatever its size. IOPS does not grow with share size, so set spec.iops for any workload that needs more.

The VPC limits the maximum IOPS by share size and refuses values out of range. For example, 10,000 IOPS needs a share of at least 500 GB, and a 300 GB share allowed about 6,000. For the exact limits, see IBM's About file storage for VPC.

docs.title: Setting IOPS
docs.text:
Set spec.iops when you need more than 100 IOPS per share. Higher IOPS costs more.

spec:
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 2000
  iops: 24000        # IOPS per share (costs more)

docs.title: When to Set Higher IOPS
docs.text:
Scenario Recommendation PVCs mostly idle (configs, static assets) Leave spec.iops unset — don't pay for unused IOPS Mixed workloads Set spec.iops for the busiest expected load; there is no burst IOPS Database PVCs with sustained random I/O Set a high spec.iops ML training with sequential large reads Leave spec.iops unset — throughput is more relevant than IOPS

See PERFORMANCE-TUNING.md — IOPS Planning for the full IOPS table and calculation examples.

docs.title: How Many VMs One Share Carries (Measured)
docs.text:
These numbers come from the PoolBench performance test on the DR lab cluster. The test adds VMs to one 3,900 GB share in steps of 15, up to 90. One VM in three runs Windows Server 2022, the others CentOS Stream 9. Each VM does 30 IOPS all the time and a burst of 300 IOPS for 45 seconds every 10 minutes (70% reads, blocks of 4, 16 and 64 KiB).

The knee is the first VM count where users would notice: more than a quarter of the VMs have a p95 latency over 20 ms, a burst is slow, an I/O stalls, or the share is at its IOPS limit. Recommended is the largest step at or below 80% of the knee, so there is room to spare.

Share IOPS Knee Recommended What happened 3,000 45 VMs 30 VMs At 45 VMs, 91% of the VMs were slow (p95 29.8 ms). At 30 VMs none were slow (p95 1.2 ms). 10,000 None up to 90 VMs 90 VMs or more No slow VMs at any step. At 90 VMs the VMs asked for 7,603 of the 10,000 IOPS IBM counts.
  • The VMs ask for more than their own IOPS suggest: IBM counts one operation for every 16 KiB of an I/O, so a share reaches its limit before the VMs' own IOPS do. PoolBench shows both numbers.
  • Making and filling new VMs is itself heavy. On a 3,000 IOPS share, 15 new VMs slowed the running VMs for about 20 minutes. Add VMs to a busy share in small groups.
  • The 20,000 IOPS tier was not measured: 90 VMs is already more than the cluster's memory allows with one node down.
  • The 3,000 IOPS result is the same from the command-line test and from the console.

To measure your own share size, speed and VM mix, use the PoolBench page in the console (see FEATURES.md).

docs.title: Binpack vs Spread
docs.text:
Factor Spread Binpack Blast radius Low — PVCs distributed evenly High — one share holds most PVCs VPC quota usage Higher — all shares active Lower — fewer shares in use IOPS distribution Even across shares Concentrated on active share Best for Production, databases, long-lived PVCs CI/CD, ephemeral, high-churn PVCs Auto-expansion Triggers when all shares fill together Triggers when active share is full

Decision rule: Use spread unless you're hitting the 300-share quota limit or running ephemeral CI/CD workloads.

docs.title: VPC Quota Budget
docs.text:
VPC accounts have a 300 file share limit shared across all consumers. Plan your budget:

VPC Share Budget Planner
========================
Account share limit:                    300
  - Stock IBM CSI driver shares:       - ___  (check: ibmcloud is shares | grep ibm-vpc-file)
  - Manually created shares:           - ___
  - Other teams/projects:              - ___
  - Safety buffer (10%):               - 30
  = Available for pool CSI:              ___

Pool allocations:
  Pool: ____________  maxShares: ___
  Pool: ____________  maxShares: ___
  Pool: ____________  maxShares: ___
  Total pool CSI shares:          ___

Check current usage: 

ibmcloud is shares --output json | jq length

If approaching the limit, consider: 1. Consolidate pools (fewer, larger pools) 2. Switch to binpack strategy (fewer active shares) 3. Increase share size to host more PVCs per share 4. Request a quota increase via IBM Cloud support ticket

docs.title: expandThresholdPercent
docs.text:
Controls when new shares are created:

Threshold Risk Profile Cost Impact Recommended For 60-70% Conservative — large buffer for burst Higher — shares sit partially empty Unpredictable burst workloads (CI/CD, batch) 80% (default) Balanced Moderate Most production workloads 90-95% Aggressive — minimal waste Lower — but PVCs may fail during expansion Stable, predictable workloads

docs.title: initialShares Formula
docs.text:
Pre-create enough shares to absorb your initial PVC burst without triggering expansion:

initialShares = ceil(initial_burst_pvc_count × avg_pvc_size_gb / (share_size_gb × threshold / 100))

Example:
  Initial burst: 200 PVCs at 10 GB each = 2000 GB
  Share size: 2000 GB, threshold: 80%
  Usable per share: 2000 × 0.80 = 1600 GB
  initialShares = ceil(2000 / 1600) = 2

  Use initialShares: 3 for safety margin

docs.title: Growth Projection
docs.text:
Use Prometheus metrics to project when you'll need more capacity:

# Current utilization
vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb / vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb * 100

# Allocation rate (GB per day)
deriv(vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb[7d]) * 86400

# Projected days to 90% utilization
(vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb * 0.9 - vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb)
/ (deriv(vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb[7d]) * 86400 + 0.001)

# PVC creation rate (per day)
increase(vpc_file_pool_allocations_total{status="success"}[7d]) / 7

Set alerts for proactive capacity management — see MONITORING.md for alerting rules.

docs.title: Pool CSI vs Stock Driver Savings
docs.text:
The pool CSI driver reduces costs by consolidating PVCs onto shared shares:

Stock driver cost (1:1 mapping):
  PVCs: 200
  Average PVC size: 5 GB
  Minimum share size: 10 GB (VPC minimum)
  Shares needed: 200
  Total billed capacity: 200 × 10 GB = 2,000 GB
  VPC shares used: 200

Pool driver cost:
  PVCs: 200
  Average PVC size: 5 GB
  Total data: 200 × 5 GB = 1,000 GB
  Share size: 2,000 GB
  Shares needed: 1 (1,000 GB fits in a single 2 TB share at 50% util)
  Total billed capacity: 2,000 GB
  VPC shares used: 1

Savings:
  Capacity billed: Same (2,000 GB) — but pool uses 1 share vs 200
  Share quota freed: 199 shares
  Provisioning speed: <1s vs 30-90s per PVC

The savings increase as PVC sizes decrease below the 10 GB VPC minimum.

docs.title: Cost Variables
docs.text: Factor Impact Share IOPS profile Higher IOPS = higher cost per GB Snapshot storage Snapshots consume share capacity (billed). A snapshot is kept on its volume's share and is charged the volume's size (a copy) or a tenth of it (an instant VM snapshot). A share without that much free space refuses the snapshot (ResourceExhausted). Snapshots do not count as PVCs. Replication storage DR destination pool is billed separately

docs.title: Small Cluster (10 nodes, <100 PVCs)
docs.text:
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: general
spec:
  zone: us-south-1
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 1000
  maxShares: 3
  initialShares: 1
  autoExpand: true
  expandThresholdPercent: 80
  allocationStrategy: spread
  defaultUID: 1000
  defaultGID: 1000
  defaultPermissions: "0755"

Budget: 3 VPC shares max. Capacity: up to 3 TB for ~300 PVCs at 10 GB average.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog.

docs.title: How versions work
docs.text:
A version is a git tag vX.Y.Z. The driver reports git describe: v0.13.2-59-g2f04e1e means 59 commits after v0.13.2.

To make a release:

  1. Move the items under Unreleased to a new heading ## [vX.Y.Z] — date.
  2. Add the section and the compatibility row to UPGRADE-GUIDE.md.
  3. Set version and appVersion in charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/Chart.yaml to X.Y.Z.
  4. Tag the merge commit vX.Y.Z and push the tag.

v0.11.0, v0.13.0 and v0.13.1 were tagged on 21 October 2026, at the commit that added their changelog entry. v0.13.2 sits at e2b780f, the last commit of 25 February 2026: the commit that first added its entry (a2c2a07) lacked the TLS work the entry names. v0.10.0 and v0.12.0 were written in the same commits as v0.11.0 and v0.13.0, so they have no tag of their own. The chart said 0.1.0 until v0.14.0.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• VM disks in backups, part 4: gateway, kubectl backup --fs and the console picker (issue #92, phase 5). The gateway makes a guest session or a guest restore for every volume the policy status shows as a VM disk, and refuses a VM disk in COS in words. Session and Restore replies have guest. kubectl backup ls with no --fs lists the file systems of the disk (with the reason beside one that cannot be read); ls, get and restore-files take --fs (a name like sda1 or a device like /dev/rhel/root) and put it before the path; notices of the session go to standard error; a VM disk session gets 20 minutes to start. The console file browser asks for a file system at the top, marks a volume that cannot be read with its reason, shows crash-copy and journal warnings, hides the tar of the whole disk and explains the hold; the restore dialog explains that the file system name stays in the restored tree. A VM that was stopped when it was backed up (copied as plain files) is read from its moments folders, like any volume. New release test part 7 (test/e2e/test-backup-files-vm.sh, stage 20), not run yet.
  • VM disks in backups, part 3: restore of files from inside a VM disk (issue #92, phase 5). BackupFileRestore has spec.guest. The restore Job runs in the guest image with the new browse --mode=restore-files (the same restore code as the driver's, now in filerestore.Main), reads the file systems inside disk.img through the read-only appliance and writes to a new claim or a new folder of an existing claim; the first name of each path is the guest file system and is kept in the restored tree. The controller holds the disk (the same per-UID hold as a browse session) before the first Job, waits for a copy that is running, and releases the hold when the restore ends. The restore records when it first held the disk (status.guestHoldStarted) and fails after 2 hours 45 minutes, so a hold that was let go cannot be taken again; each Job runs for what is left of that time (2 hours at most). The pod has two containers: the reader parses the disk and has no write access to the target and no capability; the writer (browse --mode=restore-writer) holds only the target (the claim's folder, or the share for a new claim) and CHOWN and FOWNER, never sees the disk, and checks everything the reader sends. The counts and the restored folder in the status come from the writer's own termination message (read by container name), never from the reader's, which parses the untrusted disk; the reader gives only the moment and what was left out or unreadable, and a writer with no outcome fails the restore (#347). The webhook and the controller refuse a guest restore from COS, and the controller refuses a volume that is not a VM disk or an installation without the guest image, in words. Slow for many small files (an appliance start for each). The gateway, kubectl backup and the console come in the next change.
  • VM disks in backups, part 2: the guest helper and the file system reader (issue #92, phase 5). New package pkg/guestfs shows the file systems inside a backed-up VM disk as a read-only browse.Tree: the top level folders are the guest's file systems (from virt-filesystems), and below each one virt-ls and virt-cat list and read the files. Volumes that cannot be read (LUKS, BitLocker, ReFS, ZFS, RAID members, swap, unknown types) are listed with the reason in words. Parsers are strict and fuzzed; a device name from the disk is accepted only if it is plain (a colon would add mount options), names go to the tools as separate arguments after --, never to a shell or a script. A crash copy that does not mount is read again without its journal (norecovery, noload), with a notice. browse --guest serves it (the browse API now has entry.note and info.guest, info.consistency, info.notices); Dockerfile.browse-guest builds the image from CentOS Stream 9, pinned by digest, with libguestfs, libguestfs-winsupport and guestfs-tools. The controller starts the pod (new flags --browse-guest-image, --browse-guest-kvm, --browse-guest-cpu-limit, --browse-guest-memory-limit, --browse-guest-start-timeout; Helm values backupBrowse.guest.*, off by default until the image is built and pushed). The pod has the same rights as the plain helper plus two size-limited scratch folders and, if asked, the KVM device. Nothing creates a session on a VM disk yet: the gateway, kubectl backup and the console come in the next change. The image has not been built or run (the lab does that).
  • VM disks in backups, part 1: the disk view, the disk server and the hold (issue #92, phase 5). replication.OpenDiskView shows a backed-up VM disk as it was at any restore point, read-only, rebuilt on the fly from disk.img and the undo files (no copy, no scratch space); a property test checks every moment byte for byte against RestoreDisk over random histories, including growing and shrinking disks. The new package pkg/nbd serves a view to a client as a read-only network block device on a private socket, with the request and option parsers fuzzed. BackupBrowse has spec.guest: a session on a VM disk holds the disk's next backup copy (the SubVolume annotation storage.ibmcloud.io/browse-hold, one entry per session), waits for a copy that is already running, and the replication controller makes no new copy of a held volume (held: waiting for a browse session; all disks of a running VM are held together). A hold ends with its helper and is ignored after 3 hours. Nothing creates a guest session yet: the guest helper image and the commands come in the next changes. See BACKUP-RECOVERY.md.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Listing a folder inside a VM disk works. The first lab run showed that virt-ls 1.52 refuses -l --csv ('used a flag which can only be combined with -lR mode'). The reader now runs virt-ls -lR --csv and keeps the names directly in the folder. Regular files, which virt-ls marks with -, were shown as 'other'. A folder with a very deep tree is slow to list, because -R reads the whole tree.
  • Holds on a SubVolume can no longer be wiped by another writer, and a copy that runs is waited for. Removing the last annotation with a patch made from a copy said annotations: null and wiped the other holds, so releasing an export hold or sweeping a browse hold could drop a hold that another writer had added a moment before. Hold writes now name only their own key, and the browse hold list is written only if the SubVolume is as it was read. A volume with a copy Job is not held until the Job has ended and been cleaned up: before, its status said "held" at once, the Job was never looked at again, and a browse session could start while the copy still wrote.

docs.title: [v0.16.3] — 2026-10-30
docs.text: A fix release: a new pool can no longer end with a share that has no mount target (found by beta run 2). Built from v0.16.2 plus this fix only; the Unreleased items below are not in it.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • A new pool no longer ends with a share that has no mount target (issue #366). The pool status is now saved again after a resourceVersion conflict (also when provisioning stops half way), so shares already created in VPC are recorded and the next pass does not create them again. A recorded share with no mount target now switches to the share of the same name that holds the mount target and its network interface, and the bare duplicate is deleted when no volume lives on it. Adopting a share by name prefers the one that has a mount target. Cause: when a share create call failed while building its inline mount target ("Provided Name ... -mt-vni is not unique", HTTP 500), VPC could keep a bare share of that name next to the complete one, and the next pass adopted the bare one.

docs.title: [v0.16.2] — 2026-10-29
docs.text: A fix release: a wrong COS key is named as the cause when browsing or restoring from COS.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • A wrong COS key is now named as the cause when browsing or restoring from COS. COS often answers a wrong key with only a message ("The AWS Access Key ID you provided does not exist in our records", or a signature mismatch) and no error code, so the user was told only that COS could not be read. Found in release test stage 20.

docs.title: [v0.16.1] — 2026-10-29
docs.text: A fix release. Audit Events for backup browsing and file restore are now recorded, the gateway address is filled in on a first install, and the console shows a policy's last error as an error.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Audit Events for backup browsing and file restore were refused by the API server. The gateway and the controller wrote them on the BackupBrowse or BackupFileRestore, which have no namespace, and the API server accepts an Event for such an object only in default, where many people can read. The gateway logged the Event and then failed to store it. The Events are now on the ConfigMap backup-gateway-info in the driver namespace and name the session or restore in related. Found in the first lab run of release test stage 20.
  • The policy's last error is shown as an error in the console (issue #46). On the replication policy page, the Last Error line is now a red inline alert with an icon instead of plain text, and shows - when there is no error.
  • The gateway address is filled in on a first install. The ConfigMap backup-gateway-info had an empty address after the first install on OpenShift, because the Route did not exist yet, so kubectl backup needed --gateway until a second helm upgrade. The chart now uses the host the router will give the Route.

docs.title: [v0.16.0] — 2026-10-28
docs.text: A feature release. Failover from the console: a new Failover resource plans and runs a failover on the destination cluster, for all VMs or for chosen VMs, and the console has a Recovery page for it. Files from a backup: browse, download and restore single files and folders from the backups of plain volumes, in the snapshot pool or in COS, from the command line and the console, through a new backup gateway. Two new CRDs (Failover, BackupFileRestore), new chart objects (the gateway, a browse namespace) and a new role. VM disks inside backups are not covered yet.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Release test stage 21: failover of chosen VMs, and a browser test of the Recovery page (issues #44 step 4 and #46). New stage test/release/stages/21-failover.sh (needs a second cluster: RT_DR_CLUSTER=NAME bash test/release/remote.sh start CLUSTER TAG). It replicates two running VMs and a plain volume to a receiver on the DR cluster and checks that a Plan with vms shows only the chosen VM; an Execute with a different list is refused and makes nothing; an Execute for one VM with rewindTo makes only that VM's PVCs, PVs and SubVolumes and rewinds only its two disks; the VM boots on DR from the chosen moment (no XFS errors, every logged file with its checksum, no file after the moment); a second Execute is refused as already failed over; and the second VM fails over in the Recovery page. The new Playwright test console-plugin/integration-tests/tests/recovery.spec.ts covers the VM table, the detail view, the typed VM name, the cancelled dialog and the progress to Done. The browser tests for drain, migration and clone (#46 items 5, 6 and 7) already exist (drain.spec.ts, migrate.spec.ts, clone.spec.ts, run by stage 16). Not run on a cluster yet. See TESTING.md.
  • Browse and restore files from a backup in COS, plain volumes (issue #92, phase 4). BackupBrowse and BackupFileRestore have spec.source (local or cos) and spec.fromCOS (a bucket named directly, for a cluster administrator). kubectl backup ls, get, browse and restore-files take --from-cos, with --bucket, --endpoint and --volume (and the key flags of restore --from-cos) to name a bucket. The gateway reads COS by itself when a moment is older than the oldest local restore point, or no local copy is left and an export exists, and source: cos asks for it; the gateway's volume list shows exported and exportedTime. The browse helper (cmd/browse, new flag --cos-source) and the file restore Job read the Kopia repository through the pinned Kopia program as a child process (now also in the browse image), read-only: folders are read as JSON and walked by object IDs, so a user's path is never an argument and a link leads nowhere; snapshots are chosen by tag and by the exact source path of the volume, so no other volume or policy in the bucket area is read. The backup key is unwrapped in the helper's memory; the Kopia child gets an explicit environment. The COS helper runs in the driver namespace, next to the COS and Key Protect Secrets, with no service account token and as an ordinary user, and the controller keeps a copy of the session Secret there; the keys are never copied to the browse namespace where the gateway may read Secrets. Naming a bucket directly needs the right to read each Secret it names in the driver namespace (checked by name, on every call). A wrong root key, a missing Secret, a wrong COS key and a missing repository are said in words in the session status; a session whose helper is not ready after five minutes ends with a message that names the Secrets to check. New Helm values backupBrowse.cos.*, a Role (create and delete Secrets) and a NetworkPolicy in the driver namespace. Stage 20 part 6 of the release test checks it on the lab (not run yet; it needs a COS bucket). Not yet: VM disks in COS (phases 5 and 6), and a source switch in the console file browser. See BACKUP-RECOVERY.md.
  • Restore chosen files from the console (issue #92, phase 3 second half). The file browser has a checkbox on each file, folder and link, a line with the number chosen and the total size of the files, Restore selected and Clear. The restore dialog restores into a new claim (default; optional size and storage class) or a new folder in an existing claim (turned off, with the missing rights named, for a user without them, using access reviews on the target namespace), shows what will be written, the moment, and a warning that nothing is overwritten, then follows the restore by polling every 2 seconds through its phases and shows links to the claim and folder, the counts and the size. A refusal is explained in plain words (403 names the missing right, 404, 409 suggests another name, 429 too many open restores). A file inside a chosen folder is not sent twice. Console only; no change to the gateway, the chart or the CRDs. Help link and guide section: BACKUP-RECOVERY.md.
  • Restore files from a backup into a claim, part 5: gateway and kubectl backup restore-files (issue #92, phase 2). Users can now ask for a file restore. kubectl backup restore-files --policy P --pvc NS/NAME --path A --path B --to NS/CLAIM [--existing | --new-claim --size-gb N] [--moment T] [--wait] (also --paths-file and --status NAME) calls the new gateway endpoints POST /v1/restores and GET /v1/restores/{name}. The gateway checks the user's own token and, as the user, get backupfiles in the namespace of the backed-up claim, create on persistentvolumeclaims in the target namespace and, for an existing claim, update on claims and create on pods (writing into a claim is the same power as mounting it). The access check is now a general "may this user do this in this namespace" (Authorizer.Can). The gateway reads the existing claim only after the rights are known and pins its UID in the restore, so a claim that is deleted and made again is refused. A restore is shown only to the user who asked for it. A user may have 10 restores that have not ended (backupGateway.maxOpenRestores). Each request writes an audit Event FileRestoreRequested with the user, the volume, the moment, the target and the paths. The gateway's cluster role gets get, list, create, delete on backupfilerestores and get on persistentvolumeclaims. Stage 20 part 5 of the release test checks the user path on the lab with real users.
  • Restore files from a backup into a claim, part 4: BackupFileRestore (issue #92, phase 2, resource and Job). A new cluster-scoped resource copies the files and folders you list out of one backup into a new claim (sized to the files plus 20%, at least 1 GiB, by a read-only Job that runs first) or into a new folder of an existing claim (restored-<policy>-<moment>). It never writes over a file that exists and never writes into a VM disk. A symbolic link is copied as a link and never followed, on the backup side or in the claim; setuid and setgid are removed; times and modes are kept; the owner is the one the claim is configured with. The Job is the driver program (--mode=restore-files), not a shell: the paths are a file in a ConfigMap that the restore owns. It writes a hidden staging folder in an existing claim and renames it at the end, checks the space first (the least of 200 GiB, the share's free space and the claim's size less what it holds), refuses a claim that holds disk.img, a claim with no data folder yet, a claim being restored, and a claim that was deleted and made again since the request, and removes what it wrote if anything fails (a file whose owner cannot be set fails the restore). One restore at a time writes into one claim. The validating webhook, the controller part, the chart and config/rbac roles, the backupBrowse.restoreMaxBytes and backupBrowse.restoreMaxRunning (at most 5 restores at once; more wait) values and docs are in. Users cannot ask for it yet: only a cluster administrator can make the resource; the gateway call and kubectl backup restore-files come in the next part. The file restore Job reads the backup with the browse helper's handle-based reader (now browse.ChooseRoot, moved out of the helper's main). Also: a share Job that fails now keeps the reason its container wrote.
  • Browse and download files from a backup in the console (issue #92, phase 3 first half). The Browse files action on each volume of a backup policy opens a file browser with folders in pages, breadcrumbs, a moment picker, symbolic links shown as links and never followed, names shown as escaped text, "not readable" entries, session states (starting, ready, ended) with polling and no long request, and a session close when you leave. A file downloads as a file and a folder as a tar, through the console plugin proxy with the person's own token. The gateway has a new GET /v1/sessions/{name}/download route (same session, rights, size limit and audit Event as the POST calls) and now sets Content-Disposition: attachment, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Content-Security-Policy: sandbox; default-src 'none', Cache-Control: no-store and a fixed content type on every file and tar reply, because the console serves the reply from its own origin. The chart adds a backup-gateway entry to the ConsolePlugin proxy (only when the gateway runs; the PoolBench entry is kept) and a fileBrowse key to the settings ConfigMap that tells the console whether to show the action. The file restore dialog is not part of this change. See BACKUP-RECOVERY.md.

  • Chart tests for the gateway and the browse namespace now run in make test-scripts. test/chart/test-gateway.sh and test-browse.sh were not listed there. test-browse.sh had a failing check (off: no Role) that matched the settings Role; it now checks that nothing is made in the browse namespace.

  • A failover can be limited to one VM or a chosen set (#328). Failover has a new optional list spec.vms (namespace/name). Empty is today's behaviour: every VM on the copy and every volume that is not a VM disk. With a list, only the chosen VMs are read, planned and failed over, all disks of a VM together; plain volumes are left out. A name that is not a running VM on the copy fails the Plan and says which VMs the copy holds. An Execute needs a finished Plan with the same source, rewindTo and vms (compared as sets). The Job (new flag --vms), the "already failed over" checks, the status and the created SubVolumes, PVs and PVCs cover only the chosen VMs, and a copy still being applied to another VM no longer blocks them. kubectl failover plan and execute take --vms ns/name,.... In the console Recovery page, "Fail over this VM" in the VM detail plans and fails over that VM only, and the confirm dialog asks for the VM name again; an explicit "Fail over all VMs" button keeps the old behaviour. Experimental.

  • The console has a Recovery page to fail over a VM from the copy (#44, step 3). Under Replication, a new Recovery page (link on the Replication tab) makes a Failover with action: Plan and shows the running VMs found on the copy: disks, disks to rewind, the moment each will show and how many moments can be chosen. Refresh makes a new plan. The copy to read is filled in when the cluster has one replication receiver, and chosen by the operator when it has several. A VM opens to its disks (a disk that must be rewound says it copies the whole disk and takes minutes) and its moments, newest first. Fail over opens a dialog that lists the VMs, the moment, the disks to rewind and the PVCs that will be made, asks for the DR pool, and needs a typed confirmation. It then makes an Execute with the source and rewindTo of the confirmed plan; a moment other than the one on screen first makes a new plan with that rewindTo. A failover covers everything on the copy, so with more than one VM the dialog says so and the operator types the source name. While a copy is applied to a disk the Job refuses; the page shows the refusal and offers force only behind a second warning. The page shows the phase, a still-working state with the time it has run, the created PVCs with links, and the message of a failed Failover. A warning shows when the newest copy is older than twice the schedule of the policy that wrote it (when that policy is on this cluster).
