docs.title: Golden Image Workflow for KubeVirt VMs
docs.text:
Hidden feature. Golden images are hidden. The code is kept for possible later use, and a pool that sets spec.goldenImages in YAML still works. The console pool form no longer offers golden images. The recommended way to make VMs is the standard OpenShift Virtualization catalog: pick a catalog image and choose the pool's StorageClass for the boot disk. See Create a VM with its boot disk on a pool and CDI compatibility.

This document explains how to configure golden OS images for one-click VM creation from the OpenShift Virtualization UI or CLI.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The OpenShift Virtualization catalog offers two ways to create a VM, each backed by a different Kubernetes resource:

DataSource (Image) Template What it is A pointer to a bootable disk image (PVC or VolumeSnapshot) A complete VM blueprint (CPU, memory, disks, network, cloud-init) Catalog tab InstanceTypes — user picks an image + an instance type (CPU/RAM preset) Templates — user clicks and gets a fully configured VM API cdi.kubevirt.io/v1beta1 DataSource template.openshift.io/v1 Template Flexibility High — any image can be paired with any instance type Low — opinionated, ready-to-go Use case Power users who want to choose their own sizing Quick-start VMs with sensible defaults

The golden image syncer creates both so that pool-backed images appear in both catalog tabs.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
CDI (Containerized Data Importer) manages golden OS images for OpenShift Virtualization. On clusters where the default StorageClass is ODF/Ceph, CDI imports and snapshots golden images on Ceph. These Ceph-backed golden images cannot be cloned to NFS pool storage, which causes the "Create VM" UI flow to fail with UnrecognizedDataSourceKind.

The driver supports two modes for golden image availability, selected automatically based on whether the pool StorageClass is the cluster default.

docs.title: Mode 1: Native CDI (Recommended)
docs.text:
When: The pool StorageClass is annotated as the cluster default.

In this mode, CDI handles everything natively: - CDI DataImportCron imports OS images directly onto pool storage - CDI creates VolumeSnapshot via the CSI snapshotter sidecar - VM creation uses CDI clone (CSI CreateVolumeFromSnapshot) - Cross-namespace cloning works via CDI host-assisted cloning

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
# 1. Make the pool StorageClass the default
kubectl annotate sc ibm-vpc-file-pool \
  storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true

# 2. Remove default from old StorageClass (only one default allowed)
kubectl annotate sc ocs-storagecluster-cephfs \
  storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class-

# 3. Delete existing CDI DataVolumes so DataImportCrons re-create them
#    on the new default StorageClass
kubectl delete dv --all -n openshift-virtualization-os-images

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# Wait ~5 minutes per image for CDI to re-import
kubectl get pvc -n openshift-virtualization-os-images
kubectl get volumesnapshots -n openshift-virtualization-os-images

# Check controller logs
kubectl logs deploy/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller -c controller | grep golden

Then test from the UI: Virtualization > Catalog > Select OS > Create VirtualMachine.

docs.title: Mode 2: Custom Syncer
docs.text:
When: Another StorageClass (e.g., ODF/Ceph) is the cluster default.

The controller runs a background syncer that: 1. Discovers OS images from CDI DataImportCron resources 2. Creates a CDI DataVolume for each image on the pool StorageClass. CDI downloads the image and converts it to raw format. 3. Creates a DataSource and an OpenShift Template for VM creation from the UI catalog

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Add goldenImages to your FileSharePool spec:

apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: general-purpose
spec:
  zone: us-south-1
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 1000
  maxShares: 10
  defaultPermissions: "0777"
  defaultUID: 107
  defaultGID: 107
  goldenImages:
    enabled: true
    targetNamespaces:
      - pool-tutorial
      - default
    # Optional: only sync specific images (substring match)
    # imageFilter:
    #   - centos
    #   - fedora
    # Optional: golden PVC size (default: 15 GB)
    # pvcSizeGB: 15

docs.title: What the Syncer Creates
docs.text:
For each discovered image and each target namespace:

Resource Name Purpose DataVolume golden-{imageName} CDI imports the image from the registry onto the pool StorageClass. The source is the DataImportCron's registry URL with pullMethod: node. PVC golden-{imageName} Created by CDI for the DataVolume. Holds the raw disk image. DataSource {imageName}-{namespace}-nfs-pool CDI DataSource pointing to the golden PVC (enables InstanceTypes tab). One per golden claim. Template {imageName}-nfs-pool OpenShift VM template for UI catalog, in the target namespace

For images whose DataImportCron uses an ImageStream (the RHEL images), the syncer uses the external address that the ImageStream imports from. An example is registry.redhat.io/rhel9/rhel-guest-image.

A golden image is ready when the DataVolume phase is Succeeded. If the phase is Failed, the pool status reports Failed and the syncer publishes no catalog entry.

On rovslab (20 October 2026), CentOS Stream 9 imported in about 40 seconds. RHEL 9 took about 2.5 minutes, with one automatic retry while the node pulled the image. VMs booted from both, and the guest agent connected.

Target namespaces need no extra permissions (no anyuid grant).

Two pools must not send golden images to the same namespace. The names collide. The driver does not block this.

When you delete a pool, the driver first deletes its golden DataVolumes, PVCs and Templates in its target namespaces, and its DataSources. The syncer skips pools that are being deleted.

Note: Creating a VM from the console catalog (InstanceTypes tab) with its boot disk on the pool is being tested. It is not yet verified.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# Check golden DataVolumes
kubectl get dv -n pool-tutorial

# Check golden PVCs
kubectl get pvc -n pool-tutorial -l pool.storage.ibmcloud.io/golden-image=true

# Check Templates
oc get templates -n pool-tutorial

# Check pool status
kubectl get fsp general-purpose -o jsonpath='{.status.goldenImages}' | jq .

docs.title: Creating VMs
docs.text:
From the UI: 1. Navigate to Virtualization > Catalog 2. Find the template (e.g., centos-stream9-nfs-pool) 3. Click Create VirtualMachine 4. The boot PVC is cloned from the golden image via CSI clone (the console catalog path with the boot disk on the pool is being tested)

From the CLI: 

oc process centos-stream9-nfs-pool -n pool-tutorial \
  -p NAME=my-vm \
  -p CLOUD_USER_PASSWORD=mypassword \
  | oc apply -n pool-tutorial -f -

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The E2E VM clone test validates the full syncer-driven golden image pipeline:

# Run the test (requires ROKS or ROVS + OpenShift Virtualization + CDI)
make test-vm

# With options
./test/e2e/test-vm-clone.sh --zone eu-de-1 --keep

# Available flags
#   --keep          Don't clean up on success
#   --namespace NS  Override namespace (default: e2e-vm-test)
#   --pool POOL     Override pool name (default: e2e-vm-pool)
#   --zone ZONE     Override zone (default: eu-de-1)
#   --image FILTER  Override image filter (default: centos-stream-9)
#   --timeout SECS  Override total timeout (default: 900)

The test creates a pool with goldenImages.enabled=true and lets the syncer handle image discovery, DataVolume creation, and template creation. It then creates a VM from the syncer-generated template, waits for the CSI clone Job to complete, and verifies the VM boots with connectivity checks.

Runtime: ~13-14 minutes.

The test handles cleanup automatically (before and after), but if you use --keep or the script crashes, see TESTING.md — Manual Cleanup for the 8-step teardown procedure and stuck-namespace recovery.

docs.title: Golden Image Shows Failed (DataVolume)
docs.text:
Symptom: The pool status shows a golden image in phase Failed.

# Check the DataVolume phase
oc get dv -n pool-tutorial

# See the events and the reason
oc describe dv golden-centos-stream9 -n pool-tutorial

CDI retries some failures by itself. A DataVolume that stays Failed needs a retry. To retry, delete the DataVolume. The syncer makes a new one on the next cycle:

oc delete dv golden-centos-stream9 -n pool-tutorial

docs.title: DataVolume "was not made by pool"
docs.text:
Symptom: The pool status shows Failed with a message like DataVolume ns/golden-<image> was not made by pool <pool> ...; delete it to let the pool make it.

Cause: A DataVolume named golden-<image> already exists in the target namespace, and the pool did not make it. It has no pool labels, or its source URL or StorageClass is different. The syncer refuses to use it, and publishes no catalog entry.

Fix: Check the DataVolume. If you do not need it, delete it. The syncer then makes its own on the next cycle.

oc get dv golden-centos-stream9 -n pool-tutorial -o yaml
oc delete dv golden-centos-stream9 -n pool-tutorial

docs.title: PVC Stuck in Pending
docs.text:
# Check if pool has capacity
kubectl get fsp general-purpose

# Check CSI provisioner logs
kubectl logs deploy/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller -c csi-provisioner

docs.title: Template Not Appearing in UI
docs.text:
Templates must have these labels to appear in the Virtualization catalog: - template.kubevirt.io/type: base - os.template.kubevirt.io/{imageName}: true - workload.template.kubevirt.io/server: true

Verify: 

oc get template centos-stream9-nfs-pool -n pool-tutorial -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}'

docs.title: Syncer Not Running
docs.text:
The syncer only runs in custom mode (when no pool SC is default). Check: 

kubectl logs deploy/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller -c controller | grep "golden"

If you see "Native CDI golden image mode active", your pool SC is the default and CDI handles everything.

docs.title: Helm Values Reference
docs.text: Complete reference for all configurable parameters in the ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi Helm chart.

docs.title: General
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description nameOverride string "" Override the chart name used in resource names fullnameOverride string "" Override the full resource name prefix

docs.title: Image
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description image.repository string de.icr.io/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/driver Container image repository for the CSI driver image.tag string "" Image tag. Empty means v plus the chart appVersion (never latest). Pin to a specific version or digest in production image.pullPolicy string IfNotPresent Image pull policy (Always, IfNotPresent, Never) imagePullSecrets list [] List of image pull secret names for private registries

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
VPC infrastructure configuration. On managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters, all four values are auto-discovered. Only set these for self-managed clusters or to override auto-discovery.

Parameter Type Default Description config.region string "" IBM Cloud region (e.g., us-south). Auto-discovered from secret provider endpoint config.vpcID string "" VPC ID. Auto-discovered from ibm-cloud-provider-data ConfigMap config.subnetID string "" Worker subnet IDs for mount targets, comma-separated. Each share's mount target goes in the subnet in the pool's zone. Auto-discovered from ibm-cloud-provider-data ConfigMap config.resourceGroupID string "" Resource group ID for VPC file share creation

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
Settings for the CSI controller Deployment (runs the Pool Manager and CSI controller server).

Parameter Type Default Description controller.replicas int 1 Number of controller replicas. Only 1 is active (leader election) controller.healthPort int 8081 Port for /healthz and /readyz endpoints controller.podSecurityContext object {seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}} Pod security context of the controller. Off OpenShift the chart adds fsGroup: 65532 unless you set one, so the non-root user can read the webhook key controller.securityContext object no escalation, runAsNonRoot, drop ALL Container security context of csi-controller. The image runs as user 65532 controller.sidecarSecurityContext object no escalation, drop ALL Container security context of the controller sidecars (provisioner, resizer, snapshotter, liveness probe, secret provider). Their user is not changed controller.resources.requests.cpu string 50m Controller CPU request controller.resources.requests.memory string 128Mi Controller memory request controller.resources.limits.memory string 512Mi Controller memory limit controller.tolerations list [] Tolerations for controller pod scheduling controller.nodeSelector object {} Node selector for controller pod placement controller.affinity object {} Affinity rules for controller pod scheduling

docs.title: Node
docs.text:
Settings for the CSI node agent DaemonSet (runs on every worker node).

Parameter Type Default Description node.kubeletDir string /var/data/kubelet Kubelet root directory. ROKS/ROVS/IKS uses /var/data/kubelet (the real path). Standard Kubernetes uses /var/lib/kubelet node.metricsPort int 9810 Port of the node agent's HTTPS metrics endpoint (per-share used bytes, NFS latency and IOPS). Its certificate follows webhook.certProvider (manual needs the secret <release>-ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-node-metrics-certs). The node agent uses the host network, so the port must be free on the node. 0 turns the endpoint, its Service and its ServiceMonitor off node.shareStatsInterval string 30s How often the node agent reads the NFS statistics of its shares node.registrarHealthPort int 9809 Port for the node-driver-registrar health endpoint. Must not conflict with other hostNetwork services. Stock IBM VPC file CSI uses 9808 node.securityContext object {privileged: true, runAsUser: 0} Container security context of csi-node. It must stay privileged and root to mount NFS on the host node.resources.requests.cpu string 50m Node agent CPU request node.resources.requests.memory string 64Mi Node agent memory request node.resources.limits.memory string 256Mi Node agent memory limit node.tolerations list [{operator: Exists}] Tolerations for node agent pods. Default tolerates all taints so the agent runs on every node node.nodeSelector object {} Node selector for node agent pod placement node.affinity object {} Affinity rules for node agent pod scheduling

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description logLevel int 4 klog verbosity level. 2 = normal ops, 4 = detailed, 6 = trace

docs.title: Secret Provider
docs.text:
Controls how the IBM Cloud API key is injected into the controller.

Parameter Type Default Description secretProvider.managed bool true Use the storage-secret-sidecar for automatic API key injection (managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS). Set to false for self-managed clusters secretProvider.sidecar.image string icr.io/obs/armada-storage-secret:v1.2.75 Container image for the storage-secret-sidecar

docs.title: Clone Worker
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description cloneWorker.interval string 10s Background clone worker poll interval (Go duration)

docs.title: Golden Image Syncer
docs.text:
Hidden feature. The code is kept for possible later use. The recommended way to make VMs is the standard OpenShift Virtualization catalog.

Parameter Type Default Description cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit string 8Gi The controller keeps the memory limit of CDI's copy pods at least this high, through the OpenShift Virtualization HyperConverged setting spec.resourceRequirements.storageWorkloads. CDI's default of 600M is too small for copies onto NFS: the pod is killed. On rovslab, a 25 GB copy failed with 2Gi and finished with 8Gi. Empty turns the check off goldenImageSyncer.interval string 5m Background golden image syncer poll interval (Go duration). Controls how often the syncer checks for new CDI DataImportCrons and updates golden images

docs.title: Backup Browse
docs.text:
Browse a backup and restore single files (issue #92). Added in phase 1 of docs/specs/2026-10-22-backup-file-restore.md.

Parameter Type Default Description backupBrowse.enabled bool true Turns browse sessions on. When off, the controller gets no --browse-image and the chart renders no browse Role or NetworkPolicy backupBrowse.namespace string ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-browse The namespace of browse sessions: their helper pods and one Secret for each. The chart makes it. It holds nothing else, so the gateway's right to read Secrets there reaches nothing else. It is labelled for the Pod Security level baseline, because the helper runs as root with every capability dropped (it reads backups made by other users); restricted would refuse it. On OpenShift the chart adds one SecurityContextConstraints that allows exactly that for the namespace's default account backupBrowse.image.repository string de.icr.io/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/browse The browse helper image (Dockerfile.browse) backupBrowse.image.tag string "" Empty means the tag of the driver image backupBrowse.idle string 15m A session ends after this long without use backupBrowse.maxLife string 2h A session ends after this long, even if in use backupBrowse.maxSessions int 5 Open sessions in the cluster. More wait backupBrowse.maxSessionsPerNamespace int 2 Open sessions for the claims of one namespace. More wait backupBrowse.restoreMaxBytes int 214748364800 The most one file restore (BackupFileRestore) writes, 200 GiB. A restore of more is refused before it copies. It is a controller setting and works even when backupBrowse.enabled is false backupBrowse.restoreMaxRunning int 5 File restores that run at once in the cluster. More wait, oldest first. Each running restore holds a Job and two share mounts. Works even when backupBrowse.enabled is false backupBrowse.cos.enabled bool true Browse and restore files from backups that a policy exported to COS (spec.export). The helper pods that read COS run in the release namespace, next to the COS and Key Protect Secrets (a pod mounts only Secrets of its own namespace), so those keys are never copied to the browse namespace where the gateway may read Secrets. The chart adds a Role there (the controller may create and delete Secrets, for the copy of each session's token and certificate) and a NetworkPolicy that lets only the gateway reach those pods. Off: no such pods, no Role, no NetworkPolicy, and a session or restore from COS fails with "not turned on" backupBrowse.cos.cpuLimit string "" CPU limit of the helper pod that reads COS. Empty means 1 backupBrowse.cos.memoryLimit string "" Memory limit of the helper pod that reads COS. Empty means 1Gi (Kopia and its cache need more than a helper that reads a folder) backupBrowse.cos.startTimeout string 5m A session on COS ends if its helper is not ready after this long, usually because a Secret named by the export block is missing or lacks a key; the message names the Secrets to check backupBrowse.guest.enabled bool false Browse the files inside a VM disk without starting the VM (issue #92, phase 5). Needs the guest image (Dockerfile.browse-guest, CentOS Stream 9 with libguestfs), so it is off until you have built and pushed it. While a session is open, the next backup copy of that one disk waits (held: waiting for a browse session), for at most the hard limit of a session. Keep backupBrowse.maxLife at 2h30m or less: a hold older than 3 hours is ignored backupBrowse.guest.image.repository string de.icr.io/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/browse-guest The VM disk helper image backupBrowse.guest.image.tag string "" Empty means the tag of the driver image backupBrowse.guest.kvmDevice bool false Ask the helper pod for the KVM device (devices.kubevirt.io/kvm). With it the appliance starts in about 1.5 seconds, without it in about 12 (and every folder opened or file read starts one). A pod that asks waits until a node has the device, so turn it on only where nodes have it backupBrowse.guest.cpuLimit string "" CPU limit of the helper pod. Empty means 1 backupBrowse.guest.memoryLimit string "" Memory limit. Empty means 1Gi (the appliance peaked at about 550 MiB in the lab) backupBrowse.guest.startTimeout string 20m A session on a VM disk ends if its helper is not ready after this long. It covers waiting for a backup copy that is being written (5 minutes at most) and the start of the appliance (10 minutes at most)

The chart also makes, in the browse namespace, a Role that lets the controller make, change and delete Secrets there (the session Secrets, and copies of the image pull secrets, which the controller copies from the release namespace), and a NetworkPolicy that lets only the backup gateway pods of the release namespace reach the helper pods, on port 8443. Moving from the earlier part: sessions that were open in the release namespace are not followed; they end by themselves within 2 hours and their objects are removed with them.

docs.title: Backup Gateway
docs.text:
The one door to browse sessions (issue #92). Users talk to it with their own Kubernetes token (kubectl backup ls/get/browse). It needs backupBrowse.enabled.

Parameter Type Default Description backupGateway.enabled bool true Turns the gateway on backupGateway.replicas int 1 The gateway keeps no state backupGateway.url string "" The address that goes in the ConfigMap backup-gateway-info, which kubectl backup reads. Empty uses https://<route.host>, the host of the existing Route, or on a first install on OpenShift the host the router will give the Route (<release>-gateway-<namespace>.<ingress domain>); if none is known, users pass --gateway backupGateway.tls.secretName string "" Empty: on OpenShift the service CA makes the serving certificate. Elsewhere you must name a Secret (tls.crt, tls.key) in the release namespace, or the gateway pod cannot start backupGateway.route.enabled bool true A reencrypt Route, made only where the OpenShift Route API exists. The router answers with the cluster's ingress certificate for the host, then encrypts again to the gateway (the service CA certificate, which the router trusts). Traffic is encrypted on both legs backupGateway.route.host string "" Empty lets OpenShift choose the host backupGateway.sessionWait string 20s How long a request that asks to wait (?wait=true) holds for the helper pod to be ready. Keep it under your proxy's timeout (the OpenShift router cuts a request after 30 seconds). kubectl backup does not ask to wait: it polls backupGateway.maxDownloadBytes int 53687091200 The largest single file or tar a user may download (50 GiB) backupGateway.maxOpenRestores int 10 File restores one user may have that have not ended. A request over the limit is refused (HTTP 429) backupGateway.resources object small Requests and limits

When the gateway runs on OpenShift, the chart also adds a backup-gateway entry to the ConsolePlugin proxy (user token, the gateway Service on port 8443) and sets fileBrowse: "true" in the settings ConfigMap, so the Backups pages show Browse files. There is no value for either.

The chart also makes the ClusterRoles backup-file-reader and backup-file-restorer (see BACKUP-RECOVERY.md), a ServiceAccount for the gateway with only the rights it needs, and the ConfigMap backup-gateway-info that every signed-in user may read (that one ConfigMap and no other).

docs.title: PoolBench
docs.text:
The storage performance test service (docs/specs/2026-10-25-poolbench.md). Off by default. When on, the chart renders one Deployment (--mode=poolbench, the driver image), its own service account, a cluster role, a run role, the collector Service, and the results volume.

Parameter Type Default Description poolBench.enabled bool false Turns the PoolBench service on poolBench.interval string 15s Time between two passes of the runner poolBench.results.size string 5Gi Size of the volume that keeps the test VMs' raw results until a run is deleted poolBench.results.storageClass string "" Class of the results volume; empty uses the cluster's default class poolBench.podSecurityContext object seccomp RuntimeDefault Pod security context. Where the user ID is fixed (off OpenShift, or in kube-system) the chart adds fsGroup: 65532 unless you set one, so the service can write the results volume poolBench.securityContext object non-root, read-only root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped Container security context poolBench.resources object 50m CPU, 64Mi memory requested, 256Mi limit Container resources

Rights: cluster-wide the service may make and delete namespaces, pools and backup policies (the backup event), list nodes and pods (for the room check), read images, read and update PoolBench objects, and bind one role, <release>-poolbench-run. It binds that role to itself in each run's own namespace; the role gives it secrets, claims (it also labels them), VMs, disks, pods and pod exec there and nowhere else. RBAC cannot limit namespace deletes or role bindings by name, so where the cluster has ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (Kubernetes 1.30 and later, OpenShift 4.17 and later) the chart adds a policy that lets the service make and delete only namespaces, pools and backup policies named poolbench-*, delete only a namespace, pool or policy that carries the run label, make only a backup policy for one poolbench-* namespace that copies to that run's backup pool and exports nowhere, and bind only the run role, only in such a namespace. It reads the node agents' metrics for the share's counters, trusting their certificate as the ServiceMonitors do (the service CA, or the ca.crt of <release>-node-metrics-certs). Its own metrics (port 8443) are scraped like the controller's; their certificate is the secret <release>-poolbench-certs, made by the OpenShift service CA or cert-manager, or by you with webhook.certProvider=manual. Without that secret the pod does not start. When the console plugin is on, the chart also adds a proxy poolbench to the ConsolePlugin: the console passes the person's own token to port 8444 of the service, which checks with a TokenReview and an access review that the person may get the run before it returns its raw results. The console trusts the service's certificate only when it comes from the OpenShift service CA (webhook.certProvider=openshift).

docs.title: Replication Receiver
docs.text:
Configuration for the driver-to-driver cross-region replication receiver. Deploy this on the destination cluster. Source cluster sync-client Jobs upload data via HTTPS.

Parameter Type Default Description replicationReceiver.enabled bool false Enable the replication receiver Deployment, Service, and Route replicationReceiver.pvcName string "" Pre-created PVC name for the destination NFS mount. It is also the claim a Failover reads when it names none replicationReceiver.authSecretName string "" Secret name containing a token key for bearer token authentication replicationReceiver.runAsUser int 107 User the receiver runs as. It writes destination VM disks, and KubeVirt runs QEMU as 107 replicationReceiver.runAsGroup int 107 Group the receiver runs as replicationReceiver.securityContext object no escalation, runAsNonRoot, drop ALL, seccomp RuntimeDefault Container security context of the receiver replicationReceiver.resources.requests.cpu string 100m Receiver CPU request replicationReceiver.resources.requests.memory string 256Mi Receiver memory request replicationReceiver.resources.limits.memory string 1Gi Receiver memory limit. The receiver needs about 100 MiB itself. Pages of files on NFS count against the limit and the kernel drops them as it needs room, so the memory shown for a busy receiver stays near the limit; that is normal. The receiver forces its data out every 32 MiB and drops cached pages. A 512Mi limit survived an 11 GiB VM disk send in a lab test; the default adds room replicationReceiver.tls.enabled bool false Enable native TLS on the receiver (certificates provisioned by cert-manager) replicationReceiver.tls.additionalDNSNames list [] Extra DNS SANs for the receiver TLS certificate (e.g., custom ingress hostnames). On OpenShift, the Route hostname is added automatically replicationReceiver.tls.certManager.issuerKind string Issuer cert-manager issuer kind: Issuer (namespace-scoped) or ClusterIssuer replicationReceiver.tls.certManager.issuerName string "" cert-manager issuer name. Leave empty to create a self-signed Issuer automatically

docs.title: Replication
docs.text:
Controller-side replication Job configuration.

Parameter Type Default Description replication.image string "" Override container image for replication Jobs. When empty, the driver image is used for receiver-mode (sync-client) Jobs; CentOS Stream 9 is used for direct-NFS (rsync) Jobs

docs.title: VM Snapshots
docs.text:
See VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md.

Parameter Type Default Description vmSnapshots.method string auto auto: a snapshot of a KubeVirt VM disk is instant (a new overlay file, nothing copied) where the KubeVirt Sidecar feature gate is on, and a copy elsewhere. It adds the VM hook webhook. copy: every VM disk snapshot is a copy, and there is no VM hook webhook. Red Hat does not support the Sidecar feature gate vmSnapshots.enableSidecarGate bool false Turn on the KubeVirt Sidecar feature gate, which instant snapshots need. A hook Job adds one entry to the HyperConverged kubevirt.kubevirt.io/jsonpatch annotation after each install and upgrade, and keeps the other entries. Only that Job's service account gets rights on HyperConverged: get and update on the object named kubevirt-hyperconverged, nothing else. The gate is cluster-wide: once it is on, anyone who can create or edit a VM can add a hook sidecar container to that VM's pod (see SECURITY.md). Setting it back to false or uninstalling does not turn the gate off, because VMs with instant snapshots cannot start without it. Needs vmSnapshots.method=auto. Red Hat does not support settings made through that annotation vmSnapshots.launcherImage string "" KubeVirt's virt-launcher image, which has qemu-img, for the Jobs that change a stopped VM's snapshot files and that restore instant snapshots. Empty reads it from the virt-operator Deployment in the namespace of the KubeVirt resource

The chart also renders a ConfigMap ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-settings in the release namespace. It holds vmSnapshotMethod, the value of vmSnapshots.method, and no secret. A Role lets every signed-in user get that one ConfigMap by name, and nothing else in the namespace. The console reads it to show whether snapshots are instant or copies.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Prometheus metrics and alerting configuration.

Parameter Type Default Description metrics.port int 8080 Port for the /metrics endpoint metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled bool true Create a Prometheus ServiceMonitor. The chart creates it only when the cluster has the monitoring.coreos.com/v1 API. The console plugin's charts need it metrics.serviceMonitor.interval string 30s Scrape interval for the ServiceMonitor metrics.monitoring.mode string auto Where scraping and alerts live on OpenShift. auto: in the monitoring namespace when the cluster has the Prometheus Operator API and the OpenShift console and webhook.certProvider=openshift; enabled: always (needs certProvider=openshift, else the render fails); disabled: in the release namespace. Needs user workload monitoring on: see MONITORING.md metrics.monitoring.namespace string ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring Namespace for the ServiceMonitor objects, the PrometheusRule and the metrics Services. The chart creates it, without a platform monitoring label metrics.scraper.serviceAccount string prometheus-k8s Service account bound to the chart's metrics-reader ClusterRole (get on /metrics) so it can scrape the node agents. Empty creates no binding metrics.scraper.namespace string openshift-monitoring Namespace of that service account metrics.alerts.shareUsedWarning int 85 Percent of one share's size written (real used bytes) that triggers a warning metrics.alerts.shareUsedCritical int 95 Percent of one share's size written that triggers a critical alert metrics.alerts.nfsLatencySeconds number 0.1 Average seconds per NFS read or write request on one share that triggers a warning metrics.alerts.nfsMinOpsPerSecond number 1 The latency alert is judged only while the share does at least this many read or write requests a second metrics.alerts.shareIOPSWarning int 0 Read plus write operations a second on one share (all nodes) that trigger a warning. 0 turns the alert off metrics.alerts.enabled bool true Create the PrometheusRule (only when the cluster has the Prometheus Operator API) metrics.alerts.allocationFailuresPerSecond number 0.1 Failed volume allocations per second that trigger a critical alert metrics.alerts.allocationP99Seconds number 5 P99 allocation time in seconds that triggers a warning metrics.alerts.apiErrorsPerSecond number 0.05 Failed VPC API calls per second that trigger a warning metrics.alerts.replicationLagSeconds int 7200 Replication lag in seconds that triggers a warning metrics.alerts.replicationFailures int 3 Replication failures in a row that trigger a critical alert metrics.alerts.backupLateSeconds int 43200 A volume with no backup for this long triggers a warning (use twice the schedule) metrics.alerts.exportLateSeconds int 43200 An export to COS, or a moment waiting, this old triggers a warning metrics.alerts.snapshotPoolWarning int 75 Snapshot pool share use (percent) that triggers a warning metrics.alerts.snapshotPoolCritical int 85 Snapshot pool share use (percent) that triggers a critical alert; new backups stop at 85 metrics.alerts.shareUtilizationWarning int 90 Percent of one share's size allocated to PVCs that triggers a warning metrics.alerts.utilizationWarning int 80 Pool utilization percentage that triggers a warning alert metrics.alerts.utilizationCritical int 95 Pool utilization percentage that triggers a critical alert

docs.title: Console Plugin
docs.text:
OpenShift Console dynamic plugin for visual pool management. On by default, and installed only on clusters with the OpenShift console (ConsolePlugin v1 API, OpenShift 4.14+). On other clusters the chart leaves it out.

Parameter Type Default Description consolePlugin.enabled bool true Install the OpenShift Console dynamic plugin and turn it on in the console. Set false to leave it out consolePlugin.image.repository string de.icr.io/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/console-plugin Plugin container image repository consolePlugin.image.tag string "" Plugin image tag. Empty means v plus the chart appVersion consolePlugin.securityContext object no escalation, runAsNonRoot, drop ALL, seccomp RuntimeDefault Container security context of the plugin (its image already runs as user 1001) consolePlugin.replicas int 2 Number of plugin pod replicas consolePlugin.port int 9443 HTTPS port for the plugin Service. TLS certs are auto-provisioned by the OpenShift service-ca operator consolePlugin.resources.requests.cpu string 10m CPU request consolePlugin.resources.requests.memory string 50Mi Memory request consolePlugin.resources.limits.memory string 128Mi Memory limit

The chart turns the plugin on in the console for you. A hook Job runs after each install and upgrade and adds ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi to the console's plugin list (console.operator.openshift.io/cluster, spec.plugins). It keeps every other plugin. Before helm uninstall, a second hook Job removes only this plugin from the list. If you upgrade with consolePlugin.enabled=false, the same Job removes it after the upgrade. The Jobs use the driver image and a service account that can only read and update that one object.

docs.text:
Disable the managed secret sidecar and provide VPC config explicitly:

config:
  region: us-south
  vpcID: r006-abc12345-6789-def0-1234-567890abcdef

  resourceGroupID: a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6

Then create a Secret with the IBM Cloud API key:

kubectl create secret generic ibm-cloud-credentials \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --from-literal=api-key=<your-api-key>

docs.title: SDK
docs.text:
Use the official IBM VPC Go SDK: github.com/IBM/vpc-go-sdk

Documentation: https://github.com/IBM/vpc-go-sdk

Install: 

go get github.com/IBM/vpc-go-sdk@latest

docs.title: Authentication — Using secret-common-lib
docs.text:
We reuse the same authentication infrastructure as the stock IBM CSI drivers. This means our driver works out of the box on any ROKS/ROVS/IKS cluster — no separate API key setup required.

Import the shared library: 

go get github.com/IBM/secret-common-lib@latest

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
IBM's secret-common-lib reads credentials from Kubernetes secrets that already exist on managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters. It supports two authentication methods:

  1. API key — IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=iam + IBMCLOUD_APIKEY (traditional)
  2. Pod identity / Trusted profiles — IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=pod-identity + IBMCLOUD_PROFILEID (no long-lived keys)

The library handles IAM token exchange, caching, and renewal automatically.

docs.title: Secret Lookup Order
docs.text:
The library checks credentials in this order: 1. ibm-cloud-credentials secret (key: ibm-credentials.env) — preferred 2. storage-secret-store secret (key: slclient.toml) — legacy fallback

On managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters, storage-secret-store is pre-populated by the add-on system. The ibm-cloud-credentials secret is the newer format and supports pod identity.

docs.title: Kubernetes Secrets Format
docs.text:
ibm-cloud-credentials (preferred — env file format, base64-encoded): 

# API key auth:
IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=iam
IBMCLOUD_APIKEY=<api-key>

# Or pod identity auth (no long-lived key):
IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=pod-identity
IBMCLOUD_PROFILEID=<trusted-profile-id>

storage-secret-store (legacy — TOML format): 

[Bluemix]
iam_url = "https://iam.cloud.ibm.com"
iam_api_key = "<api-key>"

[VPC]
g2_token_exchange_endpoint_url = "https://iam.cloud.ibm.com"
g2_riaas_endpoint_url = "https://us-south.iaas.cloud.ibm.com/v1"
g2_resource_group_id = "<resource-group-id>"
g2_api_key = "<api-key>"

docs.title: ConfigMaps Used
docs.text:
The library and our driver also read these ConfigMaps (pre-populated on managed clusters):

  • ibm-cloud-provider-data — contains VPC ID and subnet IDs
  • ibm-cloud-cluster-info — contains cluster ID and account ID
  • cloud-conf (optional) — JSON with region, RIAAS endpoint, resource group ID

docs.title: Managed vs. Unmanaged Provider
docs.text:
Mode IKS_ENABLED env How It Works Managed (ROKS/ROVS/IKS) true Sidecar container watches secrets, auto-refreshes tokens via projected service account token, LRU cache for multi-secret support Unmanaged (self-managed OCP/K8s) false Reads secret directly in-process, no auto-refresh, pod restart required on key rotation

On ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters, use managed mode. On self-managed clusters, use unmanaged mode.

docs.title: Client Initialization
docs.text:
package ibmcloud

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"

    secretlib "github.com/IBM/secret-common-lib/pkg/secret_provider"
    "github.com/IBM/go-sdk-core/v5/core"
    "github.com/IBM/vpc-go-sdk/vpcv1"
    "golang.org/x/time/rate"
    "k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes"
)

type Client struct {
    vpcService     *vpcv1.VpcV1
    secretProvider secretlib.SecretProviderInterface
    region         string
    rateLimiter    *rate.Limiter
}

// NewClient creates a VPC API client using the cluster's existing credentials.
// It uses secret-common-lib to read API keys or pod identity tokens from the
// same secrets that the stock IBM CSI drivers use.
func NewClient(k8sClient kubernetes.Interface, region string) (*Client, error) {
    // Initialize the secret provider (reads IKS_ENABLED env to choose managed/unmanaged)
    secretProvider, err := secretlib.NewSecretProvider(k8sClient, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to initialize secret provider: %w", err)
    }

    // Get an IAM token from the cluster's credentials
    token, _, err := secretProvider.GetDefaultIAMToken("vpc-file-pool-csi-init", false)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to get initial IAM token: %w", err)
    }

    // Get VPC API endpoint from the secret provider
    riaasEndpoint := secretProvider.GetRIAASEndpoint()
    if riaasEndpoint == "" {
        riaasEndpoint = fmt.Sprintf("https://%s.iaas.cloud.ibm.com/v1", region)
    }

    // Create the VPC service with a bearer token authenticator
    // The token will be refreshed before each API call (see refreshToken method)
    authenticator := &core.BearerTokenAuthenticator{
        BearerToken: token,
    }

    vpcService, err := vpcv1.NewVpcV1(&vpcv1.VpcV1Options{
        Authenticator: authenticator,
        URL:           riaasEndpoint,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to create VPC service: %w", err)
    }

    return &Client{
        vpcService:     vpcService,
        secretProvider: secretProvider,
        region:         region,
        rateLimiter:    rate.NewLimiter(rate.Every(time.Second), 5),
    }, nil
}

// refreshToken gets a fresh IAM token from secret-common-lib and updates
// the VPC service authenticator. Call this before any VPC API operation.
func (c *Client) refreshToken(ctx context.Context, reason string) error {
    token, _, err := c.secretProvider.GetDefaultIAMToken(reason, false)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to refresh IAM token: %w", err)
    }

    // Update the bearer token on the authenticator
    auth, ok := c.vpcService.Service.Options.Authenticator.(*core.BearerTokenAuthenticator)
    if !ok {
        return fmt.Errorf("unexpected authenticator type")
    }
    auth.BearerToken = token
    return nil
}

// withAuth wraps a VPC API call with token refresh and rate limiting.
// Use this before every API call.
func (c *Client) withAuth(ctx context.Context, operation string) error {
    if err := c.rateLimiter.Wait(ctx); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("rate limiter: %w", err)
    }
    if err := c.refreshToken(ctx, operation); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return nil
}

docs.title: Pod Identity Setup (for clusters that use Trusted Profiles)
docs.text:
If the cluster uses pod identity instead of API keys, the controller Deployment needs a projected service account token volume:

# In the controller Deployment spec
volumes:
  - name: vault-token
    projected:
      sources:
        - serviceAccountToken:
            path: vault-token
            expirationSeconds: 600
containers:
  - name: csi-controller
    volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
        name: vault-token

The secret-common-lib managed provider automatically uses this projected token when IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=pod-identity.

docs.title: Fallback: Standalone API Key (Self-Managed Clusters)
docs.text:
On self-managed clusters that don't have the IBM CSI add-on installed, there won't be a storage-secret-store or ibm-cloud-credentials secret. In that case, the operator creates the ibm-cloud-credentials secret manually:

# Create the credentials env file
cat > /tmp/ibm-credentials.env << 'EOF'
IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=iam
IBMCLOUD_APIKEY=<your-api-key>
EOF

# Create the Kubernetes secret
kubectl create secret generic ibm-cloud-credentials \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --from-file=ibm-credentials.env=/tmp/ibm-credentials.env

rm /tmp/ibm-credentials.env

The secret-common-lib will find and use this secret automatically. 

---

## File Share Operations

### Create File Share

Called by the Pool Manager when a new share is needed in a pool.

**This is a SLOW operation (30-90+ seconds).** Never call this in the CSI CreateVolume hot path.

Every share is created in **security group access mode** with one inline mount target. IBM ended new VPC-mode mount targets: the API returns HTTP 501 `shares_not_implemented` for them (seen in eu-de, October 2026), and VPC access mode reaches End of Support on 6 May 2027.

```go
type CreateShareInput struct {
    Name             string
    Zone             string
    Profile          string
    SizeGB           int64
    IOPS             *int64
    ResourceGroupID  string
    Tags             []string
    EncryptInTransit bool
    SubnetID         string   // worker subnet in Zone; required
    SecurityGroupIDs []string // groups on the mount target's network interface
}

func (c *Client) CreateFileShare(ctx context.Context, input CreateShareInput) (*ShareInfo, error) {
    // ... profile, zone, size, IOPS, resource group, tags, initial owner 65534 ...

    if input.SubnetID == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("create share %q: subnet ID is required for the mount target", input.Name)
    }
    sharePrototype.AccessControlMode = core.StringPtr("security_group")
    sharePrototype.MountTargets = []vpcv1.ShareMountTargetPrototypeIntf{
        // A virtual network interface (VNI) in SubnetID, protected by SecurityGroupIDs.
        securityGroupMountTarget(input.Name+"-mt", input.SubnetID, input.SecurityGroupIDs,
            input.EncryptInTransit, input.ResourceGroupID),
    }

    // Create (adopting an existing share of the same name on HTTP 400 "already exists"),
    // wait for "stable", then poll until the mount target's mount_path is known.
}

The NFS server and the export path both come from the mount target's mount_path, for example 10.250.0.18:/83ad9ea6_1be6_.... The export path is specific to the share; it is never /. A mount target that has an IP address but no mount_path yet is not usable, and the driver leaves its address empty until the path appears.

docs.title: Create Share Mount Target
docs.text:

type CreateMountTargetInput struct {

    SubnetID         string
    SecurityGroupIDs []string
    EncryptInTransit bool
}

func (c *Client) CreateShareMountTarget(ctx context.Context, shareID string, input CreateMountTargetInput) (*MountTargetInfo, error)

docs.title: getShareByName (Internal — Idempotent Share Lookup)
docs.text:
When CreateFileShare gets HTTP 400 "already exists" (e.g., reconciler retried after a status update conflict), this method looks up the existing share by name via ListShares with a name filter, waits for stable state, and returns its full info including mount target IPs.

func (c *Client) getShareByName(ctx context.Context, name string) (*ShareInfo, error)

docs.title: Wait for Share Stable
docs.text:
VPC file shares go through lifecycle states: pending → stable → (or failed).

func (c *Client) waitForShareStable(ctx context.Context, shareID string, timeout time.Duration) (*ShareInfo, error) {
    deadline := time.Now().Add(timeout)

    for {
        if time.Now().After(deadline) {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("timed out waiting for share %s to become stable", shareID)
        }

        info, err := c.GetFileShare(ctx, shareID)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }

        switch info.LifecycleState {
        case "stable":
            return info, nil
        case "failed":
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("share %s entered failed state", shareID)
        case "pending":
            // Still creating, wait and retry
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(10 * time.Second):
                continue
            }
        default:
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(10 * time.Second):
                continue
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Get File Share
docs.text:
type ShareInfo struct {
    ID              string
    Name            string
    LifecycleState  string    // "pending", "stable", "failed", etc.
    SizeGB          int64
    IOPS            int64
    Profile         string
    Zone            string
    MountTargets    []MountTargetInfo
    CreatedAt       time.Time
}

type MountTargetInfo struct {
    ID         string
    Name       string
    IPAddress  string    // NFS server IP or FQDN
    ExportPath string    // NFS export path (e.g. "/share_abc123"); empty defaults to "/"
    Zone       string    // VPC zone of this mount target (for cross-zone support)
}

func (c *Client) GetFileShare(ctx context.Context, shareID string) (*ShareInfo, error) {
    opts := c.vpcService.NewGetShareOptions(shareID)
    share, response, err := c.vpcService.GetShareWithContext(ctx, opts)
    if err != nil {
        if response != nil && response.StatusCode == 404 {
            return nil, ErrShareNotFound
        }
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("VPC API GetShare failed: %w", err)
    }

    info := &ShareInfo{
        ID:             *share.ID,
        Name:           *share.Name,
        LifecycleState: *share.LifecycleState,
        SizeGB:         *share.Size,
        IOPS:           *share.Iops,
        Profile:        *share.Profile.(*vpcv1.ShareProfileReference).Name,
        Zone:           *share.Zone.(*vpcv1.ZoneReference).Name,
        CreatedAt:      time.Time(*share.CreatedAt),
    }

    // Extract mount targets
    for _, mt := range share.MountTargets {
        mtRef := mt.(*vpcv1.ShareMountTargetReference)
        // Need to fetch full mount target to get IP
        mtInfo, err := c.getMountTarget(ctx, shareID, *mtRef.ID)
        if err != nil {
            continue
        }
        info.MountTargets = append(info.MountTargets, *mtInfo)
    }

    return info, nil
}

docs.title: Expand File Share
docs.text:
func (c *Client) ExpandFileShare(ctx context.Context, shareID string, newSizeGB int64) error {
    opts := c.vpcService.NewUpdateShareOptions(shareID, map[string]interface{}{
        "size": newSizeGB,
    })

    _, response, err := c.vpcService.UpdateShareWithContext(ctx, opts)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("VPC API UpdateShare (expand) failed (HTTP %d): %w", response.StatusCode, err)
    }

    // Wait for expansion to complete
    _, err = c.waitForShareStable(ctx, shareID, 5*time.Minute)
    return err
}

docs.title: Delete File Share
docs.text:
Called by Pool Manager when shrinking a pool or during cleanup.

func (c *Client) DeleteFileShare(ctx context.Context, shareID string) error {
    // First delete all mount targets
    share, err := c.GetFileShare(ctx, shareID)
    if err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, ErrShareNotFound) {
            return nil // Already deleted, idempotent
        }
        return err
    }

    for _, mt := range share.MountTargets {
        opts := c.vpcService.NewDeleteShareMountTargetOptions(shareID, mt.ID)
        _, err := c.vpcService.DeleteShareMountTargetWithContext(ctx, opts)
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("failed to delete mount target %s: %w", mt.ID, err)
        }
    }

    // Then delete the share
    // Use the If-Match header with ETag for safe deletion
    deleteOpts := c.vpcService.NewDeleteShareOptions(shareID)
    _, response, err := c.vpcService.DeleteShareWithContext(ctx, deleteOpts)
    if err != nil {
        if response != nil && response.StatusCode == 404 {
            return nil // Already deleted
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("VPC API DeleteShare failed: %w", err)
    }

    return nil
}

docs.title: List File Shares
docs.text:
Used by the reconciler to discover existing shares (e.g., on startup).

func (c *Client) ListFileShares(ctx context.Context, resourceGroupID string, tags []string) ([]*ShareInfo, error) {
    var allShares []*ShareInfo
    var start *string

    for {
        opts := c.vpcService.NewListSharesOptions()
        if resourceGroupID != "" {
            opts.SetResourceGroupID(resourceGroupID)
        }
        if start != nil {
            opts.SetStart(*start)
        }
        opts.SetLimit(100)

        result, _, err := c.vpcService.ListSharesWithContext(ctx, opts)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("VPC API ListShares failed: %w", err)
        }

        for _, share := range result.Shares {
            info := shareToInfo(&share)
            allShares = append(allShares, info)
        }

        if result.Next == nil || result.Next.Href == nil {
            break
        }
        // Parse the "start" parameter from the Next URL
        start = parseStartFromURL(*result.Next.Href)
    }

    return allShares, nil
}

docs.title: Client Interface (for Testing)
docs.text:
Define an interface so the real client can be swapped with a fake in tests:

// pkg/ibmcloud/client.go

type VPCFileClient interface {
    CreateFileShare(ctx context.Context, input CreateShareInput) (*ShareInfo, error)
    GetFileShare(ctx context.Context, shareID string) (*ShareInfo, error)
    ExpandFileShare(ctx context.Context, shareID string, newSizeGB int64) error
    DeleteFileShare(ctx context.Context, shareID string) error
    ListFileShares(ctx context.Context, resourceGroupID string, tags []string) ([]*ShareInfo, error)
    CreateShareMountTarget(ctx context.Context, shareID string, input CreateMountTargetInput) (*MountTargetInfo, error)
    GetSubnetZone(ctx context.Context, subnetID string) (string, error)
    FindSecurityGroupID(ctx context.Context, vpcID, name string) (string, error)
}

// Verify the real client implements the interface
var _ VPCFileClient = (*Client)(nil)

docs.title: Fake Client
docs.text:
// pkg/ibmcloud/fake/fake_client.go

type FakeClient struct {
    mu     sync.Mutex
    shares map[string]*ibmcloud.ShareInfo
    nextID int
}

func NewFakeClient() *FakeClient {
    return &FakeClient{
        shares: make(map[string]*ibmcloud.ShareInfo),
    }
}

func (f *FakeClient) CreateFileShare(ctx context.Context, input ibmcloud.CreateShareInput) (*ibmcloud.ShareInfo, error) {
    f.mu.Lock()
    defer f.mu.Unlock()

    f.nextID++
    id := fmt.Sprintf("r006-fake-%04d", f.nextID)

    info := &ibmcloud.ShareInfo{
        ID:             id,
        Name:           input.Name,
        LifecycleState: "stable",
        SizeGB:         input.SizeGB,
        IOPS:           1000,
        Profile:        input.Profile,
        Zone:           input.Zone,
        MountTargets: []ibmcloud.MountTargetInfo{
            {
                ID:        id + "-mt",
                Name:      input.Name + "-mt",
                IPAddress: fmt.Sprintf("10.240.0.%d", f.nextID),
            },
        },
        CreatedAt: time.Now(),
    }

    f.shares[id] = info
    return info, nil
}

// ... implement other methods similarly

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Define sentinel errors for clean error propagation:

var (
    ErrShareNotFound       = errors.New("VPC file share not found")
    ErrShareNotStable      = errors.New("VPC file share is not in stable state")
    ErrShareCreationFailed = errors.New("VPC file share creation failed")
    ErrAPIRateLimit        = errors.New("VPC API rate limit exceeded")
    ErrAuthentication      = errors.New("VPC API authentication failed")
)

Map VPC API HTTP status codes: - 404 → ErrShareNotFound - 429 → ErrAPIRateLimit (retry with backoff) - 401/403 → ErrAuthentication - 500+ → wrap with context and retry

docs.title: Rate Limiting & Token Refresh
docs.text:
IBM VPC API has rate limits. The client uses withAuth() before every API call, which combines rate limiting with token refresh:

// withAuth wraps every VPC API call with rate limiting + token refresh.
// Defined in the Authentication section above.
func (c *Client) withAuth(ctx context.Context, operation string) error { ... }

// Usage pattern in every API method:
func (c *Client) GetFileShare(ctx context.Context, shareID string) (*ShareInfo, error) {
    if err := c.withAuth(ctx, "GetFileShare"); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    // ... actual API call ...
}

The rate limiter is set to 5 requests/second by default. This is conservative and can be tuned via a flag or ConfigMap.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The IBM VPC client reads configuration from the cluster's existing secrets and configmaps, plus the FileSharePool spec:

Config Source Description IAM credentials ibm-cloud-credentials or storage-secret-store secret (via secret-common-lib) API key or pod identity — already present on managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters VPC API endpoint secret-common-lib GetRIAASEndpoint() or derived from zone Supports private endpoints automatically Resource group ID secret-common-lib GetResourceGroupID() or FileSharePool.spec.resourceGroup Pool spec overrides if set region Derived from FileSharePool.spec.zone (e.g., "us-south" from "us-south-1") VPC API region vpcID --vpc-id, or ConfigMap kube-system/ibm-cloud-provider-data key vpc_id VPC where shares and mount targets are created subnetIDs --subnet-id (comma-separated), or ConfigMap ibm-cloud-provider-data key vpc_subnet_ids Worker subnets. Each mount target goes in the one in the pool's zone securityGroupIDs FileSharePool.spec.securityGroupIDs, or the cluster group kube-<cluster_id> (ConfigMap kube-system/cluster-info key cluster_id) The cluster group already allows all traffic between workers and the mount target

The client should be created once per FileSharePool (since different pools could be in different regions), cached by the Pool Manager. Token refresh is handled by secret-common-lib — the client calls refreshToken() before each API operation.

docs.title: Installation Guide — IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver
What This Driver Does
docs.text:
In Kubernetes, applications request storage using Persistent Volume Claims (PVCs). Normally, each PVC creates its own dedicated VPC file share — which is slow (30-90 seconds per share) and wastes VPC quota.

This CSI driver takes a different approach: it creates a pool of large VPC file shares up front, then carves out subdirectories for each PVC. Think of it like a shared hard drive where each application gets its own folder. PVCs bind in seconds instead of minutes, and many PVCs share a single VPC file share.

A CSI driver (Container Storage Interface) is a plugin that teaches Kubernetes how to provision and mount a specific type of storage. This one teaches Kubernetes how to use IBM VPC file shares in a pooled way.

docs.title: Installation Overview
docs.text:
The end-to-end process from source code to a working driver on your cluster:

  1. make build — compile the Go source code into a binary
  2. docker build / podman build — package the binary into a container image
  3. docker push / podman push — upload the image to a container registry so your cluster can pull it
  4. helm upgrade --install — deploy the driver onto the cluster (creates controller, node agents, RBAC, etc.)
  5. make test-e2e — run automated tests against the live driver to verify everything works

Each step is covered in detail below.

docs.title: Cluster Requirements
docs.text:
• IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service (IKS) or Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Cloud (ROKS or ROVS), version 1.28+
  • VPC Gen2 networking (Classic infrastructure is not supported)
  • Worker nodes with topology.kubernetes.io/zone and topology.kubernetes.io/region labels (set automatically by IBM Cloud — you don't need to do anything)

docs.title: IBM Cloud Requirements
docs.text:
• An IBM Cloud account with VPC Infrastructure permissions
  • An API key with the following IAM roles:
  • VPC Infrastructure Services: Editor or Administrator (to create/manage file shares)
  • Kubernetes Service: Editor (if deploying via managed add-on in the future)
  • A VPC with at least one subnet in the target availability zone
  • Security groups on worker nodes must allow TCP port 2049 (NFS) inbound and outbound — this is the port that NFS (Network File System) uses to share files over the network

docs.title: Webhook Certificates
docs.text:
The driver uses admission webhooks — these are Kubernetes guards that validate your configuration before accepting it (e.g., rejecting a FileSharePool with an invalid zone). Webhooks require TLS certificates for secure communication.

On OpenShift (ROKS or ROVS), the simplest choice is the built-in service CA. Set webhook.certProvider=openshift. It needs no extra operator. ROVS clusters do not include cert-manager.

To use cert-manager instead (the chart default):

# Install cert-manager if not already present
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/latest/download/cert-manager.yaml

# Verify it's running (all pods should show STATUS=Running)
kubectl get pods -n cert-manager

If you prefer to manage webhook TLS certificates manually, set webhook.certProvider=manual. Create the Secret <release>-ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-webhook-certs (keys tls.crt and tls.key, for the DNS name <release>-ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-webhook.<namespace>.svc) before you install, and set webhook.caBundle to the base64-encoded PEM of the CA that signed it:

--set webhook.certProvider=manual --set webhook.caBundle="$(base64 < ca.crt | tr -d '\n')"

The chart refuses to render in manual mode without webhook.caBundle.

When you switch between certificate modes on a running install, delete the old <release>-ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-webhook-certs Secret first. For about a minute after the switch, until the controller reloads the new certificate, requests to the webhooks fail with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority, and creating or changing the driver's resources is refused. Seen on rovslab-prod-eude, 2026-10-19.

To disable webhooks entirely, set webhook.enabled=false. The controller then serves no webhooks and needs no certificate. Invalid custom resources are then accepted without checks.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text:
You'll need these command-line tools installed on your workstation:

Tool What it does Install kubectl or oc Talks to your Kubernetes/OpenShift cluster kubectl, oc helm v3.10+ Package manager for Kubernetes — installs the driver and all its components in one command helm docker or podman Builds container images from source code docker, podman ibmcloud CLI Authenticates with IBM Cloud Container Registry so you can push images ibmcloud make Runs predefined build commands from the project's Makefile — saves you from typing long go build commands Pre-installed on macOS/Linux

docs.title: Verify Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting, confirm you can reach your cluster and that it's properly configured:

# Confirm cluster access — this lists your worker nodes
kubectl get nodes -o wide

# Check node labels — each node must have a zone label so the driver
# knows which availability zone to create file shares in
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.metadata.labels.topology\.kubernetes\.io/zone}{"\n"}{end}'

# Verify NFS port is open in security group
# The VPC security group attached to worker nodes must have TCP 2049 allowed,
# otherwise nodes won't be able to mount the NFS file shares
ibmcloud is security-groups --output json | jq '.[] | select(.name | contains("kube")) | .rules[] | select(.port_min == 2049)'

docs.title: Step 1: Build and Push the Driver Image
docs.text:
Why this step? Kubernetes runs applications as container images — lightweight, self-contained packages that include the application and everything it needs to run. We need to: 1. Compile the Go source code into a binary (make build) 2. Package that binary into a container image (docker build or podman build) 3. Push the image to a registry where your cluster can download it

make build is a shortcut that runs the Go compiler with the right flags. The project's Makefile defines these shortcuts so you don't need to remember long commands.

# Clone the repository (skip if you already have it)
git clone https://github.com/IBM/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi.git
cd ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi

# Compile the Go source code into a binary
make build

Set your image coordinates — these tell the build tools where to store the image:

# The container registry to push to. IBM Cloud Container Registry (ICR)
# has regional endpoints: icr.io (US), de.icr.io (EU), au.icr.io (AP), etc.
export REGISTRY=icr.io

# Your ICR namespace (a folder in the registry to organize your images)
export NAMESPACE=your-icr-namespace

# A version tag based on the current git commit — ensures each build is unique
export VERSION=$(git describe --tags --always)

# The full image name including registry, namespace, and version tag
export IMAGE=${REGISTRY}/${NAMESPACE}/vpc-file-pool-csi:${VERSION}

Build the container image using docker or podman (they do the same thing — podman doesn't need a background daemon, which is useful on macOS):

# Option A: docker
docker build -t ${IMAGE} .

# Option B: podman (macOS, Fedora, RHEL — no Docker daemon required)
podman build -t ${IMAGE} .

# You can also use the Makefile target (auto-detects docker or podman):
#   make docker-build IMAGE_NAME=${REGISTRY}/${NAMESPACE}/vpc-file-pool-csi VERSION=${VERSION}
# Note: Do NOT include a tag in IMAGE_NAME — the Makefile appends :$(VERSION) automatically.

The image also holds the Kopia command-line program (pinned in the Dockerfile by version and SHA-256; the build stops if the checksum does not match). Only the COS export Jobs run it. The driver does not link it, and the image build needs to reach github.com to fetch it. To move to another Kopia version, change KOPIA_VERSION and KOPIA_SHA256 together, using the checksum in checksums.txt of the official release.

Push the image to IBM Cloud Container Registry so your cluster nodes can pull it:

# Authenticate with ICR — this stores a temporary token that docker/podman
# uses when pushing
ibmcloud cr login --region ${REGISTRY%%.*}

# Upload the image (use whichever tool you built with)
docker push ${IMAGE}
# or: podman push ${IMAGE}

If you're iterating locally and have a private registry or use OpenShift's internal registry:

# OpenShift internal registry
oc registry login
docker tag ${IMAGE} default-route-openshift-image-registry.apps.<cluster>/kube-system/vpc-file-pool-csi:${VERSION}
docker push default-route-openshift-image-registry.apps.<cluster>/kube-system/vpc-file-pool-csi:${VERSION}

docs.title: Step 2: Verify Credentials
docs.text:
Why this step? The driver needs to authenticate with the IBM Cloud VPC API to create and manage file shares. It uses an API key stored as a Kubernetes Secret (an encrypted key-value store that keeps sensitive data out of your YAML files and container images).

The driver uses secret-common-lib to authenticate — the same library used by the stock IBM CSI drivers. This means it reads credentials from secrets that already exist on your cluster.

docs.title: Managed Clusters (ROKS / ROVS / IKS) — Nothing to Do
docs.text:
On managed clusters, IBM Cloud automatically creates and maintains the credentials for you. Just verify they exist:

# This secret contains the API key for VPC API access
kubectl get secret storage-secret-store -n kube-system

# This ConfigMap tells the driver which VPC and subnet to use
kubectl get configmap ibm-cloud-provider-data -n kube-system

If both exist, skip to Step 3. The driver will use these automatically.

docs.title: Self-Managed Clusters — Create Credentials
docs.text:
If you're running on a self-managed OpenShift or Kubernetes cluster, create the credentials manually:

# Create a service ID — a non-human identity for the driver to use
ibmcloud iam service-id-create vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --description "Service ID for VPC File Pool CSI Driver"

# Grant it permission to manage VPC Infrastructure (file shares, mount targets)
ibmcloud iam service-policy-create vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --roles Editor --service-name is

# Generate an API key for that service ID
ibmcloud iam service-api-key-create vpc-file-pool-csi-key vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --description "API key for VPC File Pool CSI Driver" \
  --output json

# Store the API key as a Kubernetes Secret
# (replace <paste-api-key-here> with the actual key from the previous command)
cat > /tmp/ibm-credentials.env << 'EOF'
IBMCLOUD_AUTHTYPE=iam
IBMCLOUD_APIKEY=<paste-api-key-here>
EOF

kubectl create secret generic ibm-cloud-credentials \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --from-file=ibm-credentials.env=/tmp/ibm-credentials.env
rm /tmp/ibm-credentials.env

# Tell the driver which VPC and subnet to use
kubectl create configmap ibm-cloud-provider-data \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --from-literal=vpcID=<your-vpc-id> \
  --from-literal=subnetID=<your-subnet-id>

For pod identity (Trusted Profiles) setup or more details, see API-KEY-SETUP.md.

docs.title: Step 3: Install the Driver
docs.text:
Why Helm? Installing a CSI driver involves creating many Kubernetes resources: Deployments, DaemonSets, ServiceAccounts, RBAC roles, a CSIDriver object, and more. Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes (like apt or brew, but for cluster applications). Instead of applying dozens of YAML files manually, Helm installs everything in one command and lets you customize settings with --set flags.

The helm upgrade --install command is idempotent — it installs the first time and upgrades on subsequent runs, so you can safely re-run it.

docs.title: Option A: Helm Chart (Recommended)
docs.text:
# Managed clusters (ROKS / IKS) — region, VPC, and subnet auto-discovered:
helm upgrade --install ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/ \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set image.repository=${REGISTRY}/${NAMESPACE}/vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --set image.tag=${VERSION} \
  --set image.pullPolicy=Always \
  --set 'imagePullSecrets[0].name=all-icr-io'

# Self-managed clusters — provide VPC config explicitly:
# helm upgrade --install ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
#   charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/ \
#   --namespace kube-system \
#   --set image.repository=${REGISTRY}/${NAMESPACE}/vpc-file-pool-csi \
#   --set image.tag=${VERSION} \
#   --set image.pullPolicy=Always \
#   --set 'imagePullSecrets[0].name=all-icr-io' \
#   --set config.region=us-south \
#   --set config.vpcID=<YOUR_VPC_ID> \
#   --set config.subnetID=<YOUR_SUBNET_ID>

What gets installed: - A Deployment (the controller) — the brain that manages file share pools, creates subdirectories for PVCs, and talks to the IBM VPC API - A DaemonSet (the node agent) — runs on every worker node, responsible for mounting NFS shares and bind-mounting subdirectories into pods - RBAC roles — permissions that allow the driver to read/write Kubernetes resources like PVCs and CRDs - A CSIDriver object — registers the driver with Kubernetes so it knows to route storage requests to it - A StorageClass — tells Kubernetes "when someone asks for storage of this type, use this CSI driver"

Image pull secrets: Your cluster nodes need permission to download the driver image from IBM Cloud Container Registry. Managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters have a pre-configured secret called all-icr-io that handles this. Without it, pods fail to start with an unauthorized / ErrImagePull error. Verify it exists:

kubectl get secret all-icr-io -n kube-system

On some clusters, including ROVS, all-icr-io exists only in the default namespace. Copy it into kube-system:

kubectl get secret all-icr-io -n default -o json \
  | jq 'del(.metadata.namespace,.metadata.uid,.metadata.resourceVersion,.metadata.creationTimestamp,.metadata.managedFields,.metadata.ownerReferences)' \
  | kubectl apply -n kube-system -f -

ROVS note: Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization Service (ROVS) clusters have the same kubelet path as ROKS. They do not include cert-manager, so set webhook.certProvider=openshift. If the cluster logs in to IBM Cloud with a trusted profile, link the driver's service account to it first. See API-KEY-SETUP.md.

ROKS note: On Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Cloud (ROKS), the kubelet root directory is /var/data/kubelet (not the standard /var/lib/kubelet). The kubelet is the agent on each node that manages pods — the CSI node agent needs to know where it stores volume data. Add node.kubeletDir:

helm upgrade --install ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/ \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set image.repository=${REGISTRY}/${NAMESPACE}/vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --set image.tag=${VERSION} \
  --set image.pullPolicy=Always \
  --set 'imagePullSecrets[0].name=all-icr-io' \
  --set node.kubeletDir=/var/data/kubelet

Helm values reference:

Value Required Default Description image.repository Yes — Container image registry path image.tag Yes — Image tag image.pullPolicy No IfNotPresent Image pull policy (Always recommended during iterative testing) imagePullSecrets No [] Image pull secrets for private registries. On managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS, set to [{name: all-icr-io}] config.region No Auto-discovered IBM Cloud region (e.g., us-south). Auto-discovered from the secret provider RIAAS endpoint on managed ROKS/ROVS/IKS clusters config.vpcID No Auto-discovered VPC ID where shares will be created. Auto-discovered from the ibm-cloud-provider-data ConfigMap on managed clusters config.subnetID No Auto-discovered Worker subnet IDs for NFS mount targets, comma-separated. Auto-discovered from ibm-cloud-provider-data on managed clusters. Each share's mount target goes in the subnet in the pool's zone config.resourceGroupID No Auto-discovered Resource group for billing. Auto-discovered from the secret provider on managed clusters controller.replicas No 1 Controller replicas (leader-elected) controller.resources No {requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 128Mi}, limits: {memory: 512Mi}} Controller CPU/memory resource requests and limits node.kubeletDir No /var/data/kubelet Kubelet root directory. ROKS and ROVS use /var/data/kubelet (the Helm default). The Go binary default is /var/lib/kubelet for raw manifest deployments node.resources No {requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}, limits: {memory: 256Mi}} Node agent CPU/memory resource requests and limits logLevel No 4 klog verbosity (2=normal, 4=detailed, 6=trace) webhook.enabled No true Enable validating admission webhooks webhook.port No 9443 Webhook server port webhook.certProvider No cert-manager TLS certificate provider: cert-manager, openshift or manual cloneWorker.interval No 10s Background clone worker poll interval goldenImageSyncer.interval No 5m Golden image syncer poll interval cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit No 8Gi Minimum memory limit for CDI's copy pods; the controller raises it in the OpenShift Virtualization settings. Empty turns this off secretProvider.managed No true Enable managed secret provider sidecar (ROKS/ROVS/IKS) secretProvider.sidecar.image No icr.io/obs/armada-storage-secret:v1.2.75 Secret provider sidecar container image

docs.title: Option B: Raw Manifests
docs.text:
If you prefer not to use Helm, you can install the driver by applying Kubernetes YAML files directly. This gives you full visibility into what's being created, but you have to manage each file individually.

# 1. Install CRDs (Custom Resource Definitions)
#    CRDs extend Kubernetes with new resource types: FileSharePool, SubVolume, etc.
#    Without these, Kubernetes wouldn't understand what a FileSharePool is.
kubectl apply -f config/crd/

# 2. Install RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)
#    These give the driver permission to create PVs, read PVCs, update CRDs, etc.
kubectl apply -f config/rbac/

# 3. Edit the deployment manifests with your image and config
#    (or use kustomize — a kustomization.yaml is provided)
export IMAGE=${REGISTRY}/${NAMESPACE}/vpc-file-pool-csi:${VERSION}

# Using sed for quick substitution:
sed -i "s|image: .*vpc-file-pool-csi.*|image: ${IMAGE}|g" config/deploy/controller.yaml config/deploy/node.yaml

# 4. Deploy the controller and node agents
kubectl apply -f config/deploy/csidriver.yaml
kubectl apply -f config/deploy/controller.yaml
kubectl apply -f config/deploy/node.yaml

# 5. (Optional) Install custom StorageClasses
#    StorageClasses are auto-created when you create a FileSharePool.
#    Only apply this if you need custom SC parameters:
# kubectl apply -f config/deploy/storageclass.yaml

CLI flags reference (for raw manifest deployments — these map to Helm values above):

Flag Default Description --endpoint unix:///csi/csi.sock CSI gRPC endpoint --node-id (required) Kubernetes node name --mode controller controller, node, receiver, sync-client, check-receiver, apply-vm-disk, send-vm-disk, or restore-vm-disk, restore-files (the copy Job of a BackupFileRestore), unwrap-backup-key, backup-gateway, register-console-plugin, or unregister-console-plugin, or enable-sidecar-gate, or failover (the Job for a Failover resource), or poolbench (the PoolBench service, a Deployment when poolBench.enabled; all but the first three and poolbench are run as Jobs; check-receiver is run by the console's receiver setup; register-console-plugin, unregister-console-plugin and enable-sidecar-gate are the chart's hook Jobs) --region Auto-discovered IBM Cloud region --vpc-id Auto-discovered VPC ID for mount targets --subnet-id Auto-discovered Worker subnet IDs for mount targets, comma-separated; the controller uses the one in each pool's zone --kubelet-dir /var/lib/kubelet Kubelet root directory (ROKS/ROVS: use /var/data/kubelet) --clone-worker-interval 10s Clone worker poll interval --golden-image-sync-interval 1h Golden image syncer poll interval (the Helm chart sets 5m) --node-metrics-addr :9810 Node mode: listen address of the HTTPS metrics endpoint with per-share used bytes and NFS statistics.
