Set by the Helm chart --receiver-auth-token-file /etc/replication/token File with the bearer token the receiver requires (receiver mode) --receiver-listen-addr :8443 Listen address of the receiver (receiver mode) --receiver-endpoint "" URL of the destination receiver (sync-client and check-receiver modes). Set by the replication controller --auth-token-file /etc/replication/token File with the bearer token the sync client sends (sync-client and check-receiver modes) --ca-cert-file "" CA certificate file for verifying receiver TLS cert (sync-client and check-receiver modes). Empty = system trust store --source-path "" Mounted source NFS path (sync-client mode). Set by the replication controller --dest-base-path "" Destination base path (sync-client mode). Set by the replication controller --sub-path "" SubVolume sub path (sync-client mode). Set by the replication controller --subvolume-name "" SubVolume CR name (sync-client mode). Set by the replication controller --metadata-json "" Serialized SubVolume metadata (sync-client mode). Set by the replication controller --staging-path "" VM disk copy staging file (apply-vm-disk mode). Set by the replication controller --disk-path "" Disk image to replace (apply-vm-disk mode). Set by the replication controller --from, --to "" Moments the destination disk and the copy show, RFC 3339 (apply-vm-disk mode). Set by the replication controller --full false The copy holds the whole disk (apply-vm-disk mode). Set by the replication controller --keep 24h How long restore points are kept (apply-vm-disk and send-vm-disk modes). Set by the replication controller --backup-disk, --out-disk "" The backed-up VM disk to read and the new disk to write (restore-vm-disk mode). Set by the backup restore Job --restore-moment "" Moment to restore, RFC 3339; empty for the latest (restore-vm-disk mode). Set by the backup restore Job --restore-files-spec "" JSON of the file restore: mode (measure, new-claim or folder), where the backup and the claim are mounted, owner, limits (restore-files mode). Set by the file restore Job --restore-files-paths "" The file that lists the paths to restore, one per line in escaped form. Paths are never arguments (restore-files mode). Set by the file restore Job --vm-group "" namespace/name of the VM that owns the disk (send-vm-disk mode). Set by the replication controller --copy-id "" Name of this copy attempt; a repeat with the same name resumes it (send-vm-disk mode). Set by the replication controller --poolbench-collector-addr :8080 Where the collector listens for the test VMs (poolbench mode) --poolbench-collector-url "" How the test VMs reach the collector, http://<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:8080 (poolbench mode). Set by the chart --poolbench-metrics-addr, --poolbench-metrics-cert-dir :8443, "" Metrics endpoint over HTTPS with token login; an empty folder makes a self-signed certificate (poolbench mode) --poolbench-results-addr :8444 Where the raw results are served to the console's plugin proxy, over HTTPS with the metrics certificate; each request carries the person's token, and the service checks that they may get the run (poolbench mode) --poolbench-health-addr :8081 Health probe endpoint (poolbench mode) --poolbench-results-dir /results Folder for the raw results of the test VMs (poolbench mode) --poolbench-interval 15s Time between two passes of the runner (poolbench mode) --poolbench-run-role, --poolbench-service-account "" The ClusterRole the service binds to its own service account in each run's namespace (poolbench mode). Set by the chart --node-metrics-service, --node-metrics-ca "" The node agents' metrics Service and the file with the CA of their certificate, for the share's counters (poolbench and controller modes). Set by the chart --node-metrics-account "" Controller mode: the service account whose short-lived token the controller sends to the node agents, so that copies of running VM disks can follow the load on the share. It may only read their /metrics. Without it, or without --node-metrics-service, the copies run at a fixed speed. Set by the chart

Key unwrap flags (--mode=unwrap-backup-key, run by the COS export and restore Jobs):

Flag Default Description --kp-region "" Key Protect region --kp-instance "" Key Protect instance ID --kp-root-key "" Key Protect root key ID --wrapped-key-file "" File with the backup key wrapped by Key Protect --api-key-file "" File with the IBM Cloud API key for Key Protect --emergency-key-file "" Optional file with the readable backup key, used only when Key Protect is down --key-out "" File to write the readable key to, mode 0400; it must not exist

Backup gateway flags (mode backup-gateway, set by the backupGateway.* chart values):

Flag Default Description --gateway-listen :8443 Address to listen on --gateway-tls-cert-file, --gateway-tls-key-file (required) The serving certificate. It is read again when the files change. The gateway is never served in plain HTTP --gateway-browse-namespace ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-browse Where the session Secrets are --gateway-session-wait 20s How long a request that asks to wait holds for the session to be ready; keep it under the proxy timeout --gateway-max-download-bytes 53687091200 Largest single file or tar --gateway-max-open-restores 10 File restores one user may have that have not ended. More are refused --gateway-auth-cache 10s How long a token review is kept; 0 checks every call. The right on the namespace is checked on every call regardless

Browse session flags of the controller (set by the backupBrowse.* chart values):

Flag Default Description --browse-image "" Image of the browse helper. Empty turns browse sessions off --browse-namespace ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-browse Namespace of the helper pods and the session Secrets --browse-guest-image "" Image of the helper that reads the file systems inside a VM disk. Empty turns browsing inside VM disks off --browse-guest-kvm false Ask the VM disk helper pod for the KVM device (devices.kubevirt.io/kvm) --browse-guest-cpu-limit "" CPU limit of the VM disk helper pod. Empty means 1 --browse-guest-memory-limit "" Memory limit of the VM disk helper pod. Empty means 1Gi --browse-guest-start-timeout 20m A session on a VM disk ends if its helper is not ready after this long --browse-image-pull-secrets "" Comma-separated names of the Secrets, in the driver namespace, that pull the browse image from a private registry. The chart sets it from imagePullSecrets --browse-idle 15m End a session after this long without use --browse-max-life 2h End a session after this long, even if in use --browse-max-sessions 5 Open sessions in the cluster. More wait --browse-max-sessions-per-namespace 2 Open sessions for the claims of one namespace. More wait --browse-cos true Let sessions and file restores read backups exported to COS. Their helper pods run in the driver namespace. Set by backupBrowse.restoreMaxBytes --file-restore-max-running 5 How many file restores run at once in the cluster. More wait. Set by backupBrowse.restoreMaxRunning

Flag Default Description --mode (required) browse-server --root (required unless --cos-source) The latest copy of the backup, mounted read-only --moments "" The folder of earlier moments (20261022T091500Z, ...). Needed for --at --at "" Read the newest moment at or before this time (RFC 3339) instead of the latest copy --tls-cert-file, --tls-key-file (required) The session certificate and key. The API is never served in plain HTTP --token-file (required) File that holds the session token (at least 16 characters) --cos-source "" JSON that names a backup exported to COS (endpoint, bucket, prefix, policy, volume, Key Protect root key; no secret in it). docs.title: On ROKS and ROVS: turn on user workload monitoring (required for alerts)
docs.text:
The driver's alerts and scraping live in the namespace ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring, which only OpenShift's user workload monitoring reads. Without it nothing evaluates the alerts. An admin turns it on once (the chart does not change this setting):

oc -n openshift-monitoring get configmap cluster-monitoring-config -o jsonpath='{.data.config\.yaml}'   # look for enableUserWorkload: true
# If it is missing, add "enableUserWorkload: true" to config.yaml:
oc -n openshift-monitoring edit configmap cluster-monitoring-config

See "Where alerts run on OpenShift" in MONITORING.md for why, and how to check it works.

docs.title: Step 4: Create a File Share Pool
docs.text:
Why this step? The driver is now installed, but it doesn't have any storage to hand out yet. A FileSharePool tells the driver to create one or more VPC file shares and use them as a pool. When applications request storage (via PVCs), the driver allocates a subdirectory on an existing share in the pool — no need to create a new VPC share each time.

Think of it like pre-provisioning a bookshelf: you buy the shelf (the VPC file share) once, then add books (PVCs) to it as needed.

Create a pool for your target zone (see also examples/basic/pool.yaml for a ready-to-use template):

# pool-general.yaml
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: general-purpose
spec:
  zone: us-south-1                   # Must match your worker node zone
  profile: dp2                        # VPC file storage performance profile
  shareSizeGB: 2000                   # 2 TB per share
  maxShares: 10                       # Up to 10 shares (20 TB total capacity)
  initialShares: 1                    # Create 1 share immediately
  autoExpand: true                    # Auto-create new shares when pool fills up
  expandThresholdPercent: 80          # Trigger expansion at 80% allocated
  allocationStrategy: spread          # Distribute PVCs evenly across shares
  defaultPermissions: "0755"
  defaultUID: 1000                    # UID owner for subdirectories
  defaultGID: 1000                    # GID owner for subdirectories
  resourceGroup: "your-resource-group-id"
  tags:
    - "env:production"
    - "managed-by:file-pool-csi"

kubectl apply -f pool-general.yaml

Wait for the pool to initialize (the first VPC file share takes 30-90 seconds to create):

# Watch pool status — press Ctrl+C when PHASE shows "Ready"
kubectl get filesharepools -w

# Detailed status (once ready)
kubectl get filesharepool general-purpose -o yaml

The pool is ready when status.phase is Ready and at least one share shows state: stable.

Automatic StorageClass: When the pool reaches Ready, the controller automatically creates a StorageClass named after the pool (e.g., general-purpose). A StorageClass is how Kubernetes knows which storage backend to use when you create a PVC — it's the link between "I want 10 Gi of storage" and "use this CSI driver with this pool". You do not need to create StorageClasses manually.

For tiered pools, one StorageClass per tier is created (e.g., general-purpose-standard, general-purpose-premium).

To opt out of automatic StorageClass creation, add the annotation storage.ibmcloud.io/skip-storageclass: "true" to the FileSharePool.

docs.title: Check all components are running
docs.text:
# CSI Driver registered — Kubernetes knows about our storage plugin
kubectl get csidriver vpc-file-pool.csi.ibm.io

# Controller pod (should be Running with all containers ready, e.g. 6/6)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller

# Node agent pods (one per worker node, all Running)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=node

# CRDs installed — the custom resource types the driver uses
kubectl get crd filesharepools.storage.ibmcloud.io
kubectl get crd subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io

# Pool is ready
kubectl get filesharepools

# StorageClass auto-created (named after the pool)
kubectl get storageclass general-purpose

docs.title: Smoke test with a PVC
docs.text:
This creates a PVC (Persistent Volume Claim) — a request for storage — and a pod that writes a file to it. If the file appears, everything is working end-to-end: Kubernetes asked the CSI driver for storage, the driver allocated a subdirectory on the pool, and the node agent mounted it into the pod.

# Create a test PVC (using the auto-created StorageClass named after the pool)
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: test-pool-pvc
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: general-purpose
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
EOF

# Should bind within seconds (not minutes!) — press Ctrl+C once STATUS=Bound
kubectl get pvc test-pool-pvc -w

# Check a SubVolume was created — this is the internal record of the allocation
kubectl get subvolumes

# Create a test pod that writes to the PVC
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-pool-pod
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
    - name: test
      image: busybox
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo 'Hello from pool CSI' > /data/test.txt && cat /data/test.txt && sleep 3600"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: test-pool-pvc
EOF

# Verify the pod is running and the file was written
kubectl logs test-pool-pod

# Clean up
kubectl delete pod test-pool-pod
kubectl delete pvc test-pool-pvc

If the PVC binds and the pod writes successfully, the installation is complete.

docs.title: Automated end-to-end tests
docs.text:
Instead of (or in addition to) the manual smoke test above, you can run the automated e2e tests. These are test scripts that live in test/e2e/ and do the same thing — create pools, PVCs, and pods, then verify everything works — but automatically and with more thorough checks.

The tests run on your workstation using go test, but they talk to the cluster remotely via your kubeconfig. The driver must already be deployed on the cluster (Steps 1-4 above) — the tests don't install it, they just exercise it.

# Set required environment variables — these tell the tests which zone
# and subnet to use when creating pools
export E2E_HOME_ZONE=us-south-1           # Your worker node zone
export E2E_ACCESSOR_ZONE=us-south-2       # A second zone for cross-zone tests
export E2E_ACCESSOR_SUBNET_ID=<subnet-id> # Subnet ID in the accessor zone

# Run the tests (compiles and runs test/e2e/*.go from your laptop)
make test-e2e

The tests create resources with an e2e- prefix and clean them up automatically when done. Two scenarios are tested:

  • BasicPool — creates a single-zone pool, provisions a PVC, mounts it in a pod, verifies it works
  • CrossZone — creates a pool with accessor zones, verifies multi-zone NFS access

docs.title: OpenShift Console Plugin
docs.text: The driver includes an OpenShift Console dynamic plugin that provides a visual dashboard for managing file share pools, SubVolumes, snapshots, and replication policies directly from the OpenShift web console.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• OpenShift 4.14+ with the ConsolePlugin v1 API
  • The CSI driver must already be installed (Steps 1-4 above)

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The plugin is on by default. On a cluster with the OpenShift console, a plain Helm install deploys it as a separate Deployment with its own Service. TLS certificates are auto-provisioned by the OpenShift service-ca operator (no cert-manager dependency for the plugin). On a cluster without the OpenShift console, the chart leaves the plugin out.

The chart also turns the plugin on in the console. A hook Job adds ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi to the console's plugin list after each install and upgrade, and keeps the other plugins. Before helm uninstall, a hook Job removes only this plugin from the list.

To leave the plugin out, set consolePlugin.enabled=false. If it was on before, the upgrade removes it from the console's plugin list.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text: Navigate to Admin → VPC File Pools in the OpenShift console. You should see the pool dashboard with capacity gauges and share status.

docs.title: Building the Plugin Image
docs.text:
If building from source:

make console-plugin-docker-build
# Pushes as: de.icr.io/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/console-plugin:$(VERSION)

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: Why is upgrading safe? The CSI driver runs as pods, but the actual NFS mounts are handled by the Linux kernel on each node. When the driver pods restart during an upgrade, existing mounts are unaffected — your applications keep reading and writing without interruption.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/ \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set image.tag=${NEW_VERSION}

The controller Deployment will rolling-update (replace one pod at a time). The node DaemonSet will update node-by-node.

docs.title: Raw Manifests
docs.text:
# Update image in manifests, then:
kubectl apply -f config/deploy/controller.yaml
kubectl apply -f config/deploy/node.yaml

docs.title: CRD Upgrades
docs.text:
If the new version introduces CRD field changes:

# Apply updated CRDs (additive changes are safe)
kubectl apply -f config/crd/

# For breaking changes, check the release notes and migration guide

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
Important order: Delete PVCs before the pool, and the pool before the driver. If you delete the driver first, there's nothing left to clean up the VPC file shares.

# 1. Delete all PVCs using the pool StorageClass first
kubectl delete pvc -l storageClassName=ibm-vpc-file-pool --all-namespaces

# 2. Wait for all SubVolumes to be cleaned up
kubectl get subvolumes  # Should be empty

# 3. Delete the FileSharePool(s)
#    WARNING: This deletes the underlying VPC file shares and all data on them
kubectl delete filesharepool --all

# 4. Uninstall the driver
helm uninstall ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi -n kube-system
# or, if you used raw manifests:
kubectl delete -f config/deploy/
kubectl delete -f config/rbac/

# 5. Remove CRDs (only if no resources remain)
kubectl delete -f config/crd/

# 6. Remove the API key secret (if you created one manually)
kubectl delete secret ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-secret -n kube-system

Warning: Deleting a FileSharePool will delete all VPC file shares in the pool and all data on them. Ensure all PVCs are deleted and data is backed up before removing a pool.

docs.title: Installation Troubleshooting
docs.text: If something goes wrong during installation, start with these quick checks:

docs.title: Pool stuck in Initializing
docs.text:
kubectl describe filesharepool <pool-name>
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller -c csi-controller --tail=100 | grep -i "error\|fail"

Common causes: wrong zone, invalid profile, VPC quota exceeded, TCP 2049 blocked, API key permissions.

docs.title: Driver pods CrashLoopBackOff
docs.text:
kubectl logs -n kube-system <pod-name> -c csi-controller --previous

Common causes: missing API key secret, wrong image tag, RBAC misconfiguration.

docs.title: Pods stuck in ErrImagePull
docs.text:
The cluster nodes can't download the driver image. This usually means the imagePullSecrets weren't set:

# Check if the all-icr-io secret exists
kubectl get secret all-icr-io -n kube-system

# Re-install with imagePullSecrets if missing from your Helm command
helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/ \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set 'imagePullSecrets[0].name=all-icr-io' \
  # ... other --set flags

docs.title: Pods stuck in ContainerCreating for a long time
docs.text:
Check the pod events for details:

kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n kube-system

If you see transient sd-bus or create container timeout errors, these are typically temporary — the kubelet will retry automatically.

For the full troubleshooting guide (PVC issues, mount failures, pool problems, VPC API errors, and more), see TROUBLESHOOTING.md.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text: Explicit list of what the IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver does not support, why, and available workarounds. For the meaning of project words, see CONTEXT.md.

docs.title: Quota Enforcement
docs.text:
What: Per-PVC quotas are advisory only. The driver records a requested size in the SubVolume CR and reports it via NodeGetVolumeStats, but does not enforce a hard capacity limit per subdirectory.

Why: VPC file shares expose a single NFS filesystem. NFS does not support per-directory quotas, and the VPC API provides no mechanism for subdirectory-level enforcement. Linux project quotas (xfs_quota) are not available on NFS mounts.

Workaround: Monitor per-PVC usage with the kubelet volume metrics (kubelet_volume_stats_*, which the node agent feeds through NodeGetVolumeStats) and alert at the threshold you want. The metrics.alerts.utilizationWarning and metrics.alerts.utilizationCritical Helm values control alert thresholds at the pool level.

Roadmap: No change planned — this is a fundamental NFS/VPC limitation.

docs.title: Snapshots and Clones
docs.text:
What: Volume snapshots (VolumeSnapshot) and volume cloning (dataSource in PVC) are implemented via directory-level copies on the NFS share. The controller has no NFS access, so a Kubernetes Job in the driver's namespace does each copy: cp -a from the source subdirectory to a .snapshots/ directory on the same share, and back again for a restore. A restored claim stays Pending until its copy has finished. Clones use a similar copy mechanism, and every clone is asynchronous: the SubVolume CR is created with cloneStatus=Pending, and the clone worker runs a Kubernetes Job that completes the copy. NodePublishVolume gates mount until the clone is Complete.

Limitations: - Snapshots and clones are not instantaneous — they are full data copies proportional to the source volume size. - A snapshot of a volume that is being written is not one point in time: files can change while the copy runs. Stop or freeze the workload before the snapshot if you need a consistent copy. The exception is a disk that a running KubeVirt VM uses: that snapshot is a QEMU copy at one moment, with the guest frozen for a moment (see below). - A snapshot of a running VM is made for each disk (each claim) as KubeVirt asks for it, but the driver copies all the pool disks of the VM at one moment, so the snapshots of the disks fit each other. A snapshot of one disk of a multi-disk VM therefore also copies the other disks to temporary files; the files of a disk that no snapshot claims within 10 minutes are deleted, and each share needs room for them. A disk that is not on a pool is not part of the moment. The copy starts at 15 MB/s and adapts to the load on the share, so the time a disk takes depends on that load; set vmCopySpeedLimitMBps on the VolumeSnapshotClass for the highest speed, or vmCopyAdaptive: "false" for a fixed speed (default 20 MB/s). Red Hat does not support the QEMU commands this uses. - Cross-share clones require the async path (no same-share optimization). - Per-PVC quota enforcement limitations (see above) also apply to cloned volumes. - No incremental or COW snapshots — each snapshot is a full copy.

Workaround: For very large volumes where copy time is unacceptable, consider application-level backup/restore tools.

Roadmap: Phase 4a (snapshots) and Phase 4b (clones) are complete.

docs.title: Instant VM disk snapshots (Experimental)
docs.text: Where the KubeVirt Sidecar feature gate is on, a VM disk snapshot is instant instead of a copy. See VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md. Its limits: - Support: the Sidecar feature gate is not supported by Red Hat, and on OpenShift it is set through a jsonpatch annotation on HyperConverged, which marks the cluster TaintedConfiguration. On ROVS, IBM's add-on manages that resource. - Gate off: a VM whose disks have instant snapshots does not start while the gate is off; the webhook says so. Turn the gate on, or run kubectl pool-snapshots flatten <vm>, which deletes the VM's snapshots. - Restore is a copy. OpenShift restores a snapshot into new PVCs; the driver writes each with one sparse qemu-img convert. Instant restore is not built. - One disk per plain VolumeSnapshot. All disks of a VM at one moment come from an OpenShift VM snapshot, which freezes the guest first. - Replication and backups of a VM disk make a full copy after each snapshot, because QEMU's list of changed blocks stays with the frozen file. A stopped VM's disk with snapshots is not copied at all (its status says so): a copy of its folder would give the far site an old disk.img. It is copied again while the VM runs, or after kubectl pool-snapshots flatten. - No clone of a disk with instant snapshots: restore one of its snapshots instead. A copy of the folder would not be a clone. - The disk file must be owned by UID 107 (the QEMU user). Only the owner can make the frozen file read-only. For another owner, the snapshot fails before anything changes, and the message names the owner and the fix (chown 107:107). - At most 16 snapshots per disk. Hot-plugged disks are not supported. - A deleted claim's folder stays while any of its instant snapshots exists.

docs.title: Volume Group Snapshots
docs.text:
What: Volume group snapshots (VolumeGroupSnapshot) are not active. The code and the record type exist, but nothing watches a VolumeGroupSnapshot, the hooks never run, and the CSI group snapshot service is not registered, so Kubernetes' group snapshot API cannot reach the driver. There is no plan to turn it on (issue #100). The console does not show them.

Not needed for VMs: a snapshot of a running VM with several disks already shows one moment (see the VM snapshot section above). KubeVirt does not use group snapshots.

The notes below describe the design, not a working feature.

How it works: Group snapshots iterate through the source PVCs sequentially, creating individual snapshots for each member. The order can be controlled via the csi.ibm.com/copy-order parameter (comma-separated PVC names). Two failure policies are supported:

  • Abort (default): If any member snapshot fails, all previously completed snapshots are rolled back and the operation returns an error.
  • Continue: If a member snapshot fails, the operation continues with remaining members and returns a PartialFailure status. Successfully completed snapshots are preserved.

Limitations: - Snapshots are sequential, not atomic — there is an inconsistency window between the first and last member snapshot (tracked in status.inconsistencyWindow). - Each member snapshot is a full directory copy (same as single-volume snapshots), so total time is proportional to the combined size of all source volumes. - All source PVCs must belong to the same pool. - Requires Kubernetes 1.32+ for the external VolumeGroupSnapshot API (the CSI-level RPCs work with any Kubernetes version).

Workaround: For applications requiring point-in-time consistency across volumes, quiesce writes at the application level before triggering the group snapshot.

Not working on ROVS (tested 19 Oct 2026, ROVS 4.21): nothing calls these RPCs. The chart runs csi-snapshotter without group snapshots turned on, and that sidecar only knows the upstream groupsnapshot.storage.k8s.io API. OpenShift has its own groupsnapshot.storage.openshift.io API, and only on clusters with a non-default feature set. See GitHub issue #14.

Roadmap: None. The code stays, and there is no plan to turn it on (issue #100).

docs.title: Cross-Region Replication and Disaster Recovery
docs.text:
What: The driver includes a built-in replication controller (Phase 4d) for cross-region disaster recovery. A ReplicationPolicy CRD defines which SubVolumes to replicate, the destination NFS server (reachable over Transit Gateway), and a schedule interval. The controller periodically copies SubVolume data from the source pool to the destination with rsync (direct NFS) or tar over HTTPS (receiver).

How it works: The replication controller runs as a background goroutine alongside the CSI controller. For each active ReplicationPolicy on schedule: 1. Lists SubVolumes in the source pool (optionally filtered by label selector) 2. Copies each matched SubVolume's directory to the destination, with rsync (direct NFS) or tar over HTTPS (driver to driver) 3. Updates per-SubVolume and per-policy replication status 4. Tracks consecutive failures and pauses the policy after exceeding maxRetries

Limitations: - File-level consistency only (without hooks). Each individual file is consistent (NFS close-to-open semantics), but cross-file consistency is NOT guaranteed unless pre/post-sync hooks are configured to quiesce application writes. See CROSS-REGION-DR.md for detailed consistency analysis. - Plain file replication is not suitable for databases or for running VM disks. Actively written disk images and databases with WALs will produce corrupted replicas. The controller copies the disks of a running KubeVirt VM with QEMU at one moment instead (Experimental, see FEATURES.md). Use IBM VPC block storage replication or application-level replication for these workloads. - Requires pre-configured cross-region network connectivity (Transit Gateway or VPN) and a pre-existing destination FileSharePool. - Failover is manual. Automated failover is explicitly out of scope due to limited consistency guarantees.

Best suited for: Static assets, model weights, log aggregation, workloads with non-zero RPO tolerance, and workloads that support quiesce hooks for application-consistent replication.

Workaround for unsupported workloads: Use application-level replication (PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL Group Replication, etc.) or IBM VPC block storage snapshots for crash-consistent DR.

Roadmap: Phase 4d (replication) and Phase 5 (hooks + incremental rsync) — implemented.

docs.title: statfs Reports Share-Level Stats
docs.text:
What: df and statfs calls inside a pod report the total capacity and usage of the entire NFS share, not the individual subdirectory.

Why: This is an NFS protocol limitation. NFS statfs returns filesystem-level statistics; there is no per-directory equivalent.

Workaround: Use NodeGetVolumeStats (exposed via kubectl describe pvc) for accurate per-PVC usage based on du. The kubelet volume metrics also report per-PVC usage.

Roadmap: No change planned — NFS protocol limitation.

docs.title: Migration from Stock CSI Driver
docs.text:
What: Migrating from the standard IBM VPC File CSI driver (1:1 PVC-to-share mapping) to the pool CSI driver requires data copying because the two drivers use fundamentally different storage models.

Why: Kubernetes does not support in-place changes to a PV's CSI driver. Migration requires creating new PVCs on the pool driver and copying data from the old PVCs.

Tool: The kubectl-migrate CLI tool automates the migration workflow:

# Build the migration tool
make build-migrate

# 1. Plan: discover PVCs to migrate
kubectl migrate plan --namespace default --storage-class ibm-vpc-file-5iops --target-pool general-purpose

# 2. Execute: migrate a specific PVC (creates new PVC, rsync data, verify)
kubectl migrate execute --namespace default --pvc my-data --target-pool general-purpose --target-storage-class general-purpose

# 3. Status: check migration progress
kubectl migrate status --namespace default

The tool creates a new PVC on the pool driver, launches a temporary pod that rsyncs data from the old PVC to the new one, and compares file counts. The new PVC is named <old name>-pooled. A pool's StorageClass has the same name as the pool, so --target-storage-class is the pool name. If the file counts differ, the pod fails and the tool reports the migration as failed. The pod uses the OpenShift tools image from the cluster's own registry (openshift/tools:latest), so it needs no package install and no pull secret, and it runs under the restricted rules as the user id that OpenShift gives the namespace. A user with only the edit role can run it. Because that user is not root, the copy cannot set owners or modes: the new files belong to the namespace's user (the same user that other pods of the namespace run as), and a file with mode 0600 or 0700 owned by someone else cannot be read, so it is not copied and the file counts differ. If a workload needs fixed owners (for example a VM disk that must belong to UID 107), set them after the copy. The old PVC is NOT deleted automatically — you switch your workloads to the new PVC and delete the old one when ready.

Limitations: - The tool finds the cluster like kubectl: the --kubeconfig flag, then the KUBECONFIG variable, then ~/.kube/config. - Migration speed depends on data volume and NFS throughput. - Applications must tolerate brief downtime or support live migration at the application layer. - The tool does not handle StatefulSet ordinal PVC naming automatically — migrate each PVC individually.

docs.title: IBM Cloud Satellite
docs.text:
What: Not supported. The driver requires IBM Cloud VPC infrastructure.

Why: Cloud Satellite locations do not have access to the VPC file share API. Satellite uses different storage backends (local disks, NetApp, etc.).

Workaround: Use the storage drivers provided by IBM Cloud Satellite for your location's infrastructure.

Roadmap: No support planned.

docs.title: VPC Classic Infrastructure
docs.text:
What: Not supported. The driver requires VPC Gen2 infrastructure.

Why: VPC Classic (Gen1) uses a different file storage API that is not compatible with the vpc-go-sdk file share operations used by this driver.

Workaround: Migrate to VPC Gen2 infrastructure. IBM has deprecated VPC Classic.

Roadmap: No support planned — VPC Classic is deprecated.

docs.title: Share Draining (Graceful Evacuation)
docs.text:
What: The driver supports graceful share draining via spec.drainShares. Adding a share ID to this list marks it as "draining," which excludes it from new allocations. The reconciler tracks drain progress in status.drainStatus, reporting remaining SubVolumes per share. Once all SubVolumes are removed (via application redeployment with new PVCs or manual PVC deletion), the share is reported as fully drained.

Note: Draining prevents new allocations to the share but does not automatically migrate existing data. Applications must be redeployed or PVCs manually deleted to complete the drain.

Usage: 

spec:
  drainShares:
    - "r006-share-to-drain"

Monitor progress via status.drainStatus or the DrainComplete condition.

docs.title: Hard NFS Mounts
docs.text:
What: The driver defaults to soft NFS mounts. Custom mount flags from the StorageClass are merged with the safe defaults (nfsvers=4.1,soft,timeo=600,retrans=3), so soft is always present unless the StorageClass explicitly includes hard.

Why: Hard NFS mounts cause pods to hang indefinitely if the NFS server becomes unreachable. With pooled storage, a single unresponsive share could freeze many pods simultaneously. Soft mounts return errors after the retry timeout, allowing applications to handle failures gracefully.

Override: If your workload requires hard mounts (e.g., applications that must not see transient I/O errors), add hard to the StorageClass mountOptions. This will replace the soft default. Use with caution — a VPC file share outage will cause all pods using hard-mounted shares to hang until the share recovers.

Safe customization: Adding options like noatime, rsize=1048576, or timeo=300 to the StorageClass will merge with the defaults without removing soft. Only hard explicitly replaces soft.

Roadmap: No change planned — soft remains the recommended and default setting.

docs.title: Cross-Zone Node Failover
docs.text:
What: Cross-zone accessor bindings (spec.accessorZones) create mount targets in multiple VPC zones, but the node agent always selects the mount target IP matching the node's own zone. If all nodes in a zone are lost, pods rescheduled to a different zone will use that zone's mount target IP (if configured). There is no automatic failover to a different zone's mount target for an already-mounted share.

Why: NFS mount targets are zone-local. A mount target in us-south-1 is only reachable from nodes in us-south-1. The driver selects the correct zone IP at mount time, not dynamically at runtime.

Workaround: Configure accessorZones for all zones where worker nodes may be scheduled. This ensures mount targets exist in every zone before pods arrive.

Roadmap: No change planned — this is by design. Zone-local mount targets are a VPC networking constraint.

docs.title: CDI (Containerized Data Importer) Compatibility
docs.text:
What: VMs come from the standard OpenShift Virtualization catalog. You pick a catalog image and choose the pool's StorageClass for the boot disk. CDI copies the image onto the pool. CDI registry import also works with the pool CSI driver.

Measured on rovslab, 20 October 2026:

  • CDI's copy pods have a default memory limit of 600 MB. A copy of RHEL 9 from Ceph onto a pool was killed for lack of memory, 3 of 3 times (also onto IBM VPC File). With a 2 GB limit it finished in 77 s.
  • A 25 GB copy from Ceph with a 2Gi limit was killed 6 times and never finished. With an 8Gi limit it finished in 134 s and the checksum matched. Memory sat at the limit, so a much larger disk is not proven.
  • A VM from the standard RHEL 9 catalog image onto a pool had its guest agent after 103 s.
  • A CDI DataVolume with a registry source, on a pool StorageClass, imported CentOS Stream 9 in about 40 seconds and RHEL 9 in about 2.5 minutes.

Earlier versions of this document said that CDI is incompatible with this driver, and later that a copy from Ceph onto a pool still fails. Both statements are out of date.

Copy pod memory limit: The controller keeps the memory limit of CDI's copy pods at least 8Gi, through HyperConverged spec.resourceRequirements.storageWorkloads (the setting Red Hat documents). It checks at start-up and every 5 minutes. If storageWorkloads is not set, it sets CDI's defaults with the memory raised (limits CPU 750m and memory 8Gi, requests CPU 100m and memory 60M). If it is set, the controller changes only limits.memory. It never lowers a limit. Each raise logs a warning and adds 1 to vpc_file_pool_cdi_copy_limit_raised_total. Helm value: cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit.

ROVS caveat: IBM says the virtualization add-on is pre-configured and cannot be modified, and IBM's add-on creates the HyperConverged object. The driver changes one field of it. After an add-on update, check the metric and the controller log for a new warning, and check the limit again (see TROUBLESHOOTING.md). Where changing HyperConverged is not allowed, set cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit="". Then catalog copies of large disks onto the pool fail.

Golden images (hidden): The pool's golden image syncer uses CDI registry import. It is kept for possible later use, and the console pool form no longer offers it. The standard catalog is the recommended way. See GOLDEN-IMAGE-WORKFLOW.md.

Important: KubeVirt requires raw format disk images for filesystem-mode PVCs. It passes them to QEMU with "driver":"file" (no qcow2 format layer). If a qcow2 image is written to the PVC without conversion, the VM shows "No bootable device". CDI converts the image automatically. Convert by hand (qemu-img convert -f qcow2 -O raw) only if you write images to the pool yourself.

StorageProfile: The controller automatically patches CDI's StorageProfile CR for each pool StorageClass, setting claimPropertySets: [{accessModes: ["ReadWriteMany"], volumeMode: Filesystem}] and cloneStrategy: csi-clone, so CDI asks the driver to make clones. CDI's snapshot clone does not work with this driver, and CDI's host-assisted copy pods need a memory limit above their 600 MB default when they write onto NFS (see above). The patch sets claimPropertySets only when it is empty, but it sets cloneStrategy to csi-clone whenever it has any other value, so a change you make to cloneStrategy is overwritten on the next reconcile. The patching is non-fatal (errors are logged but don't block reconciliation). CDI detection is cached — if CDI is not installed, the check runs once and is skipped on subsequent reconciles.

Golden Image Automation (hidden): The driver includes a golden image syncer that automates OS image provisioning for KubeVirt. Two modes are supported:

  1. Native CDI mode: Make the pool StorageClass the cluster default. CDI then imports and snapshots golden images on pool storage.
  2. Custom syncer mode: When another StorageClass is the default, enable spec.goldenImages on the FileSharePool. The controller discovers CDI DataImportCron images and imports each one with a CDI DataVolume on the pool StorageClass. It also creates CDI DataSource CRs (for the InstanceTypes catalog tab) and OpenShift Template CRs (for the Templates catalog tab). Creating a VM from the InstanceTypes tab with its boot disk on the pool is being tested.

See GOLDEN-IMAGE-WORKFLOW.md for setup instructions.

docs.title: KubeVirt NFS Permissions (root_squash)
docs.text:
What: KubeVirt's virt-handler calls chown(mountDir, 107, 107) on every filesystem-mode PVC mount. IBM Cloud VPC file shares enforce NFS root_squash — root (UID 0) is mapped to nobody (UID 65534). Without sec=sys, the NFS mount defaults to sec=null (anonymous auth) where chown fails for all UIDs and VMs cannot start.

Why: VPC file shares in security-group mode default-negotiate to sec=null unless the client explicitly requests sec=sys (AUTH_UNIX). With sec=null, all operations are anonymous (UID 99), chown is impossible, and virt-handler fails with preparing host-disks failed: chown ... operation not permitted.

Fix: The CSI driver mounts with sec=sys in its default NFS mount options (matching the stock IBM VPC File CSI driver). With sec=sys, standard Unix UID/GID credentials are sent in NFS RPCs, root_squash maps only UID 0, and chown works for non-root UIDs.

Configure the FileSharePool for KubeVirt: 

spec:
  defaultPermissions: "0777"
  defaultUID: 107
  defaultGID: 107

If you write boot disk images to the pool yourself, convert qcow2 to raw format first (see CDI Compatibility above). CDI does this for you when it imports an image. For a manual conversion, use quay.io/centos/centos:stream9 which provides qemu-img via dnf install. The pod runs as root to install packages; due to NFS root_squash the raw file is created as UID 65534. Use chmod 0666 so the QEMU user (UID 107) can read and write the image.

Note: If mounting with custom StorageClass mountOptions, always include sec=sys. Omitting it causes NFS to negotiate sec=null, breaking chown and KubeVirt.

Roadmap: Fixed in v0.10.0 (sec=sys mount option). See TUTORIAL.md for a complete worked example.

docs.title: NFS Encryption in Transit
docs.text:
What: IBM Cloud VPC File Storage supports optional encryption in transit (IPsec) for NFS connections, but this feature is not available on bare metal servers or RHCOS-based virtual server instances.

Why: IBM Cloud's encryption in transit implementation uses IPsec between the compute host and the file share mount target. This mechanism is not supported on:

  • Bare metal servers — IPsec for file shares is not available on VPC bare metal.
  • RHCOS-based virtual server instances — Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (used by ROKS, ROVS and other OpenShift worker nodes) is explicitly unsupported.
  • Only supported on regular VPC virtual server instances running non-RHCOS Linux distributions.

Since ROKS and ROVS worker nodes run RHCOS, encryption in transit cannot be enabled for this driver on ROKS or ROVS clusters. NFS traffic travels unencrypted within the VPC network.

Mitigations: - Data at rest is always encrypted (provider-managed or customer-managed keys via Key Protect / HPCS). - VPC network traffic is isolated to your VPC — it does not traverse the public internet. - Use VPC security groups to restrict NFS traffic (TCP 2049) to only your worker node subnets (see SECURITY.md hardening checklist).

Roadmap: No change planned — this is an IBM Cloud platform limitation. Monitor the VPC file storage documentation for updates to supported compute types.

docs.title: VPC Account Quota
docs.text:
What: IBM Cloud VPC accounts are limited to 300 file shares per account. This quota is shared with the standard IBM VPC File CSI driver.

Why: This is an IBM Cloud platform limit, not a driver limitation.

Workaround: The pool driver significantly reduces share consumption by hosting many PVCs per share. A single pool with 5 shares can serve hundreds of PVCs. Request a quota increase via IBM Cloud support if needed.

Roadmap: No change planned — platform quota.

docs.title: Alerts Need User Workload Monitoring (OpenShift)
docs.text: The driver runs in kube-system, which OpenShift's platform monitoring does not read, and Red Hat does not support labelling it so that it does. The chart puts the ServiceMonitor objects and the alerts in the namespace ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring for user workload monitoring. If user workload monitoring is off, there are no alerts at all (and the controller logs a warning at start). The cluster admin must set enableUserWorkload: true in openshift-monitoring/cluster-monitoring-config; see MONITORING.md. The monitoring namespace needs webhook.certProvider=openshift; with another provider the chart keeps the older layout in the release namespace.

docs.title: Backups to a Snapshot Pool
docs.text:
What: a BackupPolicy backs up selected PVCs and VMs into a snapshot pool (see BACKUP-RECOVERY.md).

Limitations: - A volume stays on the share it was first backed up to. Backups are not moved when a share is added or fills up, and a share that holds backups must not be removed from the pool. - Above 85% full, the policies stop new backups of that share and never delete backups to make room. Free space with kubectl backup delete or a shorter keepFor. - Backups of a deleted volume stay on the share, and can be restored, until the keep time has passed since the last backup. kubectl backup delete removes the backups of a volume. - A backup of a volume that is not a VM disk is a file copy. It is as consistent as the files are. - Backups are in the same VPC as the data, and are not encrypted or locked beyond what the file share does. Export to a COS bucket with a lock (spec.export) is built. Export and restore into the same cluster were proved against real IBM Cloud in stage 18 of the release test. Not yet proved: the emergency-key restore and a restore in the other (DR) cluster. - A restore needs the snapshot pool to be ready, and waits while a copy is being written to the backup of that volume.

docs.title: Monitoring Guide — IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver
docs.text: Complete metrics reference, alerting rules, and dashboard templates for operating the pool CSI driver in production.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The controller exposes Prometheus metrics on :8080/metrics over HTTPS (callers need a token that may get /metrics). All metrics use the vpc_file_pool_ or pool_csi_ prefix and follow the Prometheus naming conventions.

The driver emits 37 metrics across nine categories:

Category Metrics Purpose Allocation 9 PVC provisioning health and capacity VPC API 2 API call success rate and latency Snapshots 2 Snapshot operation tracking Clones 2 Clone operation tracking Group Snapshots 4 Multi-PVC snapshot coordination Replication 5 Cross-region DR health CDI 1 CDI copy pod memory limit Backup 6 Backup policy health, age of backups, fullness of the snapshot pool and lateness of the export to COS Share (node agent) 6 Bytes written on each share, and NFS operations, latency and bytes of each share, read by the node agents

The PoolBench service, when it is turned on, adds its own PoolBench metrics for the VMs of a performance test run.

docs.title: Where alerts run on OpenShift
docs.text:
On OpenShift (ROKS and ROVS) the alerts and the scraping need user workload monitoring to be on. If it is off, nothing evaluates the alerts, and no alert ever fires.

Why: the driver must stay in kube-system (the managed API key secret storage-secret-store lives there). OpenShift's platform monitoring reads only namespaces labelled openshift.io/cluster-monitoring=true, and Red Hat says not to put that label on namespaces that are not part of the platform, and not to create your own ServiceMonitor or PrometheusRule objects in kube-* or openshift-* namespaces. So platform monitoring cannot read the driver where it lives.

What the chart does instead (metrics.monitoring.mode: auto, which applies when the cluster has the Prometheus Operator API and the OpenShift console and webhook.certProvider=openshift):

  • It makes a small namespace, ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring (change it with metrics.monitoring.namespace). It has no platform monitoring label.
  • The two ServiceMonitor objects (controller and node agents) and the PrometheusRule live in that namespace. User workload monitoring reads them.
  • Two Services there have no selector. The controller keeps their Endpoints up to date every minute (the controller pod's IP, and the IP of each ready node agent; node agents use the host network). Kubernetes mirrors them to EndpointSlices.
  • The ServiceMonitor objects send the token of a service account in that namespace (kept in a Secret, because user workload monitoring does not read files) and trust the OpenShift service CA from a ConfigMap in that namespace. They check the certificate against the names of the Services in kube-system, which is what the service CA issued it for.
  • The chart never changes cluster-monitoring-config.

The admin step. Turn user workload monitoring on once per cluster. The chart does not do this, because it is a cluster-wide setting that belongs to the cluster admin:

# If the ConfigMap does not exist yet:
cat <<'YAML' | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cluster-monitoring-config
  namespace: openshift-monitoring
data:
  config.yaml: |
    enableUserWorkload: true
YAML
# If it exists, add "enableUserWorkload: true" to its config.yaml instead:
oc -n openshift-monitoring edit configmap cluster-monitoring-config

How to check that alerts are evaluated:

oc -n openshift-user-workload-monitoring get pods          # prometheus-user-workload and thanos-ruler-user-workload are Running
oc -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring get servicemonitor,prometheusrule,endpoints
oc -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring get events           # no UserWorkloadMonitoringOff warning

In the console, Observe > Alerting shows the driver's alerts under "Alerting rules" (choose the monitoring project). The controller also checks at start: if user workload monitoring is off it logs a warning and records a UserWorkloadMonitoringOff event on the monitoring namespace. It checks only at start, so restart the controller after you turn it on to clear the warning.

On clusters without OpenShift (or with metrics.monitoring.mode=disabled) the ServiceMonitor objects and the PrometheusRule stay in the release namespace, as before, and your Prometheus must read that namespace.

Red Hat sources:

  • Turning on user workload monitoring (enableUserWorkload: true in cluster-monitoring-config; needs cluster-admin; then check that the prometheus-operator, prometheus-user-workload and thanos-ruler-user-workload pods run in openshift-user-workload-monitoring): OpenShift 4.18 documentation (the setting is the same in 4.21, as tested on rovslab-dr-eude running 4.21.31), Configuring user workload monitoring.
  • Support guidance that you should not create your own ServiceMonitor objects in openshift-* or kube-* projects: https://access.redhat.com/node/7024333.
  • Support guidance that you should not put the openshift.io/cluster-monitoring label on your own namespaces: https://access.redhat.com/solutions/6992399.
  • Keeping a project out of user workload monitoring (label openshift.io/user-monitoring=false; the monitoring namespace of this chart must not have it): Disabling monitoring for user-defined projects (Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS documentation; the label works the same way in OpenShift Container Platform).

docs.title: Prometheus Operator (ServiceMonitor)
docs.text:
The node agents serve their own metrics (the "Share Metrics (Node Agent)" section) over HTTPS on port node.metricsPort (9810). The caller must send a bearer token that the API server accepts, and its user must be allowed to get the URL /metrics. The chart makes a headless Service and a second ServiceMonitor (<release>-node) that send the pod's service account token, and it binds a <release>-metrics-reader ClusterRole to metrics.scraper.serviceAccount (prometheus-k8s in openshift-monitoring). The node agent serves a certificate that Prometheus checks (the token it sends is its own, so it must not go to a stranger). The certificate comes from webhook.certProvider, as for the webhooks: openshift asks the service CA (the ServiceMonitor trusts the service CA bundle that OpenShift's Prometheus mounts); cert-manager makes a Certificate; manual needs a secret <release>-ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-node-metrics-certs with tls.crt, tls.key and ca.crt, made by you, in the release namespace. With the last two the ServiceMonitor trusts ca.crt of that secret. The name it checks is <release>-ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-node-metrics.<namespace>.svc. The node agents need to read FileSharePools to name the shares. Set node.metricsPort=0 to turn the endpoint off.

The controller's :8080/metrics is HTTPS with the same token login and a certificate Prometheus checks, from webhook.certProvider (secret <release>-ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-metrics-certs for manual). Anything that scraped it over plain HTTP, such as your own Prometheus config, must now use https, a bearer token and the CA.

The Helm chart creates a ServiceMonitor for the controller when the cluster has the Prometheus Operator API (monitoring.coreos.com/v1). OpenShift has it. To turn it off, set metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=false.

The console plugin's charts read these metrics. Without the ServiceMonitor, they show no data. The console queries 19 of the first 22 metrics on its other pages, and the other three are charted in the Monitoring tab's "Group Snapshot and CDI Activity" section; the two per-share metrics are used by the VPCFilePoolShareNearlyFull alert and have no panel; the VM copy metrics named in the VM-safe replication spec do not exist yet, so they have no panel.

docs.title: OpenShift User Workload Monitoring
docs.text:
On OpenShift, user workload monitoring must be on for Prometheus to read the ServiceMonitor in kube-system:

oc -n openshift-monitoring get configmap cluster-monitoring-config -o yaml | grep enableUserWorkload

Check that Prometheus scrapes the controller (tested on ROVS 4.21):

oc -n openshift-user-workload-monitoring exec -c prometheus prometheus-user-workload-0 -- \
  curl -s 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=vpc_file_pool_share_count'

docs.title: Manual Scrape Config (prometheus.yml)
docs.text:
If not using the Prometheus Operator, add a scrape job:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'vpc-file-pool-csi'
    kubernetes_sd_configs:
      - role: pod
        namespaces:
          names: ['kube-system']
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app_kubernetes_io_component]
        regex: controller
        action: keep
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_container_port_number]
        regex: "8080"
        action: keep
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_namespace]
        target_label: namespace
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_name]
        target_label: pod

docs.title: Verifying Scrape
docs.text:
# Port-forward to the metrics endpoint
kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-metrics 8080:8080 &

# Check that metrics are being exported
curl -s http://localhost:8080/metrics | grep vpc_file_pool | head -20

# Clean up
kill %1

docs.title: Allocation Metrics
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_allocations_total Counter pool, status Total subvolume allocations. status is success, error, deallocate_success or deallocate_error. vpc_file_pool_allocation_duration_seconds Histogram pool Time to allocate a subvolume. Buckets: 10ms to ~163s (exponential). vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb Gauge pool Total pool capacity in GB across all shares. vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb Gauge pool Total allocated (requested) capacity in GB. vpc_file_pool_share_count Gauge pool Number of VPC file shares in the pool. vpc_file_pool_max_shares Gauge pool Most shares the pool may have (spec.maxShares). vpc_file_pool_share_total_gb Gauge pool, share Provisioned size of one share of the pool in GB. share is the VPC share name. vpc_file_pool_share_allocated_gb Gauge pool, share Capacity allocated to PVCs on one share, in GB. This is what PVCs asked for, not what they wrote. vpc_file_pool_pvc_count Gauge pool Number of active PVCs (SubVolumes) in the pool.

Normal ranges:

Metric Healthy Range Investigate If allocations_total{status="error"} 0 Any errors — check controller logs allocation_duration_seconds < 1s (p99) > 5s — pool may be expanding or unhealthy capacity_gb - allocated_gb > 20% of capacity < 10% — pool approaching full share_count 1 to maxShares At maxShares — cannot auto-expand

docs.title: VPC API Metrics
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_api_calls_total Counter operation, status Total VPC API calls. operation is the API method (e.g., create_share, get_share). status is success or error. vpc_file_pool_api_call_duration_seconds Histogram operation VPC API call duration. Buckets: 100ms to ~1638s (exponential).

Normal ranges:

Metric Healthy Range Investigate If api_calls_total{status="error"} 0 in steady state Sustained errors — check VPC API status, auth, quotas api_call_duration_seconds 1-90s for create_share, < 5s for get_share > 120s — VPC API may be degraded

docs.title: Snapshot Metrics
docs.text: Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_snapshots_total Counter pool, operation, status Snapshot operations. operation: create, delete, restore. status: success, error. vpc_file_pool_snapshot_duration_seconds Histogram pool, operation Time for snapshot operations. Proportional to data size.

docs.title: Clone Metrics
docs.text: Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_clones_total Counter pool, status Clone operations by outcome. status: success, error (request accepted or rejected by the controller), async_success, async_error (copy Job finished). vpc_file_pool_clone_duration_seconds Histogram pool Time from the clone worker picking up a clone to the end of its copy Job.

docs.title: Group Snapshot Metrics
docs.text: Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_group_snapshots_total Counter pool, operation, status Group snapshot operations. operation: create, delete. vpc_file_pool_group_snapshot_duration_seconds Histogram pool, operation Time for group snapshot operations (total, all members). vpc_file_pool_group_snapshot_member_count Histogram pool Number of PVCs per group snapshot. Buckets: 1 to 20. vpc_file_pool_group_snapshot_inconsistency_window_ms Histogram pool Time between first and last member copy in milliseconds. Lower is better for consistency.

docs.title: Replication Metrics
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Description pool_csi_replication_sync_total Counter policy, source_pool, result Replication sync attempts. result: success or failure. pool_csi_replication_sync_duration_seconds Histogram policy, source_pool Duration of replication sync cycles. pool_csi_replication_lag_seconds Gauge policy, source_pool Current replication lag (seconds since last successful sync). This is your RPO indicator. pool_csi_replication_consecutive_failures Gauge policy, source_pool Current consecutive failure count. Policy pauses after exceeding maxRetries. pool_csi_replication_subvolume_count Gauge policy, source_pool Number of SubVolumes being replicated per policy.

Normal ranges:

Metric Healthy Range Investigate If replication_lag_seconds < 2x the schedule interval > 3x schedule — sync is falling behind replication_consecutive_failures 0 > 0 — check connectivity to destination NFS replication_sync_duration_seconds < schedule interval > schedule — syncs overlap, data too large

docs.title: CDI Metrics
docs.text: Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_cdi_copy_limit_raised_total Counter none Times the controller raised the memory limit of CDI's copy pods (HyperConverged spec.resourceRequirements.storageWorkloads) to cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit. The controller also logs a warning each time. The first raise is normal. A later raise means something, such as an update of IBM's add-on, put the old value back.

docs.title: Share Metrics (Node Agent)
docs.text:
Each node agent reads the NFS shares mounted on its node, every --share-stats-interval (30 s). It reads the NFS counters in /proc/self/mountstats and runs statfs on the share mount, up to 8 mounts at once; it never walks the files. pool and share are the same names as the controller's per-share metrics. A share mounted on several nodes is reported by each node (the scrape adds an instance label), so use max by (pool, share) for the space metrics and sum by (pool, share) for the traffic counters. A share that is mounted nowhere has no series. A share whose pool cannot be found has pool="unknown".

Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_share_used_bytes Gauge pool, share Bytes written on the share (size minus free, from statfs). Absent when statfs fails or takes more than 10 s; after a failure the node agent does not try that mount again for 5 minutes. vpc_file_pool_share_size_bytes Gauge pool, share Size of the share as the NFS client sees it. vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_operations_total Counter pool, share, op NFS operations done by this node. op is read, write or other (all metadata calls). rate() of read and write is the IOPS. vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_rtt_seconds_total Counter pool, share, op Seconds spent between sending a request and getting the reply (the network and the server). vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_execute_seconds_total Counter pool, share, op Seconds from queueing a request to its end (the round trip plus the wait in the client). Latency per request is rate(execute) / rate(operations). vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_bytes_total Counter pool, share, direction Bytes read from and written to the share.

Latency per request, per share:

sum by (pool, share, op) (rate(vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_execute_seconds_total{op=~"read|write"}[5m]))
/ (sum by (pool, share, op) (rate(vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_operations_total{op=~"read|write"}[5m])) > 0)

docs.title: Backup Metrics
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_backup_volumes Gauge policy Number of volumes a backup policy backs up. vpc_file_pool_backup_stalest_age_seconds Gauge policy Age of the newest backup of the volume that was backed up longest ago. A volume that was never backed up counts from the time the policy was made. This is the RPO indicator of a backup policy. vpc_file_pool_backup_oldest_age_seconds Gauge policy Age of the oldest backup the policy keeps. It should stay near keepFor. vpc_file_pool_backup_export_oldest_unexported_age_seconds Gauge policy Age of the oldest backup moment that is in the snapshot pool and not yet in COS. 0 when everything is exported. Only for policies with spec.export. vpc_file_pool_backup_export_newest_age_seconds Gauge policy Age of the newest export to COS (the moment it sent). Before the first export, it counts from the time the policy was made, once a backup exists. Only for policies with spec.export. This is the RPO indicator of the COS copy. vpc_file_pool_backup_snapshot_pool_used_percent Gauge pool, share Percent of a share of the snapshot pool that is used, read by a Job about every 10 minutes (df). The controller cannot see this from custom resources: a pool counts only claims, not backups. Above 85%, the policies stop new backups to that share.

Copy results of backups are in the replication metrics: the policies the controller makes are named backup-<policy>-<source pool>.

Alert when a backup is late, using twice the schedule as the limit (here 12 hours for a 6-hour schedule):

- alert: BackupLate
  expr: vpc_file_pool_backup_stalest_age_seconds > 12 * 3600
  for: 15m
  annotations:
    summary: "Backup policy {{ $labels.policy }} has a volume with no backup for over 12 hours"

Alert when the copy in COS is late, using twice the export schedule as the limit (here 12 hours for a spec.export.schedule of 6h; with no export schedule, use twice the backup schedule). The first alert is the age of the newest export; the second is a moment that waits too long to go out:

- alert: ExportLate
  expr: vpc_file_pool_backup_export_newest_age_seconds > 12 * 3600
  for: 15m
  annotations:
    summary: "Backup policy {{ $labels.policy }} has not exported to COS for over 12 hours"

- alert: ExportMomentWaiting
  expr: vpc_file_pool_backup_export_oldest_unexported_age_seconds > 12 * 3600
  for: 15m
  annotations:
    summary: "Backup policy {{ $labels.policy }} has a backup moment that has waited over 12 hours to go to COS"

An export problem never stops the backups to the snapshot pool. status.volumes[].exportError says what failed.

Alert before the snapshot pool reaches the limit, and when it has. At 85% the policies on the pool stop new backups; they never delete backups to make room, so the fix is more space or a shorter keepFor:

- alert: SnapshotPoolNearlyFull
  expr: vpc_file_pool_backup_snapshot_pool_used_percent > 75
  for: 30m
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "Snapshot pool {{ $labels.pool }} is {{ $value }}% full; new backups stop at 85%"

- alert: SnapshotPoolFullBackupsStopped
  expr: vpc_file_pool_backup_snapshot_pool_used_percent > 85
  for: 15m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Snapshot pool {{ $labels.pool }} is {{ $value }}% full; new backups are stopped"

docs.title: PoolBench Metrics
docs.text:
The PoolBench service publishes these for the test VMs of a performance test run (docs/specs/2026-10-25-poolbench.md). Each test VM sends one result after each load phase; the values are those of the VM's last phase. The console's live graphs read them. The series of a run go away when the run is deleted.

Metric Type Labels Description poolbench_vm_iops Gauge run, vm, os, phase Reads plus writes a second of the VM's last phase. phase is steady or burst. poolbench_vm_latency_seconds Gauge run, vm, os, phase, quantile Latency of the last phase at quantile 0.5, 0.95 and 0.99, the worse of read and write. Total latency, which includes the wait before the I/O is sent. poolbench_vm_throughput_bytes_per_second Gauge run, vm, os, phase Read plus write throughput of the last phase. poolbench_vm_stalls_total Counter run, vm, os Phases whose longest I/O took more than 5 seconds. poolbench_vm_results_total Counter run, vm, os Result lines received. poolbench_vm_last_result_timestamp_seconds Gauge run, vm, os Time of the last result. A VM that stops sending is stuck or cannot reach the service. poolbench_run_vms Gauge run, os Test VMs of the run, by OS (linux, windows). 0 after the cleanup. poolbench_run_ready_vms Gauge run Test VMs of the run that have said they are ready. poolbench_run_step Gauge run The current step, from 1.

The chart scrapes the service like the controller: with a ServiceMonitor in the release namespace, or, with user workload monitoring, through a Service in the monitoring namespace whose Endpoints the controller keeps. The metrics port serves a certificate for <release>-poolbench.<namespace>.svc from the same source as the other metrics certificates (webhook.certProvider).

docs.title: Alerting Rules
docs.text:
The chart ships these alerts as a PrometheusRule (on by default; it is made only when the cluster has the Prometheus Operator API). Set the limits under metrics.alerts (see HELM-VALUES.md). A pool with no capacity, or a driver with no traffic, gives no alert. The rules are tested with promtool in make test-scripts.

Alert Severity Fires when VPCFilePoolUtilizationWarning / Critical warning / critical Pool use is above 80% / 95% VPCFilePoolOverCommitted critical More is allocated than the pool has VPCFilePoolShareNearlyFull warning One share has more than 90% of its size allocated for 15 minutes. With the binpack strategy shares fill one after another on purpose, so expect this alert there; raise metrics.alerts.shareUtilizationWarning or turn it off by setting it to 100. VPCFilePoolShareUsedHigh / Critical warning / critical One share has more than 85% / 95% of its size written (real used bytes) for 15 minutes. Max over the nodes that mount it. VPCFilePoolShareNFSLatencyHigh warning Reads or writes on one share take more than 0.1 s each on average for 10 minutes. Judged only while the share does at least 1 such request a second, so an idle share gives no alert and no NaN. VPCFilePoolShareIOPSHigh warning Reads plus writes on one share, all nodes together, are above metrics.alerts.shareIOPSWarning per second. Off by default (value 0): set it near the IOPS of the share profile. VPCFilePoolAtMaxShares warning The pool has its most shares and use is above the warning limit VPCFilePoolControllerDown critical No metrics from the controller for 5 minutes VPCFilePoolAllocationFailures critical More than 0.1 failed allocations per second VPCFilePoolAllocationSlow warning P99 allocation time above 5 s VPCFilePoolAPIErrors warning More than 0.05 failed VPC API calls per second VPCFilePoolSnapshotFailures warning Snapshot operations fail VPCFilePoolReplicationLagHigh / ReplicationFailing warning / critical Lag over 2 h, or more than 3 failures in a row VPCFilePoolBackupLate warning A volume has no backup for over 12 h VPCFilePoolExportLate / ExportMomentWaiting warning The COS copy is over 12 h late VPCFilePoolSnapshotPoolNearlyFull / Full warning / critical A snapshot pool share is above 75% / 85%

Per-share NFS latency and IOPS come from the node agents, which read the NFS client counters of each staged share (the vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_* metrics). The two alerts for them judge only a share that has real traffic.

Console dashboard. The dashboard's "Firing Alerts" card asks the cluster Prometheus (/api/prometheus) for firing alerts named VPCFilePool*. It also asks which alert rules that Prometheus has loaded; if it has none of the driver's, the card says so and does not claim that no alert is firing. OpenShift's platform Prometheus loads rules only from namespaces it watches (openshift-*, or kube-* with the openshift.io/cluster-monitoring label); if the chart is installed in another namespace, the rules need user workload monitoring, which the console queries through a different route that this card does not use.

The examples below are older hand-written rules, kept to show how to write your own. They use different names; if you load them as well as the chart's, you get two alerts for the same problem.

docs.title: Critical Alerts
docs.text:
These require immediate attention — they indicate data loss risk or service degradation.

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: vpc-file-pool-csi-critical
  namespace: kube-system
  labels:
    app: vpc-file-pool-csi
spec:
  groups:
    - name: vpc-file-pool-csi.critical
      rules:

        - alert: PoolAtMaxCapacity
          expr: |
            vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb / vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb > 0.95
            and
            vpc_file_pool_share_count >= vpc_file_pool_share_count
          for: 5m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "Pool {{ $labels.pool }} is over 95% allocated"
            description: "Pool {{ $labels.pool }} has less than 5% capacity remaining. New PVC requests will fail if the pool cannot expand. Check maxShares and VPC quota."
            runbook_url: "TROUBLESHOOTING.md#pool-full--maxshares-reached"

        - alert: PoolAtMaxShares
          expr: vpc_file_pool_share_count >= 300
          for: 1m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "Pool {{ $labels.pool }} may be at VPC account share limit (300)"
            description: "The pool has 300+ shares, which is the VPC account default limit. New share creation will fail."
            runbook_url: "TROUBLESHOOTING.md#quota-exceeded-300-shares"

        - alert: AllocationFailureRate
          expr: rate(vpc_file_pool_allocations_total{status="error"}[5m]) > 0.1
          for: 5m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "High allocation failure rate in pool {{ $labels.pool }}"
            description: "More than 0.1 allocation failures per second sustained for 5 minutes. PVC creation is failing."
            runbook_url: "TROUBLESHOOTING.md#pvc-issues"

        - alert: ControllerDown
          expr: absent(up{job="ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-metrics"} == 1)
          for: 5m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "VPC File Pool CSI controller is down"
            description: "No metrics received from the controller for 5 minutes. New PVC operations are blocked."

        - alert: ReplicationPaused
          expr: pool_csi_replication_consecutive_failures > 3
          for: 10m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "Replication policy {{ $labels.policy }} is paused due to failures"
            description: "Replication has {{ $value }} consecutive failures and is likely paused. DR data is stale."
            runbook_url: "CROSS-REGION-DR.md"

docs.title: Warning Alerts
docs.text:
These indicate potential issues that should be investigated during business hours.

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: vpc-file-pool-csi-warning
  namespace: kube-system
  labels:
    app: vpc-file-pool-csi
spec:
  groups:
    - name: vpc-file-pool-csi.warning
      rules:

        - alert: PoolNearCapacity
          expr: vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb / vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb > 0.85
          for: 10m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "Pool {{ $labels.pool }} is over 85% allocated"
            description: "Pool is nearing capacity. Verify autoExpand is enabled and maxShares has room."

        - alert: AllocationSlowdown
          expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(vpc_file_pool_allocation_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) > 5
          for: 10m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "Slow PVC allocations in pool {{ $labels.pool }}"
            description: "P99 allocation latency is {{ $value }}s (expected < 1s). Pool may be expanding or degraded."

        - alert: VPCAPIErrorRate
          expr: rate(vpc_file_pool_api_calls_total{status="error"}[10m]) > 0.05
          for: 10m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "VPC API errors for {{ $labels.operation }}"
            description: "Sustained VPC API errors detected. Check API key validity and VPC service status."

        - alert: ReplicationLagHigh
          expr: pool_csi_replication_lag_seconds > 7200
          for: 30m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "Replication lag exceeds 2 hours for policy {{ $labels.policy }}"
            description: "DR data is {{ $value | humanizeDuration }} behind. RPO may be violated."

        - alert: SnapshotFailures
          expr: rate(vpc_file_pool_snapshots_total{status="error"}[10m]) > 0
          for: 10m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "Snapshot failures in pool {{ $labels.pool }}"
            description: "Snapshot {{ $labels.operation }} operations are failing. Check share health and capacity."

        - alert: GroupSnapshotHighInconsistency
          expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(vpc_file_pool_group_snapshot_inconsistency_window_ms_bucket[1h])) > 60000
          for: 30m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "Group snapshot inconsistency window exceeds 60s in pool {{ $labels.pool }}"
            description: "Large data volumes are causing wide inconsistency windows. Consider using pre-snapshot hooks for quiescing."

docs.title: Capacity Planning
docs.text:
# Pool utilization percentage
vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb / vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb * 100

# Free capacity per pool (GB)
vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb - vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb

# Allocation rate (PVCs per hour)
rate(vpc_file_pool_allocations_total{status="success"}[1h]) * 3600

# Projected hours to full at current allocation rate
(vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb - vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb)
/ (deriv(vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb[1h]) + 0.001)

# Average PVC size (GB)
vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb / (vpc_file_pool_pvc_count > 0)

# PVCs per share
vpc_file_pool_pvc_count / (vpc_file_pool_share_count > 0)

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
# P50/P95/P99 allocation latency
histogram_quantile(0.5, rate(vpc_file_pool_allocation_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(vpc_file_pool_allocation_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(vpc_file_pool_allocation_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

# VPC API call rate by operation
rate(vpc_file_pool_api_calls_total[5m])

# P95 VPC API latency by operation
histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(vpc_file_pool_api_call_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

# API error ratio
rate(vpc_file_pool_api_calls_total{status="error"}[5m])
/ rate(vpc_file_pool_api_calls_total[5m])

docs.title: Replication
docs.text:
# Current replication lag (RPO indicator)
pool_csi_replication_lag_seconds

# Sync success rate
rate(pool_csi_replication_sync_total{result="success"}[1h])
/ rate(pool_csi_replication_sync_total[1h])

# Average sync duration
rate(pool_csi_replication_sync_duration_seconds_sum[1h])
/ rate(pool_csi_replication_sync_duration_seconds_count[1h])

# SubVolumes per replication policy
pool_csi_replication_subvolume_count

docs.title: Anomaly Detection
docs.text:
# Allocation rate spike (> 3x normal over 24h baseline)
rate(vpc_file_pool_allocations_total{status="success"}[5m])
> 3 * avg_over_time(rate(vpc_file_pool_allocations_total{status="success"}[5m])[24h:5m])

# Sudden capacity drop (possible mass deletion)
delta(vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb[5m]) < -100

# Share count instability (shares being created/removed frequently)
changes(vpc_file_pool_share_count[1h]) > 5

docs.text:
1. Copy the JSON below
