docs.title: Part 6: Replication and Failover
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 1: Pool Creation | Part 2: Snapshots & Clones | Part 3: Group Snapshots & Hooks | Part 4: Pool Configuration | Part 5: Golden Images | Part 6 | Part 7: Monitoring | Part 8: Migration & Console | Part 9: COS Backup Bucket

Step-by-step guide to setting up cross-region disaster recovery replication between two clusters, pausing and resuming sync, using lifecycle hooks, inspecting metadata, and performing failover to bring workloads online at the DR site.

Source cluster: ROKS eu-de (Frankfurt) Destination cluster: ROKS us-east (Washington, DC) -- or same cluster for testing

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
You need two ROKS or ROVS clusters with the CSI driver deployed (source and destination). For a single-cluster walkthrough, you can use the same cluster for both roles.

Verify the CSI driver is running on the source cluster:

# Controller pod (6/6 Running)
oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=controller

# Node pods (Running on each schedulable node)
oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=node

# CSI Driver registered
oc get csidriver vpc-file-pool.csi.ibm.io

# CRD installed
oc get crd replicationpolicies.storage.ibmcloud.io

Verify the same on the destination cluster (switch kubeconfig or context as needed).

For direct NFS mode, the destination NFS share must be reachable from the source cluster over IBM Transit Gateway or VPN. For driver-to-driver mode, only HTTPS connectivity between clusters is required: the source cluster's nodes must be able to reach the destination cluster's Route address. On ROKS and ROVS the Route is on the cluster's public ingress address, so the nodes need outbound internet access.

Driver-to-driver mode also needs a pool on the destination cluster for the receiver's volume, and either cert-manager (for the receiver's own certificate) or the Route's TLS (see Step 6c). Check cert-manager on the destination cluster:

oc get crd certificates.cert-manager.io

A new ROKS or ROVS cluster does not have it.

docs.title: Overview: Two Replication Modes
docs.text:
The CSI driver supports two replication modes, each suited to different network topologies:

Direct NFS mode -- The source cluster mounts the destination NFS share and uses rsync to transfer SubVolume data. This requires NFS reachability between clusters (Transit Gateway or VPN). Supports rsync incremental sync for bandwidth efficiency.

Driver-to-driver mode -- The source cluster creates Jobs that tar SubVolume data and upload it via HTTPS PUT to a receiver pod on the destination cluster. Works across any network that allows HTTPS. The receiver extracts the tar stream to the destination NFS share.

The rsync and tar copies apply to volumes that are not disks of a running VM. The controller copies a running VM's disks with QEMU instead. See Running VMs.

docs.title: Step 1: Clean Up Any Previous Tutorial Resources
docs.text:
REPL_POOL=repl-pool
REPL_NS=pool-tutorial-repl

# 1. Delete pods and PVCs
oc delete pods --all -n ${REPL_NS} --force --grace-period=0 --ignore-not-found
oc delete pvc --all -n ${REPL_NS} --timeout=60s --ignore-not-found

# 2. Delete this tutorial's ReplicationPolicies, by name.
# ReplicationPolicy is cluster-wide. Never use --all on a cluster that others share.
oc delete replicationpolicy dr-driver dr-with-hooks dr-with-http-hooks --ignore-not-found

# 3. Grace period for CSI to cascade SubVolume deletes
sleep 5

# 4. Force-clean orphan SubVolumes
for sv in $(oc get subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io \
    -l storage.ibmcloud.io/pool=${REPL_POOL} -o name 2>/dev/null); do
    oc patch "$sv" --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
done
oc delete subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io \
    -l storage.ibmcloud.io/pool=${REPL_POOL} --ignore-not-found

# 5. Delete pool
oc delete filesharepool ${REPL_POOL} --timeout=60s --ignore-not-found || {
    oc patch filesharepools.storage.ibmcloud.io ${REPL_POOL} \
        --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
    oc delete filesharepool ${REPL_POOL} --ignore-not-found
}

# 6. Delete namespace
oc delete namespace ${REPL_NS} --timeout=60s --ignore-not-found

docs.title: Step 2: Set Up Variables, Namespace, and Source Pool
docs.text:
# Shell variables used throughout this tutorial
export REPL_POOL=repl-pool
export REPL_NS=pool-tutorial-repl

# Create namespace
oc create namespace ${REPL_NS}

Create the source pool:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: ${REPL_POOL}
spec:
  zone: eu-de-1
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 100
  iops: 100
  maxShares: 2
  initialShares: 1
  autoExpand: false
  allocationStrategy: spread
  defaultPermissions: "0777"
  defaultUID: 107
  defaultGID: 107
EOF

What this does: - Creates a pool named repl-pool in eu-de-1 with a single 100 GB share - Uses the dp2 profile at 100 IOPS (sufficient for tutorial data) - Directories are owned by UID 107 (QEMU user), suitable for KubeVirt workloads

Watch the pool initialize:

oc get filesharepools -w

Wait until PHASE shows Ready:

NAME        ZONE      PROFILE   SHARES   CAPACITY   ALLOCATED   PVCS   PHASE
repl-pool   eu-de-1   dp2       1        100        0           0      Ready

docs.title: Step 3: Provision PVCs with Test Data
docs.text:
Create three PVCs with writer pods to populate test data:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: repl-app-data
  namespace: ${REPL_NS}
  labels:
    app: repl-demo
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: ${REPL_POOL}
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: repl-app-logs
  namespace: ${REPL_NS}
  labels:
    app: repl-demo
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: ${REPL_POOL}
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: repl-app-config
  namespace: ${REPL_NS}
  labels:
    app: repl-demo
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: ${REPL_POOL}
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 2Gi
EOF

Verify PVCs are bound:

oc get pvc -n ${REPL_NS}

Expected output:

NAME              STATUS   VOLUME       CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
repl-app-data     Bound    pvc-aaa...   5Gi        RWX            repl-pool      5s
repl-app-logs     Bound    pvc-bbb...   5Gi        RWX            repl-pool      5s
repl-app-config   Bound    pvc-ccc...   2Gi        RWX            repl-pool      5s

Write test data to each PVC:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: repl-writer
  namespace: ${REPL_NS}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: writer
      image: busybox
      command:
        - sh
        - -c
        - |
          echo "Application database export - \$(date)" > /data/db-dump.sql
          dd if=/dev/urandom of=/data/payload.bin bs=1M count=10 2>/dev/null
          echo "Data written: \$(ls -lh /data/)"
          echo "Access log entry - \$(date)" > /logs/access.log
          echo "Error log entry - \$(date)" > /logs/error.log
          echo "Logs written: \$(ls -lh /logs/)"
          echo "app.replicas=3" > /config/app.properties
          echo "db.host=10.0.0.5" >> /config/app.properties
          echo "Config written: \$(cat /config/app.properties)"
          echo "All test data written successfully."
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        - name: config
          mountPath: /config
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: repl-app-data
    - name: logs
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: repl-app-logs
    - name: config
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: repl-app-config
EOF

Wait for the writer to complete and verify:

oc get pod repl-writer -n ${REPL_NS} -w
# Wait for STATUS=Completed

oc logs repl-writer -n ${REPL_NS}

Verify SubVolumes and pool capacity:

oc get subvolumes -o wide
oc get filesharepools
# Expected: ALLOCATED=12, PVCS=3

Clean up the writer pod:

oc delete pod repl-writer -n ${REPL_NS}

docs.title: Step 4: Direct NFS Replication
docs.text:
Direct NFS mode uses rsync Jobs to transfer SubVolume data from the source pool's NFS share to a destination NFS share. The destination share must be reachable from source cluster worker nodes over Transit Gateway or VPN.

Note: Replace 10.240.0.50 with the actual NFS mount target IP of your destination share, and destinationExportPath with its export path. A share in security group mode (the only mode for new shares) exports a path such as /299a1485_593a_403d_98da_b0958e446b16, not /. With / the sync Jobs fail. Both values are in the destination pool's status (status.shares[].mountTargetIP and status.shares[].exportPath), or in the mount_path of ibmcloud is share-mount-target <DEST_SHARE_ID> <MOUNT_TARGET_ID> (<ip>:<export path>).

Create a ReplicationPolicy:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: ReplicationPolicy
metadata:
  name: dr-direct
spec:
  sourcePoolName: ${REPL_POOL}
  destinationNFSServer: "10.240.0.50"
  destinationExportPath: "/299a1485_593a_403d_98da_b0958e446b16"   # the export path of your destination share
  destinationBasePath: "/pvcs"
  schedule: "5m"
  incrementalSync: true
  maxParallelSyncs: 2
  bandwidthLimitMbps: 100
  maxRetries: 3
EOF

What this does: - Replicates all SubVolumes in repl-pool to the destination NFS server at 10.240.0.50 - Syncs every 5 minutes using rsync incremental mode (only changed files are transferred) - Runs up to 2 SubVolume syncs in parallel - Limits rsync bandwidth to 100 Mbps to avoid saturating the Transit Gateway link - Pauses the policy after 3 consecutive failures

Watch the policy status:

oc get replicationpolicies -w

Expected output after the first sync cycle:

NAME        SOURCE      DEST           SCHEDULE   PHASE    LAST SYNC
dr-direct   repl-pool   10.240.0.50    5m         Active   2026-02-25T14:30:00Z

Inspect per-SubVolume replication status:

oc get replicationpolicy dr-direct -o yaml | grep -A 20 subVolumeStatuses

Expected output:

  subVolumeStatuses:
  - subVolumeName: pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777
    lastSyncTime: "2026-02-25T14:30:02Z"
    bytesSynced: 10485760
  - subVolumeName: pvc-bbb11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777
    lastSyncTime: "2026-02-25T14:30:03Z"
    bytesSynced: 2048
  - subVolumeName: pvc-ccc11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777
    lastSyncTime: "2026-02-25T14:30:01Z"
    bytesSynced: 128

docs.title: Optional: Filter Which SubVolumes Are Replicated
docs.text:
By default, all SubVolumes in the source pool are replicated. Use subVolumeSelector to replicate only a subset:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: ReplicationPolicy
metadata:
  name: dr-selective
spec:
  sourcePoolName: ${REPL_POOL}
  destinationNFSServer: "10.240.0.50"
  destinationExportPath: "/"
  destinationBasePath: "/pvcs"
  schedule: "15m"
  maxRetries: 3
  subVolumeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: repl-demo
EOF

What this does: - Only replicates SubVolumes whose parent PVCs have the label app: repl-demo - Uses a 15-minute schedule (less frequent than the full-pool policy)

docs.title: Optional: Custom rsync Flags
docs.text:
Direct NFS mode supports extra rsync flags via rsyncOptions. Dangerous flags (--daemon, --server, --rsh, --rsync-path) are rejected by the validating webhook.

spec:
  rsyncOptions:
    - "--compress"
    - "--exclude=*.tmp"

Clean up the selective policy (keep dr-direct for the next steps):

oc delete replicationpolicy dr-selective --ignore-not-found

docs.title: Step 5: Pause and Resume Replication
docs.text:
To temporarily stop replication (for example, during maintenance), annotate the policy:

oc annotate replicationpolicy dr-direct storage.ibmcloud.io/paused=true

Verify the phase changes to Paused. The controller checks the annotation about every 30 seconds, so wait a minute:

oc get replicationpolicies

Expected output:

NAME        SOURCE      DEST           SCHEDULE   PHASE    LAST SYNC
dr-direct   repl-pool   10.240.0.50    5m         Paused   2026-02-25T14:30:00Z

What this does: - The replication controller detects the storage.ibmcloud.io/paused: "true" annotation - Status phase is updated to Paused - No new sync Jobs are created while paused - In-flight Jobs are allowed to complete

To resume replication, remove the annotation:

oc annotate replicationpolicy dr-direct storage.ibmcloud.io/paused-

Verify the phase returns to Active:

oc get replicationpolicies

Expected output:

NAME        SOURCE      DEST           SCHEDULE   PHASE    LAST SYNC
dr-direct   repl-pool   10.240.0.50    5m         Active   2026-02-25T14:30:00Z

The next sync cycle will run at the scheduled interval from when the policy was resumed.

Clean up the direct NFS policy before moving to driver-to-driver mode:

oc delete replicationpolicy dr-direct

docs.title: Step 6: Driver-to-Driver Replication
docs.text:
Driver-to-driver mode is the recommended approach when Transit Gateway NFS reachability is not available or when you want HTTPS-based replication with authentication and TLS.

The source cluster creates Jobs that tar SubVolume data and upload it via HTTPS PUT to a receiver pod on the destination cluster. The receiver extracts the tar stream to the destination NFS share.

docs.title: Step 6a: Generate an Auth Token
docs.text:
Generate a shared bearer token used to authenticate the source cluster to the destination receiver:

export REPL_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
echo "Replication token: ${REPL_TOKEN}"

Save this token -- you will need it on both clusters.

docs.title: Step 6b: Set Up the Destination Cluster
docs.text:
Switch to the destination cluster context (or use a separate terminal with the destination kubeconfig):

# Switch context (adjust to your cluster name)
oc config use-context dest-cluster

Create the auth token Secret on the destination cluster:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: repl-receiver-token
  namespace: kube-system
type: Opaque
stringData:
  token: "${REPL_TOKEN}"
EOF

What this does: - Creates a Secret in kube-system containing the bearer token - The receiver pod reads this token file and validates incoming requests

You also need a destination PVC. It is the receiver's data volume, so it lives on a pool on the destination cluster. The pool repl-pool exists only on the source cluster, so make a pool on the destination cluster first. Use a zone of the destination cluster. The pool can be small: the volume only has to hold the data you replicate.

export DR_POOL=dr-repl-pool

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: ${DR_POOL}
spec:
  zone: eu-de-3      # a zone of the destination cluster
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 20
  iops: 100
  maxShares: 1
  initialShares: 1
  autoExpand: false
  defaultPermissions: "0777"
  defaultUID: 107
  defaultGID: 107
EOF

oc get filesharepool ${DR_POOL}    # wait for PHASE Ready

Then make the volume on that pool:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: repl-destination-data
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: ${DR_POOL}
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
EOF

Note: If you are testing on the same cluster, you can use any RWX PVC. For a real DR setup, this PVC would be on a pool in the destination region. Make it big enough for everything you replicate.

docs.title: Step 6c: Enable the Receiver via Helm
docs.text:
Upgrade the Helm release on the destination cluster to enable the replication receiver. Use the chart that matches the image you run (the chart in the same release as the driver image). A chart that is newer than the image can stop the controller from starting.

Option A: the receiver has its own certificate (needs cert-manager).

helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set replicationReceiver.enabled=true \
  --set replicationReceiver.pvcName=repl-destination-data \
  --set replicationReceiver.authSecretName=repl-receiver-token \
  --set replicationReceiver.tls.enabled=true

What this does: - Deploys the replication receiver as a Deployment in kube-system - Mounts the destination PVC at /data inside the receiver container - Configures TLS with a self-signed certificate from cert-manager - Creates a Service (ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-replication-receiver) on port 8443 - Creates an OpenShift Route with TLS passthrough (auto-detected on OpenShift clusters) - Provisions a cert-manager Certificate with SANs for the Service and Route hostnames

Without cert-manager, this command fails with no matches for kind "Certificate" in version "cert-manager.io/v1", and nothing is changed.

Option B: the Route provides the TLS (no cert-manager). Set tls.enabled=false. The receiver then speaks plain HTTP inside the cluster, and the OpenShift Route ends the TLS with the cluster's ingress certificate. A ROKS or ROVS ingress certificate is signed by a public CA, so the source cluster trusts it without a CA Secret (skip Step 6d, and leave destinationCACertSecretRef out of the policy). The bearer token still protects the receiver.

helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set replicationReceiver.enabled=true \
  --set replicationReceiver.pvcName=repl-destination-data \
  --set replicationReceiver.authSecretName=repl-receiver-token \
  --set replicationReceiver.tls.enabled=false

The Route is now of type edge instead of passthrough.

Verify the receiver is running:

oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver

Expected output:

NAME                                                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-replication-receiver-5d8f9c7b4-x2k9j  1/1     Running   0          30s

Verify the Route is created:

oc get route -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver

Note the Route hostname (e.g., ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-replication-receiver-kube-system.apps.dest-cluster.example.com). You will need this for the source cluster configuration.

export RECEIVER_HOST=$(oc get route -n kube-system \
    -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver \
    -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.host}')
echo "Receiver endpoint: https://${RECEIVER_HOST}"

Check that the receiver answers (with Option B this also shows that the Route certificate is trusted). The first call needs no token and returns 200. The second shows that the token is needed: 401.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://${RECEIVER_HOST}/api/v1/health
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://${RECEIVER_HOST}/api/v1/auth-check

docs.title: Step 6d: Extract the CA Certificate
docs.text:
Option A only. (With Option B, skip this step and Step 6e's CA Secret.) The self-signed CA certificate must be trusted by the source cluster. Extract it from the cert-manager Secret:

oc get secret ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-receiver-certs -n kube-system \
    -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d > /tmp/receiver-ca.crt
cat /tmp/receiver-ca.crt

Note: If the cert-manager Secret does not contain a ca.crt key (some issuer configurations store it differently), use tls.crt instead. For production, use a trusted CA (e.g., Let's Encrypt via ClusterIssuer).

docs.title: Step 6e: Set Up the Source Cluster
docs.text:
Switch back to the source cluster context:

oc config use-context source-cluster

Create the CA certificate Secret on the source cluster (Option A only):

oc create secret generic repl-receiver-ca -n kube-system \
  --from-file=ca.crt=/tmp/receiver-ca.crt

Create the auth token Secret on the source cluster (same token):

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: repl-source-token
  namespace: kube-system
type: Opaque
stringData:
  token: "${REPL_TOKEN}"
EOF

docs.title: Step 6f: Create the Driver-to-Driver ReplicationPolicy
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: ReplicationPolicy
metadata:
  name: dr-driver
spec:
  sourcePoolName: ${REPL_POOL}
  destinationBasePath: "/pvcs"
  schedule: "5m"
  maxParallelSyncs: 2
  maxRetries: 3
  destinationEndpoint: "https://${RECEIVER_HOST}"
  destinationAuthSecretRef: "repl-source-token"
  destinationCACertSecretRef: "repl-receiver-ca"   # Option A only: leave this line out with Option B
EOF

What this does: - Sets destinationEndpoint to the receiver's HTTPS URL, which triggers driver-to-driver mode - References the auth token Secret (repl-source-token) for Bearer token authentication - References the CA certificate Secret (repl-receiver-ca) for TLS verification (Option A only; with Option B the source trusts the Route's public certificate) - Omits destinationNFSServer because data is uploaded via HTTPS, not mounted via NFS - The controller creates Jobs that tar each SubVolume directory and PUT it to the receiver

Watch replication status:

oc get replicationpolicies -w

Expected output after the first sync:

NAME        SOURCE      DEST   SCHEDULE   PHASE    LAST SYNC
dr-driver   repl-pool          5m         Active   2026-02-25T15:00:00Z

Note: The DEST column is blank because driver-to-driver mode uses destinationEndpoint instead of destinationNFSServer.

How long this takes. Expect 10 to 15 minutes for the three volumes, not seconds:

  • maxParallelSyncs: 2 starts two volumes at once. The third waits for the next check of the policy (deferred: parallel limit in the status).
  • The controller looks at a running cycle only on its schedule (every 5 minutes here). The data of a small volume is at the destination within a minute, but the policy shows sync in progress and an empty LAST SYNC until the next check.

Follow the Jobs while you wait: oc get jobs -n kube-system | grep repl-. To see the per-volume status:

oc get replicationpolicy dr-driver -o json | jq -c '.status.subVolumeStatuses[] | {sv: .subVolumeName, last: .lastSyncTime, err: .lastError, bytes: .bytesSynced}'

Verify data arrived on the destination cluster by switching context and checking the receiver pod's NFS mount:

oc config use-context dest-cluster

# Exec into the receiver pod to inspect the destination data
RECEIVER_POD=$(oc get pods -n kube-system \
    -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver \
    -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

oc exec -n kube-system ${RECEIVER_POD} -- ls -la /data/pvcs/

You should see directories for each replicated SubVolume (named pvc-<uuid>).

Switch back to the source cluster:

oc config use-context source-cluster

docs.title: Step 7: Replication Hooks
docs.text:
ReplicationPolicy supports pre-sync and post-sync hooks that run before and after each replication cycle. Use hooks to freeze application I/O, notify external systems, or validate replicated data.

Two things to do before you try the examples:

  1. Pause the dr-driver policy from Step 6, so two policies do not copy the same pool at the same time:
oc annotate replicationpolicy dr-driver storage.ibmcloud.io/paused=true
  1. An exec hook runs in a running pod that matches its podSelector. The writer pod from Step 3 is gone and had no labels. Start a pod that the hook can find. If no pod matches, the hook fails with no pod found in <namespace> matching labels, and with onError: Abort the cycle fails.
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: repl-app
  namespace: ${REPL_NS}
  labels:
    app: repl-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 107
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
EOF

docs.title: Exec Hook Example: Freeze Application Before Sync
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: ReplicationPolicy
metadata:
  name: dr-with-hooks
spec:
  sourcePoolName: ${REPL_POOL}
  destinationBasePath: "/pvcs"
  schedule: "10m"
  maxRetries: 3
  destinationEndpoint: "https://${RECEIVER_HOST}"
  destinationAuthSecretRef: "repl-source-token"
  destinationCACertSecretRef: "repl-receiver-ca"   # Option A only: leave this line out with Option B
  preSyncHooks:
    - name: freeze-app
      type: exec
      exec:
        podSelector:
          app: repl-demo
        namespace: ${REPL_NS}
        command:
          - sh
          - -c
          - "echo 'Freezing application I/O...' && sync"
      timeoutSeconds: 30
      onError: Abort
  postSyncHooks:
    - name: thaw-app
      type: exec
      exec:
        podSelector:
          app: repl-demo
        namespace: ${REPL_NS}
        command:
          - sh
          - -c
          - "echo 'Resuming application I/O...'"
      timeoutSeconds: 30
      onError: Continue
EOF

What this does: - preSyncHooks runs freeze-app before each sync -- executes a command in the first pod matching app: repl-demo in the ${REPL_NS} namespace - If the pre-sync hook fails, onError: Abort cancels the sync cycle - postSyncHooks runs thaw-app after the sync completes - If the post-sync hook fails, onError: Continue logs the error but does not affect the sync result

The pre-sync hook runs when a cycle starts, and the post-sync hook runs when the whole cycle has finished. With three volumes and one sync at a time, a cycle spans several checks of the policy, so the two hooks can be many minutes apart (see the timing note in Step 6f). Check that they ran in the controller log:

oc logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller -c csi-controller --tail=3000 | grep -E 'Running hook|Hook (succeeded|failed)'

A hook that works logs Hook succeeded for freeze-app (phase Pre) and for thaw-app (phase Post).

docs.title: HTTP Hook Example: Notify a Webhook Endpoint
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: ReplicationPolicy
metadata:
  name: dr-with-http-hooks
spec:
  sourcePoolName: ${REPL_POOL}
  destinationBasePath: "/pvcs"
  schedule: "15m"
  maxRetries: 3
  destinationEndpoint: "https://${RECEIVER_HOST}"
  destinationAuthSecretRef: "repl-source-token"
  destinationCACertSecretRef: "repl-receiver-ca"   # Option A only: leave this line out with Option B
  postSyncHooks:
    - name: notify-slack
      type: http
      http:
        url: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/T00000000/B00000000/XXXXXXXX"
        method: POST
        headers:
          Content-Type: "application/json"
      timeoutSeconds: 10
      onError: Continue
EOF

What this does: - After each successful sync, sends an HTTP POST to a Slack webhook URL - The headers field sets the Content-Type for the request - onError: Continue ensures a notification failure does not affect replication status

The URL above is a placeholder. The Slack service answers it with 404, so the controller log shows Hook failed ... HTTP POST returned 404 and the cycle still finishes. Use your own webhook URL.

Clean up the hook-based policies:

oc delete replicationpolicy dr-with-hooks dr-with-http-hooks --ignore-not-found
oc delete pod repl-app -n ${REPL_NS} --ignore-not-found

docs.title: Step 8: Metadata Sidecar
docs.text:
The replication controller writes a .subvolume-metadata.json file alongside each replicated SubVolume directory on the destination. This metadata is used by the failover CLI to reconstruct SubVolume CRs, PVs, and PVCs on the DR cluster.

Inspect the metadata on the destination cluster:

oc config use-context dest-cluster

RECEIVER_POD=$(oc get pods -n kube-system \
    -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver \
    -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

# List replicated SubVolume directories
oc exec -n kube-system ${RECEIVER_POD} -- ls /data/pvcs/

# Read the metadata file for one SubVolume (replace pvc-xxx with actual name)
oc exec -n kube-system ${RECEIVER_POD} -- cat /data/pvcs/pvc-xxx/.subvolume-metadata.json

Example metadata output:

{
  "subVolumeName": "pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777",
  "spec": {
    "poolName": "repl-pool",
    "shareID": "r010-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx",
    "shareMountTargetIP": "10.240.1.10",
    "shareExportPath": "/xxxxxxxx_xxxx_xxxx_xxxx_xxxxxxxxxxxx",
    "subPath": "/pvcs/pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777",
    "requestedGB": 5,
    "pvName": "pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777",
    "pvcName": "repl-app-data",
    "pvcNamespace": "pool-tutorial-repl",
    "uid": 107,
    "gid": 107,
    "permissions": "0777",
    "reclaimPolicy": "Delete"
  },
  "labels": {
    "storage.ibmcloud.io/pool": "repl-pool",
    "storage.ibmcloud.io/share-id": "r010-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
  },
  "lastSyncTime": "2026-02-25T15:00:02Z",
  "replicationPolicy": "dr-driver"
}

Key fields: - subVolumeName -- the SubVolume CR name on the source cluster - spec.pvcName and spec.pvcNamespace -- the original PVC name and namespace (used by failover to recreate PVCs) - spec.requestedGB -- the PVC size to recreate - spec.subPath -- the subdirectory path within the NFS share - spec.shareID, spec.shareMountTargetIP and spec.shareExportPath -- where the volume lived on the source share. Failover does not use them: the DR PV points at the DR share - labels -- the labels of the SubVolume, not of the PVC - lastSyncTime -- when this SubVolume was last synced (used to calculate RPO) - replicationPolicy -- which ReplicationPolicy produced this replica. If two policies copy the same pool, this is the one that wrote last

Switch back to the source cluster:

oc config use-context source-cluster

docs.title: Step 9: Failover
docs.text:
When the source cluster or region is unavailable, use the kubectl failover CLI to bring workloads online at the DR site. The CLI reads .subvolume-metadata.json files from the destination NFS mount and creates matching SubVolume CRs, PVs, and PVCs on the DR cluster.

If the source cluster is still alive, stop replication first, so no copy arrives while you fail over (skip this if the source is lost):

oc config use-context source-cluster
oc annotate replicationpolicy dr-driver storage.ibmcloud.io/paused=true --overwrite

docs.title: Step 9a: Plan the Failover
docs.text:
The tool reads the replicated folders from where the destination share is mounted. The receiver pod already mounts it at /data. The driver image does not contain the tool, so put the tool in the receiver pod (the binary is for Linux x86; make build-failover makes it, with GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 on another system):

oc config use-context dest-cluster

RECEIVER_POD=$(oc get pods -n kube-system \
    -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver \
    -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

oc exec -i -n kube-system ${RECEIVER_POD} -- \
    sh -c 'cat > /tmp/kubectl-failover && chmod +x /tmp/kubectl-failover' < bin/kubectl-failover

oc exec -n kube-system ${RECEIVER_POD} -- /tmp/kubectl-failover plan --nfs-mount-path /data

Note: You can also run the tool on any host that mounts the destination share over NFS (a VSI in the VPC, for example) and reaches the DR cluster's API. The commands below then read kubectl failover ... and --nfs-mount-path is where you mounted the share. Part 13 shows that way. From the receiver pod, the tool uses the pod's own service account to talk to the cluster, so no kubeconfig is needed.

Example output:

Failover Plan
=============
NFS Mount Path:  /data
SubVolumes:      3
RPO (max age):   5m12s

SUBVOLUME                                     PVC               NAMESPACE            SIZE (GiB)  LAST SYNC      POLICY
pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777      repl-app-data     pool-tutorial-repl   5           5m12s ago      dr-driver
pvc-bbb11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777      repl-app-logs     pool-tutorial-repl   5           5m10s ago      dr-driver
pvc-ccc11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777      repl-app-config   pool-tutorial-repl   2           5m11s ago      dr-driver

To execute failover, run:
  kubectl failover execute --nfs-mount-path /data --dr-pool <POOL> --dr-share-ip <IP>

What this does: - Scans /data/pvcs/ for directories containing .subvolume-metadata.json - Lists each discoverable SubVolume with its PVC name, namespace, size, and age since last sync - Calculates the RPO (recovery point objective) as the age of the oldest last sync time

docs.title: Step 9b: Find the DR Share and Dry-Run the Failover
docs.text:
Failover makes a PV for each volume. A PV must name its folder by the path from the root of the DR share. The replicated volumes are not at the root of the share: the receiver's data volume repl-destination-data is itself a folder on the DR pool's share, and the replicated volumes are inside it. So you need the share's address, its export path and the folder of the receiver volume:

export DR_IP=$(oc get filesharepool ${DR_POOL} -o jsonpath='{.status.shares[0].mountTargetIP}')
export DR_EXPORT=$(oc get filesharepool ${DR_POOL} -o jsonpath='{.status.shares[0].exportPath}')
RECV_PV=$(oc get pvc -n kube-system repl-destination-data -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}')
RECV_SUB=$(oc get subvolume ${RECV_PV} -o jsonpath='{.spec.subPath}')

# The tool adds /pvcs/pvc-<uuid> to this path.
export DR_EXPORT_PATH="${DR_EXPORT%/}${RECV_SUB}"
echo "${DR_IP} ${DR_EXPORT_PATH}"

Preview what resources would be created without making changes:

oc exec -n kube-system ${RECEIVER_POD} -- /tmp/kubectl-failover execute \
    --nfs-mount-path /data \
    --dr-pool ${DR_POOL} \
    --dr-share-ip ${DR_IP} \
    --dr-export-path "${DR_EXPORT_PATH}" \
    --dry-run

Example output:

[dry-run] Would create SubVolume pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777
[dry-run] Would create PV dr-pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777 (nfs://10.245.3.8/8fbb32db_4f8e_4012_b074_27fbae9536be/pvcs/pvc-cfc98075-51ab-4cdf-98e1-ca5307debf19/pvcs/pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777)
[dry-run] Would create PVC pool-tutorial-repl/repl-app-data (bound to dr-pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777)
...

What this does: - For each SubVolume, shows the SubVolume CR, PV, and PVC that would be created - PV names are prefixed with dr- to avoid conflicts with source cluster PV names - PVCs retain their original names and namespaces from the metadata - No resources are created in dry-run mode

Check the PV path. It must end in /pvcs/pvc-<uuid> after the receiver's folder. Without --dr-export-path, the path is /pvcs/pvc-<uuid> from the root of the share, which is not where the receiver wrote the data, and the volume would be empty or would not mount.

docs.title: Step 9c: Execute the Failover
docs.text:
The tool creates each PVC in the namespace it had on the source cluster. Make that namespace on the DR cluster first (or pass --namespace to put every PVC in one namespace). Then run the failover:

oc create namespace ${REPL_NS}

oc exec -n kube-system ${RECEIVER_POD} -- /tmp/kubectl-failover execute \
    --nfs-mount-path /data \
    --dr-pool ${DR_POOL} \
    --dr-share-ip ${DR_IP} \
    --dr-export-path "${DR_EXPORT_PATH}"

Example output:

Preparing running VM disks (rolling back unfinished copies, rewinding where needed)...
Created SubVolume pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777
Created PV dr-pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777
Created PVC pool-tutorial-repl/repl-app-data
...

What this does: - Creates SubVolume CRs on the DR cluster matching the source metadata - Creates PVs that point to the DR share's NFS mount target IP and the path of each volume inside the receiver's folder - Creates PVCs in the original namespaces, pre-bound to the new PVs - All operations are idempotent -- running execute again skips already-existing resources (if the namespace was missing, create it and run execute again)

Optional flags: - --namespace override-ns -- override the PVC namespace (useful when DR uses a different namespace layout) - --dr-export-path is also what you use for older shares in VPC access mode, which have an NFS export path of their own. Here it is needed for a different reason: the receiver's folder

Note: The PVCs that the tool makes do not name a StorageClass, so a cluster with a default StorageClass shows that class in the PVC (for example ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd). The PVC is bound to its PV by name, so this does not change where the data is.

docs.title: Step 9d: Check Failover Status
docs.text:
Verify the failover resources were created correctly:

oc exec -n kube-system ${RECEIVER_POD} -- /tmp/kubectl-failover status

Example output:

SUBVOLUME                                     PVC               NAMESPACE            PVC PHASE  POLICY
pvc-aaa11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777      repl-app-data     pool-tutorial-repl   Bound      dr-driver
pvc-bbb11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777      repl-app-logs     pool-tutorial-repl   Bound      dr-driver
pvc-ccc11111-2222-3333-4444-555566667777      repl-app-config   pool-tutorial-repl   Bound      dr-driver

What this does: - Lists all SubVolumes with the storage.ibmcloud.io/failover-source label - Shows the PVC phase for each -- Bound means the PVC is ready for use - Workloads deployed to the DR cluster using these PVC names will automatically mount the replicated data

Verify PVCs are bound:

oc get pvc -n ${REPL_NS}

To check the data, start a pod that mounts a PVC and compare a file with the source. For example, cksum /data/payload.bin gives the same numbers on the source volume and on the DR volume.

At this point, you can deploy your application workloads on the DR cluster using the same PVC names, and they will access the replicated data.

Switch back to the source cluster:

oc config use-context source-cluster

docs.title: Running VMs
docs.text:
A VM that is running is not copied with rsync. The controller freezes the guest for a moment, copies all of its disks at that one moment, and keeps restore points at the destination. At failover, rewind before you start the VM:

kubectl failover plan --nfs-mount-path /data --list-moments
kubectl failover execute --nfs-mount-path /data --prepare-only --rewind-to 2026-10-20T10:30:00Z

The policy fields vmCopyAdaptive (default true), vmCopySpeedLimitMBps (the highest speed; none by default) and restorePointKeepHours (default 24) control the copy speed and how long the destination keeps restore points. An adaptive copy starts at 15 MB/s for each disk, speeds up while the share the VM reads is quiet, and slows down when the share's latency passes vmCopyMaxLatencyMs (default 15). Without the node agents' metrics, or with vmCopyAdaptive: false, the copy runs at the fixed vmCopySpeedLimitMBps (default 20; 0 means no limit).

See CROSS-REGION-DR.md, "Running VM disks", for the details and the lab results.

docs.title: Source Cluster
docs.text:
oc config use-context source-cluster

REPL_POOL=repl-pool
REPL_NS=pool-tutorial-repl

# 1. Delete this tutorial's ReplicationPolicies, by name (they are cluster-wide:
#    never use --all on a cluster that others share)
oc delete replicationpolicy dr-driver dr-with-hooks dr-with-http-hooks --ignore-not-found

# 2. Delete replication Jobs, temp PVCs and temp PVs of these policies. The
#    controller removes them when a cycle ends; check that none are left.
#    (The label repl-temp=true marks the temp objects of EVERY policy, so do not
#    delete by that label alone.)
for pol in dr-driver dr-with-hooks dr-with-http-hooks; do
    oc delete jobs,pvc -n kube-system -l storage.ibmcloud.io/repl-policy=${pol} --ignore-not-found
    oc delete pv -l storage.ibmcloud.io/repl-policy=${pol} --ignore-not-found
done

# 4. Delete source Secrets
oc delete secret repl-source-token -n kube-system --ignore-not-found
oc delete secret repl-receiver-ca -n kube-system --ignore-not-found

# 5. Delete pods and PVCs
oc delete pods --all -n ${REPL_NS} --force --grace-period=0 --ignore-not-found
oc delete pvc --all -n ${REPL_NS} --timeout=60s --ignore-not-found

# 6. Grace period for CSI to cascade SubVolume deletes
sleep 5

# 7. Force-clean orphan SubVolumes
for sv in $(oc get subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io \
    -l storage.ibmcloud.io/pool=${REPL_POOL} -o name 2>/dev/null); do
    oc patch "$sv" --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
done
oc delete subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io \
    -l storage.ibmcloud.io/pool=${REPL_POOL} --ignore-not-found

# 8. Delete pool-owned PVs
oc get pv -o json | jq -r "
    .items[]
    | select(.spec.csi.driver == \"vpc-file-pool.csi.ibm.io\")
    | select(.spec.csi.volumeAttributes.pool == \"${REPL_POOL}\")
    | .metadata.name" | xargs -r oc delete pv

# 9. Delete pool
oc delete filesharepool ${REPL_POOL} --timeout=60s --ignore-not-found || {
    oc patch filesharepools.storage.ibmcloud.io ${REPL_POOL} \
        --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
    oc delete filesharepool ${REPL_POOL} --ignore-not-found
}

# 10. Delete namespace
oc delete namespace ${REPL_NS} --timeout=60s --ignore-not-found

# 11. Verify VPC shares are being deleted
ibmcloud is shares --all-resource-groups

docs.title: Destination Cluster
docs.text:
oc config use-context dest-cluster

# 1. Delete the failover resources (if you ran failover). The tool labels the
#    SubVolumes but not the PVs; its PVs are named dr-<SubVolume name>.
oc delete pvc --all -n ${REPL_NS} --timeout=60s --ignore-not-found
for sv in $(oc get subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io \
    -l storage.ibmcloud.io/failover-source -o name 2>/dev/null); do
    oc delete pv "dr-${sv#*/}" --ignore-not-found
    oc delete "$sv" --ignore-not-found
done
oc delete namespace ${REPL_NS} --timeout=60s --ignore-not-found

# 2. Disable the receiver via Helm
helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set replicationReceiver.enabled=false

# 3. Delete the destination Secret, the receiver's volume and the destination pool
oc delete secret repl-receiver-token -n kube-system --ignore-not-found
oc delete pvc repl-destination-data -n kube-system --ignore-not-found
oc delete filesharepool ${DR_POOL} --timeout=120s --ignore-not-found

# 4. Verify the VPC shares are being deleted
ibmcloud is shares --all-resource-groups

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: What Command List replication policies oc get replicationpolicies Policy details oc describe replicationpolicy <name> Per-SubVolume sync status oc get replicationpolicy <name> -o yaml Pause replication oc annotate replicationpolicy <name> storage.ibmcloud.io/paused=true Resume replication oc annotate replicationpolicy <name> storage.ibmcloud.io/paused- List replication Jobs oc get jobs -n kube-system -l storage.ibmcloud.io/repl-temp=true Replication Job logs oc logs -n kube-system job/<job-name> Receiver pod status oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver Receiver health check curl -k https://<receiver-route>/api/v1/health Receiver token check (needs the token) curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://<receiver-route>/api/v1/auth-check Receiver logs oc logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver Failover plan kubectl failover plan --nfs-mount-path <path> Failover dry-run kubectl failover execute --nfs-mount-path <path> --dr-pool <pool> --dr-share-ip <ip> --dr-export-path <path> --dry-run Failover execute kubectl failover execute --nfs-mount-path <path> --dr-pool <pool> --dr-share-ip <ip> --dr-export-path <path> Failover status kubectl failover status List VM moments kubectl failover plan --nfs-mount-path <path> --list-moments Controller logs oc logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller -c csi-controller --tail=50

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text: Continue to Part 7: Monitoring to set up Prometheus metrics, alerting rules, and a Grafana dashboard for the CSI driver -- including replication-specific metrics like sync duration and failure counts.

docs.title: Part 7: Monitoring
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 1: Pool Creation | Part 2: Snapshots & Clones | Part 3: Group Snapshots & Hooks | Part 4: Pool Configuration | Part 5: Golden Images | Part 6: Replication & Failover | Part 7 | Part 8: Migration & Console | Part 9: COS Backup Bucket

Set up Prometheus monitoring for the CSI driver: enable metric scraping, explore the main metrics, deploy alerting rules, trigger a test alert, and import a Grafana dashboard.

Cluster: ROKS eu-de (OpenShift Virtualization enabled) Zone: eu-de-1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Verify the CSI driver is running:

# Controller pod (6/6 Running)
oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=controller

# Node pods (3/3 Running on each schedulable node)
oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=node

# CSI Driver registered
oc get csidriver vpc-file-pool.csi.ibm.io

Verify the Prometheus Operator is installed (standard on OpenShift):

# Should show the prometheus-operator pod Running
oc get pods -n openshift-monitoring -l app.kubernetes.io/name=prometheus-operator

docs.title: Step 1: Set Up Variables and Namespace
docs.text:
export POOL_NAME=monitored-pool
export TUTORIAL_NS=pool-tutorial-monitoring

oc create namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS}

docs.title: Step 2: Create a Pool and Provision PVCs
docs.text:
Create a pool to generate metrics:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: ${POOL_NAME}
spec:
  zone: eu-de-1
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 100
  iops: 100
  maxShares: 3
  initialShares: 1
  autoExpand: false
  allocationStrategy: spread
  defaultPermissions: "0777"
  defaultUID: 107
  defaultGID: 107
EOF

autoExpand is off so that the pool stays at 100 GB. In Step 5 you fill it past 85%. With autoExpand: true the pool would add a second share at 80% and the alert would never fire.

Wait for the pool to reach Ready:

oc get filesharepools ${POOL_NAME} -w

Provision several PVCs to generate allocation metrics:

for i in 1 2 3; do
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: monitoring-test-${i}
  namespace: ${TUTORIAL_NS}
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: ${POOL_NAME}
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
EOF
done

Verify all PVCs are bound:

oc get pvc -n ${TUTORIAL_NS}

Expected output:

NAME                 STATUS   VOLUME           CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS     AGE
monitoring-test-1    Bound    pvc-xxxxxxxx     10Gi       RWX            monitored-pool   10s
monitoring-test-2    Bound    pvc-yyyyyyyy     10Gi       RWX            monitored-pool   10s
monitoring-test-3    Bound    pvc-zzzzzzzz     10Gi       RWX            monitored-pool   10s

Verify pool capacity:

oc get filesharepools ${POOL_NAME}
# ALLOCATED should show 30, PVCS should show 3

docs.title: Step 3: Enable ServiceMonitor
docs.text: The controller serves Prometheus metrics on :8080/metrics. A ServiceMonitor tells Prometheus where to scrape.

docs.title: Method A: Helm Values (Recommended)
docs.text:
The chart creates the ServiceMonitors by default (metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled is true). It does so only when the cluster has the Prometheus Operator API, which OpenShift has. On OpenShift the chart puts them in its own namespace, ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring (metrics.monitoring.namespace), and OpenShift's user workload monitoring must be on. See MONITORING.md. Check that they exist:

oc get servicemonitors -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring

If you turned it off, enable it again:

helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true \
  --set metrics.serviceMonitor.interval=30s

What this does: - Creates the ServiceMonitors for the controller and the node agents - Tells Prometheus to scrape the controller's :8080/metrics endpoint every 30 seconds

docs.title: Method B: Without Helm
docs.text: The controller serves its metrics over HTTPS and wants a bearer token that may get /metrics, so a plain ServiceMonitor with no TLS or token settings does not work. Copy the settings from the chart's servicemonitor.yaml, or see MONITORING.md.

docs.title: Verify Scraping
docs.text:
Port-forward to the controller pod and check raw metrics:

oc port-forward -n kube-system deploy/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller 8080:8080 &
PF_PID=$!
sleep 2

# The endpoint is HTTPS and needs a token that may "get" /metrics.
# A plain http:// call fails with "Client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server".
TOKEN=$(oc create token prometheus-k8s -n openshift-monitoring --duration=10m)
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" https://localhost:8080/metrics | grep vpc_file_pool | head -20

kill $PF_PID

Expected output (after allocating 3 PVCs; the allocated_gb and pvc_count gauges can lag a minute behind):

# HELP vpc_file_pool_allocations_total Total number of subvolume allocations
# TYPE vpc_file_pool_allocations_total counter
vpc_file_pool_allocations_total{pool="monitored-pool",status="success"} 3
# HELP vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb Total allocated capacity in GB
# TYPE vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb gauge
vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb{pool="monitored-pool"} 30
# HELP vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb Total pool capacity in GB
# TYPE vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb gauge
vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb{pool="monitored-pool"} 100
# HELP vpc_file_pool_pvc_count Number of PVCs in the pool
# TYPE vpc_file_pool_pvc_count gauge
vpc_file_pool_pvc_count{pool="monitored-pool"} 3
# HELP vpc_file_pool_share_count Number of VPC file shares in the pool
# TYPE vpc_file_pool_share_count gauge
vpc_file_pool_share_count{pool="monitored-pool"} 1

docs.title: Step 4: Key Metrics Walkthrough
docs.text: The driver exposes 37 metrics across nine categories. This section walks through the first six categories (24 metrics) with PromQL queries and explains what to look for. The backup, CDI and per-share (node agent) metrics are in MONITORING.md.

docs.title: Allocation Metrics (9 metrics)
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_allocations_total Counter pool, status Total allocations. status=success or error vpc_file_pool_allocation_duration_seconds Histogram pool Time to allocate. Buckets: 10ms-163s vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb Gauge pool Total pool capacity in GB vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb Gauge pool Total allocated capacity in GB vpc_file_pool_share_count Gauge pool Number of VPC shares in the pool vpc_file_pool_max_shares Gauge pool Most shares the pool may have (spec.maxShares) vpc_file_pool_share_total_gb Gauge pool, share Provisioned size of one share in GB vpc_file_pool_share_allocated_gb Gauge pool, share Capacity allocated to PVCs on one share in GB vpc_file_pool_pvc_count Gauge pool Number of active PVCs

Key PromQL queries:

# Allocation success rate (per minute over 5m window)
rate(vpc_file_pool_allocations_total{status="success"}[5m]) * 60

# Pool utilization percentage
vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb / vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb * 100

# Free capacity per pool (GB)
vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb - vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb

# P99 allocation latency
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(vpc_file_pool_allocation_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

What to look for: - allocations_total{status="error"} should be 0 in steady state. Any errors indicate pool issues. - allocated_gb / capacity_gb > 0.85 means the pool is nearing capacity. Verify autoExpand is enabled. - P99 allocation latency should be under 1 second. Values above 5 seconds indicate the pool is expanding or degraded.

docs.title: VPC API Metrics (2 metrics)
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_api_calls_total Counter operation, status API calls by operation (create_share, get_share, etc.) vpc_file_pool_api_call_duration_seconds Histogram operation API call duration

Key PromQL queries:

# API error rate (percentage over 5m)
rate(vpc_file_pool_api_calls_total{status="error"}[5m])
/ rate(vpc_file_pool_api_calls_total[5m]) * 100

# P95 API latency by operation
histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(vpc_file_pool_api_call_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

What to look for: - Sustained error rates above 5% indicate VPC API issues (check API key validity, VPC quotas, service status). - create_share calls take 30-90 seconds (normal). get_share should be under 5 seconds.

docs.title: Snapshot Metrics (2 metrics)
docs.text: Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_snapshots_total Counter pool, operation, status operation=create, delete, restore vpc_file_pool_snapshot_duration_seconds Histogram pool, operation Snapshot operation duration

docs.title: Clone Metrics (2 metrics)
docs.text: Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_clones_total Counter pool, status Clone operations by outcome vpc_file_pool_clone_duration_seconds Histogram pool Time from the clone worker picking up a clone to the end of its copy Job

docs.title: Group Snapshot Metrics (4 metrics)
docs.text:
Note: VolumeGroupSnapshot is not active. Nothing acts on it yet (issue #100), so these four metrics stay empty.

Metric Type Labels Description vpc_file_pool_group_snapshots_total Counter pool, operation, status operation=create, delete vpc_file_pool_group_snapshot_duration_seconds Histogram pool, operation Total group snapshot duration vpc_file_pool_group_snapshot_member_count Histogram pool Members per group snapshot vpc_file_pool_group_snapshot_inconsistency_window_ms Histogram pool Time between first/last member copy

docs.title: Replication Metrics (5 metrics)
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Description pool_csi_replication_sync_total Counter policy, source_pool, result result=success, error, skipped pool_csi_replication_sync_duration_seconds Histogram policy, source_pool Sync cycle duration pool_csi_replication_lag_seconds Gauge policy, source_pool Current replication lag (RPO indicator) pool_csi_replication_consecutive_failures Gauge policy, source_pool Consecutive failure count pool_csi_replication_subvolume_count Gauge policy, source_pool SubVolumes per policy

Key PromQL queries:

# Replication lag (RPO indicator) — should be less than 2x schedule interval
pool_csi_replication_lag_seconds

# Replication sync success rate
rate(pool_csi_replication_sync_total{result="success"}[1h])
/ rate(pool_csi_replication_sync_total[1h])

# Consecutive failures — any value above 0 needs investigation
pool_csi_replication_consecutive_failures

What to look for: - lag_seconds > 7200 (2 hours) means RPO may be violated. - consecutive_failures > 3 means the policy is likely paused. Check connectivity to the destination NFS mount or receiver endpoint. - Sync duration should be less than the schedule interval. If syncs overlap, the data volume is too large for the configured interval.

docs.title: Step 5: Alerting Rules
docs.text:
The chart already ships a PrometheusRule named ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi (metrics.alerts.enabled is true by default). Its alerts are named VPCFilePool..., for example VPCFilePoolUtilizationWarning. See MONITORING.md for the full list. Check it:

oc get prometheusrules -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring

The rules below are examples to show how an alert is written. If the chart rules are active, you do not need them, and applying both sends two alerts for one problem. Apply them only for learning, and delete them in Cleanup. They go in the chart's monitoring namespace: user workload monitoring limits a rule to the metrics of its own namespace, and the driver's metrics are in that one.

docs.title: Critical Alerts
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: vpc-file-pool-csi-critical
  namespace: ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring
  labels:
    app: vpc-file-pool-csi
spec:
  groups:
    - name: vpc-file-pool-csi.critical
      rules:
        - alert: PoolAtMaxCapacity
          expr: |
            (vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb / vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb) > 0.95
          for: 5m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "Pool {{ \$labels.pool }} is over 95% allocated"
            description: "Pool has less than 5% capacity remaining. New PVC requests will fail if the pool cannot expand."

        - alert: AllocationFailureRate
          expr: rate(vpc_file_pool_allocations_total{status="error"}[5m]) > 0.1
          for: 5m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "High allocation failure rate in pool {{ \$labels.pool }}"
            description: "More than 0.1 allocation failures per second sustained for 5 minutes."

        - alert: ControllerDown
          expr: absent(up{job="ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-metrics"} == 1)
          for: 5m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "VPC File Pool CSI controller is down"
            description: "No metrics received from the controller for 5 minutes. PVC operations are blocked."

        - alert: ReplicationPaused
          expr: pool_csi_replication_consecutive_failures > 3
          for: 10m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "Replication policy {{ \$labels.policy }} is paused due to failures"
            description: "Replication has {{ \$value }} consecutive failures. DR data is stale."
EOF

What this does: - Defines four critical alerts that fire when pool capacity, allocation health, controller availability, or replication health is compromised - Uses the for clause to avoid transient spikes triggering alerts

docs.title: Warning Alerts
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: vpc-file-pool-csi-warning
  namespace: ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring
  labels:
    app: vpc-file-pool-csi
spec:
  groups:
    - name: vpc-file-pool-csi.warning
      rules:
        - alert: PoolNearCapacity
          expr: (vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb / vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb) > 0.85
          for: 10m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "Pool {{ \$labels.pool }} is over 85% allocated"
            description: "Pool is nearing capacity. Verify autoExpand is enabled and maxShares has room."

        - alert: ReplicationLagHigh
          expr: pool_csi_replication_lag_seconds > 7200
          for: 30m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "Replication lag exceeds 2 hours for policy {{ \$labels.policy }}"
            description: "DR data is stale. RPO may be violated."
EOF

Verify the rules were created:

oc get prometheusrules -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring -l app=vpc-file-pool-csi

Expected output:

NAME                            AGE
vpc-file-pool-csi-critical      10s
vpc-file-pool-csi-warning       5s

docs.title: Trigger a Test Alert
docs.text:
Allocate more PVCs until the pool exceeds 85% utilization to trigger the PoolNearCapacity warning.

The pool has 100 GB total and currently 30 GB allocated (3 PVCs at 10 GB each). To exceed 85%, allocate 60 more GB:

for i in 4 5 6 7 8 9; do
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: monitoring-test-${i}
  namespace: ${TUTORIAL_NS}
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: ${POOL_NAME}
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
EOF
done

Verify the pool utilization:

oc get filesharepools ${POOL_NAME}
# ALLOCATED should show 90, which is 90% of 100 GB (SHARES stays 1)

After the for: 10m hold-off period, the PoolNearCapacity alert fires. The chart's VPCFilePoolUtilizationWarning alert (default threshold 80%, hold-off 5 minutes) fires too. Check in the OpenShift Console under Observe > Alerting, or query Prometheus directly:

# Port-forward to Prometheus (OpenShift thanos-querier: HTTPS on 9091, needs a token)
oc port-forward -n openshift-monitoring svc/thanos-querier 9091:9091 &
PQ_PID=$!
sleep 2

TOKEN=$(oc create token prometheus-k8s -n openshift-monitoring --duration=10m)
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" 'https://localhost:9091/api/v1/rules' | \
  python3 -c "import sys,json; rules=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(r['name'],r.get('state','')) for g in rules['data']['groups'] for r in g['rules'] if 'Pool' in r['name']]"

kill $PQ_PID

docs.title: Step 6: Grafana Dashboard
docs.text: Import a pre-built dashboard for a visual overview of pool health.

docs.title: Import Instructions
docs.text:
1. Open Grafana (OpenShift Console > Observe > Dashboards, or your standalone Grafana instance)
  2. Go to Dashboards > Import
  3. Paste the JSON below and click Load
  4. Select your Prometheus data source
