docs.title: Dashboard Tour
docs.text:
After importing, the dashboard has five rows:

  • Row 1 (Top stats): Pool utilization gauge (color-coded: green/yellow/orange/red at 0/70/85/95%), PVC count, share count, and free capacity per pool.
  • Row 2 (Allocation activity): Allocation rate over time (success vs error) and allocation latency percentiles (P50/P95/P99). Spikes in the error series or elevated P99 latency indicate pool issues.
  • Row 3 (VPC API): API call rate by operation and status, plus P95 API latency by operation. Use this to detect VPC API degradation.
  • Row 4 (Replication lag): Current replication lag per policy. The chart should stay below your RPO target. Rising lag means syncs are falling behind.
  • Row 5 (Replication sync): Average sync duration per policy. If this exceeds the schedule interval, syncs are overlapping and the data volume is too large.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Note: In production, keep the ServiceMonitor and PrometheusRules running. This cleanup removes only the examples you applied by hand.

POOL_NAME=monitored-pool
TUTORIAL_NS=pool-tutorial-monitoring

# 1. Delete PVCs
oc delete pvc --all -n ${TUTORIAL_NS} --timeout=60s

# 2. Grace period for CSI to cascade SubVolume deletes
sleep 5

# 3. Force-clean orphan SubVolumes
for sv in $(oc get subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io \
    -l storage.ibmcloud.io/pool=${POOL_NAME} -o name 2>/dev/null); do
    oc patch "$sv" --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
done
oc delete subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io \
    -l storage.ibmcloud.io/pool=${POOL_NAME} --ignore-not-found

# 4. Delete pool (force-remove finalizer if stuck)
oc delete filesharepool ${POOL_NAME} --timeout=60s || {
    oc patch filesharepools.storage.ibmcloud.io ${POOL_NAME} \
        --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
    oc delete filesharepool ${POOL_NAME}
}

# 5. Delete the example alerting rules from Step 5
oc delete prometheusrule vpc-file-pool-csi-critical -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring --ignore-not-found
oc delete prometheusrule vpc-file-pool-csi-warning -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring --ignore-not-found

# 6. The chart's own ServiceMonitors stay

# 7. Delete namespace
oc delete namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS} --timeout=60s

# 8. Verify VPC shares are being deleted
ibmcloud is shares

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: What Command Raw metrics endpoint curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://localhost:8080/metrics \| grep vpc_file_pool Port-forward to controller oc port-forward -n kube-system deploy/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-controller 8080:8080 List ServiceMonitors oc get servicemonitors -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring List PrometheusRules oc get prometheusrules -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring -l app=vpc-file-pool-csi Check active alerts oc get prometheusrules -n ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-monitoring -o yaml Pool utilization query vpc_file_pool_allocated_gb / vpc_file_pool_capacity_gb * 100 Replication lag query pool_csi_replication_lag_seconds P99 allocation latency histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(vpc_file_pool_allocation_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) API error rate rate(vpc_file_pool_api_calls_total{status="error"}[5m]) Helm enable monitoring (on by default) helm upgrade ... --set metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true --set metrics.alerts.enabled=true

docs.title: Helm Values Reference
docs.text:
The full set of monitoring-related Helm values:

metrics:
  port: 8080                     # Metrics endpoint port
  serviceMonitor:
    enabled: true                # Create ServiceMonitor CR (needs the Prometheus Operator API)
    interval: 30s                # Scrape interval
  alerts:
    enabled: true                # Create the PrometheusRule (needs the Prometheus Operator API)
    utilizationWarning: 80       # Warning threshold (%)
    utilizationCritical: 95      # Critical threshold (%)

The chart's PrometheusRule has more alerts than the examples in Step 5, and more thresholds under metrics.alerts. See HELM-VALUES.md for all of them.

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text: • Part 8: Migration & Console -- Migrate PVCs from the stock IBM VPC File CSI driver and explore the OpenShift console plugin

docs.title: Part 8: Migration and Console Plugin
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 1: Pool Creation | Part 2: Snapshots & Clones | Part 3: Group Snapshots & Hooks | Part 4: Pool Configuration | Part 5: Golden Images | Part 6: Replication & Failover | Part 7: Monitoring | Part 8 | Part 9: COS Backup Bucket

Migrate PVCs from the stock IBM VPC File CSI driver to the pool-based driver, then enable and explore the OpenShift Console dynamic plugin for visual pool management.

Cluster: ROKS eu-de (OpenShift Virtualization enabled) Zone: eu-de-1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Verify the CSI driver is running:

# Controller pod (6/6 Running)
oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=controller

# Node pods (2/2 Running on each schedulable node)
oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=node

# CSI Driver registered
oc get csidriver vpc-file-pool.csi.ibm.io

For the migration section, the stock IBM VPC File CSI driver should also be installed (standard on ROKS clusters):

oc get csidriver vpc.file.csi.ibm.io

For the console plugin section, you need OpenShift 4.14+ with the ConsolePlugin v1 API:

oc api-resources | grep consoleplugins

docs.title: Step 1: Set Up Variables and Namespace
docs.text:
export POOL_NAME=ops-pool
export TUTORIAL_NS=pool-tutorial-ops

oc create namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS}

docs.title: Step 2: Create a Pool
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: ${POOL_NAME}
spec:
  zone: eu-de-1
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 100
  iops: 100
  maxShares: 3
  initialShares: 1
  autoExpand: true
  expandThresholdPercent: 80
  allocationStrategy: spread
  defaultPermissions: "0777"
  defaultUID: 107
  defaultGID: 107
EOF

Wait for the pool to reach Ready:

oc get filesharepools ${POOL_NAME} -w

Verify the auto-created StorageClass:

oc get sc ${POOL_NAME}

docs.title: Step 3: Install kubectl-migrate
docs.text: The migration CLI is a kubectl plugin that discovers PVCs on the stock driver and copies their data to pool-backed PVCs.

docs.title: Build from Source
docs.text:
cd /Users/neiltaylor/Projects/roks_new_file_csi
go build -o kubectl-migrate ./cmd/migrate/

docs.title: Install to PATH
docs.text:
sudo cp kubectl-migrate /usr/local/bin/
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/kubectl-migrate

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl migrate version

Expected output:

kubectl-migrate dev

docs.title: Step 4: Create a Test PVC on the Stock Driver
docs.text:
To demonstrate migration, create a PVC using the stock IBM VPC File CSI driver's StorageClass and write test data to it:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: legacy-app-data
  namespace: ${TUTORIAL_NS}
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: ibmc-vpc-file-1000-iops
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: legacy-writer
  namespace: ${TUTORIAL_NS}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: writer
      image: busybox
      command:
        - sh
        - -c
        - |
          echo "Important application data - migration test" > /data/app-config.txt
          echo "Database export 2024-01-15" > /data/db-export.sql
          dd if=/dev/urandom of=/data/binary-blob.bin bs=1M count=5
          echo "Migration source verification checksum:"
          md5sum /data/*.txt /data/*.sql /data/*.bin
          ls -la /data/
          sleep 3600
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: legacy-app-data
EOF

What this does: - Creates a PVC on the stock IBM VPC File CSI driver - Writes several test files (text config, SQL export, binary blob) - Prints checksums for verification after migration

Wait for the pod to be running, then capture the checksums:

oc get pod legacy-writer -n ${TUTORIAL_NS} -w
# Wait until Running, then:
oc logs legacy-writer -n ${TUTORIAL_NS}

Note the checksums from the output -- you will compare these after migration to verify data integrity.

Stop the writer pod (migration requires the PVC to not be actively mounted by running pods):

oc delete pod legacy-writer -n ${TUTORIAL_NS}

docs.title: Step 5: Migration Plan
docs.text:
Discover which PVCs are eligible for migration:

kubectl migrate plan \
  --namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS} \
  --storage-class ibmc-vpc-file-1000-iops \
  --target-pool ${POOL_NAME}

Expected output:

Migration Plan
==============
Namespace:          pool-tutorial-ops
Source StorageClass: ibmc-vpc-file-1000-iops
Target Pool:        ops-pool
PVCs found:         1
Total size:         10 GiB

NAME              SIZE (GiB)  PHASE   SHARE ID        PODS
legacy-app-data   10          Bound   r010-xxxxxxxx#r010-yyyyyyyy   (none)

To migrate a PVC, run:
  kubectl migrate execute --namespace pool-tutorial-ops --pvc <PVC_NAME> --target-pool ops-pool --target-storage-class <POOL_SC>

What this does: - Scans the namespace for PVCs using the specified StorageClass - Shows each PVC's size, phase, backing share ID, and any pods currently mounting it - The PODS column shows (none) because we deleted the writer pod -- migration requires no active mounts

docs.title: Step 6: Migration Dry Run
docs.text:
Preview what the migration will do without making any changes:

kubectl migrate execute \
  --namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS} \
  --pvc legacy-app-data \
  --target-pool ${POOL_NAME} \
  --target-storage-class ${POOL_NAME} \
  --dry-run

What this does: - Validates the source PVC exists and is not actively mounted - Validates the target pool exists and has capacity - Shows the migration plan without creating any resources

Expected output:

[dry-run] Would create target PVC pool-tutorial-ops/legacy-app-data-pooled (size: 10Gi, storageClass: ops-pool)
[dry-run] Would create migration pod pool-tutorial-ops/migrate-legacy-app-data
[dry-run] Would rsync data from legacy-app-data to legacy-app-data-pooled
[dry-run] Source PVC would NOT be deleted

SUCCESS: dry-run completed

docs.title: Step 7: Migration Execute
docs.text:
Run the actual migration:

kubectl migrate execute \
  --namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS} \
  --pvc legacy-app-data \
  --target-pool ${POOL_NAME} \
  --target-storage-class ${POOL_NAME}

What this does: - Creates a new PVC (legacy-app-data-pooled) on the pool driver - Spawns a temporary migration pod (migrate-legacy-app-data) that mounts both the source and target PVCs - Uses rsync to copy all data from the source PVC to the target PVC, then compares file counts - Reports success when the copy completes

The command waits for the new PVC, starts the pod, streams the rsync log, and ends with the SUCCESS line:

SUCCESS: Migration completed in 27s. New PVC: pool-tutorial-ops/legacy-app-data-pooled. Update your workloads to use the new PVC, then delete the old PVC when ready.

If you stop the command early, or run it in another terminal, watch the migration pod with:

kubectl migrate status --namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS}

Expected output during migration:

POD                         SOURCE PVC       TARGET PVC              PHASE      STARTED
migrate-legacy-app-data     legacy-app-data  legacy-app-data-pooled  Running    2026-02-25 10:30:15

Wait for the phase to show Succeeded:

# Poll until complete
while true; do
    kubectl migrate status --namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS} 2>/dev/null | grep -q Succeeded && break
    sleep 5
done
kubectl migrate status --namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS}

Expected output on completion:

POD                         SOURCE PVC       TARGET PVC              PHASE      STARTED
migrate-legacy-app-data     legacy-app-data  legacy-app-data-pooled  Succeeded  2026-02-25 10:30:15

docs.title: Verify Data Integrity
docs.text:
Mount the new pool-backed PVC and compare checksums:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: migration-verifier
  namespace: ${TUTORIAL_NS}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: verifier
      image: busybox
      command:
        - sh
        - -c
        - |
          echo "Migrated data verification checksums:"
          md5sum /data/*.txt /data/*.sql /data/*.bin
          echo ""
          echo "File listing:"
          ls -la /data/
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: legacy-app-data-pooled
EOF

Wait for the verifier to complete, then compare:

oc get pod migration-verifier -n ${TUTORIAL_NS} -w
# Wait for Completed, then:
oc logs migration-verifier -n ${TUTORIAL_NS}

The checksums should match the ones from Step 4. All files should be present with identical sizes.

Verify the new PVC is on the pool:

# New PVC is on the pool StorageClass
oc get pvc legacy-app-data-pooled -n ${TUTORIAL_NS}

# SubVolume exists
oc get subvolumes -o wide | grep legacy-app-data-pooled

# Pool shows the allocation
oc get filesharepools ${POOL_NAME}

Clean up the migration pod and verifier:

oc delete pod migration-verifier -n ${TUTORIAL_NS}

Production note: After verifying the migrated data, update your application's PVC reference from legacy-app-data to legacy-app-data-pooled, then delete the original PVC to free the stock VPC file share.

docs.title: Migrate in the console
docs.text:
The console can do the same migration. On the Pools tab, choose Migrate volumes into a pool.

  1. Choose the source storage class and the namespace. The table lists the claims.
  2. A claim that a pod uses cannot move: the row names the pods. Stop the application first.
  3. Choose Migrate, pick the target pool, and confirm. The page refuses a claim that does not fit the free space of the pool.
  4. The page makes the new claim <name>-pooled and the pod migrate-<name>, as the kubectl migrate tool does. The row shows the copy, with a link to the pod log. When it says "Copied", point your application at the new claim.

The page never deletes the old claim. Delete it yourself when you are sure the new one is right.

docs.title: Step 8: Console Plugin -- Enable
docs.text: The OpenShift Console dynamic plugin provides a visual interface for managing pools, SubVolumes, snapshots, and replication policies.

docs.title: Enable via Helm
docs.text:
The plugin is on by default. If you installed the chart with consolePlugin.enabled=false, turn it on:

helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set consolePlugin.enabled=true

What this does: - Deploys the console plugin as a 2-replica Deployment in kube-system - Creates a Service on port 9443 with TLS certificates auto-provisioned by the OpenShift service-ca operator - Registers a ConsolePlugin CR with the OpenShift Console - Runs a hook Job that adds the plugin to the console's plugin list and keeps the other plugins

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
# ConsolePlugin CR exists
oc get consoleplugin ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi

# Plugin pods are running
oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=console-plugin

# Plugin is registered with the console
oc get console.operator.openshift.io cluster -o jsonpath='{.spec.plugins}'

Expected output:

["ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi"]

After a few seconds, refresh the OpenShift Console. A new "IBM VPC File Pools" item appears under Storage in the left sidebar.

docs.title: Step 9: Console Plugin -- Tour
docs.text: The console plugin adds the following pages to the OpenShift Console. The pages are tabs of one "IBM VPC File Pools" page under Storage.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The first tab shows a high-level overview of all pools:

  • Stat cards at the top: Total Pools (with health indicator), Total Capacity (allocated vs total), Total SubVolumes, and Active Alerts (pools not in Ready state)
  • Performance metrics row: Allocation rate (per hour), P95 allocation latency (color-coded: green < 100ms, yellow < 500ms, red > 500ms), and VPC API health (calls/min, error rate, P95 latency)
  • Capacity breakdown: Aggregate capacity donut chart on the left, per-pool capacity bars on the right with share count indicators
  • Replication status (conditional -- only shown when ReplicationPolicy CRs exist): Replication lag per policy (color-coded), sync rate, and consecutive failures
  • Operations activity: Snapshot count and clone count with average duration
  • Recent activity table: The 10 most recently created SubVolumes with name, pool, PVC, size, phase, and age

docs.title: Pools (FileSharePool)
docs.text:
• List page: All FileSharePools with capacity bars, share counts, phase status, zone, and profile. Click any pool name to view details.
  • Create page: A step-by-step wizard with preset configurations (Standard Workloads, KubeVirt VMs, High-IOPS Database). Configure zone, profile, share size, IOPS, max shares, allocation strategy, auto-expand settings, and default permissions. Includes a YAML editor fallback for advanced users.
  • Details page: Full pool specification, status summary, list of shares with IDs and mount target IPs, capacity bar, and associated SubVolumes table.

docs.title: SubVolumes
docs.text:
• List page: Filterable list of all SubVolumes with columns for name, pool, PVC namespace/name, size, share ID, and phase. Filter by pool name or phase.
  • Create page: Create a SubVolume manually (rarely needed -- PVCs create them automatically).
  • Details page: SubVolume spec (pool, PVC reference, requested GB, share ID, sub-path), status (phase, clone status), and conditions table.

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text:
• List page: All Snapshot CRs with pool, source SubVolume, creation time, size, and phase.
  • Create page: Select a SubVolume to snapshot, provide a name, and create. Validates that the source SubVolume exists and is in a healthy state.
  • Details page: Snapshot metadata, source SubVolume reference, creation timestamp, and restore action.

For the disk of a running VM, a snapshot is a QEMU copy or an instant snapshot, not a plain file copy. See Part 2.

docs.title: Replication Policies
docs.text:
• List page: All ReplicationPolicy CRs with source pool, destination, mode (direct NFS or driver to driver), schedule, lag indicator (color-coded), and phase.
  • Create page: Wizard for configuring replication mode, source and destination pools, schedule (an interval such as 15m), parallel sync count, and hook configuration. Validates destination connectivity.
  • Details page: Policy spec, current lag (gauge), last sync time, consecutive failure count, replicated SubVolume list, and conditions table.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
• Time range selector at the top (1h, 6h, 24h, 7d)
  • Capacity overview: Donut chart and per-pool capacity bars with PVC and share counts
  • Stat cards: Total PVCs, utilization percentage (color-coded), VPC API health, and replication status
  • Time series charts: Capacity utilization over time, PVC count over time, VPC API call rate (by status), VPC API P95 latency
  • Allocation activity (expandable section): Allocation rate over time and P95 allocation latency over time
  • Replication charts (conditional): Replication lag and sync rate over time
  • Prometheus connection diagnostic: Shows a warning banner if Prometheus is unreachable or if no CSI driver metrics are found, with instructions to enable the ServiceMonitor

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
POOL_NAME=ops-pool
TUTORIAL_NS=pool-tutorial-ops

# 1. Delete pods and PVCs
oc delete pods --all -n ${TUTORIAL_NS} --force --grace-period=0 --ignore-not-found
oc delete pvc --all -n ${TUTORIAL_NS} --timeout=60s

# 2. Grace period for CSI to cascade SubVolume deletes
sleep 5

# 3. Force-clean orphan SubVolumes
for sv in $(oc get subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io \
    -l storage.ibmcloud.io/pool=${POOL_NAME} -o name 2>/dev/null); do
    oc patch "$sv" --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
done
oc delete subvolumes.storage.ibmcloud.io \
    -l storage.ibmcloud.io/pool=${POOL_NAME} --ignore-not-found

# 4. Delete pool (force-remove finalizer if stuck)
oc delete filesharepool ${POOL_NAME} --timeout=60s || {
    oc patch filesharepools.storage.ibmcloud.io ${POOL_NAME} \
        --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
    oc delete filesharepool ${POOL_NAME}
}

# 5. Delete namespace
oc delete namespace ${TUTORIAL_NS} --timeout=60s

# 6. Verify VPC shares are being deleted
ibmcloud is shares

Note: The console plugin remains enabled after cleanup. To disable it, upgrade with the plugin off. A hook Job removes only this plugin from the console's plugin list: 

helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set consolePlugin.enabled=false

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: What Command Build migrate CLI go build -o kubectl-migrate ./cmd/migrate/ Migration plan kubectl migrate plan --namespace <ns> --storage-class <sc> --target-pool <pool> Migrate PVC (dry run) kubectl migrate execute --namespace <ns> --pvc <name> --target-pool <pool> --target-storage-class <sc> --dry-run Migrate PVC kubectl migrate execute --namespace <ns> --pvc <name> --target-pool <pool> --target-storage-class <sc> Migration status kubectl migrate status --namespace <ns> Enable console plugin helm upgrade ... --set consolePlugin.enabled=true Check plugin status oc get consoleplugin ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi Plugin pods oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=console-plugin Disable plugin Remove only this entry from spec.plugins (see the note above); never set the list to [], which disables every plugin

docs.title: Helm Values Reference (Console Plugin)
docs.text:
consolePlugin:
  enabled: true                     # The console plugin is on by default
  image:
    repository: de.icr.io/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/console-plugin
    tag: latest
  replicas: 2                       # Plugin pod replicas
  port: 9443                        # HTTPS port (TLS auto-provisioned by service-ca)
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: 10m
      memory: 50Mi
    limits:
      memory: 128Mi

docs.title: Series Summary
docs.text:
This concludes the 9-part tutorial series for the IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver. Here is a summary of what each part covers:

Part Tutorial What You Learned 1 Pool Creation, PVCs, and KubeVirt VMs Created a pool, provisioned PVCs, launched a VM with NFS-backed disks 2 Snapshots and Clones Point-in-time snapshots, restore from snapshot, clones 3 Group Snapshots and Hooks Not active: the driver does not act on group snapshots 4 Pool Configuration Multi-tier pools, allocation strategies, auto-expansion, share draining 5 Golden Images Hidden, optional feature: golden image provisioning from CDI sources 6 Replication and Failover Cross-region DR with direct NFS and driver-to-driver modes, failover 7 Monitoring Prometheus metrics, ServiceMonitor, alerting rules, Grafana dashboard 8 Migration and Console Plugin PVC migration from stock driver, OpenShift console plugin walkthrough 9 A COS bucket for backups Manual setup of a locked, versioned COS bucket for backup export

For production operations, see: - Day 2 Operations -- Health checks, draining, failover procedures - Troubleshooting -- Common issues and solutions - Monitoring -- Full metrics reference and PromQL cookbook - Capacity Planning -- Sizing guidance and cost estimation

docs.title: Part 9: A COS bucket for backups (manual setup)
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 1: Pool Creation | Part 2: Snapshots & Clones | Part 3: Group Snapshots & Hooks | Part 4: Pool Configuration | Part 5: Golden Images | Part 6: Replication & Failover | Part 7: Monitoring | Part 8: Migration & Console | Part 9

Make an IBM Cloud Object Storage (COS) bucket that the backup export can use: a locked, versioned bucket, a key that can only write to it, and a network rule that lets only the cluster and your admin addresses reach it. This is the setup that kubectl backup cos-setup does for you (see docs/specs/2026-10-21-backup-cos-export.md). Follow these steps by hand if you want to see each one. They are what we ran on the lab on 21 October 2026, and each one was checked.

Note: kubectl backup cos-setup automates these steps (run it with --dry-run first; see BACKUP-RECOVERY.md). It was run against real IBM Cloud in stage 18 of the release test. The command also makes the backup key and wraps it with Key Protect. These manual steps do not. This page stays the tested manual procedure and the reference for what the command makes.

Account: the one that holds your cluster. Region: the bucket is in the cluster's region (eu-de here).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The IBM Cloud CLI with the cloud-object-storage, cbr plugins, and your login (ibmcloud login). You need the right to make COS instances, IAM roles, service IDs and CBR rules. This is an owner task. The driver never does it.
  • The resource group of the cluster: ibmcloud target -g <group>.
  • Kopia on your laptop, to check the key at the end (brew install kopia).
  • A note of the admin addresses that should reach the bucket (your office or VPN address). Step 6 uses them.

Set names once. Change them for your account:

export RG=rovslab-prod-eude-rg          # resource group of the cluster
export COS=pool-csi-backup-test-cos     # COS instance name
export BUCKET=pool-csi-backup-test-$(date -u +%m%d%H%M)   # bucket names are unique worldwide
export SID=pool-csi-backup-test-driver  # service ID that owns the driver's key
export ROLE=PoolCsiBackupWriter         # custom role

docs.title: Step 1: Make a COS instance
docs.text:
ibmcloud resource service-instance-create $COS cloud-object-storage standard global \
  -g $RG -d premium-global-deployment-iam

The CLI asks which deployment you want if you leave out -d. Use premium-global-deployment-iam. Note the instance ID and tell the COS plugin to use it:

COS_GUID=$(ibmcloud resource service-instance $COS --output json | jq -r '.[0].guid')
ibmcloud cos config crn --crn "crn:v1:bluemix:public:cloud-object-storage:global:a/<account-id>:${COS_GUID}::"

Use the account ID from ibmcloud target. The standard plan costs nothing until you store data.

docs.title: Step 2: Make the bucket, with versioning and object lock
docs.text:
ibmcloud cos bucket-create --bucket $BUCKET --class smart --region eu-de
ibmcloud cos bucket-versioning-put --bucket $BUCKET --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled --region eu-de
ibmcloud cos object-lock-configuration-put --bucket $BUCKET \
  --object-lock-configuration '{"ObjectLockEnabled":"Enabled"}' --region eu-de

Check it:

ibmcloud cos bucket-versioning-get --bucket $BUCKET --region eu-de          # Status: Enabled
ibmcloud cos object-lock-configuration-get --bucket $BUCKET --region eu-de  # Object Lock Status: Enabled

There is no default keep time on the bucket. Each backup policy sets its own (spec.export.keepFor and lock). The shortest keep time is 25 hours: Kopia needs the keep time to be at least its maintenance interval plus 24 hours. Use 25 hours for tests and 30 days or more for real backups. A locked object cannot be deleted by anyone before its time ends, and COS bills it until then.

docs.title: Step 3: Make a role that can write, but not delete or unlock
docs.text:
IBM's standard Writer role can also delete versions and skip Governance locks, so a stolen key could erase backups. Make a custom role with only what the export needs:

P=cloud-object-storage; A=""
for a in account.get_account_buckets bucket.get bucket.get_basic bucket.head bucket.get_location \
         bucket.get_versioning bucket.get_versions bucket.get_object_lock_configuration bucket.get_uploads \
         object.get object.get_version object.head object.head_version object.put object.post \
         object.post_initiate_upload object.put_part object.post_complete_upload object.get_uploads \
         object.delete_upload object.delete object.get_object_lock_retention \
         object.get_object_lock_retention_version object.put_object_lock_retention \
         object.put_object_lock_retention_version object.post_extend_retention; do A="$A,$P.$a"; done
ibmcloud iam role-create $ROLE -n "Pool CSI backup writer" \
  -d "Backup export: read, write, extend locks, hide with a delete marker. No delete of versions, no skip of locks, no bucket changes." \
  --service-name cloud-object-storage --actions "${A#,}"

What the role leaves out on purpose:

Left out Why object.delete_version A delete with this role only adds a delete marker. The data stays. object.bypass_governance_retention The key cannot skip a lock. bucket.put_*, bucket.delete_bucket The key cannot change or delete the bucket.

object.delete is kept because Kopia hides data it no longer needs. A hidden object is still there. Your restore command (run with your own login) removes the hiding marks first.

docs.title: Step 4: Make the driver's key, limited to this one bucket
docs.text:
ibmcloud iam service-id-create $SID -d "Driver key for the backup export bucket"
ibmcloud iam service-policy-create $SID --roles "Pool CSI backup writer" \
  --service-name cloud-object-storage --service-instance $COS_GUID \
  --resource-type bucket --resource $BUCKET

The role is called by its display name (Pool CSI backup writer) in the policy, not by $ROLE. Now make an HMAC key (the S3 style key that Kopia uses) for the service ID. Write it to a private file. Do not print it.

mkdir -p ~/.config/pool-csi && chmod 700 ~/.config/pool-csi
ibmcloud resource service-key-create pool-csi-backup-test-hmac \
  --instance-name $COS --service-id $SID --parameters '{"HMAC":true}' --output json \
  > ~/.config/pool-csi/cos-key.json
chmod 600 ~/.config/pool-csi/cos-key.json

IBM Cloud also adds a policy to the service ID by itself when it makes the HMAC key: the Writer role on the whole COS instance, not on one bucket. Delete it, or this key can write to every bucket in the instance (ibmcloud iam service-policies $SID, then ibmcloud iam service-policy-delete $SID <policy-id> for the one with no resource type and no resource). kubectl backup cos-setup finds this one policy, which did not exist before the HMAC key, and deletes it; it leaves any other wide policy for you to remove. The secret is shown once, so cos-setup writes the key file the moment the key is made.

The access key and secret are in .credentials.cos_hmac_keys of that file. Later they go into a Kubernetes Secret in the driver namespace (spec.export.credentialsSecret). Never put them in a repository or a log.

docs.title: Step 5: Check what the key can and cannot do
docs.text:
Use Kopia, because it is what the driver runs. This makes a small repository in the bucket without a lock:

export KOPIA_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 24)       # keep it with the key file
AK=$(jq -r .credentials.cos_hmac_keys.access_key_id ~/.config/pool-csi/cos-key.json)
SK=$(jq -r .credentials.cos_hmac_keys.secret_access_key ~/.config/pool-csi/cos-key.json)
kopia repository create s3 --bucket $BUCKET --endpoint s3.eu-de.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud \
  --access-key "$AK" --secret-access-key "$SK" --prefix smoke-nolock/
mkdir -p /tmp/smoke && echo hello > /tmp/smoke/a.txt && kopia snapshot create /tmp/smoke

Expected: the repository is made and the snapshot is saved. Then try what must be refused. With rclone, giving the key through the environment (not on the command line):

export RCLONE_CONFIG_T_TYPE=s3 RCLONE_CONFIG_T_PROVIDER=IBMCOS \
  RCLONE_CONFIG_T_ACCESS_KEY_ID="$AK" RCLONE_CONFIG_T_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="$SK" \
  RCLONE_CONFIG_T_ENDPOINT=s3.eu-de.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud
rclone lsf T:$BUCKET/smoke-nolock/     # works: lists the Kopia files
rclone rmdir T:$BUCKET                 # Expected: 403 AccessDenied (DeleteBucket)

A delete of one object with this key adds a delete marker and removes nothing; we saw it accepted. A delete of a version must be refused. We did not test that one yet: the release test checks it (see the spec).

The test objects stay in the bucket. Only you can remove them, with your own login (see "Clean up").

docs.title: Step 6: Lock the bucket to the cluster (CBR)
docs.text:
A context-based restriction (CBR) rule makes COS refuse the bucket to every address except the ones you list. If the key leaks, it is useless from anywhere else. A rule needs a network zone: a list of addresses and VPCs.

If you already have a zone for the cluster (the lab has rovslab-prod-eude-allowed: the cluster VPC and the admin addresses), use it. Otherwise make one:

ibmcloud cbr zone-create --name backup-bucket-allowed \
  --description "Cluster VPC and admin addresses" \
  --vpc "<crn of the cluster VPC>" --addresses "<admin ip>,<another admin ip>"

Find the VPC CRN with ibmcloud is vpcs. Put your own admin address in the zone, or you lose access to the bucket from your laptop (setup, list and restore run with your login, from your machine).

Make the rule. It covers this one bucket and only the data plane (the S3 calls), so IBM Cloud can still manage the instance:

ibmcloud cbr rule-create \
  --description "Backup bucket: only the cluster VPC and the admin addresses" \
  --service-name cloud-object-storage --service-instance $COS_GUID \
  --resource-type bucket --resource $BUCKET \
  --zone-id <zone id> \
  --api-types crn:v1:bluemix:public:context-based-restrictions::::api-type:data-plane \
  --enforcement-mode enabled

Check it from an address that is not in the zone. We did this on the lab by pointing the rule at a zone with a made-up address for a minute: the same Kopia/rclone call returned AccessDenied at once, and worked again at once when we put the real zone back. A rule is also checked for the cluster: the first export Job must still work with the rule on. Run one before you trust the bucket for real backups.

Notes: - ibmcloud cbr rule-update replaces the whole rule, so give it every flag again. - A VPC in a zone counts only for traffic that comes over IBM's private network. A cluster that reaches COS through its public gateway would be refused. Use the private (direct) endpoint, or the private endpoint gateway in the next part. - Use --enforcement-mode report first if you are unsure. COS then only records what it would refuse.

docs.title: Recommended: a virtual private endpoint (VPE) for COS
docs.text: For real backups, give the cluster's VPC a virtual private endpoint gateway for COS in the same region. It gives COS a private address inside your subnet. Backup traffic then stays on IBM's private network and does not need the public gateway. With the CBR rule above, the bucket is reachable only from inside the VPC and from the admin addresses. It adds a small hourly charge and one security group rule (outbound HTTPS from the workers to the gateway). Make it in the console (VPC, Virtual private endpoint gateways) or with ibmcloud is endpoint-gateway-create. It is not needed for a lab test.

docs.title: What the lab shows after this setup
docs.text: Check Result Kopia repository create and snapshot with the key Worked Delete the bucket with the key 403 AccessDenied Call from an address not in the CBR zone AccessDenied at once Call from the admin address in the zone Worked

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Locked objects cannot be removed before their time ends (25 hours at the shortest). Then, with your own login:

ibmcloud cbr rule-delete <rule id>
# delete every object version and delete marker (the driver's key cannot), then the bucket
ibmcloud cos object-versions --bucket $BUCKET --region eu-de --output json   # lists Versions and DeleteMarkers
ibmcloud cos object-delete --bucket $BUCKET --key <key> --version-id <id> --region eu-de --force
ibmcloud cos bucket-delete --bucket $BUCKET --force
ibmcloud resource service-key-delete pool-csi-backup-test-hmac -f
ibmcloud iam service-id-delete $SID -f
ibmcloud iam role-delete $ROLE
ibmcloud resource service-instance-delete $COS -f

Delete the key file ~/.config/pool-csi/cos-key.json too.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The backup export itself (the spec.export block, kubectl backup cos-setup, kubectl backup restore --from-cos) is described in BACKUP-RECOVERY.md and in docs/specs/2026-10-21-backup-cos-export.md. Part 6: Replication and Failover covers replication between sites.

docs.title: Part 10: Backup and Restore
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 1: Pool Creation | Part 10

Back up a volume on a schedule into a pool that holds only backups. Change the volume, wait for a second backup, and restore the volume as it was at the first moment. Then delete the backups. The words moment, restore point and snapshot pool are defined in CONTEXT.md.

Time: about 30 minutes, most of it waiting for backups. Status: backups are Experimental. See BACKUP-RECOVERY.md for the full reference.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The driver runs on your cluster, with the admission webhooks on (the chart default). See Part 1.
  • The kubectl-backup plugin is on your path. Build it with make build-backup and copy bin/kubectl-backup to a directory in your PATH. Check it:
kubectl backup version
  • Your login can create cluster-wide resources (pools and policies).

docs.title: Step 1: Set variables and make the namespace
docs.text:
export NS=pool-tutorial-backup
export DATA_POOL=tut-data
export SNAP_POOL=tut-backups
export POLICY=tut-nightly

oc create namespace ${NS}

docs.title: Step 2: Make a data pool and a snapshot pool
docs.text:
The data pool holds your volume. The snapshot pool holds only backups, so a lost or full data share does not take the backups with it. The driver refuses a snapshot pool that holds any volume, and it refuses to make a volume on a pool that a policy uses as its snapshot pool.

Pick the zone of your cluster's workers:

export ZONE=$(oc get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.labels.topology\.kubernetes\.io/zone}{"\n"}{end}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | awk 'NR==1{print $2}')
echo ${ZONE}

for p in ${DATA_POOL} ${SNAP_POOL}; do
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: ${p}
spec:
  zone: ${ZONE}
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 100
  iops: 3000
  maxShares: 1
  initialShares: 1
  autoExpand: false
  allocationStrategy: spread
  defaultPermissions: "0777"
EOF
done

Wait until both pools are Ready. A share takes one to three minutes.

oc get filesharepool ${DATA_POOL} ${SNAP_POOL}

Expected: PHASE is Ready for both. The driver also makes a StorageClass with the name of each pool.

docs.title: Step 3: Make a volume and write some files
docs.text:
The label backup: "yes" on the PVC is what the policy selects.

cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: files
  labels:
    backup: "yes"
spec:
  storageClassName: ${DATA_POOL}
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  volumeMode: Filesystem
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
EOF

Run a pod that writes the first content and then waits:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: files-writer
spec:
  containers:
    - name: writer
      image: registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal:latest
      command: ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
      args:
        - |
          mkdir -p /data/a
          echo first > /data/a/1
          echo first > /data/keep
          touch /data/written
          sleep 36000
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: files
EOF

oc wait -n ${NS} --for=condition=Ready pod/files-writer --timeout=300s
oc exec -n ${NS} files-writer -- test -f /data/written && echo written

Expected: written.

docs.title: Step 4: Make the backup policy
docs.text:
The policy backs up every PVC with the label backup=yes in the namespace pool-tutorial-backup, every 5 minutes, and keeps each backup for 48 hours. The shortest schedule is one minute. The shortest keep time is one hour.

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: BackupPolicy
metadata:
  name: ${POLICY}
spec:
  snapshotPool: ${SNAP_POOL}
  schedule: 5m
  keepFor: 48h
  namespaces: [${NS}]
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      backup: "yes"
EOF

Check the policy:

oc get backuppolicy ${POLICY}

Expected: PHASE is Active. If it is Error, run oc get backuppolicy ${POLICY} -o jsonpath='{.status.message}'. The usual cause is a snapshot pool that is not Ready yet.

The controller makes a ReplicationPolicy named backup-${POLICY}-... for each source pool. Do not edit it. The backup controller sets it back.

docs.title: Step 5: Wait for the first backup
docs.text:
kubectl backup list --policy ${POLICY}

Repeat until the row for ${NS}/files shows a time under LAST BACKUP. This takes as long as the first copy. The row shows sync in progress in the ERROR column until the first copy ends, and shows the time within seconds after that.

Expected:

POLICY     VOLUME                    VM  LAST BACKUP           OLDEST                POINTS  CONSISTENCY  STATE   ERROR
tut-nightly  pool-tutorial-backup/files  -   2026-10-22T10:05:12Z  2026-10-22T10:05:12Z  0       FileCopy     active

FileCopy means the volume is a plain volume. The files were copied one by one, so the backup is only as consistent as the files. See CONTEXT.md. POINTS counts the earlier moments you can restore. It is 0 after the first backup.

Write down the time under LAST BACKUP. This is the first moment.

export FIRST=$(oc get backuppolicy ${POLICY} -o jsonpath='{.status.volumes[0].lastBackupTime}')
echo ${FIRST}

docs.title: Step 6: Change the volume and wait for a second backup
docs.text:
oc exec -n ${NS} files-writer -- bash -c 'echo second > /data/a/1; echo new > /data/b; rm /data/keep'

Wait for POINTS to reach 1:

kubectl backup list --policy ${POLICY}

Expected: POINTS is 1, and OLDEST is the first moment. The volume now has two moments. A new moment is made every 5 minutes whether or not the files change, so POINTS is higher if you waited longer. Restore a moment from before the change: FIRST, or OLDEST.

docs.title: Step 7: Restore the first moment to a new PVC
docs.text:
A restore makes a new PVC. It never writes over a volume that exists. The command waits until the copy ends.

kubectl backup restore --policy ${POLICY} --pvc ${NS}/files --to ${NS}/files-first \
  --moment ${FIRST} --wait

Expected: the command prints the phases Pending, Provisioning, Restoring, then Done: pool-tutorial-backup/files-first holds the backup of <time>. The new PVC uses the StorageClass of the backed-up claim, unless you pass --storage-class. Without --moment, the restore uses the latest backup.

Mount the new PVC and look at it:

cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: files-check
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: check
      image: registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal:latest
      command: ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
      args: ["cat /data/a/1; ls /data"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: files-first
EOF

oc wait -n ${NS} --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/files-check --timeout=300s
oc logs -n ${NS} files-check

Expected: the output is first, then a listing with a, keep and written, and no b. The restored volume holds the files as they were at the first moment.

The pod waits while the copy runs. A pod that mounts the new PVC does not start until the restore ends.

docs.title: Step 8: See the state of the restore
docs.text:
oc get backuprestore

Expected: one row, PHASE Done. A failed restore shows Failed, and status.message says why.

docs.title: Step 9: Delete the backups of a volume
docs.text:
First stop the policy from backing up the volume. Remove the label, then wait for one backup cycle (5 minutes). kubectl backup list then shows the volume as retained.

oc label pvc -n ${NS} files backup-
kubectl backup list --policy ${POLICY}

Delete the backups. The command measures them, shows the paths and the size, and asks you to type the volume as namespace/name:

kubectl backup delete --policy ${POLICY} --pvc ${NS}/files

Use --yes instead of the typed answer in a script. Without a terminal, the command refuses to continue unless you pass --yes. The controller never deletes backups by itself before the keep time. The command refuses while the policy still backs up the volume, and while a restore of the volume runs.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
oc delete pod -n ${NS} files-writer files-check --ignore-not-found --force --grace-period=0
oc delete backuprestore --all
oc delete backuppolicy ${POLICY}
oc delete namespace ${NS} --timeout=120s
oc delete filesharepool ${DATA_POOL} ${SNAP_POOL}

Deleting a policy keeps its backups on the share. Deleting a pool deletes its VPC shares and everything on them, including backups. The driver blocks the pool delete while volumes or snapshots remain on it, so wait for the namespace to go first.

docs.title: VMs
docs.text: A BackupPolicy backs up a VM through its disks. If any disk of a VM has the label, all its disks are backed up together at one moment. The status shows FileSystemConsistent or CrashConsistent. Restore each disk at the same --moment and make a VM from the new PVCs. See BACKUP-RECOVERY.md.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A backup policy copies selected volumes into a snapshot pool on a schedule.
  • kubectl backup list shows each volume, its moments and its consistency.
  • kubectl backup restore makes a new PVC at any kept moment.
  • kubectl backup delete removes backups on purpose.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Part 14: Restore a snapshot in the console
  • Part 9: A COS bucket for backups sends backups out of the VPC.

docs.title: Part 11: Instant VM Snapshots
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 1: Pool Creation | Part 11

Take a snapshot of a running VM in seconds, whatever the disk size. Delete a snapshot while the VM runs. Restore a snapshot to a new VM. Then remove all snapshots of the VM. The words instant snapshot, chain and Sidecar gate are defined in CONTEXT.md.

Time: about 45 minutes. The restore is a copy, so it takes longer for a large disk. Status: Experimental. Read VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md and the limits in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md first.

Red Hat does not support the KubeVirt Sidecar feature gate that this feature needs. OpenShift Virtualization then reports TaintedConfiguration=True. Use a test cluster. On ROVS, IBM's add-on manages the HyperConverged object; the driver changes one field of it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• OpenShift Virtualization on your cluster, and virtctl.
  • A running VM whose disks are PVCs on a pool StorageClass. Its guest runs the guest agent (qemu-guest-agent). This tutorial calls the VM my-vm in the namespace vms. Change the names to match yours.
  • Each disk file (disk.img) is owned by the QEMU user (UID 107). The driver makes the frozen file read-only from inside the VM pod, as UID 107, and only the owner can do that. If another user owns the file, the driver refuses before it changes anything: the VolumeSnapshot or VM snapshot fails with a message that names the owner, and the disk chain stays as it was. A disk that you made by hand as root on NFS (as in Part 1) is owned by nobody unless you run chown 107:107 on it. Run the chown, then take the snapshot again.
  • A VolumeSnapshotClass for the driver exists. The chart makes ibm-vpc-file-pool (see volumeSnapshotClass in HELM-VALUES.md).
  • The driver runs with the admission webhooks on, and vmSnapshots.method=auto (the chart default). See HELM-VALUES.md.
export NS=vms
export VM=my-vm
oc get vmi -n ${NS} ${VM} -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{"\n"}'

Expected: Running.

docs.title: Step 1: Turn on the Sidecar gate
docs.text:
Check the gate first:

oc get kubevirt -A -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.configuration.developerConfiguration.featureGates}{"\n"}'

If the list contains "Sidecar", go to step 2. Otherwise turn it on. Choose one way.

With the chart. Upgrade the release with vmSnapshots.enableSidecarGate=true. A Job turns the gate on after each install and upgrade. It adds one entry to the kubevirt.kubevirt.io/jsonpatch annotation of HyperConverged and keeps the other entries.

helm upgrade <release> charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi -n kube-system --reuse-values \
  --set vmSnapshots.enableSidecarGate=true

By hand. Use the script in the repository. It edits only its own entry:

hack/sidecar-gate.sh on <cluster name> <kubeconfig>

Check again. The gate shows after a minute or two, because KubeVirt reconciles it.

Expected: the list now contains "Sidecar".

The chart never turns the gate off. Turning it off is always a step you take (see Step 7).

docs.title: Step 2: Find the disk files
docs.text:
The VM has one volume for each disk. Each volume is a PVC, and each PVC has a SubVolume. Before any snapshot, a disk is one file, disk.img:

export CLAIM=$(oc get vm -n ${NS} ${VM} -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.volumes[0].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName}')
export PV=$(oc get pvc -n ${NS} ${CLAIM} -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}')
echo "claim ${CLAIM}, volume ${PV}"
oc get subvolume ${PV} -o jsonpath='{.status.diskChain}{"\n"}'

Expected: an empty line. status.diskChain is empty for a volume with no snapshots. If your VM boots from a dataVolume volume, use .dataVolume.name in place of .persistentVolumeClaim.claimName.

docs.title: Step 3: Take a snapshot of the running VM
docs.text:
A VirtualMachineSnapshot snapshots all disks of the VM at the same moment. OpenShift freezes the guest for that moment. You can also use the VM Snapshots tab in the console.

cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualMachineSnapshot
metadata:
  name: ${VM}-snap1
spec:
  failureDeadline: 1h
  source:
    apiGroup: kubevirt.io
    kind: VirtualMachine
    name: ${VM}
EOF

oc wait -n ${NS} vmsnapshot/${VM}-snap1 --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded --timeout=300s

Expected: the snapshot is Succeeded within a few seconds. The VM keeps running.

Look at the disk now:

oc get subvolume ${PV} -o jsonpath='{.status.diskChain}{"\n"}'

Expected: a list with two files, for example ["snap-a1b2c3.qcow2","disk.img"]. The newest file is first. The VM now writes to snap-a1b2c3.qcow2. disk.img is the snapshot and is read-only. Nothing was copied.

To see how each disk snapshot was made, find the Snapshot resource of the first disk:

VSC=$(oc get vmsnapshot -n ${NS} ${VM}-snap1 -o jsonpath='{.status.virtualMachineSnapshotContentName}')
VS=$(oc get vmsnapshotcontent -n ${NS} ${VSC} -o json | jq -r '.spec.volumeBackups[0].volumeSnapshotName')
CONTENT=$(oc get volumesnapshot -n ${NS} ${VS} -o jsonpath='{.status.boundVolumeSnapshotContentName}')
HANDLE=$(oc get volumesnapshotcontent ${CONTENT} -o jsonpath='{.status.snapshotHandle}')
oc get snapshots.storage.ibmcloud.io ${HANDLE##*/} -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.storage\.ibmcloud\.io/snapshot-method}{"\n"}'

Expected: instant. If it says vm or file, the snapshot was a copy. Read status.methodReason of the Snapshot. The usual reason is that the Sidecar gate is off.

docs.title: Step 4: Take a second snapshot
docs.text:
Make a change in the guest first, so the snapshots differ. Then snapshot again.

virtctl ssh -n ${NS} cloud-user@vmi/${VM} -c 'echo two | sudo tee /var/tmp/marker-two && sync'

cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualMachineSnapshot
metadata:
  name: ${VM}-snap2
spec:
  failureDeadline: 1h
  source:
    apiGroup: kubevirt.io
    kind: VirtualMachine
    name: ${VM}
EOF

oc wait -n ${NS} vmsnapshot/${VM}-snap2 --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded --timeout=300s
oc get subvolume ${PV} -o jsonpath='{.status.diskChain}{"\n"}'

Change the user name in virtctl ssh to the user of your guest image. virtctl ssh needs an SSH key in the guest. A VM that has only a password (like the one in Part 1) cannot use it: log in on the console and make the file there.

Expected: a chain of three files. A disk may have at most 16 snapshots.

docs.title: Step 5: Delete the first snapshot while the VM runs
docs.text:
A file in the chain cannot just be deleted, because newer files depend on it. The driver merges the next newer file into it, and QEMU does this while the VM runs.

oc delete vmsnapshot -n ${NS} ${VM}-snap1
oc get subvolume ${PV} -o jsonpath='{.status.diskChain}{" "}{.status.chainOperation}{"\n"}'

While the merge runs, status.chainOperation names it. No other snapshot or merge of the disk starts then. A merge takes about as long as copying the changed parts, not the whole disk. Repeat the command until chainOperation is empty.

Expected: the chain has two files, and the VM was never stopped.

docs.title: Step 6: Restore a snapshot to a new VM
docs.text:
OpenShift restores a snapshot by making new PVCs. The driver writes each with one sparse copy of the snapshot (qemu-img convert). The restore is a copy, so it takes time in proportion to the data.

cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualMachineRestore
metadata:
  name: ${VM}-restore
spec:
  target:
    apiGroup: kubevirt.io
    kind: VirtualMachine
    name: ${VM}-copy
  virtualMachineSnapshotName: ${VM}-snap2
  patches:
    - '{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/spec/domain/devices/interfaces/0/macAddress"}'
EOF

oc wait -n ${NS} vmrestore/${VM}-restore --for=jsonpath='{.status.complete}'=true --timeout=3600s
virtctl start ${VM}-copy -n ${NS}

The patches line removes the MAC address, so the copy does not clash with the original. Remove that line if your VM has no network interface with a fixed MAC address.

Expected: the new VM starts and has the file /var/tmp/marker-two.

A snapshot of a VM disk cannot be cloned. Restore the snapshot instead.

docs.title: Step 7: Remove all snapshots (flatten)
docs.text:
To go back to plain disks, delete all snapshots of the VM. The flatten command does it and waits until every disk is one disk.img again.

kubectl pool-snapshots flatten ${VM} -n ${NS}

Expected: the command lists the snapshots and asks you to type the VM name. Then it deletes them and prints Done: every disk of vms/my-vm is a plain disk.img. Use --yes to skip the question.

A VM with snapshots does not start while the Sidecar gate is off. Flatten first, then remove the Sidecar entry from the kubevirt.kubevirt.io/jsonpatch annotation, or run hack/sidecar-gate.sh off.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
oc delete vm -n ${NS} ${VM}-copy --ignore-not-found
oc delete vmrestore -n ${NS} ${VM}-restore --ignore-not-found
oc delete vmsnapshot -n ${NS} ${VM}-snap1 ${VM}-snap2 --ignore-not-found

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Backups and replication of a disk with instant snapshots make a full copy after each snapshot. A stopped VM's disk with snapshots is not copied until the VM runs or the disk is flattened.
  • A VM with snapshots gets a small extra container (the VM hook) when it starts. The driver adds it by itself. The hook needs the Sidecar gate.
  • Hot-plugged disks are not supported.

docs.text:
