docs.title: Part 12: Replicating Running VMs
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 6: Replication and Failover | Part 12 | Part 13: Failover of Running VMs

Copy a running VM with all its disks to a second cluster, while the VM keeps running. Check that every copy shows one moment for all disks, and see which copies are file-system consistent. The words moment, restore point, change list and receiver are defined in CONTEXT.md.

Time: about 1 hour, most of it waiting for the first copy. Status: Experimental. Read CROSS-REGION-DR.md, "Running VM disks", for the design and the lab results.

How it works, in short:

  1. The controller freezes the guest file systems for a moment. QEMU (the program that runs the VM) starts a copy of every disk of the VM at that one moment. The guest thaws.
  2. QEMU writes the copy slowly, 20 MB/s for each disk by default, so the VM keeps its speed.
  3. A Job sends the copy to the receiver on the destination cluster. The receiver applies it.
  4. QEMU keeps a change list. The next copy holds only the blocks that changed.
  5. Before the receiver changes a block, it saves the old contents in an undo file. The undo files are restore points.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Two clusters, with the driver on both: the source (where the VM runs) and the destination (the DR cluster). The clusters reach each other over HTTPS. The source cluster needs no NFS route to the destination.
  • A running VM on a pool StorageClass on the source cluster, with the guest agent (qemu-guest-agent) running. Without the guest agent, copies are crash consistent.
  • oc, helm, jq, openssl, virtctl, and the repository checkout (for the chart). Use the chart from the same release as the driver image that runs on the destination cluster.
  • The source nodes must be able to reach the receiver's address on the destination cluster. The address is a Route on the destination cluster's ingress, which on ROKS and ROVS is a public address, so the nodes need outbound internet access.
  • A pool on the destination cluster with room for the receiver volume (Step 1) and a pool zone that exists on the destination cluster.

Set the names. This tutorial calls the VM my-vm in the namespace vms and the source pool vm-pool:

export SRC_KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/source-config
export DR_KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/dr-config
export NS=vms
export VM=my-vm
export SRC_POOL=vm-pool
export DR_POOL=dr-vm-pool
src() { oc --kubeconfig "${SRC_KUBECONFIG}" "$@"; }
dr() { oc --kubeconfig "${DR_KUBECONFIG}" "$@"; }

Check the VM on the source cluster:

src get vmi -n ${NS} ${VM} -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{" agent="}{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="AgentConnected")].status}{"\n"}'

Expected: Running agent=True.

docs.title: Step 1: Make the destination pool and the receiver volume
docs.text:
On the destination cluster, make a pool. The receiver runs as UID 107, the same user as QEMU. Give the pool the same owner, so a failed-over VM can open its disk.

export ZONE=$(dr get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.labels.topology\.kubernetes\.io/zone}{"\n"}{end}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | awk 'NR==1{print $2}')

cat <<EOF | dr apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: ${DR_POOL}
spec:
  zone: ${ZONE}
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 500
  iops: 3000
  maxShares: 1
  initialShares: 1
  autoExpand: false
  defaultUID: 107
  defaultGID: 107
  defaultPermissions: "0777"
EOF

dr get filesharepool ${DR_POOL}

Wait for Ready. The receiver needs a volume that is big enough for all the disks you replicate, plus room for restore points:

cat <<EOF | dr apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: repl-destination-data
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  storageClassName: ${DR_POOL}
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 200Gi
EOF

docs.title: Step 2: Start the receiver
docs.text:
Make a token. Both clusters need it.

export REPL_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)

dr create secret generic repl-receiver-token -n kube-system --from-literal=token="${REPL_TOKEN}"

Enable the receiver on the destination cluster. Use the release name and chart path of your install:

helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi \
  --kubeconfig ${DR_KUBECONFIG} -n kube-system --reuse-values \
  --set replicationReceiver.enabled=true \
  --set replicationReceiver.pvcName=repl-destination-data \
  --set replicationReceiver.authSecretName=repl-receiver-token \
  --set replicationReceiver.tls.enabled=true

The receiver writes whole disks through NFS. Pages of files on NFS count against the container's memory limit, so the memory use of a busy receiver stays near the limit; that is normal, because the kernel drops the pages as it needs room. The receiver forces its data out every 32 MiB and drops the cached pages, and the default limit is 1Gi (see HELM-VALUES.md). Older versions with a 512Mi limit were killed (OOMKilled) during the first copy of an 11 GiB disk.

The chart makes a Deployment, a Service, a TLS certificate (it needs cert-manager) and, on OpenShift, a Route.

No cert-manager? A new ROKS or ROVS cluster has none, and the command above then fails with no matches for kind "Certificate" in version "cert-manager.io/v1" (nothing is changed). Use the Route's TLS instead: set --set replicationReceiver.tls.enabled=false. The Route then ends the TLS with the cluster's ingress certificate, which is signed by a public CA. The source trusts it without a CA Secret, so skip the repl-receiver-ca Secret below and leave destinationCACertSecretRef out of the policy in Step 3. See Part 6, Step 6c.

Check the receiver and get the address:

dr get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver
export RECEIVER_HOST=$(dr get route -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.host}')
echo https://${RECEIVER_HOST}

Expected: one pod 1/1 Running, and a host name.

Copy the token (and, if the receiver has its own certificate, the CA certificate) to the source cluster:

# Only with the receiver's own certificate (cert-manager):
dr get secret ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-receiver-certs -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d > /tmp/receiver-ca.crt
src create secret generic repl-receiver-ca -n kube-system --from-file=ca.crt=/tmp/receiver-ca.crt

# Always:
src create secret generic repl-source-token -n kube-system --from-literal=token="${REPL_TOKEN}"

(base64 -d is base64 -D on older macOS.)

docs.title: Step 3: Make the replication policy
docs.text:
On the source cluster, make a policy for the pool that holds the VM disks. The policy copies every volume of the pool. To copy only some, add subVolumeSelector (see Part 6).

cat <<EOF | src apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: ReplicationPolicy
metadata:
  name: vm-to-dr
spec:
  sourcePoolName: ${SRC_POOL}
  destinationEndpoint: https://${RECEIVER_HOST}
  destinationAuthSecretRef: repl-source-token
  destinationCACertSecretRef: repl-receiver-ca   # leave this line out if the Route provides the TLS
  destinationBasePath: /repl
  schedule: 15m
  maxRetries: 3
  maxParallelSyncs: 2
  vmCopyAdaptive: true
  restorePointKeepHours: 24
EOF

The fields that matter for a VM:

  • vmCopyAdaptive (default true) makes the copy of each disk start at 15 MB/s, speed up while the share the VM reads is quiet, and slow down when the share's average latency passes vmCopyMaxLatencyMs (default 15 ms). vmCopySpeedLimitMBps sets the highest speed; by default there is none. With vmCopyAdaptive: false it is the fixed speed instead (default 20; 0 means no limit). At 20 MB/s a VM kept 93% of its write speed in a lab test. The copy counts empty space too, so a first copy of a large disk takes long.
  • restorePointKeepHours is how long the destination keeps earlier moments. It is 24 by default. The disk uses more space the more the VM writes.
  • schedule is how often a new copy starts.

docs.title: Step 4: Watch the first copy
docs.text:
src get replicationpolicy vm-to-dr
src get replicationpolicy vm-to-dr -o json | jq -c '.status.subVolumeStatuses[] | {sv: .subVolumeName[0:16], phase: .vmCopy.phase, moment: .copyMoment, consistency, err: .lastError}'

The phase of a copy is Copying while QEMU writes the staging file, and Sending while a Job applies it at the destination. The first copy is a full copy. At 20 MB/s, a 20 GB disk needs about 17 minutes, and a 100 GB disk about 1.5 hours.

Expected after the first copy: every disk of the VM has the same copyMoment, consistency is FileSystemConsistent, and vmCopy is empty.

Plan on this: in a lab test, a 12 GiB root disk and a 2 GiB data disk took 10 minutes to copy at 20 MB/s, and 4 more minutes to send. The first status can appear several minutes after you create the policy.

If a copy fails, the status shows it: lastError of the disk says apply Job failed for <volume> (<reason>), for example when the receiver was restarted during the upload. The next cycle starts a new copy by itself. A receiver that was killed while it stored records cuts away the damaged end of its upload record, and the Job resumes. You do not need to clean up. To see why a Job failed, read the log of its pod while it runs: src logs -n kube-system <pod>.

consistency can also be CrashConsistent. Then consistencyReason says why, for example that the guest agent did not answer. A VM that starts from a crash consistent copy may need a file-system check, as after a power loss.

docs.title: Step 5: Watch an incremental copy and the restore points
docs.text:
Write something in the guest, and wait for the next cycle (15 minutes):

KUBECONFIG=${SRC_KUBECONFIG} virtctl ssh -n ${NS} cloud-user@vmi/${VM} -c 'head -c 50000000 /dev/urandom | sudo tee /var/tmp/big >/dev/null; sync'
src get replicationpolicy vm-to-dr -o json | jq -c '.status.subVolumeStatuses[] | {sv: .subVolumeName[0:16], moment: .copyMoment, bytes: .bytesSynced, points: .restorePoints, oldest: .oldestRestorePoint}'

Change cloud-user to the user of your guest image. Set the cluster with the KUBECONFIG variable, as above. With virtctl ssh --kubeconfig ... the connection helper reads the default kubeconfig instead, and the command fails with virtualmachineinstance ... "my-vm" not found. If ssh says Too many authentication failures, add -i <key> -t "-o IdentitiesOnly=yes".

Expected: the second copy sends far less than the disk size (about the 50 MB you wrote, plus whatever the guest wrote). restorePoints is now 1, and oldestRestorePoint is the first moment. Each further copy adds a restore point, until restorePointKeepHours passes.

docs.title: What changes a copy
docs.text:
• Live migration of the VM cancels the copy.
  • A restart or a move of the VM loses the change list. The next copy sends only the blocks that differ from the destination disk.
  • A hot-plugged disk is skipped.
  • A snapshot of the VM at the same time makes the copy wait. Copies and snapshots of one VM take turns.
  • A stopped VM is copied as a folder, as a plain volume is. A stopped VM whose disk has instant snapshots is not copied (see Part 11).
  • A running VM that has instant snapshots gets a full copy after each snapshot.

docs.title: See it in the console
docs.text: Open the replication policy page. For each disk, it shows the moment of the last copy and whether it is file-system or crash consistent. It also shows the restore points and the phase of a copy in progress. See Part 8.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
On the source cluster:

src delete replicationpolicy vm-to-dr
src delete secret -n kube-system repl-receiver-ca repl-source-token --ignore-not-found

Delete the temporary objects of a policy if any are left (the controller removes them when a copy ends). Use the policy name, because other policies have temporary objects too:

src delete jobs,pvc -n kube-system -l storage.ibmcloud.io/repl-policy=vm-to-dr --ignore-not-found
src delete pv -l storage.ibmcloud.io/repl-policy=vm-to-dr --ignore-not-found

On the destination cluster, keep the receiver and the data if you go on to Part 13. To remove them:

helm upgrade ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi --kubeconfig ${DR_KUBECONFIG} -n kube-system --reuse-values --set replicationReceiver.enabled=false
dr delete pvc -n kube-system repl-destination-data
dr delete secret -n kube-system repl-receiver-token
dr delete filesharepool ${DR_POOL}

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A policy copies a running VM at one moment for all disks, and sends only changed blocks after the first copy.
  • The status says which moment a copy shows and how consistent it is.
  • The destination keeps restore points so you can start the VM from an earlier moment.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: • Part 13: Failover of running VMs

docs.title: Part 13: Failover of Running VMs
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 12: Replicating Running VMs | Part 13

Start a replicated VM on the destination (DR) cluster. Choose the moment it starts from: the newest one, or an earlier restore point. The words failover, rewind, moment and restore point are defined in CONTEXT.md.

Time: about 30 minutes, plus the time to copy a disk if you rewind. Before you start: finish Part 12, so the destination holds copies of a VM with at least one good copy of every disk.

What the failover tool does and does not do:

  • It reads the metadata that replication left on the destination share. It creates a SubVolume, a PersistentVolume and a PVC for each volume on the DR cluster.
  • For a running VM, it picks the newest moment that all disks of the VM can show, so the disks fit each other. It rolls back a copy that stopped half way.
  • It does not make the VM, start the workload or change DNS. You apply the VM definition yourself.

Rewind before you start the VM. A VM that runs on the latest disk writes to it. After that, the disk no longer matches its restore points, and the tool refuses to rewind it. If you may want an earlier moment, rewind first.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The destination cluster from Part 12: the receiver, the pool dr-vm-pool, and the volume repl-destination-data in kube-system.
  • A place to run the failover tool where the destination share is mounted. The tool reads the replicated folders from a mounted share. There are two ways:
  • A host that can reach the destination share over NFS and the DR cluster's API. A VSI in the destination VPC works. A host in another VPC usually cannot reach the share (the NFS port times out).
  • A pod next to the share. The receiver pod cannot do this: it has no rights on the Kubernetes API. Make a pod that mounts the receiver volume (repl-destination-data, at /data) and runs under a service account that may create SubVolumes, PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims and read FileSharePools. This is the way used in the steps below.
  • The failover tool, built for Linux x86 (the failover pod and most hosts):
make build-failover        # makes bin/kubectl-failover; set GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 on another system

For a host, copy it to /usr/local/bin/ and check kubectl failover version.

The failover pod. Make a service account with these rights and a pod that mounts the receiver volume. Any image with a shell works; the driver image does:

cat <<EOF | dr apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: failover-tool, namespace: kube-system}
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata: {name: failover-tool}
rules:
  - {apiGroups: ["storage.ibmcloud.io"], resources: ["subvolumes"], verbs: ["get", "list", "create"]}
  - {apiGroups: ["storage.ibmcloud.io"], resources: ["filesharepools"], verbs: ["get", "list"]}
  - {apiGroups: [""], resources: ["persistentvolumes", "persistentvolumeclaims"], verbs: ["get", "list", "create"]}
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata: {name: failover-tool}
roleRef: {apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io, kind: ClusterRole, name: failover-tool}
subjects: [{kind: ServiceAccount, name: failover-tool, namespace: kube-system}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: failover-tool, namespace: kube-system}
spec:
  serviceAccountName: failover-tool
  imagePullSecrets: [{name: all-icr-io}]
  securityContext: {runAsUser: 107, runAsGroup: 107, runAsNonRoot: true, seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}}
  containers:
    - name: tool
      image: de.icr.io/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/driver:<your image tag>
      command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
      securityContext: {allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}}
      volumeMounts: [{name: data, mountPath: /data}]
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: repl-destination-data}
EOF
dr wait --for=condition=Ready pod/failover-tool -n kube-system
dr exec -i -n kube-system failover-tool -- sh -c 'cat > /tmp/kubectl-failover && chmod +x /tmp/kubectl-failover' < bin/kubectl-failover
failover() { dr exec -n kube-system failover-tool -- /tmp/kubectl-failover "$@"; }

Below, failover <args> is the pod way. On a host, read kubectl failover <args> instead, and add --kubeconfig ${DR_KUBECONFIG} to execute and status. Delete the pod, the ClusterRole and the binding when the failover is done.

Set the names from Part 12:

export DR_KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/dr-config
export DR_POOL=dr-vm-pool
dr() { oc --kubeconfig "${DR_KUBECONFIG}" "$@"; }

docs.title: Step 1: Stop replication (only if the source still runs)
docs.text:
If the source cluster is alive, pause the policy, so no copy arrives while you fail over:

oc --kubeconfig ${SRC_KUBECONFIG:-~/.kube/source-config} annotate replicationpolicy vm-to-dr storage.ibmcloud.io/paused=true

If the source cluster is lost, skip this step.

docs.title: Step 2: Find the destination share
docs.text:
Find the share's address and the folder of the receiver volume on the DR cluster:

export DR_IP=$(dr get filesharepool ${DR_POOL} -o jsonpath='{.status.shares[0].mountTargetIP}')
export DR_EXPORT=$(dr get filesharepool ${DR_POOL} -o jsonpath='{.status.shares[0].exportPath}')
export RECV_PV=$(dr get pvc -n kube-system repl-destination-data -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}')
export RECV_SUB=$(dr get subvolume ${RECV_PV} -o jsonpath='{.spec.subPath}')
echo "${DR_IP} export='${DR_EXPORT}' receiver folder=${RECV_SUB}"

In the failover pod, the receiver volume is mounted at /data, so the replicated folders are in /data/repl/pvcs:

dr exec -n kube-system failover-tool -- ls /data/repl/pvcs
export FAILOVER_PATH=/data/repl

On a host, mount the whole share. The share needs sec=sys:

sudo mkdir -p /mnt/dr
sudo mount -t nfs4 -o nfsvers=4.1,sec=sys,soft,timeo=600,retrans=3 ${DR_IP}:${DR_EXPORT:-/} /mnt/dr
ls /mnt/dr${RECV_SUB}/repl/pvcs
export FAILOVER_PATH=/mnt/dr${RECV_SUB}/repl

Expected: one folder pvc-<uuid> for each replicated volume. In Part 12 the policy used destinationBasePath: /repl, so the failover path is the receiver folder plus /repl.

docs.title: Step 3: Plan the failover
docs.text:
failover plan --nfs-mount-path ${FAILOVER_PATH}

Expected: a table with one row for each volume. The columns are SubVolume, PVC, namespace, size, age of the last copy and policy. Then the RPO (the age of the oldest last copy) and a list of the VMs with the moment each will show:

Running VM disks
  VM vms/my-vm shows the moment 2026-10-22T11:15:00Z
    pvc-aaa...: in place
    pvc-bbb...: in place

in place means the disk already shows that moment, so it is used as it is. The tool refuses with "a copy is still being applied" if a copy is in progress. Wait for it to end, or add --force, which rolls the unfinished copy back first.

To use an earlier moment, list the moments that all disks of each VM can show (newest first):

failover plan --nfs-mount-path ${FAILOVER_PATH} --list-moments

The list reaches back as far as restorePointKeepHours of the policy (24 hours by default). Choose one:

export MOMENT=2026-10-22T10:45:00Z
failover plan --nfs-mount-path ${FAILOVER_PATH} --rewind-to ${MOMENT}

Expected: the plan now says rewind (copies the whole disk into a new folder) for the disks that are ahead of the moment. The tool uses the newest moment at or before --rewind-to.

docs.title: Or use the Failover resource and the console
docs.text:
The same plan and failover can run without a shell. On the DR cluster, a cluster admin creates a Failover (or uses the Recovery page in the console). The receiver's data claim is a claim that the driver provisioned, and the controller finds its share address by itself. Part 12 used destinationBasePath: /repl, so the copies are in the repl folder of the claim, and the Failover must say so with basePath:

dr apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: Failover
metadata:
  name: plan-1
spec:
  action: Plan
  basePath: /repl
YAML
dr get failover plan-1 -o yaml

Expected: phase: Planned, with the VMs and the moments in the status. If basePath is wrong, the Plan fails and says which folder it looked for; if it finds copies in another folder it names the basePath to use. An Execute needs a Plan with the same basePath and a drPool. The Recovery page does not set basePath: with a destinationBasePath other than /, make the Plan and the Execute with kubectl as above, or use destinationBasePath: / for the policy.

docs.title: Step 4: Rewind the disks (optional)
docs.text:
Skip this step if the plan says in place for every disk and you want the newest moment.

failover execute --nfs-mount-path ${FAILOVER_PATH} --prepare-only --rewind-to ${MOMENT}

--prepare-only rolls back unfinished copies and rewinds the disks, then stops. It needs no cluster and no pool name. Each rewound disk goes into a new folder next to the original, named <volume>.rewind-<epoch>. The latest disk is not changed. A rewind copies the whole disk, so it can take minutes (about 2.5 minutes for 14 GiB in a lab test).

Expected: one line for each rewound disk: pvc-... rewound into /pvcs/pvc-....rewind-<epoch>. The tool prints Warning: skipping ...rewind-...: metadata file not found for these folders in later commands. This is harmless.

docs.title: Step 5: Make the volumes on the DR cluster
docs.text:
Each PV must name its folder by the path from the root of the share. The replicated volumes are inside the receiver volume's folder, so pass that path with --dr-export-path. The tool adds /pvcs/pvc-<uuid> to it.

export DR_EXPORT_PATH="${DR_EXPORT%/}${RECV_SUB}/repl"

The tool makes each PVC in the namespace it had on the source cluster, so make that namespace first (or pass --namespace to put every PVC in one namespace):

dr create namespace vms --dry-run=client -o yaml | dr apply -f -

docs.title: The newest moment
docs.text:
failover execute --nfs-mount-path ${FAILOVER_PATH} \
  --dr-pool ${DR_POOL} --dr-share-ip ${DR_IP} --dr-export-path "${DR_EXPORT_PATH}" --dry-run

failover execute --nfs-mount-path ${FAILOVER_PATH} \
  --dr-pool ${DR_POOL} --dr-share-ip ${DR_IP} --dr-export-path "${DR_EXPORT_PATH}"
failover status

Expected: Created SubVolume, Created PV and Created PVC for each volume (the dry run shows three lines for each volume and makes nothing). The PV path ends in .../repl/pvcs/pvc-<uuid>. The status table shows each PVC as Bound after a few seconds. The PVs have the prefix dr-. The PVCs keep the namespace and name they had on the source cluster. Running execute again skips what exists.

The PVs carry the pool's NFS mount options, including sec=sys, and the PVCs name no StorageClass, so the cluster default class does not apply. Check: dr get pv dr-pvc-<uuid> -o jsonpath='{.spec.mountOptions}'.

docs.title: An earlier moment (after Step 4)
docs.text:
Add --rewind-to ${MOMENT}. A dry run shows the rewound folder (...pvc-<uuid>.rewind-<epoch>) in each PV path and checks it the same way as a real run:

failover execute --nfs-mount-path ${FAILOVER_PATH} \
  --dr-pool ${DR_POOL} --dr-share-ip ${DR_IP} --dr-export-path "${DR_EXPORT_PATH}" \
  --rewind-to ${MOMENT} --dry-run

failover execute --nfs-mount-path ${FAILOVER_PATH} \
  --dr-pool ${DR_POOL} --dr-share-ip ${DR_IP} --dr-export-path "${DR_EXPORT_PATH}" \
  --rewind-to ${MOMENT}

Apply the current SubVolume CRD (config/crd) first: older ones refuse the .rewind-<epoch> folder.

docs.title: Step 6: Start the VM
docs.text:
Apply the VM definition on the DR cluster. Keep these in version control, or export them from the source cluster while it is alive. Remove status, metadata.uid, metadata.resourceVersion and the macAddress of the interface, and set spec.runStrategy to Halted, so the VM does not start before you say so. Every volume must name the PVC that you made above.

dr apply -n vms -f my-vm.yaml
virtctl start my-vm -n vms --kubeconfig ${DR_KUBECONFIG}
dr get vmi -n vms -w

Expected: the VM boots. The guest agent connects. The kernel log shows no file-system errors if the copy was FileSystemConsistent.

Check your data. For a VM that logs files, count the files and compare their checksums to the log. In a lab test with a VM that wrote a file and logged its checksum every 2 seconds, a VM started from the rewound disk had exactly the files up to the chosen moment (and not the file written later), and a VM started from the newest moment had all the files up to the last copy. All checksums matched. Both VMs started in under a minute.

After the VM runs, the disk no longer fits its restore points. failover execute --prepare-only --rewind-to ... now refuses with "has changed since its last copy". To try another moment, fail over again from copies that no VM has used.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
dr delete vm -n vms my-vm
dr delete pvc -n vms --all
sudo umount /mnt/dr      # only if you mounted the share on a host

The PVs that failover made have names that start with dr-. Their SubVolumes have the label storage.ibmcloud.io/failover-source. Both have the reclaim policy Retain, so deleting a PVC keeps the data on the share. Delete the PVs and SubVolumes last, when you no longer need the data. The data of the rewound disks is in the .rewind-<epoch> folders of the receiver volume. They are deleted with the receiver volume.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• kubectl failover plan shows the RPO and the moment each VM will show.
  • --list-moments and --rewind-to choose an earlier restore point.
  • --prepare-only rewinds the disks before any VM runs on them.
  • execute makes the PVCs. You apply the VM definition and start the VM.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Part 6: Replication and Failover for plain volumes.
  • CROSS-REGION-DR.md, "Running VM disks".

docs.title: Part 14: Restore a Snapshot in the Console
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 8: Migration and Console | Part 14

Make a snapshot of a volume in the OpenShift console, change the volume, and restore the snapshot to a new PVC without writing any YAML. Then check the data in the new PVC. The words snapshot and restore are defined in CONTEXT.md.

Time: about 15 minutes. Scope: this page restores a snapshot, which stays on the same share as its volume. The console has a Backups tab for backups. To back up, restore and delete backups in the console, see Part 16. To do the same with kubectl backup, see Part 10.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The console plugin is on. In the chart it is consolePlugin.enabled (the default). In the console, the menu Storage shows IBM VPC File Pools. See Part 8 if it does not.
  • A pool and a StorageClass, and a VolumeSnapshotClass for the driver (the chart makes ibm-vpc-file-pool). See Part 1.
  • oc, to write and read files. You can do those steps in the console terminal instead.

docs.title: Step 1: Make a volume with data
docs.text:
export NS=pool-tutorial-console
oc create namespace ${NS}

cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-data
spec:
  storageClassName: ibm-vpc-file-pool
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal:latest
      command: ["/bin/bash", "-c", "echo before > /data/state; sleep 36000"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: app-data
EOF

oc wait -n ${NS} --for=condition=Ready pod/app --timeout=300s
oc exec -n ${NS} app -- cat /data/state

Change storageClassName if your pool has another StorageClass.

Expected: before.

docs.title: Step 2: Make the snapshot in the console
docs.text:
1. Open Storage, then IBM VPC File Pools, then the Snapshots tab.
  2. Choose Create snapshot.
  3. Under Source volume, choose pool-tutorial-console/app-data. The list shows only claims on a StorageClass of this driver.
  4. Leave the name, or type app-data-before. The snapshot goes in the namespace of the claim.
  5. Choose Create.

If the page says No snapshot class for this driver, make a VolumeSnapshotClass first (the chart makes one when volumeSnapshotClass.create is true).

Expected: the snapshot appears in the list. Its Ready column shows it as ready when the copy has ended. A snapshot of a plain volume is a copy of its folder (a Job runs it), so a large volume takes time. A snapshot of a VM disk is a QEMU copy or an instant snapshot. See CONTEXT.md.

docs.title: Step 3: Change the volume
docs.text:
oc exec -n ${NS} app -- bash -c 'echo after > /data/state; echo new > /data/new-file'
oc exec -n ${NS} app -- cat /data/state

Expected: after.

docs.title: Step 4: Restore the snapshot to a new PVC
docs.text:
1. On the Snapshots tab, open the snapshot. Or open the row menu (the three dots) of the snapshot.
  2. Choose Restore to new PVC.

The button is off, with a reason, in two cases: the snapshot is not ready yet, or no VolumeSnapshot points to it. A Snapshot object made directly, without a VolumeSnapshot, has none. Create a VolumeSnapshot for it first.

The form has defaults:

Field Default Notes Name <source claim>-restored The name of the new claim. It must not exist. Namespace The snapshot's namespace You cannot change it. This is a Kubernetes rule. Size (GiB) The snapshot's size You can make it bigger, not smaller. Storage class The class of the source claim Only classes of this driver are offered. Access mode From the source claim Volume mode From the source claim
  1. Leave the defaults and choose Restore.

If a VM uses the source claim, the form shows a warning. The warning says the snapshot may be a plain file copy that does not boot. That text is older than the driver. A snapshot of a running VM's disk is now a QEMU copy or an instant snapshot. Check status.consistency of the Snapshot (FileSystemConsistent is best) before you rely on it.

Expected: the page shows a banner. It says Restoring: the copy is starting, then a progress bar with the bytes copied, then The restored volume is ready. The new claim stays Pending until the copy ends. If the copy fails, the banner shows the error and keeps the claim. The action only makes a new claim. It never replaces an existing volume.

Check the claim:

oc get pvc -n ${NS}

Expected: app-data and app-data-restored, both Bound.

docs.title: Step 5: Check the data
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: check
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: check
      image: registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal:latest
      command: ["/bin/bash", "-c", "cat /data/state; ls /data"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: app-data-restored
EOF

oc wait -n ${NS} --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/check --timeout=300s
oc logs -n ${NS} check

Expected: the log shows before and a listing with state only. The file new-file is not there, because it was made after the snapshot.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
oc delete namespace ${NS}

This deletes the PVCs. Delete the snapshot in the console first (Snapshots tab, row menu, Delete), because it holds space on the share until you delete it. A pool cannot be deleted while snapshots exist on it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• You can make and restore a snapshot from the console.
  • A restore always makes a new claim, and the claim waits until the copy ends.
  • This page restores snapshots. Backups restore in the console on the Backups tab (Part 16) or with kubectl backup restore.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Part 16: Backups, clones and replication setup in the console
  • Part 10: Backup and restore
  • Part 2: Snapshots and clones does the same with YAML.

docs.title: Part 15: Make a VM from the Catalog on a Pool
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 1: Pool Creation | Part 15

Make a virtual machine (VM) from the OpenShift Virtualization catalog, with its boot disk on a pool. You pick an image and an instance type, and you choose the pool's StorageClass for the boot disk. CDI (the Containerized Data Importer) copies the image onto the pool. Then the VM starts. This is the recommended way to make a VM on a pool. The driver needs no special image setup.

Time: about 30 minutes, most of it waiting for the image copy. On rovslab (24 October 2026, driver v0.14.1, OpenShift 4.21), the copy of the CentOS Stream 9 image onto a 100-IOPS share took about 13 minutes for the first VM and about 7 minutes for a second VM. Status: Beta. See FEATURES.md (the CDI copy limit feature). This page was run end to end on rovslab on 24 October 2026, both in the console and with YAML. Scope: this page makes a VM from a catalog image. It does not use the pool's golden images, which are hidden. See FEATURES.md.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The driver runs on the cluster (Part 1).
  • OpenShift Virtualization is installed. Check that its HyperConverged object exists:
oc get hyperconverged -n openshift-cnv

Expected: one object named kubevirt-hyperconverged.

  • A login that can make a namespace, a VM and read cluster-wide objects such as StorageProfiles.

docs.title: Step 1: Use a pool that suits VMs
docs.text:
A VM disk needs a pool whose folders belong to the QEMU user. KubeVirt runs QEMU as user and group 107. The pool must set defaultUID: 107, defaultGID: 107 and defaultPermissions: "0777". Without them, the VM can fail to start with preparing host-disks failed: chown ... operation not permitted (KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md).

If you have the pool from Part 1, it already sets them. Check:

export POOL_NAME=my-pool
oc get filesharepool ${POOL_NAME} \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.defaultUID}{" "}{.spec.defaultGID}{" "}{.spec.defaultPermissions}{"\n"}'

Expected: 107 107 0777.

If you have no pool yet, make one. Use the zone of your workers (oc get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone). The share must hold the VM disk, so the example makes a 100 GB share. More IOPS make the image copy faster.

cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1
kind: FileSharePool
metadata:
  name: ${POOL_NAME}
spec:
  zone: eu-de-1
  profile: dp2
  shareSizeGB: 100
  iops: 3000
  maxShares: 3
  initialShares: 1
  autoExpand: true
  expandThresholdPercent: 80
  allocationStrategy: spread
  defaultPermissions: "0777"
  defaultUID: 107
  defaultGID: 107
EOF

oc get filesharepools -w

Expected: PHASE shows Ready after the first share is made. Part 1 explains each field.

docs.title: Step 2: Check the StorageClass and the CDI StorageProfile
docs.text:
The controller makes a StorageClass with the name of the pool. A pool with tiers gets one StorageClass for each tier, named <pool>-<tier>.

oc get sc ${POOL_NAME}

Expected: one StorageClass with the provisioner vpc-file-pool.csi.ibm.io.

CDI makes a StorageProfile for each StorageClass. A StorageProfile tells CDI which access mode and volume mode to ask for when it makes a disk. The controller patches the profile of every pool StorageClass when CDI is installed.

oc get storageprofile ${POOL_NAME} -o jsonpath='{.spec}{"\n"}'

Expected: the output holds "claimPropertySets":[{"accessModes":["ReadWriteMany"],"volumeMode":"Filesystem"}] and "cloneStrategy":"csi-clone".

If the StorageProfile is not found, CDI has not made it yet. The controller patches it on a later reconcile, so check again in a minute. If the fields stay empty, read the controller log:

oc logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=controller \
  -c csi-controller --tail=200 | grep -i storageprofile

docs.title: Step 3: Check the copy pod memory limit
docs.text:
CDI's copy pods have a default memory limit of 600 MB. When a copy pod writes onto NFS, the file cache counts against that limit, and the pod is killed for lack of memory (OOMKilled). The controller keeps the limit at least 8Gi. It sets limits.memory in the storageWorkloads field of the HyperConverged object. It checks at start-up and every 5 minutes. It only raises the limit and never lowers it. The Helm value is cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit (default 8Gi).

oc get hyperconverged -n openshift-cnv kubevirt-hyperconverged \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.resourceRequirements.storageWorkloads}{"\n"}'

oc get cdi -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.config.podResourceRequirements}{"\n"}'

Expected: both outputs show limits.memory of 8Gi or more.

On ROVS, IBM manages the virtualization add-on, and IBM says it cannot be modified. The driver changes one field of the HyperConverged object that IBM's add-on makes. After an add-on update, check the limit again. If the controller must not change HyperConverged, set cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit="". Then catalog copies of large disks onto the pool fail. See KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md.

docs.title: Step 4: Make the VM in the console
docs.text:
1. Make a project (namespace) for the VM. The steps below use pool-tutorial-vm.
export NS=pool-tutorial-vm
oc create namespace ${NS}
  1. In the OpenShift console, open Virtualization, then Catalog, in the project pool-tutorial-vm. The page is called Create new VirtualMachine. Stay on the InstanceTypes tab.
  2. Under Select volume to boot from, choose a catalog image, such as centos-stream9 or rhel9.
  3. Under Select InstanceType, keep the default (for example U series, u1.medium) or choose another.
  4. Under VirtualMachine details, set Name, and set Storage class to the pool's StorageClass. It has the name of the pool (my-pool in the example). Keep the Disk size, or make it bigger.
  5. Choose Create VirtualMachine.

These labels are from OpenShift 4.21. Other versions can name them differently. The three choices are the same: the image, the instance type and the StorageClass of the boot disk.

Go to Step 6 to watch the copy.

docs.title: Step 5: Make the same VM with YAML (optional)
docs.text:
The console makes a VirtualMachine with a dataVolumeTemplate. The template has a sourceRef that points to a catalog DataSource. You can make the same object with oc.

List the catalog DataSources. The catalog images are in the namespace openshift-virtualization-os-images:

oc get datasource -n openshift-virtualization-os-images

Pick one and set its name. The names depend on your cluster, so this page does not give one.

export DS=<name from the list>

A DataSource can carry the names of a default instance type and a default preference. Read them:

oc get datasource ${DS} -n openshift-virtualization-os-images \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.instancetype\.kubevirt\.io/default-instancetype}{"\n"}{.metadata.labels.instancetype\.kubevirt\.io/default-preference}{"\n"}'

If a name is empty, list the choices and pick one:

oc get virtualmachineclusterinstancetype
oc get virtualmachineclusterpreference

export INSTANCETYPE=<instance type name>
export PREFERENCE=<preference name>

Make the VM. The storage block leaves out the access mode and the volume mode. CDI takes them from the StorageProfile of Step 2, which is why that profile matters. Make the size at least as big as the image needs.

cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachine
metadata:
  name: catalog-vm
spec:
  runStrategy: Always
  instancetype:
    name: ${INSTANCETYPE}
  preference:
    name: ${PREFERENCE}
  dataVolumeTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: catalog-vm-rootdisk
      spec:
        sourceRef:
          kind: DataSource
          name: ${DS}
          namespace: openshift-virtualization-os-images
        storage:
          storageClassName: ${POOL_NAME}
          resources:
            requests:
              storage: 30Gi
  template:
    spec:
      domain:
        devices:
          disks:
            - name: rootdisk
              disk:
                bus: virtio
      volumes:
        - name: rootdisk
          dataVolume:
            name: catalog-vm-rootdisk
EOF

Expected: virtualmachine.kubevirt.io/catalog-vm created. If the instance type is namespaced rather than cluster-wide in your cluster, add kind: VirtualMachineInstancetype under instancetype, and the same for the preference. Check the fields against the VirtualMachine CRD with oc explain virtualmachine.spec.instancetype.

docs.title: Step 6: Watch the copy
docs.text:
oc get datavolume -n ${NS} -w

Expected: the DataVolume of the VM moves through its phases, and the PROGRESS column rises until the phase is Succeeded. In the console, the VM page shows the same progress.

Look at the pods and the PVC while it runs:

oc get pods,pvc -n ${NS}

Expected: the PVC catalog-vm-rootdisk is Pending while the copy runs, and becomes Bound when the DataVolume is Succeeded (the PVC and the DataVolume have the same name). CDI copies into a temporary claim on the pool, then hands the volume to your PVC. The CDI pods and the temporary claim are in the namespace of the catalog images, not in ${NS}:

oc get pods,pvc -n openshift-virtualization-os-images

If you used the console, the PVC has the name of the VM with -volume added (for example console-vm-volume). It is also on the VM's Storage tab.

If the CDI pod restarts and the progress goes back to zero, go to If the copy fails.

docs.title: Step 7: Check that the VM boots and has its guest agent
docs.text:
export VM=catalog-vm
oc get vmi -n ${NS} ${VM}
oc get vmi -n ${NS} ${VM} \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="AgentConnected")].status}{"\n"}'

Expected: the VMI is Running, and the second command prints True. The guest agent starts a little after the guest boots, so repeat the second command if it prints nothing. If you used the console, change VM to the name of your VM.

For a look at the screen, open the VM in the console and choose its Console tab.

docs.title: Step 8: Find the boot disk on the pool
docs.text:
Each PVC on a pool has a SubVolume object. The SubVolume has the name of the PV that the PVC uses. SubVolumes are cluster-wide, so you need no namespace.

export PVC=catalog-vm-rootdisk
export PV=$(oc get pvc -n ${NS} ${PVC} -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}')
oc get subvolume ${PV} -o jsonpath='{.spec.poolName}{" "}{.spec.shareID}{" "}{.spec.subPath}{" "}{.status.phase}{"\n"}'

Expected: the name of your pool, a share ID, a folder such as /pvcs/pvc-<uuid>, and the phase Bound. The disk is the file disk.img in that folder, on that share.

See the file from inside the VM's pod. The VM's virt-launcher pod has the disk under /var/run/kubevirt-private/vmi-disks/<disk name>/:

LAUNCHER=$(oc get pods -n ${NS} -l vm.kubevirt.io/name=${VM} -o name | head -1)
oc exec -n ${NS} ${LAUNCHER} -c compute -- ls -l /var/run/kubevirt-private/vmi-disks/

Expected: one folder for each disk. For the YAML of Step 5, and for a VM made in the console, it is rootdisk. List that folder to see disk.img:

oc exec -n ${NS} ${LAUNCHER} -c compute -- ls -l /var/run/kubevirt-private/vmi-disks/rootdisk/

Expected: a file disk.img. CDI wrote it in raw format. KubeVirt needs raw format for a disk on a file system, and CDI converts the catalog image for you.

docs.title: If the copy fails
docs.text:
The CDI pod shows OOMKilled, the DataVolume keeps restarting, and the progress goes back to zero. The memory limit of the copy pods is too low. The limit is too low if cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit is empty, if the controller cannot patch HyperConverged, or if something put the old value back, such as an update of IBM's add-on on ROVS.

  1. Run the two checks of Step 3.
  2. Check that cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit is not empty.
  3. Check that the controller's ClusterRole allows get, list and patch on hco.kubevirt.io hyperconvergeds.
  4. The controller corrects the limit within 5 minutes. Restart the controller to make it check at once.
  5. Look for a warning in the controller log, and check the metric vpc_file_pool_cdi_copy_limit_raised_total:
oc logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi,app.kubernetes.io/component=controller \
  -c csi-controller | grep -i "CDI copy pod memory limit"
  1. If a raise happens again and again, something resets the value. On ROVS, ask IBM support.
  2. Delete the failed DataVolume and make the VM again. The copy starts from zero:
oc delete datavolume -n ${NS} catalog-vm-rootdisk

The full steps are in TROUBLESHOOTING.md.

The VM says "No bootable device". The disk is not in raw format. CDI converts the catalog image, so check the DataVolume with oc describe datavolume -n ${NS} catalog-vm-rootdisk. See TROUBLESHOOTING.md.

The VM does not start and the event names a chown error. The pool does not set defaultUID: 107. Go back to Step 1.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Delete the VM first. The DataVolume that the VM made goes with it, then its PVC, then its SubVolume.

oc delete vm -n ${NS} catalog-vm
oc get pvc -n ${NS}
oc get subvolume ${PV}

Expected: the PVC list is empty. The last command says the SubVolume is not found. If you made the VM in the console, delete it there, or use the name of your VM.

oc delete namespace ${NS}

If you made the pool only for this page, delete it after the namespace is gone. A pool cannot be deleted while volumes exist on it, and deleting a pool deletes its VPC shares:

oc delete filesharepool ${POOL_NAME}

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A VM from the catalog needs only a pool with defaultUID: 107, defaultGID: 107 and defaultPermissions: "0777", and the pool's StorageClass for the boot disk.
  • The controller patches the CDI StorageProfile of the pool's StorageClass, and keeps the memory limit of CDI's copy pods at 8Gi or more.
  • The boot disk is one raw file, disk.img, in the folder of the volume's SubVolume.
  • On ROVS, check the copy pod limit again after an update of the add-on.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Part 14: Restore a snapshot in the console
  • Part 1: Pool creation, PVCs and KubeVirt VMs writes a disk image onto a pool by hand.
  • KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md has the measured results for CDI.

docs.title: Part 16: Backups, Clones and Replication Setup in the Console
docs.text:
Tutorial Series: Index | Part 6: Replication & Failover | Part 10: Backup and Restore | Part 14: Restore a Snapshot in the Console | Part 16

Do three jobs in the OpenShift console, with no YAML. First, back up a volume on a schedule, restore it, and delete its backups. Second, clone a volume to a new PVC. Third, set up a replication receiver: paste its token and certificate, let the console make the Secrets, and check the connection. The words backup, moment, restore point and snapshot pool are defined in CONTEXT.md.

Time: about 45 minutes for parts A and B, most of it waiting for backups. Part C needs a second cluster. Status: backups are Experimental (BACKUP-RECOVERY.md). This page was run end to end on rovslab on 24 October 2026 (driver v0.14.1, OpenShift 4.21), with a second cluster for part C. Scope: the console does not run kubectl backup cos-setup. Part A shows what the COS tab does and links to the commands.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The console plugin is on. In the console, the menu Storage shows IBM VPC File Pools (Part 8).
  • The data pool, the snapshot pool and the labelled volume of Part 10, Steps 1 to 3. They give you the namespace pool-tutorial-backup, the pools tut-data and tut-backups, and the PVC files with the label backup=yes. The steps below use those names.
  • oc, to check the results. You can use the console terminal instead.
  • Your login may create BackupPolicy and BackupRestore objects. Without the right, the console switches the button off, names the missing right and shows YAML for an administrator.
  • For part C only: a second cluster with a running replication receiver (Part 6, Step 6a to 6c).
export NS=pool-tutorial-backup
export POLICY=tut-console
oc get pvc -n ${NS} files --show-labels

Expected: files is Bound and has the label backup=yes.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Backups tab
docs.text: Open Storage, then IBM VPC File Pools, then the Backups tab. The list is empty, and says "No BackupPolicies found".

docs.title: Step 2: Make a policy with the form
docs.text:
1. Choose Create BackupPolicy.
  2. Fill in the form:
Field What to enter Name tut-console. The name is also a label value on the volumes the policy backs up, so you cannot change it later. Snapshot pool tut-backups. Only a pool that holds no workload claims and has a ready share can be chosen. The other pools are listed but switched off, with the reason. Schedule Choose Custom and type 5m. The presets are 1h, 6h, 12h and 24h. The least is 1 minute. Keep for 48h. The links under the box (1 day, 7 days, 30 days) fill it in. The least is 1 hour. Labels Key backup, value yes, then Add label. A policy with no labels is refused. Namespaces pool-tutorial-backup. Empty means all namespaces. VM copy speed limit (MB/s per disk) Leave it. It matters only for VM disks.
  1. Look under Labels. A line counts the claims that match. It says 1 claim matches. If it says No claim matches yet. Check the labels., the label is wrong.
  2. The blue box at the top of the form says that backups stop when the snapshot pool is more than 85% full. Nothing is deleted to make room, and backups start again when the use falls to 85% or less.
  3. Choose Create.

The form checks the same limits as the admission webhook. If the webhook still refuses the policy, the page shows its message under Creation failed.

Expected: the page of the policy opens. Its Phase shows Unknown for a few seconds, then Active. Check from a terminal:

oc get backuppolicy ${POLICY}

Expected: PHASE is Active. If it is Error, the page shows a red banner with the reason. The usual cause is a snapshot pool that is not Ready yet.

docs.title: Step 3: Read the list and the policy page
docs.text:
Go back to the Backups tab. The list has one row for each policy, with these columns:

Column Meaning Name A link to the policy page. Snapshot Pool, Schedule, Keep The settings of the policy. Phase Active, Suspended or Error. Volumes How many volumes the policy backs up. Stalest Backup How old the oldest "last backup" is. It says No backup yet until the first backup ends. Export On or Off: whether the policy also sends backups to COS.

When a policy is in the Error phase because its snapshot pool is more than 85% full, a red banner above the table says so and links to the pool.

Open the policy. The Overview tab shows the settings (Snapshot Pool, Schedule, Keep, Volumes picked by label, Namespaces, VM Copy Speed Limit, Export to COS). Below them is a table with one row for each volume:

Column Meaning Claim namespace/name of the PVC. A volume that the policy no longer backs up says No longer backed up, kept until <date>. VM The VM that uses the disk, or -. Last Backup, Oldest Backup How long ago. A restore can go back as far as the oldest. Restore Points How many older moments, besides the newest, a restore can go back to. Size What the newest backup wrote, for a VM disk. A plain volume shows -: its file copy does not count bytes. Consistency File copy for a plain volume. File-system consistent or Crash consistent for a VM disk. A crash consistent copy has an orange label. Error The last error, or -. Export The COS state of the volume.

Expected: the table has one row, pool-tutorial-backup/files. Its Consistency is File copy once the first backup ends. The first backup takes as long as the first copy. A new backup is made every 5 minutes.

Wait until Last Backup shows a time. Then wait for Restore Points to reach 1, which takes one more cycle.

docs.title: Step 4: Suspend and resume the policy
docs.text:
Suspend stops new backups. The backups that exist stay.

  1. On the policy page, choose Suspend. Or open the menu (the three dots) of the policy on the Backups list and choose Suspend.

Expected: Phase is Suspended, and the page shows an information box Backups are suspended. The button now reads Resume. The phase can take up to 20 seconds to change on the page.

  1. Choose Resume.

Expected: Phase is Active again.

The same menu has View Details, Edit and Delete. Edit opens the same form, with the name switched off.

docs.title: Step 5: Restore a volume with the Restore form
docs.text:
A restore makes a new PVC. It never writes over a volume that exists.

  1. On the policy page, open the menu (the three dots) of the row pool-tutorial-backup/files and choose Restore.

The page is called Restore from a backup. The fields:

Field Default and notes Volume The volume you chose. A volume that is gone is listed too, with (no longer backed up), until its backups pass the keep time. A line below shows the oldest and the newest backup. Latest backup / At a moment Latest backup is on. With At a moment, a Moment field appears. Choose a time in your time zone. The restore uses the newest backup at or before it. The page refuses a time before the oldest backup. Namespace The namespace of the backed-up claim. New claim name files-restored. The page refuses a name that exists. Storage class Same as the backed-up claim, with the class name. Only classes of this driver are offered.
  1. Leave the defaults and choose Restore.
  2. A box asks Restore from this backup? It says that a new claim is made, that nothing is overwritten, and that the copy takes time. Choose Restore.

Expected: a banner follows the restore through these titles:

  1. Restoring: the request is starting
  2. Restoring: making the new volume
  3. Restoring: copying the backup into the new volume
  4. The restored volume is ready, with the line Restored the latest backup, from <time>.

If the restore fails, the banner is red and says The restore failed with the message. Nothing was written over an existing volume. The banner links to the new claim. Choose Back to the policy to leave the page.

Check from a terminal:

oc get backuprestore
oc get pvc -n ${NS}

Expected: one BackupRestore with PHASE Done, and the PVC files-restored.

docs.title: Step 6: Check the restored data
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | oc apply -n ${NS} -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: files-check
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: check
      image: registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal:latest
      command: ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
      args: ["cat /data/a/1; ls /data"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: files-restored
EOF

oc wait -n ${NS} --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/files-check --timeout=300s
oc logs -n ${NS} files-check

Expected: the output is first, then a listing with a, keep and written. A pod that mounts the new claim does not start until the restore ends.

To restore an earlier moment, repeat Step 5 and choose At a moment. The line under Volume shows the oldest and the newest backup. Enter a time in your own time zone.

docs.title: Step 7: Delete the backups of a volume
docs.text:
Delete backups is the only destructive action of the Backups tab. It removes all backups of one volume, for good. The volume itself is not touched.

First see the refusal. The policy still backs up files, so:

  1. On the policy page, open the menu of the row pool-tutorial-backup/files and choose Delete backups.

Expected: the box is called Delete backups of pool-tutorial-backup/files. It shows a warning, The backups of this volume cannot be removed now, and the text Policy tut-console still backs up pool-tutorial-backup/files: remove the label that selects it, or delete the policy, wait for the next backup cycle, then try again. Nothing starts. Close the box.

The box also refuses while a restore of the volume has not ended. The text is Restore <name> of <claim> has not ended; wait for it, then try again.

Now stop the policy from backing up the volume. Remove the label, and wait for one backup cycle (5 minutes):

oc label pvc -n ${NS} files backup-

Expected: after one cycle, the row of the volume says No longer backed up, kept until <date>.

  1. Open Delete backups on the row again. The console starts a short Job in kube-system that only measures the backups. The box says Measuring the backups on the snapshot pool....
  2. When the measure ends, a red box says This removes all backups of pool-tutorial-backup/files from policy tut-console, for good. It shows the two folders, the size and the number of moments.
  3. Type pool-tutorial-backup/files in the box. The button Delete backups turns on only when the text matches exactly.
  4. Choose Delete backups.

Expected: the box says Removing the backups on the snapshot pool..., then The backups are removed, with Removed the backups of pool-tutorial-backup/files (<size>). The console removes its Jobs when they end. If the folders are empty, the box says No backup data found and stops. If the delete fails, it says The delete stopped. You can try again.

The Jobs run in kube-system with your own rights. Without them, the box names the missing rights and shows the command kubectl backup delete --policy tut-console --pvc pool-tutorial-backup/files for an administrator. After a policy is deleted, its status no longer says where its backups are. Then use kubectl backup delete --pool ... --volume ... (Part 10).

docs.title: Step 8: Look at the COS tab
docs.text:
A policy can also send its backups, encrypted, to an IBM Cloud Object Storage (COS) bucket. Open the policy and choose the COS tab.

For a policy with no export, the tab says This policy does not export to COS. The tab shows:

  • Set up the export. A guide with four steps. It shows the kubectl backup cos-setup command with your names filled in (Region, Resource group, Bucket, Key Protect root key CRN, VPC CRN, Admin addresses, Folder in the bucket (optional)). The console does not run it, because it needs your own IBM Cloud login and the console must not hold an IBM Cloud API key. After you run it on your machine, you paste what it wrote:
  • Step 2. Make the Secrets. Paste the two Secret files and the Key Protect API key, then choose Make the Secrets. The console makes the Secrets in kube-system. It sends each once, never reads a Secret back, and leaves a Secret that exists already as it is.
  • Step 3. Save the export to the policy. Paste the spec.export block that the command printed, then choose Save the export to the policy.
  • Step 4. Check that it works. A line says whether volumes have reached COS.
  • What is in the bucket. The button List COS contents runs a read-only Job and shows the volumes and their moments. It is off while the policy has no export.
  • Restore from COS. A link, also on the Backups list. It makes a restore from the bucket, and works in a cluster that has no policy.

For a policy with an export, the tab also shows Export settings and Export state of each volume.

Make the bucket by hand with Part 9. The commands and the full export are in BACKUP-RECOVERY.md.

docs.title: Part B: Clone a volume
docs.text: A clone is a new PVC with a copy of the data of another PVC. A Job copies the data in the background.

docs.title: Step 9: Clone with "Clone to new PVC"
docs.text:
1. Open the SubVolumes tab. Find the row whose PVC is pool-tutorial-backup/files.
  2. Open the menu of the row and choose Clone to new PVC. Or open the SubVolume page and choose the button Clone to new PVC.

The action is off, with a reason, in these cases: the volume is not Bound yet, or a copy into the volume is still running.

The page is called Clone to new PVC. The fields:

Field Default and notes Name files-clone. Namespace The namespace of the source claim. You cannot change it. This is a Kubernetes rule. Size (GiB) The size of the source volume. You can make it bigger, not smaller. The page shows the free space of the pool. Storage class The class of the source claim. Only classes of this driver are offered. Access mode, Volume mode Copied from the source claim.
  1. Leave the defaults and choose Clone.

If a VM uses the source claim, the page warns A VM uses this claim: the clone is a plain file copy made while the VM runs, so the cloned disk may not boot. Here no VM uses files.

docs.title: Step 10: Follow the clone
docs.text:
Expected: a banner follows the clone:

  1. Cloning: the copy is starting
  2. Cloning: copying <size> from the volume, with a bar that shows Copied <size> of <size>
  3. The cloned volume is ready, with The claim files-clone is Bound.

If the copy fails, the banner is red: Cloning failed, with the error. The claim is not deleted. Choose Back to volumes to leave the page.

The claim is Bound at once: the driver makes the claim and copies the data behind it. A pod that mounts the claim waits until the copy ends. The banner follows the copy, not the claim. In driver v0.14.1 and earlier, the banner showed the last title as soon as the claim was Bound, before the copy ended. To see the copy itself, open the SubVolume of the clone (it has the same name as the PV of the claim). The Clone Progress card shows the bar, Started At, Completed At and any Clone error. The Clone Status column of the SubVolumes list shows the same.

oc get pvc -n ${NS}
oc get subvolumes -o wide

Expected: the PVCs files, files-restored and files-clone are Bound.

docs.title: Part C: Set up a replication receiver
docs.text: A receiver is a pod on the destination cluster. It takes the data of a replication policy over HTTPS. The form needs the receiver's address, its token, and its certificate. This part uses two clusters. The destination cluster runs the receiver. The source cluster runs the console you use.

docs.title: Step 11: Get the token and the certificate from the destination
docs.text:
On the destination cluster, read the token that you put in the receiver's Secret. Part 6 names it repl-receiver-token, with the key token:

oc get secret repl-receiver-token -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d; echo

Get the address of the receiver:

oc get route -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=replication-receiver \
  -o jsonpath='https://{.items[0].spec.host}{"\n"}'

If the receiver has its own certificate (Part 6, Option A), copy the CA certificate as well. If the Route provides the TLS with a public authority (Option B), you need no certificate.

oc get secret ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-receiver-certs -n kube-system \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d

Expected: a long token, an https:// address, and for Option A a block that starts with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----.

docs.title: Step 12: Fill in the replication form
docs.text:
On the source cluster, open Storage, IBM VPC File Pools, the Replication tab, and choose Create ReplicationPolicy.

Field What to enter Name dr-console. The console names the Secrets and the check Job after it. Enter the name first. Source Pool Name tut-data. Replication Mode Driver-to-Driver (cross-region). Receiver Endpoint The https:// address. The form refuses http://. Token and certificate Make new Secrets from what I paste. The other choice, Use Secrets that already exist, asks for the names of Secrets in kube-system (Auth Secret Name with the key token, CA Cert Secret Name (optional) with the key ca.crt). Token Paste the token. CA certificate (optional) Paste the certificate in PEM form. Leave it empty when a public authority signed the receiver's certificate. SubVolume Selector Add the label tutorial = receiver-setup, with Add. See the note below.

Note: Create makes a real policy. Without labels in the SubVolume Selector, every SubVolume in the pool is replicated. A label that no volume has replicates none. Use this to test the receiver without copying data.

docs.title: Step 13: Check the connection
docs.text:
Choose Check connection. The console does three things:

  1. It makes the Secrets dr-console-receiver-token and dr-console-receiver-ca in kube-system. The token goes once from the browser to this cluster's API server. The console keeps no copy and never reads a Secret back. If a Secret with that name exists and the console did not make it, the form stops and says so.
  2. It starts a short Job in kube-system, with the driver image. The Job tests, in order, that the receiver answers, that its certificate is trusted, and that it accepts the token.
  3. It shows the result.

Expected: an information box, Checking the receiver, then a green box, The receiver is ready: The receiver answered, its certificate is trusted, and the token is accepted.

If the check fails, a red box, The check failed, gives one reason: cannot connect, certificate not trusted, token refused, receiver storage not reachable, or receiver has no auth-check call; update it. Fix the cause and choose Check connection again. Changing any field turns the check off, and you must run it again.

Create turns on only after the check passes. If your account may not make Jobs in kube-system, the form says You cannot run the check, and you can make the policy without it. A wrong address, token or certificate then shows up only when the first copy runs. If your account may not make Secrets there, the form says You cannot make Secrets in kube-system. Ask an administrator to make them, then choose Use Secrets that already exist.

Check the Secrets from a terminal. The check Job removes itself after ten minutes.

oc get secret -n kube-system dr-console-receiver-token dr-console-receiver-ca

Expected: both Secrets exist. With no certificate pasted, only the token Secret exists.

docs.title: Step 14: Make the policy and read the Receiver status
docs.text:
Leave Destination Base Path and Schedule as they are (/pvcs and 15m), and choose Create.

Expected: the policy page opens. It shows the label Driver-to-Driver, the Receiver Endpoint, and a line Receiver Status. The status is Checking... until the controller's first result, then Reachable. If it says Not reachable, the reason follows. The controller repeats the same checks once for each schedule. A failing check does not stop replication.

Open the Replication tab. The list has a Receiver column with the same state.

oc get replicationpolicy dr-console -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}{"\n"}'

Expected: a condition of type ReceiverReachable with status True.

docs.title: Step 15: Delete the policy and the Secrets it made
docs.text:
1. On the policy page, choose Delete.
  2. The box asks Delete ReplicationPolicy? It has a tick box that is off: Also delete the Secrets the receiver setup made (dr-console-receiver-token, dr-console-receiver-ca). The box appears only for Secrets named <policy name>-receiver-token and <policy name>-receiver-ca that this policy uses and no other policy uses.
  3. Tick the box and choose Delete.

The console deletes a Secret only after it proves that the Secret carries the label that the setup put on it. A Secret that you made yourself with the same name is left alone, and a message names it.

oc get secret -n kube-system dr-console-receiver-token dr-console-receiver-ca

Expected: both Secrets are not found.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Delete the backup policy in the console (Backups tab, row menu, Delete). The box says that new backups stop, and that the backups already made stay on the snapshot pool. If any remain, use Delete backups first (Step 7).

oc delete pod -n ${NS} files-check --ignore-not-found
oc delete namespace ${NS} --timeout=120s
oc get backuprestore   # delete the ones you made with: oc delete backuprestore <name>
oc delete filesharepool tut-data tut-backups

Deleting a pool deletes its VPC shares and everything on them, including backups. The driver blocks the delete while volumes remain, so wait for the namespace to go first. The destination cluster keeps the receiver and anything replicated to it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• The Backups tab makes and changes a policy with a form, suspends and resumes it, restores a volume to a new claim, and deletes the backups of a volume after a typed confirmation.
  • Delete backups refuses while the policy still backs up the volume or a restore runs, and it asks you to type the claim.
  • Clone to new PVC copies a volume to a new claim in the same namespace.
  • The replication form makes the receiver Secrets, checks the connection, and shows the receiver's state on the list and the policy page. The delete box removes the Secrets that the setup made.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:

  • Part 9: A COS bucket for backups
  • Part 6: Replication and failover sets up the receiver and runs a failover.

docs.title: Tutorial Series — IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver
docs.text:
Hands-on tutorials covering every major capability of the pool CSI driver. Each part is self-contained with its own setup and cleanup — follow them in any order after Part 1. The words used here are defined in CONTEXT.md.

Cluster: ROKS (OpenShift Virtualization enabled)

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text: Part Tutorial What You'll Learn 1 Pool Creation, PVCs, and KubeVirt VMs Create a pool, provision PVCs, launch a VM with NFS-backed boot and data disks 2 Snapshots and Clones Point-in-time snapshots, restore from snapshot, clones (asynchronous, Job-based) 3 Group Snapshots and Hooks Group snapshots are not active; what to use instead, and lifecycle hooks on replication 4 Pool Configuration Multi-tier pools, spread vs binpack strategies, auto-expansion, share draining 5 Golden Images CDI native mode and custom syncer for automatic KubeVirt golden image provisioning 6 Replication and Failover Direct NFS and driver-to-driver cross-region replication, pause/resume, failover CLI 7 Monitoring Prometheus metrics (37 metrics), ServiceMonitor, alerting rules, Grafana dashboard 8 Migration and Console Plugin PVC migration from stock driver, OpenShift console plugin walkthrough 9 COS Bucket for Backups Locked COS bucket, a key that cannot delete or unlock, a CBR rule that limits it to the cluster 10 Backup and Restore Back up a volume on a schedule to a snapshot pool, list the moments, restore one, delete backups 11 Instant VM Snapshots Turn on the Sidecar gate, snapshot a running VM in seconds, merge, restore, flatten 12 Replicating Running VMs Copy a running VM with all disks at one moment to a second cluster through a receiver 13 Failover of Running VMs Plan, rewind and fail over replicated VMs with kubectl failover 14 Restore a Snapshot in the Console Make a snapshot and restore it to a new PVC in the OpenShift console 15 Make a VM from the Catalog on a Pool Pick a catalog image and an instance type, choose the pool's StorageClass for the boot disk, and let CDI copy the image 16 Backups, Clones and Replication Setup in the Console Schedule and restore backups, clone a volume, and set up a replication receiver in the console

docs.title: Reading Order
docs.text: Parts 2-16 are independent of each other, except that Part 13 follows Part 12. Pick whichever is relevant to your use case.

docs.title: Prerequisites (All Parts)
docs.text:
Every tutorial assumes:

  1. ROKS or ROVS cluster with OpenShift Virtualization enabled (for VM tutorials)
  2. CSI driver deployed — controller and node pods running: 
    oc get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi
  3. IBM Cloud CLI with VPC infrastructure plugin (ibmcloud is)
  4. oc and virtctl CLI tools installed

docs.title: Namespace Convention
docs.text:
Each tutorial uses a unique namespace to avoid conflicts:

Part Namespace 1 pool-tutorial 2 pool-tutorial-snapshots 3 none (Part 3 has no steps to run) 4 pool-tutorial-config 5 pool-tutorial-golden 6 pool-tutorial-repl 7 pool-tutorial-monitoring 8 pool-tutorial-ops 10 pool-tutorial-backup 11 vms (your own VM) 12 vms (your own VM) 13 vms (your own VM) 14 pool-tutorial-console

Tutorials can be run concurrently on the same cluster without interference.

docs.title: Upgrade Guide — IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver
docs.text: This guide covers upgrading the driver between versions without data loss or downtime.

docs.title: Pre-Flight Checklist
docs.text:
Before upgrading, complete every item:

  • [ ] Read the CHANGELOG.md entry for the target version — note breaking changes, new CRD fields, and required actions
  • [ ] Verify pool health — all pools should be in Ready phase: 
    kubectl get filesharepools
# All pools should show Phase: Ready
  • [ ] Back up CRD resources (pools and subvolumes are the source of truth for all state): 
    kubectl get filesharepools -o yaml > backup-pools.yaml
kubectl get subvolumes -o yaml > backup-subvolumes.yaml
kubectl get snapshots.storage.ibmcloud.io -o yaml > backup-snapshots.yaml 2>/dev/null
kubectl get replicationpolicies -o yaml > backup-replication.yaml 2>/dev/null
kubectl get volumegroupsnapshots -o yaml > backup-groupsnapshots.yaml 2>/dev/null
  • [ ] Check for in-flight operations — no PVCs should be in Pending state and no clones should be in progress: 
    kubectl get pvc --all-namespaces | grep Pending
kubectl get subvolumes -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.spec.cloneStatus=="InProgress")]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}'
  • [ ] Verify you have the correct target version of the Helm chart or manifests
  • [ ] Confirm cluster meets the compatibility requirements for the target version (see below)
