docs.title: Examples — IBM VPC File Pool CSI Driver
docs.text: Ready-to-use examples for common deployment patterns. Each example can be applied directly with kubectl apply -f.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before using these examples, ensure: 1. The CSI driver is installed (INSTALL.md) 2. At least one FileSharePool is Ready (the basic/ example creates one) 3. A StorageClass exists for the pool (the basic/ example creates one)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Directory Description basic/ Minimal setup: pool, StorageClass, PVC, and pod multi-zone/ Pools across availability zones with WaitForFirstConsumer statefulset/ StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates shared-rwx/ ReadWriteMany PVC shared across deployment replicas tiered/ Performance tiers: standard and high-IOPS pools custom-permissions/ Restricted UID/GID/permissions via StorageClass retain/ Keep data after PVC deletion (reclaimPolicy: Retain)

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# 1. Create the pool and StorageClass
kubectl apply -f examples/basic/pool.yaml
kubectl apply -f examples/basic/storageclass.yaml

# 2. Wait for the pool to be Ready (30-90 seconds for initial share creation)
kubectl get filesharepools -w

# 3. Create a PVC and pod
kubectl apply -f examples/basic/pvc.yaml
kubectl apply -f examples/basic/pod.yaml

# 4. Verify
kubectl get pvc my-app-data          # Should be Bound
kubectl logs my-app-pod              # Should show "Hello from pool CSI"

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
# Delete examples in reverse order
kubectl delete -f examples/basic/pod.yaml
kubectl delete -f examples/basic/pvc.yaml
kubectl delete -f examples/basic/storageclass.yaml
kubectl delete -f examples/basic/pool.yaml

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Replace us-south-1 / us-south-2 zones with your actual VPC zones
  • Replace your-resource-group-id with your IBM Cloud resource group ID
  • Pool creation triggers a VPC file share creation (30-90 seconds)
  • PVC binding is near-instant once the pool is Ready

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
The diagrams in the docs are draw.io files saved as .drawio.svg. One file is both the picture and the source:

  • GitHub and any Markdown viewer show it as an image.
  • draw.io (the desktop app, the web app at app.diagrams.net, or the VS Code extension) opens it for editing, because the file holds a copy of the diagram.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• The text explains. The diagram shows. A diagram has labels on its parts and short labels on its arrows (two to four words). No sentences, no numbered steps, no notes. The explanation stays in the Markdown text next to the diagram.
  • One idea per diagram. If a diagram needs a legend of more than three entries, split it.
  • Every diagram is next to the text it shows, with alt text that names what it shows: ![The hook sidecar opens the newest file of the chain](images/vm-instant-snapshots-hook.drawio.svg).
  • Names match the doc. Use the same words for the same parts as the text.
  • When the text changes, change the diagram. A diagram that disagrees with its text is a defect.

docs.title: File names
docs.text: <doc-name>-<what-it-shows>.drawio.svg, in lower case, in this folder. Example: vm-instant-snapshots-hook.drawio.svg for VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
Part Fill Line Notes Area: cluster, node, zone, region none #8d8d8d, dashed Label at top left, 12 px, #525252 Group: pod, share, bucket #f4f4f4 #a8a8a8 Label at top left, 12 px Component: a container, controller, service #ffffff #525252, or #0f62fe (1.5) for the part the diagram is about Name in bold Optional or added part #edf5ff #0f62fe (1.5), dashed File shape=note, #ffffff #8d8d8d; #198038 (1.5) for live or healthy Name in bold; state on a second line Problem, failure, data loss #fff1f1 #da1e28 (1.5) Only where the doc describes a failure Arrow #525252; colour of its target when it helps Label 11 px, #525252, with a background
  • Font: Helvetica, 12 px for parts, 11 px for arrow labels. Courier New for paths.
  • Corners: rounded=1, arcSize=8 for components, arcSize=4 for areas and groups.
  • Space: at least 100 px between boxes that an arrow with a label joins. No label may touch a box.
  • Flow goes left to right, or top to bottom. Arrows do not cross.
  • No icons, no shadows, no gradients, no 3D.
  • Width at most 800 px.

docs.title: Making or changing a diagram
docs.text:
1. Open the .drawio.svg file in draw.io, edit it, and save. draw.io keeps the .drawio.svg format.
  2. To make one from a script, write the draw.io XML to a temporary .drawio file and export it: 
    /Applications/draw.io.app/Contents/MacOS/draw.io -x -f svg -e -b 10 -o docs/images/<name>.drawio.svg <name>.drawio
    -e puts the diagram into the SVG, so it stays editable. Do not commit the temporary .drawio file.
  3. Look at the result as a PNG before you commit (-f png -s 2). Check that no label touches a box or another label.

docs.title: Storage and VM benchmark tools compared with our performance test
docs.text:
Date: 2026-10-24

Question answered: how does our planned test (many everyday VMs on one NFS share, find the "knee", recommend 80 percent of it) compare with mature storage and VM benchmarks, and what should we change?

docs.title: How to read this file
docs.text:
• Every claim has a source URL beside it. All sources are the tool's own documentation, source code, specification, or the vendor's own pages. I read them directly unless the text says otherwise.
  • "Not confirmed" means I could not find a primary source. I do not state it as fact. All such items are also listed in the last section.
  • Terms are defined once, where first used.
  • Our design is in docs/specs/2026-10-24-performance-test-30-vms.md and test/perf/ on the branch worktree. At the time of reading, run-tier.sh only implements the steady-state ramp. It has no boot storm, patch window, migration, snapshot, or backup step yet, and no Windows (diskspd) profile. The comments below on those parts are about the spec.

docs.title: 1. Summary table
docs.text: Tool What it is for How it defines load How it finds capacity or pass/fail Source fio General I/O generator (Linux and others) Job file: block size, read/write mix, queue depth, optional rate limit (rate_iops) None built in. latency_target can search for the highest load under a latency limit. steadystate can stop a job when a metric is stable https://github.com/axboe/fio/blob/master/HOWTO.rst diskspd Microsoft I/O generator for Windows Command line: block size, write percent, threads, outstanding I/O, throttle -g (IOPS form -g<n>i since 2.1) None built in. Has -W warm-up and -C cool-down https://github.com/microsoft/diskspd/wiki/Command-line-and-parameters and https://github.com/microsoft/diskspd/blob/master/README.md HCIBench (VMware) Wrapper that deploys many VMs and runs Vdbench or fio in each, for hyper-converged storage Number of VMs, disks per VM, threads per disk, or a parameter file. "Easy Run" picks the counts itself Easy Run profiles try to hold p95 latency under 1, 3 or 5 ms for small random I/O. Otherwise the user compares runs https://github.com/vmware-labs/hci-benchmark-appliance/blob/main/HCIBench_User_Guide.pdf VMmark 4 (VMware) Cluster benchmark. A "tile" is one fixed group of application VMs Add tiles to add load. Infrastructure operations (vMotion, clone and deploy) run alongside Score is peak load with quality of service met. Exact thresholds: not confirmed https://blogs.vmware.com/cloud-foundation/2024/05/09/introducing-vmmark-4/ SPECvirt Datacenter 2021 Datacenter VM benchmark, tile based Add tiles. Phased run of 90, 30 and 60 minutes Peak is where another tile fails quality of service in any tile, or does not raise the score. Per-workload p90 and p95 response limits https://www.spec.org/virt_datacenter2021/docs/designoverview.html and https://www.spec.org/virt_datacenter2021/docs/runrules.html SPC-1 Block storage benchmark for business applications Requested I/O rate, split in fixed streams. One "stimulus scaling unit" is a user group that makes up to 500 IOPS Valid only if average response time is at most 30 ms in every phase. Needs an 8 hour sustain test and a repeat test https://storageperformance.org/sites/default/files/files/specifications/SPC1_v391_final.pdf SPECstorage Solution 2020 File-server (NFS and SMB) benchmark A "business metric" per workload (builds, video streams, and others). LOAD, INCR_LOAD, NUM_RUNS give a ramp Curve of business metric against response time. Needs at least 10 load points in one run. Latency pass rule: not confirmed https://www.spec.org/storage2020/docs/usersguide.pdf and https://www.spec.org/storage2020/docs/runrules.pdf SNIA SSS PTS 2.0.2 Test method for one solid state drive Prescribed workloads in "rounds" Steady state: in a 5 round window, range under 20 percent of the mean and slope under 10 percent https://www.snia.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/SNIA-SSS-PTS-2.0.2.pdf KubeVirt perf and scale tests Control plane tests (VM creation latency, API load) Create 100 minimal VMIs with 100 ms between each P50 and P95 creation-to-running latency. No disk I/O https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/docs/perf-scale-benchmarks.md kube-burner Tool to create and measure Kubernetes objects at scale, including VMs Job files that create objects Measurements include vmiLatency and pvcLatency. Red Hat's VM-and-storage example boots VMs only and runs no I/O inside them https://kube-burner.github.io/kube-burner/latest/measurements/ and https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2024/09/04/use-kube-burner-measure-red-hat-openshift-vm-and-storage-deployment-scale IBM File Storage for VPC (dp2) The system under test IOPS limit set per share, by share size IBM publishes limits, not latency expectations https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-file-storage-profiles

docs.title: Facts behind the table
docs.text:
fio: - rate_iops caps IOPS. With a block size range, "the smallest block size is used as the metric" (HOWTO, rate_iops). - rate_process default is linear: "fixed delays between I/Os that gets adjusted based on I/O completion rates". poisson models a random request flow (HOWTO, rate_process). - ramp_time runs the workload "before logging any performance numbers" (HOWTO, ramp_time). - steadystate plus steadystate_duration use a rolling window and stop the job when a criterion (iops, bw, lat, and their slopes) falls inside a limit. Default duration 0 means off (HOWTO, steadystate options). - clat_percentiles reports completion latency percentiles. lat_percentiles reports total latency (submission plus completion). percentile_list sets the percentiles (HOWTO, "Measurements and reporting"). - direct=1 is non-buffered I/O, usually O_DIRECT (HOWTO, direct). - randrepeat seeds the random generators "in a predictable way so the pattern is repeatable across runs". Default: true (HOWTO, randrepeat). randseed sets the seed. - write_hist_log and log_hist_msec write latency histograms over time (HOWTO, write_hist_log). - slat, clat, lat: lat is "the time from when fio created the I/O unit to completion" (https://fio.readthedocs.io/en/latest/fio_doc.html, section "Interpreting the output").

diskspd: - -W warm-up (before measurement), -C cool-down, -d duration, -L latency statistics, -D IOPS statistics interval (text output gives standard deviation, XML gives the series), -Sh is the same as -Suw (unbuffered and write-through), -w write percent, -g<n>i throttle in IOPS (wiki; README for version 2.1). - The README says the latency histogram "now reports to 9-nines" in text and XML output (version 2.0.17a note).

HCIBench: - Easy Run and the three latency profiles, and the general-purpose workloads "4K, 70% Read, 100% Random" and "8K, 50% Read" (guide, "Easy Run" section). - Start points: for best IOPS, 4 VMs per ESXi host, 8 data disks per VM, 4 threads per disk. For best latency, 2 VMs per host, 4 disks, 1 thread (guide, "Best Practice" in the test configuration section). - "We strongly recommend selecting to Prepare Virtual Disk Before Testing to allow blocks being allocated to avoid first write penalty as well as the read served by memory only" (guide, test configuration best practice). - "Clear Read/Write Cache Before Each Testing" is only for vSAN OSA, a two-tier design (guide). - A "Testing Duration" field overrides the elapsed time in the parameter files (guide). - Mixed Workload Mode (version 3.0 and later) runs groups of VMs with different parameter files at the same time (guide). - Disk initialisation options ZERO, RANDOM, NONE: https://blogs.vmware.com/cloud-foundation/?p=24181

SPECvirt Datacenter 2021: - Scaling is "an increasing number of tiles. Peak performance is the point at which the addition of another tile (or fraction of a tile) either fails the Quality of Service (QoS) criteria in any tile or fails to improve the overall metric" (design overview, 2.2.2). - Measurement interval is three phases: initial load 90 minutes, host provisioning 30 minutes, final load 60 minutes (design overview, 2.5). - Mail server: 90 percent of response times at most 150 ms and 95 percent at most 170 ms. Web server 190 and 210 ms. Collaboration server 385 and 425 ms. This applies "for every tile" (run rules, 4.4.1.1). These are application transaction times, not disk times. - HammerDB needs at least 200 new-order transactions a second in every tile (run rules, 4.4.1.2). - The older SPECvirt_sc2010 used a tile of six VMs, one of them idle "to represent VMs in a typical user environment which are not running at full capacity" (https://research.spec.org/icpe_proceedings/2012/p251.pdf).

SPC-1 (v3.9.1): - The spec uses "stimulus scaling unit" (SSU), not "BSU". One SSU is "a community of users who collectively generate up to 500 I/O's per second" (clause 1.2.2). "BSU" was the older name. I did not check older versions. - Average response time is computed per test phase "and cannot exceed 30 milliseconds. If ... exceeds that 30-millisecond constraint for any TEST PHASE, the MEASUREMENT is invalid" (6.3.2.4). - Phases (Table 6-1): sustain at 100 percent load, transition at least 3 minutes, measurement at least 8 hours. Then a response time ramp down through 100, 95, 90, 80, 50 and 10 percent and back up, each with at least 3 minutes transition and 10 minutes measurement. Then repeatability phases at 10 and 100 percent. - Sustain throughput must be within 5 percent of the reported result (6.3.3.2). Repeat throughput must be above the reported result minus 5 percent (6.3.8.5). Repeat average response time at 10 percent load must be within 5 percent or 1 ms of the first (6.3.8.6). - Repeat phases use "a statistically distinct sequence of I/O REQUESTS to assure that prior cache contents do not affect the results" (6.3.8.7). - "The HOST SYSTEM(s), shall not cache or buffer any data associated with implementing the ASUs" (4.2.1.2). - Steady state is "throughput and response time are stable and sustainable". A gradual constant drift or a sudden permanent change fails it (5.1.1). - Response time is "COMPLETION TIME minus START TIME" (glossary).

SPECstorage Solution 2020: - Workloads: SWBUILD, VDA, EDA_BLENDED, AI_IMAGE, GENOMICS (user guide, parameter BENCHMARK). There is no VDI workload in this version. (The older SPECsfs2014 had one; I read that only in a secondary news article, so it is not confirmed.) - Load ramp: set LOAD, INCR_LOAD and NUM_RUNS (user guide, section 3). Auto mode -a "finds maximum passing load value" (user guide, command line list). The pass rule behind "passing": not confirmed. - Run rules 5.3: at least 10 load points in one run, spaced evenly within 30 percent of nominal. "Any invalid data points will invalidate the entire run." Run rules 5.4: overall response time is the area under the curve divided by peak throughput. - Run rules 5.2: cloud storage components "should be (re-)initialized to the fullest extent possible and documented". - User guide: "Ensure that your test network is idle ... Results obtained on production networks may not be reproducible." - The guide's sample output shows "Test run time = 300 seconds, Warmup = 300 seconds" and a latency band histogram. I did not confirm these are defaults.

SNIA PTS 2.0.2 (section 2.1.24): steady state needs both (a) range of the tracked value within the measurement window at most 20 percent of its average, and (b) slope of the best linear fit changes the value by at most 10 percent of the average. The measurement window is 5 rounds (2.1.13). Pre-conditioning is writing data to bring the device to steady state, either with an unrelated workload (workload independent) or the test workload itself (workload dependent) (2.1.18). The spec is for single SSDs. I use it only for the generic ideas.

KubeVirt and Red Hat: - KubeVirt's benchmark doc "doesn't mention storage or disk I/O": it covers creation latency (P50, P95), CPU and memory of KubeVirt components, and API call counts. - kube-burner lists vmiLatency, pvcLatency, dataVolumeLatency, volumeSnapshotLatency among its measurements. - Red Hat's 2024 article uses kube-burner to boot 10 namespaces of 50 VMs that clone a boot disk, and reports vmiLatency percentiles. It says the workload "only boots the VMs and waits for them to reach Running" and treats I/O inside the VMs as a possible future step. - Red Hat has a blog post and reference architecture about OpenShift Virtualization performance and boot storms. The search snippets mention them, but the page itself returned HTTP 404 when I fetched it, so I treat it as not confirmed.

IBM File Storage for VPC (https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-file-storage-profiles): - The dp2 table of share size against IOPS range matches pkg/ibmcloud/share_profiles.go as quoted in our spec. - "IOPS values are based on a 16 KB block size for all profiles, with a 50-50 random workload. Each 16 KB of data that is read or written counts as one read/write operation. A single write of less than 16 KB counts as a single write operation." - dp2 maximum bandwidth is IOPS times 256 KB, capped at 8192 Mbps. - "For the 96,000 IOPS to be realized, a single file share must be accessed by multiple virtual server instances. A single file share that is accessed by one client is limited to 48,000 IOPS." - "A single session can achieve up to 64 KB block size transfer. To use the max allowable bandwidth, you need multiple concurrent sessions to the share." - Mounting needs NFS 4.1 or higher, and sec=sys (https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-file-storage-mount-RHEL). - Encryption in transit "can decrease performance" and workloads that bypass VSI caching "might have a substantial performance impact" (https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-file-storage-planning). - I found no IBM page that states latency expectations or a benchmark method for File Storage for VPC.

docs.title: 2. Gap analysis
docs.text: Each item gives: what mature tools do, what we do, whether it matters for our goal, and the change. Our goal is a sizing table of how many everyday VMs one NFS share carries before users notice.

docs.title: Gap 1. Warm-up and steady-state detection
docs.text:
• Mature tools: SPC-1 forces a transition of at least 3 minutes before each 10 minute measurement and an 8 hour sustain (Table 6-1). fio has ramp_time and steadystate. diskspd has -W. SNIA defines steady state with a 20 percent range and 10 percent slope test. HCIBench tells you to write the disks first (see gap 3).
  • We do: a 5 minute settle before each 45 minute window (run-tier.sh, SETTLE_MIN). There is no check that the window was stable. The settle is a fixed time, not a test. Each fio run is a new process with no ramp_time, so the first seconds of every phase include start-up.
  • Matters: yes, moderately. New VMs added at each step boot, write to their disks, and may still be copying clone data. A drifting step gives a wrong p95.
  • Change (small): after collection, test each step for stability using the SNIA idea. Split the window into 5 minute bins, take the share-level IOPS and average latency per bin, and mark the step "not stable" if the range exceeds 20 percent of the mean or the slope exceeds 10 percent. Report unstable steps and do not use them for the knee unless repeated. Add --ramp_time=30 to each fio call so the first seconds are not counted (small; note the HOWTO says ramp time adds to runtime).

docs.title: Gap 2. Run length and number of repeats
docs.text:
• Mature tools: SPC-1 runs each point 10 minutes but demands an 8 hour sustain and two repeats (6.3.3, 6.3.8). SPECvirt Datacenter measures for 3 hours in three phases. SPECstorage needs at least 10 load points in one run and voids the run if one is invalid. Repeat tolerance in SPC-1 is 5 percent.
  • We do: 45 minutes a step, one pass per tier. The spec repeats "the first full run ... once at its knee step".
  • Matters: yes. Cloud storage speed varies by hour (our own spec says so). One sample per step cannot show whether a difference is real. Our steps are also coarse: 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90. A knee at 45 gives a recommendation of 36, rounded down to 30. That is a large rounding loss.
  • Change (medium): (a) after the first knee, add one step halfway between the last good step and the knee (for example 37 or 38) so the answer is not a 15 VM guess. (b) Repeat the knee step and the step below it, at least once more, on a different hour. Accept the knee only if both runs agree. Use an SPC-1-like band (for example p95 within 10 percent or 2 ms). (c) At the end of the ramp, run the 15 VM step again and compare with the first 15 VM step. This is the SPC-1 repeatability idea (6.3.8.6) and it detects backend drift during the day.

docs.title: Gap 3. Working set versus cache (is 2 GB per VM enough?)
docs.text:
• Mature tools: SPC-1 forbids host caching of the test data (4.2.1.2) and uses a different request sequence on repeat phases (6.3.8.7). HCIBench says to write every disk first so reads are not "served by memory only", and offers cache clearing on vSAN OSA. SPECstorage says to re-initialise cloud components "to the fullest extent possible". I did not find a primary statement of a required ratio of working set to cache size in any of them. HCIBench's working-set setting: not confirmed.
  • We do (profile.sh): --direct=1 and --size=2G on the load disk, with --ioengine=libaio. No pre-write of the area. No randrepeat=0, no randseed.
  • What this means:
  • direct=1 removes the guest page cache (HOWTO, direct). It does not remove the node's NFS client cache or any cache on the file server. Whether QEMU opens the disk file with direct I/O in our VMs: not confirmed. The VM definition has to be checked.
  • fio's randrepeat default is true: the random pattern is "repeatable across runs". Each steady phase and burst phase starts a new fio process with the same options, so each process reads and writes the same sequence of offsets again, every 10 minutes. After the first period those blocks can be in a cache. At 30 IOPS average and about 34 KB average I/O size, one steady phase touches well under the 2 GB area, so every repeat revisits mostly the same early blocks. The result would be too fast, and it would be too fast more as time goes on. This is a real defect in the current profile.sh, not a theory, though I did not run it. I did not verify the size of the effect.
  • Never-written regions: if the disk file is sparse, reads of unwritten blocks may be answered without reading media. How the IBM backend treats this: not confirmed. HCIBench's advice to write first covers it.
  • Aggregate size is not the issue (90 VMs times 2 GB is 180 GB). The per-VM random area and the repeated pattern are.
  • Matters: yes, strongly. It can make the share look better than it is, and the sizing table would then recommend too many VMs.
  • Change:
  • (small) Add --randrepeat=0 or a per-phase --randseed to every fio call. Add the same on diskspd (-z with a changing seed).
  • (small) Write the area once before measuring (a sequential fill with large blocks), as HCIBench advises. Measure the fill time in the smoke run, because IBM counts operations in 16 KB units.
  • (small) Cross-check cache effects in the smoke run: compare the sum of guest read IOPS with the share's NFS read operations from the node agent counters that the driver already exports. If the guests report far more reads than the share saw, a cache is absorbing them.
  • (medium) Use a larger area per VM than 2 GB (for example most of the load disk) and check by a short A/B run (2 GB against the larger area) that read latency does not change. If it changes, the larger one is the right default.
  • (small) Check the VM definition for the disk cache mode and write it in the results.

docs.title: Gap 4. Latency as a percentile or an average
docs.text:
• Mature tools: SPC-1 validity uses average response time (at most 30 ms) and also publishes frequency distributions and response time graphs (10.9.x). SPECvirt Datacenter uses p90 and p95 limits per workload in every tile. HCIBench Easy Run targets p95. SPECstorage reports average operation latency with latency bands in its sample output. Which of these is "right" is a choice, but percentiles are the common choice for user-visible behaviour.
  • We do: p95 of read latency per VM, from fio JSON completion latency, taken from steady phases only. Per VM we use the highest p95 across the phases in the window (perf_vm_stats). Burst phases are excluded from the p95 and only count in the stall test. Write latency is parsed but not used in the knee.
  • Matters: yes, in three ways.
  • Taking the highest p95 across phases is a maximum of a percentile. It is sensitive to one bad phase and to the number of phases. It is not a standard statistic.
  • Bursts are what users notice (boot, patching, scans), and the knee ignores their latency.
  • Percentiles from separate phases cannot be combined by averaging them. Pooling needs histograms.
  • Change:
  • (small) Record per-VM p95 for the steady phase and, separately, p95 and p99 for the burst phase. Apply a burst rule (for example burst p95 under a looser limit such as 50 ms) as a second condition, set in the spec.
  • (small) Use write p95 too, since 30 percent of the I/O is writes.
  • (medium) Capture a latency histogram per VM per step (write_hist_log with log_hist_msec, HOWTO) so the step p95 and p99 are computed by pooling, not by taking a maximum or an average of percentiles. For diskspd, use the XML output, which includes the histogram (README).
  • (small) Also report the share-level average NFS latency, as SPC-1 and SPECstorage do, next to the p95.

docs.title: Gap 5. Coordinated omission
docs.text:
Definition: coordinated omission is when a load generator slows its own requests when the system is slow, so the slow period produces fewer samples and the measured latency looks better than users would see.

  • What fio's documentation says:
  • The io_submit_mode=offload entry says offloading "avoids skewed latency reporting if I/O gets backed up on the device side (the coordinated omission problem)", and that it "cannot reliably be used with async IO engines" (HOWTO).
  • rate_process=linear uses "fixed delays between I/Os that gets adjusted based on I/O completion rates" (HOWTO). That wording suggests the rate adapts to completions, but I could not confirm from the documentation what happens to the intended start time of a late I/O.
  • lat is measured "from when fio created the I/O unit to completion", and clat from submission to completion (fio_doc, "Interpreting the output"). Our parser uses clat_ns, which excludes any wait before submission.
  • Answer to your question: the fio documentation does not say that, with rate_iops, latency is measured from the intended start time. It names coordinated omission as a known problem and offers offload mode, which it says not to use with async engines. We use libaio, which is an async engine. So the claim "fio with rate_iops measures from the intended start" is not confirmed, and the safe assumption is that it does not.
  • diskspd: the README says only that version 2.2 "improved" latency measurement. Coordinated omission is not mentioned. Not confirmed.
  • Matters: yes, for the stall and tail figures. In a near-stall, a single fio process with queue depth 4 can stop issuing, and the time it waited is not in clat. The p95 then looks fine while the user waits.
  • Change:
  • (small) Record the achieved IOPS against the target for every phase. A shortfall (for example below 90 percent of the target) is the sign that the generator was held back. Treat a step with a shortfall as failed or unreliable. SPC-1 also requires the measured load to match the intended load within a tolerance (5.2.9).
  • (small) Also keep lat (total latency) by adding --lat_percentiles=1, and use it instead of clat.
  • (medium) Test the generator itself once, outside the cluster: run the same fio command against a local device that is made slow on purpose and see whether the reported p95 and achieved IOPS reveal the slowdown. This answers the "not confirmed" above for the versions we use.
  • (medium) Consider --rate_process=poisson for arrivals that look like real users. This does not fix omission. It only changes the spacing.

docs.title: Gap 6. How the knee or pass line is chosen
docs.text:
• Mature tools:
  • SPC-1: average response time at most 30 ms in every phase, and the reported figure must also hold in a sustain and in repeats (6.3.2.4, 6.3.3, 6.3.8).
  • SPECvirt Datacenter: per-workload p90 and p95 limits, and every tile must pass (run rules 4.4.1.1). One failing tile ends the run. Peak is also where the overall score stops rising.
  • HCIBench Easy Run: p95 targets of 1, 3 and 5 ms for small random I/O on flash storage.
  • VMmark: quality of service exists, thresholds not confirmed. A VMware forum post puts the VMmark 2 era DVD Store limit at 500 ms. That is a forum post, not a primary source.
  • IBM: no published latency expectation (not confirmed).
  • We do: a step is a knee if more than 25 percent of VMs have p95 read latency over 20 ms for the step, or any stall, or a boot storm over twice the first, or the share at its limit.
  • Assessment:
  • 20 ms p95 for disk reads is in the same range as SPC-1's 30 ms average ceiling, and stricter, since a p95 is higher than the average. It is a reasonable first value. I found no primary source that says 20 ms is the point where everyday users notice. The number stays a decision.
  • "More than a quarter of VMs" is looser than SPECvirt Datacenter's "every tile". It is also easy to change. It should be a stated parameter.
  • "Any stall" over 5 s across up to 90 VMs and 45 minutes is a very sensitive rule. One event (a live migration, a snapshot, a backup) will trigger it. Our spec plans to run those operations during the 30 VM step. Left as written, they decide the knee.
  • The boot storm rule compares the storm at N VMs with the storm at 15 VMs. A storm of 30 VMs is naturally longer than one of 15, so "twice as long" can fire from VM count alone. In report.sh the baseline is taken from the first row, but the spec runs the first storm at 30 VMs, so the baseline would be empty and the rule would not fire. The runner does not run a boot storm yet.
  • "Share at its limit" uses NFS operations a second compared with the configured IOPS (run-tier.sh, 95 percent). IBM counts one operation per 16 KB. A 64 KB I/O counts as four. With 4 KB to 64 KB blocks, the share can reach its IBM limit when the NFS operation count looks lower. Whether the NFS client's operation count tracks IBM's 16 KB unit: not confirmed.
  • Change:
  • (small) Keep 20 ms, but compute the knee at 10, 20 and 30 ms and publish all three. The data already exists, so this is cheap, and it shows how sensitive the result is.
  • (small) Make the 25 percent and 20 ms values report parameters, and show also the result for "any VM over limit" (the SPECvirt style).
  • (medium) Split each step into a baseline window and an event window. Apply the knee rule only to the baseline window. Report the migration, snapshot and backup as separate deltas against the baseline. VMmark treats infrastructure operations as a separate load added to the application tiles (VMmark 4 blog), though how it scores them is not confirmed.
  • (small) Compare boot storms per VM (seconds per VM, or time to last VM against count), and run the baseline storm at the first step. Add a test to test-perf.sh for an empty baseline.
  • (medium) Express the share load in IBM's unit: for each fio I/O, count ceil(size / 16 KiB). Compare that with the share limit. This needs the block size mix from the fio output or a fixed known distribution.

docs.title: Gap 7. Synchronised or random bursts
docs.text:
• Mature tools: VMmark and SPECvirt use tiles with each workload on a predefined stress pattern. SPECvirt Datacenter says tiles "may be started in rapid succession or in delayed sequences" with delay factors (design overview, 2.5). SPC-1 spreads its load over streams at fixed intensities. I found no primary text about synchronised bursts as a design choice.
  • We do: random start offsets per VM, set from the boot id (profile.sh), plus a separate synchronised "patch window" and boot storm in the spec.
  • Matters: it is a good approach. Real peaks line up (patch, backup, boot). A random mix shows the everyday case and a synchronised one shows the worst case.
  • Change (small): record the offsets (or seed them from a run seed) so a repeat run can use the same pattern or a changed one on purpose. Report the result of the synchronised phase beside the random phase, and do not mix them into one knee figure. The spec already separates them; keep it so.

docs.title: Gap 8. Does low average with bursts match published VM profiles?
docs.text:
• Mature tools: HCIBench's "general purpose" Easy Run workload is 4K, 70 percent read, 100 percent random, at the maximum rate the system gives (guide), and OLTP is 8K, 50 percent read. IBM rates dp2 at 16 KB blocks, 50/50 random. The SPECvirt tile includes an idle VM to represent VMs not at full load (2012 paper). SPECstorage 2020 has no VDI workload. I did not find a primary published profile for everyday desktop or server VMs in IOPS terms. The View Planner (VMware VDI benchmark) search did not return its guide, so VDI profile: not confirmed.
  • We do: 20 to 50 IOPS average, 300 IOPS bursts of 30 to 60 s every 10 to 15 minutes, 70/30, 4K to 64K block mix. The spec states these are defaults taken from the issue and not measured from a real fleet.
  • Matters: yes, because the answer scales almost directly with the assumed load. The result is only true for this profile. The spec says so.
  • Change:
  • (small) State plainly in the sizing table that the numbers are for this stated profile, with the source "owner's defaults, not measured".
  • (medium) Measure real averages and bursts from a real cluster if one is available (guest disk counters over a week) and replace the defaults. Not a benchmark change, but the biggest effect on the answer.
  • (small) Add a sensitivity run: the same ramp at half and at double the average rate for one tier. This shows how the knee moves with load, as SPC-1 shows it with its ramp.
  • Note for balance: HCIBench-style closed-loop "maximum rate" runs would answer a different question (the peak the share gives), which our spec does not need. The rate-limited approach is the right one for "how many VMs".

docs.title: Gap 9. Per-VM and aggregate reporting
docs.text:
• Mature tools: SPC-1 and SPECstorage report aggregates. SPECvirt and VMmark report per tile and require every tile to pass. HCIBench reports aggregates across all VMs and keeps the per-VM files (guide).
  • We do: both: per-VM p95 (share of VMs slow) and share-level NFS IOPS and average latency from the node agents.
  • Matters: this is a strength. One missing piece is a reconciliation: the sum of guest IOPS should match the share's NFS operations after allowing for block splitting.
  • Change (small): write both numbers in steps.csv and flag a step where they differ by more than a set margin. This also feeds gap 3.

docs.title: Gap 10. Variance and confidence
docs.text:
• Mature tools: SPC-1 states a 5 percent repeatability band. SPECstorage run rules mention a margin of error of 1 percent (peak business metric) and 5 percent (response time) for later general-availability results and say the margins "may be larger for black-box cloud publications" (run rules, item 5). SNIA uses the 20 and 10 percent steady state tests. None of the sources I read gives confidence intervals.
  • We do: no variance reporting. One run per step, one repeat at the knee.
  • Matters: yes. A sizing table without a spread invites false precision.
  • Change (medium): for each step record the spread across VMs (median, p90 and maximum of the per-VM p95), and for the knee step and the one below it, the result from at least two runs. Publish the range (low and high) in the table beside the recommended count. Agree a repeat band up front (SPC-1 uses 5 percent; a cloud share will need wider, so choose 10 percent and write it down).

docs.title: Gap 11. Noisy neighbours on shared cloud storage
docs.text:
• Mature tools: SPECstorage says an idle network and idle solution are needed, and says results on shared production networks "may not be reproducible". Its run rules allow larger margins for cloud and require documenting how cloud parts were re-initialised. SPC-1 requires the sponsor to do nothing between phases and not restart the system (6.3.2.6, 6.3.2.7). None offers a method for measuring a shared backend you do not control.
  • We do: the lab cluster is idle, which is good for the compute side. The IBM storage backend is shared and not controllable. The spec says to repeat the knee step.
  • Matters: yes. A noisy period during one step could move the knee by a whole step.
  • Change:
  • (medium) Add a fixed probe: a small fixed-rate fio job on a separate small share (or a fixed VM on the same share, low rate) that runs for the whole test, with the same settings at every step. If the probe's p95 changes by more than the repeat band without a change in our load, the step is tagged "backend noise" and repeated. This is my design, not a method from a source.
  • (small) Record the time of day, the zone, and the share's IOPS setting for each step. Start all three tiers at similar times of day.
  • (small) The 15 VM repeat at the end (gap 2) is the cheap version of the same check.

docs.title: Gap 12. NFS client behaviour and concurrency
docs.text:
• IBM's page says a single session reaches only a 64 KB transfer size and that full bandwidth needs "multiple concurrent sessions to the share". It also says one client is limited to 48,000 IOPS on a 96,000 IOPS share. I found no IBM advice on mount options for performance beyond sec=sys, NFS 4.1 and _netdev, and no advice on nconnect (not confirmed).
  • We do: the driver mounts each share once per node, so all VMs on a node share one NFS client mount. Three workers carry the whole load. The high tier is 20,000 IOPS, below the 48,000 single-client limit, but each node is one client.
  • Matters: the node mount may be a limit before the share is. If one node's single session saturates, the knee is a driver or client limit, not the share. This is useful to know but must not be mixed up with the share limit.
  • Change (small): add per-node NFS counters to the report (the node agents already export per-share counters). Check whether load is spread evenly across the three nodes. Note in the results which limit was reached. Record the mount options in the results.

docs.title: Gap 13. VM-level scale tooling
docs.text:
• KubeVirt's own test and the Red Hat kube-burner example measure creation latency and the control plane, not guest disk I/O. The Red Hat article calls guest I/O a possible future step. Our test fills that gap, but we also should use their measurements for the boot side.
  • Change (small): for boot storm timing, use the same measure as kube-burner's vmiLatency (VM creation to ready, phase by phase), so numbers can be compared with Red Hat's published method. The spec already measures "time for each VM to boot and report its guest agent". Keep it and record percentiles (P50, P95, P99), as KubeVirt and kube-burner do.

docs.title: 3. Where we are at least as good
docs.text:
• Rate-limited, per-VM load. Most storage benchmarks push for maximum rate. HCIBench's Easy Run does this. Ours holds each VM at a fixed low average, which answers "how many VMs" directly. SPC-1 and the SPEC tile benchmarks also use fixed intensity, so this matches the mature method.
  • Real VMs in the real stack. HCIBench runs on VMs on a hypervisor, and so do we, through the CSI driver, NFS and KubeVirt. The KubeVirt and Red Hat tools I found boot VMs but run no guest I/O (Red Hat article).
  • Mixed guest operating systems. HCIBench Easy Run and SPC-1 use one kind of generator. Our plan mixes Linux (fio) and Windows (diskspd) and keeps the same share. Windows is not built yet.
  • Boot storm, patch window, and live operations together with steady load. VMmark 4 includes infrastructure operations; SPC-1 and SPECstorage do not have a counterpart. The KubeVirt tools do not test them against disk load.
  • Per-VM pass counting. A share-wide average can hide a few suffering VMs. Counting VMs over the limit is closer to what users feel than SPC-1's average.
  • Both guest and share measurements. We have the node agent counters, a second independent view that most guest-only tools (HCIBench's fio runs) lack.
  • Stall rule. A 5 s stall rule catches freezes that p95 hides. SPC-1 and SPECvirt have no stall rule in the clauses I read.
  • Cleanup and cost control. The planned sweep and VPC check match the care SPECstorage asks for in re-initialising the system.

docs.title: 4. Where we are weaker
docs.text:
• Cache and repeated patterns. The fio default randrepeat=true repeats the same offsets every phase (gap 3). No data pre-write. Cache mode of the VM disk unchecked. This is the most important weakness because it makes results optimistic.
  • Latency measured without correction for waiting. We use completion latency with a rate-limited async generator and no shortfall check (gap 5).
  • Stability and repeats. No steady state test (gap 1). One pass per step, with a repeat at the knee only (gap 2). SPC-1 requires 8 hour sustain and repeats. SPECvirt measures 3 hours. Our run is 8 hours for the whole ramp, with less than 1 hour at the answer.
  • Rule design. The knee rule mixes planned events with steady load (gap 6). The boot storm baseline is inconsistent between the spec and report.sh. The share-limit test uses a different unit from IBM's (gap 6).
  • Burst latency is not judged. Only steady phases set the p95.
  • No spread or confidence reported (gap 10), and no noisy neighbour control (gap 11).
  • Step size is coarse near the answer (gap 2).
  • Profile not measured from a real fleet (gap 8). This is the largest uncertainty in the final number, and no benchmark design removes it.
  • Windows side not built. diskspd needs -g<n>i (version 2.1 or later), -W, a changing seed, and unbuffered, write-through I/O (-Sh). Whether diskspd's default is buffered: not confirmed from what I read.

docs.title: 5. Recommended changes, in order of value
docs.text:
Size: small is under half a day, medium is one to two days, large is more than two days. The sizes are my estimates.

  1. Stop the repeated random pattern (add --randrepeat=0 or a new --randseed per fio call; the same for diskspd). Small. Gap 3.
  2. Write the test area once before measuring, and check cache effects (fill step, compare guest reads with share NFS reads in the smoke run, record the VM disk cache mode). Small. Gap 3.
  3. Record achieved against target IOPS per phase and use lat (total latency) not only clat. Treat a shortfall as an unreliable step. Small. Gap 5.
  4. Count share load in IBM's 16 KB units and use that for the "at limit" test. Small to medium. Gap 6.
  5. Separate the baseline window from the event window (migration, snapshot, backup) and apply the knee rule only to the baseline. Medium. Gap 6.
  6. Add burst-phase and write latency to the rules, and pool latency histograms instead of taking a maximum of p95 values. Medium. Gap 4.
  7. Repeat runs and a repeat band. Run the knee step and the one below at least twice, end the ramp with a repeat of the 15 VM step, publish a range. Medium. Gaps 2, 10, 11.
  8. Add an intermediate step after the first knee (bisect) so rounding down to 80 percent does not cost a whole step. Small. Gap 2.
  9. Add a stability check (SNIA-style 20 percent range and 10 percent slope) per step, and ramp_time in each fio call. Small. Gap 1.
  10. Publish the knee at 10, 20 and 30 ms, and make the 25 percent and 20 ms values parameters. Small. Gap 6.
  11. Fix the boot storm baseline (storm at the first step, compare per VM) and add a unit test for an empty baseline. Small. Gap 6.
  12. Add a fixed-rate probe against backend noise. Medium. Gap 11.
  13. Test the generator's latency reporting on a deliberately slow local device, to settle the coordinated omission question for our fio and diskspd versions. Medium. Gap 5.
  14. Add per-node counters and a guest-versus-share reconciliation to steps.csv. Small. Gaps 9, 12.
  15. Sensitivity run at half and double the average rate on one tier. Medium (lab time rather than build time). Gap 8.
  16. Replace the default profile with a measured one when real fleet data exists. Large, and outside the test code. Gap 8.

docs.title: 6. Not confirmed
docs.text:
• VMmark: the exact quality-of-service thresholds, scoring formula, and run lengths of VMmark 3 and 4. The VMmark user guide link I found was a Broadcom community page, not the PDF. VMmark 4 blog: https://blogs.vmware.com/cloud-foundation/2024/05/09/introducing-vmmark-4/ does not describe scoring or thresholds.
  • VMmark default run length (3 hours, turbo 30 minutes) and the 500 ms DVD Store limit: seen only in VMware community forum posts, which are not primary documentation.
  • HCIBench: warm-up inside the workload, recommended test durations and repeat counts, working-set percentage, how latency percentiles are reported (only the Easy Run p95 targets and "latency details" appear in the guide). Recommended durations (900 to 1800 s trial, 6 hours formal) appeared only in a StorageReview article.
  • SPECstorage Solution 2020: the exact pass or fail rule for latency or for requested against achieved load ("passing" in auto mode), default warm-up and run times, and whether a VDI workload ever existed in 2020 (the SPECsfs2014 VDI workload is mentioned only by a news article).
  • SPC-1: I read v3.9.1 only. The term "BSU" does not appear in it. The SPC-1 ratio of data set size to cache: not confirmed.
  • fio: whether rate_iops with libaio measures latency from the intended start time. The documentation does not say this, and I did not test it.
  • diskspd: latency percentile list in the output, whether the default is buffered or unbuffered, and any coordinated omission handling.
  • IBM File Storage for VPC: published latency expectations, a recommended benchmark method, NFS client mount tuning (nconnect, rsize, wsize) beyond sec=sys, NFS 4.1 and _netdev, and how the NFS operation count maps to IBM's 16 KB unit.
  • KubeVirt and OpenShift Virtualization: an official guide for many-VM storage tests. KubeVirt's own tests and Red Hat's kube-burner article cover creation latency only. The Red Hat blog and reference architecture on performance, scale and boot storms could not be fetched (HTTP 404), so I did not use them.
  • Published VDI or "everyday VM" IOPS profiles from a primary source (View Planner, SPECsfs2014 VDI, or similar).
  • Whether the VMs' disk files are opened with direct I/O by QEMU in our setup, and what the effect of randrepeat is on our measurements. These need a check in the smoke run.
  • Whether the shared IBM backend uses a server-side cache that a 2 GB area would stay inside.

docs.title: Typical VM sizes, VM capacity of rovslab-dr-eude, and the shares needed
docs.text:
Date: 2026-10-24

Question answered: what does an everyday Linux or Windows Server VM look like, how many fit on the 3-node cluster rovslab-dr-eude, and how many dp2 shares do they need?

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
• Recommended size for the sums: Linux 2 vCPU, 4 GiB, 50 GiB disk. Windows Server 2 vCPU, 8 GiB, 80 GiB disk. Disk sizes are my estimate (no source gives a typical disk).
  • Memory is the limit, not CPU or pod count. With no memory overcommit and a mix of 2/3 Linux and 1/3 Windows: 132 VMs on all 3 nodes, and 66 VMs if one node can fail.
  • Those VMs need 7,920 GiB (3 nodes) or 3,960 GiB (N+1) of provisioned disk, and about 2,300 to 4,600 average guest IOPS (3,700 to 7,400 IBM operations, at 1.6 operations per I/O of the test's block mix). If every VM bursts to 300 IOPS together, the need is 31,680 (N+1) or 63,360 (3 nodes) IBM operations.
  • Proposal at 80 percent fill: N+1 is 2 shares of 3,000 GB at 16,000 IOPS. All 3 nodes is 4 shares of 3,000 GB at 16,000 IOPS. These are estimates.
  • The running performance test on DR (one share at 3,000, 10,000 and 20,000 IOPS, up to 90 VMs) measures the real VMs per share. Put its number into the formula in section 8 and it replaces my IOPS-based share count.

docs.title: How to read this file
docs.text:
• Every number has a source link beside it. "My estimate" means no source exists and I chose the number. "Lower confidence" means only a secondary source exists.
  • Units: Red Hat and KubeVirt use MiB and GiB. IBM writes GB and KB. I treat IBM's GB as 10^9 bytes and its KB as 1,024 bytes where IBM does not say. The cluster's memory figures are converted from the bytes Kubernetes reports to GiB (388.9 GB allocatable per node is 362.15 GiB).
  • Sections 1 to 3 are research. Sections 4 to 8 are calculations.

docs.title: 1. Typical VM sizes: what the sources say
1.1 Vendor minimums (these are floors, not typical sizes)
docs.text:
Item Value Source Windows Server 2022, RAM 1 GB Server Core, 2 GB with Desktop Experience https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/get-started/hardware-requirements Windows Server 2025, RAM 2 GB Server Core. 2 GB with Desktop Experience, 4 GB recommended same page Windows Server, CPU and disk 1.4 GHz 64-bit processor. 32 GB system disk, "an absolute minimum" same page Windows Server, recommended size Microsoft says a recommended size "is unrealistic" to state, and tells you to test same page RHEL 9, RAM 1.5 GiB minimum for install from local media or NFS. 3.5 GiB for network install on x86_64. No recommended figure on the page https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/9/html/interactively_installing_rhel_from_installation_media/system-requirements-and-supported-architectures_rhel-installer RHEL 9, disk 10 GiB minimum same page

Not found: the RHEL 10 page. I did not read it. Other websites quote "2 GB, 4 GB recommended" for RHEL 9. I could not trace that to a Red Hat page, so I do not use it.

docs.title: 1.2 Platform sizing guides (these show sizes people plan with)
docs.text:
Source What it defines Link KubeVirt common-instancetypes, u1 series "General purpose", 1:4 vCPU to memory ratio, burstable CPU. nano 1 vCPU 512Mi, micro 1/1Gi, small 1/2Gi, medium 1/4Gi, 2xmedium 2/4Gi, large 2/8Gi, xlarge 4/16Gi, 2xlarge 8/32Gi https://github.com/kubevirt/common-instancetypes/blob/main/README.md KubeVirt common-instancetypes, o1 series Same sizes as u1 (no 2xmedium). The only difference is that memory is overcommitted for higher density same page Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization Cluster Sizing Guide 3.1.0 (June 2026) "Reasonable starting points" when real data is missing: Micro 1 vCPU 1 GiB. X-small 1/4 GiB. Small 2/8 GiB. Medium 4/24 GiB. Large 8/48 GiB. X-large 16/64 GiB. XX-large 32/96 GiB. It says to use real utilisation data when you have it https://access.redhat.com/articles/7107457 (PDF attachment openshift_virtualization_cluster_sizing_guide_v3.1.0.pdf, link on that page: https://access.redhat.com/node/7107457/40/0/23834985) Our own performance test spec Linux 1 vCPU 2 GB. Windows Server 2022 2 vCPU 4 GB. 20 to 50 IOPS average, 300 IOPS bursts docs/specs/2026-10-24-performance-test-30-vms.md

The Red Hat guide's sizes are for a large estate (its example is 1,700 VMs with an average of 4.7 vCPU and 22.4 GiB). They are bigger than "everyday small" VMs. The guide gives no disk size and no IOPS.

docs.title: 1.3 Real estates (lower confidence)
docs.text:
I found no primary, published estate average from Dell Live Optics, Broadcom/VMware, AWS, Azure or Google. What I found:

Source What it gives Confidence Dell Live Optics help pages: https://www.dell.com/support/kbdoc/en-ie/000299118/live-optics-optical-prime-vtab and https://www.dell.com/support/kbdoc/en-ae/000299135/live-optics-optical-prime-vmware-guest-vm-performance How Live Optics works out per-VM averages of vCPU, memory and disk used. It publishes no global averages Method only, no numbers Microsoft Azure Migrate documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/migrate/ Tool documentation. No estate averages found Method only, no numbers One consultant's analysis of one estate of 756 VMs: https://occasional-it.com/2020/04/19/smart-sizing-2-analysis/ Average 3.5 vCPU (range 1 to 29), 9.2 GB vRAM (2 to 128), 72 GB disk used (1.3 to 1,698). Source of the data is not named. Dated April 2020 Lower confidence. One estate, secondary Nutanix sizing lab answers: https://sizing-workshop.readthedocs.io/en/latest/datacollection/rvtools-lab1-answers/rvtools-lab1-answers.html Three example clusters, 4.0 to 5.3 vCPU per core. Totals only, no per-VM figure Lower confidence. Training example

The 756-VM estate has a mean that is pulled up by a few big VMs (the maxima are 29 vCPU, 128 GB and 1.7 TB). The typical VM is smaller than the mean. This is my reading of the ranges, not a figure from the source.

docs.title: 1.4 Disk IOPS per VM (lower confidence)
docs.text:
Source What it gives Confidence Cisco lab blog, Windows 7 desktops on an all-flash array: https://news-blogs.cisco.com/datacenter/vdi-the-missing-questions-9-how-many-storage-iops Steady state about 11 read plus 7 write IOPS per desktop (about 18). Boot storm about 260 read IOPS per desktop at peak, about 133 sustained for 5 to 6 minutes. The author says not to design from these numbers Lower confidence. Desktops, not servers. Lab test Our performance spec Server VMs at 20 to 50 average and 300 burst. These are the issue's defaults, not measured Assumption

I found no primary source for the IOPS of an everyday server VM. The numbers in sections 5 to 7 use the spec's 35 average (the middle of 20 to 50) and 300 burst. The Cisco figures are the same order of size.

docs.title: 2. Table of typical small, medium and large VMs
docs.text:
Size Linux (vCPU / RAM / disk) Windows Server (vCPU / RAM / disk) Average IOPS Source of each number Small 1 / 2 GiB / 20 GiB 2 / 4 GiB / 60 GiB 20 Linux: u1.small (1.2); RHEL floor of 1.5 GiB and 10 GiB (1.1). Windows: 2025 "4 GB recommended" and 32 GB floor (1.1). Test spec sizes (1.2). Disk is my estimate Medium 2 / 4 GiB / 50 GiB 2 / 8 GiB / 80 GiB 35 Linux: u1.2xmedium (1.2). Windows: between Red Hat X-small and Small (1.2). Disk is my estimate. IOPS: spec middle Large 4 / 16 GiB / 100 GiB 4 / 16 GiB / 120 GiB 50 u1.xlarge (1.2). Close to the 3.5 vCPU, 9.2 GB mean of one estate (1.3). Disk is my estimate

Where sources disagree: for RAM a medium VM runs from 4 GiB (u1.medium) to 8 GiB (Red Hat Small) to 9.2 GB (one estate's mean). For vCPU it runs from 1 to 4.

Recommended size for the calculations: medium. Linux 2 vCPU, 4 GiB, 50 GiB. Windows 2 vCPU, 8 GiB, 80 GiB. Reasons: - It sits above every vendor floor (1.1) and equals a named KubeVirt size for Linux (1.2). - It sits below the Red Hat example sizes, which are for big estates, and below the one-estate mean, which large VMs inflate. - The test spec uses smaller VMs (Linux 1/2, Windows 2/4). Section 4.5 repeats the sums with those sizes, so the test and the plan can be compared.

docs.title: 3. What a VM costs the cluster
3.1 Memory overhead of the virt-launcher pod
docs.text:
Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization 4.20 gives this formula (https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.20/html/virtualization/installing, section "Virtual machine memory overhead"; I read the single-page version, https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.20/html-single/virtualization/index):

  • Overhead per VM is about 0.002 x requested memory, plus 218 MiB, plus 8 MiB per vCPU, plus 16 MiB per graphics device, plus extra overhead.
  • Extra overhead: 1 GiB for each SR-IOV device or GPU, 256 MiB for SEV, 53 MiB for TPM.
  • The Red Hat Cluster Sizing Guide uses the same formula (https://access.redhat.com/articles/7107457).
  • Overhead is added on top of the guest memory. The pod requests guest memory plus overhead.

The KubeVirt user guide says only that the default memory overhead is 32Mi for "additional system resources" and does not give this formula (https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/resources_requests_and_limits/). I use the Red Hat formula because it covers the whole pod.

I do not add graphics devices, SR-IOV, GPU, SEV or TPM. Windows Server 2022 needs no TPM. A vTPM would add 53 MiB per VM, which is under 1 percent.

VM Guest memory Overhead Memory request Linux 2 vCPU 4 GiB 4,096 MiB 8.2 + 218 + 16 = 242 MiB 4,338 MiB = 4.237 GiB Windows 2 vCPU 8 GiB 8,192 MiB 16.4 + 218 + 16 = 250 MiB 8,442 MiB = 8.245 GiB

docs.title: 3.2 CPU request
docs.text:
KubeVirt asks for 1/cpuAllocationRatio core per vCPU. The ratio defaults to 10 (https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/resources_requests_and_limits/; the Red Hat guide says the same, https://access.redhat.com/articles/7107457). Your cluster has 10, so each vCPU requests 0.1 core. A 2 vCPU VM requests 0.2 core.

I did not add the small CPU requests of the other containers in the virt-launcher pod. I have no source for them. At 0.2 core per VM the CPU limit is far from binding (section 4), so a few extra millicores do not change the result.

docs.title: 3.3 Pod count
docs.text: Each VM is one virt-launcher pod, so one pod per VM. The limit is 250 pods per node (your measurement). I do not know how many pods the other workloads use. I show the pod limit with those pods ignored, which is the best case.

docs.title: 4.1 Free room (from your measurements)
docs.text:
Node Allocatable memory Requested Free memory Allocatable cores Requested Free cores 1 362.15 124.97 237.2 95.68 40.2 55.48 2 362.15 105.56 256.6 95.68 48.5 47.18 3 362.15 115.79 246.4 95.68 47.3 48.38 All 3 1,086.45 346.32 740.1 287.04 136.0 151.04

Memory is in GiB, converted from the bytes Kubernetes reports (for example, 388,858,399,457 bytes allocatable is 362.15 GiB). Cores are cores.

For N+1, one node fails and its other workloads restart on the two that remain. So I take the capacity of two nodes and subtract all the existing requests:

  • Memory: 2 x 362.15 = 724.3, minus 346.32 = 378.0 GiB free.
  • Cores: 2 x 95.68 = 191.36, minus 136.0 = 55.36 cores free.
  • Pods: 2 x 250 = 500, minus the pods of other workloads (not known).

This treats memory as one pool. Real scheduling leaves small gaps on each node, so the true count is a little lower.

docs.title: 4.2 No memory overcommit (the default)
docs.text:
Mix: 2/3 Linux, 1/3 Windows, so a group of 3 VMs is 2 Linux plus 1 Windows. One group requests 2 x 4.237 + 8.245 = 16.72 GiB and 0.6 core.

Case By memory By CPU (0.2 core per VM) By pods (ignoring other pods) Binds All 3 nodes, Linux only 740.1 / 4.237 = 174 151.04 / 0.2 = 755 750 Memory All 3 nodes, Windows only 740.1 / 8.245 = 89 755 750 Memory All 3 nodes, mix 740.1 / 16.72 = 44.3, so 44 groups = 132 VMs (88 Linux, 44 Windows) 755 750 Memory N+1, Linux only 378.0 / 4.237 = 89 55.36 / 0.2 = 276 500 less other pods Memory N+1, Windows only 378.0 / 8.245 = 45 276 500 less other pods Memory N+1, mix 378.0 / 16.72 = 22.6, so 22 groups = 66 VMs (44 Linux, 22 Windows) 276 500 less other pods Memory

docs.title: 4.3 With memory overcommit (not on in your cluster; shown for comparison)
docs.text:
How it works (Red Hat docs, https://docs.redhat.com/ko/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.21/html/virtualization/virt-configuring-higher-vm-workload-density, and the Cluster Sizing Guide, https://access.redhat.com/articles/7107457): - The HyperConverged setting is memoryOvercommitPercentage. The scheduler counts "assigned memory x (100 / percentage)" for each VM. 200 percent counts half of the guest memory. The docs allow 100 to 400 percent. - It needs swap on every worker, set up with a MachineConfig. The wasp-agent component is deployed when the percentage is above 100 at the time the HyperConverged CR is first created. Swap should be at least as large as the overcommitted RAM (OKD copy of the same procedure: https://docs.okd.io/4.21/virt/post_installation_configuration/virt-configuring-higher-vm-workload-density.html). - Only Burstable VM pods can swap. Without swap, Red Hat says overcommit is "strongly discouraged": the node's out-of-memory killer can end a running VM. - Red Hat says the path of the setting differs between versions. Check it against the version you run. I read the 4.21 page only through a search result summary and the OKD copy, not the full Red Hat page, because the page was too large for my fetch tool.

I assume the overhead from section 3.1 is not reduced. I could not confirm that from the docs.

Setting Linux request Windows request Group of 3 3 nodes (mix) N+1 (mix) 100 percent (now) 4.237 GiB 8.245 GiB 16.72 GiB 132 VMs 66 VMs 200 percent 2,048 + 242 = 2.237 GiB 4,096 + 250 = 4.245 GiB 8.72 GiB 740.1 / 8.72 = 84 groups = 252 VMs 378.0 / 8.72 = 43 groups = 129 VMs

At 200 percent, CPU requests still allow 755 VMs (3 nodes) or 276 VMs (N+1), so memory still binds. The N+1 count of 129 VMs also uses 129 of the 500 pod places that remain.

This is a count of what the scheduler allows. It is safe only if the VMs' real memory use is about half of their configured memory (Red Hat: the working set decides, https://access.redhat.com/articles/7107457). I do not assume it is on.

docs.title: 4.4 Real CPU
docs.text:
CPU requests (0.1 core per vCPU) are bookkeeping, not use. A check against real demand:

  • Red Hat plans CPU at 4:1 (4 vCPU per physical core) in its worked example. That turns a 4.7 vCPU average VM into about 1.2 cores (https://access.redhat.com/articles/7107457).
  • VMware's design guide says 1:1 to 3:1 is "not typically an issue", 3:1 to 5:1 may show performance loss, and 6:1 or more often causes problems. It quotes these as rules of thumb, not measurements. Source: VMware vCloud Architecture Toolkit, section 5.8, https://download3.vmware.com/vcat/vmw-vcloud-architecture-toolkit-spv1-webworks/Core%20Platform/Architecting%20a%20vSphere%20Compute%20Platform/Architecting%20a%20vSphere%20Compute%20Platform.1.019.html. I read this only through a search result summary, not the page. Lower confidence.
  • An old Dell/vKernel paper says physical servers averaged only 5 to 15 percent use (https://virtualizationreview.com/~/media/ECG/Tech%20Library%202013/04/DELL%20VKERNEL%20APRIL/Dell%20%20%20Best%20Practices%20for%20Oversubscription%20of%20CPU%20%20Memory%20and%20Storage%20in%20vSphere%20Virtual%20Environments_0.ashx). It is about 10 years old. I read it only through a search summary. Lower confidence.

Sums with my sizes (every VM has 2 vCPU, so 2 vCPU each):

Case VMs vCPU At 4:1 (0.25 core per vCPU) At 15 percent of a vCPU 3 nodes 132 264 66 cores 40 cores N+1 66 132 33 cores 20 cores

Compare with the free room in 4.1: the surviving two nodes have 191 allocatable cores. Real use of the other workloads is not known (I have only their requests), so I cannot say how much of that is idle. VM CPU is not the limit at these counts under either assumption.

docs.title: 4.5 Same sums with the test spec's smaller VMs
docs.text:
Linux 1 vCPU 2 GiB: overhead 4.1 + 218 + 8 = 230 MiB, request 2.225 GiB. Windows 2 vCPU 4 GiB: 242 MiB overhead, request 4.237 GiB. A group of 3 requests 8.69 GiB.

Case Mix VMs 3 nodes, no overcommit 740.1 / 8.69 = 85 groups = 255 VMs N+1, no overcommit 378.0 / 8.69 = 43 groups = 129 VMs

So the 90-VM test fits in the N+1 case (129 VMs) with room to spare.

docs.title: 5. Disk, IOPS and throughput of the maximum VM count
5.1 Capacity
docs.text:
My disk sizes: Linux 50 GiB, Windows 80 GiB (section 2).

Case Linux Windows Provisioned total N+1 (66 VMs) 44 x 50 = 2,200 GiB 22 x 80 = 1,760 GiB 3,960 GiB (4,252 GB) 3 nodes (132 VMs) 88 x 50 = 4,400 GiB 44 x 80 = 3,520 GiB 7,920 GiB (8,504 GB)

Thin files: this driver's VM disks are raw files, and raw files on NFS can be sparse, so unwritten space uses nothing (docs/VM-DISK-FORMATS.md, "Sparse Files and Thin Provisioning"; its example is 100 GB logical, 12 GB used). The pool counts logical (requested) size, not used size, when it places a volume (same file). So the share must be sized for the provisioned total, even if real use is lower. One estate averaged 72 GB used per VM (1.3), which is above my disk sizes, so I do not assume large savings.

Not confirmed: whether a cloned disk stays sparse. I searched docs/VOLUME-CLONING.md and pkg/pool/clone*.go for "sparse" and found nothing. A clone that copies the full size would use the full logical size. Treat clones as full size until tested.

docs.title: 5.2 IOPS and throughput
docs.text:
IOPS per VM: average 35 (range 20 to 50) and burst 300 (section 1.4, spec).

Case Average (35 each) Range at 20 to 50 Typical peak: 10 percent of VMs burst, rest at 35 Worst case: all VMs burst at 300 N+1 (66) 2,310 1,320 to 3,300 7 x 300 + 59 x 35 = 4,165 19,800 3 nodes (132) 4,620 2,640 to 6,600 13 x 300 + 119 x 35 = 8,065 39,600

These are guest I/Os. IBM counts more (next list).

The 10 percent burst share is my estimate. The worst case is the spec's patch window (all VMs at 300 for 10 minutes).

How IBM counts operations (https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-file-storage-profiles): "IOPS values are based on a 16 KB block size for all profiles, with a 50-50 random workload. Each 16 KB of data that is read or written counts as one read/write operation. A single write of less than 16 KB counts as a single write operation." (The repo's earlier research quotes the same text.) So:

  • IBM operations = sum over I/Os of ceil(size / 16 KB). An I/O of 16 KB or less counts as 1. A 64 KB I/O counts as 4.
  • My IOPS figures above are guest I/Os: what a VM does. The share's limit is in IBM operations. The two are not the same when an I/O is larger than 16 KB.

The 1.6 factor. The performance test's block mix (test/perf/profile.sh, PERF_BLOCK_MIX) gives each I/O size a share of the I/Os. Each size counts as a number of IBM operations by the rule above:

I/O size Share of the I/Os IBM operations each Adds 4 KiB 50 percent 1 0.5 16 KiB 30 percent 1 0.3 64 KiB 20 percent 4 0.8 Average 1.6

So one guest I/O of this mix counts as 1.6 IBM operations on average. A VM that does 300 I/Os a second uses 300 x 1.6 = 480 of the share's IOPS. The test computes the same factor (perf_ibm_ops_per_io) and reports ibm_ops_demand = guest IOPS x 1.6 beside the share's own count.

With the factor: - Average: N+1 2,310 x 1.6 = 3,696 IBM operations a second. 3 nodes 4,620 x 1.6 = 7,392. - All VMs burst together: N+1 19,800 x 1.6 = 31,680. 3 nodes 39,600 x 1.6 = 63,360. - One share with 33 VMs all bursting: 33 x 300 = 9,900 guest I/Os, but 9,900 x 1.6 = 15,840 IBM operations. This is why section 6 proposes 16,000 IOPS per share, not 12,000.

Limit of the factor: the mix is the test's model of an everyday VM, not a measurement of real VMs. Larger I/O (backup scans, boot, file copies) raises the factor. A mix of only 4 KiB and 16 KiB I/O gives 1.0; a 1 MiB I/O counts as 64. Replace 1.6 with the factor of the real workload when it is known.

Throughput: - IBM sets the maximum bandwidth as IOPS x 256 KB. The dp2 maximum is 8,192 Mbps (same IBM page). - The mix's average I/O is 0.5 x 4 + 0.3 x 16 + 0.2 x 64 = 19.6 KiB. Average throughput is 35 x 19.6 KiB = 0.67 MiB/s per VM: about 44 MiB/s for N+1 and 88 MiB/s for 3 nodes. - Worst case (all burst): N+1 19,800 x 19.6 KiB = about 379 MiB/s, 3 nodes about 758 MiB/s, so about 190 MiB/s per share in either proposal. That is far under the 8,192 Mbps (about 1,000 MiB/s) dp2 limit of one share.

docs.title: 6. Proposed dp2 shares
docs.text:
IBM rules used (https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-file-storage-profiles, https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-quotas, https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-file-storage-vpc-about): - Size 10 to 32,000 GB. Allowed IOPS depend on size. The table is the one in docs/specs/2026-10-24-performance-test-30-vms.md and matches IBM's page: 2,000 to 3,999 GB allows 200 to 40,000 IOPS. 4,000 to 7,999 GB allows 300 to 40,000. 8,000 to 15,999 GB allows 500 to 64,000. - Up to 300 file shares per account per region. One mount target per share per VPC. 256 hosts per mount target. - A share used by one client is limited to 48,000 IOPS. The 96,000 maximum needs several clients (IBM profile note). Not a limit at these sizes.

Headroom: fill each share to 80 percent at most. This is the default target utilisation in docs/CAPACITY-PLANNING.md (80 percent). Reasons: thin disks grow as VMs write (warning in docs/VM-DISK-FORMATS.md), snapshots use share space (a copy is charged the volume's size, an instant VM snapshot a tenth of it; docs/CAPACITY-PLANNING.md), and a share without room refuses a snapshot.

Capacity needed at 80 percent fill: - N+1: 4,252 GB / 0.8 = 5,315 GB. - 3 nodes: 8,504 GB / 0.8 = 10,630 GB.

Proposal (estimate until the test result replaces it):

Case Shares Size each IOPS each Total capacity Total IOPS Fill N+1, 66 VMs 2 3,000 GB 16,000 6,000 GB 32,000 71 percent 3 nodes, 132 VMs 4 3,000 GB 16,000 12,000 GB 64,000 71 percent

Why 16,000 IOPS: each share carries 33 VMs in both cases. If all of them burst at 300, that is 9,900 guest I/Os, or 33 x 300 x 1.6 = 15,840 IBM operations a second. 16,000 covers that. This meets the worst case on paper. It assumes the test's block mix and an even spread of VMs across shares. If the burst I/O is larger, the IBM count is higher and this is too low. 16,000 is under the 48,000 limit for a share used by one client. The 3,000 GB size is in the 2,000 to 3,999 GB row, which allows up to 40,000 IOPS, so there is room to raise IOPS without resizing.

Two shares in the N+1 case means a lost share takes half the VMs. Four shares limits that to a quarter. More, smaller shares spread the risk but each smaller share allows fewer IOPS (a 1,000 to 1,999 GB share allows up to 20,000). I did not choose on cost, because no budget was set. Cost of the IOPS is not calculated here.

docs.title: 7. Where the numbers are weak
docs.text:
• Memory is the limit in every case. Anything that changes VM memory changes the count in direct proportion. A group at Red Hat's "Small" size (2/8 GiB) for all VMs would give fewer VMs than shown.
  • Average and burst IOPS are assumptions. The performance test measures them.
  • Disk sizes are my estimates. Used space could be much lower, but clones may not be sparse.

docs.title: 8. Swap in the performance test result
docs.text:
A performance test is running on DR now: one share at 3,000, 10,000 and 20,000 IOPS, with up to 90 VMs. It finds how many VMs one share carries before latency rises. Its result replaces my IOPS-based share count (section 6). The formulas, so you can put the measured number in:

  • VMs per share (measured) = the knee count x 0.8. The spec recommends 80 percent of the knee.
  • Shares for the IOPS = ceil(VM count / VMs per share at the chosen IOPS tier).
  • Shares for the capacity = ceil((provisioned GiB / 0.8) / share size in GB).
  • Shares needed = the larger of the two.
  • Check the result against the cluster limit: VM count = the smaller of the memory, CPU and pod counts in section 4.

Example with a made-up number: if one 16,000 IOPS share carries 40 VMs at the safe point, then for 66 VMs: ceil(66 / 40) = 2 shares for IOPS, and ceil(5,315 / 3,000) = 2 for capacity. Shares needed = 2.

The test's VMs are the smaller test sizes (Linux 1/2, Windows 2/4). The IOPS per VM does not depend on RAM, so the count carries over. Disk per VM is larger in my sizing, so re-check the capacity formula.

docs.title: Decisions I made
docs.text:
• Used medium VMs: Linux 2 vCPU 4 GiB 50 GiB, Windows 2 vCPU 8 GiB 80 GiB.
  • Used the Red Hat 4.20 overhead formula (0.002 x memory + 218 MiB + 8 MiB per vCPU), not the KubeVirt 32Mi note.
  • Converted the cluster's memory from bytes to GiB.
  • For N+1, moved all existing workloads onto the two surviving nodes before counting free room.
  • Pooled memory across nodes and ignored fragmentation.
  • Ignored the other pods' count and the small CPU requests of the virt-launcher helper containers.
  • Used 35 average and 300 burst IOPS from the spec because I found no primary source for server VMs.
  • Used a 10 percent burst share for "typical peak" and all VMs for "worst case".
  • Kept the pool count at logical (provisioned) disk size and 80 percent fill.
  • Sized IOPS per share for the all-burst case at the test's block mix (1.6 IBM operations per I/O).
  • Chose 3,000 GB shares so IOPS can rise to 40,000 without resizing.
  • Did not assume memory overcommit is on.

docs.title: Claims I could not source
docs.text:
• A typical disk size (provisioned or used) for small, medium and large VMs: no source. The only data point is one estate at 72 GB used.
  • Published estate averages (vCPU, RAM, disk, IOPS) from Dell Live Optics, Broadcom, AWS, Azure or Google: not found. Their pages describe methods only.
  • IOPS of an everyday server VM: no primary source. Only desktop lab figures (Cisco) and the spec's assumption.
  • RHEL 10 system requirements: not read.
  • A recommended RHEL 9 RAM figure on a Red Hat page: the page gives only minimums.
  • Whether memory overcommit also shrinks the per-VM overhead: not confirmed.
  • Whether VM clone copies stay sparse: not found in the repo docs or code.
  • CPU requests of the other containers in the virt-launcher pod: no source.
  • Pod count of the existing workloads on the cluster: not measured.
  • The VMware vCAT section 5.8 and the Dell/vKernel paper were read through a search summary only.

docs.title: Spec: One unattended test run after each release update
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-19. Status: draft for review.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
After you update the driver on a cluster, one command checks every feature, through the API and the web console, and measures storage speed. Nobody needs to watch it. At the end it gives one pass or fail report, and it leaves nothing behind on the cluster or in the VPC.

"Done" means: - One command runs every stage below against rovslab-prod-eude. - A full run finishes unattended, and you can read the result on one screen. - A stage that fails does not stop the other stages, and the run still cleans up everything. - Speed results are saved, so each run is compared with the last one.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
Part What it does State test/e2e/test-vm-clone.sh Pool, image import, clone, VM boot Passed on rovslab, 19 Oct test/e2e/*_test.go Basic pool, cross-zone pool, replication objects only Not run on rovslab console-plugin/integration-tests/ 24 browser tests for the console plugin Last changed February; not run on ROVS /bench skill fio in a pod Instructions for Claude, not a script

No end-to-end test exists for: volume expansion, auto-expand, snapshots and restore, group snapshots, clones of plain volumes, share draining, webhooks, metrics, golden images, real replication, VM live migration, the PVC migration tool, or controller and node restarts.

Found while writing this spec: group snapshots do not work on ROVS. The driver's snapshot sidecar runs without group snapshots, and it only knows the upstream API. rovslab has OpenShift's own copy, groupsnapshot.storage.openshift.io/v1beta1, and only because its feature set is not the default. The fix is tracked in GitHub issue #14. Until then, the group snapshot stage reports SKIP with this reason.

Testing between regions is a separate script, written later. This run tests replication within one cluster only.

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text:
• Where: on the build server pool-csi-build, not on your laptop. You start it with one command from the laptop. It keeps running after you close the laptop.
  • Entry point: make test-release CLUSTER=rovslab-prod-eude. A Bash script, test/release/run.sh, runs the stages in order. Each stage is one file in test/release/stages/. Bash and oc match the existing VM clone test, and the build server already has them.
  • Access: at the start, the laptop copies a kubeconfig and a short-lived IAM token to the build server. The run deletes both when it ends. No credential is stored in the repo or kept on the server.
  • Safety:
  • The run refuses to start unless the cluster name matches CLUSTER.
  • Everything it makes is in namespaces and pools named rt-<run id>-....
  • It never touches any other object. The cluster has other lab work on it.
  • Each stage has a set-up step, checks, and its own clean-up, all with time limits. It ends as PASS, FAIL or SKIP, and a SKIP always gives its reason. A stage that times out counts as FAIL, and the run moves on.
  • Clean-up always runs, also after a failure or an interrupted run. It then checks that no rt- objects, VPC shares or VPC mount targets are left. Any leftover counts as a FAIL.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
Each line says what the stage proves, and how it checks the result itself, not the status the driver reports.

  1. Pre-flight. The driver runs the expected version (from the start-up log line). All pods are ready, and the CRDs and webhooks answer. CDI's copy pod memory limit is at least 8Gi (added by 2026-10-20-cdi-copy-limit.md). No rt- leftovers exist from an earlier run.
  2. Pool.
  3. A pool reaches Ready.
  4. Its share uses security group access mode, and its mount target is in the pool's zone (read from the VPC API).
  5. Its StorageClass exists.
  6. A pool with a security group that does not exist shows Degraded and creates no share.
  7. Volumes.
  8. Two pods on different workers write and read the same file.
  9. Owner and permissions match the pool settings.
  10. Deleting the PVC removes its SubVolume and its directory.
  11. Growth.
  12. A PVC is resized, and the pod sees the new size.
  13. A small pool with auto-expand adds a second share when it fills.
  14. Snapshots.
  15. A VolumeSnapshot is restored to a new PVC. Its files match the source checksums.
  16. A snapshot of a running VM that writes nonstop is restored, and a VM boots from it. Added by 2026-10-20-vm-safe-replication.md (the stage file is 06-vm-snapshots.sh, which runs test/e2e/test-vm-snapshot.sh).
  17. Group snapshots. A group snapshot of two PVCs is restored. Both match. If the cluster has no group snapshot API, the stage is SKIP.
  18. Clones.
  19. A clone of a PVC matches its source.
  20. A pod that uses the clone cannot start until the copy is done.
  21. VMs from the standard catalog (stage 08-vms, in a namespace with no extra permissions). Changed by 2026-10-20-cdi-copy-limit.md: golden images are hidden, so this stage no longer tests them.
  22. A VM made from the standard catalog (CentOS Stream 9), with its boot disk on the pool, boots, and its guest agent connects.
