  23. The VM live-migrates to another worker without a restart and keeps running.
  24. CDI copies 25 GB of random data from Ceph onto the pool, and the checksum matches. This re-tests CDI's copy pod memory limit on every run.
  25. Merged into stage 8. It was the golden image check; golden images are no longer tested.
  26. Replication. Replication runs between two pools on the same cluster, in direct NFS mode and in receiver mode. The copies at the destination match the source checksums. Pausing a policy stops new syncs. The VM checks below come from 2026-10-20-vm-safe-replication.md. Each one is added when its part of that spec ships.
    • A running VM is replicated while it writes nonstop to two disks. A VM boots from the copy, and its guest agent connects. The kernel log shows no file system errors.
    • In the copy, every file the VM logged before the freeze matches its checksum, and both disks show the same moment.
    • The next cycle sends only changed blocks: far fewer bytes than the disk size.
    • The source VM live-migrates. The next cycle is a compare pass, sends far fewer bytes than the disk size, and the copy still boots.
    • The receiver is stopped in the middle of applying a copy. After it restarts, the copy boots and shows either the old or the new moment, never a mix.
    • A stopped VM is copied with rsync, and it is still stopped afterwards.
    • The VM writes a marker file in each of three cycles. A rewind to the second restore point boots, has the first two markers and not the third. The latest copy still has all three.
    • The source VM live-migrates while a full copy runs. The migration succeeds within one controller cycle, and the next cycle makes a good copy.
    • Until the new copy method ships, a running VM volume is skipped with an error, and no rsync copy is made.
    • The guest pause and the VM slowdown during a copy are saved to test/release/history.csv. More than 20% worse than the last run is a warning.
  27. Draining. A share marked for draining gets no new volumes, and the pool counts the volumes left on it. Taken off the drain list, the share takes new volumes again.
  28. Restarts.
    • The controller pod is deleted. A new one takes over, and every pool and volume is unchanged.
    • A node agent pod is deleted. A pod that is writing to a volume keeps writing.
  29. Webhooks. Bad objects are refused, each with the expected message. Examples: a bad permissions value, a change to an immutable field, and limits out of range.
  30. Migration tool. kubectl-migrate copies a PVC from IBM's own VPC File class into a pool. The data matches.
  31. Metrics.
    • Prometheus has the driver metrics, with non-zero values after the earlier stages.
    • Each pool reconciles about once a minute. Today's loop bug made it about 30 times a minute.
  32. Console.
    • The browser tests run with a token, so no IBMid sign-in is needed.
    • A screenshot of each plugin tab is saved with the report.

  33. Speed. fio runs these tests, 60 seconds each:

    • sequential read and write with 1 MB blocks
    • random read and write with 4 KB blocks
    • a 70/30 random mix

    They run in three places: - a pod on a pool volume - a pod on a PVC from IBM's own class ibmc-vpc-file-3000-iops, as a baseline - inside a VM disk on pool storage

    The pool's shares get 3,000 IOPS, the same as the baseline. Results go to speed.csv in the run folder and to history.csv next to the run folders on the build server, because the test scripts folder is replaced on each run. The VM prints its results on its serial console, which the stage reads from the VM pod's log.

    First run on rovslab (20 October, run 1020-1303): pool volume, IBM baseline and VM disk all gave about 3,000 IOPS random 4 KB and 187 MB/s sequential 1 MB, the share's limit. A result more than 20% worse than the last run is a warning, not a FAIL, because cloud storage speed varies. 18. Backup. From 2026-10-20-vm-safe-replication.md, added when backup ships. - Built so far (stage 18 in test/release/stages/18-backup.sh, not run on a cluster yet). It runs test/e2e/test-backup.sh and checks its log. A BackupPolicy backs up a running VM with two disks and a pod volume to a separate snapshot pool, with a 5-minute schedule. The policy lists three volumes: the VM disks as FileSystemConsistent, the pod volume as FileCopy. The VM disks restored at the oldest moment boot with no XFS errors, and every file the VM logged is on the data disk with its checksum. The pod volume restored at the oldest moment holds the first content, and at the latest moment the changed content. A pod volume whose claim was deleted can be restored. The stage gets 100 minutes because the script takes 60 to 90. The second part, the COS export (part 6 of 2026-10-21-backup-cos-export.md), is in the same stage and script, built and not run on a cluster: with COS settings it adds spec.export (Compliance lock, 25 hours, a prefix new for each run), checks exportedTime and exportedBytes, runs kubectl backup cos-list, restores the three volumes from COS into a second namespace, boots the VM and checks the checksums and the pod volume; COS_DR_KUBECONFIG repeats the restore in the other cluster of the lab pair. Without settings those checks are reported as not checked. The stage time limit is 180 minutes. The bullets below that are not in this stage yet: three snapshots with a keep count, and the encryption and lock checks (a delete with the driver's key, an attempt to shorten a lock). - A backup policy takes three snapshots of a running VM and of a normal PVC, into a separate snapshot pool. - The oldest and the newest snapshot are restored. The VM boots from each, and the PVC files match their checksums. - With a keep count of 2, the third snapshot merges the oldest one away. The remaining snapshots still restore and boot. - The newest snapshot is exported to COS and restored from COS to a new PVC. The VM boots from it. - A known text string written in the VM cannot be found in any object in the bucket, which shows that the data is encrypted. - The driver's key cannot delete or shorten the lock of a backup. The run uses Compliance with a 1-day keep time, in a test bucket with a rule that deletes objects when their lock ends. So those objects stay for one day after the run, and are not counted as left behind. - The run uses its own rt-<run id>/ prefix in one test bucket, and deletes that prefix at the end. 19. Clean-up and report.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
• One screen: the version tested, each stage's result and time taken, the speed table compared with the last run, and anything left behind.
  • Saved files: a report folder on the build server with the logs, screenshots and fio output. It is copied back to the laptop.
  • Exit code: the run exits non-zero if any stage fails.

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text:
Stage by stage, smallest first. Each stage is proven on rovslab before the next one is written. These are real cluster tests, so TDD here means: 1. Define the check. 2. See it fail where a feature is broken, or prove that it can fail. 3. Then see it pass.

The bugs that the stages find are fixed in the same PRs, the same way as before.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
These figures are estimates from today's runs, not measurements of the full run.

  • Run time: about 2 to 3 hours. The VM, golden image and speed stages take the longest.
  • VPC shares:
  • about 8 small shares (100 GB or less) for up to 3 hours
  • one 2 TB, 3,000 IOPS share for the speed stage
  • one 500 GB, 10,000 IOPS share for the VM stage
  • one baseline PVC from IBM's class

All are deleted at the end. - Build server: running for the length of the run. - Work: about 5 PRs: - the runner, with stages 1 to 3 - data stages 4 to 7 - VM and golden image stages 8 and 9 - replication, draining, restarts and webhooks, stages 10 to 13 - the migration tool, metrics, console and speed stages, 14 to 17

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The run uses the cluster's own VMs for "VSI" tests. A VPC VSI outside the cluster cannot use this driver.
  • Replication is tested between two pools on rovslab. Testing between regions is a second script (your decision, 19 Oct).
  • Speed tests use 3,000 IOPS shares and compare with IBM's own 3,000 IOPS class. That is the most useful comparison for the money.
  • A slower speed result is a warning, not a failure.
  • The run executes on the build server, never on the laptop.
  • Credentials are passed in at the start and deleted at the end.
  • A stage that fails does not stop the run, and clean-up always runs.
  • Anything left behind after the run counts as a failure.
  • The run is started by hand after an update. It is not run on a schedule or from CI, because each run costs money.
  • It is written in Bash with oc, the same as the existing VM clone test.
  • The VM replication and backup checks test Linux VMs only. Windows freeze is tested once, in the lab test of the VM replication spec, because the run has no Windows image.
  • Stages 8 and 9 are one stage: the VM checks need the golden image, so testing them apart would make the image twice.
  • Object lock is tested with a 1-day Compliance lock. The test bucket deletes those objects by itself the next day.

docs.title: Spec: Run on ROVS, move to security group access, fix what the test found
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-19. Status: built. The design was implemented and merged on 19 and 20 October 2026 (PRs #3, #6, #7, #9). This file is kept as the record of the decisions.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
The driver creates pools, serves volumes and boots a cloned VM on a ROVS cluster (rovslab-prod-eude), and on new ROKS clusters. Every share it makes uses security group access mode. Every problem found on the way is fixed in this repo.

"Done" means the VM clone test passes on rovslab-prod-eude, the console plugin shows real pools there, CI is green on main, and the docs describe what the driver does now.

docs.title: What we found
docs.text:
Measured on rovslab-prod-eude (ROVS 4.21.31, 3 bare metal workers in eu-de-3) on 19 October 2026, unless a line says otherwise.

# Problem Effect 1 The driver creates file shares in VPC access mode. IBM has deprecated that mode (End of Support 6 May 2027). The API now refuses it: a share with a VPC-mode mount target fails with HTTP 501 shares_not_implemented. A share without a mount target is created in security group mode, and a VPC-mode mount target cannot then be added (HTTP 400). Seen in zones eu-de-1 and eu-de-3. The driver cannot create usable storage on any new cluster. Not ROVS-specific. 2 The driver reads a security-group mount target's export path as /. The real mount path has a share-specific export, for example 10.250.0.18:/83ad9ea6_1be6_.... Even with #1 fixed, every NFS mount would fail. 3 The driver uses the first subnet in vpc_subnet_ids, whatever zone the pool is in. On a multi-zone cluster, a pool's mount target can land in the wrong zone. 4 A pool reported phase Ready, "2 shares ready", while neither share had a mount target. The pool looks healthy but cannot serve one volume. 5 When no share was usable, volume requests failed with "no available capacity", and the pool grew to its share limit. A 500 GB, 10,000 IOPS share was created that could never be used, at a real cost. 6 The second share was created by a code path that passes no VPC, subnet or security group details. Shares created by auto-expansion never get a mount target. 7 Existing pools on VPC-mode shares have no migration path. None were found in this account (eu-de, all resource groups). Out of scope (19 Oct): this is a new app, so no VPC-mode shares exist, and the driver must not change existing shares. 8 CI has failed on main since February: 34 errcheck lint errors (mostly in pkg/replication/), and the integration tests do not compile (a test fake no longer satisfies the Kubernetes client interface). All unit tests pass. Real failures cannot be seen among the old ones. 9 The E2E VM clone test defaults to zone eu-de-1. All rovslab workers are in eu-de-3. The test fails on any cluster outside eu-de-1 unless you know the flag. 10 The container image logs version="dev". The Dockerfile build does not stamp the version. You cannot tell which build is running. 11 Every CSI health probe is logged at the default log level: about 3 lines per second. Real events are hard to find in the controller log. 12 webhook.certProvider=manual never sets the CA bundle on the webhook config, so every API call to the webhook fails TLS. With webhook.enabled=false, the controller still starts the webhook server, which needs certificates. Found by reading the code; not yet run. Both documented alternatives to cert-manager are likely broken. 13 The /deploy skill assumes Docker and does not set the pull secret or the certificate option. Following it on this Mac and on ROVS fails. 14 VPC-NETWORKING.md, the tutorials and the E2E script describe only ROKS and VPC access mode. The docs describe a setup that no longer works. 15 The OpenShift console plugin (console-plugin/) has never been built, deployed or tested on ROVS. It is off by default, and its image is not in this account's registry. Unknown whether pool management in the web console works. 16 Clones of small volumes were meant to copy at once, inside the create call. That path is switched off in code, because the controller cannot reach NFS. Every clone now runs as a background Job. The unused path and its size setting are still in the code, and VOLUME-CLONING.md and CLAUDE.md still describe it. The docs promise a fast path that does not exist, and the dead code misleads anyone who reads it.

Already fixed and merged in PR #3: webhook certificates through the OpenShift service CA, the trusted profile and pull secret install steps, and x86 image builds.

docs.title: Security group access mode (fixes 1, 2, 3, 6)
docs.text:
Every new share is created in security group mode, with one mount target. The mount target gets a virtual network interface (VNI), which is a network port with its own IP address, in a worker subnet.

  • Subnet: the cluster's worker subnet in the pool's zone. The driver reads all IDs in vpc_subnet_ids, asks the VPC API for each subnet's zone, and picks the one that matches spec.zone. If no subnet matches, the pool reports an error and creates nothing.
  • Security group: the cluster's own group, kube-<cluster_id>, with the cluster ID read from the cluster-info configmap. IBM's file driver uses this group on rovslab. The group already allows all traffic between its members, so the workers can reach NFS port 2049 with no rule change. A new optional pool field, securityGroupIDs, overrides it.
  • Mount path: read the server and export path from the mount target's mount_path in every mode. Never assume /.
  • One code path: initial provisioning, auto-expansion and mount-target recovery all build the request in one place. Then a share can never be created without its mount target details.
  • Other zones: pods in other zones mount the same mount target across zones. IBM documents cross-zone mounting for security group mode. The VM clone test on a multi-zone cluster proves it; until then, the docs say that it is untested.

docs.title: Pool health (fixes 4, 5)
docs.text:
• A share counts as ready only when it is stable and has a mount target with an IP address.
  • A pool is Ready only when at least one share is ready. Otherwise it is Degraded, with a condition that names the cause.
  • Auto-expansion runs only when the ready shares are full. It never adds a share because the existing ones have no mount target.

docs.title: Migrating existing VPC-mode shares (7): dropped
docs.text: This is a new app. Every share it creates uses security group access mode, and it must not change existing shares. So there is no conversion, no warning and no runbook.

docs.title: Console plugin (fixes 15)
docs.text:
• Build and push the plugin image for x86, the same way as the driver image.
  • Turn it on in the rovslab install (consolePlugin.enabled=true), with the same pull secret.
  • Check each tab against real objects: the dashboard, pools, volumes, snapshots, group snapshots, replication policies and monitoring. Each tab must show what oc get shows, and the create and edit forms must make valid objects.
  • Show the new pool states from this spec: Degraded and the cause of an unusable share.
  • Make the plugin's own lint and unit tests run in CI, if they do not already.

docs.title: Housekeeping (fixes 8–14, 16)
docs.text:
• Fix all 34 lint errors properly. For example, return close errors where they matter, not _ = everywhere. Make the integration tests compile and pass.
  • E2E script: read the zone from the worker nodes when --zone is not given.
  • Dockerfile: stamp the version, as make build already does.
  • Log CSI probes at a detailed level, V(6), not at V(4).
  • Webhooks: manual mode takes the CA bundle from a chart value. With webhook.enabled=false, the controller registers no webhooks. Run both on rovslab, not only in tests.
  • /deploy skill: use podman or Docker, set the pull secret, and use webhook.certProvider=openshift on OpenShift.
  • Clones: delete the unused synchronous path and its size setting, and correct VOLUME-CLONING.md and CLAUDE.md to say that every clone runs as a Job.
  • Docs: VPC-NETWORKING.md describes security group mode; ROKS-only wording becomes "ROKS or ROVS" where both are true; record what this spec changes in CHANGELOG.md and FEATURES.md.

docs.title: How we prove it
docs.text:
Every change starts with a failing test. Unit tests use the fake VPC client. Then, on rovslab-prod-eude:

  1. Create a pool. Its share has a security-group mount target in eu-de-3, and the pool reaches Ready.
  2. Run the VM clone test with the zone read from the nodes. A cloned CentOS Stream VM boots to a login prompt, checked on the VNC screen and not only on the serial console.
  3. Create a pool whose share cannot get a mount target, for example with a security group ID that does not exist. The pool shows Degraded and does not grow.
  4. The console plugin loads in the rovslab web console. Each tab shows the same objects as oc get, checked by screenshot.
  5. CI is green on the PR, with Lint, Test and Build all passing.

docs.title: Order of work
docs.text:
1. CI fixes (8), so that each later PR shows its own failures.
  2. Security group mode and the mount path (1, 2, 3, 6), together with pool health (4, 5), as one PR. Then the VM clone test on rovslab.
  3. Housekeeping (9–14, 16).
  4. Console plugin (15), after step 2, so it can show the new pool states.

Each step is a separate PR that is merged before the next one starts.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
• Each run of the VM clone test creates one 500 GB, 10,000 IOPS share for about 15 minutes. The test then deletes it.
  • The work is about 4 PRs. Step 2 is the largest.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• New shares always use security group mode. There is no setting to choose VPC mode, because the API refuses it.
  • The default security group is the cluster's own kube-<cluster_id> group, the same as IBM's file driver. You can give a different group per pool.
  • One mount target per share, in the pool's zone. Other zones mount it across zones.
  • A pool with no usable share is Degraded, not Ready, and it does not grow.
  • No migration of VPC-mode shares: the app is new, and existing shares are never changed (your decision, 19 Oct).
  • I fix the CI failures first, so each later PR has a clean signal.
  • The 34 lint errors get real fixes, not blanket "ignore the error" lines.
  • The fixes found by reading code (problem 12) are tested on the cluster before I call them fixed.
  • The console plugin is in scope. It is tested after the security group change, because it must show the new pool states.

docs.title: Spec: VMs use the standard catalog; the driver keeps CDI's copy limit at 8 GB
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-20. Status: approved in chat: "hide the converter/golden images just in case we need it in the future. have an installation task that checks/updates the cdi to 2GB and we use the cdi from now on", then "yes, build it with 8GB" after the 25 GB test below.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
To make a VM from the standard OpenShift catalog with its boot disk on a pool, CDI copies the catalog image onto the pool. CDI's copy pod may use at most 600 MB of memory. When it writes onto NFS, the file cache counts against that limit and the pod is killed.

What was measured on rovslab, 20 October:

Test Result CDI copy of RHEL 9 from Ceph onto a pool, 600 MB limit Killed for lack of memory, 3 of 3 (also onto IBM VPC File) The same copy, 2 GB limit Done in 77 s, peak 1.95 GB VM from the standard RHEL 9 catalog image onto a pool, 2 GB limit Guest agent after 103 s VM from a RHEL 9 master copy already on the pool (driver copy) Guest agent after 154 s CDI copy of 25 GB of random data from Ceph onto a pool, 2 GB limit Killed 6 times, restarts from zero each time, never finishes The same copy, 8 GB limit Done in 134 s, checksum matches; memory sat at the limit Driver copy of 25 GB on the pool (512 MB limit) Done in 160 s, checksum matches

Research: Red Hat documents HyperConverged.spec.resourceRequirements.storageWorkloads as the way to change CDI's pod limits, and its example uses 2Gi. CDI has a known problem with file cache under the 600 MB limit; its fix covers only image conversion, not plain disk copies. IBM's ROVS docs say the virtualization add-on is pre-configured and cannot be modified, and do not mention this setting.

docs.title: The driver keeps CDI's copy limit at 8 GB
docs.text:
• When OpenShift Virtualization is installed, the controller (leader only) reads the HyperConverged object at start-up and every 5 minutes.
  • If CDI's copy pod memory limit is missing or below the target, it raises it:
  • If storageWorkloads is not set, it sets CDI's own defaults with the memory limit raised: limits CPU 750m and memory 8Gi, requests CPU 100m and memory 60M.
  • If storageWorkloads is set, it changes only limits.memory.
  • It never lowers a limit and never changes any other field.
  • Each time it raises the limit, it logs a warning and adds 1 to the metric vpc_file_pool_cdi_copy_limit_raised_total. A raise after the first one means something, such as IBM's add-on, put the old value back.
  • Helm value cdi.copyPodMemoryLimit (default 8Gi) sets the target. An empty value turns the check off. Controller flag: --cdi-copy-pod-memory-limit.
  • The controller ClusterRole gets get, list and patch on hco.kubevirt.io hyperconvergeds.

docs.title: Golden images are hidden
docs.text:
• The golden image code stays, so it can be used again. It is off unless a pool turns it on, as today.
  • The console's pool form no longer offers golden images, and its "VM storage" preset no longer turns them on. The pool details page still shows golden image status if a pool has it.
  • The docs mark golden images as hidden and kept for possible later use. They point to the standard catalog instead.
  • The old converter is already deleted. It can be restored from git history (before PR #27).

docs.title: Release test
docs.text:
• Stage 01 checks that CDI's copy pod memory limit is at least 8Gi.
  • Stage 08 makes its VMs from the standard catalog (CentOS Stream 9) with the boot disk on the pool. It still checks boot, guest agent, and live migration without a restart. It also copies 25 GB of random data from Ceph onto the pool with CDI and checks the checksum, so every run re-tests the limit. The golden image checks are removed from the run; their unit tests stay.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The driver does the check and the raise, not a one-time install step, so a reset by IBM's add-on is undone within 5 minutes and shows up as a warning and a metric.
  • 8 GB is the target. 2 GB (Red Hat's example) worked for a RHEL image but failed for 25 GB of data; 8 GB worked for 25 GB. CDI's memory sat at the limit, so a much larger disk is not proven. The workers have about 500 GB of memory each.
  • The driver only raises the limit. If someone sets a higher one, it is left alone.
  • The Helm value can turn the check off, for clusters where changing HyperConverged is not allowed.
  • Pool StorageProfiles keep cloneStrategy: csi-clone, so copies from one pool disk to another are made by the driver.
  • The release test no longer tests golden images, because they are hidden.

docs.title: Spec: golden images are made by CDI, not by our converter
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-20. Status: approved in chat ("if we don't need the converter, we should get rid of it").

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A pool with golden images turned on makes a ready-to-boot disk image of each OS in each target namespace. Today our own converter Job does this: it installs tools, downloads the container disk, unpacks it, converts it to raw, and patches the boot sector. It was written because CDI, the cluster's own image importer, was thought not to work with this driver.

The release test run (stage 08, 20 October) and a check next to it found:

Finding Consequence The converter runs as root in the app's namespace No golden image unless that namespace has the anyuid permission The syncer makes the golden disks again while their pool is being deleted A pool with golden images can never be deleted Catalog entries (DataSources) stay after their pool is deleted The VM catalog shows images whose disks do not exist. Five such entries were on rovslab Every catalog entry for an image has the same name Only the first namespace, of the first pool, gets a catalog entry

docs.title: What was measured on rovslab, 20 October
docs.text:
• CDI import from the registry onto pool storage works. CentOS Stream 9 from quay.io/containerdisks/centos-stream:9 imported in about 40 seconds. A VM booted from it with BIOS, and its guest agent connected. RHEL 9 from registry.redhat.io/rhel9/rhel-guest-image: see "RHEL 9 result" below.
  • CDI clone of the cluster's own image onto pool storage does not work reliably. Cloning the RHEL 9 image from Ceph: CDI's upload pod (memory limit 600 MB) was killed for lack of memory after 10 seconds, then could not restart because the half-written disk.img existed. The same failure was seen once on 18 October.
  • VMs on pool storage work. A VM made from the golden image template booted, its guest agent connected, and it live-migrated to another worker without a restart.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• The syncer keeps its job: for each image and each target namespace, make a golden disk, a Template, and a catalog entry. Only the way the disk is made changes.
  • The golden disk is a CDI DataVolume in the target namespace, on the pool's StorageClass, named golden-<image> as before. CDI downloads and converts the image itself. Its source is the image's registry address, pulled by the node (pullMethod: node), the same way the cluster's own image jobs pull it.
  • For images whose cluster job uses an internal ImageStream (the RHEL images), the syncer uses the external address that the ImageStream itself imports from, for example registry.redhat.io/rhel9/rhel-guest-image. The node's pull secret already allows it.
  • The golden disk is ready when the DataVolume has succeeded. CDI retries a failed import itself.
  • Catalog entries are named <image>-<namespace>-nfs-pool, one per golden disk.
  • Deleting a pool first deletes its golden DataVolumes, claims, Templates and catalog entries, in every namespace. The syncer skips a pool that is being deleted.
  • Removed: the converter Job and its script, the goldenImages.converterImage setting, the internal registry permission (RoleBinding) the converter needed, and the controller's permissions that only the converter used.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Unit tests: the DataVolume the syncer makes (source, StorageClass, size, labels), readiness from the DataVolume phase, the external address for ImageStream images, pool deletion clean-up, and the skip of a pool being deleted.
  • Release test stage 08 runs in a namespace with no extra permissions and checks: golden image ready, Template, catalog entry pointing at this pool's disk, VM boot and guest agent, live migration, pool deletion, and nothing left in the shared images namespace.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• CDI downloads from the registry. It does not clone the cluster's existing image, because that clone ran out of memory on this cluster twice.
  • The golden disk is made once and not refreshed when a newer OS image comes out. This is the same as today. Delete the golden disk to get a fresh one on the next sync.
  • Disk images are no longer patched to set the boot flag. The CDI-made CentOS disk booted without it. If an image does not boot, stage 08 will show it.
  • The converterImage setting is removed, not kept as an unused field. This is a new app, so no existing pools need it.
  • Two pools must not send golden images to the same namespace. That is documented, not blocked.

docs.title: Spec: deletes, snapshots and restores act on the share data
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-20. Status: in progress (fix for a data-safety bug found by the release test run).

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The controller has no NFS access. Its pool manager was built with no file operations, so four operations skip their data step and still report success:

Operation What happens today Consequence Delete a volume The volume's folder stays on the share Pool shows space as free, but the share is still full of old data Create a snapshot No copy is made; the snapshot reports ready A snapshot that holds nothing Restore a snapshot No copy is made; the volume is empty A restore that "succeeds" with no data Delete a snapshot Nothing is removed (no data to remove today)

Even with file access, the old code could not work: it joined paths to one local folder and had no idea which share a path belongs to.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
All four data steps run as short Kubernetes Jobs, the same way volume clones already copy data.

  • A share Job mounts one share root (or two, for a restore onto a different share) through a temporary PersistentVolume and claim, and runs one shell step: remove a folder, or copy a folder.
  • Share Jobs run in the driver's own namespace (from the pod's namespace, default kube-system), as root. Measured on rovslab on 2026-10-20: root in such a pod can read, copy (owners kept) and delete another user's private files on a VPC file share (sec=sys).
  • Each Job is named from the operation and the volume or snapshot name, so a retry finds the same Job. On success the Job, claim and volume are removed. On failure they are removed and the operation reports an error; the next retry starts a new Job.
  • A failed copy removes its partial folder before it ends.
  • A delete first stops a copy that is still writing into the same folder (an unfinished restore or snapshot), and answers "in progress" until that copy has stopped.
  • Every path is checked against the volume or snapshot path rules before it goes into a step.

docs.title: Per operation
docs.text:
• Delete a volume: the first call starts the remove Job and answers "in progress". The CSI provisioner retries. When the Job has succeeded, the volume record is deleted and the space is given back to the pool. The space comes back only after the data is gone.
  • Create a snapshot: the snapshot record is written first as not ready, and the copy Job starts. The CSI snapshotter calls again until the snapshot is ready. When the Job has succeeded, the record is marked ready. If the Job fails, the record is deleted and its space given back, so the next call starts again. A short API error changes nothing.
  • Restore a snapshot: the new volume's record is written first, with phase Creating, so the chosen share keeps its reservation across retries. The copy Job copies the snapshot folder into the new volume folder, then sets owner and permissions. Until it succeeds, the call answers "in progress" and the claim stays Pending. No pod can mount a half-restored volume.
  • Delete a snapshot: like deleting a volume.

"In progress" is gRPC Aborted. The CSI sidecars treat it as "not final" and retry. If a claim is deleted while its restore runs, the provisioner finishes the create and then deletes the volume.

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
• Unit tests for the Job runner and for each manager operation (Job not started, running, succeeded, failed).
  • Release test stage 3 (delete removes the folder) passes on rovslab.
  • New release test stage 5: write data, snapshot, restore to a new claim, compare checksums, delete the snapshot and check its folder is gone.

docs.title: Not in this change
docs.text:
• Volume clones still run their Job in the claim's namespace. That needs the anyuid permission in every user namespace. Moving clones to share Jobs is the next change.
  • Group snapshots still do not work on ROVS (issue #14). This change only stops the group code from reporting a group as complete before its copies finish: the group stays InProgress, and later calls check the copies again.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Data steps run as Jobs, not inside the controller. Giving the controller NFS mounts would make it a privileged pod and would block CSI calls for minutes on large copies.
  • Jobs run in the driver's namespace, not the user's, so no user namespace needs extra permissions.
  • A deleted volume's space is freed only after its data is removed, not before.
  • A restore keeps the claim Pending until the copy is done, instead of binding at once and blocking the mount. This needs no new fields and no change to the node agent.
  • A failed Job is removed and retried on the next call, without a retry limit. The CSI sidecars already slow their retries down over time.
  • The old in-process copy and remove code paths for these four operations are removed, with their unit tests. They never ran in a real controller. New tests cover the Job-based behaviour.
  • The Job uses the same image as clone Jobs (quay.io/centos/centos:stream9).
  • The Job runner reads through the API directly, not the controller's cache, so it never acts on an old view of a Job or pod.
  • A retried create for a restore or clone always goes to the pool manager. Only plain volumes are answered from the existing record.

docs.title: Spec: VM disk replication in receiver mode, and failover to a chosen moment
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-20. Status: draft for review. This is step 5 of 2026-10-20-vm-safe-replication.md. Read that spec first.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: When this step is done: - In receiver mode (destinationEndpoint set), running VM disks replicate safely, with the same guarantees as direct NFS mode. Today receiver mode skips them. - Each changed block crosses the network once, not three times. - After a full copy to a disk that already exists, only the blocks that differ cross the network. - Failover of a VM with several disks always gives disks from the same moment, even if a copy stopped half way, and even if the source region is gone. - You can fail over to an earlier restore point, for example before ransomware.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
• Direct NFS mode (step 4): the apply Job writes into the far-site disk over NFS. It saves old blocks in undo files first. Each changed block crosses the network about three times.
  • Receiver mode: sync-client Jobs send a tar stream to an HTTPS receiver. The receiver extracts files. It does not know about VM disks, and the controller skips VM volumes in this mode.
  • Failover (cmd/failover): reads one metadata file per SubVolume and creates the SubVolume, PV and PVC. It treats every PVC alone. It does not know which PVCs belong to one VM, and it does not look at undo files.
  • pkg/replication/undo.go already has apply, roll back, rewind and prune. It works on a local folder, so the receiver can call it unchanged.

docs.title: A new receiver call for VM disks
docs.text:
The sync client sends the staging file in three calls. All use the existing token and TLS.

  1. Compare POST /api/v1/vmcopy/{subvolume}/compare. The client sends a SHA-256 hash for each 64 KiB block of the staging file's data. It only sends this for a full copy. The receiver compares the hashes with its own disk and answers with the list of blocks that differ. For a change-only copy, this call is skipped, because every listed block already changed.
  2. Upload PUT /api/v1/vmcopy/{subvolume}/{copyID}. The client sends only the needed blocks, as a stream of offset, length and data. The receiver writes them to a sparse staging file in an .repl-incoming folder next to the disk. The call can be repeated with the same copyID; the receiver keeps what it has and asks only for the rest.
  3. Commit POST /api/v1/vmcopy/{subvolume}/{copyID}/commit. The client sends the disk size, the moments from and to, and a hash of the whole upload. The receiver checks the hash. Then it calls ApplyCopy, the same function direct NFS mode uses, on its local copy of the folder. So the undo file is written at the far site, and each changed block crosses the network once.

The from check. The receiver compares from with the moment its disk shows now. If they differ (a copy was lost, or someone else changed the disk), it answers 409. The client then does a full copy with the compare call. No copy is applied on top of the wrong base.

Safety rules for the receiver: - The receiver uses os.Root on the volume folder, as undo.go does. A link in the folder cannot send a write outside it. - It refuses a block whose offset plus length is beyond the declared disk size. It refuses a declared size above a limit in the policy (default 2 TiB). - It allows one call per disk at a time. A second commit for the same disk waits or answers 429. - It deletes .repl-incoming files older than 24 hours. - The subvolume name must match ^pvc-[a-f0-9-]{36}$, as today.

docs.title: Several disks of one VM commit together
docs.text:
A VM with two disks must not end with disk 1 at moment B and disk 2 at moment A for long. The client works in two phases:

  1. Upload all disks of the VM (steps 1 and 2 above). Nothing is applied yet.
  2. Send commit for each disk, one after the other.

If the client stops between two commits, the disks show different moments. That is allowed, and failover handles it (next section). The next cycle finishes the commits, because the uploaded files are still there.

docs.title: The VM group and the moment, in the metadata
docs.text:
Failover can only choose a common moment if it knows which volumes belong to one VM, and what moment each disk shows. The metadata file of each SubVolume gets two new fields: - vmGroup: namespace and VM name, taken from the source VM pod when the copy is made. - vmMoment: the moment the disk shows. The receiver writes it in the same commit step, after the disk is marked applied.

The moment of a disk is also known without the metadata: it is the to of the newest applied undo file. For a disk with no undo file yet, the metadata is the only record. If the two disagree, the undo file wins, because it is written first.

docs.title: Failover picks the latest common moment
docs.text:
For a VM, failover now does this:

  1. Check that no commit is running on the disks (a lease file with a time limit, written by the receiver). If one is running, stop and say so. With --force, wait for its limit to pass.
  2. Roll back any unfinished copy on each disk (Recover). This needs nothing from the source region.
  3. List, for each disk, the moments it can show: its current moment, and the from of each applied undo file.
  4. Choose the newest moment that every disk can show. If you gave --rewind-to, choose the newest common moment at or before that time.
  5. Disks that already show that moment are used in place, as today. Other disks are rewound into a new disk (Rewind writes a new file and leaves the latest disk unchanged). The new disk gets its own folder, and the PV points to it.
  6. Print the moment chosen, for each disk the moment it started at, and the RPO. If a disk is rewound, say how much extra space it needs.

If no moment is common to all disks (the 24 hour history was pruned on one disk only), failover stops and lists the moments each disk has. It never mixes moments.

New flags: --rewind-to <RFC3339 time> and --list-moments (print the common moments and exit).

docs.title: Remove the receiver-mode skip
docs.text: The controller stops skipping VM volumes in receiver mode and uses the QEMU path with the three calls above. Hot-plugged disks are still skipped, as in direct NFS mode, because the volume list does not include them.

docs.title: Metrics and status
docs.text: Status adds, for each VM volume: the mode used (receiver or direct), whether the last cycle was a compare pass, and bytes sent. New metrics: bytes skipped by the compare pass, and commit failures by reason (409, hash mismatch, size limit).

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
This step is 3 PRs. Each adds its release test checks in the same PR.

  1. Receiver calls and the VM group. The three calls, the from check, the incoming folder and its clean-up, the safety rules, and the new metadata fields. Tests: unit tests with a fake disk for each refusal; a test that a stopped upload resumes; a test that a wrong from gives 409.
  2. Controller and client in receiver mode. The sync client sends the three calls. The controller removes the skip. The compare call for full copies. Two-disk commit order. Test: extend test/e2e/test-vm-replication.sh with a receiver-mode run on rovslab (two pools; the receiver runs in the same cluster, as in the existing receiver tests). It checks bytes sent are near the changed bytes, not three times that.
  3. Failover. Latest common moment, --rewind-to, --list-moments, the lease check, the rewind into a new disk. Test: stop a commit between two disks (a test hook), run failover, boot the VM, and check that both disks show one moment. Then rewind to an older restore point, boot, and check that the checksums match that moment. Add this to release test stage 10.

Not in this step: the two-region test with Windows (step 6), and any change to snapshots or backup.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• Hashing. The compare call makes the client read the whole staging file once and hash it. This costs CPU and local read time, but no network. A 100 GB disk takes a few minutes. It happens only after a VM move or restart.
  • Space at the far site. Unchanged from step 4: up to one more disk for 24 hours of restore points. A rewind needs one more full disk until you delete it.
  • Receiver is a new write path to far-site data. It writes disk files, so a bug can corrupt a disk. The undo file protects the previous moment. The safety rules above and the shared ApplyCopy code limit the risk. Tests for refusals are part of PR 1.
  • Failover with a long wait. If a commit hangs, failover waits for the lease to end, or you use --force. During a real disaster, --force is the right choice, because Recover makes it safe.
  • Rewind is slower than a normal failover. It copies the whole disk, then applies undo files. A 100 GB disk takes minutes. A failover to the latest moment is as fast as today.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Receiver mode uses the same apply code as direct NFS mode (ApplyCopy), run at the far site. One method, tested once.
  • The client sends block hashes first, so a compare pass sends only the blocks that differ.
  • A copy is applied only if the far-site disk shows the moment the copy starts from. If not, the client does a full copy with the compare pass.
  • A VM's disks are uploaded first and committed one after the other. A stop between commits is allowed; failover fixes it.
  • Failover chooses the newest moment that all disks of a VM can show. It never mixes moments, and it stops if there is no common one.
  • Failover on a disk with an unfinished copy rolls it back first. It needs nothing from the source region.
  • A rewind makes a new disk and leaves the latest one unchanged, so you can try another moment.
  • Failover learns which volumes belong to one VM from a vmGroup field in the metadata.
  • A running commit blocks failover until its lease ends; --force skips the wait.
  • The default size limit for one disk in a receiver call is 2 TiB, set per policy.
  • Hot-plugged disks stay skipped in receiver mode, as in direct NFS mode.
  • This step does not change snapshots, backup or the Windows test. Those stay in steps 6 to 9.

docs.title: Spec: Replicate and back up running VMs safely
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-20. Status: draft for review.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Replication copies the disks of running VMs to the other region, and each copy is safe to boot. Safe means: every disk of a VM shows the same single moment. A copy never mixes data from before and after that moment.

"Done" means: - A running VM's disks replicate on the policy's schedule, and the VM keeps running. - After failover, the copy boots and its file systems mount without errors. - If the VM has a guest agent, the copy is file-system consistent. If it does not, the copy is crash consistent, the same as a power cut. The status says which. - A VM with several disks gets all its disks from the same moment. - Only changed blocks cross between regions in normal operation. - The driver never copies a running VM disk with rsync again. - Optional backup: on a schedule, the driver keeps local snapshots in a separate snapshot pool, and can also export them to IBM Cloud Object Storage (COS). Both use the same safe copy as replication.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
Replication copies files with rsync, on a schedule. For VM disks this is unsafe. rsync reads disk.img while the VM writes to it, so the copy mixes blocks from different moments. CROSS-REGION-DR.md already says VM disks are not supported, but the controller copies them anyway, without a warning.

OpenShift Virtualization will get a supported backup feature with change tracking (KubeVirt v1.8; Veeam says it is a Tech Preview in OpenShift 4.22). rovslab runs 4.21 (KubeVirt v1.7.4), so we cannot use it yet.

Snapshots have the same problem. A snapshot copies the volume's files into /pvcs/.snapshots/ on the same share. For a running VM, that copy is also unsafe. Because it is on the same share, it is also lost if the share is lost. The driver has no backup to COS.

docs.title: Test on rovslab, 20 Oct
docs.text:
The controller can ask QEMU, the program that runs each VM, for a copy. Every VM pod has libvirt 10.10 and QEMU 9.1. I tested this with a CentOS Stream 9 VM on a pool volume. During the test the VM wrote about 200 MB/s without a pause.

Check Result Freeze the guest file systems, start the copy, thaw Guest paused for 0.1 s Boot the full copy Booted. All 150 checked files matched. The last file is the last one written before the freeze Change tracking through libvirt Refused: "checkpoint for disk vda unsupported for storage type raw" Change tracking in QEMU memory Works on our raw disks Copy of changes only, applied to the full copy, then boot 3 GB in 16 s, compared with 224 s for the full copy. Booted, all 150 files matched Live migration The change list is gone after the migration Guest write speed during the copy 20 times slower during the full copy, 10 times slower during the change-only copy. The copy was written to the same file share as the VM disk Size of a full copy 40 GB for a 40 GB disk with 5 GB of data, because the copy was not sparse

Red Hat does not support this method. You accepted that on 20 Oct, until the supported feature arrives.

docs.title: Which volumes take the VM path
docs.text:
On each cycle, the controller checks every volume in the policy. A volume takes the VM path if a running VM uses it. The controller finds this from the VM pod that mounts the volume.

  • Running VM: QEMU makes the copy (below).
  • Stopped VM, or no VM: rsync is safe, because nothing writes to the disk. The controller checks that the VM is still stopped after the copy. If the VM started during the copy, the controller discards the result and tries again on the next cycle.
  • Running VM, but the QEMU path fails: the controller skips the volume and reports an error. It never falls back to rsync.

docs.title: Take a copy at one moment
docs.text:
The controller runs commands in the VM pod. On OpenShift, a user may run commands in a pod only if it could also create that pod. VM pods run under the kubevirt-controller security policy (SCC), so the controller's account gets use on that one SCC. Kasten and IBM Backup and Recovery have the same permission for the same reason. This gives the account no new power to start pods. It cannot create pods directly. A pod can run as this account only in kube-system, where OpenShift applies no SCC at all, so the Jobs the controller already creates there are unrestricted. Found in the end-to-end test on 20 Oct: without it, every copy failed with "exec operation is not allowed because the pod's security context exceeds your permissions".

  1. Freeze the guest file systems through the guest agent, with KubeVirt's own freeze tool in the VM pod.
  2. The tool thaws the guest by itself after a timeout, even if the controller never sends the thaw. The controller sets 30 s. So a lost connection cannot leave the guest frozen.
  3. If there is no guest agent, skip this step.
  4. If the freeze fails, thaw and go on without it. Example: on a Linux guest with SELinux, one file system with a missing label makes the whole freeze fail.
  5. In both cases the copy is marked "crash consistent", and the status shows the guest's error.
  6. In one QEMU step, for all disks of the VM: start a new change list, and start a copy of each disk as it is at this moment.
  7. Thaw the guest. The guest is paused for about 0.2 s.
  8. QEMU writes the copy to a staging file in the VM's own volume, at a speed limit.
  9. A copy Job sends the staging file to the other region (below), then deletes it. The Job runs as the same user as QEMU, because only that user can delete the file.

If the VM must move during a copy. A VM cannot live-migrate while QEMU copies its disks: the move fails, and the VM stays where it is (tested 20 Oct). A worker drain or a cluster update would wait for the copy. So the controller watches for a requested move. When it sees one, it cancels the copy and deletes the staging files. The move then works, and the next cycle starts a new copy. A move waits at most one controller cycle, 30 s by default.

Reading the staging file. The staging file is in QEMU's qcow2 format. The driver image cannot install qemu-img, so the driver reads the format itself. It accepts only what QEMU makes for a copy, and it refuses anything else. A staging file lies in a volume that other pods in the namespace can write, so the reader checks every table against the file size.

The staging file is sparse: it holds only the data the disk really uses (a full copy) or the blocks that changed (a change copy). In the step 1 test, a full copy of a 40 GB disk with 5 GB of data was 5.1 GB.

Speed limit. Without a limit, the copy uses all the share's bandwidth, and the VM's writes were 16 to 19 times slower. At 20 MB/s per disk, the VM kept 93% of its normal write speed. The policy has a speed setting, 20 MB/s per disk by default. A higher limit gives a shorter copy and a lower RPO, but slows the VM more.

The limit counts empty disk space too. A full copy of a 20 GB disk with 2 GB of data took about 18 minutes at 20 MB/s (tested 20 Oct). Change copies are not affected. Full copies happen only on the first copy and after a VM moves or restarts.

Why not read the disk over the network. The earlier draft read the disk from QEMU over the network, with no staging file. Step 1 showed that this cannot work. The VM pod forwards every incoming connection to the guest, so nothing outside the pod can reach QEMU. The only other way is through the node, with a privileged reader. That stays a possible later change, because the node agent is already privileged.

docs.title: Send only changed blocks
docs.text:
• Change list. QEMU keeps a change list (a dirty bitmap) for each disk, in memory. Each copy starts a new list at its moment. The list of the last copy that reached the other region stays until the next copy has reached it too. So if a copy fails, the next one still includes every block that changed since the last good copy.
  • Normal cycle: QEMU writes only the blocks in that list to the staging file.
  • First copy, or after the change list is lost: a live migration or a VM restart erases the lists. The controller sees that the list is gone and asks QEMU for a full copy. The staging file of a full copy holds only the data the disk really uses.
  • Compare pass. When a full copy reaches a far-site disk that already exists, only the blocks that differ are written, and only those go into the undo file (below). In direct NFS mode the Job compares the blocks itself, so it reads the far-site data once over the network; that costs about as much as sending it. Receiver mode will compare at the far site, from checksums, so only the blocks that differ cross the network.
  • The Job never reads the VM's live disk file. It reads only staging files, which do not change while it reads them.

docs.title: Apply the copy in the other region
docs.text:
The far-site disk must never be left half updated, and a rewind must be possible. One method serves both, and it works in direct NFS mode, where nothing of ours runs in the other region:

  1. Before it changes any block, the Job reads the far-site disk's current contents of every block it will change, and writes them to an undo file next to the disk. Then it marks the undo file complete.
  2. It writes the new blocks into the disk.
  3. It marks the undo file applied. The undo file is now a restore point: it can take the disk back to the moment before this copy.

If the Job stops during step 2, the disk is half updated, but the complete undo file is at the far site. The next Job, or failover, first rolls the disk back from that undo file to the previous good moment. This needs nothing from the source region, so it also works after the source region is lost. An undo file that is not complete is deleted; the disk was not touched yet.

In direct NFS mode each changed block crosses the network about three times: the old block is read and written to the undo file, and the new block is written. Receiver mode will do steps 1 to 3 at the far site, so each block crosses once.

Failover rolls back any applied-but-not-marked copy first. It refuses to use a disk while a Job is applying a copy.

Full copies in step 3. Step 3 sent whole disks and swapped each one in only when complete. Step 4 changes this to the method above, so the first copy after the change gives the first restore point.

docs.title: Restore points in the other region
docs.text:
The far site keeps the copies of the last 24 hours, so you can rewind if bad data reached the VM, for example ransomware or a broken update. Each policy has a keep time, 24 hours by default.

  • Each copy's undo files form one restore point. A restore point covers all disks of a VM at the same moment.
  • The disk itself always holds the latest copy. So a failover to the latest copy is as fast as today.
  • To rewind, failover makes a new disk from the latest one, then applies the undo files from newest to oldest, back to the chosen moment. The latest disk is not changed, so you can rewind again to a different moment.
  • When an undo file is older than the keep time, the next Job deletes it. Undo files are deleted oldest first, so the remaining ones always form a complete chain back from the latest copy.
  • After a compare pass, the undo file holds only the blocks that differed. So a VM move does not cost a full disk of storage.
  • The policy status lists the restore points.

docs.title: What the status shows
docs.text:
For each VM volume, the policy status shows: - the moment the last good copy shows - "file-system consistent" or "crash consistent" - whether the last cycle was a change-only cycle or a compare pass, and the bytes sent - the oldest and newest restore points in the other region

New metrics: copy type, guest pause time, and how long the VM was slowed by a copy.

docs.title: Optional backup: snapshot pool and COS
docs.text:
A new BackupPolicy resource turns backup on. It has a schedule, a snapshot pool, how long to keep local snapshots, and optional COS settings. Backup is off unless you create a policy.

A policy selects VMs by label, and covers all disks of each VM, taken at one moment. It can also select normal PVCs by label. One VM belongs to at most one backup policy. If two policies match a VM, the webhook refuses the second one.

Local snapshots in their own pool. A snapshot pool is a normal pool that holds only snapshots. It uses its own VPC file shares, so a lost or full data share does not take the snapshots with it.

  • Each scheduled snapshot uses the safe copy above: QEMU for running VMs, a file copy for everything else.
  • VM disks are kept as a chain: one full copy, then one change file for each later snapshot. This uses the same change list as replication. The 20 Oct test showed that a change file applied to its full copy boots.
  • Other volumes are kept with rsync and hard links. A file that did not change takes no extra space.
  • When a snapshot passes its keep time, the driver merges it into the next one in the chain, so the chain stays short.
  • Restore makes a new PVC from any snapshot, as restore does today.

Export to COS (optional). After each local snapshot, the driver uploads it to a COS bucket.

  • It reads from the snapshot pool, not from the VM, so the export does not slow the VM.
  • It uses Kopia, an open-source Go backup library. Kopia splits data into chunks, uploads only chunks that COS does not already have, and encrypts the data before upload. Writing this ourselves would take months. Kopia is also what Velero and Kasten use.
  • It has its own keep time, usually longer than the local one.
  • Each policy has its own area in the bucket. So the locks of one policy cannot affect another. The cost: two policies do not share identical chunks, so storage is a little higher.

Setup command for COS. You run it once, with your own IBM Cloud login. It is in the console plugin and in the CLI. It:

  • creates the COS instance, if you do not give an existing one
  • creates the bucket, with object lock turned on and no fixed keep time, so each policy decides
  • sets your Key Protect root key for the bucket
  • creates a key for the driver, with a custom role on this one bucket only. The role can read, write, and extend locks. It cannot delete a version of an object, skip a lock, or change the bucket settings. IBM's standard Writer role is not used, because it can skip Governance locks.
  • gives the driver the Reader role on the root key in Key Protect. Reader can encrypt and unlock the backup key, but cannot delete the root key.
  • creates the backup key (below), has Key Protect encrypt it, and shows the readable key to you once

The driver itself never creates or deletes a COS instance or bucket. If someone takes over the cluster, they get only the driver's key, and that key cannot remove a lock. An uninstall or a clean-up of the driver never touches the bucket.

Encryption. Backups are encrypted in three places:

  • on the way to COS, with HTTPS
  • inside COS, with COS encryption and your Key Protect root key. While object lock is on, COS stops anyone from deleting that root key, so nobody can make the backups unreadable by deleting it
  • before upload, by Kopia with the backup key, so COS only ever holds encrypted data

The backup key is protected by Key Protect. Key Protect encrypts the backup key with the same root key as the bucket. Only that encrypted copy is stored: in a Kubernetes Secret, and next to the backups in COS. The readable key is never stored. When the driver needs the key, it asks Key Protect to unlock it, and keeps it only in memory.

  • Because it is the bucket's root key, object lock also protects it from deletion.
  • If the cluster is lost, a restore in another cluster reads the encrypted copy from COS and asks Key Protect to unlock it.
  • If you remove the driver's access in Key Protect, the driver can no longer read or write backups.

Emergency copy. Key Protect runs in one region. If that region is down, Key Protect cannot unlock the key. So the setup command shows the readable key once, and you keep a copy outside IBM Cloud, for example in a password manager. A restore can use it instead of Key Protect. Without either Key Protect or this copy, nobody can read the backups, including IBM and us.

Immutable backups. Each policy sets a keep time for its COS backups, and either Compliance lock or no lock:

  • Compliance: nobody can delete or change a backup before its keep time ends. That includes you, your account admins and IBM. This is the default for a new policy, with a keep time of 30 days.
  • None: no lock.

A change to a policy affects only new backups. A backup in Compliance mode keeps its lock to the end, even if you change or delete the policy. COS bills a locked backup until its lock ends. IBM requires the account to stay in good standing while any lock is active.

What the step 1 test showed (Kopia 0.23.1, IBM COS, 20 Oct):

  • Kopia locks its data, its indexes and its repository files in COS. Restore matched the checksums. No readable text from the backup was found in any object.
  • No role could shorten a Compliance lock.
  • Governance mode does not protect against a stolen driver key. IBM's Writer role can skip Governance locks. A custom role without that permission stops the skip. But the driver also needs permission to extend locks, and with it the driver can shorten a Governance lock. So Governance is not offered.
  • Locks must be extended. A chunk that a new backup still uses keeps the lock from its first upload. Kopia extends the locks of chunks that are still in use during its maintenance run. This needs the "extend locks" permission, which is safe in Compliance mode. Kopia requires the keep time to be at least the maintenance interval plus 24 hours. The driver sets the maintenance interval to fit.
  • A delete by the driver's key only hides data. COS adds a delete marker, and the data stays. But Kopia cannot read hidden data. So the restore command, run with your own login, first removes any delete markers. The driver's key cannot remove them.
  • Restore from COS makes a new PVC in any cluster that runs the driver, including a cluster in another region. This is the last line of defence if both regions lose their pools.

Fix for today's snapshots. A snapshot of a running VM volume also uses the safe copy, not a file copy.

docs.title: Later: switch to the supported feature
docs.text: The part that takes the copy is one replaceable piece. When the clusters run the OpenShift version with the supported backup feature, we replace that piece. The transfer, the receiver and failover stay the same.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
1. Lab test (done, 20 Oct). Results:
  2. Reading the disk over the network: cannot work, see above. The plan uses the staging method.
  3. Two disks: one QEMU step copies both at the same moment. The far-site disks booted, and both showed the same last write.
  4. Speed limit: at 20 MB/s per disk, the VM kept 93% of its write speed.
  5. Sparse staging files: 5.1 GB for a 40 GB disk with 5 GB of data.
  6. A full copy plus two change copies, applied at the far site, booted with all files intact.
  7. Linux freeze fails if a file system has no SELinux label. The design now falls back to a crash-consistent copy.
  8. Windows freeze: tested in step 6 (21 Oct). The freeze goes through VSS and the copy is file-system consistent; see step 6.
  9. COS and Kopia: see "Immutable backups" below.
  10. Stop unsafe copies. The controller detects running VMs and skips their volumes with a clear error. This ships first and by itself, because today's behaviour makes copies that cannot boot.
  11. Copy at one moment. Freeze, take the view, thaw, read the full disk, and send it. Cancel the copy when the VM must move. Lab test of the parts, 20 Oct:
  12. KubeVirt's freeze tool is in the VM pod. Freeze took 0.11 s, thaw 0.03 s, and the automatic thaw worked.
  13. A live migration during a copy fails, and the VM keeps running where it was. After the copy is cancelled, the migration took 8 s.
  14. The speed limit counts empty disk space (above).
  15. The staging file is owned by the QEMU user, and only that user can delete it.
  16. End-to-end test, 20 Oct (test/e2e/test-vm-replication.sh, direct NFS mode, two pools on the driver): a CentOS VM with a 20 GB root disk and a 10 GB data disk wrote a file every 0.1 s. Both disks showed the same moment and were file-system consistent. The far-site copy booted with no XFS errors, and all 1,579 files written before the freeze matched their checksums; the last one was written at the moment of the freeze. Data sent: 1.98 GB and 118 MB. The test pool's shares had 100 IOPS at first, and the copy ran at about 3 MB/s per disk; at 3000 IOPS it ran at the speed limit. So the copy time depends on the share's IOPS as well as the speed limit.
  17. Change-only cycles, safe apply with undo files, and restore points, in direct NFS mode. Parts: change lists in the copy piece; the undo-file apply and roll-back; the controller and a keep time per policy. This took over the safe-apply part of step 5, because direct NFS mode has no far-site receiver to do it.
  18. Receiver mode for VM disks, and failover changes. The receiver does the same apply at the far site, and compares checksums for the compare pass. Failover rolls back an unfinished copy and can rewind to any restore point.
  19. Test across two regions, with a failover and a boot of a Linux VM and a Windows VM. This includes the first test of Windows freeze and thaw. Then update CROSS-REGION-DR.md, FEATURES.md and the tutorial. Done 21 Oct on two clusters in Frankfurt (no second region exists in the lab): Linux and Windows Server 2022 both passed. A new Windows VM can take about 40 minutes before its guest agent runs commands.
  20. Safe snapshots of running VMs, using the copy from step 3.
  21. Backup to a snapshot pool: the BackupPolicy resource, the chain of change files, hard-link snapshots, merging, and restore.
  22. Export to COS: the setup command, Kopia upload, encryption, keep time, lock modes per policy, and restore from COS into another cluster. Then add a backup stage to the release test run.

About 5 PRs for replication after the lab test, and 3 more for backup.

docs.title: Tests in the release test run
docs.text:
Each part of this plan adds its checks to the unattended release test run, in the same PR as the code. The checks are listed in 2026-10-19-release-test-run.md: stage 5 (snapshot of a running VM), stage 10 (VM replication) and stage 18 (backup). Each check looks at the result itself: the copy boots, the files match their checksums, and the bytes sent. It does not trust a status field.

The run needs one COS bucket for the backup stage. I will ask you to create it when backup is built.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• VM slowdown during a copy. Without a limit, a VM that writes nonstop was 16 to 19 times slower during a copy. The default limit of 20 MB/s per disk kept 93% of its speed. A slower copy makes a longer copy window, so this is a trade-off between RPO and VM speed. The policy has a setting for it.
  • Restore point space. The far site keeps the old contents of every block that changed in the last 24 hours. A VM that rewrites much of its disk each day needs up to one more disk of space at the far site.
  • VM moves wait for the copy to cancel. A move waits up to one controller cycle, 30 s by default. A full copy that is cancelled starts again from the beginning.
  • Staging space. Each copy needs free space in the VM's volume for its staging file, until the Job has sent it: the used data for a full copy, the changed blocks for a change copy.
  • Red Hat does not support it. An OpenShift Virtualization update can change the VM pod and break this method. Each release test run will include a VM replication stage, so we find a break before you do. If it breaks, VM volumes are skipped with an error. They are never copied unsafely.
  • Security. The controller runs commands in VM pods, which needs use on the kubevirt-controller SCC (above). The staging files stay in the VM's own volume; the apply Job mounts only that volume's folder and refuses links.
  • Backup cost. A snapshot pool is extra VPC file shares, paid for as normal shares. COS is paid for each GB stored, and only changed chunks are added after the first upload. A cost estimate goes into this spec once you choose the keep times.
  • New dependency. Kopia, for the COS export only.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Running VM disks are never copied with rsync. If the safe method fails, the volume is skipped and reported.
  • Step 2 (stop unsafe copies) ships first, before the new copy method exists.
  • A VM without a guest agent still replicates, as a crash-consistent copy. The status says so.
  • Stopped VMs still use rsync, with a check that the VM stayed stopped.
  • After a migration or restart, a compare pass sends only the blocks that differ, not the whole disk.
  • The far-site disk is updated through a change file, so it is never left half written.
  • Replication copies disks only. VM definitions are not replicated. After failover, you create the VMs from your own definitions, as today.
  • Change tracking stays in QEMU memory, because libvirt refuses it on our raw disks. Changing the disk format is out of scope.
  • The copy piece is built to be replaced by OpenShift's supported backup feature later.
  • Every part adds its release test checks in the same PR as its code.
  • Backup is optional and off by default. It is a separate BackupPolicy, not part of replication, so you can use either one without the other.
  • Local snapshots go to their own pool, never to the data share.
  • VM disk snapshots are a chain of change files, and old ones are merged. Other volumes use hard-link snapshots.
  • The COS export reads from the snapshot pool, never from the running VM.
  • The COS export uses Kopia (chunking, encryption, upload of new chunks only), instead of our own format.
  • A backup policy selects whole VMs by label. A VM can be in only one backup policy.
  • A setup command that you run creates the COS instance, the bucket and the driver's key. The driver never creates or deletes buckets.
  • The driver's COS key can write to one bucket only, and cannot remove locks.
  • Backups in COS are always encrypted. Key Protect protects the backup key with the bucket's root key, so the readable key is never stored.
  • The setup command shows the readable key once, as an emergency copy for when Key Protect is down. You keep it outside IBM Cloud.
  • Key Protect is required for COS export.
  • Each policy sets a keep time, and either Compliance lock or no lock. A new policy defaults to Compliance for 30 days.
  • Governance lock is not offered. Tested on 20 Oct: it cannot stop a stolen driver key from shortening the lock, while still letting the driver extend locks.
  • The driver's COS key uses a custom role: read, write and extend locks. It cannot delete versions, skip locks or change the bucket.
  • The restore command removes delete markers first, with your login.
  • When a Linux or Windows guest cannot freeze, the copy goes ahead as crash consistent, and the status shows why.
  • The copy uses a sparse staging file in the VM's own volume, at 20 MB/s per disk by default. Reading the disk over the network is not possible (tested 20 Oct).
  • Each policy has its own area in the bucket, so storage is slightly higher than one shared area.
  • Snapshots of running VMs are fixed to use the safe copy, as part of this work.
  • Backup is built after replication, because it reuses the safe copy and the change list.
  • Multi-disk VMs are copied at one moment as part of this work. Group snapshots (issue #14) stay a separate issue.
  • The far site keeps restore points for 24 hours by default, set per policy. You chose 24 hours on 20 Oct.
  • Safe apply and restore points use one method: undo files written at the far site before the disk changes. It works in direct NFS mode, which has nothing of ours at the far site. The cost there is about three network crossings per changed block; receiver mode will need one.
  • Direct NFS mode has no checksum compare pass. After a VM move, the Job reads the far-site data once to compare, which costs about as much as sending it.
  • A failed copy loses nothing: the change list of the last good copy is kept until the next copy reaches the far site.
  • Step 4 builds this for direct NFS mode first, because that is the mode that copies VMs today. Receiver mode follows in step 5.
  • Restore points are undo files: the disk always holds the latest copy, so failover to the latest copy stays fast. A rewind is slower, because it must apply undo files.
  • A rewind makes a new disk and leaves the latest copy unchanged.
  • Step 3 keeps no restore points. They start in step 5.
  • The guest freeze uses KubeVirt's own freeze tool, which thaws the guest by itself after 30 s.
  • When a VM must move, the controller cancels the copy. A move is more important than a copy.
  • The default speed limit stays at 20 MB/s per disk, even though full copies are slow, because full copies are rare.
  • The driver reads QEMU's staging file format itself, and refuses any part of the format that QEMU does not use for a copy.
  • The copy Job runs as the QEMU user, so it can delete the staging file.
  • The driver's controller account may use the kubevirt-controller security policy, as Kasten and IBM Backup and Recovery do. OpenShift requires it to run commands in VM pods. It adds no new power to start pods, because the controller's Jobs in kube-system already skip SCC checks.

docs.title: Spec: export backups to IBM Cloud Object Storage (COS)
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-21. Status: draft for review. This is step 9 of 2026-10-20-vm-safe-replication.md. It builds on 2026-10-21-backup-to-snapshot-pool.md (step 8, built and merged). Read both first. The main spec already sets the design (Kopia, Key Protect, Compliance lock). This spec turns it into things we can build and test.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: When this step is done: - A BackupPolicy can send its backups to a COS bucket, as well as keep them in the snapshot pool. - The copy in COS is encrypted before it leaves the cluster, and nobody can delete or change it before its keep time ends. That includes a person who has taken over the cluster. - If the VPC, the cluster and both regions lose their pools, you can restore a volume from COS into a new cluster that runs the driver. - Sending to COS never slows a running VM. It reads from the snapshot pool, not from the VM.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
On the policy. A new optional block spec.export:

  • bucket, endpoint and prefix (the bucket and where it is)
  • credentialsSecret (the driver's COS key, made by the setup command)
  • keepFor (how long COS backups are kept, default 30d) and lock (Compliance or None, default Compliance). Both are set on each policy, so a test policy can use a short lock and a real policy a long one. The webhook refuses a keep time below the minimum (see "The shortest lock")
  • schedule (how often to send, default after each local backup moment)

Without export, nothing changes from step 8.

Commands. Three, all in kubectl backup:

  • kubectl backup cos-setup — run once, with your own IBM Cloud login. Makes the COS instance (or uses yours), the bucket with object lock, the driver's key, and the backup key. Shows the readable backup key once.
  • kubectl backup restore --from-cos ... — makes a new PVC from a COS backup, in any cluster. Same flags as the local restore, plus the bucket.
  • kubectl backup cos-list — lists what is in the bucket for a policy: volumes and moments.

Status. Each volume in the policy status gets exportedTime (the moment of the newest copy in COS), exportedBytes and exportError. The console shows them next to the local backup.

Metrics and alerts. A gauge for the age of the oldest unexported moment, and one for the age of the newest export. An alert for "export late", using twice the schedule, as for local backups.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A local backup of a volume finishes (step 8). It has a moment.
  2. If the policy has export, the controller starts an export Job in the driver namespace for that volume. The Job mounts the snapshot pool's share read-only, at the volume's backup folder and its .moments folder.
  3. The Job unlocks the backup key (below), opens the Kopia repository in the bucket (the area of this policy only), and makes a Kopia snapshot of the two folders. It is tagged with the moment and the volume name. Kopia sends only chunks that COS does not have yet.
  4. The Job writes its result (bytes sent, moment) in its termination message. The controller puts it in the status, as it does for other Jobs.
  5. Kopia's maintenance run (a second Job, once a day) extends the locks of chunks still in use and removes snapshots past their keep time. The keep time of the lock is at least the maintenance interval plus 24 hours (Kopia's rule, tested on 20 Oct).

One export Job runs at a time for each policy, so a slow upload does not pile up. A moment that is not yet exported when the next one is made is exported as part of the next snapshot (Kopia sees both folders), so nothing is skipped; the older moment is still tagged and restorable.

What goes to COS: the whole backup folder (the latest whole copy) and the earlier moments (undo files) of every volume. A restore from COS therefore gives the same choice of moments as a local restore.

Where Kopia comes from. We add the Kopia command-line program to the driver image, at a pinned version and checked by its SHA-256. The Job runs it as a child process. We do not link Kopia into the driver as a Go library, because that would add a large number of Go dependencies to the controller, which must stay small and easy to review. Kopia is only used by the Job.

Credentials. Three secrets, all in the driver namespace:

  • the COS key of the driver (an HMAC key for the S3 interface, limited to the one bucket by the custom role)
  • the driver's IBM Cloud API key with the Reader role on the Key Protect root key
  • the backup key, encrypted by Key Protect (the readable key is never stored)

The Job, not the controller, asks Key Protect to unlock the backup key. The key stays in the Job's memory. The controller never sees it.

docs.title: Setup command
docs.text:
As in the main spec: the user runs it with their own login. It uses the IBM Cloud APIs for COS, Key Protect and IAM. In order:

  1. Check the account: Key Protect instance exists, and the account is in good standing (locks need that).
  2. Make or reuse the COS instance. Make the bucket: object lock on, no default keep time, encrypted with the user's Key Protect root key. The bucket's region is the user's choice; we show the cost note below.
