  3. Make the custom role (read, write, extend locks; no delete of versions, no skip of locks, no change of bucket settings) and a service ID with that role on the one bucket. Make an HMAC key for it.
  4. Give the service ID the Reader role on the root key.
  5. Make the backup key, have Key Protect wrap it, store the wrapped copy in a Secret and in the bucket. Show the readable key once. Ask the user to confirm they saved it.
  6. Print the spec.export block to paste into the policy.

The setup command never runs in the cluster, and the driver never creates or deletes a bucket or an instance.

docs.title: Restore from COS
docs.text:
1. The command reads the wrapped key from the bucket (or from the Secret in this cluster) and unlocks it with Key Protect, or with the emergency copy if the user passes it with --backup-key-file.
  2. With the user's own login, it removes any delete markers in the bucket area (the driver's key cannot; a delete by that key only hides data).
  3. It starts a Job that opens the repository read-only, restores the chosen snapshot into a scratch folder on a share, then the existing restore Job (step 8) copies the volume or applies the undo files, as for a local restore. This reuses the tested path.
  4. The new PVC is held back from pods until the copy ends, as for a local restore. It never writes over an existing volume.

In a new cluster the policy and the snapshot pool need not exist. The command needs only the bucket, the endpoint, the keys, and a pool to restore into.

docs.title: The shortest lock
docs.text:
Each policy sets its own lock mode and keep time, so tests use a short lock. The shortest possible lock is a little over 1 day, not 1 day. Kopia needs the keep time to be at least its maintenance interval plus 24 hours, because it extends the locks of chunks still in use at each maintenance run (tested 20 Oct). The driver sets the maintenance interval from the keep time, with 1 hour as the shortest. So:

  • the webhook refuses a keep time below 25 hours
  • release tests and lab runs use keepFor: 25h with lock: Compliance, and the hourly maintenance run. Their data is then billed for 25 hours and can be deleted after that
  • a real policy defaults to 30 days

docs.title: Not in this step
docs.text:
• No Governance lock (the main spec explains why).
  • No export of volumes that are not in a BackupPolicy.
  • No console screen for the setup or the restore from COS (the status is shown; the screens come later).
  • No other object stores. IBM COS only. The Kopia S3 interface would allow others later.
  • No restore of a VM definition. Only disks and volumes, as in step 8.

docs.title: Build order
docs.text:
Status: part 1 built and merged (tested against a local Kopia repository, not yet against MinIO or a real bucket, and the image was not built). Part 2 built (PR open): spec.export, the status fields, the webhook rules, the export and maintenance Jobs driven by the controller, Kopia retention, the two metrics and the alert examples; tested with fakes and a local Kopia repository, not on a cluster and not against a bucket. Part 4 built (PR open): kubectl backup cos-setup and package pkg/cossetup, tested with httptest fakes of the IBM Cloud APIs, not run against real IBM Cloud; it keeps its own small Key Protect wrap client until pkg/keyprotect is joined. Part 4 decisions: it does not make the service ID's API key for the Key Protect unlock (it gives the service ID Reader on the root key; the API key and its Secret belong to part 3); the bucket is recognised as made by the command by a marker object; the wrapped key sits in the bucket at _pool-csi-setup/backup-key.wrapped.json; after making an HMAC key it removes the instance-wide Writer policy that IBM Cloud adds for the key by itself (found by comparing the service ID's policies before and after the key is made; first live run, issue #138), then checks that the service ID has no policy wider than the one bucket and stops with a message if it has (a policy that was there before is never removed). Part 3 built (PR open): the Jobs unwrap the backup key with Key Protect in memory (the driver mode unwrap-backup-key, package pkg/keyprotect); spec.export has a required keyProtect block (instanceID, region, rootKeyID, apiKeySecret) and an optional emergencyKeySecret; tested with a fake Key Protect HTTP server, not against a real instance (none exists yet). Part 5 built (PR open): kubectl backup restore --from-cos, kubectl backup cos-list, spec.fromCOS on BackupRestore, delete marker clean-up; tested with fakes, httptest and a local Kopia repository, not against a real bucket. Part 6 built (PR open): the COS part of release test stage 18, in test/e2e/test-backup.sh with helpers in test/e2e/lib/backup-cos.sh; tested with stub scripts only, not run on a cluster, a bucket or Key Protect. Part 6 decisions: see the end of "Decisions I made for you". Part 6 fix after the first real run (rovslab, 2026-10-22): the check counted two cos-list lines per volume, but the pod volume was exported once, so it could never pass; it now needs one export per volume, waits at most 30 minutes, prints the cos-list output and exit status when it fails, and lets the restore checks run before the script ends with a failure. Part 5 decisions: the claim name, class and size are not in COS, so the command takes --volume pvc-..., --storage-class and --size-gb; a restore picks the oldest export made at or after the moment (it holds the earlier moments as undo files), or the newest; cos-list runs a read-only Job in the cluster (no Kopia needed on the laptop) and lists export moments, cut at about 3.5 KB; with --backup-key-file the readable key goes into a temporary Secret that the command removes when the restore ends, and Key Protect is never called; the delete marker clean-up removes markers only, by version, in the policy's area; a scratch folder that cannot be removed is logged and does not fail the restore. Part 3 decisions: the emergency key is used only when Key Protect is unreachable (no connection, a 5xx or a 429), never after a refusal, so a wrong root key or API key is not hidden; the Secrets reach the Job as read-only files, not environment variables, so the Kopia child never holds the API key; the readable key file is removed once Kopia has its password; the API key Secret has the key apikey, and cos-setup prints the command to make it but does not make the API key itself; an emergency key Secret in the cluster is optional and weaker than an emergency copy kept outside IBM Cloud. Part 2 decisions: the maintenance Job runs every maintenance interval (a day, or an hour for a 25-hour keep time) rather than a fixed once a day, so the lock extension keeps pace with a short lock; snapshots past the keep time are deleted by age in the maintenance Job, because Kopia can expire only by count; a failed export is retried after 5 minutes; the controller keeps exporting while a policy is suspended.

Each part is a PR with its tests, and updates the docs and the release test run in the same PR.

  1. Kopia in the image and the export Job. Image change (pinned, checked). A new mode of the Job runner: export, run against a local test repository (a folder), then against MinIO in CI for the S3 path. Status fields.
  2. The controller, status, metrics, alerts. spec.export, the webhook rules (lock mode, keep time at least the maintenance interval plus 24 hours), the export Jobs and the maintenance Job.
  3. Key handling. Wrapped key, Key Protect unlock in the Job, emergency key. Tested against a Key Protect instance in the lab.
  4. cos-setup. Built against the real IBM Cloud APIs with a throw-away account section; the custom role and the permissions are verified by a test that tries to do what the role must refuse.
  5. Restore from COS and cos-list. Includes the delete marker clean-up.
  6. Release test: stage 18, second part. Export the three volumes (an export holds the newest copy and the earlier moments as undo files, so two moments need only one export; cos-list prints one line per export, and a pod volume that does not change is exported once), then restore from COS into a second namespace, boot the VM, check the checksums. A second run restores into the other cluster of the lab pair.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Unit tests with fakes for the controller, the status, the webhook and the Job script.
  • A local Kopia repository test in CI (folder), and an S3 test against MinIO in CI.
  • On the lab and a real bucket: export, a second export that sends only changed chunks (check the bytes), a delete with the driver's key (check only a marker is made and the restore command repairs it), an attempt to shorten a lock with every key we hold (must fail), and a restore into another cluster.
  • A test that the logs and the status never contain a key or secret.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• COS storage. Paid for each GB stored. The first upload is the size of the data; later ones add only changed chunks and the undo files. Locked data is billed until its lock ends, so a 30 day Compliance lock on a policy means 30 days of billing even after you delete the policy. A cost table for the lab (size, keep time, price per month) goes in this spec after you choose keep times; the formula is: stored GB × price per GB per month × (keep days ÷ 30), plus the changed data per day × keep days.
  • Compliance lock cannot be undone. A wrong keep time (for example 10 years by mistake) costs money for that time and cannot be shortened, even by IBM. The setup command and the webhook ask for a clear confirmation of the keep time above 90 days.
  • Key loss. Without Key Protect and without the emergency copy, nobody can read the backups. The setup command makes the user confirm the copy.
  • New dependency. Kopia (a program in the image, used only by the export and restore Jobs). It is open source, used by other backup products, and tested in step 1.
  • Same account. COS in the same IBM Cloud account as the cluster is better than nothing, but an account takeover reaches both. The lock protects against deletes by a stolen driver key, not against a stolen account owner. A bucket in a second account is possible (the user gives the endpoint and key); we do not set it up.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• cos-setup writes the COS key file the moment the HMAC key is made, before any check, because IBM Cloud shows the secret once. The "never deletes anything" rule has one exception: the instance-wide Writer policy that IBM Cloud adds to the service ID when the HMAC key is made. The command deletes only a policy that matches (this service ID, the COS service, this instance, no resource type, no resource) and that was not there before the key was made, and says so in the printed steps. Any other wide policy still stops the command. If the HMAC key exists already, the command makes no second one and says its secret cannot be shown again; delete the key to get a new one. A key file that exists without its HMAC key stops the command before it makes a key (issue #138).

  • Export is a block on the existing BackupPolicy, not a new resource. One policy, one schedule, one place to look.

  • The export reads from the snapshot pool, mounted read-only, never from a running VM.
  • We run the Kopia program as a child of the Job. We do not link it into the driver.
  • The Job unlocks the backup key. The controller never holds it.
  • Export is off unless the policy has spec.export.
  • A new export block defaults to Compliance lock and 30 days. Lock mode and keep time are set on each policy. Tests use Compliance for 25 hours, the shortest Kopia allows (the owner asked for 1 day; 1 day is 1 hour short of Kopia's rule).
  • A keep time above 90 days needs a typed confirmation, because it cannot be undone.
  • One export Job runs at a time for each policy. A missed moment goes out with the next one.
  • Restore from COS reuses the step 8 restore Job, so there is one restore path to test.
  • COS restore into a new cluster needs no policy and no snapshot pool in that cluster.
  • Only IBM COS for now.
  • The bucket is locked to the cluster with a context-based restriction (CBR) rule: the cluster VPC and the admin addresses only. A virtual private endpoint (VPE) for COS in the cluster's VPC is recommended for real backups and not needed for lab tests. The setup command offers both, and docs tutorial 9 shows the manual steps. The admin addresses must be in the zone, or cos-setup, cos-list and restore --from-cos fail from a laptop.
  • The setup command is built last of the key parts, after the export works against MinIO and a real bucket by hand.
  • Maintenance runs every maintenance interval, not on a fixed daily timer: a day for a normal keep time, an hour for the 25-hour test lock. This keeps lock extension ahead of a short lock.
  • Snapshots past the keep time are deleted by age in the maintenance Job. Kopia can only expire by count, so the export tells Kopia to keep every snapshot and the Job does the expiry.
  • A failed export is tried again after 5 minutes, and a volume that keeps failing does not hold up the others.
  • While the export of a volume runs, the next local backup of that volume waits, so the export reads a disk that does not change. See 2026-10-27-export-reads-a-steady-disk.md.
  • The controller keeps exporting while a policy is suspended: suspend stops new local backups, not the copy of moments that already exist.
  • A failed maintenance run is written to the controller log and tried again; it is not in the status yet.
  • Release test (part 6): the COS checks run inside the existing stage 18 script, on the same policy and the same three volumes, so the VM is built once. They are on when COS_BUCKET is set (in the environment or in ~/.config/pool-csi/cos-stage.env) and reported as "not checked" otherwise. A partly filled configuration fails the stage at the start, before the 60 to 90 minutes of setup.
  • The test needs an existing bucket (made by cos-setup), the HMAC key file cos-key.json, the Key Protect API key file kp-apikey.json and the backup-key-secret.yaml that cos-setup --secret-file wrote, all in ~/.config/pool-csi. It makes its own copies of the three Secrets, named after the run, and deletes them. Values go from file to file to Secret and are never on a command line or in the log.
  • Each run uses a new prefix, stage18/<run name>-<date and time>, with lock: Compliance and keepFor: 25h. The objects stay in the bucket and are billed for 25 hours; the test says so in its output and in the report.
  • The restore in the other cluster is part of the same run, switched on by COS_DR_KUBECONFIG (with remote.sh, COS_DR_CLUSTER=rovslab-dr-eude). It needs the driver and a free zone there; it makes its own pool, namespace and Secrets and removes them. A separate second run is not needed: the prefix is new for each run, so a separate run could not find the first one's exports.
  • The restore from COS skips the delete marker clean-up (--skip-marker-cleanup): the test deletes nothing in the bucket, and the lab run has no IBM Cloud login on the build server.
  • The test restores the two VM disks and the pod volume at the oldest and the newest moments, as the local part does, into a pool made for the purpose, so the restore has room (the scratch copy needs space for a full volume).

docs.title: Needs from you
docs.text:
• A COS bucket for the release test, and a Key Protect root key in the lab account. Needed from build part 3 on. I will build parts 1 and 2 without them (local repository and MinIO). Say if you want me to make them with the setup command once it exists instead.
  • Keep times (local and COS) that a customer would choose, to fill in the cost table.

docs.title: Spec: backup to a snapshot pool
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-21. Status: draft for review. This is step 8 of 2026-10-20-vm-safe-replication.md. Read that spec first. Step 9 (export to COS) is a separate spec: 2026-10-21-backup-cos-export.md.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: When this step is done: - You create one BackupPolicy. On its schedule, the driver backs up the VMs and PVCs you selected, into a pool that holds only backups. - A lost or full data share does not take the backups with it, because the backup pool uses its own VPC file shares. - You can restore any backup moment of a volume to a new PVC, in the same cluster, with one command. - A VM with several disks is backed up at one moment, and a restored VM boots. - Backups older than the keep time go away by themselves.

docs.title: A change from the main spec
docs.text:
The main spec said: keep a VM disk as a chain, one full copy and then one change file per backup, and merge the oldest into the next one.

This spec keeps the latest backup as a whole disk, and keeps older moments as undo files. This is what replication already does at the far site (step 4). Reasons: - Restoring the latest backup, the most common case, is a plain copy. In a chain, it must apply every change file. - Dropping an old backup is deleting its undo file. In a chain, it is a merge that rewrites data. - The code exists and is tested on two clusters: ApplyCopy, Rewind, and the prune of old undo files. A chain would be new code.

So a VM backup is a replication to a pool in the same cluster, with a longer keep time. The rest of this spec is what is new on top of that.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
• A ReplicationPolicy can send a pool's volumes to a destination pool by NFS (direct mode). It copies running VMs safely, at one moment for all disks of a VM, and sends only changed blocks after the first copy.
  • The destination keeps restore points (undo files) for restorePointKeepHours, and kubectl failover execute --rewind-to makes a disk as it was at a moment.
  • Replication selects volumes with a label selector, and skips nothing silently.
  • Snapshots (steps 1 to 7) live on the same share as the volume.

docs.title: The BackupPolicy resource
docs.text:
Cluster-scoped. Fields: - snapshotPool: the pool that holds the backups. It must be a pool that no workload claim uses. The webhook refuses a policy that names a pool with claims, and refuses a data pool that also is a backup pool. - schedule: an interval such as 6h, like replication. - selector: a label selector for PVCs. A VM is selected through its disks: if any disk matches, the whole VM is backed up. Namespaces can be limited with namespaces. - keepFor: how long backups are kept, such as 30d. The default is 7 days. - vmCopySpeedLimitMBps: the same limit as for replication. Default 20. - suspend: stops new backups. Existing backups stay.

The status lists each backed-up volume with its last backup moment, its oldest backup moment, the bytes written, the consistency, and the last error.

One volume belongs to at most one backup policy. The webhook refuses a second policy that selects the same labels in an overlapping namespace. (A volume can be both backed up and replicated; these are different policies.)

docs.title: How a backup runs
docs.text:
The controller makes and owns a ReplicationPolicy for each BackupPolicy. It points at the snapshot pool, uses the same schedule and selector, and sets restorePointKeepHours from keepFor. Replication does the copy: QEMU for running VM disks, at one moment for all disks of a VM, and changed blocks only after the first copy. The BackupPolicy status is read from the owned policy.

The owned policy is marked as owned. The webhook refuses edits by hand, and deleting the BackupPolicy deletes it. Deleting the policy does not delete the backups; a separate command does that (below).

docs.title: Volumes that are not VM disks
docs.text: Replication keeps only the latest files of such a volume. Backups of them need old moments too. For these volumes the backup uses hard links: - Each backup moment is a folder in the snapshot pool. A backup copies from the previous moment's folder with rsync --link-dest. A file that did not change takes no extra space. - A backup folder is consistent only as much as the files are: it is a file copy of a live volume, as snapshots of pods are today. The policy status says FileCopy, not FileSystemConsistent. For a database, use a hook (the hooks of replication work on backup policies too). - Folders older than keepFor are removed, oldest first.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
A new command, kubectl backup: - kubectl backup list --policy NAME shows each volume and its backup moments. - kubectl backup restore --policy NAME --pvc NS/NAME --moment TIME --to-pvc NAME [--namespace NS] makes a new PVC in the cluster's data pool with the contents at that moment. --moment takes the nearest earlier backup. Without it, the latest backup is used. - For a VM, --vm NS/NAME restores all disks of the VM at one moment, to new PVCs with a suffix. The command prints the VM's disk names. It does not create the VM.

A restore copies the backup (after a rewind if the moment is not the latest) into a new volume with a Job, as restore from a snapshot does today. The new PVC stays Pending until the copy has finished.

docs.title: Keep time and clean-up
docs.text:
• Undo files and hard-link folders older than keepFor are removed on each cycle.
  • If the snapshot pool is more than 85% full, the policy stops new backups and reports the error. It does not delete backups early. (A full pool is an alert; losing backups to make room would hide the problem.)
  • kubectl backup delete --policy NAME --pvc NS/NAME removes the backups of a volume, after you confirm. It is never run by the controller.

docs.title: Status and metrics
docs.text: New metrics: backups made, bytes written, last backup age per policy, and oldest backup age per policy. Alert rules go into MONITORING.md: no backup within twice the schedule, and the pool above 85%.

docs.title: What this step does not do
docs.text:
• No COS export, no encryption, no locks. That is step 9.
  • No restore into another cluster. That is step 9.
  • No console screens. They come after the command works.
  • No restore of a whole VM definition. You restore disks and attach them to a VM.

docs.title: Changes to code and docs
docs.text:
• New: BackupPolicy CRD and webhook, a controller that owns ReplicationPolicy objects, the hard-link backup Job, the kubectl backup plugin (like kubectl failover), the 85% check.
  • api/v1alpha1: run make generate. Update CRD-SPEC.md.
  • Docs: FEATURES.md, BACKUP-RECOVERY.md, MONITORING.md, HELM-VALUES.md (RBAC), CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: More than one share in the snapshot pool (issue #71)
docs.text:
A snapshot pool may have several shares. Each volume is backed up to one share, chosen when the volume is first backed up and kept for good, because its backups and its change lists are on that share.

  • Where a new volume goes: the ready share below 85% that holds the fewest volumes (counted over all backup policies on the pool). Ties go to the first share in the pool's list. If no share qualifies, the volume waits and its error says so.
  • Where it is written down: shareID in the volume's entry in the policy status. A restore and kubectl backup delete read it. An entry without one was made when the pool had one share; it belongs to the first share.
  • How it is copied: one replication policy for each source pool and share. The SubVolumes carry a storage.ibmcloud.io/backup-share label that the replication policy selects on. The policy for the first share keeps its old name, so an upgrade keeps the change lists of running VM copies.
  • The 85% rule: read for each share. Only the copies to a full share are paused. New volumes avoid it.
  • Not done: backups are never moved between shares, and a share that holds backups must not be removed from the pool.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Unit tests with fakes: the owned policy is made from the backup policy and follows its changes; the webhook refuses overlap and a pool with claims; hard-link folders and their clean-up; the 85% rule; restore picks the nearest earlier moment.
  • Release test stage 18: back up a running VM with two disks and a pod volume. Make a second backup. Restore the VM disks at the first moment and the pod volume at the second. The restored VM boots, every logged file matches its checksum, and the restored pod volume matches its checksums. Delete the data share's volume and restore it from the backup.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• Space. The snapshot pool needs about one copy of the selected data, plus the changes in keepFor. A VM that rewrites half its disk each day for 30 days needs up to 15 extra disks of undo files. The first policy shows the numbers in its status so you can size the pool.
  • Extra VPC shares. The snapshot pool is normal VPC file shares, paid for as normal shares.
  • Same cluster. These backups are lost if the VPC itself is lost. Step 9 (COS) and replication cover that.
  • Replication and backup of one VM share the VM. Copies take turns, so each waits for the other. A VM under both policies is copied about twice per cycle.
  • File copies are not application-consistent. Only VM disks get the freeze. Use hooks for databases.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Backups keep the latest copy whole and older moments as undo files, the same as replication. This replaces the "chain of change files" in the main spec.
  • A BackupPolicy is a thin layer: it makes and owns a ReplicationPolicy to the snapshot pool.
  • Default keep time is 7 days. Default speed limit is 20 MB/s.
  • A VM is backed up whole if any of its disks matches the selector.
  • One volume belongs to one backup policy.
  • Non-VM volumes use rsync --link-dest folders and are reported as file copies.
  • A snapshot pool above 85% stops new backups. It never deletes backups to make room.
  • Deleting a policy keeps the backups. Removing them is a separate, confirmed command.
  • Restore is a command first (kubectl backup). The console comes later.
  • Restore makes new PVCs. It never writes over an existing volume.
  • A snapshot pool can have more than one share. A volume stays on the share it was first backed up to, so adding a share never moves backups (issue #71).
  • A new volume goes to the ready share with room that holds the fewest volumes. If none has room, it waits.
  • The 85% limit is for each share, not for the pool.

docs.title: Spec for #46 item 4: receiver mode setup in the console
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-21. Status: draft for review.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: An operator can set up replication to a receiver (driver-to-driver mode) from the console, with no YAML and no kubectl. "Done" means: the form makes the token Secret and the CA Secret, tests that the receiver answers and accepts the token, and only then creates the ReplicationPolicy. A wrong address, a wrong token or a wrong certificate shows a plain message before the first copy is due, not as a failed cycle an hour later.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
• The create form has the receiver address, the name of the token Secret and the name of the CA Secret as plain text fields. The operator must make both Secrets first, in the kube-system namespace of the source cluster, with the keys token and ca.crt. Nothing checks them.
  • The receiver has one open health call (GET /api/v1/health). It checks that the receiver's NFS path is reachable. It does not check the token or the certificate, because it needs neither.
  • The destination base path is a field with the default /pvcs.
  • A mistake shows up late: the first sync-client Job fails, the policy shows an error, and the operator reads Job logs.

docs.title: 1. The check cannot run in the browser
docs.text: The receiver is on another cluster and often has a self-signed certificate. A browser call to it fails on certificate trust and on cross-origin rules, and it would send the token from the operator's laptop. So the check runs inside the source cluster, the same place the real copies run.

docs.title: 2. One new receiver call and one new check command (driver change)
docs.text:
• The receiver gets GET /api/v1/auth-check. It needs the bearer token and returns 200 with the base path and the receiver's version. It changes nothing. A wrong token gets 401.
  • The sync-client binary (already in the driver image) gets a check command with the same flags as a copy (--endpoint, --token-file, --ca-cert-file). It calls the health call, then the auth-check call, and prints one result line: ok, or a short reason (cannot connect, certificate not trusted, token refused, receiver storage not reachable). The exit code is 0 only for ok.

docs.title: 3. The console flow
docs.text:
The "Receiver" part of the form becomes a guided step:

  1. Address. HTTPS URL. The form refuses http:// with a plain reason.
  2. Token. A password field. The operator pastes the token (it is in the receiver's Secret on the destination cluster; the form says where to find it and gives the one command).
  3. Certificate. A text box for the CA certificate (PEM), with the note "leave empty when the receiver's certificate comes from a public authority". The form checks that the text starts with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----.
  4. Base path. Default /pvcs. Unchanged.
  5. Check connection. The console creates the two Secrets (named <policy name>-receiver-token and <policy name>-receiver-ca, labelled as made by the console) and one Job in kube-system that runs sync-client check from the driver image. The form shows the result line. On success the Create button turns on. On failure the form shows the reason, and the operator fixes the field and checks again.
  6. Create. Makes the ReplicationPolicy with the two Secret names filled in. The Job is deleted when the check ends (a short time-to-live is set on it, in case the page is closed).

If the operator already has Secrets, the form still accepts their names (the form today). Then the check runs against those Secrets, and the console makes no new ones.

docs.title: 4. What the console never does
docs.text:
• It never reads a Secret back. It can only create one. The token is sent once, from the browser to the source cluster's API server, and is not kept anywhere else (not in browser storage, not in a log).
  • It never changes the destination cluster. Setting up the receiver itself (Helm values, Route, certificate) stays a documented task. A later spec can add a "destination checklist" page.
  • It never deletes a Secret it did not make. A Secret it made is deleted with the policy only if the operator ticks a box on the delete dialog.

docs.title: 5. Access
docs.text: Making a Secret and a Job in kube-system needs rights the operator may not have. The form asks the cluster if the operator may (an access review). If not, it says which objects are needed and shows the YAML to give to an administrator. It does not fail half way.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
1. Driver: the receiver's auth-check call and the sync-client check command, with tests (Go, table tests, a TLS test with a self-signed certificate, as the receiver tests have today). One PR.
  2. Console: the guided step, the check Job and the access review, with tests. One PR.
  3. Release test: a check against a real receiver. This needs two clusters, so it belongs to the replication stage (10).

About 2 PRs plus the release stage. Docs: CROSS-REGION-DR.md (the setup steps get a console route), CRD-SPEC.md (no change to the CRD), FEATURES.md, CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• Low risk to data: nothing here copies data. The new receiver call changes nothing and needs the token.
  • One driver change (new call, new command). It must not weaken the receiver: the new call uses the same token check as the upload calls.
  • Making Secrets from the console puts a token through the browser. It goes to the cluster's API server over TLS, as any other Secret made in the console does.
  • The check Job adds a pod in kube-system for a few seconds.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The check runs inside the source cluster, never in the browser.
  • The check proves three things in order: the receiver answers, the certificate is trusted, the token is accepted. The health call alone proves only the first.
  • A new, read-only receiver call is added for the token check, instead of trying a real upload.
  • The console makes the Secrets (create only). It never reads one back.
  • Create stays off until the check passes. An operator who wants to skip the check uses YAML.
  • The destination cluster is not changed from the console. Its setup stays in the documents.
  • The Secrets the console makes are named from the policy name and are deleted with the policy only if the operator agrees.

docs.title: Spec: instant VM snapshots (overlay files)
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-21. Status: approved ("spec agreed continue"); updated with the lab check results the same day. It replaces the VM path of 2026-10-21-vm-safe-snapshots.md (step 7) for clusters that allow it. How the method works, with the lab evidence, is in VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md. Read that first.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
When this is done: - A snapshot of a running VM's disk takes a few seconds, whatever the disk size. No disk data is copied. - An OpenShift VM snapshot (VirtualMachineSnapshot) of a VM with several disks gives disks from one moment: the moment OpenShift froze the guest. The snapshot reports that moment truthfully. - Deleting a snapshot merges its file away while the VM runs. The merge copies only the data that changed. - A VM with snapshots restarts and live-migrates without losing data. - If anything that this method needs is missing, the VM refuses to start rather than start on the wrong data. - Restoring a snapshot to a new disk is one copy pass. - VMs are made the normal way: from the standard OpenShift catalog, with the pool's StorageClass. Nothing is added to the VM. The driver adds its hook to each running instance by itself.

Gap against the goal (VMware-like): in VMware, "revert to snapshot" is instant. Here, an OpenShift restore always makes new PVCs, so a restore is a copy of the disk. A 500 GB disk with 50 GB used takes minutes. Making restore instant is part 2 at the end; it is not in this build.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
• A snapshot of a running VM disk is a full QEMU copy at 20 MB/s by default, then a second full copy by a Job. A 500 GB disk takes about 7 hours.
  • The copy starts after CreateSnapshot has returned, so the reported moment is wrong. On the lab cluster, OpenShift froze the guest for 1 second, then our driver froze it again 3 seconds later, for one disk only (21 Oct, VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md). Disks of one VM come from different moments. This is the root cause of issue #14.
  • The driver can already run commands in a VM's virt-launcher pod (pkg/vmcopy, using pods/exec).

docs.title: When the instant method is used
docs.text:
CreateSnapshot uses the instant method when all of these are true: 1. The volume is the disk of a KubeVirt VM (a virt-launcher pod mounts the claim, or the VM is stopped and its spec names the claim). 2. The KubeVirt Sidecar feature gate is on. The driver reads it from the KubeVirt resource on each call. 3. The VM is running or stopped. A running VM does not need the hook for its first snapshot. The hook is only needed when a VM with a chain starts. 4. The disk is not a hot-plugged disk. 5. The disk's chain has fewer than 16 snapshot files.

Otherwise, it uses the existing copy method, and the Snapshot status says why (status.method: copy, status.methodReason).

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
• The cluster admin turns on the KubeVirt Sidecar feature gate. On OpenShift this is a jsonpatch annotation on the HyperConverged resource. It marks the cluster configuration as TaintedConfiguration, and Red Hat does not support it. INSTALL.md gets the steps and the support warning.
  • Helm value vmSnapshots.method: auto (instant when possible, the default) or copy (never instant).

docs.title: The hook
docs.text:
• A new mutating webhook on VirtualMachineInstance create adds the hooks.kubevirt.io/hookSidecars annotation, only when both are true:
  • at least one of the VM's disks is a pool claim with a chain (a snapshot exists), and
  • the Sidecar feature gate is on. With the gate off, KubeVirt refuses any VMI with the hook annotation ("sidecar feature gate is not enabled"), so adding it would stop the VM from starting.
  • A VM without snapshots is never changed.
  • The hook uses KubeVirt's own sidecar-shim image, with a script from a ConfigMap. This is the setup tested in the lab. The controller keeps the ConfigMap ibm-vpc-file-pool-vm-hook in every namespace that has a pool claim.
  • The webhook also writes the current top file of each disk into a VMI annotation, storage.ibmcloud.io/disk-top-<volume>, read from the SubVolume status. The hook script opens that file as qcow2 instead of disk.img. With no annotation, the disk is opened as plain disk.img, as today.
  • After every snapshot and merge, the controller updates that annotation on the running VMI. A live migration does not need it: the target takes the chain from the running VM (lab check 2). The annotation is for the next start.
  • The webhook is set to failurePolicy: Ignore. Missing the hook is made safe by the read-only rule below, not by blocking all VMs.

docs.title: The read-only rule (safety)
docs.text:
• Once a file is frozen as a snapshot, the driver makes it read-only (chmod 0444). QEMU only reads frozen files, so this does not affect a VM that runs with its chain.
  • If a VM with a chain starts without the hook, QEMU tries to open disk.img for writing, fails, and the VM does not start. It never writes to a frozen file. A write to a frozen file would damage every snapshot built on it.
  • The driver raises an event and an alert metric when a VM with a chain is found running or starting without the hook.

docs.title: Taking a snapshot
docs.text:
For a running VM, inside CreateSnapshot: 1. If OpenShift has frozen the guest (VMI status.fsFreezeStatus is frozen), do not freeze again. Otherwise ask for a freeze (--quiesce). If the guest agent cannot freeze, take the snapshot anyway and mark it crash-consistent. 2. Run virsh snapshot-create-as <domain> --disk-only --atomic --no-metadata in the compute container, for this disk only. The new file is snap-<n>.qcow2 in the disk's folder. 3. Read the real chain back from QEMU (virsh domblklist, qemu-img info --backing-chain). Save it in the SubVolume status (status.diskChain). 4. Make the frozen file read-only. Update the VMI annotation. 5. Copy replication's change list to the new top file, so incremental replication keeps working. 6. Return ReadyToUse: true with the creation time from step 2.

For a stopped VM: a Job runs qemu-img create -f qcow2 -b <top> -F <format> snap-<n>.qcow2, then steps 3 to 6. The next start uses the new file through the hook.

A snapshot request that is not from OpenShift (a plain VolumeSnapshot) for one disk of a multi-disk VM covers only that disk. To cover all disks at one moment, use an OpenShift VM snapshot. It freezes the guest first, and each disk's snapshot lands inside that freeze. On the lab cluster, the freeze lasted 1 second and each instant snapshot took about 2 seconds, so the freeze timeout matters. The default KubeVirt timeout is longer than this, but this needs a lab check (see below).

docs.title: Deleting a snapshot (merge)
docs.text: Rule: the snapshot's frozen file F has one child C (the next file up the chain). Merge C into F. Then F takes C's place, and the snapshot that owned C (or the live disk) now owns F. - Running VM, C is the live top: virsh blockcommit --active --pivot. - Running VM, C is in the middle: virsh blockcommit --top C --base F. - Stopped VM: a Job runs qemu-img commit. - F is read-only, and a merge into a read-only file fails. So the driver makes F writable just before the merge. If the merge fails, it makes F read-only again. If C was the live top, F is now the live top and stays writable. - Then delete C's file, update the chain in the SubVolume status and the VMI annotation. - A merge and a live migration cannot run at the same time. The driver waits and retries for up to 30 minutes, then returns an error that the snapshotter retries.

docs.title: Restore to a new disk
docs.text:
CreateVolume from a snapshot runs qemu-img convert -O raw from the snapshot's frozen file (which reads its own backing files) into the new folder's disk.img. This is one pass and keeps the disk sparse. It uses the existing share-data Job runner and the async restore flow.

A restore and a merge on the same disk never run at the same time. A per-volume lock enforces this.

docs.title: Deleting a disk that has snapshots
docs.text: When a claim is deleted and its disk still has snapshots, the driver keeps the folder as retained, until the last snapshot is deleted. Then it removes the folder. This matches the CSI rule that a snapshot outlives its source.

docs.title: Space
docs.text:
• An overlay file starts small and grows with the changes written after the snapshot. In the worst case it grows to the disk size.
  • Each snapshot is charged 10 % of the disk size against pool capacity. Real use is measured by the node agent and shown in the Snapshot status and a metric.
  • The existing alert on share usage covers a share that fills. A full share pauses the VM's writes; it does not lose data.

docs.title: When the Sidecar gate is turned off
docs.text:
• New snapshots fall back to the copy method.
  • VMs with chains will not start (read-only rule). The driver raises an alert at once.
  • A new kubectl pool-snapshots flatten <vm> command merges all of a VM's snapshots back into disk.img. It works on a running VM, or by Job on a stopped VM. After that, the VM starts without the hook. Its snapshots are gone; the command says so and asks for confirmation.

docs.title: Other features that touch VM disks
docs.text:
• Replication and backup (pkg/vmcopy): they copy the live disk through QEMU, which reads through the chain. They must keep working. Their change list moves to the new top file at each snapshot (step 5 above).
  • Restore of a backup into a disk (restore-vm-disk, PR #68): refuses a disk that has a chain. The user deletes or flattens snapshots first.
  • Clone of a VM disk: a clone flattens the chain (qemu-img convert), the same as a restore.
  • Golden images: not affected; they are plain raw files.
  • Group snapshots: unchanged by this spec. An OpenShift VM snapshot gives one moment for all disks without them.

docs.title: Code and docs that change
docs.text:
• pkg/vmsnap (new): take, merge and flatten, using the Execer from pkg/vmcopy.
  • pkg/pool/manager.go: choose the method; call pkg/vmsnap; keep retained folders.
  • pkg/webhook: new mutating webhook for VMIs.
  • api/v1alpha1: SubVolumeStatus.DiskChain; SnapshotStatus.Method, MethodReason, ChainFile; then make generate and CRD-SPEC.md.
  • Helm chart: the webhook, the ConfigMap, vmSnapshots.method, RBAC to patch VMIs and read the KubeVirt resource; HELM-VALUES.md.
  • cmd/ : the flatten command.
  • Docs: VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md (from design to built), FEATURES.md, KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md, CONSISTENCY-MODEL.md, INSTALL.md, TROUBLESHOOTING.md, MONITORING.md, CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Lab checks (done, rovslab, 21 Oct)
docs.text:
1. KubeVirt keeps the read-only bits. A VM with a chain started with the hook, and disk.img stayed 0444. Without the hook, the VM did not start: QEMU said "Could not open .../disk.img: Permission denied". The read-only rule works, so the webhook keeps failurePolicy: Ignore.
  2. A live migration straight after a snapshot keeps the chain, even for a VM started with no hook at all. The target takes the chain from the running VM.
  3. With the gate off, KubeVirt refuses a VMI that has the hook annotation. So the webhook adds the hook only when the gate is on and the VM has a chain (see "The hook").
  4. Time limits: a VirtualMachineSnapshot fails after 5 minutes by default, and the chart runs csi-snapshotter with --timeout=300s. OpenShift held the freeze for 1 second with a fast CreateSnapshot. An instant snapshot takes 2 to 5 seconds per disk.
  5. The IBM add-on did not undo the jsonpatch annotation, nor the driver's own HyperConverged change from 20 Oct. Only KubeVirt's operator wrote to the resource since then.

New finding: a merge into a read-only file fails. The merge rule above handles it.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Unit tests, written first, with a fake Execer: method choice, the chain record, the merge rule for each position in the chain, the read-only rule, the per-volume lock, retained folders, and the fallback when the gate is off.
  • E2E on rovslab, Linux and Windows:
  • Make the VM from the standard catalog with the pool StorageClass, in the console. Take a snapshot from the console's Snapshots tab. It must be instant.
  • A 2-disk VM with a counter writer on both disks. Take an OpenShift VM snapshot. Restore it. The counters must match.
  • Snapshot time for a 100 GB disk must be under 10 seconds.
  • Restart, live migration and live migration right after a snapshot.
  • Delete the oldest, a middle and the newest snapshot; restart; check marker files.
  • Remove the hook from a VM with a chain: the VM must not start.
  • Turn the gate off: snapshots fall back to copy; flatten works.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• Support: the Sidecar gate is not supported by Red Hat, and it changes a resource that IBM's add-on manages. Every customer cluster needs it. This is the main risk, and it is a product decision, not a technical one.
  • Data safety: a write to a frozen file damages every later snapshot. The read-only rule is the guard, and lab check 1 must pass.
  • Build effort: about two to three weeks for code, tests and docs, plus lab time. It reuses the exec, Job and restore code that exists.

docs.title: Part 2 (not in this build): instant restore
docs.text: A restored disk could be a new overlay file in the new folder, on top of the snapshot's frozen file in the old folder. That makes a restore instant, like VMware's revert, but it ties the new disk to the old folder. It needs its own spec.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The instant method is the default wherever the cluster allows it. The copy method stays for clusters without the Sidecar gate.
  • The hook uses KubeVirt's own shim image and a ConfigMap, as tested. No new image to pull into user namespaces.
  • The webhook adds the hook only to VMs that have snapshots, and only while the gate is on. It does not block VM starts if it is down. Safety comes from the read-only rule.
  • Chain state lives in the SubVolume status. After each change the driver reads the real chain from QEMU, and the real chain wins.
  • At most 16 snapshot files per disk. More are refused with a clear message, because long chains slow reads.
  • A plain VolumeSnapshot covers one disk. All disks at one moment comes from an OpenShift VM snapshot. No new group snapshot work.
  • Deleting a snapshot is a merge into its own file, so other snapshots never move.
  • A restore is a full, sparse copy. Instant restore is part 2.
  • A claim with snapshots keeps its folder until the last snapshot goes.
  • Each snapshot is charged 10 % of the disk size; real use is measured and shown.
  • Turning the gate off never deletes data. VMs with chains refuse to start until you run flatten.
  • The wrong-moment bug in the copy method and the other snapshot bugs found on 21 Oct are fixed in separate issues, not in this build. The exception is the restore size check (#98), which the restore path needed.
  • Changed while building: replication makes a full copy after each snapshot instead of moving its change list to the new file. Moving it safely would need the change list and the snapshot in one QEMU step, which libvirt does not offer; a full copy is always correct.
  • Changed while building: a clone of a disk with snapshots is refused instead of flattened. Restoring a snapshot does the same job.
  • Changed while building: new files name their backing file by file name only, and the stopped-VM and restore Jobs run in KubeVirt's virt-launcher image (it has qemu-img), mount only the folders they need, and check the chain before they open it.
  • Changed after review: deleting a snapshot of a running VM no longer waits for the merge. The driver starts it, checks on it at each retry, and finishes it when QEMU is ready. While a merge or a Job changes a disk, every other snapshot or delete of that disk waits.
  • Changed after review: a Job changes a stopped VM's disk only when there is no VM pod and no VM instance for it, so a VM that is just starting is never touched.
  • Changed after review: if a snapshot command reports an error but the chain shows the snapshot was made, the snapshot counts as made (crash consistent). The new file is never deleted then.
  • Changed after review: a restore whose claim was deleted before it finished no longer blocks snapshot deletes.
  • The release test has a new stage 19 for instant snapshots. It runs when the gate is on; stage 06 (the QEMU copy) runs when it is off. The console tab, Windows, removing the hook and the gate-off fallback stay manual checks.

docs.title: Spec: snapshots of a running VM with several disks show one moment
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-21. Status: draft for review. Issue #14. This extends 2026-10-21-vm-safe-snapshots.md, which left several disks out.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: When this is done: - A KubeVirt snapshot of a running VM with two or more pool disks gives disks that fit each other. Every file that one disk names is on the other disk. A VM restored from the snapshot boots with all its disks from one moment. - Each disk's Snapshot shows the same copy moment. - Snapshots of VMs with one disk, and of everything else, work as they do now.

docs.title: What the lab showed (21 Oct 2026, rovslab-dr-eude)
docs.text:
A running VM with a system disk and a data disk. A writer puts file n on the data disk, then logs it on the system disk. - KubeVirt made one VolumeSnapshot per disk and called the VM snapshot done after 11 s. It does not wait for our copies, and it never calls the group snapshot API. - Our driver copied the disks one after the other: the data disk at 13:16:25 and the system disk at 13:17:45, 80 s apart. startVMSnapshotCopy makes snapshots of one VM take turns. - In the restored VM, 725 of 1,154 logged files were missing on the data disk. Each disk was sound alone.

Making the group snapshot API work would not help: KubeVirt does not use it.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
The driver copies all pool disks of the VM at one moment, when the first disk's snapshot request arrives. Later requests for the same VM use that copy.

  1. Find the disks. When a CreateSnapshot for a running VM disk starts its copy, the controller lists every pool disk the VM pod mounts (replication already does this). It starts one QEMU copy for all of them (vmcopy.Copier.Start already takes a list of volumes and gives one moment).
  2. The first Snapshot owns the copy. Its status.vmCopy lists every disk with its staging file. It watches the QEMU copy as it does today.
  3. Other Snapshots join. When a request for another disk of the same VM arrives while a copy set exists for that VM, the new Snapshot records the set (same copy id and moment, its own staging file) and does not start a QEMU copy. When the QEMU copy is done, each Snapshot starts its own apply Job and becomes ready.
  4. A set that nobody claims is dropped. KubeVirt makes all VolumeSnapshot objects within seconds. A staging file that no Snapshot claims within 10 minutes of the QEMU copy is deleted. A request that arrives after that starts a new set.
  5. One disk, or no sibling. A VM with one pool disk behaves as today. A lone VolumeSnapshot of one disk of a multi-disk VM also copies every disk, and drops the others after the wait.
  6. Failure. A migration cancels the whole set and every joined Snapshot tries again, up to 3 times as now. A Snapshot that is deleted before its apply Job leaves the set; the set ends when none is left.
  7. The apply Jobs write each disk's disk.img into its own snapshot folder, as today. Restore is unchanged.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
• Time and space for a lone snapshot. A snapshot of one disk of a VM with a 500 GB data disk still copies the data disk to a staging file, and drops it after 10 minutes. The staging files sit in each disk's folder on its share, so the share needs room for them. This is the price of one moment for all disks.
  • More code in the part that moves the copy forward. The controller must keep one copy set per VM across several Snapshot resources. The tests below cover the cases where this breaks.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Unit tests with the fake copier: two Snapshots of one VM share one copy and one moment; a third request after 10 minutes starts a new set; a migration cancels the set and both Snapshots retry; delete of one Snapshot while the other finishes; a controller restart in the middle; a one-disk VM is unchanged.
  • Lab test: test/e2e/test-vm-snapshot-2disk.sh (PR #86) is the check. It must report MISSING=0 and copy moments within 1 s. Stage 06 of the release test runs it.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• All pool disks of the VM are copied at one moment, even when only one disk was asked for. A guess at which disks belong together would be less safe than the extra copy.
  • The wait for sibling requests is 10 minutes. KubeVirt needs seconds. A longer wait only costs staging space.
  • A disk of the VM that is not on a pool is not copied. A VM that mixes pool disks and other storage does not get one moment across both. (The first draft said the Snapshot would say so in its status. It does not: the driver cannot know that a disk on other storage matters.)
  • Restore and the group snapshot API do not change. KubeVirt does not use the group API, so the API stays as a separate item.
  • The 2-disk test stays in stage 06 and fails until this is built. A failing test is the honest state.

docs.title: Spec: safe snapshots of running VMs
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-21. Status: draft for review. This is step 7 of 2026-10-20-vm-safe-replication.md. Read that spec first.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: When this step is done: - A snapshot of a PVC that a running VM uses shows one moment, and the guest file system is consistent. A VM restored from it boots. - The snapshot does not stop the VM for more than a fraction of a second. - Snapshots of everything else (stopped VMs, pods, databases) work as they do today. - You see in the Snapshot's status whether it is file-system consistent or crash consistent.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
• CreateSnapshot makes a Snapshot resource and starts a Job that copies the volume's folder to /pvcs/.snapshots/snap-<name> on the same share. For a running VM this is an unsafe copy: the Job reads the disk file while the VM writes to it, so the snapshot mixes moments. This is the same defect that step 2 removed from replication.
  • Replication already has the safe copy (pkg/vmcopy): freeze the guest, start a QEMU copy of the disk, thaw, wait, then an apply-vm-disk Job turns the staged file into a raw disk.img. Lab results are in the main spec. Linux and Windows both passed on 21 Oct.
  • Restore (RestoreSnapshot) copies the snapshot folder into a new volume. It does not care how the folder was made.

docs.title: Which snapshots take the new path
docs.text: CreateSnapshot looks for a KubeVirt pod (virt-launcher or hotplug-disk) that runs or starts and mounts the source claim. This is the same check replication uses, and it moves to a shared place so both call it. - No such pod: the file copy, as today. - A pod exists: the VM path below.

docs.title: The VM path
docs.text:
1. The Snapshot gets status.vmCopy, a small record of the copy: the VM pod, the staging file, the copy id and the phase. It has the same shape as replication's vmCopy state.
  2. The controller freezes the guest, tells QEMU to copy this one disk, and thaws. The copy goes to a staging file in the volume's own folder.
  3. When QEMU has finished, the controller starts an apply-vm-disk Job. It writes a raw disk.img into the snapshot folder on the same share. It has no undo file and no change list, because a snapshot is always a full copy. The Job deletes the staging file.
  4. The Snapshot becomes ready. Its status shows the copy moment and consistency: FileSystemConsistent, or CrashConsistent if the guest could not freeze.

A background loop in the controller moves the copy forward every 10 seconds. Snapshots do not depend on the snapshotter calling CreateSnapshot again, because a copy takes minutes.

docs.title: Failure cases
docs.text:
• Live migration. A migration cancels the copy, as in replication. The controller removes the staging file and tries again, up to 3 times, one minute apart. After that the Snapshot fails with a message that names the migration.
  • The VM stops during the copy. If the QEMU copy fails because of this, the controller starts again with the file copy, because the disk is now at rest.
  • A VM starts during a file copy. When a file copy ends, the controller checks again for a VM pod. If one is there, it deletes the snapshot folder and starts again on the VM path.
  • Delete during a copy. The controller cancels the QEMU copy, removes the staging file and the snapshot folder, and then removes the Snapshot.
  • A copy that runs too long. QEMU does not report how far a copy is, so progress cannot be measured. A copy that runs longer than 2 hours plus twice the time the disk needs at the speed limit is cancelled and counts as one try. (Changed during the build: the first draft said "no progress for 2 hours".)
  • Controller restart. The record in status.vmCopy lets the new leader carry on. If the VM pod is gone, the try is cancelled.

docs.title: Speed limit
docs.text: A VolumeSnapshotClass parameter vmCopySpeedLimitMBps limits how much the copy slows the VM. The default is 20, the same as for replication. A 20 GB disk takes about 20 minutes at this limit (lab, 20 Oct), because empty space counts. A higher limit is faster and slows the VM more.

docs.title: What this step does not do
docs.text:
• It does not make several disks match. A snapshot is one PVC. (Matching several disks was added later: see 2026-10-21-multi-disk-vm-snapshots.md.)
  • No chain of change files and no merging. Every snapshot is a full copy. The chain belongs to the backup step (step 8).
  • No change to restore, or to group snapshots.

docs.title: Changes to code and docs
docs.text:
• api/v1alpha1: SnapshotStatus gets vmCopy, consistency and consistencyReason. Run make generate. Update CRD-SPEC.md.
  • New: the copy loop for Snapshots, in pkg/pool. The Job builder shares code with replication's.
  • Docs: FEATURES.md, KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md (one disk per snapshot), BACKUP-RECOVERY.md, CHANGELOG.md.
  • Metrics: the existing snapshot metrics count VM snapshots too. No new metric.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Unit tests with the fake copier: the VM path starts, advances and finishes; a migration retries three times and then fails; a VM starts during a file copy; delete during a copy; a restart in the middle.
  • Lab test on rovslab (the release test stage 5): a CentOS VM writes a file every 0.1 s with its checksum in a log. Take a VolumeSnapshot while it runs. Restore it to a new PVC and boot a VM from it. The file system has no errors and every logged file matches its checksum. Repeat with the Windows VM.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• Slower snapshots of running VMs. The old copy was fast and wrong. A safe snapshot takes as long as a full copy: about 20 minutes for a 20 GB disk at the default limit.
  • Space. A snapshot of a running VM is a full copy of the allocated blocks, on the same share as the disk. Hard-link or chain snapshots come with step 8.
  • Red Hat does not support the QEMU commands this uses. The same risk as for replication. The step is easy to replace later with the supported feature.
  • A snapshot on the same share is lost with the share. This step does not change that. Step 8 puts snapshots in their own pool.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• A VM disk snapshot is a full copy every time. Chains wait for the backup step.
  • The snapshot path is chosen by looking for a running VM pod. There is no new setting to turn on.
  • One PVC per snapshot. Matching several disks stays with group snapshots (issue #14).
  • The default speed limit is 20 MB/s, the same as replication. A class parameter can change it.
  • A migration retries the copy three times, one minute apart, and then fails.
  • A copy that runs longer than 2 hours plus twice the expected time is cancelled. Progress cannot be measured, so a time limit replaces "no progress".
  • A snapshot never removes the change lists that replication keeps. It only checks that no other copy runs in the VM, and waits if one does. Replication waits the same way.
  • The status says whether the snapshot is file-system consistent or crash consistent. A crash-consistent snapshot is still ready to use; it is not an error.
  • If the VM stops during the copy, the controller falls back to the file copy.
  • The copy runs in a loop in the controller. It does not wait for the snapshotter to ask again.

docs.title: Spec: browse a backup and restore single files (issue #92)
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-22. Status: draft for review. It builds on 2026-10-21-backup-to-snapshot-pool.md (step 8) and 2026-10-21-backup-cos-export.md (step 9). Read both first. Facts here come from the code on main on 22 Oct 2026.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
The owner's goal is: like Veeam. Look inside a backup, pick one file or folder, and get it back, without restoring the whole volume.

When this is done: - Plain volumes: a user lists folders and files of any backup moment, reads or downloads a file, and restores files or folders to a new or an existing claim. In the console and with kubectl backup. - VM disks: the same, for the files inside the guest's file systems (XFS, ext4, NTFS, and LVM volumes inside the guest). The VM is not started and does not need to exist. - Browsing is read-only. It never changes a backup, and it never writes to a VM disk. - It works for backups in the snapshot pool and for backups exported to IBM Cloud Object Storage (COS). - Who may browse follows Kubernetes access rules (RBAC).

docs.title: What is not reachable on this platform
docs.text:
Said first, so there is no surprise later. Size of each gap:

Part of the Veeam experience Can we meet it? Gap Plain volumes, local and COS Yes, fully None VM guest: ext4, XFS, btrfs, NTFS, LVM Yes, in a helper pod with no special rights, by running a tiny read-only appliance VM (see "VM disks"). Proven on the lab on 22 Oct 2026 (see "Phase 0 results") A disk opens and a file reads in about 1.5 seconds with KVM, and about 12 seconds without it Older moments of a VM disk, instantly Yes, with a small read-only disk server that rebuilds the old view on the fly New code, the riskiest part of this spec VM guest file systems that need a key: BitLocker, LUKS No. Without the guest's key nobody can read them, Veeam included You can only restore the whole disk (works today) VM guest: ReFS, Storage Spaces, ZFS No. Linux has no safe reader for them Same: whole disk only. Veeam reads ReFS through a Windows helper. We have none Put a file back into the guest's own disk, in place No. A file system that a VM is using must not be written from outside, and writing into a stopped guest from a pod is not safe either The file goes to a claim or to a download. The user copies it into the VM A mounted Windows disk that was not shut down cleanly (hibernate, fast start) Partly. Read-only works. Recent writes may be missing Shown as a warning on the session

docs.title: What exists today (from the code)
docs.text:
• Layout of a backup on the snapshot pool. One folder per volume: /backup/<policy>/pvcs/<volume> holds the latest whole copy. Earlier moments are in /backup/<policy>/.moments/pvcs/<volume>/. For a plain volume a moment is a folder of hard links, named like 20261022T091500Z. For a VM disk the latest copy is one raw file, disk.img, and earlier moments are "undo files" (the old contents of the blocks that changed). replication.RestoreDisk rebuilds an older disk by applying undo files to a copy of the latest. The status of each policy lists the volumes with their sub path, share and moment times (BackupVolumeStatus).
  • Restore today is a whole volume: BackupRestore (cluster scoped) makes a new claim, holds pods back, and a Job copies the volume in. Nothing lists files.
  • Helper pods are Kubernetes Jobs in the driver namespace (kube-system by default). They mount the NFS shares themselves, may mount them read-only (jobShape.readOnly), and run as root. The controller has no NFS access. On OpenShift, kube-system has no security rules applied, so these Jobs need no special SCC today (the chart comment says so, and the release tests prove it).
  • Path safety. util.ValidateBackupPath and ValidateBackupMomentsPath check the shape of every backup path. The disk code opens files through a folder handle that refuses symbolic links (openVolume).
  • COS export. A Job copies the backup folder and the moments folder of one volume into a Kopia repository in the bucket, encrypted with a backup key that the Job unlocks with Key Protect in memory. One policy has one area in the bucket. A restore from COS (BackupRestore.spec.fromCOS) runs a Job that restores one Kopia snapshot into a scratch folder and then reuses the normal restore Job.
  • Console. The console plugin is a static page set served by nginx. It has no page for backups at all today (no BackupPolicy model, no list). It has no server side to stream a file.
  • KubeVirt images. The controller already finds the virt-launcher image from virt-operator (discoverLauncherImage). The driver image has no qemu-img and no file system tools for guests.

docs.title: Design that meets the goal
docs.text: Three parts: a browse session (a helper pod per open backup), a gateway (the one door that users talk to, which checks access), and a file restore (a Job that copies chosen paths out).

docs.title: 1. The browse session
docs.text:
A new cluster-scoped resource, BackupBrowse, describes one open session: the policy, the volume (namespace/name of the claim), the moment (default: latest), whether it reads the snapshot pool or COS, and for a VM disk which guest file system (see below). Users never create or see this resource. The gateway makes it after the access check. The backup controller (the same leader that runs backups) reconciles it:

  1. It starts a helper pod (a Job with one pod, in the driver namespace) that mounts only this volume's folders, read-only, down to the NFS export. For COS it mounts nothing from NFS and gets the COS and Key Protect Secrets as read-only files, as the export Job does.
  2. The pod runs the browse binary (cmd/browse, mode browse-server). It serves a small API on a private port over TLS, with a random session token and a certificate made for this session alone (the controller makes a key and a self-signed certificate, keeps them with the token in a Secret that the BackupBrowse owns, and mounts it into the pod; the gateway trusts exactly that certificate, no other and no CA): list a folder (paged, 1000 entries), stat, read a byte range, stream a file, stream a folder as a tar. The API takes paths relative to the volume only. It cannot be asked for anything outside it.
  3. The controller writes status.phase (Starting, Ready, Closed, Failed), the pod address and a message. A session ends when it is idle for 15 minutes (default), when it has lived 2 hours (hard limit), or when the gateway closes it. Then the Job is deleted.

Path safety in the helper (the main risk for a plain volume, since a backup is attacker-supplied data): - Symbolic links are listed as links, with their text, and are never followed. A download of a link is refused. A restore copies it as a link. - Every open goes through a folder handle that refuses links and .. (the same method as openVolume; Linux openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH). A test uses a backup that holds a link to /etc and to ../../other-volume. - File names are sent as raw bytes encoded in the API, shown escaped in the console, and never put into a shell command. The restore Job gets paths as a list in a file, not as arguments. - The pod has no service account token (automountServiceAccountToken: false), no host paths, no extra capabilities, a read-only root file system, and a NetworkPolicy that lets only the gateway reach its port, and traffic to it is encrypted with TLS (no plain HTTP in the cluster).

Files that the pod cannot read. NFS on VPC always squashes root to an ordinary user. A backup file with mode 0600 owned by another user may then be unreadable to the helper. This must be tested in Phase 1 on the lab before the design is called done. The list shows such files as "not readable" instead of failing. The same question applies to the existing restore Job, which copies as root; Phase 1 settles both.

Idle and cleanup. Every object of a session (the Job, its share volume and claim, the Secret) is named and labelled with the UID of the BackupBrowse, never its name, so a session deleted and made again with the same name cannot get the old session's Secret or pod. Pods carry a label and an owner reference to the BackupBrowse. The controller removes sessions past their limits, pods whose session is gone, and any session older than 2 hours after a restart. A limit on open sessions (default 5 in the cluster, 2 per namespace) makes extra requests wait with a clear message.

docs.title: 2. Plain volumes
docs.text: The helper reads the latest copy at .../pvcs/<volume> or a moment folder under .moments. A moment folder is already a normal folder of files, so listing is instant. The list of moments comes from the policy status plus the folder names. A moment that the keep time removes while someone browses it gives "this moment was removed by the keep time", not a crash. The latest copy is rewritten by the next backup, one file at a time and with a rename, so a file is whole or old, never half-written; the page says "the latest copy may change while you look".

docs.title: 3. VM disks
docs.text:
A backup of a VM disk is one raw disk. The file systems are inside it, so something must understand partitions, LVM and the guest's file systems, without starting the VM and without root on the node.

Recommended: a small read-only appliance VM inside the helper pod (libguestfs). libguestfs is the library that KubeVirt's own virtctl guestfs and Red Hat's VM migration tool use. It starts a tiny VM with its own Linux kernel, attaches the disk read-only, and that kernel reads XFS, ext4, btrfs, NTFS (read-only) and LVM. The pod needs no extra rights: no privileged mode, no loop devices, no CAP_SYS_ADMIN, no FUSE, no host paths. It runs as root only inside its own pod, like today's Jobs, and works under the OpenShift rules if the driver namespace has them (see "OpenShift rules"). With the KVM device (devices.kubevirt.io/kvm, the device KubeVirt already uses) the appliance is fast. Without KVM (a ROKS cluster with virtual workers) it works with software emulation, slower. Both were tested in Phase 0 (see "Phase 0 results").

How it is wired: 1. A disk server (new code). The pod starts a read-only disk server in Go that shows the VM disk to the appliance as a network block device on a local socket. For the latest moment it reads disk.img. For an older moment it reads disk.img and the undo files newer than that moment, newest first, and returns the old contents of each changed block. This is the same rule as Rewind, but without writing a copy. No scratch space and no wait, however big the disk is. The server only answers reads; its export is marked read-only. 2. The appliance gets that device as a read-only drive and mounts the guest file systems read-only. libguestfs gives the list: partitions, LVM volumes, type, size, and which looks like the system volume. The console shows them as a picker. 3. The browse API in the pod asks the appliance for lists and file contents and relays them in the same API as a plain volume. So the console and the command line see one kind of session.

Why not the cheaper routes: - Restore the whole disk to a scratch claim, then look inside (RestoreDisk plus a mount). Does not meet the goal: it restores the whole volume, which is what the owner asked to avoid. A 500 GB disk takes minutes to hours and needs 500 GB of scratch. - Mount the disk with a loop device in a privileged pod. Meets the goal for ext4 and XFS only if the node allows it, but it is a security risk: a privileged pod, with a guest kernel-parser bug running in the node's kernel. A hostile VM disk can then reach the node. We will not use it. - Pure Go readers (go-ext4, go-ntfs, go-xfs). Partly meets the goal: no appliance, faster start, but each file system needs a separate, immature reader, none does LVM, and we would own their bugs. It is a possible later fast path for ext4 only.

Safety of reading a guest file system. The disk is read-only at four layers: the NFS mount, the disk server, the appliance's drive flag, and the mount flag. The appliance is thrown away when the session ends. A broken or hostile file system can crash the appliance, not the node. The appliance has no network.

Dirty file systems. A backup of a running VM is a crash copy unless the freeze worked (the status says which: FileSystemConsistent or crash-consistent). A read-only mount of a crash copy may not be allowed to replay the journal. The helper then mounts with the "do not replay" option (norecovery for XFS, noload for ext4). The page shows a notice: "this copy was taken while the VM was running; the newest changes may be missing." Phase 0 showed that a read-only XFS mount with norecovery works in the appliance.

Not read: encrypted and unusual file systems. If the helper finds BitLocker, LUKS, ReFS, Storage Spaces or ZFS it lists the volume as "cannot be read here" with the reason. Nothing is skipped silently.

Backups and browsing of the same VM disk. The next backup copy writes into disk.img and adds undo files. A session on a VM disk holds a lease on that volume, so the backup controller waits for that volume's next copy while a session is open, for at most 2 hours (the hard limit of a session). The policy status shows "waiting for a browse session". Reason: a half-applied copy has the disk and the undo files out of step, and the disk server must see a steady state. Cost: a backup of that one volume can be late by up to 2 hours. Other volumes are not held back. (A later version could let the disk server follow a copy in progress, as Recover does, and remove the wait. It is not needed for the goal.)

docs.title: 4. Backups in COS
docs.text:
COS backups are in a Kopia repository. The helper opens it read-only with the same Secrets the export Job uses: the backup key is unlocked by Key Protect in the helper's memory, as in step 9. The controller never holds it.

  • Plain volumes. Kopia lists a folder in a snapshot and fetches the chunks of one file, so listing and getting one file does not download the volume. Meets the goal fully.
  • VM disks. The disk server reads disk.img and the undo files as objects in the repository, by byte range, with a read cache on an emptyDir (default 5 GiB). The rest of the path is the same as for the snapshot pool. Meets the goal, with slower reads than the pool (each read may go to COS); a guest start of several minutes is likely. To be measured in Phase 6.
  • Where Kopia comes from. The step 9 spec keeps Kopia out of the controller. This is kept: the helper is a separate binary (cmd/browse) in its own image, not the controller. For plain volumes it runs the pinned Kopia program as a child, as the export Job does. For VM disks, a range read needs Kopia as a Go library in that separate binary. This is the one new dependency, and it is limited to the browse image. If Phase 6 shows the library is not workable, the fall-back is to fetch disk.img and the undo files of the one moment into scratch space first. That fall-back does not meet the goal for large disks, and we would say so in the product.
  • Whole area of the bucket. The helper's credentials can read the whole policy area, which has other namespaces' volumes. The API accepts only the one volume's path, and a test tries to reach another volume with traversal and with crafted snapshot names. This is the weakest point of COS browsing and is tested hard (see "Tests").
  • A new cluster, no policy. kubectl backup browse --from-cos takes the same flags as restore --from-cos (bucket, endpoint, volume). It is for cluster administrators because it needs the Secrets in the driver namespace.

docs.title: 5. Where restored files go
docs.text:
A new resource, BackupFileRestore, cluster scoped like BackupRestore, made by the gateway for the user. It holds a session reference or the volume and moment, a list of paths, and the target. Three targets:

  1. New claim. The controller makes a new claim (same method as BackupRestore: size, class, held back from pods until the copy ends) and a Job copies the chosen paths into it. The tree under the volume's root is kept: restoring /var/www/html/index.php gives /var/www/html/index.php in the new claim. Size of the claim defaults to the total of the chosen files plus 20%, at least 1 GiB, and the user can raise it. For a VM guest the claim is a plain file-system claim; a VM disk is never the target.
  2. Existing claim, as a new folder. Files go to a new folder in the claim, restored-<policy>-<moment>/, never over existing files. A name that exists gets a suffix. The Job mounts the claim's folder on the share, like the other share Jobs. It refuses if the claim is a VM disk claim (it holds disk.img), if the claim is being restored, or if the free space is not enough (checked before it copies). The files get the claim's configured owner (defaultUID and defaultGID, for example 107 on KubeVirt pools), as the existing restore does.
  3. Download. From the console or kubectl backup get: one file as a stream; a folder or several files as one tar stream (a tar file; no zip). The stream passes through the gateway and the helper. Limits are in the next section.

Putting a file back where it was (in place, over the original) is not offered, for plain volumes either. A restore never writes over existing files. This matches step 8 ("it never writes over a volume that exists"). The user copies from the restored folder.

For a VM guest, targets 1 and 2 give plain files in a claim. The user attaches that claim to the VM or a pod and copies in the guest. This is the gap in the table.

docs.title: 6. The gateway and access control
docs.text:
One door. A new small Deployment, backup-gateway, in the driver namespace. The console reaches it through the console plugin proxy (the OpenShift console forwards the signed-in user's token). kubectl backup reaches it through an OpenShift Route (or an Ingress on other clusters) with the user's token. Users never need rights in the driver namespace, and never see the helper pods, BackupBrowse or the Secrets.

Who may do what. The gateway checks every call with the Kubernetes API, as the user, by a token review and a SubjectAccessReview. The rule is by the namespace of the backed-up claim, because that is who owned the data:
