Action Needs List backups and moments of volumes of namespace N get on backupfiles (group storage.ibmcloud.io) in N Browse a backup, read and download files of N get on backupfiles in N Restore files out of N's backup to a claim get on backupfiles in N, plus create on persistentvolumeclaims in the target namespace T. For an existing claim, also update on persistentvolumeclaims in T Browse a COS backup without a policy (--from-cos) cluster administrator (it needs the driver's Secrets)

backupfiles is a rights-only name: no such object is ever stored. It exists so that RBAC can say "may read backups of this namespace". The chart ships two ClusterRoles, backup-file-reader (get) and backup-file-restorer (get), and aggregates the reader into the built-in admin role, so a namespace admin can read their own namespace's backups with no setup. Another namespace's backup needs a RoleBinding made by someone who has rights in that namespace. A deleted claim's backup still belongs to its old namespace. If the namespace itself is gone, only a cluster administrator can browse it.

A person in namespace B who wants a file from the backup of namespace A, to put into B, needs get backupfiles in A and the PVC rights in B. Without the first, they get a plain "forbidden", the same as any other Kubernetes object. The gateway never shows the existence of volumes in a namespace to a person without rights there.

Audit. Each session start, download, and restore writes a Kubernetes Event on the BackupBrowse and a log line: user, namespace, volume, moment, and the paths (not the contents). A user cannot read the Events of the driver namespace; the cluster administrator can. A test checks that no API key, token or file content reaches logs or Events.

docs.title: 7. Limits
docs.text:
Limit Default Why Folder listing page 1000 entries Large folders stay fast Session idle time 15 min Frees the pod and the lease Session hard limit 2 hours Stops a forgotten session from holding backups Open sessions 5 in the cluster, 2 per namespace Each VM session used about 550 MiB in the lab (Phase 0) Helper pod plain: 200m CPU, 256 MiB; VM guest: 1 CPU, 1 GiB Appliance memory (lab peak 550 MiB) One file download 50 GiB Stream, no temporary copy One restore 200 GiB or the free space of the target, whichever is less The Job checks first Appliance start 10 minutes, then the session fails with the reason Software emulation is slow Restore Job time 4 hours A hard stop for a stuck copy

All defaults are Helm values (backupBrowse.*) and are listed in HELM-VALUES.md with the phase that adds them.

docs.title: 8. User stories
docs.text:
Console: 1. As a namespace admin, I open Backups, pick a policy, see my volumes, pick a volume and a moment, and press Browse files. A plain volume opens at once. A VM disk shows "Starting the reader" for a few seconds and then a picker of the disk's file systems. 2. I click into folders, search the current folder by name, tick files and folders, and press Download (one file, or a tar for several) or Restore to a claim (new claim, or a folder in an existing one). 3. I see the status of the restore (copying, done, failed) and a link to the new claim. 4. A VM backup shows the notice about a crash copy, and a lock icon on volumes that cannot be read, with the reason.

Command line (kubectl backup, same plugin as today): - kubectl backup ls --policy P --pvc NS/NAME [--moment TIME] [--disk N] [--fs /dev/sda2] [PATH], lists a folder. For a VM disk without --fs it lists the file systems it found. - kubectl backup get --policy P --pvc NS/NAME [--moment TIME] [--fs ...] PATH [--out DIR] downloads a file, or a folder as a tar or an unpacked folder. - kubectl backup restore-files --policy P --pvc NS/NAME [--moment TIME] [--fs ...] --path A --path B --to NS/CLAIM [--new-claim --size-gb N | --existing] [--wait]. - kubectl backup browse ... opens a session by hand and prints its name, so repeated ls and get calls reuse it. Without it each command reuses an open session of the same user, volume and moment, or opens one. - The same commands take --from-cos --bucket B --endpoint HOST --volume pvc-... for a cluster administrator.

docs.title: OpenShift rules (security context constraints)
docs.text:
• Plain volume helper: runs as root in its pod with all capabilities dropped, on a read-only NFS mount. No special rule. It is the same as today's share Jobs.
  • VM guest helper: also unprivileged. It asks for the KVM device through the KubeVirt device plugin (devices.kubevirt.io/kvm: 1) when the node has it. Without it, no request, and software emulation. It needs a writable /tmp and /var/tmp (an emptyDir with a size limit). It needs no SCC beyond what the driver namespace already allows.
  • If the driver is installed in a namespace where OpenShift does apply SCCs (not kube-system), the chart ships one SCC, pool-csi-browse, that allows running as root with no capabilities and no host access, and the controller gets use on it only. The release test checks that this SCC and the pod pass admission.
  • Image. The VM helper image is our own image, built from CentOS Stream 9 with the libguestfs, libguestfs-winsupport and guestfs-tools packages, pinned by digest, with our static Go binary copied in (CGO_ENABLED=0). Phase 0 ruled out the libguestfs image of OpenShift Virtualization: it has no NTFS support. It is not built from UBI: UBI repositories do not have the qemu and libguestfs packages (the same reason the converter pod uses the CentOS image).
  • NTFS rule. The RHEL and CentOS builds of libguestfs read NTFS only when one of the virt- tools runs it (for example virt-ls and virt-cat). A program that uses the library directly gets "unsupported filesystem type". So the helper reads Windows disks by running virt-ls and virt-cat, as the packaging intends. It must not pretend to be one of those tools.
  • Never: privileged pods, hostPath, loop devices, FUSE, or kernel mounts of a guest file system on the node.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Unit tests (every phase). The disk server against Rewind: for each moment, a read must equal RestoreDisk byte for byte (property test, random writes, several moments, an unfinished copy ignored). Path rules: links, .., very long names, names with newlines and invalid UTF-8, a link to the helper's own files. Gateway: every row of the access table, with a fake SubjectAccessReview, including "forbidden gives no hint that the volume exists". Controller: session start, idle timeout, hard limit, limits on open sessions, orphan cleanup after a restart, the lease on VM volumes. BackupFileRestore: all three targets, a name clash, a target that is a VM disk claim, not enough space.
  • COS. Kopia against a local repository and MinIO in CI: list, one file, one volume's path only, a hostile snapshot name, a range read of a large file, the cache size.
  • Chart tests (make test-scripts). The gateway and its NetworkPolicy render; the two ClusterRoles and the aggregation; the SCC only when asked for; the console proxy entry; Helm values documented.
  • Console tests. The new pages: list, breadcrumb, selection, the picker, disabled states, the warning texts; no file content is put into a URL.
  • Release test, new stage 20 (stage 19 is the instant snapshots stage) in test/e2e, run on the lab pair:
  • Plain pod volume with a known tree (links, a 0600 file owned by another user, a name with spaces and an accented letter). Two backup moments. Browse both, download a file and check its checksum, restore a folder to a new claim and to an existing one, and compare checksums. Check that the backup folder is byte-identical before and after (a recorded hash of the tree).
  • Linux VM with an XFS root on LVM and an ext4 data disk, with a log of files and checksums (as stage 18). Browse the latest and the first moment without starting the VM; stop the VM first for one run. Restore a file; compare. Check the disk image is byte-identical after.
  • A Windows or NTFS disk image (a small prepared image; the lab has no Windows licence, so the image is made with ntfs-3g tools and checked as a disk, not as a boot).
  • COS: browse and restore the same plain volume and the VM disk from the bucket of stage 18, in the second cluster of the pair.
  • Access: a test user with only a RoleBinding in the other namespace gets "forbidden", gets access after a binding, and loses it after the binding is removed.
  • Cleanup: no helper pod, BackupBrowse or scratch left after the run, and a killed controller leaves none after a restart.
  • A backup due during a VM session waits and then runs after it closes.
  • What the lab cannot test: a customer's own Windows disks, BitLocker/ReFS (checked only that they are reported as unreadable, using a small image header), and the speed of very large disks. The report says so.

docs.title: Build plan: phases, one PR each
docs.text:
Sizes: S is a day or less of work, M a few days, L a week or more. Each PR has its tests, updates FEATURES.md, BACKUP-RECOVERY.md, HELM-VALUES.md, CRD-SPEC.md, MONITORING.md and CHANGELOG.md, and extends stage 20 for its part.

  1. Spike on the lab (S, risk check). Run the libguestfs image in a pod on ROVS with and without the KVM device. Measure: start time, listing, reading a file, memory. Try XFS, ext4, NTFS, LVM, a crash copy, a hibernated NTFS, and a disk served over a socket from a small test server. Decide the image and how to find it. Results are added to this spec in a PR that holds no product code. If it fails (for example the appliance cannot start in a pod under the cluster's rules), the VM part of the goal is re-stated with the real gap before more is built.
  2. Plain volumes, snapshot pool, command line (L). BackupBrowse, the helper in cmd/browse and its image, the controller part, the gateway, the access rules and ClusterRoles, kubectl backup ls/get/browse, limits, cleanup, audit Events. Settles the "squashed root cannot read 0600 files" question.
  3. Restore of files (M). BackupFileRestore, the Job, the three targets, kubectl backup restore-files, the space check, ownership.
  4. Console (L). The file browser, download, the file restore dialog, help texts and the plugin proxy entry. The Backups pages themselves (policies, volumes, moments) come from 2026-10-22-console-backup-ui.md, which reserves a "Browse files" action on each volume row and moment for this phase. Build those pages first.
  5. COS, plain volumes (M). Kopia read-only helper, --from-cos for ls/get/restore-files, the tests that block reaching another volume.
  6. VM disks in the snapshot pool (L, the riskiest). The disk server with undo-file rebuild and its property tests; the lease and the backup wait; the appliance helper; the file system picker; norecovery handling; the console picker; the crash-copy notices; the unreadable-volume list.
  7. VM disks in COS (M). Kopia library range reads and the cache; speed measurements; the fall-back decision if needed.
  8. Release test stage 20 final and docs (S). The stage is extended per phase; this PR makes it one run for the lab pair, adds the two-cluster COS run and the cleanup checks, and writes the user tutorial.

Total: about 4 to 6 weeks of agent work, with the lab as the slowest part (stage 20 runs about an hour). Phases 1 to 4 deliver the whole plain-volume goal and can be deployed and tested before phases 5 and 6 are done.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• Biggest technical risk: the VM path (phases 5 and 6). It has three new parts: the disk server, the appliance in a pod, and the COS range reads. Phase 0 removed the first doubt: the appliance runs in an ordinary pod on ROVS. If that ever changes, the fall-back is a helper that restores one volume to scratch space and then reads it. That does not meet the goal; the gap would be shown to you before we build it.
  • Security risk: reading hostile data (a backup of a compromised VM). The appliance is the main defence. For plain volumes the risk is path tricks, handled by handle-based opens and tests.
  • Backups held back: a VM session delays that volume's next backup by up to 2 hours. A noisy user could do it repeatedly; the per-namespace limit and the audit trail bound it.
  • Resources: each VM session takes about 2 CPU and 2 GiB on a worker for its life. The limit of 5 open sessions bounds it.
  • COS cost: reads from COS cost egress and requests. Browsing one file is cheap; browsing a VM disk reads only the blocks the file system asks for, but a first mount reads a lot of metadata. Measured in phase 6 and added here.
  • New dependencies: the libguestfs image (pinned, from Red Hat's own OpenShift Virtualization release) and, in phase 6 only, Kopia as a library in the browse binary. Nothing new in the controller.
  • Time to first value: the end of phase 2 gives command-line browse and restore of plain volumes.

docs.title: Phase 0 results (22 Oct 2026, rovslab-dr-eude)
docs.text:
The test ran in a new namespace, in a pod with no special rights: a random non-root user, all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, the default seccomp profile, and only /tmp and /var/tmp as emptyDir folders. The pod asked for the KVM device (devices.kubevirt.io/kvm: 1). The workers are bare-metal bx2d.metal.96x384 nodes, each with the KVM device.

Check Result The appliance starts in an ordinary pod Yes. No privileged mode, no host paths, no extra rights Open a disk, mount read-only and read one file, with KVM About 1.3 to 1.6 seconds for XFS, ext4 on LVM, and LVM listing The same without KVM (software only) About 12 seconds Memory The appliance used about 260 MiB; the whole container peaked at about 550 MiB XFS, ext4, LVM Read correctly with the OpenShift Virtualization image NTFS with the OpenShift Virtualization image No. The image has no NTFS support: no libguestfs-winsupport, no ntfs-3g, and its kernel has no NTFS driver NTFS with CentOS Stream 9 packages (libguestfs-winsupport) Yes, through virt-ls and virt-cat. A direct library call is refused by design ("unsupported filesystem type") virt-copy-out and virt-tar-out on an NTFS data disk with no operating system No: they need to find an operating system. Use virt-ls and virt-cat per file for data disks Read-only XFS mount with norecovery Works Disk served over a local socket by nbdkit -r Reads work. A write through it is refused

What this changes in the spec: the VM path is proven to start quickly; the helper image is our own CentOS Stream 9 image; Windows disks go through the virt- tools; the VM helper needs 1 CPU and 1 GiB, not 2 and 2.

Not yet tested: a real Windows disk with BitLocker or a hibernated system, btrfs, and very large disks. Phase 5 covers them.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Users talk to one small gateway, never to helper pods or driver resources. The gateway checks Kubernetes access on every call.
  • Access follows the namespace of the backed-up claim, through a rights-only name backupfiles. Namespace admins get read access to their own namespace by default; everything else needs a RoleBinding.
  • Restoring a file out needs read rights on the source namespace and create rights on the target namespace. No new super-user role.
  • Browsing from COS without a policy is for cluster administrators only.
  • A VM disk is browsed through a small read-only appliance VM in an unprivileged pod, not through a privileged mount on the node. We do not use privileged pods for this.
  • Older moments of a VM disk are shown by a read-only disk server that rebuilds the old view on the fly. We do not restore a scratch copy, because that would restore the whole volume.
  • A VM session holds the next backup of that one volume for up to 2 hours. Other volumes are not held.
  • Files are never put back in place, and nothing is ever written into a VM's own disk. Files go to a new claim, to a new folder in an existing claim, or to a download.
  • A restore to an existing claim goes into a new folder and never over existing files; it refuses a VM disk claim.
  • BitLocker, LUKS, ReFS, Storage Spaces and ZFS guests are listed as "cannot be read here". Their only route is the whole-disk restore that exists.
  • Symbolic links in a backup are shown and copied as links and never followed.
  • Defaults: 15 minutes idle, 2 hours hard limit, 5 sessions in the cluster and 2 per namespace, 50 GiB for one download, a listing page of 1000 entries.
  • The browse helper is a separate binary and image. Kopia stays out of the controller. Kopia as a library is allowed in the browse image only.
  • A short spike (phase 0) came before any VM work. It passed on 22 Oct 2026.
  • The VM helper image is built by us from CentOS Stream 9, because the OpenShift Virtualization libguestfs image cannot read NTFS.
  • Windows disks are read through the virt-ls and virt-cat tools, which is the use the packaging allows.
  • The Backups pages in the console are built by the backup screens spec (2026-10-22-console-backup-ui.md). This work adds the file browser to them.
  • Plain volumes are finished and usable (phases 1 to 4) before VM disks start.
  • No restore of single mail items or database rows (Veeam's application-level explorers). Files and folders only.

docs.title: Needs from you
docs.text:
• Nothing blocks phases 1 to 4. Phase 0 is done.
  • Whether phases 5 and 6 (VM disks) must be in the first deployment, or can follow it. I assumed they follow.

docs.title: Changes made while building (23 Oct 2026)
docs.text:
• The helper API is served over TLS with a per-session self-signed certificate, pinned by the gateway. Decided by the coordinator after a security review: the stream carries other namespaces' file contents and the token, and pod traffic is not encrypted by default.
  • Objects of a session are named by the UID of the BackupBrowse, not its name (security review: a reused name must never reuse an old Secret or pod).
  • The release test stage is 20, not 19.
  • The helper image is separate; the gateway runs in the driver image.
  • Helper pods, their Secrets and the NetworkPolicy live in their own namespace, ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-browse (chart value backupBrowse.namespace), which holds nothing else. Reason (security review of part 3): the gateway must read the session Secrets, and the driver namespace (kube-system) holds the cluster's IBM Cloud API key and other Secrets that a compromised gateway could then read. The gateway's Role for Secrets is in the browse namespace only; the controller has a Role there, and copies the image pull secrets into it. The helper needs root (to read backups made by other users), so the namespace is labelled Pod Security baseline (not restricted), and on OpenShift the chart adds one SCC (runAsUser: RunAsAny, all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, no host path, only PVC/secret/projected/emptyDir/configMap/downwardAPI volumes) for the namespace's default account. This replaces the earlier text that said the controller gets use on the SCC.
  • The gateway reads the rights as get backupfiles on the claim's namespace and runs in the driver image (--mode=backup-gateway). Users reach it through a reencrypt Route on OpenShift (a passthrough Route would show the service certificate, which is for the service name and not for the Route host); kubectl backup finds the address in the ConfigMap backup-gateway-info.
  • The audit Events are written in the driver namespace on the ConfigMap backup-gateway-info, with the BackupBrowse in related (the API server refuses Events of a cluster-scoped object outside default, which many people can read).
  • A session belongs to the user who made it; another user, even with the same rights, sees "no such session".
  • The helper has a /v1/moments call so that kubectl backup ls --moments can list the moment folders.
  • The console file browser (phase 3, first half) downloads with a GET route on the gateway, GET /v1/sessions/{name}/download?type=file|tar&p=<base64 name>..., because a browser can stream a large download to disk only from a GET. It takes the same steps as the POST calls. Every file and tar reply now carries Content-Disposition: attachment, nosniff, a sandbox Content-Security-Policy and no-store, since the console proxy serves it from the console's own origin. The console shows the action when the settings ConfigMap says fileBrowse: "true".

docs.title: Changes made while building phase 2 (28 Oct 2026)
docs.text:
• The restore Job is the driver program (--mode=restore-files, package pkg/filerestore), not a shell script with cp -a. It reads the backup through the browse helper's handle-based reader and writes the target the same way (mkdirat, symlinkat, openat with O_EXCL and O_NOFOLLOW, no link followed). Reason: an existing claim is open to its users, so the target is as untrusted as the backup.
  • Paths are spec.paths, a list of escaped strings (the form kubectl backup ls prints), kept in a ConfigMap that the restore owns and mounted as a file. At most 1000 paths, 256 KiB together.
  • The squashed-root question, write side: the order is times, then mode, then owner for a file, and a folder is finished only after everything in it is written (like cp -a, which the lab proved). The owner is the one the pool configures for the claim (defaultUID, defaultGID); without one, the backup's owner is kept. If an owner cannot be set, the restore fails and removes what it wrote. Stage 20 part 4 checks both cases on the lab (a pool with owner 107 and a pool with none, files of users 1000 and 2000).
  • Into an existing claim the Job writes a hidden folder .restoring-<restore UID> and renames it to restored-<policy>-<moment> (a suffix if the name exists). NFS has no rename that refuses to replace; the name is checked just before.
  • The Job mounts the whole share that holds the target claim (the claim's folder may not exist before the Job, and a folder that does not exist cannot be mounted), and opens only the claim's folder below it, one name at a time. An existing claim whose folder does not exist yet is refused.
  • A new claim is sized by a read-only measure Job first (skipped when sizeGB is given), because the controller has no NFS access.
  • The claim's UID is pinned (spec.targetUID, set by the gateway; otherwise the first UID the controller sees), so a claim deleted and made again is refused. The new claim made for a restore carries the restore's name and UID as annotations, and both must match.
  • The Job keeps only the CHOWN and FOWNER capabilities. It has a 4 hour deadline.
  • Limit of one restore: the least of 200 GiB (backupBrowse.restoreMaxBytes), the free space of the share, and, for an existing claim, its size less what it holds.
  • The setuid and setgid bits are removed from everything restored.
  • At most 5 file restores run at once in the cluster (backupBrowse.restoreMaxRunning); the others wait, oldest first. Without a limit, any user with the rights could start unlimited Jobs that mount shares.
  • A refusal by the Job (no room, a VM disk claim, a missing path, an owner it cannot set) ends the Job with exit code 0 and the reason in its termination message. A Job that failed with a non-zero code is started again by Kubernetes in the same pod, which loses the message. The controller reads error in the outcome as a failed restore. Only a Job that was stopped, or ran out of its 4 hours, ends as a failed Job, and then the reason is "the copy Job failed or ran out of time".
  • One rare repeat can happen: a Job's objects are removed when it succeeds, before the controller saves Done. If that save fails, the next pass runs the Job again, and an existing claim gets a second folder (-2). Nothing is lost or written over.
  • The gateway call is POST /v1/restores (answer 202) and GET /v1/restores/{name}. It checks get backupfiles in the source namespace first, then create on claims in the target namespace (and, for an existing claim, update on claims and create on pods: writing into a claim is the same power as mounting it), and only then looks at the target claim and takes its UID. Paths are stored in one canonical escaped form. A restore is shown only to the user who asked. A user may have 10 restores that have not ended (backupGateway.maxOpenRestores).
  • kubectl backup restore-files defaults to a new claim; --existing chooses a new folder in an existing claim.

docs.title: Changes made while building phase 4 (28 Oct 2026)
docs.text:
• The COS helper pod and the COS file restore Job run in the driver namespace, not in the browse namespace. The COS key, the wrapped backup key and the Key Protect API key are Secrets there, and a pod mounts only Secrets of its own namespace. Copying them to the browse namespace would let a compromised gateway (which may read Secrets there) decrypt every policy's area of the bucket. So the controller keeps a second copy of each session's token and certificate in the driver namespace, owned by the session, and a NetworkPolicy there lets only the gateway reach those pods. The chart gives the controller a Role in the driver namespace that can create and delete Secrets and nothing else. This replaces the earlier text "for COS it mounts nothing from NFS and gets the Secrets as the export Job does" only in where the pod runs.
  • The reader is a Go package, pkg/cosbrowse, used by the helper and by the restore Job. It talks to the Kopia program through two calls (list the snapshots as JSON, show one object by ID). Folders are parsed from Kopia's JSON; the sed and awk of the restore script are not used for names a tenant wrote.
  • The helper unwraps the backup key itself, in process (pkg/keyprotect), and gives it to the Kopia child in an explicit environment. The browse image carries the same pinned Kopia as the driver image; a test keeps the version and checksum equal, and checks that the Dockerfile copies every package the binary imports.
  • A snapshot belongs to a volume only if its volume tag and its exact source path say so. The export Job's mount point is /share0.
  • The source of a session is local or cos. The gateway chooses COS when the moment is older than the oldest local restore point or no local copy is left, and an export exists; source: cos asks for it. A bucket named directly is fromCOS, which needs the right to read every Secret the request names, in the driver namespace.
  • A COS session that is not ready after five minutes ends in words (backupBrowse.cos.startTimeout).
  • Not done in this phase: the source switch in the console file browser; it needs the console files that the restore dialog work is changing, and the gateway already chooses the source for a moment that only COS holds.

docs.title: Spec for #46 item 9: backups in the console
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-22. Status: draft for review.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
An operator can do everything the backup tools and resources can do from the console, with no YAML and no kubectl: see what is backed up and how fresh it is, make and change a backup policy, restore a volume or a VM disk to a new PVC at a chosen moment, remove the backups of one volume, set up the COS export as far as a browser can, and list and restore from COS. "Done" means each row of the table below has a console route, and a release-test browser stage proves restore and delete.

Out of scope here, and kept as a clear seam: browsing a backup and restoring single files is in docs/specs/2026-10-22-backup-file-restore.md (issue #92). This spec only reserves a "Browse files" action on each backup moment and each volume row, which that spec fills in. Until it is built the action is not shown.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
The console has no backup page. The driver has these (all in cmd/backup and the resources BackupPolicy and BackupRestore):

Task Today Console route in this spec See backups: volumes, newest and oldest moment, restore points, bytes, consistency, errors kubectl backup list, BackupPolicy.status.volumes Backups page, policy details page See that new backups stopped because the snapshot pool is over 85% status.phase=Error and message Banner on both pages, with link to the pool Make, change, suspend, delete a policy YAML Create/edit form, Suspend/Resume, Delete Restore to a new PVC, newest or at a moment kubectl backup restore, BackupRestore Restore page Remove all backups of one volume kubectl backup delete (measure Job, typed confirmation, delete Job) Delete backups action Export to COS: set up bucket, keys, lock kubectl backup cos-setup (needs the person's IBM Cloud login) Guide only; see below List volumes and moments in COS kubectl backup cos-list (read-only Job) COS tab Restore from COS, even in another cluster restore --from-cos Restore page, source "COS" Export status per volume (exportedTime, exportedBytes, exportError) status.volumes Same table Backup metrics and alerts Prometheus Panels on Monitoring; alerts already show on the dashboard's Firing Alerts card

docs.title: Pages (under Pools, one new tab "Backups")
docs.text:
1. Backups list. One row per BackupPolicy: snapshot pool, schedule, keep time, phase, number of volumes, stalest volume age, export on or off. A phase of Error shows the message in plain words. Help buttons on the status columns like the other lists (column-help.ts).
  2. Policy details. Overview card (the spec, in plain words), a volumes table (claim, VM, last backup, oldest backup, restore points, size, consistency, error, export state; a retained volume is marked "no longer backed up, kept until "), and per-row actions: Restore, Delete backups, and the reserved Browse files (hidden until #92 is built). Crash-consistent copies carry a warning label, as on the replication page. Card help like card-help.ts.
  3. Create and edit form. Snapshot pool (only pools of the snapshot kind), schedule, keep time, label selector and namespaces (with a live count of the PVCs that match, so a wrong selector shows at once), VM copy speed limit (same explanation as the replication form), suspend. The form explains the 85% stop. The console shows the admission webhook's message instead of copying its rules.
  4. Restore page. Source: this cluster (policy and claim, or a volume that is gone) or COS. Moment: "latest" or a picker listing the real moments (from the status for the snapshot pool, from the COS list Job for COS). Target namespace and name (must not exist; checked live), storage class (default: the class of the backed-up claim; for COS also the size, which COS does not keep). A confirm dialog says: a new PVC is made, nothing is overwritten, the copy takes time. Progress reuses the snapshot-restore banner: BackupRestore.status.phase, the restored moment, and the message on failure.
  5. Delete backups. Same steps as the CLI, as a dialog: the console starts the measure Job, shows how much would go ("12 GiB, 9 moments"), and asks the operator to type the claim name before it starts the delete Job. It refuses while the policy still backs the volume up (the label is still there) or a restore of that volume is running, with the CLI's wording. It is the only destructive action.
  6. COS tab. Shows the policy's export settings and the per-volume export state. List COS contents runs the read-only list Job and shows volumes and moments. COS credentials are never shown.

docs.title: Where the work runs
docs.text: The measure, delete and list steps are Jobs. The console creates the same Jobs the CLI creates, with the user's own rights, and reads the result from the Pod's termination message (the pattern of the receiver check). To keep the Go and TypeScript Job specs in step, the Go builders write a golden JSON file and a console test builds the Job from the same input and compares it (the pattern of the migration Jobs). Restore needs no Job from the console: it creates one BackupRestore object, as the CLI does.

docs.title: COS setup: what a browser can and cannot do
docs.text: cos-setup creates the bucket, the keys, the Key Protect wrap and the CBR rule with the person's own IBM Cloud login. The console has no IBM Cloud login and must not hold an IBM Cloud API key. So the console does not run cos-setup. It shows a "Set up the export" guide: the exact command with the person's names filled in, what each flag means, and the spec.export block the command prints, with a text box to paste it. The console then does what it can: creates the two Secrets from pasted manifests (the pattern of the receiver setup, never reading a Secret back), writes spec.export into the policy, and shows whether the export works (from exportedTime and exportError). This is the one part of the goal a browser cannot reach, and it is stated, not hidden. Closing it would need a driver-side setup service that takes a short-lived IAM token from the person. That is a security design of its own and is not assumed here.

docs.title: Access
docs.text: Each action asks the cluster, by access review, whether the person may do it (create BackupRestore, edit BackupPolicy, create Jobs and Secrets in the driver namespace). If not, the action is disabled, the missing right is named, and the YAML for an administrator is shown, as in the receiver setup.

docs.title: The seam to the file-restore spec
docs.text:
• Each volume row and each moment gets a Browse files action, shown only when the file-restore feature is present (the console reads a flag from the place it reads other driver settings).
  • The Restore page takes a ?moment= query value and the Delete dialog takes ?claim=, so #92 can link to them.
  • This spec does not say how files are listed, previewed or restored. If #92 needs a field on BackupRestore (a list of paths), it is added there, and the Restore page shows it.

docs.title: Plan (about 7 small PRs, in this order; each has jest tests, help text, FEATURES.md and CHANGELOG.md lines)
docs.text:
1. Types, models, and the read-only Backups list and policy details (no driver change).
  2. Restore page and progress banner (snapshot pool source).
  3. Create, edit, suspend and delete policy.
  4. Go: the Job builders for measure, delete and COS list write golden files; TypeScript builders compare to them.
  5. Delete backups dialog.
  6. COS tab: list Job, restore from COS, export state.
  7. Export setup guide with Secret creation and the spec.export write.

Then a release-test browser stage for restore and delete (it needs a cluster and a browser).

Docs touched: FEATURES.md, CHANGELOG.md, BACKUP-RECOVERY.md (the console route next to each kubectl step), MONITORING.md if panels are added.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• Pages 1 to 4 are low risk: they read the resources or create one BackupRestore, which never overwrites a volume.
  • Delete is the one dangerous action. The typed confirmation, the measure step that shows the size first, the refusals above, and the golden-file tests limit the risk.
  • The Job specs are copied into TypeScript, so a drift test is required.
  • The effort is larger than the earlier console items: about 7 PRs, mostly forms and tables.
  • COS setup stays partly on the CLI. That is the one place the console cannot match the CLI, and it is a platform limit.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The goal is full parity with the CLI and the resources, so the plan is 7 PRs, not a read-only page.
  • Restore and policy changes are done directly by the console; it creates the same objects the CLI creates.
  • Delete backups needs the measure step and a typed claim name, like the CLI.
  • The console does not run cos-setup, because a browser has no IBM Cloud login and must not hold an API key. It guides, and does the Secret and spec parts.
  • Browsing and single-file restore are left to the #92 spec; this one keeps only a hidden "Browse files" action and two link parameters.
  • The Job specs are tied to Go by golden files, as for migration.
  • Backups is a new tab under Pools, not a new top-level page.

docs.title: Spec: snapshots of a whole pool (share-level snapshots)
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-22. Status: draft for review. It builds on 2026-10-21-backup-to-snapshot-pool.md, 2026-10-21-backup-cos-export.md, 2026-10-22-backup-file-restore.md and 2026-10-21-instant-vm-snapshots.md. Read the backup spec first. Facts about the driver come from the code on main on 22 Oct 2026. Facts about IBM Cloud come from the IBM docs and carry a link. Where the docs are unclear, this spec says "to verify in the lab" and puts the check in phase 0.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
The owner's question was: is there a use case for a snapshot of the pool or share?

Yes. Today the driver uses no IBM share snapshot. It keeps snapshots per volume, as file copies or QEMU copies (see docs/CONTEXT.md). An earlier decision kept it that way because a share holds many tenants' volumes, and a share snapshot cannot give back one volume without touching the others (docs/CONSISTENCY-MODEL.md). That reason is still true for a restore in place. It does not stop us using share snapshots in other ways.

The goal of this spec: an administrator can protect and recover a whole pool quickly, in minutes whatever its size. The administrator and the tenants can also recover single volumes or VM disks from the same pool-level moment, without touching other tenants.

Two real uses: 1. Fast recovery of a whole pool after ransomware, a bad mass change, or a script that deleted many folders. One share snapshot covers every volume on the share, and it is ready in seconds. 2. A steady, same-moment source for backups and replication. They read a frozen view of the share, not live files that change while they copy.

docs.title: What IBM Cloud gives us (facts, with sources)
docs.text:
All links are on cloud.ibm.com. "Gen 1" means the dp2 profile that this driver uses.

Fact Source A snapshot is taken with the VPC API (POST /shares/{id}/snapshots), the CLI, the console or Terraform. It is stable "within seconds". Only one snapshot a minute. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-create The first snapshot copies all the share's contents. Later snapshots hold only the changes. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-about Up to 750 snapshots per dp2 share. Together they cannot pass 100 TB per share. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-about and https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-planning Shares in access mode vpc cannot have snapshots. Shares in access mode security_group can. The driver makes only security_group shares (pkg/ibmcloud/vpc_client.go: AccessControlMode = "security_group"). https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-about (Limitations) Snapshots live in the same zone and on the same share. They cannot be copied to another zone or region. When the share is deleted, its snapshots are deleted. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-about You cannot take a snapshot of a share in a degraded state, or of a replica share. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-about A replica share (zonal replication) receives the source's snapshots at the next sync. Snapshots on a replica cannot be deleted by hand. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-create Restore is "make a new share from the snapshot". There is no restore in place. The new share has the same profile, zone and encryption. It can be bigger, and you can choose its IOPS. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-restore The new share starts with pointers to the old data. It is in state pending while IBM copies the data. You can mount it and read and write at once while it is pending. In pending you cannot make a replica or a snapshot of it. You cannot delete the source snapshot until the copy ends. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-restore Single files: the share shows a hidden read-only folder /.snapshot at the top of the mount. It has one subfolder for each snapshot, named by the snapshot's fingerprint. You can read it with normal commands. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-restore ("Restoring files from a snapshot") Cost: you pay for the storage in GB-hours. A snapshot kept for part of a month is charged for those hours. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-about Schedules: IBM "Backup for VPC" runs a plan on shares that carry a matching user tag. Up to 10 policies per region, 4 plans per policy. Retention by days (1 to 1000) or by count. It needs a service-to-service authorization for file storage. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-backup-service-about The size of snapshots is reported within 15 minutes. Activity Tracker records create, delete and change of snapshots. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-fs-snapshots-about IBM says a backup or snapshot restore is a manual step that takes time and is not a disaster-recovery product. https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/vpc?topic=vpc-backup-service-about The Go SDK in go.mod (vpc-go-sdk v0.80.0) has CreateShareSnapshot, GetShareSnapshot, ListShareSnapshots, UpdateShareSnapshot, DeleteShareSnapshot and a pager. A share is made from a snapshot with the source_snapshot field of the share prototype. The driver's own client has none of these yet. vpcv1/vpc_v1.go in the module cache; pkg/ibmcloud/client.go

docs.title: To verify in the lab (phase 0)
docs.text:
The docs are silent or unclear on these. Each one decides part of the design below.

  1. When is the moment captured? At the API call, or when the snapshot becomes stable? The API has a captured_at field. If the moment is the call time, snapshots of all shares can be called in parallel and fit within a second or two.
  2. Does the one-a-minute limit apply per share or per account? The design assumes per share.
  3. What does a snapshot of a share with open NFS writers contain? Expected: crash consistent (like a power loss). Prove it with a running VM.
  4. Is /.snapshot visible on our mounts? Our mount is sec=sys, NFS version 4.x, through the share's mount target in security_group mode, and the node mounts the share root. Check that ls /mnt/share/.snapshot/ works, that a read of a file in it is correct, and that it works from a Job pod and from a node mount.
  5. How long does a new share from a snapshot take to be mountable, for 1 TB and 10 TB shares with a lot of data? And how fast is I/O during pending? IBM does not give figures. This is the number that decides "minutes, any size".
  6. How long does pending last, and do we know when it ends? (Share state stable.) This sets how long a restored share is pinned (see "Limits").
  7. Does a snapshot change the IOPS or latency of the share while it is taken, while it holds a lot of changes, and while a restore from it is pending?
  8. Does a snapshot use the share's free space (the driver's capacity numbers) or is it billed and counted apart? Check df before and after. The price per GB-hour for dp2 snapshots is not in the pages above; read it from the catalog (ibmcloud-global-catalog-pricing) before we promise a cost.
  9. What IAM role does the driver's API key need to create, list, delete snapshots and to make a share from a snapshot? Check the key from API-KEY-SETUP.md.
  10. Two pages disagree on what happens to a share backup when its share is deleted. One says the backups are deleted. Another says backups "remain available". Check with the share's own snapshots too. The design assumes the safe reading: they are deleted with the share.
  11. Does a share made from a snapshot keep our folder layout and file owners? Expected yes. Check that a KubeVirt disk file boots from it, and that the mount target we create (in security_group mode) works on it with sec=sys.
  12. Does the VPC replication of a share carry its snapshots to a replica in another zone? (This is how a pool snapshot could survive the loss of a zone. The driver does not use VPC replication today. This check only sizes an option.)

docs.title: What exists today (from the code)
docs.text:
• A pool is one or more dp2 shares in one zone. A volume is a folder /pvcs/pvc-<uuid> on one share. The SubVolume records the share (shareID, shareMountTargetIP, shareExportPath), the folder and the claim.
  • A PV carries the share's address in its volumeAttributes (server, share, subDir). A PV's attributes cannot be changed after it is made. The node plugin reads them in NodeStageVolume. It already reads the SubVolume for the clone gate.
  • A pool cannot adopt a share that already exists. Shares are made by the pool manager only.
  • The controller has no NFS access. Everything that touches files runs as a Job that mounts the share (pkg/pool/share_job*.go).
  • Freezing a running VM's file systems through the guest agent already exists (pkg/vmsnap, pkg/vmcopy). The guest thaws by itself after 30 seconds at most.
  • A backup of a plain volume is a hard-link folder made by rsync from the live folder. A backup of a running VM is a QEMU copy that sends only changed blocks.
  • BackupRestore and the browse and file-restore design already copy a backup into a new claim, with the access rules by the namespace of the claim.
  • Metrics, alert rules, a console plugin and a release-test harness exist.

docs.title: Design that meets the goal
docs.text: Four parts: a pool snapshot (one moment for all shares), pool snapshot policies (schedule and keep time), volume recovery from a pool snapshot (no effect on others), and pool recovery (new shares, then a controlled switch).

docs.title: 1. Taking a pool snapshot
docs.text:
A new cluster resource, PoolSnapshot. It names a pool, and its status lists one VPC share snapshot per share of the pool. The controller makes it, on a schedule or on request.

Steps, in order:

  1. Write the manifest. A short Job on each share writes /.pool-manifest.json at the share root: the list of volumes on that share with their claim (namespace and name), size, folder, owner and mode, VM chain files, and clone state, and the pool's name. The snapshot then carries it. This is what lets us recover a volume whose SubVolume is gone, and tell the administrator what a restore will lose. (The PoolSnapshot status holds only the counts and a hash, so it stays small with thousands of volumes.)
  2. Freeze (optional, on by default for VMs). For each running VM that has a disk on the pool, ask the guest agent to freeze, as the VM snapshot code does now. The freeze runs for one short window. The window is bounded: the controller thaws everything when all share snapshots have been called, or after a time limit (default 20 seconds, never above the guest's own 30), whichever comes first. The status records, for each VM, FileSystemConsistent or CrashConsistent and why. A VM with no guest agent is taken as crash consistent. A plain volume is a file copy, as today.
  3. Call the snapshots in parallel, one per share, tagged pool-csi:<pool>:<snapshot name>. The calls go through the driver's client with its rate limit. With 10 shares this needs about two seconds.
  4. Thaw.
  5. Wait for each snapshot to be stable. Record its fingerprint and its captured_at time.

Same moment across shares. One share snapshot is one moment for its share. Several shares are called within a second or two of each other, not at the same instant. IBM gives no way to snapshot several shares as one unit. The effect: - A volume is entirely on one share. For every volume, and every VM disk, the snapshot is one moment. This is the case that matters. - A VM with disks on two shares could see its disks about one or two seconds apart. With the freeze on, the guest wrote nothing between the two calls, so the disks agree. Without a freeze, the guest sees a crash between its disks, which a file system or database normally repairs. - The status records the spread (latest captured_at minus earliest) and the list of VMs that have disks on more than one share. A spread above a limit (default 10 seconds) makes the snapshot Degraded, and the policy takes another. - Phase 0 check 1 may show that the spread is zero. Then this section simplifies.

A VM with a chain of instant snapshots is safe: the chain files are plain files on the share, so the snapshot has them all.

Failures. If one share cannot be snapshotted (degraded, rate limit, API error), the controller deletes the snapshots it made for this pool snapshot and retries, up to a limit. It never leaves a half pool snapshot marked ready. The pool snapshot states are Pending, Ready, Degraded (taken, but spread too large or a freeze failed) and Failed. Only Ready is offered for a pool recovery. Degraded is still usable for single volume recovery.

Share state. A share that is itself pending after a restore cannot be snapshotted (see "Limits"). The policy skips it and raises an alert.

docs.title: 2. Schedules and keep time
docs.text:
A new cluster resource, PoolSnapshotPolicy: pool, schedule (an interval such as 1h, minimum 15 minutes), keepFor (default 3d) and keepLast (default 6, the minimum number to keep whatever their age), freeze (VMs by default, or None), and suspend.

The driver runs the schedule. We do not use IBM Backup for VPC for the pool snapshots. Reasons, in plain words: - IBM's plans run per share and know nothing of the others. They cannot give one moment across a pool, cannot freeze guests, and cannot write the manifest. - They need a service-to-service authorization and an account-level policy (10 per region). That is more setup, and a failure there is silent. - The driver still marks its snapshots with a user tag, so an administrator sees them in the IBM console.

Removal of old snapshots: the controller deletes the share snapshots of a pool snapshot that is older than keepFor, keeping at least keepLast. It never deletes a pool snapshot that a restore uses. The limits that bound the plan: 750 snapshots per share and 100 TB of snapshot data per share, and one snapshot a minute. At an hourly schedule with 3 days kept, a share holds about 72. The webhook refuses a policy whose keepFor / schedule is above 500 (the margin leaves room for manual snapshots).

Space and cost. A snapshot holds only the changes since the one before it. A pool where VMs rewrite a lot (disk images change all the time) grows faster than a pool of documents. The first policy shows the snapshot size in its status (read from the VPC, which reports it within 15 minutes) so the administrator sees the growth. The price is per GB-hour, to verify (check 8).

docs.title: 3. Recovering one volume or VM disk from a pool snapshot
docs.text:
This is the case that matters most, and it needs no new share and no wait.

The pool snapshot shows each old moment of the share as a read-only folder: /.snapshot/<fingerprint>/. A volume's folder at that moment is /.snapshot/<fingerprint>/pvcs/pvc-<uuid>. The existing restore Job already copies a folder into a new claim. It gets one new source: this path. So:

  • kubectl backup list --pool-snapshots shows the moments of a claim. kubectl backup restore --from-pool-snapshot <name> --pvc NS/NAME --to-pvc NEW makes a new PVC with the contents at that moment. It never writes over an existing volume. The new PVC is held back from pods until the copy ends, like a restore today.
  • For a VM, --vm NS/NAME restores all its disks at the one moment. It prints the disk names; the user attaches them to a VM. (Same as for backups.)
  • The manifest tells us the claim's original size, owner and mode, and the chain files, so a deleted volume can be restored too. The new volume's SubVolume gets the chain list from the manifest.
  • The copy time grows with the size of the volume. A 500 GB disk takes minutes, not seconds. Phase 0 measures it. A later phase may offer an instant variant (below).
  • Other tenants are not touched. The Job reads one folder, read-only, and writes only into the new volume. The tenants' live folders are never written.

Files in the browse feature. The browse and file-restore design (2026-10-22-backup-file-restore.md) works on a path. A pool snapshot is one more source for it: the same helper pod, with the read-only mount of one /.snapshot/<fingerprint>/pvcs/<volume> folder. File-level restore from a pool snapshot then comes at no new design cost. It is a later phase.

Instant variant (later, optional). Make a new share from the snapshot, and point a PV at the volume's folder on it. A VM boots at once while IBM copies the data. This is VMware's "instant recovery". It adds a tenant volume on a recovery share, and later needs a move into the live pool. It is not needed to meet the goal, so it comes last.

docs.title: 4. Recovering the whole pool
docs.text:
IBM can only restore into new shares. So a pool recovery has two stages. The first is safe and changes nothing. The second is the switch, and the administrator approves it.

A new cluster resource, PoolRestore: pool, poolSnapshot, and mode.

Stage 1: side by side (changes nothing). - For each share, make a new share from its snapshot: same profile, zone and encryption, the same size, the same IOPS, a mount target in the same subnet and security group as the original (the driver's own function makes it). The shares are made in parallel, so the time is that of one share (30 to 90 seconds for the API, plus the pointer setup; phase 0 check 5 gives the real figure). The size of the data does not matter, because the new share starts with pointers. - The status shows, for each share, the new share, its state, and whether IBM's copy has ended. - The manifests are read (by a Job on each new share) and compared with the live SubVolume list. The status reports three lists: volumes in both (will be back as they were), volumes created after the snapshot (their data is not in the snapshot; they will be lost by a switch), and folders in the snapshot with no volume now (deleted since; they can be restored one by one). - At this point the administrator can already recover single volumes from the new shares if they want, or stop and delete them.

Stage 2: the switch (the administrator approves it). A switch is a planned outage of the pool. It needs the administrator to say approve: true on the PoolRestore, after reading the three lists. 1. Quiesce. The pool refuses new volumes (retriable error, as when a pool is expanding). The controller lists the pods that use claims of this pool. It does not stop other people's workloads. The administrator stops them, or sets force: true, which accepts that those pods lose their mount. The switch waits until none remain (or force). 2. Switch each share. The pool's share list and every matching SubVolume get the address of the new share (shareID, mount target, export path). The old shares leave the pool and become retired. They are not deleted. Their snapshots stay too (the pool snapshot stays pinned, see "Limits"). 3. Mark the lost volumes. A SubVolume for a volume created after the snapshot has no folder on the new share. It is marked LostByRestore. The node plugin refuses to mount it (the same way the clone gate does, with a clear message). It must never give a pod a silent empty folder. The administrator decides: delete it, or restore it from a backup. 4. Node plugin reads the address from the SubVolume. This is a change to NodeStageVolume: the PV's own attributes are old after a switch and cannot be edited, so the node plugin uses the SubVolume's current share address when it differs. Without this change a switch would need every PV to be deleted and made again. 5. Unquiesce. Pods can start. Their claims mount the new shares. 6. Old shares. Kept for retireFor (default 7 days), then listed for deletion. Deletion is a separate confirmed command, never automatic. This is the rollback: before then, a second PoolRestore can switch back. (The old shares still hold the data from after the snapshot, including what the ransomware did. The administrator may need them for a forensic look.)

Other modes. - mode: Copy: leave the live pool as it is, and copy chosen volumes out of the new shares. This is the same as stage 1 plus single volume recovery. It does not need an outage, but it takes time in proportion to the data. It does not meet "minutes, any size" for a whole pool. - There is no restore in place. IBM does not offer it.

The honest gap: the first hours after a switch. While IBM copies the data into a restored share, that share is pending. We cannot snapshot it or replicate it, and the snapshot we restored from cannot be deleted. So for a period after a pool recovery there is no pool snapshot of the new shares. The length depends on the data and is unknown until check 6. During it, the driver's backups to the snapshot pool continue, and the administrator is told in the pool status and by an alert. If the lab shows this is many hours for a large pool, it is the main weakness of this design, and the answer is to keep the backups running and to not restore a pool to a share that is ransomware-affected twice in a row.

docs.title: Tenancy and access (RBAC)
docs.text:
• Pool snapshots are an administrator thing. PoolSnapshot, PoolSnapshotPolicy and PoolRestore are cluster resources. Only cluster administrators (the chart's admin ClusterRole) can see or change them. Tenants never see the pool, the shares, or other tenants' volumes.
  • A tenant can recover their own volumes with the same rule as backups: the right is by the namespace of the claim that owned the data. The gateway from the file-restore spec (or the plain BackupRestore path) checks it as the user. The rights-only name is backupfiles, as there. A new pair of verbs is not needed: reading a pool snapshot's copy of a volume of namespace A needs get backupfiles in A, and making the new PVC needs the usual rights in the target namespace. A person without the right gets "forbidden", and cannot tell whether the volume exists.
  • A deleted namespace. The manifest records the namespace of each volume. If the namespace is gone, only an administrator can restore it.
  • A pool snapshot never gives a tenant a view of the share. The restore Job mounts one volume's folder only, read-only, and the tenant sees the result only as a new PVC. The Job runs in the driver namespace with the same safety rules as the other jobs: paths checked against the folder pattern, no links followed, nothing written outside the new volume.
  • Ransomware thinking. An attacker with the cluster admin role, or with the VPC API key, can delete a share and its snapshots with it. Pool snapshots are not a lock. For that, use the COS export with a Compliance lock (step 9). Say so in the docs.

docs.title: How it works with backups and replication
docs.text:
• Backup from a share snapshot (the steady source). A backup of a plain volume reads from /.snapshot/<fingerprint>/pvcs/<volume> of the newest Ready pool snapshot, instead of the live folder. A read-only, frozen source gives a true same-moment copy of every plain volume of the pool, which the live rsync cannot. The backup's consistency for these volumes changes from FileCopy to CrashConsistent (the state of the share at one moment). The backup policy gets a source field: Live (today, the default) or PoolSnapshot. It needs a PoolSnapshotPolicy on the pool, and the backup waits for a snapshot that is newer than its last run, or asks for one.
  • VM disks keep the QEMU path. A running VM's backup is a QEMU copy that sends only changed blocks, and it is file-system consistent with the freeze. Reading a whole disk file from a snapshot every time would read all its blocks, because a file snapshot has no change list. So VM disks do not move to the snapshot source. A stopped VM's disk can use it.
  • Replication. A replication of a plain volume (rsync) can read from the snapshot too (source: PoolSnapshot on the policy), for the same reason. VM replication does not change.
  • A pool snapshot is not a backup. It is on the same share and zone. It dies with the share and the zone. The documents will say this in the first paragraph, and the console will show "same share" on it.
  • Snapshot of the backup pool. A PoolSnapshotPolicy can name a snapshot pool too. That protects backups from a mistaken delete of folders (not from a deleted share).
  • Zone loss. IBM copies snapshots to a zonal replica share. If phase 0 check 12 passes, a later phase may offer an option to make a replica of each share. This is a separate feature (cost: a second set of shares) and is not in the build plan.

docs.title: Limits and rules
docs.text:
• 750 snapshots per share, 100 TB per share, one a minute. The policy checks these and refuses a plan that cannot fit.
  • A share in pending after a restore cannot be snapshotted, and the snapshot it came from cannot be deleted until the copy ends. The controller pins that pool snapshot and does not remove it.
  • The first snapshot of a share copies all its contents. Phase 0 checks how long the first one takes and what it does to the IOPS of a busy share.
  • A pool snapshot of a pool that is expanding or draining includes only the shares that exist and are stable at that moment. The status lists them. A share added later is not in it. A restore of that pool snapshot does not touch the later share.
  • A share that is failed or degraded cannot be snapshotted. The pool snapshot becomes Failed and the policy retries.
  • All share snapshots of one pool snapshot have the same keep time.
  • A pool snapshot is useless once a share is deleted (its snapshots go with it). The controller refuses to remove a share from the pool or delete it while a Ready pool snapshot depends on it, unless the administrator uses force.
  • No tiers special case: all shares in all tiers of a pool are in the pool snapshot.

docs.title: Monitoring and alerts
docs.text:
New metrics (listed in MONITORING.md when they are built): - pool_snapshot_total (by pool and result), pool_snapshot_duration_seconds, pool_snapshot_spread_seconds - pool_snapshot_age_seconds (newest Ready for each pool), pool_snapshot_count (by pool) - pool_snapshot_share_bytes (snapshot size, by pool and share) - pool_snapshot_freeze_failures_total - pool_restore_phase (by pool), pool_restore_share_pending (shares still copying)

New alert rules, in the chart with rule tests: - no Ready pool snapshot within twice the schedule - a pool snapshot Degraded or Failed three times in a row - a share with more than 600 snapshots (limit 750) - snapshot data above 50 percent of the share size - a restored share pending for more than 24 hours - a pool with a policy but no snapshot after a restore (the gap above)

docs.title: Console and command line
docs.text:
• Command line: kubectl pool-snapshots already exists for VM flatten. Add kubectl pool-snapshots take|list|delete, and kubectl pool-restore plan|start|approve|status|retire. kubectl backup restore --from-pool-snapshot is for volumes (tenant-safe, goes through the access checks).
  • Console (administrator): a Pool snapshots page for each pool: the list with state, time, spread and size; "Take now"; the policy form; a Restore wizard that shows the three lists and the quiesce list before the approve button. A tenant sees their volume's restore points, under the existing volume page, once the file-restore console work lands.
  • Every dangerous step (approve a switch, force, delete retired shares) asks the user to type the pool name.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Unit (fakes). The fake VPC client gets share snapshots and share-from-snapshot. Tests: all-or-nothing creation (one share fails, the others are deleted); the spread rule; the freeze window ends at the time limit; the manifest has every volume; retention keeps keepLast and never removes a pinned snapshot; the policy limits; the webhook refusals; the three lists of a PoolRestore; a switch updates every SubVolume and marks the lost ones; the node plugin uses the SubVolume address and refuses LostByRestore; from-pool-snapshot path checks (no .., no links); access checks per namespace.
  • Chart tests. Roles, the new CRDs, the alert rules (with promtool rule tests), the new values.
  • Release test stage on the lab (rovslab). Make a pool of two shares with a plain volume and a two-disk VM (one disk on each share if possible). Write known files with checksums. Take a pool snapshot with the freeze. Then: (1) delete a volume, restore it from the snapshot, check the checksums; (2) restore the VM's disks at the one moment and boot the VM; (3) run PoolRestore stage 1 and check the three lists; (4) switch (with the VM stopped) and check that the pods mount the new shares, a volume created after the snapshot is refused with a clear message, and the old shares are retired; (5) switch back. Clean up all shares at the end.
  • Failure test. Make the snapshot of the second share fail. The first share's snapshot must be deleted and the pool snapshot must be Failed.

docs.title: Build plan: phases, one PR each
docs.text:
Phase What Meets 0 Lab checks 1 to 12 of the IBM facts, with the numbers written into this spec. No product code. Decides the rest 1 VPC client: create, get, list, delete share snapshot and share-from-snapshot, in the real and fake clients. IAM check. Foundation 2 PoolSnapshot, the manifest Job, parallel snapshots, all-or-nothing, the freeze window, metrics. On request only. Use 1 (protect) 3 PoolSnapshotPolicy: schedule, keep time, limits, webhook, alerts, chart. Use 1 (protect) 4 Volume and VM disk recovery from a pool snapshot: the /.snapshot source for the restore Job, kubectl backup restore --from-pool-snapshot, access checks. Single-volume goal 5 PoolRestore stage 1 (side by side) and the three lists. Whole-pool goal (half) 6 PoolRestore stage 2: quiesce, switch, LostByRestore, node plugin reads the SubVolume, retired shares, rollback. Whole-pool goal 7 Backup and replication read from the snapshot (source: PoolSnapshot) for plain volumes. Use 2 8 Console pages and the release test stage. (Release-test pieces for earlier phases are added in those phases.) Usability 9 (optional) File-level browse from a pool snapshot; instant recovery volume. Extra

Size, honestly: phases 1 to 4 are about the size of the backup step 8 (new CRDs, a controller, a Job, a command). Phase 6 is the largest and riskiest: it changes how the node plugin finds a volume and moves every SubVolume of a pool. Total: about 8 PRs, 2 to 3 of them large.

docs.title: Does the design meet the goal?
docs.text: Part of the goal Met? Why Protect a whole pool, any size, snapshot in seconds Yes, if checks 1, 3 and 7 pass One snapshot call per share, in parallel Same moment for every volume Yes for each volume (one share each). Within about 2 seconds for a VM with disks on two shares, closed by the freeze IBM has no cross-share snapshot Recover a whole pool in minutes, any size Yes for the new shares and the switch, if checks 5 and 6 pass. IBM makes the new share from pointers, usable while pending Recover single volumes without affecting tenants Yes, by copy. The time grows with the volume The restore reads one read-only folder and writes a new PVC Whole-pool recovery in place No IBM has no restore in place. We use new shares and a switch Survive the loss of the share, zone or VPC No Snapshots live and die with the share. Use backups and COS for that Protect against an attacker who has the cloud API key No They can delete the share and its snapshots. Use a COS lock A pool snapshot of the new shares right after a restore No, for a time IBM forbids it while the share is pending Zero outage for a whole-pool recovery No A switch needs the pods to stop. Mode Copy avoids the outage but is slow

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Recommended: the design above (driver-run pool snapshots, /.snapshot single-volume recovery, side-by-side restore then a switch). Meets the goal except the rows marked No, which IBM's platform rules out.
  • Only IBM Backup for VPC plans on the shares, no driver code. Does not meet the goal. No same moment across shares, no freeze, no manifest, no volume-level recovery, no switch. It is cheap and may do for an administrator who only wants a safety net. It can run next to the design above.
  • Only single-volume recovery (phase 4), no pool recovery. Does not meet the goal (a whole pool would be recovered volume by volume, at the speed of the data). Useful first step; it is phases 1 to 4.
  • Restore a pool by copying all volumes out. Does not meet "minutes, any size". It is mode Copy.

docs.title: Cost, effort and risk
docs.text:
• IBM cost. Snapshot storage in GB-hours (price to verify, check 8). A restored share costs as a normal share for as long as it exists, so a stage 1 that nobody switches or deletes is a bill. The controller reports restored shares older than 7 days. A switch leaves the old shares billed until deleted (default 7 days).
  • Effort. About 8 PRs. The riskiest are phase 6 (the switch) and the first lab numbers (phase 0). If check 5 shows that a restored share is slow while pending, the "minutes" promise is weaker, and the spec must be changed before phase 5 starts.
  • Risk: the switch. It changes where every volume of a pool lives. Mitigations: nothing is deleted, the old shares are retired and can be switched back, the lost volumes are blocked not emptied, and the administrator must approve after seeing three lists.
  • Risk: freeze. A freeze of many VMs for 20 seconds can stall their I/O. It is off for freeze: None. The time limit is hard. A freeze failure makes a VM CrashConsistent, never blocks the snapshot.
  • Risk: false safety. A pool snapshot is not a backup. The documents, the console and the alert text say so.
  • Risk: IBM facts wrong. Twelve checks are listed in phase 0. Phases 2 and later do not start until the checks that they depend on are written into this spec.
  • Docs to update when built: FEATURES.md, BACKUP-RECOVERY.md, CRD-SPEC.md (new CRDs), MONITORING.md, HELM-VALUES.md, CONSISTENCY-MODEL.md (the line that says "this driver does not use share snapshots"), KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md, API-KEY-SETUP.md (new IAM rights), CHANGELOG.md, a new tutorial.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Pool snapshots are an extra tool. They do not replace per-volume snapshots or backups.
  • The driver runs the schedule. We do not use IBM Backup for VPC plans for pool snapshots.
  • A pool snapshot is one VPC share snapshot per share, called in parallel. It is Ready only if all of them worked, else all are removed.
  • Running VMs are frozen for a short, bounded window by default. A failed freeze gives a crash-consistent copy and never stops the snapshot.
  • A manifest of the volumes is written onto each share before the snapshot, so a deleted volume can be recovered and a restore can say what it loses.
  • A single volume or VM disk is recovered by copying from the read-only /.snapshot folder into a new PVC. It never writes over a live volume.
  • A whole-pool recovery uses new shares from the snapshots. It has two stages: side by side first, then a switch that the administrator approves.
  • The switch needs the pool's pods to be stopped. The driver does not stop other people's workloads by itself. force is the administrator's choice.
  • Volumes created after the snapshot are blocked from mounting after a switch, not given an empty folder.
  • Old shares are retired, kept 7 days, and deleted only by a confirmed command. That is the rollback.
  • The node plugin will read a volume's share address from the SubVolume, because a PV's own address cannot be changed.
  • Default schedule floor is 15 minutes. Default keep time is 3 days and at least 6 snapshots.
  • Backup and replication of plain volumes can read from a pool snapshot (opt in). VM disks keep the QEMU path, because it sends only changed blocks.
  • Tenants may recover their own volumes using the same namespace rule as backups. Pool snapshots, shares and restores of a whole pool are administrator only.
  • Pool snapshots are not protection against loss of the share, the zone, or the VPC API key. The documents say so plainly.
  • Phase 0 (lab checks) comes first, and later phases wait for the numbers they depend on.

docs.title: Spec: continuous data protection for VMs (RPO of seconds)
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-22. Status: draft for review. Nothing in this spec is built yet.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Tier-1 VMs (databases, ERP) lose at most a few seconds of writes when the source site is lost. The DR site can start the VM as it was at any chosen second in a retention window. This is what Zerto and Veeam CDP offer.

"Done" means a lab test passes on two clusters in different VPCs:

  • A write-heavy VM runs. We kill its source node in the middle of a write burst.
  • The VM starts at the DR site at the newest safe second. At most 5 seconds of acknowledged writes are missing.
  • We pick an earlier second from the last 4 hours. The VM starts as it was at that second. Checksums of files written before that second match. Nothing written after it is present.
  • A VM with several disks shows the same second on every disk.
  • The VM's disk writes are not slowed by more than the limit in "Effect on the VM".

Two parts of the goal need care, and this spec says so plainly:

  • RPO of seconds through a live migration or a node crash. One of the two ways to tap the writes (the QEMU tap) cannot do this. It loses the journal for the time it takes to resync. The other way (the file-system tap) can. See "Which write tap".
  • One exact second across several VMs. No design can promise it, because the VMs write on different nodes. We offer coordinated bookmarks instead. See "Several VMs".

docs.title: Words used here
docs.text:
• RPO: how much recent data you lose. "RPO 5 seconds" means the last 5 seconds of writes may be missing.
  • Journal: an ordered record of every write to a disk. With it you can rebuild the disk as it was at any second.
  • Write tap: the part that sees each write of a running VM disk and passes a copy on.
  • Relay: a small service on the source node. It receives the copies from the tap, keeps them in order, and sends them to the DR site.
  • Bookmark: a marked point in the journal where the guest file systems were frozen. A VM started from a bookmark needs no file-system check.
  • Batch: all writes of one short window (1 second by default), joined into one unit. Each batch end is a point you can recover to.
  • Undo journal: at the DR site, the old contents of every block that a batch changed. It is the finer form of the undo files that exist today.
  • Crash consistent: the disk looks as after a power cut. A database repairs itself from that state.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
All facts in this section come from the code and the docs in this repository.

  • Replication of a running VM is a QEMU copy of all disks at one moment, on a schedule (5 minutes is the practical floor). The controller sends QMP commands (QEMU's control commands) through virsh in the VM pod (pkg/vmcopy). Red Hat does not support this. The owner accepted that on 20 Oct.
  • Between copies QEMU keeps a change list (a dirty bitmap) in memory. The next copy sends only the changed blocks. A live migration or a restart erases the list (lab, 20 Oct). The next copy is then a full compare pass.
  • The copy goes to the destination through the receiver: an HTTPS service with a bearer token (pkg/replication/receiver*.go). The call model is one session per copy: upload a staging file, compare, commit.
  • At the destination, ApplyCopy first writes the old contents of every block it will change into an undo file, then writes the new blocks. The disk always holds the newest copy. Undo files give restore points for 24 hours by default (restorePointKeepHours). Rewind builds an older disk by copying the newest one and applying undo files backward. kubectl failover plan|execute --rewind-to uses it. A disk that a VM has run on cannot be rewound.
  • Unfinished applies are rolled back at failover (Recover).
  • A copy cannot run during a live migration. The controller cancels the copy when it sees the move. Long copies slow the VM: the lab saw 10 to 20 times slower writes when the copy shared the VM's file share.
  • Instant snapshots (snap-*.qcow2 overlay files) need the KubeVirt Sidecar gate, which Red Hat does not support. The hook is a sidecar container in the VM pod.
  • Issue #89 and PR #105 gave the receiver its own ServiceAccount with no role, no API token, no capabilities, a token check in constant time, and a rule that it writes only into pvc-<uuid> folders. TLS on by default was left for later.
  • IBM file share replication runs at most every 15 minutes (the FAQ says hourly; verify). It does not meet this goal. docs/specs/2026-10-22-zone-loss.md (PR #199) says the same.
  • CROSS-REGION-DR.md rejects file-level streaming (inotify) because NFS gives no write events. That reasoning does not apply here. We tap writes inside QEMU or in a mount that we control, not on the share.

docs.title: Key questions this design answers
docs.text: Question Answer Can QEMU send every write of a running disk somewhere else? Yes. blockdev-mirror copies a disk's writes to a target over NBD, in background or write-blocking mode. Docs: "blockdev-mirror: Start mirroring a block device's writes to a new destination." write-blocking: "when data is written to the source, write it (synchronously) to the target as well." background: "copy data in background only." A running job can switch from background to write-blocking, but not back (QEMU commit "mirror: implement mirror_change method", 2023). Does a mirror give us a journal? No. A mirror makes the target a copy of the disk. It sends no log of writes, no order and no time. The journal must come from our own server at the other end of the connection. Is background mode enough? No. It copies blocks later, from a list of changed blocks. It gives no order across disks and no history. Only write-blocking gives a usable order. Can today's restore points grow into a journal? Partly. The model stays: the disk holds the newest data, and undo records go back in time. The format and the calls are new. Today one undo file covers one copy. A journal needs thousands of small records an hour, and a way to stop in the middle of a file. How do all disks of a VM stay at the same second? All disks' writes must pass one sequencer on the source node, with the mirror in write-blocking mode. Separate mirror jobs have no shared order. The relay (below) is that sequencer. Does it work for plain volumes, not only VM disks? Not in this design. The QEMU tap sees only VM disks. A file-system tap could also see plain volumes, but a folder of files also needs create, rename and delete in the journal. That is a much larger job, and it is out of scope. Does Red Hat support it? Not the QEMU tap: the driver works with QEMU directly, as today's VM copies do. The sidecar tap would also need the Sidecar gate. The file-system tap changes nothing in KubeVirt or QEMU, but we must ask Red Hat whether a CSI driver that serves files through a user-space mount is supported (to verify). What if the link to DR is slow? With a relay on the same node, write-blocking waits for the relay, not for the DR site. The link then decides how far the DR site lags, not how fast the VM writes. What happens on a live migration? Probably the mirror stops and a resync is needed (not proven). The QEMU docs say lists of changed blocks can move with a VM, but our lab lost them, so this is probably off under libvirt. Phase 0 tests it. Can IBM share replication do this instead? No. It copies every 15 minutes or more (IBM docs).

docs.title: Research: QEMU and KubeVirt facts
docs.text:
Sources are the official docs. Items marked "verify in the lab" are not proven for our VM pods (libvirt 10.10, QEMU 9.1 on OpenShift 4.21).
