  1. Mirror jobs. blockdev-mirror mirrors a node of the block graph to a target that we create with blockdev-add. Sync modes: full, top, none (only new writes), bitmap. After the job is ready, "the source and destination are synchronized". Cancelling it then leaves a point-in-time copy. Completing it switches the guest to the target. Source: Live Block Device Operations, QMP reference.
  2. Copy mode. copy-mode is background (default) or write-blocking (since QEMU 3.0). query-block-jobs shows actively-synced. Source: QMP reference. The docs do not say what happens to the guest when the target stalls. Verify in the lab.
  3. NBD as target. QEMU's NBD client connects out. The VM pod forwards incoming connections to the guest (lab, 20 Oct), but outgoing connections work. The nbd block driver has reconnect options (reconnect-delay). Verify the exact option names for QEMU 9.1.
  4. Dirty bitmaps. In-memory bitmaps track writes. Only qcow2 files can store a bitmap on disk. Our disks are raw, so bitmaps are in memory only. The docs say bitmaps can migrate with a live migration. Our lab lost them. Verify why. Source: Dirty Bitmaps and Incremental Backup.
  5. Backup and fleecing. blockdev-backup copies a point in time. The copy-before-write filter copies the old contents of a cluster to a target before the guest overwrites it. It has target, bitmap, on-cbw-error, cbw-timeout and min-cluster-size. discard-source exists since QEMU 9.1. This is built for a point in time, not for a stream of every write. Source: QMP reference.
  6. qemu-storage-daemon. A long-running QEMU process without a VM. It builds block nodes, exports them (NBD, vhost-user-blk, FUSE, VDUSE), runs block jobs, and is controlled by QMP. NBD servers can use TLS through --object tls-creds-*. Exports are read-only unless writable=on. Source: qemu-storage-daemon. It has no write journal of its own.
  7. KubeVirt and OpenShift Virtualization backup. Changed block tracking arrives in KubeVirt v1.8. Veeam says it is a Tech Preview in OpenShift 4.22 and that Kasten reads QEMU's dirty bitmap. It is a periodic backup API (push a full or changed-block copy), not a write stream. It cannot give an RPO of seconds. The gate name and the API shape are not confirmed. Sources: Veeam blog, Red Hat 4.22 release notes (I could not read the Technology Preview section; verify).
  8. Hook sidecar. Our hook can change the VM's domain XML before start, as the instant snapshot hook does. It needs the Sidecar gate.

docs.title: Options compared
docs.text:
Each option is tested against the goal. "Goal" means: RPO of seconds in steady state, any second in the window, one second on all disks of a VM.

# Option Steady-state RPO of seconds Any second Same second on all disks Survives live migration with no RPO loss Survives node crash with no divergence Effect on VM Meets the goal? 1 blockdev-mirror straight to an NBD server at the DR site In background mode, no bound. In write-blocking mode, yes, but every write waits for the WAN round trip (10 to 30 ms between regions) Only if the DR server journals No (one job per disk, no shared order) No No Severe in write-blocking No. Fails on write speed or on order 2 blockdev-mirror in write-blocking mode to a node-local relay, which journals and ships to DR (the QEMU tap) Yes Yes (1 s batches) Yes (one relay orders all disks) No. The mirror stops. A resync of unknown size follows Not unless the relay keeps a durable spool Small (the relay answers from memory) In steady state, yes. Not through a migration or a crash. 3 blockdev-backup or copy-before-write with fleecing, run every few seconds No. A cycle needs a guest freeze (0.1 to 0.2 s) and the lab saw 10 to 20 times slower writes during a copy. A 10 second cycle is not workable Only at cycle points Yes (one transaction) No Yes Severe No. Keep it as the fallback when the journal breaks 4 Write-splitting layer in the hook sidecar: qemu-storage-daemon exports the disk to the VM over NBD (loopback) and tees writes to a journal Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes (with a durable spool) All reads and writes pass one more hop. Breaks the instant snapshot and QEMU copy code, because the file leaves the VM's own block graph Yes, at the highest cost, and it needs the Sidecar gate 5 File-system tap (new): the CSI node plugin serves the VM disk file through a user-space mount that tees each write to the relay (the file-system tap) Yes Yes Yes (one daemon per node orders all disks) Yes Yes (with a durable spool) Every read and write passes the user-space daemon. Highest risk to I/O speed Yes, if its speed is acceptable 6 KubeVirt incremental backup (changed block tracking) No (periodic) No Yes Yes (supported API) Yes Moderate No. A good later replacement for the periodic copy 7 Synchronous mirror to DR, write-blocking straight to a receiver within the same region (round trip 2 ms or less) RPO 0 Yes if journaled Needs the relay No Yes Adds one round trip to every write Yes, for zone loss only. Not for cross-region 8 IBM share replication No (15 minutes or more) No No n/a n/a None No. 9 In-guest or application replication (database log shipping, for example) Yes for that application Per application Per application Yes Yes Per application Outside the driver. Fine to use next to it

docs.title: In one paragraph
docs.text: A relay on each source node receives a copy of every write to the disks of protected VMs. It numbers the writes in the order they arrive, groups them into 1 second batches, compresses them and sends them over TLS to the receiver at the DR site. The receiver stores each batch durably, then applies it to the replica disk, after saving the old block contents in an undo journal. The replica disk always holds the newest data. So a failover to the newest second is as fast as today. A failover to an earlier second applies undo records backward. Bookmarks, made with a guest freeze every 5 minutes, mark points where the file systems are consistent.

docs.title: Which write tap
docs.text:
The tap is the part that sees each write. The relay, the transport, the DR journal, the failover and the console are the same for every tap. We build them once. The tap is replaceable, as the copy piece was for replication.

Tap 1: QEMU mirror into the relay (build first). - The controller sends QMP commands to the VM's QEMU, as pkg/vmcopy does today. It adds an NBD target that points at the node's relay, and starts blockdev-mirror with sync=none and copy-mode=write-blocking. Every guest write then goes to the disk file and to the relay. The guest write completes when both finish. - Order is correct: the guest issues a dependent write only after the first write completes. In write-blocking mode that means the relay already holds the first write. So any prefix of the relay's order is a state the disks could really have had. This is why one relay gives the same second on all disks. - The relay is a separate DaemonSet, not part of the CSI node plugin. A driver upgrade then does not drop the connection. The NBD client uses a reconnect delay, so a relay restart of a few seconds only pauses writes for that long (verify the option). - It needs no Sidecar gate. It needs QMP, which the driver already uses and which Red Hat does not support. - The limit: when a live migration or a crash ends the QEMU process, the job ends. The new QEMU has no job and no change list. See "Live migration and restart".

Tap 2: file-system tap (build if phase 0 says Tap 1's gap is not acceptable). - For a protected VM, the node plugin serves the disk folder through a FUSE mount (a file system that runs as a normal program). The program passes each read and write to the NFS share. It tees each write to the relay before it answers. - QEMU, libvirt and KubeVirt see an ordinary file. Nothing in the VM changes. Live migration and restart work, because no QEMU job is involved. Instant snapshot overlays and QEMU copies still work. - The relay on each node journals the writes of all disks on that node, in order. After a live migration, the new node's relay continues the same journal (see "Live migration and restart"). - The risk is speed and failure. Every I/O of a tier-1 VM passes through our program. If the program dies, the mount returns errors and the VM sees disk errors. Phase 0 measures the speed. Red Hat's view on support is still to verify.

Tap 3: sidecar with qemu-storage-daemon (option 4). We do not build it. It meets the goal like Tap 2, but it needs the Sidecar gate, it moves the disk out of the VM's own block graph, and so it breaks instant snapshots and the QEMU copies. Tap 2 has none of those costs.

Recommendation. The design that meets the whole goal is the journal with Tap 2. Tap 1 meets the goal in steady state only. We build the shared parts first with Tap 1, because it needs no new data-path program and it gives a working RPO of seconds early. Phase 0 and phase 2 results decide whether Tap 2 is also built. Tap 1 alone is labelled as not meeting the goal for migration and crash.

docs.title: Source side
docs.text:
Relay. One pod per node (DaemonSet, own ServiceAccount, no Kubernetes role). For each protected VM it holds a stream. - It accepts writes from the tap. For each write it records: stream number, sequence number, disk, offset, length, bytes, and the node clock time. - It adds an empty heartbeat batch every second, so an idle VM still shows a fresh time. - Every second it closes a batch. Overlapping writes inside one batch collapse into the last one. Batch ends are the recovery points. The batch length is a policy setting (batchInterval, 1 s; 100 ms to 10 s allowed). - It compresses each batch (zstd) and sends it. It sends over one TLS connection per stream. - It keeps a batch until the receiver says it is durable at DR. - Trim and write-zeroes commands are journaled as zero ranges, not as data.

What is in the write path. For Tap 1 the guest waits for the relay to accept the write into memory. It does not wait for the network to DR. Expected cost: a loopback round trip, well under 1 ms. We measure it in phase 0. The relay adds no I/O to the VM's file share, which is the big difference from the periodic copies. Those read the disk from the same share and slowed the VM 10 to 20 times in the lab.

Durability levels (policy setting spool.durability):

Level Where an unsent batch lives A relay or node crash loses Cost memory (default) Relay memory Up to the unsent tail: the batch window plus what the link has not carried None node-disk Node-local disk, written before the guest write completes Nothing, if only the relay restarts. The tail if the node is lost A local write per batch shared A small spool file on the pool share Nothing, even if the node is lost. The tail is read by another node's relay and sent One more NFS write per batch. Doubles the write latency on that share

The default is memory. A site loss loses at most the unsent tail either way, because the DR site holds only what has arrived. The levels matter for a relay restart, a node crash and divergence (below).

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
• One TLS 1.3 connection per stream, relay to receiver, with certificates on both sides (see Security).
  • Frames: open stream (policy, volume names, epoch), batch (sequence range, time, compressed records, checksum), bookmark, heartbeat, seal.
  • The receiver answers each batch with the highest sequence it holds durably. The relay frees buffers up to there.
  • Sizing the link: see "Bandwidth".
  • The relay sends batches in order, with a window of several unacknowledged batches. One slow batch does not stop the stream.

docs.title: DR side
docs.text:
The DR cluster runs the receiver, extended with a journal service. For each disk:

  1. Receive. A batch is written to a staging journal on the DR share and flushed. The receiver then tells the relay "durable up to sequence N". This is the moment that counts for the RPO.
  2. Apply. An apply worker reads the staging batches in order. For each batch it reads the old contents of the blocks, appends them to the undo journal and flushes it, and writes the new blocks to disk.img. It then records "applied up to sequence N". The staging batch can be deleted after that. If the receiver stops in the middle, recovery knows the batch from the staging journal and the undo journal. It can finish the batch or roll it back.
  3. Result. disk.img holds the newest second. The undo journal holds how to go back.

Undo journal format. Append-only segments, one per minute. Each record: sequence, batch time, disk, offset, old data. A batch is complete only when its end marker is written. A rewind to second T applies records backward from the newest batch down to the first batch whose time is after T. It stops at a batch end, never inside a batch.

Why not keep only after-images and apply them late (the way Zerto describes its journal). Then the replica disk is hours behind. A failover to the newest second must replay hours of writes first. A failover to the newest second is the common case in a disaster, so we keep the disk current and pay for it with extra reads and writes at the DR site (below).

DR cost per incoming byte. One read of the old block, one write to the undo journal, one write to the disk. That is about 3 operations per changed block. DR shares need room for this. See "Bandwidth and size".

docs.title: Retention in two tiers
docs.text:
• Seconds tier (window, default 4 hours): every batch end is a recovery point. The undo journal keeps this.
  • Minutes tier (existing restorePointKeepHours, default 24 hours): after the seconds window, a background task merges the undo journal into one undo file per 5 minutes, using the same format as today. The restore points of the existing model take over.
  • Beyond 24 hours: backups (existing). A BackupPolicy keeps working as before.

The merge keeps the oldest block contents of each 5 minute span. A rewind to a second older than window lands on the nearest 5 minute point.

docs.title: Checkpoints with guest freeze (bookmarks)
docs.text:
• Every bookmarkInterval (default 5 minutes) the controller freezes the guest through the guest agent, as it does for copies today. The relay writes a bookmark into every disk's stream between the freeze and the thaw. The guest is paused about 0.15 s.
  • A VM without a guest agent gets a crash-consistent bookmark and the status says why, as today.
  • A bookmark is a recovery point at which file systems are consistent. A second between bookmarks is crash consistent. A database recovers from a crash-consistent state. A bookmark is better for applications that do not.
  • Lifecycle hooks (existing) run before the freeze, so an application can flush.
  • Bookmark IDs are random and unique. The same ID goes into every disk and, for a group, into every VM (below).

docs.title: Several disks of one VM
docs.text: One relay orders the writes of all disks on the node. Every batch end is the same second on all disks. Failover picks one second and applies it to every disk of the VM. The existing planner already refuses to mix moments across disks of a VM.

docs.title: Several VMs (protection groups)
docs.text:
• What we can promise. A bookmark ID shared by all VMs in a group. A coordinated freeze of the group, one VM after another, in under about 1 second in total. A recovery to that bookmark gives a consistent state per VM, and an application-consistent state across the group for applications that tolerate that.
  • What we cannot promise. One exact crash-consistent second across VMs on different nodes. The VMs write on different machines. No single writer sees their order. We can cut by clock time, and the node clocks differ by some milliseconds (chrony). A message from VM A to VM B that arrives faster than the skew can end up on the wrong side of the cut. The status shows the measured skew.
  • Zerto's protection groups are the same idea. A group is optional. By default each VM is on its own.

docs.title: Network loss
docs.text:
The relay never lets the network slow the VM, unless the policy says so.

  1. Buffer. Unsent batches stay in memory, up to spool.memoryMiB per VM (default 512), then spill to a node-local spool file up to spool.diskGiB per VM (default 10).
  2. Alert. CDPLagging fires when the RPO passes rpoWarning (default 15 s). CDPJournalBroken fires at the next step.
  3. Overflow. When both buffers are full, policy onOverflow decides:
  4. degrade (default): the relay stops journaling for this VM and tells the controller. The VM keeps full speed. The controller falls back to the existing periodic copy (5 minutes), which still has its change list. When the link returns, the copy catches up and the journal restarts from a fresh baseline. The recovery range has a hole for the broken time. The status and the console show it.
  5. block: the relay slows the guest's writes until there is room. The RPO stays bounded. The VM slows or stops during a long outage. For customers who prefer a slow VM to a hole.
  6. Catch-up after a hole. The journal does not know which blocks changed in the hole. The periodic copy's change list does (Tap 1: QEMU's list, kept always on as the safety net). The catch-up sends only those blocks. The journal is valid again from the end of the catch-up (see "Starting a journal").

docs.title: Starting a journal
docs.text:
At the start, and after every hole, the DR disk must match the source disk at some moment, and the journal must have no gap after it.

  1. Start the change list in the same QEMU step as today's copy (it already does block-dirty-bitmap-add in a transaction).
  2. Send the copy as today, as the baseline. Or send a catch-up copy of only the changed blocks.
  3. Start the mirror (sync=none, write-blocking) after the baseline starts. Writes between the baseline moment and the mirror start are in the change list. A catch-up copy sends them.
  4. Replaying the journal on top of a baseline and a catch-up gives a correct disk from the end of the catch-up onward. Blocks that were written in both windows end up right because the journal replays in order.

So the recovery range of a new journal starts at the end of the catch-up, not at the baseline moment. Before that, the periodic restore points apply.

Bench for this step: write a pattern into a VM during a start, then compare checksums of the DR disk. This is a phase 1 test.

docs.title: Live migration and restart
docs.text:
Tap 1 (QEMU mirror). The job ends with the QEMU process. What the design does:

  • A planned migration: the controller sees the request (it already does, for copies). It seals the stream: the relay flushes all batches and the receiver confirms. It stops the mirror. The migration runs. On the new node, a new mirror starts.
  • The writes between stopping the mirror and starting the new one are not in the journal. The change list is gone (lab). So the replica could differ from the source on blocks written in that window. The window is the length of the migration, 10 seconds to a few minutes.
  • The fix is a compare pass of the whole disk. Both sides compute a checksum for each 1 MiB chunk. Only differing chunks cross the link. This exists today. Its time is the disk size divided by the slower read speed. A 500 GB disk at 150 MB/s takes about 55 minutes. During it, the journal runs on top, and recovery to a second before the migration works. Recovery to a second after the migration is safe only after the compare pass ends. Until then, a site loss gives a recovery point at the seal, not at the newest second. That is an RPO of the compare pass time. This is the part of the goal Tap 1 does not meet.
  • Sizes: a VM with a 100 GB disk, about 11 minutes; 500 GB, about 55 minutes; 2 TB, about 3.7 hours. These are estimates; phase 0 measures them.
  • Cheaper ways to narrow the gap, all tested in phase 0:
  • Turn on QEMU's dirty-bitmaps migration capability, if libvirt or KubeVirt lets us. Then the change list survives and no compare pass is needed.
  • Check whether QEMU allows a migration while a mirror job runs. If it does, the mirror can run until the guest pauses, which makes the window as small as the switch-over.
  • Check whether the destination QEMU accepts blockdev-mirror before the guest resumes. KubeVirt resumes it at once, so probably not.
  • A restart: if the guest shuts down cleanly, the relay seals after the last write and the disk has not changed since. The next start checks the disk's size and change time against the seal record and starts a new mirror with no compare pass. A VM that crashed (not clean) needs the compare pass, because writes the relay never received (or lost) may be on the source disk.

Tap 2 (file-system tap). There is no job to lose. - On a migration the source node's relay and the destination node's relay both hold the stream. The receiver allows one writer at a time. The source relay seals when the guest pauses. The destination relay opens the next epoch only after the seal arrives, or after a fence time (the controller marks the old pod gone). Writes in the new epoch sort after the old epoch. - A restart is the same. A crash restart: the relay keeps a persistent record of dirty regions (a bitmap on the pool share). After a crash, only those regions are compared, not the whole disk. If spool.durability is shared, even the unsent tail survives. - So the goal holds through migration and crash.

docs.title: Failover to any point in time
docs.text:
Reuse kubectl failover. Add:

  • kubectl failover points --vm <name> lists the recovery range, the bookmarks and the holes.
  • kubectl failover plan|execute --at <time> picks the newest batch end at or before the time, on all disks of the VM. --bookmark <id> picks a bookmark. --rewind-to keeps working for the minutes tier.
  • Newest second: drain the staging journal (seconds), run Recover, create the PV and PVC as today. The disk is current. No copy.
  • Earlier second: Rewind copies the newest disk to a new folder, then applies undo records backward to the chosen batch. This copies the whole disk, as a rewind does today. It is slow for big disks (a 30 GB disk with 2 GB used took 165 s in the lab; a 500 GB disk with 50 GB used takes minutes). A faster rewind that does not copy (an overlay file, with the existing hook) is part 2; see "Phases".
  • The latest disk stays unchanged, so the admin can try a second time at a different second.
  • The newest second is chosen by the receiver: the highest batch end that all disks of the VM have. The plan shows the RPO in seconds, as plan does now.
  • Failover to a second that lies in a hole (a gap after a broken journal) is refused with the nearest valid seconds on each side.

docs.title: Failback (reverse CDP)
docs.text:
• After a failover the VM runs at the DR site. The old source disk may hold writes the DR site never received (the unsent tail). It cannot be used as is.
  • Failback is a new policy in the other direction. The first step is a compare pass of the old source disk against the running DR disk, with the same checksum method. Differing chunks flow back. Then a journal starts in the reverse direction (Tap 1 or Tap 2 at the DR site).
  • A planned failback is clean: stop the VM at the DR site, wait for the seal (zero tail), start it at the old source. No data is lost. Then the policy turns around again.
  • Today CROSS-REGION-DR.md describes failback as a reverse replication policy. This is the same, with a journal on top.

docs.title: Effect on the VM
docs.text:
These are targets for the phase 0 tests, not measured results.

  • Tap 1 write latency added: 0.5 ms or less at the 99th percentile, with a loopback relay.
  • Tap 1 throughput: 95% or more of the unprotected disk on a write-heavy fio run. The relay adds no I/O to the file share.
  • Tap 2 write latency added: 1 ms or less. Tap 2 read throughput: 90% or more. If Tap 2 misses these, we do not build it.
  • Guest pause per bookmark: 0.2 s or less (lab: 0.1 to 0.2 s).
  • A relay restart pauses writes for seconds, bounded by the reconnect delay. It must not cause I/O errors in the guest.
  • write-blocking mode in QEMU has one more risk: while the target is slow, guest writes wait. The relay answers from memory so the wait is short. If the relay is stalled, the guest stalls. The relay needs a watchdog: after a timeout it drops the stream (overflow degrade) so the guest never hangs for long. The timeout is a policy setting (default 2 s).

Phase 0 measures each of these for both taps.

docs.title: Bandwidth and size
docs.text:
Bandwidth is the write rate of the VM after batch coalescing and compression. It is not the changed-block rate that periodic copies send. A database that rewrites the same blocks again and again sends more under CDP than under 5 minute copies. The table uses assumed factors (coalescing and compression together: 2 to 1). Replace them with the phase 0 measurements.

VM write rate After 2 to 1 Link needed (bits) Journal for 4 hours DR share I/O (3 operations per block) 5 MB/s 2.5 MB/s 20 Mbit/s 36 GB 15 MB/s 20 MB/s 10 MB/s 80 Mbit/s 144 GB 60 MB/s 100 MB/s 50 MB/s 400 Mbit/s 720 GB 300 MB/s 200 MB/s (the rate in the 20 Oct lab VM) 100 MB/s 800 Mbit/s 1.4 TB 600 MB/s

Rules: - The link must carry the peak write rate for longer than the buffer can hide. Buffer time = buffer size divided by (peak minus link). A 512 MiB buffer hides a 100 MB/s surplus for about 5 seconds. - Size the DR share for 3 times the incoming rate, plus the 4 hour journal, plus the minutes tier, plus the disk itself. - Compression is cheap on the relay (zstd level 1). It uses CPU on the source node: about one core for 200 MB/s (to verify). - The cross-region link rate on IBM Cloud (Transit Gateway or VPN) is to verify in phase 0. The lab uses two different VPCs; VPN throughput can be far lower than a Transit Gateway. - A VM that writes more than the link can carry for hours cannot have an RPO of seconds, whatever the design. The console shows this before the policy is saved (a warning when the sustained write rate is above 70% of the measured link).

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• TLS and authentication. The current receiver uses a bearer token, and TLS on by default was left for later in #89. CDP carries every write of the most sensitive VMs, so TLS 1.3 with client certificates is required for a journal stream. The receiver refuses a journal stream without it. The certificates come from cert-manager, one per source cluster, with a short life.
  • Stream scope. Each stream is bound to one policy and one list of pvc-<uuid> volumes, fixed when the stream opens. The receiver refuses a write to any other volume. It checks that sequence numbers only increase and that the epoch is the current one. A replayed or forged batch is refused.
  • The receiver's rights. Unchanged in kind: own ServiceAccount, no role, no API token, no capabilities, writes only inside pvc-<uuid> folders (PR #105). The journal service adds write access to a journal/ area inside those folders. Limits: batch size, stream count, segment size, and total journal size per volume. A full journal area stops the stream (degrade) instead of filling the share.
  • Tap 1 connection on the node. QEMU in the VM pod connects to the relay over the pod network to the node. Another pod on the node could connect and send fake writes. The export name is a random secret for each stream, shared only through QMP. The relay accepts one connection per stream and checks the source address. A NetworkPolicy limits who can reach the relay's port. The OVN user-defined network (UDN) may block a VM pod from reaching the node. Verify in the lab.
  • Relay rights. It runs privileged only if Tap 2 needs it. The relay for Tap 1 needs no extra rights. It sees the plain data of every protected VM on its node. A node compromise already allows this, because the node mounts the shares.
  • Data at rest. The DR share is encrypted by IBM as every share is. The journal holds plain writes, so anyone who can read the DR share can read them. The spool on the node disk (node-disk) is also plain; it uses an encrypted node disk or an emptyDir on the node's encrypted volume (to verify on ROKS).
  • Controller. It keeps its right to run commands in VM pods (the kubevirt-controller SCC), as for copies today. No new right.
  • Red Hat support. QMP into KubeVirt VMs is unsupported (accepted on 20 Oct). A journal that stops the VM from live-migrating or hangs it on a relay stall is a new kind of risk. The owner should treat CDP VMs as a separate support class.

docs.title: How it fits with what exists
docs.text:
• Periodic replication keeps running as a safety net while the journal is healthy, but at a longer interval (default 60 minutes, off if you choose). It supplies the change list for catch-ups and a checksum scrub of the DR disk. If the journal breaks, the periodic copy takes over at its own interval (5 minutes if you set it).
  • Backups (BackupPolicy) are unchanged. They read from the local share, not from the DR site. A CDP VM can be in a backup policy.
  • Instant snapshots work with Tap 1 (QEMU does the snapshot; the mirror follows the top file; verify that a snapshot during a mirror job is allowed). With Tap 2 they work, and the journal records writes to the overlay files. Replicas then hold the overlay files too. First release: a CDP VM must have no instant snapshots (the webhook refuses the policy, or flatten first). This is simpler. Phase 4 lifts it.
  • Restore points. The minutes tier is the existing format. Rewind and failover code is reused. The journal adds a finer layer on top.
  • Zone loss (PR #199): Level 2 copies a pool to a partner pool in another zone at 5 to 10 minutes. CDP gives the same-cluster option an RPO of seconds when the receiver and relay run in the partner zone. Option 7 (a synchronous mirror within the region, 2 ms or less) can give RPO 0 there. That is an extension, not part of this build. Regional rfs shares give RPO 0 without any of this, where IBM offers them.

docs.title: Console and CLI
docs.text:
• Policy. A new cdp block in ReplicationPolicy: enabled, batchInterval, window, bookmarkInterval, onOverflow, rpoWarning, spool.{memoryMiB,diskGiB,durability}, tap (qemu or filesystem). The webhook checks it: needs the receiver mode, TLS, a guest-agent warning, no instant snapshots (first release).
  • Console. The VM page shows the live RPO, the state (Seeding, Healthy, Lagging, Broken, Resyncing), the lag in seconds and bytes, the buffer fill, and the recovery range as a bar. The bar shows bookmarks and holes. A "Recover to" picker takes a time or a bookmark and shows the plan before it runs. At the DR site, the same picker starts the failover.
  • CLI. kubectl failover points, plan --at, execute --at, --bookmark (above). kubectl failover status --vm shows the live numbers.

docs.title: Metrics and alerts
docs.text:
New metrics (names follow the existing pool_csi_ style; they go into MONITORING.md when built):

  • pool_csi_cdp_rpo_seconds{vm}: age of the oldest write not yet durable at DR. It is 0 when nothing is pending. Heartbeats prove it.
  • pool_csi_cdp_state{vm,state}.
  • pool_csi_cdp_buffer_bytes{vm,level} and pool_csi_cdp_sent_bytes_total{vm}.
  • pool_csi_cdp_write_ack_seconds{vm}: histogram of the relay's answer time. This is the cost to the guest.
  • pool_csi_cdp_apply_lag_seconds{vm} at DR.
  • pool_csi_cdp_range_seconds{vm}: length of the recovery range.
  • pool_csi_cdp_resync_progress{vm}, pool_csi_cdp_clock_skew_seconds{node}.

Alerts: CDPLagging (RPO above rpoWarning for 1 minute), CDPRpoBreach (above the policy target for 2 minutes), CDPJournalBroken, CDPResyncLong (resync over 1 hour), CDPApplyBehind, CDPJournalSpaceLow.

docs.title: Cost, effort and risk
docs.text:
Effort. In pull requests, the same unit as the earlier specs. About 25 PRs for the journal with Tap 1, and about 10 more for Tap 2. Plus lab time on two clusters. This is a larger project than the whole of VM replication (about 5 PRs). It is the biggest feature in the driver.

What it costs to run. - DR share space: the disk, the journal window, and the minutes tier. See the bandwidth table. - DR share speed: 3 operations per changed block. - Link: the VM's write rate after compression, for as long as the VM runs. Cross-region data transfer is billed by IBM (verify the price). - A relay pod on each node, with memory for buffers (512 MiB per protected VM by default). - Tap 2 adds a user-space program on the path of every I/O.

Risks, most serious first. 1. Tap 1 loses the journal on a live migration or a crash. Sized above. Phase 0 may shrink it. Tap 2 removes it. 2. A stalled relay stalls the VM (write-blocking). The watchdog and the degrade mode limit it. The test "kill the relay under load" must show no guest I/O error. 3. Tap 2 is in the I/O path. A bug or a crash in it hurts the VM. It needs the strongest testing and a soak run. It may fail the speed targets. 4. Unsupported by Red Hat. An OpenShift Virtualization update can change the VM pod and break QMP, or change how mirror jobs and migrations interact. Every release test run gets a CDP stage. 5. Hot-block workloads send far more than periodic copies do. The console warns about it. 6. DR apply lag. If the apply worker cannot keep up, failover to the newest second takes longer. The metric and alert show it. 7. Clock skew limits cross-VM cuts and the meaning of "second". 8. Complex recovery code. Undo journal recovery after a crash at any point must be correct. Property tests and crash tests cover it (see Testing).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Tests ship in the same PR as the code, as in the earlier specs.

Unit (no cluster). - Batch coalescing: later writes win, trims and zero writes are right, order across disks is kept. - Wire frames: reject bad sizes, bad checksums, a sequence that goes back, a wrong epoch, a volume that is not in the stream. - Undo journal: apply then rewind to every batch end gives the exact earlier disk (property test with random writes). A crash injected at every step of apply (stage, undo append, disk write, marker) recovers to a valid batch end. - Retention merge: a rewind before and after the merge gives the same bytes. - Hole handling: failover to a second inside a hole is refused. - Failover planner: the newest common batch end across disks. - Overflow: degrade and block behave as set.

Lab (two clusters). Source rovs-aug-2026-v2, DR rovslab-dr-eude. They are in different VPCs. The link is what the lab has (VPN or Transit Gateway). Verify the link speed first. 1. Steady state. A CentOS VM with two disks runs a writer that logs a counter with a checksum to each disk every 10 ms. Journal on. Check the live RPO stays under 5 s for 1 hour. 2. Kill the source mid-write. Power off the source worker (or delete the VM pod and cut the network) during a write burst. Fail over at the newest second. Check: the VM boots, file systems mount, and the counters on both disks end within 5 s of the kill and match each other (the same second). 3. Chosen second. Fail over to a second T from 30 minutes ago. Check: every record written before T is present and its checksum matches. No record written after T is present. Run for five different T, including one between two bookmarks and one exactly on a bookmark. 4. Window ends. Fail over to a second older than window: land on the nearest 5 minute point. Check the plan says so. 5. Link loss. Cut the link for 30 s, then 5 minutes, then 30 minutes. Check the alerts, the buffers, degrade falling back to the periodic copy, the catch-up, and a new journal. Check the VM's fio throughput is unchanged during the outage in degrade mode. 6. Live migration. Migrate the VM during the writer. Tap 1: measure the gap, the compare pass time, and the recovery point during it. Tap 2: check the journal continues with no hole. 7. Restart and crash. Clean restart, guest crash, node crash. Check divergence handling. 8. Relay restart under load. No guest I/O error. 9. Failback. Reverse resync and a planned failback with zero loss. 10. Windows. A Windows Server VM with VSS bookmarks. 11. Performance. fio random and sequential, read and write, 4 KiB and 1 MiB, with and without CDP, for each tap. Report latency percentiles and throughput. Check the targets in "Effect on the VM". 12. Release test run. Add a CDP stage with a short version of tests 1, 2, 3 and 6.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
Phase 0: lab spikes (about 2 weeks; no product code). Each answers a question that can change the design. 1. Mirror throughput: blockdev-mirror with sync=none and copy-mode=write-blocking to an NBD server on the same node (a small test server). Does it work with sync=none? Does the job report actively-synced? 2. VM write latency and fio throughput with no mirror, background, and write-blocking. Latency added per write. 3. Link loss: break the NBD connection. What does the job do? What does the guest see? Which on-target-error and reconnect options give no guest error? 4. Live migration with a running mirror job: refused or allowed? What does the destination QEMU have? Is dirty-bitmaps migration available through libvirt and KubeVirt? 5. Node-local relay reachability from a VM pod, including a pod with a primary user-defined network and a NetworkPolicy. 6. Snapshots during a mirror job (instant snapshot, blockcommit). 7. Link speed between the two lab VPCs, and the compare pass speed on a 100 GB disk. 8. FUSE tap: a pass-through FUSE mount over the NFS share, as the disk of a VM. Speed with fio. Does QEMU's O_DIRECT work? What happens on a daemon kill? Does live migration work? Ask Red Hat about support. 9. Clock skew between nodes of one cluster, and between the two lab clusters. 10. zstd cost and ratio on real write traffic (a database benchmark such as pgbench or HammerDB).

Decision at the end of phase 0: build Tap 1 first (default), or go straight to Tap 2 if Tap 1's migration gap cannot be narrowed and Tap 2's speed passes.

Phase 1: one disk, steady state, Tap 1 (about 8 PRs). Relay, wire format, receiver journal service, staging, apply with undo journal, crash recovery, starting a journal, failover to the newest second, metrics. Lab tests 1 and 2.

Phase 2: any second, several disks, bookmarks (about 6 PRs). Batches across disks, freeze bookmarks, failover points|plan --at|--bookmark, rewind from the undo journal, retention tiers. Lab tests 3 and 4.

Phase 3: failures (about 5 PRs). Memory and disk buffers, degrade and block, catch-up, migration and restart handling for Tap 1 (seal, compare pass), alerts. Lab tests 5, 6, 7, 8.

Phase 4: operations (about 5 PRs). Policy webhook, console page and picker, protection groups, failback, docs, release test stage. Lab tests 9, 10, 12.

Phase 5: Tap 2 (about 10 PRs, only if chosen). The FUSE tap, relay changes (epochs, dirty-region record), shared spool, soak tests. Lab tests 6, 7 and 11 again.

Phase 6 (optional): synchronous mode within a region. Same-region RPO 0 for the zone-loss design.

docs.title: Open items to verify in the lab
docs.text:
• sync=none with write-blocking in QEMU 9.1, and the QMP options for NBD reconnect.
  • Migration with a running mirror job; dirty-bitmaps migration under libvirt.
  • Reachability of the node relay from VM pods (UDN, NetworkPolicy).
  • Red Hat support position for a CSI driver that serves files through a user-space mount.
  • OpenShift Virtualization 4.22 Technology Preview list (changed block tracking) and the gate name.
  • Whether IBM file share replication is 15 minutes or hourly (the pages disagree).
  • Cross-region link throughput and data transfer cost.
  • Node disk encryption on ROKS for the node-local spool.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The goal is a journal of every write, shipped within seconds, with recovery to any second in a window. Periodic copies cannot do it.
  • The default window of one-second recovery points is 4 hours. After that, 5 minute points to 24 hours. You can change both per policy.
  • Recovery points are the ends of 1 second batches. A batch is the smallest step. This keeps bandwidth lower. The batch length is a setting.
  • The DR disk always holds the newest second. A failover to the newest second is fast. We pay with 3 operations at DR for each changed block.
  • A relay on each source node orders the writes. It is its own DaemonSet so a driver upgrade does not cut streams.
  • The QEMU mirror in write-blocking mode into the relay is the first tap. The guest never waits for the WAN.
  • The first tap does not keep the journal through a live migration or a node crash. It needs a resync of up to hours for big disks. I say so rather than hide it.
  • The design that meets the whole goal uses the file-system tap. I build it only if phase 0 says the first tap's gap is not acceptable and the file-system tap is fast enough.
  • I do not build the sidecar storage daemon option. It needs the unsupported Sidecar gate and breaks instant snapshots and QEMU copies.
  • The mirror straight to the DR site is rejected. It either lags without limit or adds the WAN round trip to every write.
  • Short copies every few seconds are rejected. They freeze the guest and slow the VM too much. Periodic copies stay as the fallback.
  • KubeVirt's own incremental backup is not used. It is a periodic backup, not a write stream. It may replace the periodic copy later.
  • When the link is lost and the buffers are full, the VM keeps full speed and the journal pauses (degrade). The periodic copy takes over. A block setting exists for the opposite choice.
  • Bookmarks come from a guest freeze every 5 minutes. Any second between is crash consistent. Databases recover from that.
  • Several VMs share only bookmark IDs, not an exact second. No design can order writes across nodes.
  • Journal streams need TLS 1.3 with client certificates. The old bearer token alone is not enough for this.
  • The receiver keeps its small rights from PR #105. The journal adds write access to one area in the volumes it already serves.
  • Periodic replication keeps running at 60 minutes as a safety net and for catch-ups.
  • First release: a CDP VM may not have instant snapshots. This keeps the replica format simple.
  • CDP covers VM disks only. Plain volumes stay with periodic replication.
  • Rewind to an earlier second copies the disk first, as a rewind does today. A faster rewind is later work.
  • CDP VMs are a separate support class. Red Hat does not support the QMP method, and the journal adds a risk to live migration.
  • Same-region RPO 0 (a synchronous mode) is an extension in phase 6, not part of this build.
  • The size is about 25 PRs for the first tap and 10 more for the second. Phase 0 comes first and may change it.

docs.title: Spec: survive the loss of a zone (multi-zone clusters)
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-22. Status: draft for review. Nothing in this spec is built yet.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
A ROVS or ROKS cluster has workers in three zones of one region. One zone fails. Then:

  • VMs and pods that used pool storage in that zone start again in another zone, with their data.
  • We state in advance how much recent data can be lost (the recovery point, RPO) and how long the restart takes (the recovery time, RTO). The console and the metrics show the real numbers at any moment.
  • Two copies of one VM never write to the same disk at the same time (fencing).
  • When the zone returns, the workloads can move back (failback), or can stay where they are.

"Done" means a lab test with a simulated zone loss passes for both protection levels below, and an admin can run the whole failover and failback from the console or one command.

What this spec does not promise: a VM does not keep running through a zone loss. Its memory is lost. It starts again from its disk, like a power cut. No IBM Cloud feature can change that for a VM whose host is gone.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
All facts in this section come from the code and the docs in this repository.

  • A pool lives in one zone (FileSharePool.spec.zone). Its shares and their mount targets are created in that zone.
  • A multi-zone cluster uses one pool per zone and a WaitForFirstConsumer StorageClass. The driver reads the zone of the node that the pod was scheduled to (topology.kubernetes.io/zone) and picks the pool of that zone. The example is in examples/multi-zone/.
  • A pool can list accessorZones. The driver then gives the volume a topology that allows every listed zone. VPC-NETWORKING.md says one mount target in the home zone serves all zones. KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md ("Cross-Zone Node Failover") says there is one mount target per zone. The two pages disagree. This project has not tested cross-zone mounting on a multi-zone cluster. Phase 0 settles it.
  • Pools only use the dp2 profile (zonal). The VPC client sends the profile name from the pool and has no regional-share code.
  • Replication (ReplicationPolicy) copies a pool to a destination: an NFS server or a receiver. It is built for another cluster or region. For running VMs it takes a QEMU copy of all the VM's disks at one moment, sends only changed blocks, and keeps 24 hours of restore points at the destination. kubectl failover then creates the SubVolume, PersistentVolume (PV) and PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) at the destination and picks the newest moment that all disks of a VM can show.
  • Nothing protects against the loss of a zone. If a zone fails, every volume in its pool is unavailable until the zone returns. A VM cannot start in another zone with its data.

docs.title: IBM Cloud facts (checked 22 Oct 2026)
docs.text:
Each fact has its source. Where the docs are unclear, the fact is marked "verify" and becomes a phase 0 check.

# Fact Source 1 dp2 shares are zonal: data lives in one zone. Profiles 2 A zonal share can be mounted from another zone of the region. This needs security group access mode and a mount target with a virtual network interface (VNI). Performance can drop because traffic crosses zones. About File Storage for VPC, cross-zone mount targets 3 The old vpc access mode is deprecated and cannot mount across zones. same page, and Creating replica file shares 4 Regional shares exist: profile rfs. Data is replicated synchronously across all 3 zones of the region. The docs warn of "increased latency during write operations". Profiles 5 rfs is select availability: you need special access from your IBM account team. The IBM OpenShift storage classes for it are Beta, for allowlisted accounts only. About File Storage for VPC, FAQ, ROKS storage class reference 6 rfs is listed for Frankfurt (eu-de), Dallas, London, Madrid, Washington DC and others. Not Montreal. About File Storage for VPC 7 rfs limits: 1 to 32,000 GB; IOPS fixed at 35,000 per share; bandwidth 800 Mbps by default, adjustable to 8192 Mbps for extra cost; largest file 1 TB; 300 shares per region for all profiles; no cross-region replication in this release; a share cannot change between zonal and regional. Profiles, About File Storage for VPC, limitations 8 An rfs mount target must use a VNI. The VNI belongs to a subnet in one zone, but "is accessible from any availability zone within the region, even if the owning region is temporary unavailable". Traffic stays local to the zone of the server. About File Storage for VPC, regional mount targets 9 Encryption in transit for rfs uses stunnel. The ROKS storage add-on does not support it for regional shares. Our driver does not use it today. ROKS storage class reference 10 IBM share replication copies a dp2 share to a read-only replica in another zone of the region, or another region of the same geography. It is asynchronous. The schedule is a cron expression, and runs must be at least 15 minutes apart. About file share replication, Creating replica file shares 11 The IBM FAQ says "as frequently as every hour". The other two pages say 15 minutes. Verify. FAQ 12 Replication has no automatic failover. You call a failover on the replica (ibmcloud is share-replica-failover, or POST /shares/{id}/failover). The service first tries a final sync from the source. The timeout is 300 to 3600 seconds (default 5 minutes). With fallback_policy: split, a failed final sync leaves two independent read/write shares, and the replica may lack the latest data. The relationship cannot be restored. You must set up a new replica when the source zone returns. Replication failover 13 A replica can have its own mount target. It is read-only until failover or split. Same-region replicas inherit the source's encryption. The replica profile is dp2 and you choose its IOPS. Creating replica file shares 14 Cost: file shares are billed by capacity and IOPS. A replica is a second share with its own capacity and IOPS. Data transfer between regions is billed. The docs do not say that transfer between zones is billed. Verify. FAQ 15 Share snapshots of the source are copied to the replica at the next sync. Snapshots of a replica cannot be made. The docs do not say whether a sync copies the share at one moment. Verify. About file share replication 16 OpenShift Virtualization restarts a VM with run strategy Always or RerunOnFailure on another node when its node is declared failed. On a cluster with machine health checks, this happens when a node fails the check. Otherwise an admin must delete the Node object, or the Node Health Check operator with Self Node Remediation must do it. Without this, a VM on a dead node does not move. Red Hat: Nodes 17 ROKS fact still to find: how worker pools spread across zones, and whether ROKS replaces workers by itself when a zone fails. The IBM page did not load. Verify in the lab. to verify

docs.title: What this means
docs.text:
• No synchronous copy exists for dp2. IBM offers one synchronous design only: the regional rfs share. For dp2, the best IBM gives is asynchronous replication at 15 minutes or more. That is the size of the gap: RPO 0 with rfs, and minutes with dp2. There is no dp2 option with RPO 0.
  • rfs is not general availability. We cannot promise it to every customer. It also has real limits: a fixed 35,000 IOPS per share, higher write latency, and a 1 TB largest file. A VM disk is one file (disk.img), so a disk larger than 1 TB cannot live on rfs.

docs.title: The design that meets the goal
docs.text: Two protection levels, chosen per pool. Both end in the same failover command and the same console page.

docs.title: Level 1: regional pool (RPO 0)
docs.text:
A pool can be regional. Its shares use the rfs profile. IBM keeps the data in all three zones. The pool has no home zone and no copies to manage.

When a zone fails, the shares stay up (fact 8, to verify in the lab). Nothing needs to move. The work is to fence the dead zone and restart the VMs in the other zones.

  • RPO: 0. The data is crash consistent, as after a power cut.
  • RTO: fence and restart. Target under 10 minutes after the admin confirms the loss. Measure it in phase 0.
  • Failback: nothing to copy back. When the zone returns, the admin lifts the fence. VMs can live-migrate to any zone, because the storage is the same everywhere.
  • Needs: IBM special access for rfs in the region, and a lab check that the driver can create and mount an rfs share.
  • Limits: facts 7 and 9. The pool webhook refuses a regional pool with a StorageClass that asks for more than 35,000 IOPS per share. The console warns about disks above 1 TB.

docs.title: Level 2: copied pool (RPO of minutes)
docs.text:
Each zone keeps its dp2 pool, as today. Each pool is protected by a pool in another zone. The existing replication copies the pool's volumes to the partner pool, on a schedule, in the same cluster.

  • VMs use the existing VM-safe copy. One QEMU step copies all disks of a VM at one moment. Multi-disk VMs stay consistent. Only changed blocks move. The destination keeps 24 hours of restore points.
  • Plain volumes use the existing file copy.
  • Partner layout: a ring. Zone 1 is copied to zone 2, zone 2 to zone 3, zone 3 to zone 1. Copies go into a separate folder tree on the partner pool's shares (/replica/<source pool>/). They do not appear as volumes and cannot be mounted by a pod.
  • RPO: the time since the last good copy. The copy interval is 5 minutes by default. A copy with little change takes tens of seconds, so the RPO is about 5 to 10 minutes. A VM that writes fast or has large changes can take longer, and its RPO grows. The status shows the real value for each VM, and an alert fires when it passes the target.
  • RTO: the failover command re-points each volume to its copy (below). Target 15 to 20 minutes for 50 VMs. Measure it in phase 0.
  • Failback: planned, one VM at a time, with a short outage (below).
  • Cost: the partner pool needs room for the copies and the restore points. See "Cost".

docs.title: Why not IBM share replication for Level 2
docs.text:
IBM share replication is not our recommended method. It does not meet the goal for VMs, for these reasons.

  • The shortest interval is 15 minutes, and a run takes time on top. The practical RPO is 30 minutes or more, against 5 to 10 minutes for our copy.
  • A share holds many volumes. IBM replicates the whole share, with all its capacity, whether the volumes need it or not.
  • Failover splits the pair for good. After the zone returns, you create a new replica and send the whole share again.
  • Failover is one share at a time, with no view of VMs. A VM with disks on two shares has no common moment. Our copy gives one moment for all disks.
  • The docs do not say whether a sync gives a consistent moment (fact 15). If it does not, a running VM's disk.img can be torn, which is the same fault that made us stop using rsync for VM disks.

IBM replication stays on the list as a comparison in phase 0. If the lab shows that it gives a crash-consistent moment for each share, it is a possible lower-effort method for plain volumes. It is not part of the first build.

docs.title: Options that do not meet the goal
docs.text: Option Why it does not meet the goal Do nothing; restore from backup after the zone returns Volumes stay down until the zone returns. No restart in another zone. Restore from backup (COS) into another zone Works, but the RPO is the backup interval (hours) and the RTO is hours for large disks. Keep it as the last resort. IBM share replication alone Meets "restart in another zone" with a 30 minute or worse RPO and no VM-safe moment. See above. Cross-zone mounting alone (accessor zones) Lets pods in zone 2 use a share from zone 1. It does not help when zone 1 fails, because the share is in zone 1. It is useful for load, not for survival. Application-level replication (database clusters, for example) Good, and outside this driver. We do not stop anyone from using it.

docs.title: Failure model
docs.text: Failure What happens What the design does Zone down (workers and storage in it are gone) Pods in the zone are gone. Zonal shares in it are unreachable. The goal of this spec. Failover moves the workloads. Zone down, regional pool Pods in the zone are gone. The rfs share stays up (to verify). Fence the zone, restart VMs. No data moves. Zone partition (zone is alive but cut off from the control plane or other zones) Workers in the zone keep running their VMs and keep writing to their disks. The rest of the cluster thinks they are dead. This is the dangerous case. Fencing (below). Without it, two VMs can write to one rfs disk and destroy it. One share unavailable (zone is up) Volumes on that share fail. The pool already marks a failed or degraded share and drains it. Out of scope here. Level 2 copies let an admin fail over a pool, so the zone failover command also works for one pool (--pool). Storage up, workers gone Same as zone down, for the workers only. Level 1: fence and restart. Level 2: the primary share is up, so volumes could stay. We still use the zone failover, because the VM needs workers with its data, and the data is only mountable from the zone's workers if cross-zone mounting works. Phase 0 checks cross-zone mounting from a surviving zone. If it works, a Level 2 volume can be mounted across zones with no data movement ("storage-only-up" shortcut). Control plane unavailable OpenShift on ROKS runs its control plane across zones. This spec assumes it survives one zone. Not covered.

docs.title: Placement
docs.text:
• Pools per zone stay the same. The multi-zone StorageClass with WaitForFirstConsumer places a VM's disk in the VM's zone, so reads and writes stay in-zone.
  • A regional pool has a StorageClass with WaitForFirstConsumer, but any zone is allowed. The scheduler places the VM on any node.
  • VM-to-zone affinity. A VM keeps its zone while that zone is healthy. We do not add a new rule. After a failover, the VM runs in the partner zone.
  • Spare room. To survive one zone of three, the other two zones must hold the load of the third. Each zone can run at most 66% of its capacity. The console shows the headroom and refuses a failover plan when the target zone lacks CPU, memory, or pool space (admin may override).
  • No partner by accident. The pool webhook refuses a partner in the same zone as the source, and refuses two pools that protect each other when a third zone exists (use the ring).

docs.title: New objects
docs.text:
• FileSharePool.spec.zoneProtection (Level 2 only): partnerPool (a pool in another zone), interval (default 5m), rpoTarget (default 15m), keepRestorePoints (default 24h). The controller creates and owns a ReplicationPolicy for it. The admin does not write the policy.
  • FileSharePool.spec.profile: rfs (Level 1). The zone is optional for a regional pool.
  • ZoneFailover (cluster-wide): failedZone, mode (Failover or Failback), pools (default all in the zone), rewindTo (optional), dryRun, approvedBy. Its status lists each step with a result, so the record shows what was done and when. One ZoneFailover per zone at a time.
  • FileSharePool.status.zoneState: Healthy, Suspect, Failed, FailedOver, Recovering.

docs.title: Detecting a zone loss
docs.text:
A new controller watches three signals for each zone:

  1. Node health: the share of workers in the zone that are NotReady.
  2. Storage health: the share and mount target state from the VPC API, and a small probe Job in a surviving zone that lists a folder on the share.
  3. Node agent heartbeat: each node agent already runs on every worker. A missing heartbeat from the whole zone counts as a signal.

States:

  • Suspect: signal 1 or 3 is true for 2 minutes. An alert fires. Nothing else changes.
  • Failed (proposed): two of three signals are true for 5 minutes. The console shows "Zone X looks down. Fail over?" with the plan. This is the point where a human decides.

While a zone is Suspect or Failed, the pool manager in that zone's pools stops auto-expand and stops creating shares. It never creates a replacement share in a failed zone. It keeps every SubVolume record, so no data is forgotten.

The VPC API for a failed zone can be slow or can fail. Every VPC call in this path has a time limit and is allowed to fail without blocking the rest of the plan.

docs.title: Who decides: an admin, not the controller (first release)
docs.text:
Failover is admin-triggered (console button or kubectl failover zone execute). The controller proposes it. It does not run it alone.

Why: a wrong failover is worse than a slow one. A false alarm (a network blip) with an automatic failover would start a second copy of every VM and could corrupt rfs disks. A zone loss is rare, and a few minutes for a human to confirm costs little against that risk.

An automatic mode is a later phase (phase 6). It is off by default and requires all three signals, a longer wait (15 minutes), and a limit of one automatic failover per day.

docs.title: Fencing
docs.text:
Fencing means making sure the old copy of a VM cannot write any more. It happens before any VM restarts. The command refuses to continue until every fence step is done or the admin says in writing (--accept-unfenced) that the zone is physically gone.

Fence steps, in order:

  1. Storage network. Remove the failed zone's worker subnets from the security group rules of the mount targets of the affected shares. This cuts NFS traffic from that zone at the VPC. It works from a surviving zone, because the VPC API is regional. Lab check: does removing the rule stop traffic on connections that are already open? (Security groups track connections, so it may not.)
  2. Workers. Stop the failed zone's worker instances through the VPC API, if the API answers. Otherwise delete the Node objects.
  3. Nodes in Kubernetes. Delete the Node objects of the zone. Red Hat documents this as the trigger to restart Always VMs elsewhere (fact 16). Force-delete the stuck virt-launcher pods.
  4. Taint. Taint the zone storage.ibmcloud.io/zone-failed:NoExecute so nothing schedules there. The taint is removed at failback.
  5. File lock. The NFS server drops the locks of a client that does not renew its lease. QEMU also takes a lock on its image file. If a zombie client later reconnects, it should find its state expired. Lab check: do its writes fail? This is defence in depth only. We do not rely on it.

For Level 2 the two copies are separate files, so a zombie VM in the dead zone cannot damage the copy. The risk is two diverging versions of a VM, not corruption. The failback step (below) picks the winner and the other version is kept, not deleted, until the admin removes it.

docs.title: Steps: regional pool (Level 1)
docs.text:
1. Plan: list the VMs and pods in the zone, the spare room in the other zones, and the state of the pool.
  2. Fence (above).
  3. Restart: VMs with Always or RerunOnFailure restart by themselves after step 2. The command waits and reports each VM. VMs with Halted stay off. Plain pods that belong to a Deployment or StatefulSet restart as usual.
  4. Report: the time from approval to the last VM running, and which VMs did not start.

docs.title: Steps: copied pool (Level 2)
docs.text:
1. Plan: for each volume in the failed pool, the moment of its last good copy (the RPO), the VM group, and the spare room. VMs whose disks show different moments get the newest common moment, as in the existing failover.
  2. Fence (above).
  3. Stop new copies from the failed zone. Run the existing recovery step on each copy: roll back any half-applied copy.
  4. Re-home each volume, in the same cluster:
  5. Delete the old PVC and PV objects (the data in the failed zone is not touched; the PV has Retain).
  6. Move the SubVolume record to the partner pool, to the folder of the copy.
  7. Create a new PV that points to the partner pool's share and the copy's folder, with a node affinity for the partner zone. Create the PVC again with the same name and namespace, bound to that PV.
  8. The VM object already exists in the cluster, so it restarts on its own PVC names. Nothing in the VM manifest changes.
  9. Move the copy folder out of /replica/ into /pvcs/ on the same share. This is a rename inside one share, so it is instant.
  10. Start the VMs (they start after step 2 by themselves), and wait for each.
  11. Report the RPO per VM and the moment each VM runs from.

A rewind (rewindTo) uses the existing rewind: a new disk is built from the latest disk and the undo files. It is slower and needs room for one extra disk.

Open point for phase 0: deleting and recreating a PVC that a pod used, on a node that is gone. The pvc-protection finalizer waits for the pod to end. Step 2 must have removed the pod first. The test must show that it works with a stuck pod.

docs.title: Volumes made or changed during the outage
docs.text:
• New PVCs go to the pools of the surviving zones. A PVC of a failed pool that is still Pending stays pending. The event says why.
  • DeleteVolume for a volume in a failed pool answers with a retriable error. It does not forget the volume.
  • Snapshots and backups of volumes in a failed pool are paused. The backup history is kept by volume name, so it continues after the re-home (to verify in phase 0: the backup policy selects by PVC and labels, not by pool).

docs.title: Regional pool
docs.text: Lift the fence: remove the taint, uncordon the nodes (or let the replaced workers join). VMs may stay where they are, or live-migrate back one by one. No data moves.

docs.title: Copied pool
docs.text:
The failed pool in the returned zone holds old data. It is now stale: the VMs ran on the partner pool since the failover. The driver keeps it read-only and out of use.

  1. Re-seed. The zone's pool is reconnected. A reverse protection starts: partner pool to the returned pool. The first run is a full copy with the compare pass, so only blocks that differ cross the network. The status shows the progress and the RPO.
  2. Choose when. The admin chooses a quiet time for each VM or group of VMs. The console lists the VMs and the size of the last difference.
  3. Move. For each VM: stop it, run one last copy, re-home it to the returned pool (the same steps as failover), start it. The outage is the length of the last copy plus the boot. The command refuses to move a VM while its protection is more than the RPO target behind, unless the admin accepts that.
  4. Close. When the zone's pool holds all its VMs again, the original protection (zone 1 to zone 2) resumes, and the reverse protection ends.

An admin may also choose to never fail back. The VMs stay in the partner zone and the returned pool becomes a spare. This costs nothing and has no outage.

docs.title: If both versions of a VM changed (partition case)
docs.text: If a VM kept running in the cut-off zone, its old disk has data that the copy does not have. The failover keeps the old disk as it was, under /stale/<time>/, and the status lists it. The admin can look at it with the existing backup browse feature. The driver never merges two versions.

docs.title: Consistency of VMs with several disks
docs.text:
Level 1: all disks are on rfs shares, which are synchronous. The result is as a power cut would leave it. A VM with several disks on different shares is as consistent as after a power cut, because writes reached the storage in order for each file. The guest's own journal handles the rest. This is the same state a physical server would be in.

Level 2: the existing VM copy takes all disks of a VM at one moment, and the failover picks the newest moment that all disks show. If the guest agent works, the result is file-system consistent. If not, it is crash consistent. The status says which. This is the same method as cross-region replication, so no new code is needed for it.

Plain volumes (not VM disks) in both levels: files are as consistent as the files are. A database that writes several files needs its own method (a hook, or an application-level copy).

docs.title: Interaction with other features
docs.text:
• Instant VM snapshots. The overlay files of a disk are in the disk's folder, so the copy method takes the folder as it does for cross-region replication. Phase 0 checks that a disk with a chain boots in the partner zone after a Level 2 failover. A snapshot taken in the failed zone and not yet copied is lost with the RPO.
  • Backups. The snapshot pool for backups must not be in a zone it protects. The Helm check warns if the snapshot pool is in the same zone as the pool it backs up. COS export is independent of zones and is the last-resort source.
  • Cross-region DR. A cross-region policy copies a pool to another region. After a zone failover, the volumes live in the partner pool, so the cross-region policy must follow them. The policy selects by label, and the first run after a re-home is a compare pass. The /replica/ folders are not volumes, so cross-region policies skip them.
  • Drain, auto-expand, tiers. Unchanged. The partner pool counts the copy space as used space, so auto-expand reacts to it.
  • Golden images and CDI. A CDI import in the failed zone fails and retries in a surviving zone through the normal StorageClass binding. No special handling.

docs.title: Console and command line
docs.text:
Console (a new "Zones" page in the existing plugin):

  • A row for each zone: state, workers ready, pools, protection status, spare room.
  • A row for each protected pool: partner, last good copy, RPO now against target, bytes behind.
  • A button "Fail over zone". It opens the plan: VMs, RPO for each, spare room, fence steps. The admin types the zone name to confirm. A progress view follows the ZoneFailover steps.
  • A "Fail back" button on a failed-over zone, with the VM list and the per-VM move.

Command line, extending the existing failover tool:

kubectl failover zone status
kubectl failover zone plan    --zone eu-de-1 [--pool NAME] [--rewind-to TIME]
kubectl failover zone execute --zone eu-de-1 --approve [--accept-unfenced]
kubectl failover zone failback plan|execute --zone eu-de-1 [--vm NS/NAME]

docs.title: Monitoring and alerts
docs.text:
New metrics (the 31-metric table in MONITORING.md grows):

  • zone_state{zone} (0 healthy, 1 suspect, 2 failed, 3 failed over, 4 recovering)
  • zone_protection_rpo_seconds{pool,partner} and per VM zone_protection_vm_rpo_seconds
  • zone_protection_last_success_timestamp{pool}
  • zone_headroom_ratio{zone} for CPU, memory and pool space
  • zone_failover_step_duration_seconds{step} and zone_failover_total{result}
  • zone_fence_state{zone}

Alerts:

  • Zone suspect (warning), zone failed (critical).
  • Protection behind target for 2 intervals (warning), for 6 (critical).
  • Spare room below what one zone loss needs (warning).
  • A partner pool above 85% (warning).
  • A VM running with no protection while its pool has protection on (warning).
  • A fence step failed (critical).

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Storage and traffic:

  • Level 1: rfs capacity price, and bandwidth above 800 Mbps costs extra. IBM publishes the price in the console only. Not found in the docs. Verify. No second copy to buy.
  • Level 2: the partner pool holds a copy of the protected data. VM copies hold only used blocks (the staging copy is sparse), and the restore points add up to about one more disk for each VM for 24 hours. Plan 1.2 to 2 times the protected data in the partner pool. The partner pool is still dp2, so IOPS is paid on it too.
  • IBM share replication would be 1 times the full capacity of each share plus its IOPS, whatever the data size.
  • Traffic: the copies cross zones inside the region. The docs say that data transfer between regions is billed, and do not say it for zones. Verify.

Compute: the real cost is spare room. To survive one zone of three, each zone runs at no more than 66% of its workers. That is 50% more workers than the load needs. This is the largest cost, and it is the same for both levels. It is a property of the goal, not of this driver. With two zones the spare room is 100%.

Load on the VMs: the existing copy slows a VM's writes. At the 20 MB/s default the VM kept 93% of its write speed in the lab. Level 1 has no such cost, but writes are slower than on dp2 (fact 4).

docs.title: Risk
docs.text:
• rfs is select availability. IBM can change it before general availability. Level 1 may not be offered to every customer. The design must work without it, which is why Level 2 exists.
  • rfs performance. A fixed 35,000 IOPS per share and higher write latency may not suit every VM. Phase 0 measures this with the fio benchmark we already have.
  • Fencing is hard to prove. A partition cannot be simulated exactly. The lab tests cover the controls we own (security group rule, Node delete, taint, lock). A real zone loss may differ.
  • Re-home touches PVs and PVCs. A bug here can leave a VM without a disk. The re-home keeps the old objects until the new ones are bound, and the plan shows every change first. The release test covers it.
  • Level 2 depends on the VM copy method, which Red Hat does not support (accepted on 20 Oct). A zone failover inherits that.
  • A surviving zone has less spare room than expected. The plan checks the room before it starts.

docs.title: Lab needed
docs.text:
The three current labs are single-zone. A zone loss needs a new lab:

  • A ROVS cluster in eu-de with workers in all three zones (eu-de-1, eu-de-2, eu-de-3). At least 2 workers per zone, so the other zones can take the load. Size the workers for 3 to 4 test VMs per zone.
  • A pool in each zone (Level 2), and a regional pool if IBM gives us rfs special access. Ask the IBM account team now, because this takes the longest.
  • The driver image from the build server, as for the other labs.
  • The same test VM set as the release test (Linux with the guest agent, a Windows VM, a VM with two disks, a VM with an instant-snapshot chain).

No test can switch off an IBM zone. We simulate it in two ways, and each test says which it used:

  1. Cut off: a network ACL on the zone's worker subnets that blocks all traffic to the other zones and to the storage. Workers stay running. This is the partition case and tests fencing.
  2. Gone: stop all workers of the zone through the VPC API. This tests the clean zone loss.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Each is a release test stage that runs unattended, as the other stages do.

  • Level 2, gone: write a counter file on a VM and on a plain volume every second, fail over, check that the data on the new VM is no older than the RPO, and that the VM boots. Repeat for the two-disk VM and check that both disks show one moment.
  • Level 2, cut off: as above, but the old VM keeps writing. Check that the fence stops it, that the stale disk is kept, and that no disk of the new VM changed after the failover.
  • Level 1, gone and cut off: RPO is 0 (the counter shows no gap), the VM restarts in another zone, and the cut-off VM can no longer write.
  • Failback of both levels, with the one-VM move and the outage time measured.
  • Spare room: a plan against a full surviving zone is refused.
  • Failover with a stuck pod on a missing node (the finalizer case).
  • A false alarm: the zone is Suspect for 3 minutes and then recovers. Nothing is moved.
  • Metrics and alerts fire as listed.

Unit tests cover the zone state machine, the plan builder, the re-home steps with a fake client, and the webhook rules.

docs.title: Phase 0: checks in the lab, before any code
docs.text:
Do these first. The results can change the plan.

  1. IBM access: request rfs special access for the account and region. Record the answer and the date.
  2. Cross-zone mounting: mount a dp2 share from a worker in another zone through the driver. Does it work? How slow? Does the pool need one mount target per zone, or does one serve all (the two docs disagree)?
  3. A zonal share in a dead zone: with the zone cut off, can a worker in a surviving zone still mount and use the share? (If it can, the "storage-only-up" shortcut in the failure model is real.)
  4. Share replication: create a replica in another zone. Measure the real interval, the sync time, and whether a sync is one consistent moment (write a counter during a sync). Fail over with split. Resolve fact 11. This decides whether IBM replication has any role.
  5. rfs with the driver: create an rfs share through the API, with the Go SDK we use. Mount it with sec=sys and our mount options. Check the root squash behaviour, initial_owner, the export path, a 1 TB file, and the speed with fio. Fail the zone (cut off) and measure the time until I/O works from another zone.
  6. Fencing controls: does removing a security group rule stop an open NFS connection? Does a zombie client's write fail after its lease ends? Does deleting a Node object restart an Always VM in another zone, and how long does it take?
  7. ROKS and ROVS in a zone loss: how workers are spread across zones, and whether ROKS replaces lost workers by itself. Find the IBM documentation. Add the source to this spec.
  8. PVC re-home: delete and recreate a PVC and PV under a VM whose node is gone. Does the VM start on the new PV with its name unchanged?
  9. Cost: read the price of rfs and dp2 in the console for eu-de, and the VPC rule for traffic between zones. Fill the cost section with numbers.
  10. A disk with an instant-snapshot chain after a Level 2 copy: does it boot in the partner pool?

Phase 0 ends with a short note in this folder with the results. If check 5 fails or rfs is not available, Level 1 waits and the rest goes ahead.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Sizes: S is one PR, M is 3 to 4 PRs, L is 5 or more. Each PR adds its release test checks.

Phase What Size 0 Lab checks above, and the multi-zone lab lab build plus about 1 week of work, no code 1 Zone health, status, metrics, alerts, spare room check. A failed zone's pools stop expanding and never heal in place. Docs: fix the two pages that disagree. M 2 Level 2 protection: zoneProtection on the pool, the controller-owned policy to a partner pool in the same cluster, the /replica/ layout, the RPO status, the webhook rules M 3 Zone failover for Level 2: ZoneFailover, fencing, re-home, the command and the plan. The first release test with a simulated loss. L 4 Failback for Level 2: re-seed, per-VM move, stale disk handling M 5 Level 1: rfs profile in the pool and the VPC client, regional mount target, webhook limits, fencing and restart for regional pools. Needs phase 0 checks 1 and 5. Can start after phase 1, in parallel with 2 to 4. M 6 Console "Zones" page; the optional automatic mode M

Order: phases 0 and 1 first. Then 5 and 2 to 4 in parallel if rfs is open to us, because Level 1 is the shorter path to RPO 0. If rfs is not open, 2 to 4 are the whole deliverable.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Two protection levels: a regional pool for RPO 0, and a copied pool for RPO of minutes. I did not pick one, because the regional shares are not generally available and have performance limits.
  • For dp2 there is no way to reach RPO 0 on IBM Cloud. I state the gap: minutes, not zero.
  • The copied pool uses our own VM-safe copy, not IBM share replication. IBM replication is slower (15 minutes or more), copies whole shares, and has no VM moment. It stays a phase 0 comparison only.
  • Failover is started by an admin. The controller only proposes it. A false alarm that starts a second copy of every VM is worse than a few minutes of waiting.
  • Fencing comes first and is required. The command refuses to run without it, unless the admin says in writing the zone is gone.
  • The default copy interval is 5 minutes, and the default RPO target is 15 minutes.
  • Zones copy in a ring (1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 1). It is simple and uses the existing one-destination policy.
  • The copy folders sit on the partner pool's shares under /replica/, not as volumes. A pod cannot mount a copy by mistake.
  • After a failover, volumes are re-homed in the same cluster by recreating the PV and PVC under the same names. The VM manifest does not change.
  • A stale disk from a cut-off zone is kept, never merged or deleted, until the admin removes it.
  • Failback is optional and per VM, with a short outage. Staying in the new zone forever is allowed.
  • The spare room is part of the plan. A failover plan is refused if the surviving zones cannot hold the load, unless the admin overrides.
  • A zone-loss test is simulated (blocked network, stopped workers). We cannot switch off an IBM zone.
  • A new multi-zone lab in eu-de is needed. None of the current three can test this.
  • The automatic failover is the last phase and off by default.
  • I did not use accessor zones as a protection method. They help with load, not with the loss of the zone that holds the share.

docs.title: Spec: the console shows the driver's real VM snapshot mode
