docs.text: Date: 2026-10-24. Status: draft for review. It builds on docs/VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md (the "Choosing a setting" section) and 2026-10-21-instant-vm-snapshots.md.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A person who opens the console on a cluster can see, without reading Helm values, how the driver takes VM disk snapshots there: instant or copy. The console must never say "instant" while the driver takes copies.

docs.title: What exists today (from the code)
docs.text:
• The driver has one setting, vmSnapshots.method (flag --vm-snapshot-method, in cmd/main.go): auto or copy. With copy, every VM disk snapshot is a copy, whatever the cluster allows.
  • Instant snapshots need two things at once: method=auto and the KubeVirt Sidecar feature gate turned on.
  • The console box "Instant VM snapshots: on / off / unknown" (console-plugin/src/components/common/InstantSnapshotStatus.tsx, used on the Snapshots page and the Pools page) reads only the gate, through instantSnapshotState() in console-plugin/src/utils/instant-snapshots.ts. It never sees method.

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: If the gate is on and method=copy, the box says "on" but snapshots are copies. A wrong "on" is worse than no box, because a person may rely on instant snapshots that are not happening. The gate can be turned on by anyone who can edit the cluster's HyperConverged object, so the two values can differ.

docs.title: Design that meets the goal
docs.text:
The console needs one more fact, method, and it already has the other one, the gate. The effective mode is a function of both:

method Gate Mode shown copy on, off or cannot be read Copy auto on Instant auto off Copy auto cannot be read Unknown not published (older chart) any Unknown, with the words "the driver does not report its setting"

How the console learns method. The Helm chart renders a small ConfigMap, ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi-settings, in the release namespace. It holds only non-secret settings the console wants to show. It starts with one key, vmSnapshotMethod. It is configuration written by Helm, not driver state, so the rule "all state in CRDs" is not touched.

Ordinary console users cannot read ConfigMaps in kube-system. So the chart also renders a Role that allows get on that one ConfigMap by name, and a RoleBinding for all authenticated users. Nothing else in the namespace becomes readable.

What the box says. - Instant: "VM snapshots: instant. Each snapshot starts a new small file. The KubeVirt Sidecar feature gate is on." - Copy because the gate is off (method=auto): "VM snapshots: copy. The driver would take instant snapshots, but the KubeVirt Sidecar feature gate is off." - Copy because of the setting (method=copy): "VM snapshots: copy. The driver is set to copy. Each snapshot copies the disk: slower, and it uses more storage. Nothing else on the cluster is changed." - Unknown: as today, with the reason.

The list of VMs that have instant snapshots stays, shown only in Instant mode.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
1. A chart test (test/chart/, run by make test-scripts): helm template renders the ConfigMap with the value of vmSnapshots.method, and a Role limited to that ConfigMap name. Written first and seen failing.
  2. A console unit test: the mode function returns the table above for every row, including "not published".
  3. A component test: the box text matches each mode.
  4. By hand on a cluster: copy with the gate on shows Copy (the case that is wrong today).

docs.title: Build plan
docs.text: One pull request, two commits: the chart (ConfigMap, Role, RoleBinding, test, docs/HELM-VALUES.md note), then the console (mode function, box text, tests). Update docs/VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS.md and the CHANGELOG.

docs.title: Does the design meet the goal?
docs.text: Yes. The box shows copy or instant, and it cannot say "instant" unless both conditions hold, because it combines both facts. It does not depend on monitoring being installed.

docs.title: Cost, effort and risk
docs.text:
• Effort: about a day, including the by-hand check.
  • Risk: low. The only cluster change is one read-only ConfigMap and a Role that reads that one name. A cluster on an older chart shows "Unknown", never a wrong answer.
  • Not covered: a cluster where someone edits the driver's flag by hand, not through Helm. The ConfigMap would then be wrong. Helm is the supported way, so this spec accepts that.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The box shows the driver's effective mode (copy or instant), not the raw gate.
  • The driver's setting reaches the console as a Helm-rendered ConfigMap, not a new CRD and not a metric. A metric needs monitoring installed, which is optional.
  • All authenticated users may read that one ConfigMap and nothing else in the namespace.
  • An older chart with no ConfigMap shows "Unknown" with a reason. It never guesses.
  • The list of VMs with instant snapshots appears only in Instant mode.
  • One pull request, chart first, console second.
  • With method=copy the box says Copy even when the KubeVirt gate cannot be read, because the setting alone settles the answer. (Changed while building: the first draft said Unknown.)

docs.title: draw.io diagrams for the docs
docs.text: Status: agreed and built, 2026-10-24.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Every Markdown doc that explains a structure or a flow has draw.io diagrams next to its text. The diagrams are simple and professional. They carry labels only; the explanation stays in the text. The style and file rules are in docs/images/README.md.

docs.title: Done means
docs.text:
1. Each doc in scope was read, and each section that explains a structure, a flow, a sequence of steps across parts, or a set of states has a diagram, unless the text is already short and clear without one.
  2. Each text drawing made of characters (boxes of ┌─┐, arrows of ──>) is replaced by a draw.io diagram that shows the same thing. The text drawing is removed.
  3. Every diagram follows docs/images/README.md, was looked at as a PNG, and has alt text.
  4. A list at the end of this spec names each doc in scope and its diagrams, or "no diagram" with a one-line reason.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
In scope: every .md file in docs/ and the repository root, except those listed below.

Out of scope: - CHANGELOG.md: a list of changes. - docs/specs/: build plans. They can get diagrams later. - docs/images/README.md: the style guide itself.

docs.title: How the work is split
docs.text:
Two batches, each on its own branch and pull request: - Batch 1, design docs: ARCHITECTURE, CONSISTENCY-MODEL, VOLUME-GROUP-SNAPSHOTS, VOLUME-CLONING, CROSS-REGION-DR, VPC-NETWORKING, VM-DISK-FORMATS, VM-INSTANT-SNAPSHOTS, CSI-INTERFACE, CRD-SPEC, IBM-VPC-API, GOLDEN-IMAGE-WORKFLOW, OVERVIEW, README, FEATURES, KNOWN-LIMITATIONS, SECURITY, CONTEXT, CAPACITY-PLANNING, PERFORMANCE-TUNING, TESTING, CODING-GUIDELINES, SKILL, CONTRIBUTING. - Batch 2, operations and tutorials: TUTORIAL and TUTORIAL-01 to TUTORIAL-14, INSTALL, UPGRADE-GUIDE, HELM-VALUES, API-KEY-SETUP, MONITORING, DAY2-OPERATIONS, BACKUP-RECOVERY, TROUBLESHOOTING, USER-GUIDE, DEPLOYMENT-NOTES, SUPPORT.

A tutorial links to the design doc's diagram when it shows the same thing, instead of a copy.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Diagrams are .drawio.svg files: one file that GitHub shows as a picture and draw.io opens for editing. No separate .drawio and .png pair that can drift apart.
  • All diagrams live in docs/images/, named after their doc.
  • Text drawings of boxes and arrows are replaced, not kept beside the new diagram. Folder trees and file lists stay as text, because they are easier to read and copy as text.
  • The diagrams show what the doc says. Where a doc looks wrong against the code, the diagram follows the doc, and the difference is reported, not fixed in this work.
  • The colours are IBM's grey and blue, with green for live and red only for failures.
  • The interactive pages in docs/diagrams/ stay. They teach by clicking; these diagrams sit beside the text.
  • Specs are left out of this pass.

docs.title: Spec: how many general-purpose VMs one share carries
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-24. Status: draft for review. It answers issue #118 and gives the numbers behind the share alerts of issue #117 (closed).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
An administrator can look up, for each share speed (IOPS tier), how many everyday VMs one share carries before users notice, and what the share's IOPS limit and delay look like at that point. The answer is a sizing table in docs/CAPACITY-PLANNING.md and docs/PERFORMANCE-TUNING.md, with the measurements behind it.

"Everyday VMs" means a general-purpose mix of Linux and Windows VMs, not databases: low average load, short bursts at boot, patching and backup scans.

docs.title: What exists today (from the repo and the lab clusters)
docs.text:
• The /bench skill runs fio sequential and random tests on one plain pool. It does not use VMs.
  • Release test stage 17 runs five 60-second fio tests in three places: a pod on a pool volume, a pod on IBM's own 3000-IOPS class, and inside one VM on a pool disk. It writes speed.csv, keeps a history, and warns (does not fail) when a result is 20% worse than the last run.
  • Share speed rules. IBM's dp2 table is kept in pkg/ibmcloud/share_profiles.go, and the pool admission check refuses a bad size and IOPS pair (issue #37):
Share size (GB) IOPS allowed 10 to 39 100 to 1,000 40 to 79 100 to 2,000 80 to 99 100 to 4,000 100 to 499 100 to 6,000 500 to 999 100 to 10,000 1,000 to 1,999 100 to 20,000 2,000 to 3,999 200 to 40,000 4,000 to 7,999 300 to 40,000 8,000 to 15,999 500 to 64,000 16,000 to 32,000 2,000 to 96,000
  • Measurements the driver already makes. The node agents read the NFS client counters of each share and publish vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_operations_total and vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_execute_seconds_total (by pool, share and operation). Two alerts use them: VPCFilePoolShareNFSLatencyHigh (more than 0.1 s per request on average for 10 minutes, judged only above 1 request a second) and VPCFilePoolShareIOPSHigh (off by default). Allocation time has its own histogram.
  • Room in the lab. rovslab-dr-eude has 3 workers of about 96 vCPU and 389 GB each and no pools in use. rovslab-prod-eude has 3 workers of about 64 vCPU and 512 GB each, and holds other tests.
  • A Windows Server 2022 test VM was already run on the lab (instant snapshot tests), so a Windows image exists. How it is licensed is not recorded here.

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: No test runs many VMs at once, and no test uses a Windows VM under load. So the repo cannot say how many VMs fit on one share. The guides give an IOPS model and advice by volume count and size, but no measured number of VMs per share.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text:
For each IOPS tier, one pool with one share carries a growing number of VMs. For each step the test records:

  • Per VM, from inside the guest: IOPS, throughput, and p50, p95 and p99 latency, from fio on Linux and diskspd on Windows.
  • Per share, from the node agents: NFS operations a second and average latency a request, all nodes together, with the share's IOPS limit beside them.
  • Stalls: a stall is any I/O that takes more than 5 seconds, or a guest log line that reports a blocked disk.
  • Driver: time to allocate each volume, time for each VM to boot and report its guest agent, time to take a snapshot, time for a backup.

docs.title: The load profile (one per VM)
docs.text:
• Average 20 to 50 IOPS, set with a rate limit so it does not depend on the VM's speed.
  • Bursts of about 300 IOPS for 30 to 60 seconds every 10 to 15 minutes, which stand for boot, patching and backup scans.
  • 70% reads, 30% writes, block sizes mixed from 4 KB to 64 KB.
  • Each VM gets a different start time, so bursts do not line up except in the patch window.

docs.title: The mix of VMs
docs.text: Two thirds Linux (CentOS Stream 9, 1 vCPU, 2 GB) and one third Windows Server 2022 (2 vCPU, 4 GB), at every step. So 30 VMs is 20 Linux and 10 Windows. All disks are on the one share under test.

docs.title: The tiers
docs.text:
Three runs, one for each share speed. Each uses a fresh pool with one share of 3,900 GB, made and deleted for the run. Only the IOPS changes, so the three results compare like with like. IBM allows 200 to 40,000 IOPS at that size (the 2,000 to 3,999 GB row). The disks of 90 VMs need about 3.2 TB: a copy of a catalog disk must be 30 GiB, so each Linux VM needs 32 GiB with its load disk and each Windows VM about 42 GiB. (The first draft gave each tier its own smaller share. That was wrong: 90 VMs do not fit on 200 GB, or on 3,000 GB.)

Tier IOPS set Low 3,000 Middle 10,000 High 20,000

docs.title: The steps in one run
docs.text:
1. Start 15 VMs. Wait until all report their guest agent. Run the profile for 45 minutes.
  2. Add VMs up to 30. Run 45 minutes. At this step, also run:
  3. Boot storm: stop all 30 VMs and start them together. Record how long until the last one is ready.
  4. Patch window: all 30 burst at 300 IOPS together for 10 minutes.
  5. Mixed work: while the load runs, live-migrate one VM, take one snapshot, and run one backup.
  6. Add VMs up to 45, 60, 75, 90, with 45 minutes at each step. Stop at the knee or at 90 VMs, whichever comes first.
  7. At the last step reached, repeat the boot storm.
  8. Delete every VM, the pool and the share. Check in the VPC that the share is gone.

docs.title: The knee
docs.text:
The knee is the first step where any one of these is true for 5 minutes in a row:

  • p95 read latency above 20 ms on more than a quarter of the VMs,
  • any stall,
  • the boot storm takes more than twice as long as the same storm at 15 VMs,
  • the share runs at its IOPS limit and requests queue.

The recommended count in the sizing table is 80% of the knee, rounded down to a whole step.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text: On rovslab-dr-eude. It is idle, has the room, and a mistake there does not touch the other tests on rovslab-prod-eude. The release test's name sweep (everything labelled with the run ID) cleans up at the end, the same way as the release run.

docs.title: What gets built
docs.text: A folder test/perf/ with: a script that runs one tier; the Linux and Windows VM definitions with the load profile in them (cloud-init for Linux, the prepared image for Windows); a collector that gathers the guest results and the node agent metrics; and a report step that writes the table and a CSV. It reuses the release test's library (labels, waits, sweep) and the fio code of stage 17. The test is started the same way, from the build server, so the laptop can sleep.

docs.title: The output
docs.text:
• docs/CAPACITY-PLANNING.md and docs/PERFORMANCE-TUNING.md: a table of VMs per share for each tier, the knee, the recommended count, and the p95 and p99 latency and the share IOPS used at the recommended count.
  • The raw results of each run: a CSV and a short summary kept in docs/perf/.
  • A note on whether the 0.1 s threshold of VPCFilePoolShareNFSLatencyHigh fires before the knee, with the numbers. Any change to the alert is a separate pull request.

docs.title: Tests of the test
docs.text:
• Unit tests (Bash, like the other test/ scripts) for the report step with made-up results: the knee rule, the 80% rule, and the table.
  • A smoke run first: 5 VMs on the low tier for 10 minutes, to prove the tools, the collection and the cleanup before any long run.
  • After every run, a check that nothing labelled with the run ID is left in the cluster or the VPC.

docs.title: Build plan: phases, one PR each
docs.text:
1. Tooling and smoke run. The VM definitions, the load profile, the collector, the report step and its tests; the 5-VM smoke run.
  2. First full run: the middle tier. Review the knee rule against what the data shows. Adjust the rule in the spec if it is wrong.
  3. The low and high tiers.
  4. Documentation: the sizing table in the two guides, the raw results, the alert note.

docs.title: Does the design meet the goal?
docs.text:
Yes. It finds the knee for each tier by growing the count until users would notice, up to 90 VMs, and it includes the Windows VMs, the boot storm, the patch window, and a migration, a snapshot and a backup under load. Three limits are stated, not hidden:

  • At the assumed profile, the high tier may not reach a knee by 90 VMs (90 VMs at 50 IOPS average is 4,500 IOPS; their bursts together are 27,000). If so, the table says "more than 90 at this tier", not a made-up number.
  • The result applies to this profile. A heavier VM mix (databases) needs its own run.
  • Cloud storage speed varies from hour to hour. The first full run is repeated once at its knee step, and both results go in the table.

docs.title: Cost, effort and risk
docs.text:
• Effort: about 3 to 5 days to build the tooling and the smoke run. Each full run is about 8 hours of lab time, so the three tiers are about a day of running, which can go overnight.
  • Cost: three shares of 3,900 GB for a few hours each, deleted after. The VMs use the lab cluster's spare room.
  • Risk:
  • The Windows image: if it cannot be used for a test like this (licence or no diskspd), the Windows third of the mix is replaced and the table says so. Today no Windows catalog image is ready on rovslab-dr-eude, so the Windows part needs an image brought in first. Phase 1 builds the Linux half; the Windows half waits for a decision on the image.
  • A leftover VM or share after a failed run costs money until it is deleted. The sweep and the final VPC check guard against it.
  • Results from a shared cloud backend are noisy. The repeat run and the written knee rule limit this.

docs.title: Phase 1 results (smoke runs on rovslab-dr-eude, 2026-10-24)
docs.text:
Five small Linux VMs on a 200 GB, 3,000 IOPS share, 10 minutes of measuring. It took four runs to get a good one. What each run found:

  1. The VM definition used a cloud-init field name KubeVirt does not know (secretRef is right).
  2. A copy of a catalog disk must be at least as large as the catalog disk, 30 GiB. This changed the share size in this spec (3,900 GB).
  3. fio counted every I/O of a job with a block size range as the smallest block size, so the load came out about 8 times too light (35 IOPS for a target of 300). The load is now three jobs with fixed block sizes. After the fix the VMs hit their targets: about 28 steady and 298 burst IOPS against 30 and 300.
  4. The node agents' /metrics answered HTTP 500 when a node held the same share more than once, so the share counters read zero. This was a driver bug, fixed in PR #246 and in the main-55211050 build that DR runs.

The good run: all 5 VMs ready in about 4 minutes (including the disk fill), no stall, no slow VM, no VM short of its rate, and the cleanup left nothing.

Open, to settle before the first full run. The share counters showed 982 NFS operations a second at 532 ms average, while the VMs reported about 359 IOPS and a p95 of about 1.3 ms. The two sides do not agree. Possible causes: a host cache between the guest and the share (the disk cache mode), the root disks' own traffic on the same share, or write-behind queueing in the NFS client that the guests never wait for. Every run now records the first VM's disk definition (vm1-disks.txt) to answer the first. If a cache is the cause, the guest latency is flattered and the 20 ms rule must be applied to the share-side latency, or the cache must be bypassed.

Windows VMs (built; one VM run on rovslab-dr-eude on 24 October 2026). The image is Windows Server 2022 Datacenter Evaluation, copied from rovslab-prod-eude (brs-win-image/win2k22-brs) to rovslab-dr-eude (openshift-virtualization-os-images/win2k22-perf). test/perf/prepare-windows-image.sh prepares it once: it installs fio for Windows (3.43, from the fio project's release, checked against its checksum), sets the clock to UTC, and activates the evaluation licence (online it gives 180 days; without internet it resets the grace period). run-tier.sh makes every third VM Windows (--windows-every, 0 for none). Each Windows VM gets a config disk from a ConfigMap with the fio arguments of its fill and its two phases, built by the same code as the Linux jobs, and windows/load.ps1, which fills the test area once, says PERF-READY and prints the same result line as a Linux VM. The run starts each Windows VM's load through the guest agent. The Windows VMs share one computer name and machine identity (the image is not sysprepped); that has no effect on a disk test. The first run was one Windows VM alone (--steps 1 --windows-every 1, a 200 GB share at 3000 IOPS, 10 minutes): ready 3.5 minutes after it was made, about 28 steady and 298 burst IOPS against 30 and 300, steady p95 under 1 ms, no stall. The share counted 76 NFS operations a second against 73 IOPS from the guest, so for this VM the two sides agree.

Decisions made while building it: - fio, not DiskSpd, on Windows. DiskSpd 2.2 and 2.3 both refused every job file on this Windows build ("failed to load profile, line 0, errorCode 80070057"), even one DiskSpd wrote itself, and its command line cannot give each block size its own rate. fio runs the exact Linux jobs, so the two kinds of VM compare like with like. - The run starts the load through the guest agent, not a Windows start-up task. The task stayed "Queued" and never ran, even when started by hand.

Not built yet: repeat runs and a steady-state check, the baseline and event windows, the boot storm and the other planned events. They are items 5, 7, 9 and 12 of the research file docs/research/2026-10-24-storage-benchmark-tools.md.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The real VM mix and peaks are not known, so I used the issue's defaults: 20 Linux and 10 Windows, 20 to 50 IOPS average, 300 IOPS bursts, 70/30 read/write. Change them here and the test follows.
  • "Users notice" means p95 read latency above 20 ms, or any stall over 5 seconds, or a boot storm twice as slow as at 15 VMs.
  • The recommended count is 80% of the knee.
  • Three tiers: 3,000, 10,000 and 20,000 IOPS, all on a 3,900 GB share, so only the IOPS differs.
  • The ramp goes 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90 and stops at the knee or 90.
  • The test runs on rovslab-dr-eude, not on rovslab-prod-eude.
  • The Linux VMs are small (1 vCPU, 2 GB) and the Windows VMs are 2 vCPU, 4 GB, so the disk is the thing being tested, not the CPU.
  • The tool lives in test/perf/ and results in docs/perf/.
  • Alerts are not changed by this work; it only reports whether the 0.1 s threshold fits.

docs.title: Spec: PoolBench, a storage performance test in the console
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-25. Status: draft for review. It builds on the performance test spec (2026-10-24-performance-test-30-vms.md, issue #118) and the VM capacity research (docs/research/2026-10-24-vm-sizes-and-cluster-capacity.md).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
An administrator opens the OpenShift console and, without a terminal, can:

  • set up a performance test of a file pool share with VMs, with every setting the command-line test has;
  • start it, watch it live, and control it while it runs (pause, hold, skip a step, stop);
  • see at every moment how many VMs are running, what the share does, and how the VMs feel;
  • get a final result in the style of VMware HCIBench: one row per VM count, the knee, and the recommended VM count for that share;
  • keep, compare and download the results of earlier runs.

"Comprehensive" is the bar: every fact a person needs to trust the result or to stop a bad run must be on the page, with help text. A person must never need a terminal to find out what the test is doing.

docs.title: What exists today (from the repo and the lab clusters)
docs.text:
• The command-line test in test/perf/ (run-tier.sh, collect.sh, report.sh, profile.sh, guest.sh, windows/). It runs from the build server with a kubeconfig. It makes a pool with one share, adds VMs in steps of 15 (1 in 3 Windows), lets them settle, measures, applies the knee rule, writes a CSV and a Markdown report, and cleans up. It has run the 3,000 IOPS tier (knee at 45 VMs, recommended 30) and is running the 10,000 IOPS tier on rovslab-dr-eude.
  • How the test reads the VMs today. Each guest prints one result line per load phase on its serial console. collect.sh reads the console logs after each step. So results arrive only at the end of a step, and only to the machine that runs the script.
  • Share counters. The node agents publish NFS operations, latency and bytes for each share (vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_*, see docs/MONITORING.md). Prometheus keeps them.
  • The console plugin has a Monitoring page with time graphs that read Prometheus (TimeSeriesChart.tsx, use-pool-metrics.ts), a Dashboard, and tabs under VPC File Pools for pools, volumes, snapshots, replication, migration and backups. It checks the person's rights by access review before an action (the backup UI pattern).
  • Not built in the command-line test yet: boot storm, patch window, and a live migration, snapshot and backup under load.

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: The test needs a terminal, a kubeconfig on a build server, and someone who reads logs. Nothing is live: a person sees a step's result 45 to 60 minutes after it starts. There is no control except killing the script, and no place where old results are kept and compared.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
1. A PoolBench resource (cluster-scoped, storage.ibmcloud.io/v1alpha1). Its spec holds every setting of the run. Its status holds the live state and the results table. All state is in this object, as for the other features.
  2. The PoolBench service: a new Deployment in the driver namespace, off by default (poolBench.enabled in Helm). One replica with leader election. It has its own service account, so the CSI controller's rights do not grow. It does two jobs:
  3. Runner. A reconciler moves each PoolBench through its stages and records each stage in the status. If the pod restarts, it reads the status and goes on from the same stage. It never loses a run and never starts a step twice.
  4. Collector. An HTTP endpoint inside the cluster. Each test VM sends its result line to it at the end of every load phase (Linux with curl from the cloud-init script, Windows with Invoke-WebRequest from load.ps1). The collector publishes the results as Prometheus metrics and keeps the raw lines on a small results volume.
  5. The PoolBench pages in the console plugin, a new tab "PoolBench" under VPC File Pools.

Sending results to the collector replaces reading the serial console. Results then arrive within seconds of each phase, from every VM, and the console log stays only as a fallback for a VM that cannot reach the collector.

docs.title: Safety: the test never touches real VMs' storage
docs.text:
• Every run makes its own new pool and share and its own namespace (poolbench-<run name>). Nothing is shared with other pools. Every object carries the run label, and the end of a run deletes them all and checks in the VPC that the share is gone, as the command-line test does.
  • A finalizer on PoolBench makes sure that deleting the object, or a failed run, still cleans up.
  • The test VMs still use the nodes' CPU, memory and network. The new-run form checks free room first (below) and the page says plainly that real VMs share the nodes.
  • Only a cluster administrator can create a PoolBench (cluster-scoped, plus an access review in the console). The admission webhook refuses a run that does not fit the IBM dp2 size and IOPS table, or the cluster.

docs.title: What the person can set (the new-run form)
docs.text:
Every setting has help text and a sensible default. Presets fill the form: "Quick check" (5 VMs, a shorter 120-second load period, about 25 minutes), "One tier" (the spec's full ramp), "Three tiers" (3,000, 10,000 and 20,000 IOPS one after another).

  • Share: size in GB and IOPS, with the allowed IOPS range for that size shown live from the dp2 table. The form works out the size the VMs need and warns if the share is too small.
  • VM mix: VMs per step (15), number of steps or the largest VM count (90), the Windows share of the mix (1 in 3, or none), and the Linux and Windows sizes (vCPU, memory). Windows needs the prepared image; the form shows whether it exists and when its evaluation licence ends.
  • Load profile: steady IOPS per VM, burst IOPS, burst length and gap, read and write mix, block size mix. The form shows the resulting demand per step in IOPS and in IBM operations (the 1.6 factor of the research note) beside the share's limit.
  • Timing: settle minutes and measure minutes per step. The form shows the expected total run time.
  • Knee rule: the latency limit (20 ms), the share of VMs that may be over it (a quarter), the stall time (5 s), and whether the run stops at the knee.
  • Events at a chosen step (optional): boot storm, patch window, live migration, snapshot, backup.
  • At the end: delete everything (default), or keep the VMs and pool for a look (the page then shows a "Clean up now" button and a cost warning).

Before Run, a check panel shows: free CPU and memory on the nodes against the largest step, also with one node down (the N+1 rule of the research note); the share size and IOPS and how long it will exist; whether the images exist; and anything that would block the run. The button stays off until every blocking check passes.

docs.title: The run page
docs.text:
1. Status banner. Stage and progress in plain words, for example "Step 3 of 6: 45 VMs running (15 Windows), measuring, 20 min left". Also the run's start, expected end, and share size and IOPS.
  2. Controls, each with a short note of what it does:
  3. Pause / Resume. The VMs stop their load; the clock of the step stops.
  4. Hold at this step. Keep measuring this VM count until the person says go on.
  5. Measure longer. Add minutes to the current step.
  6. Skip to the next step. End this step now; its row is marked "cut short".
  7. Stop and clean up. End the run and delete everything; confirmed with a dialog.
  8. Run an event now. Boot storm, patch window, migration, snapshot or backup, at the current step.
  9. Live graphs, all with the same time axis, a marker at the start of each step and at each event, and a range picker:
  10. VMs running, Linux and Windows stacked, and VMs that are not ready yet.
  11. IOPS: share NFS IOPS, guest IOPS, and IBM operations, against the share's IOPS limit.
  12. Latency: the VMs' p50, p95 and p99, and the share's average latency per request, against the 20 ms line.
  13. Throughput in MB/s, read and write.
  14. Slow VMs: the percent of VMs over the latency limit, against the knee threshold.
  15. Step results (the HCIBench-style table): VMs (Linux and Windows), share IOPS, guest IOPS, IBM operations and percent of the limit, p50, p95 and p99, percent of VMs slow, stalls, time to ready, and a pass or fail per step. The knee row and the recommended count are marked, with one sentence that explains the result.
  16. VMs. One row per test VM: name, OS, node, state, last IOPS, last p95, slow phases, stalls. A row opens that VM's result lines and console log.
  17. Event log. Every stage change, control action, warning and error, with the time.
  18. Downloads: step table (CSV), raw VM results (CSV), the report (Markdown), and a print view that the browser saves as PDF.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
An event is an extra test at a chosen step, on VMs that are already under load. Each event runs once, in its own stage called Event, right after the step's measuring ends. The step's own numbers, and so the knee, stay free of the event. All VMs keep their normal load during the event.

Each event writes one result: when it started and ended, its main time in seconds, and one plain sentence with the numbers. An event never fails the run. If it cannot run, the result says why and the run goes on. Every event ends at the latest 30 minutes after it started, except the backup, which gets 60 minutes because it copies whole VM disks at the backup policy's copy speed limit.

Event What it does Main time Boot storm Restarts every VM at once. The load restarts by itself on Linux (a system service) and through the guest agent on Windows. Until the last VM sends results again Patch window All VMs run the burst load without the quiet phase, for 10 minutes, as a patch scan would. Until the share's p95 is back under the limit Migration Live-migrates 10% of the VMs at once (at least 1, at most 10). Until the last migration ends; failed migrations are counted Snapshot Takes an instant snapshot of 10% of the VMs while they run. Until the last snapshot is ready Backup Backs up 10% of the VMs (at least 1, at most 10) while they run, with a backup policy, to a second small share that the run makes. Until the last backup ends

The Backup event needs no object storage bucket. The run makes a second pool of one share, sized for a full copy of the target VMs' disks and half as much again, at 3,000 IOPS so the backup share is not what slows the copy. It labels the load disks of the target VMs, makes a backup policy that selects them in the run's namespace and copies to that pool, and deletes the policy when the event ends, so it backs up once. Cleanup deletes the policy and the second pool. Because a backup policy is not tied to a namespace, the service gets get, create and delete on backup policies cluster-wide, and the admission policy lets it make only a policy named poolbench-* for one poolbench-* namespace, that copies to that run's backup pool and never exports. A run name may not end in -backups, so one run's backup pool never has the name of another run's pool; the service also refuses to use or delete a pool that carries another run's label.

docs.title: Other pages
docs.text:
• Runs list: name, share size and IOPS, state, VMs now, knee, recommended count, started, run time. A failed run shows its reason in plain words.
  • Compare: pick two or more finished runs and see their step results side by side, and one graph of p95 latency against VM count, one line per run. This is how a person reads the three tiers together.
  • Help: the knee rule, the profile, what IBM operations are, and the limits below, in plain words, linked from every card.

docs.title: Measurements kept and for how long
docs.text:
• The step table, the knee, the settings and the summary stay in the PoolBench status for as long as the object exists.
  • The raw results stay on the results volume until the PoolBench is deleted.
  • The live graphs read Prometheus. After Prometheus drops old data (15 days by default), the run page shows the step table and the raw results, but not the graphs. The page says so.

docs.title: Metrics added
docs.text: The collector publishes, per run, step and VM: guest IOPS, p50, p95 and p99 latency, slow phases and stalls; and per run: VMs running by OS, VMs not ready, current step and stage. They go into docs/MONITORING.md.

docs.title: Plan (one PR each, in this order; each with tests, help text, FEATURES.md and CHANGELOG.md lines)
docs.text:
1. The PoolBench resource and its admission checks, with make generate and docs/CRD-SPEC.md.
  2. The collector, and the guest scripts that send to it. A golden-file test keeps the Go load profile and the Bash profile the same.
  3. The runner: stages, steps, knee rule, cleanup, finalizer, restart in the middle of a run. Tested with fake clients.
  4. Helm: the Deployment, its service account and rights, the service, the results volume, metrics scraping; off by default. docs/HELM-VALUES.md.
  5. Console: runs list and run page with banner, step table, VM table and event log.
  6. Console: live graphs.
  7. Console: new-run form with presets, live checks and the check panel.
  8. Console: controls, downloads, print view and compare.
  9. Events: boot storm, patch window, migration, snapshot and backup under load, in the runner and the form.
  10. Lab check on rovslab-dr-eude: run the 3,000 IOPS tier from the console and compare with the command-line result (knee at 45, recommended 30). Both must agree within the noise of the share.

After step 10, the command-line runner stays for the build server until the console run agrees with it. Then a later PR makes run-tier.sh create a PoolBench instead of doing the work itself, so there is one runner, not two.

docs.title: Cost, effort and risk
docs.text:
• Effort: large, about 10 PRs, near the size of the backup UI. The runner (PR 3) and the run page (PRs 5 to 8) are most of it.
  • Cost: a run costs what the command-line test costs: one share for the run's length (a 3,900 GB share for about 8 hours per tier), deleted at the end. Leaving the resources kept after a run costs money until "Clean up now".
  • Risk:
  • The test VMs load the nodes' CPU and network. On a cluster with real VMs, the check panel and the N+1 rule limit this, but a run can still slow real VMs' network. The page says so before Run.
  • A run that cannot clean up (for example the VPC API is down) leaves a share that costs money. The finalizer keeps trying, and the page shows a red banner until the share is gone.
  • The PoolBench service has rights to create namespaces, VMs and pools. Its own service account, admin-only access, and the feature being off by default limit this.
  • The VMs must reach the collector over the pod network. If a cluster blocks this, the runner falls back to reading the console logs, and the live graphs then update once per step.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The name is PoolBench (the owner chose it).
  • The test runs inside the cluster as its own service, not from the build server, so the console can start it, show it live and control it.
  • The service is off by default and has its own rights, so a normal install does not gain the right to create VMs.
  • Every run makes its own pool, share and namespace and deletes them at the end, so real VMs' storage is never loaded.
  • VMs send each result to the service as it happens, instead of the service reading console logs after each step. The console log stays as a fallback.
  • Only cluster administrators can start a run.
  • The form blocks a run that does not fit the cluster with one node down.
  • The PDF comes from the browser's print view, so no PDF library is added.
  • Results stay until the run object is deleted; the graphs last as long as Prometheus keeps its data.
  • The command-line runner stays until the console run gives the same result, then becomes a thin starter for PoolBench.
  • Events run after a step's measuring, not during it, so one event cannot push a step over the knee.
  • An event never fails the run; it records why it could not run.
  • Events touch 10% of the VMs (at most 10), except the boot storm and the patch window, which touch all.
  • The Backup event needs no bucket: the run makes a second small share for the backups and removes it at the end. It comes last because it needs wider rights for the service.
  • The backup uses the backup policy's own copy speed limit, so the time is what a customer would see with the defaults.

docs.title: Spec: the VM disk copy speed adapts to the load on the share
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-26. Status: draft for review. It builds on 2026-10-21-backup-to-snapshot-pool.md (the backup copy) and 2026-10-25-poolbench.md (the backup event that measured it).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
A backup of a running VM is as fast as the share allows, and the VM is never noticeably slower because of it. A person does not have to guess a speed number.

Today the copy runs at a fixed limit, 20 MB/s for each disk (vmCopySpeedLimitMBps). The PoolBench backup event on the DR lab copied one 30 GB VM in 1,650 s at that limit. The limit is a guess. Too low, and a backup of a large VM takes hours and the restore point is old. Too high, and the copy reads the VM's own share hard enough to slow the VM.

docs.title: What exists today (from the code and the lab)
docs.text:
• The copy is a QEMU blockdev-backup job for each disk. It starts with a speed in bytes per second, set once in pkg/vmcopy/vmcopy.go (Start). The same copier makes the VM snapshots by copy (pkg/pool/snapshot_vm.go) and the backups (pkg/pool/replication_vmcopy.go).
  • QEMU can change the speed of a job that is running (block-job-set-speed). The driver does not use it yet. Lab check 1 proves it works on these VMs before anything else is built.
  • The replication controller wakes every 30 s and asks QEMU about each running copy (Progress). That is the natural moment to change the speed.
  • Each node agent already counts the reads and writes of each share and the seconds they took (the metrics vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_operations_total and vpc_file_pool_share_nfs_execute_seconds_total). PoolBench reads them to find the average latency of a share (pkg/poolbench/shares.go).
  • The VM's disk lives on the source share, and the copy reads from it. So the latency of the source share is the signal that says "the VM is being slowed".

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
On the policy. Three settings in BackupPolicy.spec:

  • vmCopySpeedLimitMBps stays. With adaptive speed on, it is the highest speed for each disk. Default 0 = no highest limit (today the default is 20). With adaptive speed off, it is the fixed speed, as before.
  • vmCopyAdaptive (new): true or false. Default true.
  • vmCopyMaxLatencyMs (new): the average share latency above which the copy slows down. Default 15. The CRD refuses a value above 20, the PoolBench limit for a slow VM.

While a copy runs. The speed starts low (15 MB/s for each disk), goes up while the source share is quiet, and goes down at once when its latency passes the limit. The replication status of the volume shows the speed now (vmCopy.speedMBps).

In PoolBench. The backup event result says how fast the copy went, the average and the highest, and what the VMs' latency did during the event compared with before it. A run can then answer "did the backup slow the VMs, and by how much".

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The copy starts at the start speed (15 MB/s for each disk).
  2. Every 30 s, for each running copy, the controller reads the average latency of the source share over the last interval (the change in execute_seconds_total divided by the change in operations_total, from every node agent, as PoolBench does).
  3. If the latency is under the limit, the speed goes up by 5 MB/s for each disk, up to the highest speed. If it is over the limit, the speed is halved, down to the start speed. A network uses the same rule to share a link: grow slowly, shrink fast.
  4. The new speed is sent to QEMU with block-job-set-speed.
  5. If the node agents cannot be read, or the share had no operations in the interval, the speed does not change. A missing reading never speeds the copy up.
  6. The speed of each copy is kept in the status (vmCopy.speedMBps of the replication policy's volume), so a restart of the controller goes on from it. Two copies on one source share both follow the same rule: both grow while the share is quiet, and both halve when it is not.

Smoothing. The reading is the median of the last three 30-second intervals, and an interval with fewer than 50 operations is not a reading. The lab (see below) showed that one 15-second interval of a busy share can swing by tens of milliseconds, so one bad interval must not decide.

The token. The controller does not send its own token to the node agents, because that token has wide rights and a node agent could be taken over. It asks the API server for a one-hour token of a separate service account (<release>-node-reader) that may do nothing but read /metrics, and renews it ten minutes before it ends.

Why share latency and not the VM's own latency. The driver cannot see inside the VM. The share latency is what every VM on that share feels, and it is already measured.

Why a slow start and a fast brake. A backup that is a little too slow costs minutes. A VM that is too slow costs the people who use it. The rule errs on the side of the VM.

docs.title: Checks before building (the lab)
docs.text:
1. block-job-set-speed on a running copy changes its speed, on a Linux and a Windows VM, and the copy still ends with a valid restore point.
  2. The average latency of a share goes up when a copy runs at high speed, so that the signal is real. Measure with PoolBench: a backup event at 20, 50 and 0 (no limit) MB/s, with the VM latency before and during.
  3. Choose the start speed, the step and the default latency limit from check 2, not from this spec.

docs.title: What the lab showed (DR, 2026-10-26)
docs.text:
Check 1 passed. On a Linux VM with a 30 GB root disk and a 4 GB load disk, block-job-set-speed changed the speed of copies that were running, up and down, within seconds. The copy followed the new speed (set to 20, 40 and 80 MB/s, it ran at about 22, 41 and 82 MB/s), and the backup still ended with "all finished". Two runs, one with speeds set by hand: 1,635 s at the fixed 20 MB/s, 555 to 720 s with raised speeds. A Windows VM was not tested; the speed is a setting of QEMU on the node, not of the guest.

Check 2 gave a first answer, not a final one. 5 VMs (steady 30 IOPS, bursts of 300) on a 200 GB, 3,000 IOPS share, one VM backing up, speed raised every two minutes. The median p95 latency of the VMs' own I/O:

Copy speed Steady Burst none (before) 0.8 ms 0.8 ms 20 MB/s 1.3 ms 2.0 ms 40 MB/s 4.0 ms 29.2 ms 80 MB/s 2.0 ms 1.1 ms unlimited 28.4 ms (worst 497 ms) 31.3 ms (worst 359 ms)

What this does show: at 20 MB/s the VMs hardly notice the copy; with no limit the VMs go far over the 20 ms limit for a slow VM. What it does not show: the middle. The 40 and 80 rows do not rise in order, because each VM result covers a 100-second test and the speed steps were two minutes long, so one result mixes two speeds. A VM-result window is too coarse for this. The signal the controller reads, the average latency of the share every 30 s, is much finer. The build therefore starts with a measurement of that signal against copy speed, with a step of at least 5 minutes, before the numbers in "How it works" are fixed.

docs.title: What is not in this step
docs.text:
• The speed of VM snapshots made by copy. They use the same copier, so they can get the same behavior later, but their deadline (vmSnapshotDeadline) is worked out from the speed limit and needs its own change.
  • Reading latency from inside the VM.
  • The export to COS. It reads the backup share, not the VM, and has its own rate.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Adaptive speed is on by default, because a number nobody can choose well should not be a setting people must set.
  • The existing speed limit becomes the highest speed, and a policy that sets one keeps it. A policy that sets nothing no longer has the 20 MB/s limit.
  • The signal is the average latency of the source share, the same one PoolBench uses.
  • The rule is: up 5 MB/s each 30 s while quiet, halve when over the limit. The numbers are first guesses; lab check 2 replaces them.
  • A missing reading never raises the speed.
  • The copy falls back to the old fixed speed (20 MB/s unless the policy says otherwise) when the controller cannot read the node agents, so a cluster without node metrics behaves as before.
  • The first build reports the speed in the replication status only. The PoolBench backup event does not report it yet.
  • Snapshots by copy keep the fixed limit in this step.
  • The PoolBench backup event reports the speed and the effect on VM latency, so the result of this work is measured, not claimed.

docs.title: Spec: a COS export reads a disk that does not change while it is read
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-27. Status: draft for review. It fixes issue #310. It builds on 2026-10-21-backup-cos-export.md (the export) and 2026-10-21-backup-to-snapshot-pool.md (the local backup).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A restore from COS gives the disk exactly as it was at the moment the export says. For a VM with two disks, both disks come back from the same moment.

docs.title: What goes wrong today
docs.text:
The export Job reads the live backup folder of a volume, then tags the result with the moment the volume had when the Job started. A local backup can be applied to the same folder while the Job reads it. The export then holds a mix of two moments under one tag. The undo files (the moments folder) are read after the disk, so the disk and its undo files can disagree.

Evidence is in the issue: in release test run 1027-1558 the root disk export took 15 minutes. The next local backup of that disk landed in the middle. The restored VM had a data disk with 556 of the 729 files that the root disk had. The check failed. The earlier full run passed only because its exports ended before the next backup.

Any export that is slower than the backup schedule can be torn. Nobody sees it until a restore.

docs.title: The change
docs.text:
While the export of a volume runs, the local backup of that volume waits. When the export ends, the backup runs at its next turn.

  1. When the controller starts an export Job for a volume, it marks the volume as held. When the Job ends (done, failed, or removed), it removes the mark.
  2. The replication controller skips a held volume in its cycle, as it already skips a volume in use by a running VM. The skip is not an error. The status says "held: export to COS running".
  3. Other volumes on the same share are not held. Only the volume being exported waits.
  4. A held volume that waits longer than its schedule is counted by the existing stale-backup metric. Nothing new to read: the age of the last restore point grows, and the alert for an old backup already covers it.
  5. If the controller restarts, the marks are rebuilt from the export Jobs that exist. A mark with no running Job is removed.
  6. A hold never lasts longer than a limit (default 6 hours). When the limit passes, the hold is removed, the export Job is stopped, and the export is marked failed with a clear message. Then it is tried again by the existing retry rule. This stops a stuck Job from stopping backups for ever.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
• Restore points of a volume get older by the length of its export. A 2 GB disk on the lab took 15 minutes. A large disk over a slow link takes longer.
  • The export spec has no sentence that says exports never hold back backups, but it implies that the two run side by side. It is changed to say that one volume's backup waits while its export runs.
  • The VM is not affected. The export still reads the snapshot pool, never the running VM.

docs.title: Why not the other two ways
docs.text:
• Freeze a copy first. Backups carry on, but it needs free space for one extra copy of the disk on the snapshot pool and one more read of the disk. Space on a full share is already the first thing that breaks in the lab. Not chosen. It stays open if the hold proves too slow for large disks.
  • Check afterwards and repeat. Nothing else changes, but on a busy schedule an export may never finish. Not chosen.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Red first, in this order:

  1. A held volume is skipped by the replication cycle, and the other volumes of its share are copied.
  2. The mark is set when an export Job starts and removed when the Job ends, fails, or is gone.
  3. After a controller restart, the mark matches the Jobs that exist.
  4. A hold past the limit is removed, the Job is stopped, and the volume shows an export error.
  5. The status shows the hold as a message, not as an error, and a held volume does not fail the policy.
  6. The metric for the age of the last backup keeps growing during a hold.

Then the lab proof: release test stage 18, full length, with the other cluster restore (COS_DR_CLUSTER). Both disks must come back from the same moment. A second run with an export made slower than the schedule on purpose (a short schedule) must also pass.

docs.title: Documents to update
docs.text: docs/specs/2026-10-21-backup-cos-export.md (add the hold), docs/BACKUP-RECOVERY.md, docs/CRD-SPEC.md (if the status gains a field), CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Wait, not freeze and not repeat. It needs no extra space and it always gives a clean export.
  • Only the volume being exported waits, not the whole share.
  • The wait is not an error. A held backup is normal, and the old-backup alert is what tells you if it lasts too long.
  • The hold has a 6 hour limit, so a stuck export cannot stop backups for ever.
  • Restore points get older during an export. I accept this, because a restore point that is wrong is worse than one that is old.
  • The export spec is changed to describe the hold. It made no promise against it, but the issue said it did; I checked and it did not.
  • No new setting for people. The 6 hour limit is fixed in the first build.

docs.title: Spec: Release v0.15.0
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-27. Status: draft for review.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Release v0.15.0 and put it on the three lab clusters: rovslab-dr-eude, rovslab-prod-eude and rovs-aug-2026-v2. After the update, the release test (make test-release) passes on rovslab-prod-eude.

"Done" means: - The tag v0.15.0 exists, and the images driver, browse and console-plugin at v0.15.0 are in de.icr.io/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi. - Each of the three clusters runs v0.15.0 for the driver and the console plugin. - The release test passes on rovslab-prod-eude, or each failure has a reason written down. - Every cluster can go back to the version it had before, with one command.

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
Fifty changes since v0.14.3. Two matter to a person who runs the driver:

  1. Copies of running VM disks adapt their speed. This covers replication, backup and snapshot copies. A copy starts at 15 MB/s, speeds up while the share the VM reads is quiet, and slows down (never below 15 MB/s) when the share is busy. In a lab backup this took 1,410 s, where the fixed 20 MB/s took 1,635 s.
  2. PoolBench, a storage performance test in the console. It is off by default (poolBench.enabled), so a cluster that does not turn it on sees no change from it. DR has it on.

Smaller: a PoolBench run from before a rule change can now be cleaned up, and a flaky receiver test is fixed.

docs.title: Why v0.15.0 and not v0.14.4
docs.text:
• It adds features: PoolBench, adaptive copy speed.
  • It adds a new resource kind (PoolBench) and new fields on BackupPolicy and ReplicationPolicy.
  • It changes a default. The fixed 20 MB/s copy speed is gone for adaptive copies. vmCopySpeedLimitMBps is now the highest speed, and unset means no highest speed. A person who relied on 20 MB/s as a ceiling must set it.

docs.title: What changes on a cluster
docs.text:
• New CRD and fields. The CRDs change in an additive way. They must be applied before or with the Helm upgrade (kubectl apply --server-side -f config/crd/).
  • New objects from the chart. A service account <release>-node-reader that can only read the node agents' /metrics; a Role that lets the controller list the node agents' endpoint slices and ask for a token of that one account; a ConfigMap <release>-node-ca that OpenShift fills with the CA. Without OpenShift's service CA, copies stay at the old fixed speed.
  • New controller flags (--node-metrics-service, --node-metrics-account, --node-metrics-ca). The chart sets them.
  • Running copies. The controller restarts in the upgrade. As in earlier releases, a copy in progress is picked up again or restarted by the next cycle. We check that on prod after the upgrade.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the release (no cluster is touched)
docs.text:
1. Run /docs-audit and fix what it finds.
  2. One pull request that:
  3. moves the Unreleased items in CHANGELOG.md under ## [v0.15.0] — 2026-10-27;
  4. adds "Upgrading to v0.15.0 (from v0.14.3)" and the compatibility row to docs/UPGRADE-GUIDE.md (new CRD, new chart objects, the changed default, what to check);
  5. sets version and appVersion in charts/ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi/Chart.yaml to 0.15.0.
  6. Squash-merge it. Tag the merge commit v0.15.0 (annotated) and push the tag.

docs.title: 2. Build and push
docs.text: On the build server, from the tagged commit: build driver, browse and console-plugin with VERSION=v0.15.0 and push all three. Check each tag exists in the registry. (An earlier release missed browse.)

docs.title: 3. DR first
docs.text: rovslab-dr-eude already runs the same code as a main build (v0.14.3-50-g77bdeb2b, rev 67). Apply the CRDs, then upgrade to v0.15.0 for both the driver and the console plugin. Check: pods roll out; the start-up line shows version=v0.15.0; no "Cannot read the latency" line in the controller log; PoolBench still works (start a Quick check and let it pass).

docs.title: 4. Production (needs your go-ahead)
docs.text: rovslab-prod-eude is on v0.14.3 (rev 47). It holds the kept namespace ovl-test (VMs ovl, ovl-r, win). Before: list the pools and copies in progress. Apply the CRDs, upgrade both images. After: every pod ready; every VM still running; node /metrics answers HTTP 200 on all nodes; one replication policy or backup shows vmCopy.speedMBps moving; ovl-test untouched.

docs.title: 5. Release test (needs your go-ahead)
docs.text: Run make test-release CLUSTER=rovslab-prod-eude on the build server. It runs about as long as the earlier runs. It needs the cluster to itself, so nothing else may run on prod. Read the report; fix or file each failure.

docs.title: 6. rovs-aug (needs your go-ahead; the cluster runs other people's VMs)
docs.text: Upgrade only after steps 4 and 5 are green and you say yes. The same checks as in step 4. Rollback is rev 15.

docs.title: Going back
docs.text:
Cluster Now Go back with rovslab-dr-eude rev 67 (main build) helm rollback ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi 67 -n kube-system rovslab-prod-eude rev 47, v0.14.3 helm rollback ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi 47 -n kube-system rovs-aug-2026-v2 rev 15, v0.14.3 helm rollback ibm-vpc-file-pool-csi 15 -n kube-system

The CRD changes are additive, so the older driver still works with them. A policy that leaves vmCopySpeedLimitMBps unset runs at 20 MB/s on the older driver, as before.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• The copy speed is new on prod. It was tested on DR with one VM and a small run. If a VM slows down on prod, set vmCopyAdaptive: false on the policy to go back to a fixed speed without a rollback.
  • PoolBench on prod stays off. We do not turn it on there in this release.
  • Not tested on a cluster: the snapshot copy speed (the lab takes instant snapshots, which copy nothing) and the speed change on a Windows VM (QEMU does the change, so we do not expect a difference).

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: About two hours of work, plus the release test run (hours, unattended). The clusters are used as they are; nothing new is created.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• The version is v0.15.0, not v0.14.4, because of new features, a new resource and a changed default.
  • DR goes first, then prod, then the release test, then rovs-aug last.
  • PoolBench stays off on prod and rovs-aug in this release.
  • I will not touch prod, run the release test, or touch rovs-aug without your yes for each.
  • The release test runs on prod, as in earlier releases, and not on DR.
  • Rollback is a Helm rollback to the revision now on each cluster. I do not remove the new CRD fields.
  • browse is built and pushed with the other two images, because an earlier release missed it.

docs.title: Spec: browse and restore files from VM disks in COS (issue #92, phase 6)
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-29. Status: speed bar agreed by the owner (29 Oct 2026); design ready for build. It fills in phase 6 of 2026-10-22-backup-file-restore.md (the parent spec). Read section 3 ("VM disks") and section 4 ("Backups in COS") of the parent first. It builds on phase 4 (COS, plain volumes, merged) and phase 5 (VM disks in the snapshot pool, PRs #337, #338, #341 and #342, not merged and not yet run on the lab). Facts here come from main and the vm-browse-c2 branch on 29 Oct 2026.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
This is the parent spec's goal, like Veeam, for the last case it does not cover yet: a VM disk whose backup is only in COS. This happens when the moment is older than every local restore point, when the snapshot pool is lost, or when the backup is opened in a different cluster.

When this is done: - A user picks a VM disk and a moment held in COS. They list the guest's file systems and folders, download a file, and restore files or folders to a new or an existing claim. In the console and with kubectl backup, exactly as for the snapshot pool. - Nothing downloads the whole disk. Only the parts of the disk that the guest's file system reads are fetched from COS. - It works in a second cluster that has the COS Secrets and no policy (--from-cos), for cluster administrators, as in phase 4.

Speed bar. The goal is met if, for a 100 GiB disk with a 30 GiB XFS or NTFS file system, using the private COS endpoint in the same region: - the file systems and the top folder show within 30 seconds of asking, - any other folder of up to 1,000 entries shows within 5 seconds, - a download or a restore starts within 2 minutes, and a 1 GiB file then downloads at 50 MiB/s or more.

This holds for the newest moment of each export. An older moment inside an export (see section 1a) is listed from the disk itself and may take up to 5 minutes; the console says so before the user waits.

The first version of this spec allowed 5 minutes for the first listing. The owner judged that too long for a user to wait, so the listing now comes from a file list saved at backup time (section 1a). The numbers are not measured yet. Phase 6a measures them. If they are missed by a wide margin, I will show you the real numbers before more is built.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
• Disk view (phase 5). pkg/replication/diskview.go shows a backed-up disk at one moment, read-only. It rebuilds the old contents from the latest disk.img and the undo files, on every read. It opens these by path on the NFS share, and it watches for a new copy starting (ErrDiskChanged).
  • NBD server (phase 5). pkg/nbd serves anything that can be read at an offset (io.ReaderAt and a size) to the appliance VM.
  • Guest helper (phase 5). The disk server and the libguestfs appliance run in one container of the helper pod and talk over a local socket. The helper pod runs in the browse namespace and holds no Secrets.
  • Guest restore Job (phase 5, #341). It is split into a reader, which parses the disk and holds no rights, and a writer, which holds only the target and CHOWN/FOWNER.
  • COS reader (phase 4). pkg/cosbrowse drives the pinned Kopia program as a child process. It lists snapshots and reads whole files with kopia show. It runs in a pod in the driver namespace, because it needs the COS key, the wrapped backup key and the Key Protect API key. A NetworkPolicy there lets only the gateway reach it.
  • What an export holds. Each export is two Kopia snapshots, tagged with the volume and the moment. One is the backup folder, which holds the latest disk.img. The other is the moments folder, which holds the undo files up to that export. A restore of a moment uses the oldest export made at or after it. Kopia cuts files into chunks of about 4 MiB on average, by content. The export does not set compression.

docs.title: What is not reachable
docs.text:
• Reading a range of a file in COS with the Kopia program alone. kopia show and kopia snapshot restore give whole files only. Mounting with kopia mount and FUSE needs /dev/fuse and extra rights, which the parent spec rules out. So either the Kopia program serves ranges another way (see 1, option A), or Kopia is used as a Go library (option B).
  • The key and a hostile disk in one pod. The phase 5 helper parses the guest's file system in the same container that serves the disk. For COS, the container that serves the disk holds the backup key, which can decrypt every volume in the policy's area of the bucket. So the phase 5 layout cannot be reused as it is. See 2.

docs.title: 1. Reading parts of disk.img and the undo files from COS
docs.text:
The disk view gets a small source interface: open a file by name for reads at an offset, and list the undo files. The NFS source is today's code, unchanged. The COS source reads the two Kopia snapshots of the chosen export. COS objects never change, so the COS source has no change check and no lease.

Two ways to read ranges. Phase 6a picks one on the lab.

  • Option A: the Kopia program, over WebDAV (preferred). kopia mount --webdav serves a snapshot as a WebDAV share on localhost, with no FUSE and no extra rights. A WebDAV GET with a Range header reads part of a file. The COS source then makes ranged HTTP reads to 127.0.0.1 inside the pod. This keeps Kopia out of our Go code, as phase 4 does, and adds no Go dependency. Not proven: that the pinned Kopia 0.23.1 serves WebDAV on Linux without trying an OS mount, and that it honours Range without reading from the start of the file. Phase 6a checks both.
  • Option B: Kopia as a Go library. Open the repository read-only in process and seek within the file object. The parent spec already allows this, in the browse binary only. Cost: a large new dependency in go.mod (the module is shared, but only cmd/browse links it), and its version must match the pinned program. Used only if option A fails.

Either way: - Cache. Kopia's own content cache, on an emptyDir on the node's disk (not memory), default 5 GiB (backupBrowse.cos.cacheSize). The first file system list reads a lot of metadata. The cache keeps later reads local. - Indexing the undo files. Today the view reads every byte of each undo file once, to index and check it. Over COS that would fetch all the changed data of the export before the first listing. The COS source indexes by reading the record headers and skipping over the data, and checks a record's data when it is read. If the undo format has no way to check one record alone, the whole-file check stays, and phase 6a measures what it costs. - Keep time. A session or restore is refused if the export's snapshots reach the end of their keep time within the session's hard limit (2 hours) plus 1 hour. Kopia maintenance must not delete the data while it is being read. Phase 6a also checks Kopia's own safety margin for data that is no longer referenced.

docs.title: 1a. A file list saved with each export
docs.text:
Reading folders straight from a disk in COS is slow: every cold read fetches a whole chunk, and a file system list touches many scattered blocks. So the listing does not read the disk.

  • When. Each export to COS of a VM disk also saves a file list of the guest's file systems at the export's newest moment. It is made from the local copy in the snapshot pool, before or while the export runs, by the phase 5 guest helper (no Secrets, unprivileged, the hostile-disk rules of phase 5).
  • What. For each file system: its label and type, and for each entry the path, type, size, mode, owner, times and link target. No file contents. The list is compressed and stored in the same Kopia repository as the export, so it is encrypted with the same backup key and kept and deleted with the export.
  • Trust. The list comes from a hostile disk, so the reader treats it as untrusted: size limits on the list and on each name, names shown escaped as phase 3 does, and paths checked against traversal. A wrong list can only show wrong names. A download or restore reads the disk itself and refuses a path that is not there.
  • Use. The COS disk server reads the list (a few MiB to tens of MiB) when the session starts and answers folder requests from it. The appliance and the disk are opened only for a download or a restore.
  • Older moments. An export holds the undo files back to the previous export, so it covers several moments, but only the newest has a list. Making a list per moment would multiply the export's work. An older moment is listed from the disk, slowly, as the first version of this spec did. 6a measures how slow.
  • No list. Exports made before this feature, or whose list failed, are browsed from the disk, slowly, with the same notice. A failed list does not fail the export: the export is the backup and comes first. The policy's status says the list failed.
  • Cost. One guest file system scan per VM disk per export, measured in 6a. If it makes exports late, the list is made after the export, from the same local moment, and the session falls back to the slow path until it exists.

docs.title: 2. Keeping the key away from the hostile disk
docs.text:
Two pods per session, as in phase 4 and #341:

  • COS disk server, in the driver namespace. It has the Secrets, the Kopia child (or library), the cache and the disk view, and it serves the disk at the chosen moment over NBD. It never parses the guest's file system. It sees only blocks.
  • Guest helper, in the browse namespace, the phase 5 image with no Secrets. It reaches the disk server over the pod network instead of a local socket. Everything else is phase 5 unchanged: the appliance, the file system picker, norecovery, and the notices.

The NBD link uses TLS with the session's own certificate, which already exists for the gateway link. The NBD server accepts only that client. A NetworkPolicy in the driver namespace allows only that guest helper pod to reach that disk server. The disk is read-only at the NBD level: the server refuses writes.

A file restore from COS uses the #341 split. The reader container gets its disk from a COS disk server pod in the same way. The writer is unchanged.

docs.title: 3. Choosing COS
docs.text: The gateway already picks COS for a plain-volume moment that only COS holds (phase 4). The same rule applies to VM disks: source: cos, or an automatic choice when there is no local copy. kubectl backup browse --from-cos and restore-files --from-cos accept a VM disk. The console file browser gets the source switch that phase 4 left out (local or COS), for plain volumes and VM disks alike.

docs.title: 4. Limits and cost
docs.text:
• A COS VM session counts as one session against the existing limits (5 in the cluster, 2 per namespace). It uses two pods: the guest helper (about 550 MiB, measured in phase 0) and the disk server (estimate 256 MiB plus Kopia's index cache, measured in 6a).
  • COS cost. Reads through the private or direct endpoint have no data transfer charge. The cost is the GET requests (class B) and, for the Standard class, nothing more. Phase 6a counts requests and bytes for the speed bar run and adds a cost line here. A browse never writes to the bucket.
  • The 5-minute start limit for COS sessions (backupBrowse.cos.startTimeout) stays for a moment with a file list. A moment without one is allowed 10 minutes. 6a sets the final values.

docs.title: 5. User stories
docs.text:
• As a namespace admin, I browse the files inside my VM's disk at a moment that is only in COS, and download one file, without a whole-disk restore.
  • As a namespace admin, I restore a folder from that disk to a new claim.
  • As a cluster admin in the DR cluster, with no policy there, I browse a VM disk from the bucket with --from-cos.
  • As anyone, if the disk is encrypted inside the guest (BitLocker, LUKS), I am told it cannot be read here and pointed at the whole-disk restore.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Disk view source interface: the existing property tests run against both sources. The COS source is fed from a local Kopia repository, built in the test as phase 4 does. Every moment must give byte for byte what RestoreDisk writes.
  • Ranges: a test reads small, unaligned and chunk-crossing ranges and counts the bytes fetched. A range read must not fetch the file from the start.
  • Isolation: the guest helper pod spec has no Secret volumes, no environment from Secrets and no API token. The disk server refuses NBD writes, a client without the session certificate, and any volume other than the session's (including traversal and crafted snapshot names, as in phase 4).
  • Keep time: a moment near the end of its keep time is refused with a clear message.
  • File list: a list made from a test disk matches the files the appliance sees. A crafted list (huge, names with .., newlines or control characters, entries outside the file system) is refused or shown escaped, and a download of a path that is only in the list is refused. A failed list leaves the export Done and says so in the policy status. A session on a moment with no list uses the slow path and says so.
  • Release test stage 20: a new part that exports a VM disk, deletes the local restore points (or uses a moment older than all of them), browses a file inside it from COS, restores a folder, and compares checksums. It runs once in prod and once from the DR cluster with --from-cos. It records the speed bar numbers, with and without the file list, in the report.

docs.title: Build plan: phases, one PR each
docs.text:
Phase 6 needs phase 5 merged and passing on the lab first.

  • 6a. Spike on the lab (S, risk check). Use a real export of a lab VM (stage 18 makes them). Try option A, then option B if A fails. Make a file list of the lab VM's disk and measure its time and size. Measure the speed bar (with the list, and the slow path without it), bytes fetched, COS requests, disk server memory, and the cost of indexing the undo files. Write the results and the choice into this spec, in a PR with no product code. If neither option meets the speed bar within a factor of 2, I stop and show you the gap.
  • 6b. COS disk server (M). The file list at export (made, stored with the export, read and checked), the source interface, the COS source, the cache, the keep-time check, the TLS NBD link, the disk server pod and its NetworkPolicy, and the guest helper over the network. Command line browse and download.
  • 6c. Restore and console (M). The file restore from COS through the #341 split, the console source switch, the help text, and stage 20's COS VM part.

Total: about 1.5 to 2.5 weeks of agent work, plus the lab runs.

docs.title: Cost and risk
docs.text:
• Biggest risk: speed. Each cold read fetches at least a 4 MiB chunk from COS. A file system list touches many small, scattered metadata blocks, so a listing from the disk may fetch hundreds of MiB. The file list (section 1a) takes this off the normal path; it remains for older moments and for exports without a list. 6a comes first to measure both.
  • Second risk: option A not working. Option B then adds a large dependency. It is still inside the browse image only.
  • Fall-back, which does not meet the goal: download the export's disk.img and undo files to scratch space first, then browse as phase 5 does. This needs a scratch claim the size of the disk and a full download for every session. I would put it in front of you as a choice, not build it quietly.

docs.title: Decisions I made for you
docs.text:
• Phase 6 starts only after phase 5 is merged and has passed on the lab.
  • A short spike (6a) comes before any product code, with a stop-and-show-you rule if speed misses the bar.
  • Speed bar: first listing within 30 seconds, other folders within 5 seconds, a download starts within 2 minutes and runs at 50 MiB/s. You judged 5 minutes for the first listing too long.
  • To meet it, each export also saves a file list of the VM disk, so folders are shown without reading the disk in COS.
  • Only the newest moment of each export gets a file list. Older moments in the export are listed slowly, up to 5 minutes, and the console says so first.
  • A failed file list never fails the export.
  • The Kopia program over WebDAV is tried first, so Kopia stays out of our Go code. The Kopia library is the second choice.
  • The pod that holds the backup key never parses the guest's file system. The disk is served over the network to the existing unprivileged guest helper.
  • The link between the two pods is encrypted and allows only the one session's client, even inside the cluster.
  • COS sessions need no hold on the next backup, because COS objects never change.
  • A moment whose keep time ends within 3 hours cannot be browsed.
  • The cache is 5 GiB on the node's disk per session, and can be changed in the chart.
  • The console gets a local or COS switch for every volume type, not only VM disks.
  • VM disks from COS follow the same session limits as everything else. There is no separate limit.

docs.title: Needs from you
docs.text:
• Nothing blocks writing 6a. It needs a lab run, which waits for your go-ahead as usual.
  • Nothing else. The speed bar is agreed: first listing within 30 seconds.
